For Julie, and for my dad.


Julie,
   Three years ago, a few months into the rendering engine, I came out of my office
and told you I thought I was onto something. You said okay. You didn’t ask what
it was, or what it was for, or when it would be done, and you didn’t ask me for
anything I could have shown you, because there was nothing to show. There was a
program that had done something it shouldn’t have been able to do, and a man who
didn’t yet know what a Turing machine was.
   You gave me the three years anyway. The nights after the lot closed. The
weekends. The hours I was in the house and not in the house, because my head was
in a wall I couldn’t get past. Every dead end, and there were more of those than
there are pages here. You never once asked me to stop, and you never once said it
was fine when it wasn’t. You just kept giving me the next evening.
   This book is what I did with them. It’s the one thing I’ve built from nothing that
I’m sure of, because I threw out every piece of it I couldn’t prove, and what’s left
holds. I know that isn’t what you gave the years for. You gave them for me. But it’s
what I have to show, and I wanted it to be worth showing.

Dad,
    The name on the cover was yours first. I asked you before I used it and you said
go ahead. You and Mom taught me that nothing is true just because somebody says
it is. This book is that lesson, six hundred pages long. I put our name on it because I
wanted one thing in the world with that name on it that nobody handed me, that I
couldn’t have faked, and that I can stand behind in front of anyone. Here it is.
    Julie carries the name now too. So the machine has it third. This is for the two
of you who had it first.

The point

The whole book is four steps, and I’ll set them out first so you know what you’re
carrying. Each step is motivated by the one before it, and the book goes up them in
order.
    One: nothing becomes something for free. Take a blank cell: a square of paper with
nothing on it, a bead that could sit in either of two dips, a bit of memory nobody
has set. Now make it a 0, and keep it a 0. Something is the case now that wasn’t
a moment ago. That moment, nothing becoming something, is always paid for. It
dissipates by happening, in any real device, in finite time, and keeping it is paid on
top, in a merge or in fresh states.
    Two: so what a computation makes the case is a resource. Computer science
charges a computation for two things, how long it runs and how much space it takes,
and the bits it erases have been counted too. What no model I found charges is the
moment a reading goes up and stays. The Thiele Machine is a model of computation
that does: the step that raises a reading that stays is the step that’s charged. Those
steps are a few events in a run, not the billions of overwrites a computer makes every
second; what they write doesn’t stay, and the toll leaves them to the erasure count
and to physics. Put the record inside the machine, then choose a window that shows
only the working part. Through that window you can watch the computation while
missing what the machine kept about it. That is the picture behind “computation is
the slice.” I will have to earn it by giving the window and the moves precise rules;
calling something a window is not enough.
    To show the definition can be met, Part III builds one example. It starts with two
counters and a line number. The computing moves add, subtract and jump. The
record moves check a claim, select a passed check and certify it. While the example
is live, the counters and line follow their own computing rules; looking only there
leaves out the record and its ledger. A failed record move can stop the example, so
that boundary belongs in the statement too. Theorem E.4 says exactly which other
computers admit the same construction and which do not. The Thiele Machine is
the definition, not the example. Here the point is the view: working states can look
alike while the full states differ in what was kept.
    The counting underneath needs its own conditions too: states, a next-state rule,
and a reading that stays. Once those are given, what follows is a theorem. Whether a
physical process fits that description is the further question stated in the Conclusion.


                                                  15
16   The point


                     Three: the structure a computation makes is made of exactly this. Structure in
                 general is a relation kept under the changes you choose; Part II takes that word
                 from the people who wrestled with it. The part a computation makes, and can’t
                 take back, is a distinction held in its state, and a 0 is the smallest one there is: the
                 ways a cell could be, sorted into piles, and one pile held. A grouping, an order, a
                 relation a later move leans on, a fact somebody found out and wrote down: each is
                 a distinction that stays, paid for the same way as the 0. Insight, in the sense this
                 book can price, is a kept distinction. The toll charges the moment it’s raised; holding
                 it up afterward adds nothing to the cost. That’s what the book’s other name, No
                 Free Insight, means.
                     Four: established is the sharpest case. Two computers can end with the same an-
                 swer, and only one of them checked it. The difference between them is a distinction
                 one of them never kept. A record that a claim was checked and closed is a 0 that
                 stays, with a check in front of it, and it’s paid for the same way. I build a machine
                 for that case, all the way down, because it’s the one where you can point at the kept
                 0 and at what it cost. It’s the sharpest case of what keeping takes, but it isn’t the
                 point. The point is the 0.
                     Step one is where the toll gets its reason. If it breaks, the toll goes back to being
                 only my choice, though the latch, the window, the diagonal and the earned record
                 are proved without it and would stand. So that’s where I start: the blank cell, taken
                 apart as far down as I can get before I hit something that holds or something I can’t
                 get under. I’ll tell you which.
                     One warning about how this went, because it explains the shape of everything
                 after it. Most of the time I had the hunch first and found the names later. Over and
                 over, somebody had been here before me. Sometimes that made my day. Sometimes
                 it pissed me off. You’ll see both.


                 Where a 0 comes from
                 Before any machine comes the cell. What does it take for there to be a 0 at all?
                     It takes three things. First, something that can be more than one way: a bead in
                 a dish of water, a speck of magnetised metal, a charge on a tiny capacitor, a square
                 of paper. Nature hands you that much, and it isn’t a 0 yet. It’s stuff that can sit in a
                 lot of arrangements.
                     Second, a sorting: somebody says which arrangements count as 0, which count
                 as 1, and which count as blank. The sorting is the first piece of structure Part II gets
                 to: the ways a thing could be, cut into piles. Without it there’s no 0, just a bead
                 somewhere. A 0 and a 1 aren’t things; they’re the two sides of a line somebody drew
                 across the ways a thing can be.
                                                                                               The point   17


    Third, a hill, because a sorting that drifts isn’t a bit; it’s noise. Something has to
hold the bead on its side of the line: a barrier it can’t climb, a latch, a dip it can’t
jiggle out of. In the laboratory you’ll meet in Part I, a bead held behind a barrier
eight times the size of its own heat jiggle stays put for about fifty minutes, and with
the barrier lowered to about twice its jiggle it hops every ten seconds. A distinction
that stays is a hill paid for in advance.
    Put the three together and you have a distinction that stays. Every 0 and every
1 in every computer is one, and so is a flag that’s up, a written number, a fact
somebody checked and wrote down.
    Now for the moment itself: the cell is blank and you write a 0. Everything that
step can take comes next, and the rest of the book only ever adds detail to it.
    It happens, so it dissipates. Any change a real device makes in a finite time to the
chances of its states, sitting in surroundings at some temperature, produces entropy;
the more time it’s given, the less it has to produce, and never none. That’s what
dissipating means here: entropy produced. Over a cycle that brings the device back
to where it started it all leaves as heat; within a single step the heat that leaves can
even be negative, when the device’s own entropy goes up.
    If the blank could have been anything, every way it might have been now lands
on one way, the 0. That landing is a merge, and it’s the step the physics premise
puts a floor under, one that survives going as slowly as you like.
    If you knew the cell was blank, nothing uncertain is removed, and no new floor
is owed. What was owed didn’t vanish. Somebody made the cell blank, by wiping a
cell that could have held anything, and that wipe was the merge. Or somebody is
still holding the fact that it’s blank, and that fact is itself a 0 somewhere, a distinction
that stays, which gets paid for when it’s wiped.
    Or you never merge at all: you write every 0 on a fresh cell and never reuse one.
That way pays in fresh states, and they never come back. An endless tape can do it
forever. A real one runs out, because a real device can tell apart only finitely many
states in a bounded place. That’s a premise about the world, not a theorem, and
nobody has measured where its ceiling sits.
    So every 0 on every tape of a machine that keeps running was bought in a merge
or in fresh states, on top of the dissipation of the moment it was written. (A machine
that stops slips past, by having no next step at all; Part I says exactly how.) Ordinary
computing looks as though it pays nothing because the tape was paid for before
the run started, by whoever made it blank. That’s the bottom of the book, and
everything above it is the same payment at a bigger size: a list kept in order, a
measurement written down, a fact checked and committed to. Each is a distinction
that stays, and each is paid for the way the 0 is.
18   The point


                 Why it has to cost
                 Now what it takes to keep that 0, made exact, and it’s the part I’m proudest of,
                 because once something stays, the choosing stops and the counting takes over. And
                 the counting is the one behind musical chairs.
                     Take any machine at all, with any number of states, finite or endless, and one
                 rule that gives the next state. Each state is one way the whole machine can be held,
                 and the machine moves from state to state, one step at a time. Watch one run and
                 keep a list of the states it has been in. Now look at the next step. There are exactly
                 three things it can do. It can land on a state this run hasn’t used yet, which spends a
                 fresh state, there and then. It can come back, for the first time, to a state the run has
                 used, other than the one it started on, and then it comes from a different state than
                 the one that got there first, so two states land on one. That’s a merge: two different
                 states with the same next state, and afterward the state they landed on can’t tell
                 you which one it came from. Or it can go round a loop: land back on the very state
                 it started from, or take a step it has already taken, which is all a run does after its
                 first return. A loop makes nothing new. There is no fourth thing a step can do, a run
                 merges at most once, and it doesn’t matter how many states there are.
                     Now make the machine keep something. Pick a yes-or-no reading of the state
                 and make it permanent: no step ever turns a yes back into a no. Start on a state
                 that reads no and let some step raise it to yes. From then on the run can never come
                 back to its start, because the start reads no and the yes never comes down. So the
                 run can’t be a loop through its start, and the first time it comes back to any state it
                 has used, that step is a merge. Either somewhere along the run two states land on
                 one, or it never comes back to a state it has used and takes a fresh one at every step,
                 forever. Raising something to keep can’t be done going round a loop, the only kind
                 of step that spends neither a merge nor a fresh state, because the loop is exactly the
                 step that makes nothing new. Keeping isn’t the only thing that pays this, though.
                 Any run that never comes back to its start merges or takes fresh states, whatever it
                 keeps; what keeping adds is that coming back is ruled out. The sharper fact is about
                 the move, and the chairs below show it: when fresh states run out, the move that
                 raises a reading that stays has to merge two states itself.
                     Do it with chairs when the room runs out. Draw a box on the floor, three chairs
                 inside, one chair outside by the door. Four people, one per chair: the four states the
                 machine could be in. The three inside already read yes. One step moves everybody
                 at once, each to the chair the rule sends them to. Nobody inside may leave, because
                 yes is permanent. The person by the door has to come in, because this is the step
                 that flips them to yes. Now finish the move, one person per chair. You can’t. Four
                 people, three inside chairs: somebody shares. Maybe the newcomer ends up on a
                 lap, maybe two insiders squeeze onto one chair; either way, two starting places share
                                                                                          The point   19


a destination. Somebody secretly picks a starting chair, the rule moves them, and
you’re told only where they ended up: at a shared chair, you can’t say where they
started. That’s the pigeonhole principle, which is old and not mine, and the chapter
“Why the toll isn’t arbitrary” (Section 3) proves it with exactly three conditions on a
rule that gives every state a next one: finitely many states that read yes, a yes that
stays, and one flip. There’s no physics in it anywhere, only counting.
    (How old is it? I went looking. A French Jesuit, Jean Leurechon, used it in 1622
to argue that two people somewhere must have exactly the same number of hairs
on their heads, which is the kind of thing you can be completely sure of and never
check. The first name for it I can find came two centuries later, from the German
mathematician Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet, who used it in print in 1842 without
naming it and in later work called it the drawer principle, the Schubfachprinzip; the
pigeons came later still. Benoît Rittaud and Albrecht Heeffer, who wrote a short
paper in 2014 on what came before Dirichlet, looked for a source for the year 1834
that turns up next to his name and found none, and neither have I. Is 1622 the
bottom? I can’t tell you. History is like that: it’s where you start digging.)
    Now give the room endless chairs inside, numbered 1, 2, 3 and on with no end,
every one taken, and the newcomer still gets a seat: everybody inside moves up one,
from chair n to chair n + 1, and chair 1 is left empty. Nobody shares. That’s David
Hilbert’s hotel, from a lecture in the 1920s, and it’s no trick. Look at what it took:
every single person inside had to get up and move one over, into a chair that was
taken a moment before, to leave one gap. Any way of doing it moves an endless
line of them, the person in the chair the newcomer takes, the one whose chair that
person took, and on with no end, and that only works because the building has
a chair past every chair. That’s the fresh-state column, paid in full on every raise.
Richard Dedekind, the German mathematician, made it the definition of infinite in
1888: a collection is infinite exactly when it can be moved one-to-one into a proper
part of itself. So finiteness doesn’t create what keeping takes. Keeping is paid for in
merges or in fresh states however many states there are, as long as every state has a
next one. What finiteness does is take fresh states off the table, and then keeping
has to be paid for in a merge.
    Turn it around and it says the same thing from the other side. A reversible
computer, one where every step can be run backwards, never merges anything,
because a step you can undo never lands two states on one. So it can only pay
for keeping in fresh states. Charles Bennett, at IBM, showed in 1973 that any
computation can be done reversibly if you give it fresh states to keep its own history
in while it works, and that’s the fresh-state column, written out as a construction.
Give a reversible computer finitely many states and it runs out. A one-to-one shuffle
of finitely many states always comes back around to where it started, so it can never
keep a flag up; whatever it raises comes back down, as long as every state has a
20   The point


                 next one. A reversible machine that stops slips past this, as Part I shows exactly,
                 and Klaus-Jörn Lange, Pierre McKenzie and Alain Tapp (2000) built such machines:
                 reversible ones that do what any deterministic machine does in the same space, up
                 to a constant factor, and stop with the answer, paying in time. Give it an endless tape
                 to keep its history on and it keeps everything, never comes back, and pays a fresh
                 stretch of tape at every step. And a reversible computer doesn’t escape dissipation
                 either. Bennett’s own only moves forward if it’s pushed, and at any speed above
                 nothing the push dissipates, and in his walker, in the long run, all of it leaves as
                 heat. Go slower and the dissipation per step drops, but it never reaches nothing for
                 a run that finishes; Part I proves that for his walker, with Schnakenberg’s formula
                 taken as the model (Theorem 1.9), and the physicists who study changes made in
                 a finite time (Tim Schmiedl and Udo Seifert for a dragged bead; Naoto Shiraishi,
                 Ken Funo and Keiji Saito for jump processes) find the same for any change in the
                 chances of a device’s states that finishes, when those states jump or drift at random
                 in surroundings at a fixed temperature. So in any real device of that kind every step
                 that actually changes something dissipates, on average. What a merge adds is a
                 floor under its heat that no slowness removes, and what fresh states buy is a way
                 around the floor, never around the dissipation of happening. Time sets how much
                 you pay above the floor. Only forever makes it zero, and a step that takes forever
                 never happens.
                     Now comes the physics, as an assumption with its name on it. Rolf Landauer, at
                 IBM, 1961, said that a step that can’t be run backwards, that merges, “requires a
                 minimal heat generation.” That’s the rule people call Landauer’s principle: when a
                 merge wipes out a difference the machine really could have been holding, its heat
                 has a floor, on average at least k B T ln 2 for every bit of difference lost, however
                 slowly it’s done. Landauer stated it for a memory whose states are alike apart from
                 what they record, a symmetric memory; when the states differ in their own entropy
                 the floor moves, and in a lopsided double well the work to erase has been measured
                 below k B T ln 2. It’s physics, it’s a premise, and no proof in this book reaches it.
                     And his next sentence is the whole problem step four is about. That heat, he
                 wrote, “serves the purpose of standardizing signals and making them independent
                 of their exact logical history.” Ordinary machines spend their merges, and their heat,
                 on forgetting how the bits got there, on purpose, so a 1 is a 1 no matter what path
                 made it. You’ll see in step four what that does to two computers that end up holding
                 the same bits. And the very same kind of step, a merge, is what it takes, on any
                 machine that keeps running and whose fresh states run out, to make something stay
                 for good.
                     So, the deepest thing I can say about keeping: not every forgetting keeps anything,
                 and wiping a scratch pad keeps nothing. But every keeping pays. On a finite machine
                 that keeps running, keeping pays by forgetting: the step that makes something stay
                                                                                          The point   21


for good lands two states on one, somewhere, maybe not where you happen to be
standing, and afterward nothing can tell which one it was. With endless fresh states
it can dodge the merge only by spending fresh states it never gets back. A verdict
keeps the decision and lets go of the arguing.
    It’s worth seeing where that payment can go and where it can’t, so you know
exactly what you’re being asked to accept. Give the machine unlimited memory and
it never has to merge, but it hasn’t got out of anything: it pays in fresh states, at
every step, forever, on top of the dissipation of every step that changes something,
and the chapter “Why the toll isn’t arbitrary” builds that machine and counts its
fresh states. Let the flag come back down and nothing is kept, so there’s no payment
for keeping; the steps still dissipate when they happen. Start the machine from a
state you already know and Landauer’s principle, in the form Part I adopts, puts no
heat floor under the merge at all (Theorem 3.17), because no uncertainty is wiped.
It’s the known blank from a couple of pages back, and what keeping takes sits where
it sat there: the step still dissipates when it happens, and the difference was already
being kept, by whoever knows the start. The toll I build in Part I charges that step
anyway, because it charges the raise, whichever way the raise is paid, for every state
the step could be handed. That’s a rule of the ledger, not a claim about heat. The
heat itself is physics. In 2012 a group in Lyon erased one bit held in a tiny bead,
kept in place by a laser, and found the average heat it gave off coming down toward
Landauer’s floor as the erasing was slowed; the principle also has serious critics, the
philosopher John Norton among them. So the counting is proved, on any machine,
the floor in heat is an assumption, and I never let those two swap places. Section 1
goes all the way down: what a distinction that stays is, why writing a single 0 on a
blank cell is already a merge, and what the lab has measured.
    So an ordinary computer pays in merges and in heat, and keeps nothing to show
for it. What I want is a model of computation that charges for keeping in the very
step that makes something stay. That’s the Thiele Machine.


What the usual models don’t count

That’s step one, and step two is what it means for computing.
    Computer science has always counted what a computation costs. How many steps
it takes is time. How many cells it needs is space. Whole fields rest on those two
counts, and on the models built to make them exact: the random-access machine of
the computer scientists Stephen Cook and Robert Reckhow (1973), which charges
each instruction a unit; the cell-probe model (1981) of Andrew Yao, which counts
only the memory cells a program reads; the input-output model of Alok Aggarwal
and Jeffrey Vitter (1988), which counts only the blocks moved between a small fast
memory and a large slow one. The random-access machine computes exactly what
22   The point


                 Turing’s machine computes, and the other two leave the computing between the
                 moves they count out of the count. They differ in what they count, and the counting
                 is the reason to have them. Manuel Blum gave two axioms in 1967 for any measure
                 of computational cost at all; they name no machine and say what every cost has to
                 satisfy.
                     Now look again at what step one found keeping takes. Every time a computation
                 makes something the case and keeps it, a bit set, a list left in order, an answer
                 written down, it pays, in a merge or in fresh states. What it pays isn’t the time
                 count: a slow step and a fast one can keep the same thing. It isn’t the space count
                 either, though fresh states are one of the two ways to pay it: a machine with a fixed
                 memory pays it by merging, over and over, in the same cells, and its space count
                 never moves. The merge half of it has been counted before. Ming Li and Paul Vitányi
                 (1996) took as axioms of a model of computation that a step that can be undone
                 costs nothing and that every bit a computation irreversibly erases costs one unit,
                 and Erik Demaine and three coauthors (2016) put that count on the random-access
                 machine, beside time and space. What none of them charges, as far as I found, is
                 the moment a chosen reading goes up and stays, whichever way keeping it is paid.
                 That’s a third thing a computation does, and it’s what this model adds. It isn’t a cost
                 in Blum’s sense once the computing itself costs nothing. Blum asks that “this run
                 costs exactly m” be decidable, and then it isn’t: a program that runs another program
                 at no cost and makes one move costing one unit if that one halts costs exactly one
                 exactly when the other halts, so deciding its cost would decide halting. (Price every
                 move at one and a run’s cost is its step count, which is a cost in Blum’s sense. And a
                 run that never stops can still show a finite count; leave its cost undefined there, as
                 Blum does, and his first axiom holds. It’s the decidability that fails.)
                     So the Thiele Machine, all of it, is a model of computation, math you can reason
                 about, the way Turing’s machine is. It has five parts and one rule: a set of states,
                 a set of moves, a step that takes a state and a move to the next state, a price on
                 each move, a whole number of units of cost, and a reading of the state, yes or no.
                 The rule, which I call the toll, says that a step that turns the reading from no to yes
                 costs at least one unit. The toll sits on the raise, not on the merge, so it charges for
                 keeping something whichever way that’s paid, in a merge or in fresh states. Two
                 more pieces come in when a result needs them: a counter in the state that adds
                 up the costs and only climbs, which is the ledger, and a window, what an outside
                 observer gets to see. The toll’s first name, the one I gave it before I understood it, is
                 No Free Insight.
                     It computes nothing new, any more than the random-access machine does. What
                 it adds is a place, in the step itself, for what a computation made the case and what
                 that cost. The reading can be any yes-or-no reading at all; the toll charges every
                 step that turns it on. The readings this book cares about are the ones that, once yes,
                                                                                            The point   23


stay yes, because those are the kept distinctions and keeping is what the merge or
the fresh states pay for. The blank cell’s “it’s a 0 now” is one. “This list has been put
in order” is one. “This claim was checked and closed” is one. The model doesn’t care
which, and for readings that stay, Part I derives the toll from what keeping takes,
on stated premises. A reading that flips back and forth isn’t a record of anything:
Part II calls it a toggle and proves it’s the latch of no event (Section 10).
    The one in the toll is one unit of cost, in the model’s own count, and it’s one
because that’s the least a whole-number count can charge and still not be free,
and the toll only says not free. A unit of cost isn’t a joule. What ties it to heat is
Landauer’s principle, named, through the merge a raise has to make when only
finitely many states read yes, and nothing else.
    And there’s one thing to hold on to through the whole book, because it’s where
readers go wrong and where I went wrong for a long time. The ledger is a count,
not a lock. It doesn’t stop anybody from doing anything. It adds up the prices you
chose for the moves that ran, writes the sum down where the machine can’t lose it,
and the toll makes each raise of the reading you chose cost at least one. It doesn’t
measure merges, fresh states or heat: a merge that keeps nothing can cost nothing,
fresh states are taken at every step and the toll asks for a unit only at the raise, and
where a merge raises nothing, a cost of one unit per raise leaves that merge out.
What ties the count to what keeping takes is a theorem, not a reading of a dial: on a
machine with finitely many states reading yes, any price list that charges merges
has to charge each raise of a reading that stays at least one. What a kept reading
means, whether a reading that’s up stands for anything, is a separate question with a
separate answer, and Part III gives it for one case: an order the step enforces, which
is the lock. A lock would work at a price of zero. The price isn’t there to make the
lock work. It’s there because, on a machine where every state has a next one, the
raise of a reading that stays merges or takes fresh states, whether anybody writes it
down or not.


What I found, what I assumed and what I chose
I didn’t invent a machine. I found one. That’s how I see this work, and I’ll be straight
about the difference between that conviction and a theorem before I do anything
else.
    That sentence walks straight into one of the oldest fights in mathematics, so I’ll
take a short trip into it first. G. H. Hardy, a Cambridge number theorist who wrote
A Mathematician’s Apology in 1940 to defend doing mathematics for its own sake,
came down on the found side about as hard as anyone ever has: mathematical
reality, he wrote, lies outside the people who study it, and the theorems they like
to call their creations are really just notes on what they saw there. The German
24   The point


                 mathematician Leopold Kronecker supposedly split the difference: God made the
                 whole numbers, and everything else is the work of people. Supposedly, because push
                 on that line and it gets thin fast. It comes down through Heinrich Weber, another
                 German mathematician, in a memorial piece written after Kronecker died, pointing
                 back to a lecture from 1886, and that’s the only source I could find anybody citing.
                 It’s a great line with one witness. (The record chapter of Part I, Section 2, stops
                 early on to ask how many witnesses a claim ought to need. The answer is more
                 than one.) None of this settles whether I found the Thiele Machine or made it up. A
                 proof doesn’t settle it either: showing what follows from the premises doesn’t decide
                 whether you found the theorem or made it. That’s why it’s labelled a conviction.
                 What it changes is how I hold the thing: like something that was already there,
                 which means I can be wrong about its shape and the shape won’t care. And to be
                 exact about what “found” covers, it covers the parts the counting forces on you, the
                 latch shape and the merge or the fresh states. The event to record, the price list,
                 and putting the count inside the step are choices, mine, and the three lists below
                 say which is which.
                     The three lists draw the line between what nothing let me choose, what I had
                 to assume, and what I did choose, because everything after this depends on where
                 it falls. Read the first list as the ground, the second as what the ground is taken to
                 stand on, and the third as the model built on it.
                     Found: what counting forces on any machine.
                 • Run a machine that gives each state exactly one next state. It takes fresh states
                   until it first comes back to one it has used; that return lands on its start or is a
                   merge, two states with one next state; and after it the run only repeats steps it
                   already took. There’s no fourth thing a step can do, and a run merges at most
                   once (Theorem 1.1).
                 • So any run that never comes back to its start merges somewhere or takes a
                   fresh state at every step. A reading that goes from no to yes and never comes
                   back rules the return out, so every run that raises it merges or takes fresh states
                   (Proposition 3.5). The sharper fact is about the move: when only finitely many
                   states read yes, the move that raises the reading merges two states (Theorem 3.1
                   for a finite machine, Proposition 3.4 when only the yes-states are finitely many).
                   A machine that can stop, with a state that has no next state at all, slips past
                   this, and Part I says exactly how (Theorem 1.2). All of that is counting, with no
                   physics in it.
                 • Over any machine at all, a record that the computation drives and that never
                   comes down is a latch on one event: it switches on the first time something
                   happens and nothing switches it off (Observation 10.1). That’s counting too,
                   given the two conditions in it.
                                                                                           The point   25


  Assumed: what the found list is taken to stand on, in the world.
• A merge of states the machine really could have been in, done in surroundings
  at some temperature, has a floor under its heat, on average, however slowly it’s
  done, in a memory whose states are alike apart from what they record. That’s
  Landauer’s principle, the premise from thermodynamics, named and assumed
  and never proved here, with its critics named.
• A real device can tell apart only finitely many states in any bounded place, so its
  fresh states run out. Nobody has measured where that ceiling sits.
• The clean start: a raised record means the event happened only because the
  record was down at the start, and that start is put in by hand. It’s a past hypothesis
  in miniature. The past hypothesis, the philosopher David Albert’s name (2000)
  for an assumed low-entropy beginning of the universe, is an idea that goes back
  to Boltzmann; several accounts of why records point to the past lean on it, and
  every theorem here about records gets its arrow from an assumed clean start
  (Section 10).
  Chosen: what the model adds, each of which could have gone another way.
• To put the account inside the step, as part of what a step is. Two things go there.
  That the record stays and the computing can’t reach it has to: the record is one
  of the five parts, a reading of the state, and a rule about the state kept by the
  step holds of every program, where a log a program keeps holds of that program
  only. The count can go there or not: it isn’t one of the five parts, it’s the sum of
  the prices along the run, so a log of the run holds the same number. I keep it in
  the step so every state carries its own count. That changes no number and no
  merge; it moves the fresh states the count takes, a fresh value for every unit of
  cost, from the log into the state. On the certified machine of Part III the step also
  keeps the order, check, then commit, then certify, for the same reason.
• The toll itself: a whole unit, at least one, on the step that raises a reading,
  whichever way keeping is paid. On a machine with finitely many states reading
  yes, for a reading that stays, it follows from a price on merging, and that price is
  a choice too. On a machine that pays in fresh states it would follow from a price
  on taking them, on a move that takes a fresh state every time it’s played, but
  counting up is such a move, so that price charges computing. Where computing
  costs nothing, a raise paid in fresh states, and the rise of a reading that can come
  down, carry the toll because I declare it.
• Which readings matter: the ones that never come down. The toll charges
  any reading’s rise; permanence is what makes the rise a case of keeping, and
  permanence is a choice. So is one next state for every state, the condition the
  stopping hole gets around.
26   The point


                 • Which event gets a record, and what price list the record pays. The latch leaves
                   both unforced. And on a machine that pays in fresh states, where the write merges
                   nothing, the record stays up because I declare that it does (Theorem 10.3).
                 • On the machine of Part III, where its ordinary computer ends and its record
                   begins, and that its step never reads the flag: the rest of the state moves by its
                   own rule and the ledger adds the instruction’s price, whichever way the flag
                   reads. Part of the first is forced: the line, and each counter or its version, have to
                   be on the computer’s side, and the flag or the trap on the record’s. The certifying
                   move’s form isn’t a second choice, and neither is its merge. With nowhere in the
                   step for a copy of the old reading to go, the flag’s two readings go to one, and the
                   state with the flag down and the same state with it up land together. A record
                   kept as a list that only grows keeps the copy, raises its reading with no merge,
                   and pays in fresh states instead.
                    The machine Part III builds is one worked demonstration of the third list, on one
                 reading. Nothing in the first list needs it.


                 What structure is made of

                 Step three says that a 0 is the smallest structure that sorts, and that the rest of
                 structure is the same thing at a bigger size.
                     A sorting of a pile into groups is a distinction: these go together, those don’t.
                 Keep it and it’s a distinction that stays, paid for the same way. An ordering is every
                 pair compared and the answers kept. A fact somebody found out and wrote down is
                 a distinction between the ways things could have been and the way they were, kept.
                 A machine can carry any of those in its state and in its rules, and each one it keeps
                 is paid for the way the 0 is. Part II goes through the people who wrestled with the
                 word structure, from Pythagoras to category theory, and comes out at that: structure
                 is distinctions held in a state.
                     That gives insight an exact meaning, a narrower one than you’d like, and I’ll be
                 honest about how narrow. Finding something out doesn’t have to pay the merge.
                 Bennett showed that you can write down what you see on a blank page without
                 merging anything, so Landauer’s floor isn’t owed; the page is what you spend, and
                 it can be handed back while the original is still there. Making it stay is what pays.
                 Learning borrows, committing pays. The insight the toll prices is the committed
                 kind, a distinction made to stay. Whether that narrower thing deserves the word is a
                 fair thing to argue about, and Part I argues it, where learning and committing get
                 pulled apart.
                     Then Part II asks what follows, on any machine, once a distinction is kept and
                 the keeping is charged. The ledger is itself a distinction that stays: a number that
                                                                                           The point   27


only climbs takes a fresh value for every unit it counts. A window that shows only
part of a state can hide the very distinction that was paid for, and when it shows a
step that paid and one that didn’t the same, before and after, no price read off the
window can be exact. A later step can be entitled to something because a distinction
stayed, and the entitlement has an exact count. Over any machine at all, a reading
the machine’s own steps turn on and nothing turns off is a latch, the blank cell’s 0
one level up. And there’s a wall no level gets past: no state codes every question
about the states.


Established

Step four is the sharpest case, and it’s the one I build a machine for.
    Two computers each get the same messy list and each end up holding it sorted.
One sorted it, and the other was handed the sorted list and copied it in. They hold
the same bits in memory, byte for byte. Ask me which is which and I can’t tell you,
and neither machine can tell you either. The difference was real: one of them ran
a check that could have come out no. It just wasn’t kept. Nothing in an ordinary
computer’s end state has to hold “this was checked,” and in these two nothing does.
Ordinary computers spend their merges on forgetting how their bits got there, on
purpose, so that a 1 is a 1 whatever path made it. They pay what step one says
keeping takes, in merges, and keep nothing for it.
    Established is the name for the difference. An answer is established when a check
that could have said no said yes, about that very answer, and the result was made
to stay. That last part is a kept distinction, a 0 in some cell that says “checked,”
and it’s paid for the same way as every other 0. Part III opens by taking that apart
(Section 14): what “could have said no” means, what settling a question is, and why
the people who thought hardest about knowledge kept landing near it.
    Then it builds one example that meets the definition, in two layers. Underneath
is an ordinary computer, as small as I could make it: two counters that add one
and take one away, which Marvin Minsky proved can compute anything a Turing
machine can, once the input is handed to them packed. Its own merges are an
ordinary computer’s merges, and the ledger leaves them alone. On top sits a record
layer whose flag is the blank cell. Raising the flag is the write of a 0: the state with
the flag down and the same state with it already up both land on one state. That
landing is a merge, the one step one is about, and once merges in that layer are
priced, the toll on the flag follows as a theorem (Theorem 3.19). The example’s toll
charges the 0 in the step itself.
    What makes a raised flag mean something is the lock, and it’s one rule: no flag
without a commitment, and no commitment without a check of that same claim
that passed, with the thing checked untouched since (a counter’s edition is how
28   The point


                 many times it has been written, so “untouched” means the edition hasn’t moved;
                 the example of Part III calls it the counter’s version). The rule is in the step, so, from
                 a clean start, it holds of every program anybody can write for the example, buggy
                 and hostile ones included. A log a program keeps tells you about that program. A
                 rule in the step tells you about all of them.
                    How far the example reaches, to other models of computation and to universal
                 machines that run it as a guest and earn its flag again, is proved too; Part III states it
                 (Section 16) and the appendices build it. That’s the reach of the case, not what the
                 book is about.


                 The four steps of the argument
                 Here are the four steps together. The proofs establish the counts and constructions;
                 the argument for carrying this account inside the machine explains why I built them.
                      Proved, step one, on any machine with one next state for every state, finite or
                 endless: every step lands on a fresh state, merges two states into one, or goes round
                 a loop, and a run that raises a reading and keeps it up can’t be on a loop through
                 its start, so it merges somewhere or takes a fresh state at every step: a merge or a
                 fresh state. On finitely many states, a noisy step that keeps the even spread and a
                 quantum step that keeps lengths can’t raise a reading that stays up either. And a
                 coarse merge forces something at every finer zoom it’s exact about (when a coarse
                 picture merges, a finer picture it’s exact about merges too, steps out of the states
                 the picture describes, or has no end), and for a bounded memory the fresh states
                 run out at an exact count. With finitely many states reading yes and a reading
                 that never comes down, every move that raises it merges states, which is Part I’s
                 counting of states. That a merge of states that were really possible carries a heat
                 floor is Landauer’s premise, and that every change a real device makes in a finite
                 time dissipates is cited physics; neither is proved here.
                      Proved, step two: with finitely many states reading yes, every schedule that
                 prices merges charges the move that raises a kept reading, which is the toll, derived;
                 and anything that obeys the toll pays at least one unit of cost every time its reading
                 goes from no to yes, which is the universal floor. Finding out doesn’t have to merge:
                 add what you see onto a blank page, so that doing it again clears the page, and
                 you learn something with no two states landing on one, so a price list on merges
                 can charge it nothing. That doesn’t mean it takes nothing: it borrows fresh states,
                 the blank page, and the copy can be handed back while the original’s still there. A
                 commitment can’t be handed back, so the toll lands on committing. Put a number
                 on that, on a finite machine whose price list charges every bit a move removes, and
                 it’s the certainty bound: what anyone learns about where a machine started is either
                 still held in its state or was paid for in units of cost, at most one bit a unit.
                                                                                            The point   29


    Proved, step three: a window that shows a step raising a kept reading and a quiet
one alike, before and after, can’t price the raise exactly, however clever it is. Over
any machine, a reading the machine’s own events turn on and nothing turns off is a
latch on one event, with two unforced choices: the price list and which event. And
no state codes every question about the states.
    Proved, step four, inside its one case, on a minimal example, six instruction kinds
on two counters, there to show the definition can be met and the record earned:
for every program anybody can write, from a clean start, a raised flag always went
through a passing check, then a commitment, then a certificate, of exactly the same
claim about exactly the same edition, with claims about any property that comes
with a checker proved to mean it and an exact test for telling properties apart,
“sorted” included (Section 15). Every such run incurred a cost of at least three, and
three is reached. The example meets a definition I call certified Thiele-complete,
which asks that the record be earned, on top of everything the bar below asks.
    Defined, and proved about, over any base and any event: a machine is Thiele-
complete when its computing is universal, costs nothing and can’t touch the record,
every other move costs one, the record stays, starts are blank, and some run’s record
tells two starts apart (Section 10.8). A clock fails it, every machine that meets
it hides its record and its ledger from its own window, and any universal base
becomes one by adding marks, all by theorem. Certified Thiele-complete is exactly
Thiele-complete with clean starts, an earned record (the chain, a checker proved
sound, claims that stay true while what they’re about is unchanged) and a claim
that could have failed added (Theorem 15.23).
    Proved, over any computer that shows two counters and a line, with a move for
each two-counter instruction and a start for any two counters, about where ordinary
computation sits: it’s the slice. Put a record layer on such a computer, a tally, a table
with room for a fact, a channel, a trap, a ledger and a flag, with check, commit
and certify its only priced moves and “this counter is at least n” as its claims, and
the result is certified Thiele-complete. Forget the layer and what’s left runs as the
computer runs until a record move fails, reaches exactly what the computer reaches,
is never moved by a check, a commitment or a certificate, and can’t see the record
or the ledger: from one start, two runs end on the same state of the computer with
the record up in one and down in the other and ledgers exactly three apart. With
no room in the table, no way of reading the result meets the definition. The other
way round, the moves of a Thiele-complete machine that cost nothing are the same
however you read it as Thiele-complete, and its window is a slice of it onto two
counters. And a machine run as one rule has no universal base and no slice, and is a
Thiele machine only as a clock or with a reading that never rises (Theorem E.4). Not
all of that could have failed. That the slice runs as the computer runs and that the
record moves leave it alone hold by construction, and its blindness follows from the
30   The point


                 second once the layer is certified. The other way round holds by construction too,
                 apart from the window being blind, which Part II proves. What could have failed
                 is that the layer is certified at all, that every Thiele-complete machine’s window is
                 blind, and that a table with no room certifies under no reading. The one-rule result
                 is short, and it rests on one choice in the toll: the price sits on the move, the same
                 from every state.
                     Argued only: that the structure a computation makes is kept distinctions, priced
                 by the toll, while a reading that undoable moves keep never rises and is never
                 charged; that’s a choice of what to price, and on a finite machine the second half is
                 proved.
                     Argued only: that an account of computation should carry what a computation
                 made the case, and what it cost, in how it steps. The proofs show that it hangs
                 together, what it follows from, and what it costs; whether it ought to be adopted is
                 a claim about what matters, which no theorem decides.
                     My proposed reason for choosing certification is that its records get copied and
                 relied on by parties who didn’t produce them. That is the pointer thesis in Part III.
                 It connects the machine to how people use records; the counting arguments work
                 with whichever record is chosen.
                     The results also have a history. By my own sorting at the back (Appendix C),
                 each piece has its neighbours standing right there. Start from the top. The small
                 machine and its universal programs carry the reference monitor’s every-program
                 move (Anderson in 1972) to a record that’s priced and earned; the two-player game
                 check in the appendices (Appendix H) is careful engineering on known mathematics.
                 The latch has the 1918 flip-flop and write-once memory for neighbours. The
                 window fact is an old fact about functions, from Edward Moore’s 1956 thought
                 experiments and Rudolf Kalman’s observability, with a price put on it. The toll
                 derived from finiteness, permanence and a price on merging is a ledger form of
                 the core underneath. And that core, what step one says keeping takes, is old
                 mathematics: the pigeonhole principle, Dedekind’s 1888 definition of infinite and
                 the finite heart of Ernst Zermelo’s 1896 recurrence argument, with Landauer and
                 Bennett on merging and Thomas Ouldridge and David Wolpert’s 2023 price in
                 entropy on the merges a finite automaton can’t avoid. For deterministic machines
                 the arrangement is old too: Ming Li and Paul Vitányi (1996) wrote that a bounded
                 memory forces erasure in the long run, and Demaine and his coauthors (2016)
                 that extra space only postpones it. What I’d defend most is there, at the bottom, in
                 the form I didn’t find: one law with three columns and no fourth, stated alike for
                 deterministic, noisy and quantum steps, with two small exact lemmas, the count of
                 fresh states for a bounded memory and every scale paying the same way, and a toll
                 on a reading that stays, which charges for keeping whichever column pays for it.
                                                                                          The point   31


   The route through the book is the route through the model: follow a step, see
which distinctions survive it, and count what the next step has to work with. Then
put the record and its price into the step itself. The example at the end shows those
choices can all be made at once.


How the book goes

Part I is what keeping costs. It covers a distinction that stays, and what every step
of every machine does to the states it has used; the smallest thing that writes what
keeping takes into its own step, as one rule, the toll; whether the rule is forced, and
on which premises; and why finding out only borrows, where committing pays.
    Part II is structure, as kept distinctions: the word itself, from the people who
wrestled with it, and then what follows on any machine once a distinction is kept
and the keeping charged: the ledger, the window, entitlement, the latch, and the
wall no level gets past.
    Part III is the sharpest case: what established means, the machine that keeps it,
how far the machine reaches, five real systems that keep records and whether they
price the write, the thesis about which kept distinction is worth paying for, and what
its ledger has to do with heat.
    Part IV brings the results together: what each establishes, which conditions it
uses, and how the constructions fit. After that comes how I got here, for anyone
who wants the story, and then the appendices, which carry the full constructions the
main text only states.

What keeping costs

         Part I is step one, and the rule step two needs. It starts at the smallest structure
     that sorts: a cell that’s blank, and then a 0. First comes what keeping takes, before
     any price list: what a distinction that stays is, what every step of every machine
     does to the states it has used, and what it costs for something to go from nothing to
     something and stay. Then the smallest machine that writes what keeping takes into
     its own step, as one rule, the toll. Then whether the rule is forced, and on which
     premises. Then the one thing that looks like it ought to pay a merge and doesn’t
     have to: finding out, which borrows fresh states instead.
CHAPTER 1




A distinction that stays

A cell can be blank, or 0, or 1, and somebody has drawn the lines between those.
Write a 0 in it and it stays a 0, and that’s the event this whole book is about, nothing
becoming something; this chapter is what it takes, before any machine and before
any price list.
    What this chapter counts is a distinction that stays. A cell on a tape that reads 0,
and not 1, and not blank, is one; a bead sitting in the left well and not the right is
one; a flag that is up is one. Anything the world can tell apart from something else
and keeps telling apart counts. It takes three things: something that can be more
than one way, a sorting of its ways into piles, and a hill that keeps it in its pile. The
point said so in pictures (“Where a 0 comes from”). Here I want two things exactly:
what every step of every machine does to the states it has used, and what it costs for
a state to be taken at all. Both answers are proofs, and every one of them is short
enough to follow on the page. Nothing in this chapter needs a price list, and the
toll, named up front, is stated exactly only in the next chapter, which writes what
keeping takes into a machine’s step; the one after asks whether it had to.


1.1 Every step does one of three things
Forget the cell for a moment, and forget finiteness. Take any machine at all, with
any number of states and any rule that gives each state exactly one next state, and
watch it run from any start. Keep a list of every state it has been in. Now look at the
next step. There are exactly three things it can do.
   It can land on a state the run has not used yet, which uses up a fresh state on
this step. The only way to stop using up fresh states is to come back to a state the
run has used: to the start, and a run that does that has kept nothing, or to another
one, which is the next thing a step can do.
   It can come back, for the first time in the run, to a state the run has used before,
and not the state it started from. Then it came from a different state than the one
that first got there, so two different states have led to the same place, and that is
what I mean by a merge: a literal collision, two different states with the same next
state. Under Landauer’s premise a merge of states that were really possible carries a
floor of heat, and no amount of going slowly lowers it.


                                                   35
36   1 A distinction that stays


                   Or it can land back on the very state it started from, or take a step the run
                has already taken. Then the machine is going round a loop, and this is certain: a
                machine with one rule for the next state, once it stands where it stood before, does
                again what it did before, forever. Every later state is one it already had, and every
                later step is one it already took, and it is computing nothing new.
                   There is no fourth thing a step can do, and every run has the same shape: fresh
                states, then at most one return, and after it nothing but steps already taken. The
                proof is one line: the first time a run comes back to a state it has used, either it
                came back to its very first state, which is a pure loop from the start, or the step that
                brought it back lands on the same state as the step that first got there, which is a
                merge. So a run merges at most once; going round the loop it settles into doesn’t
                merge again.


                Theorem 1.1 (The step law). Let a step give every state of a set exactly one next
                state, where the states can be told apart, and run it from any start x0 , writing
                x0 , x1 , x2 , . . . for the run. Either every step is fresh, landing on a state the run has
                not visited, or there is a first step that lands on a visited state, from xn to xn+1 = x j
                with j ≤ n, and then: every step before it is fresh; it lands on the start (j = 0), or
                it is a merge, coming from a different state than the one that first reached x j , so
                that two distinct states share a next state; and from x j on the run is periodic, so
                every later state is one the run already had and every later step, from xk to xk+1
                with k > n, is a step the run already took. In a run at most one pair of distinct states
                shares a next state, x j−1 and xn , and the step that first joins them is the only merge;
                later laps retake it.

                Proof. If no state repeats, every step is fresh. Otherwise take the first step that
                lands on a visited state, from xn to xn+1 , and the position j ≤ n with x j = xn+1 ;
                it is unique, because x0 , . . . , xn are all different. Every earlier step is fresh, by the
                choice of n. If j > 0, compare x j−1 , which first reached x j , with xn : both land on x j .
                They differ, because xn = x j−1 with j − 1 < n would be an earlier repeat. So two
                distinct states share a next state: a merge. Either way, since one rule gives the next
                state, xn+1 = x j gives xn+1+k = x j+k for every k, so the run repeats with period
                p = n + 1 − j from position j on. For k > n the step from xk to xk+1 is then the step
                from xk− p to xk− p+1 , taken earlier, and every later state is one of x j , . . . , xn . No later
                step merges: it lands where an earlier step from the same state landed, and the only
                two distinct states with a shared next state in the run are x j−1 and xn .
                   The step law is “nothing is kept for free” as a theorem with two hypotheses: you
                can tell states apart, and each state has one next state. The only step that neither
                uses up a fresh state nor merges is a step on a loop, and a loop makes nothing new.
                                                                1.1 Every step does one of three things   37


Anything new is a state never used before or one that two states have led to, and
that’s what keeping takes. There’s dissipation on top of it: a real step that changes
a device’s state in a real amount of time dissipates just by happening. That one is
heat against time: I prove it below for Bennett’s walker, and the physicists have it
for devices sitting in surroundings at a temperature. The reading that stays up is the
way to force “new”: a reading that was no and is now yes can never come back to
the state it started on, so the run can’t be a loop through its start. Its first return to
any state it has used, if it ever has one, is a merge; if it never has one, every state it
takes is fresh. Two chapters on, that’s the first part of Proposition 3.5, where the
fresh states get counted exactly. (After a merge the run can settle onto a loop among
states that read yes and idle there, making nothing new. The keeping was paid for
at the merge.)
    There is one hole, and it’s worth seeing exactly. Take a machine that stops, with
two states. The first reads no, the step takes it to the second, which reads yes, and
the second has no next step at all. The reading is raised, there is no merge, no fresh
state after that, nothing. The step law assumed every state has a next state, and a
machine that stops its clock dodges it. Close the hole either way and what keeping
takes comes back. Say the halted state’s next state is itself, which is the usual way
to give a stopped machine a step, and the halt is a merge: the moving state and
the halted state both land on the halted state. A physical device can also hold a
reading through its storage arrangement. What that arrangement costs is a question
about the device; the partial transition rule has not answered it. Here I can settle
the state-counting question once holding is included in a total next-state rule.


Theorem 1.2 (Halting). A partial step, one that may have no next state, can raise a
permanent reading on two states with no two states sharing a next state. Totalising
it, with the halted state stepping to itself, makes the raise a merge: the halted state
and the state that steps onto it share a next state. In general, once every halted state
steps to itself, any other state that steps onto a halted state shares that landing with
it.

Proof. States a and b, reading no on a and yes on b; a steps to b and b has no next
state. No two states step to the same state, because only a steps at all. Totalise:
b steps to b, and now a and b both step to b, a merge of two distinct states. The
general case is the same two lines: if c ̸= h steps to the halted state h and h steps to
h, then c and h share a next state.
   Stepping the halted state to itself is one way to totalise. Step it to a fresh sink
state instead and the merge only moves: the sink steps to itself, and the halted state
lands there too. On finitely many states reading yes, every way to totalise that keeps
38   1 A distinction that stays


                the reading up merges somewhere (Proposition 3.4, two chapters on). An endless
                counter offers another arrangement: the reading stays put while the full state keeps
                changing. I want to count that arrangement now, because the screen and the box
                are doing different things.

               The camera stops; the box keeps ticking
               At three o’clock the screen says 42. The program is finished. Stop filming and you
               have the computation from start to finish. Leave the camera running and the box is
               still on the desk. At 3:01 it says 42. At 3:02 it says 42.
                   Let the box’s next-state rule keep ticking. It can stay exactly where it is, or change
               something behind that screen. Imagine a wheel inside it, turning from “first holding
               state” to “second holding state” while the display never moves. The screen gives you
               42 each time. Open the box and the wheel may tell you which tick you are looking
               at.
                   Start the count one tick before completion. That unfinished state is u. Call the
               total next-state rule F, so F (u) is the first completed state and F2 (u) is the next one.
               Gather the full states that keep the answer into a set H, and require the rule to stay
               in that set once it enters. Give H room for K configurations. Two bits can have four
               configurations; these are the arrangements of the box I am counting.
                   Now ask it to hold for L samples while every distinct source in that stretch,
               including u, has a distinct successor. Suppose two holding samples repeated the
               same full state. Follow their equal successors backwards. Each cancellation takes
               one step off both sides, until the unfinished state equals a state already holding the
               answer. That is impossible. Every holding sample needs its own full configuration.


                Theorem 1.3 (Room to hold an answer). Let F : X → X be total, with distin-
                guishable states, and let H ⊆ X have K elements. Suppose u ∈
                                                                           / H, F (u) ∈ H, and
                F ( H ) ⊆ H. For L ≥ 0, put

                If F is one-to-one on DL , then the L held states F (u), . . . , F L (u) are distinct, and
                L ≤ K. In particular, among u, F (u), . . . , F K (u) there are two distinct states with the
                same successor. If instead F is one-to-one everywhere and the held region is allowed
                to be infinite, the orbit from u never repeats.

                Proof. Suppose the same full state occurs twice in the displayed stretch, first at
                position i and later at position j. If the earlier position is the start, I have already
                equated the unfinished state u with a held state, which is impossible.
                                                                                     1.2 What a kept distinction is   39


   Otherwise look one tick behind both occurrences. Those two predecessors belong
to DL , and they have the same successor. The one-to-one rule on DL says that
the predecessors must therefore be equal. Move back another tick on both sides
and repeat. You eventually reach position zero on the earlier side and position
j − i > 0 on the later side. In symbols, the repeated backward comparison has given
u = F j−i (u). The left side is unfinished; the right side has entered H and stayed
there. That is the contradiction.
    So all L held samples are distinct. There are only K states available in H, giving
L ≤ K. If the sources through F K (u) had no shared successor, use L = K + 1:
you would need K + 1 held states where only K exist. Finally, when the step is
one-to-one everywhere, the backward comparison works for any two finite positions
in the run. No repetition is possible, no matter how long you keep watching.
   Draw the smallest delayed example:
