The screen says 42 at both h1 and h2 . Only u leads to h1 ; the entry is clear. The
two arrows meet a tick later, when h1 and h2 both lead to h2 . With K holding
configurations, the run exposes a collision within its first K + 1 transitions from u.
   You can reach the bound exactly. Hand me a guest run that halts after T ≥ 1
steps, and let me use K ≥ 1 holding states. Line them up:
             prep −→ a0 −→ · · · −→ a T −1 −→ h1 −→ · · · −→ hK −→ hK .

The preparation state shows nothing yet. Each a j shows that step of the guest run.
Every h j shows its final answer. There are 1 + T + K full states. Starting at the last
running state, the first K sources have different successors. Add the next source and
the arrows meet. The box uses every holding state before exposing the collision.
   The camera can stop at 42. The box that keeps showing it still has a next step.
Include those steps and you can count exactly how long it can keep its full states
apart. 1


1.2 What a kept distinction is

Now I turn to the cell. A blank cell could be anything. Write a 0 in it and it is a
0, and it stays a 0. That moment, nothing becoming something, is an event, and
like every change a real device makes in a real amount of time, it dissipates when it
happens. Heat against time, below, says how much. And if the blank could have
been anything, fixing it to a 0 also wipes out what it could have been, and that part
   1 This is a state-capacity count. A ledger price requires a pricing rule; a heat bound requires physical

premises.
40   1 A distinction that stays


                carries a floor no slowness takes away: it’s the merge I’m about to show you. Here I
                want the other part of the price, the part for keeping it, and I want it from the step
                law and one count, the pigeonhole on the written states.
                    And the cell isn’t the lowest level. Describe whatever holds it, a bead in two dips,
                the molecules that jostle the bead, whatever holds those, and you’ve described states
                that can be told apart and a way they change: a machine of the same kind, charged
                the same way, because a merge one level up forces, one level down, either a merge
                or a state never used before, as long as the level above is exact about the level below
                and the level below stays among the states the one above describes (Theorem 1.10).
                Every level you can describe is one of these. Under all of them there’s nothing told
                apart at all, and that’s the nothing a blank cell stands for.
                    The cell has three states: blank, zero, one. The reading is “the cell is definite,” no
                on blank and yes on the other two, and a written cell stays written, so the reading is
                permanent. The move is “write a 0,” which takes blank to zero and leaves a written
                cell alone. Now look at where each state lands. Blank lands on zero, and zero
                lands on zero, so two different states have led to the same place, and writing a 0 on
                nothing is, by itself, a merge. When you don’t know whether the cell was blank or
                already 0, that merge owes Landauer’s floor on top of the dissipation of happening,
                and no slowness removes it. When you know it was blank, the floor goes where
                the knowing is, as you’ll see below. The history in which the cell was blank and the
                history in which it already held a 0 are now the same history. This is not an analogy
                to the step law; it’s the step law with three states filled in.
                    The obvious way round it is a fourth state that remembers: “0, and it was
                blank before.” Now blank lands on a state nothing else has landed on. But the
                remembering state has to go somewhere on the next write too, and it’s written, so it
                has to stay written. Every written state already has something landing on it: zero
                and one land on themselves, and the remembering state is where blank landed. So
                the remembering state has to share. In the smallest version it lands on itself, and
                then blank and the remembering state land on the same state. No finite extension
                of the cell gets out of the merge, and the reason is counting (Proposition 3.4, two
                chapters on), not bad luck. The only way to write with no merge, once every state
                has a next one, is a supply of fresh states that never runs out: a state never used
                before for every write, forever, such as a new cell of an endless tape for each one (it
                comes back two chapters on, as the first of three ways out of a theorem). That isn’t
                getting out of what keeping takes. It dodges the floor by taking a state it has never
                used, at every write, without limit, and each write still dissipates when it happens.
                Or, in a form I need below, a tape that stretches both ways with the machine stepping
                one cell along it. Every cell has one before it and one after it, nothing ever shares a
                landing, the reading “past the start” goes up on the first step and never comes down,
                                                                       1.2 What a kept distinction is   41


and the machine never returns. This is the bilateral shift, and it pays at every step
by taking a cell it has never used.


Theorem 1.4 (The write of a 0 merges, and only fresh states avoid it). (1) On
the three states blank, zero, one, with reading “definite,” writing a 0 is permanent,
raises the reading from blank, and merges blank with zero. (2) Adding a fourth
state that remembers the cell was blank, with written cells staying written, does not
avoid the merge: on the four states the write still merges two distinct states. The
same holds on any finite set of states. (3) On an endless tape, writing adds one cell
and is one-to-one; on the integers, the step “one cell along” is a bijection, raises
“past the start” on the first step, keeps it up, and after any positive number of steps
is away from where it started.

Proof. (1) Blank and zero both step to zero, and blank is not zero; zero and one step
to themselves, so a written cell stays written. (2) Blank steps to the remembering
state, and permanence sends each of the three written states, zero, one and the
remembering state, to a written state. So four states land among the three written
ones, and two of them share a landing. Whenever only finitely many states are
written the same count works: permanence sends the finitely many written states
among themselves, blank lands among them too, so one more state lands among
them than there are, and two share a landing (Proposition 3.4, two chapters on,
states it in general). (3) “Add one” on the counting numbers is one-to-one and never
returns to zero; “add one” on the integers is one-to-one and onto, sends 0 to 1, sends
every number that is at least 1 to one that is at least 1, and after k > 0 steps has
moved by k.
    The theorem leans on one thing, and I want it in the open. The write is a move
defined on every state of the cell, written ones included, and a written cell stays
written, so the state blank merges with is a cell that was already written. A write
defined only on blank, with the machine simply stopping when it meets a written
cell, merges nothing. That’s the stopping hole from above (Theorem 1.2): it buys
the 0 by having no next step at all.
    The theorem buys this: a fact is a distinction that stays, and a kept distinction is
a state the run has used and can’t give back. The machine is the thing whose own
state includes the used states it can’t give back.
    It doesn’t stop at the cell. The tape is a set of distinctions that stayed. So is the
rule for the next state, and so is the question you ask of a state. Each of the five
parts of the model is itself a definite thing where there could have been anything;
the model doesn’t charge for them, but they’re the same kind of thing it charges
for. And the model can run itself: a host that obeys the toll and runs a guest move
42   1 A distinction that stays


                for move, carrying the guest’s prices on its own ledger, pays at least one unit there
                for every step where the guest’s record went up, and Part III states one (Section 16;
                Appendix D builds it). The tower is the same kind of machine above and below.
                What no level does is hold all the questions you can ask of it: for any way of coding
                readings as states, there’s a reading no state codes, the one that answers each state
                with the opposite of what that state’s own coded reading says of it. That’s Cantor’s
                diagonal, the shape of Russell’s 1902 letter to Frege (Section 5), and the subject of
                Section 13. Put the two together and you have the regress exactly: every level runs
                the one below that way and pays again, in its own ledger, for every rise of the lower
                level’s record, and no level ever holds every question about itself.


                Theorem 1.5 (No level holds its own questions). For any set of states and any
                assignment of a yes/no reading to each state, some yes/no reading on the states is
                assigned to no state.

                Proof. Take the reading that says, of each state, the opposite of what that state’s
                assigned reading says of the state itself. If some state were assigned it, that state
                would answer itself both ways.
                    The regress has a price too. Write a 0 on a cell you know is blank and Landauer’s
                premise sets no floor: the entropy before and after are both zero (Theorem 3.17,
                two chapters on, does the arithmetic). The write still dissipates when it happens.
                What’s missing is a floor that survives going slowly, and it’s missing only for a writer
                built knowing which of blank and 0 it will be handed, like one built for this one
                cell, knowing it’s blank. A writer that writes 0 on whatever it’s handed, blank or
                0, keeps a floor on the worse of the two however slowly it goes (Section 3.7 says
                how much). So where did the floor go, for the writer built knowing? It went into
                the knowing. “This cell is blank” is a distinction that stays, a record, and the count
                Section 8 uses says how big a record like that is: naming one of a list of possibilities
                takes the rounded-up logarithm of the list’s length in yes-or-no questions, one per
                halving. Blank named among three possibilities is two questions. Blank among “it
                could have been anything” is as many as you like. Whoever knows the cell is blank
                is keeping that distinction, and the heat floor for it was paid in the knowing, or will
                be paid when that record is wiped. And the state the 0 sits in was paid for before
                the run, by whoever built the cell.


                1.3 A reversible machine keeps nothing

                Bennett’s reversible machine never lets two of its states lead to the same next state;
                that’s what reversible means. Put one on finitely many states and watch it. By the
                                                                                       1.4 Noisy steps   43


pigeonhole it has to revisit a state within as many steps as there are states. The step
law says the first revisit is a merge or a return to the start, and a merge is impossible
for it, so it returns to its start, and once it’s back at its start it does everything again.
Any reading it raised has come back down. A reversible finite machine with a next
state for every state keeps nothing, and that’s a theorem, not a slogan. One that
stops slips past, as the stopping hole above says, and keeps what it halted on. It
is the recurrence Zermelo threw at Boltzmann (Section 3 tells that story), in its
finite form, proved from the step law and the pigeonhole and nothing else. What
Bennett’s machine keeps is the fresh states it’s handed: on an endless tape it can
keep its whole history and never come back, taking a state it has never used at every
step, and the tape was paid for before the first step by whoever built it. A reversible
machine dodges the merge and its floor. A real one, in contact with its surroundings,
doesn’t dodge the dissipation of happening: run slowly it dissipates little, but never
nothing, and it pays by taking fresh states besides.


Theorem 1.6 (Reversible keeps nothing). Let a one-to-one step act on finitely many
states. From any start the run returns to the start within as many steps as there are
states, and any reading that is no at the start and never goes from yes to no is no at
every step.

Proof. Among the first (number of states) plus one states of the run, two are equal,
by the pigeonhole. Take two equal positions and cancel the one-to-one step back
from both the same number of times, until the earlier one reaches the start; the later
one then equals the start. So the run returns to the start after at most that many
steps, and from then on repeats. If the reading were yes at some step, it would stay
yes from there, in particular at a later multiple of the period, where the state is the
start, which reads no.


1.4 Noisy steps
Real states are noisy. The bead hops on its own. So take the step to be a table
of chances: from each state, the chance of landing on each state next, every row
adding to one. A permanent reading is a set of states you never leave once you’re in
it. And “no merge” has an exact noisy meaning: the step preserves the even spread.
Start with everybody spread evenly over the states, take one step, and they’re still
spread evenly; which is to say every column of the table adds to one as well as every
row. Such a step squeezes nothing on average.
    Then the cell’s count goes through with chances in place of people. A step that
preserves the even spread cannot raise a permanent reading from any state outside
44   1 A distinction that stays


                it, and not merely with small chance but with none. Count the chance flowing
                into the yes-states from everywhere. Column by column that’s one per yes-state, so
                it equals the number of yes-states. The yes-states alone already send exactly that
                much, because they never leave. What’s left over for the outside states is zero, and
                it’s a sum of chances, so each is zero. The count never used that the spread was
                even, only that every state had some chance and the step gave the spread back. A
                lopsided memory that keeps its own lopsided spread can’t raise a reading that stays
                either: weight each state by its chance and the same sum comes out.
                    And it runs the other way too. A step that can raise a permanent reading does
                not preserve the even spread, so after one step from the even spread the crowd is
                more bunched up than it was. Here is a way to measure that bunching. Draw a
                state twice, independently, using the same spread of chances. Ask whether the two
                draws match. For two equally likely states, the matching pairs have chances one
                quarter and one quarter, so a match occurs half the time. Put three quarters of the
                chance on one state and one quarter on the other: the matching chances are now
                nine sixteenths and one sixteenth, adding to ten sixteenths. Bunching has made a
                match more likely.
                    In general, a state with chance q contributes q2 to this matching chance: q for
                the first draw, times q for the independent second draw. Add those squares over all
                states. I call that total the collision weight. The step just described raises it above the
                value for an even spread.
                    There is another measure of the same change, Shannon entropy, which measures
                uncertainty in the spread. It is largest when all states are equally likely, so leaving
                that even spread lowers it. This is the quantity that enters the heat bound under
                Landauer’s premise. Section 3.7 works through its meaning in bits; the proof here es-
                tablishes the drop. Finally, when a step preserves the even spread, it cannot increase
                the collision weight of any starting spread. That last claim needs a calculation too.


                Theorem 1.7 (Noisy steps). Let a step on finitely many states be a table of chances
                with rows adding to one, and let a set of states be closed: from inside, the chance
                of leaving is zero. (1) If every column also adds to one, the chance of entering the
                closed set from any state outside it is zero. (2) If some state outside can enter the
                closed set with positive chance, then some column does not add to one, and one
                step from the even spread strictly raises the collision weight, the sum of the squared
                chances, which is least for the even spread, and it leaves a Shannon entropy strictly
                below the logarithm of the number of states. (3) If every column adds to one, one
                step never raises the collision weight of any spread.
                                                                                    1.4 Noisy steps   45


   Part (1) needs only the closed set to be finite, the rest as large as you like, and
part (3) needs no finiteness at all; part (2) needs the even spread, so it needs finitely
many states.
Proof. (1) Count the total chance sent into the closed set. Each of its columns sums
to one, so the total equals the number of states in that set. The rows belonging to
states already inside send all their chance inside, and they already supply that entire
total. Nothing remains for an outside row to contribute. Because every contribution
is nonnegative, each outside contribution is zero.
    (2) Suppose instead that an outside state contributes a positive chance of entry.
Then the conclusion of (1) fails, so its column-sum condition cannot hold: at least
one column sum differs from one. Call the number of states N and the sum of
column j c j . Starting evenly puts chance 1/N at each source, so the chance at
destination j after the step is c j /N. The column sums themselves add to N, because
the N rows each add to one. Expand the following squares and use that total:

                   ∑(c j − 1)2 = ∑ c2j − 2 ∑ c j + N = ∑ c2j − N.
                    j               j          j              j

At least one square is positive. Thus ∑ j c2j > N. Dividing by N 2 says that the new
collision weight is greater than 1/N, the old even spread’s collision weight. Now
compare the uncertainty before and after. Write q j = c j /N for the new chances.
At least one differs from 1/N. Shannon’s entropy weights each possible state’s
logarithmic uncertainty by its chance. Using the natural logarithm, written ln, its
value is
                                H (q) = −    ∑ q j ln q j .
                                            j:q j >0

The sum leaves out states with zero chance; they contribute nothing. An even spread
has N equal terms, giving H = ln N. Subtract the new entropy from that value.
Since the chances add to one, you can put ln N inside the sum:

                           ln N − H (q) =     ∑ q j ln( Nq j ).
                                             j:q j >0

I need to show that this difference is positive, even though some individual terms
may be negative.
   Use the elementary logarithm inequality ln y ≤ y − 1, with equality only at y = 1.
One way to see it is to look at y − 1 − ln y: its slope is 1 − 1/y, negative below one
and positive above one, so its least value is zero at one. Apply the inequality with
y = 1/( Nq j ) and multiply by q j . Rearranging gives
                                q j ln( Nq j ) ≥ q j − 1/N,
46   1 A distinction that stays


                with equality only when q j = 1/N. A zero chance contributes zero to the entropy
                difference, which is strictly greater than its comparison term −1/N. Add the
                comparisons over all N states. Their right sides sum to 1 − N/N = 0. At least one
                comparison is strict because the new spread is not even, so the entropy difference is
                positive.
                   (3) Fix a destination column. Because its entries add to one, its new chance is an
                average of the old chances, with those entries as weights. An average of squares is
                never less than the square of the average. To see why, call the weights wi , the old
                chances pi , and their weighted average m. Expanding gives

                         ∑ wi ( pi − m)2 = ∑ wi p2i − m2 ≥ 0,         ∑ wi = 1,     m = ∑ wi p i .
                          i                  i                         i                   i

                So the new chance squared is at most the weighted sum of the old chances squared.
                Add this comparison over all destination columns. Each old chance squared gets
                weights from its whole row, whose sum is one. The result is exactly the old collision
                weight, bounding the new one from above.


                1.5 Unitary steps

                The quantum version needs a different picture. Draw a sheet through the centre of a
                room. Call every direction along the sheet YES, and the direction straight through it
                NO. Turn the whole arrangement without stretching it. Can the sheet stay within its
                old plane while the direction through it turns into that plane? No. The turn keeps
                right angles. If the sheet still fills that plane, the direction that was at right angles to
                the whole sheet is still at right angles to it.
                    Here is what carries from that picture into the quantum statement. A quantum
                state is described by a vector. A reversible quantum step preserves lengths and
                overlaps between vectors; such a step is called unitary. The YES part is a subspace: a
                collection of directions that also contains their linear combinations. The directions
                with zero overlap with every YES direction make up its orthogonal complement.
                These are the NO states in this argument. Permanence means that a vector in the
                YES subspace stays in it after the step.
                    There is one detail to settle before the right-angle argument works. The old
                YES directions must fill the whole YES subspace after the step, leaving no missing
                direction. Choose a finite list of directions from which every YES vector can be
                assembled, with none of the listed directions assembled from the others. Such a
                list is called an independent spanning list, or a basis. A unitary step keeps the list
                independent, since any relation between its images could be reversed to give the
                same relation before the step. The images are still inside the YES subspace, and
                there are just as many independent directions as before. They therefore still span it.
                                                                                 1.5 Unitary steps   47


That is why the step fills the YES subspace, rather than merely landing somewhere
inside it.
   Now take a NO vector. Before the step it has zero overlap with every YES vector.
After the step those overlaps are still zero, and the stepped YES vectors still fill the
whole YES subspace. The stepped NO vector is therefore still NO. Repeat the step
and the same argument applies again.
   Finite dimension was used exactly once: a full finite list of independent YES
directions still fills the YES subspace after the step. Drop it and the bilateral shift,
which is unitary on an endless ladder of states, raises “past the start” on the first
step and keeps it forever, taking a state it has never used every time. A reading
that stays, which no unitary step can raise in finite dimension, is paid for either
by fresh states, a ladder of states that never comes back around, or by a step that
squeezes the even spread, which, when the squeezed states were really possible,
owes Landauer’s floor. Not every step that fails to be unitary squeezes: one that
keeps the even spread, as pure dephasing and an unread measurement do, can’t
raise a reading that stays either. The balance argument is the same one used for
noisy steps. Choose a complete set of mutually perpendicular directions, some filling
the YES subspace and the rest filling its orthogonal complement. Spread the chances
equally over those directions. This is the fully mixed state: choosing a different
complete perpendicular set gives the same mixture.
   Suppose there are N directions altogether and m of them are YES. The mixture
has chance m/N of YES. A step that preserves this mixture must leave that chance
at m/N. But the YES part already supplies all of it: it started with weight m/N,
and permanence keeps that whole weight inside YES. Every contribution from the
other directions is nonnegative, so none can contribute any chance of entering YES.
You can include any chosen NO vector among the perpendicular directions of the
complement. The same balance then rules out entry from that vector. That is why
the outside cannot get in. In finite dimension nothing is kept without one of the
two. Which way a quantum measurement pays when its outcome is kept isn’t settled
here. The collapse models people test keep the even spread too, so the heat the
experiments look for is the heat of the noise those models add, not a Landauer price
on a kept outcome; I come back to them below.



Theorem 1.8 (Unitary steps). Let a unitary map a finite-dimensional subspace into
itself. Then it maps the orthogonal complement into itself: a state orthogonal to the
subspace remains orthogonal after every step.
48   1 A distinction that stays


                Proof. Call the step U and the YES subspace Y. Choose a basis of Y, meaning an
                independent list from which every vector in Y can be assembled. The step sends that
                list to an equally long independent list inside Y, so its images are another basis of Y.
                    Take any vector x orthogonal to Y. To test whether Ux is still orthogonal, choose
                any vector y in Y. Because the images fill Y, there is a vector z in Y with Uz = y.
                Unitarity preserves the overlap, written with angle brackets, so

                                          ⟨Ux, y⟩ = ⟨Ux, Uz⟩ = ⟨ x, z⟩ = 0.
                The last equality holds because x is orthogonal to every vector in Y, including z. The
                choice of y was arbitrary, so Ux is orthogonal to all of Y. This is the same condition
                I started with, and it survives every further step.


                1.6 Going faster gives off more heat

                Everything so far was what keeping takes. What comes next is the dissipation of
                happening at all, and no device in contact with its surroundings escapes it. Bennett’s
                own reversible computer is a walker on a line that is pushed forward a little: at
                each tick it steps forward with some chance and back with the rest. Its speed is the
                difference between the two. Every step it takes is one-to-one; it merges nothing
                and owes no floor. The entropy it gives off per tick is Schnakenberg’s formula for a
                biased walk, the speed times the logarithm of the forward-to-backward ratio, and
                that number is strictly positive at any speed other than zero, because both factors
                have the same sign. The only walker that gives off nothing is the one with no drift,
                as likely to step back as forward. This is the point that going slower doesn’t get you
                out of paying, now as a theorem: at any speed you actually run it, every tick gives
                off heat on average.
                    The exchange rate has a floor as well. Heat per net step forward, counted in
                units of kT, is the logarithm of the forward-to-backward ratio, and that logarithm is
                at least the speed. So walking a distance costs at least distance times speed in heat
                and takes distance over speed in time, and heat times time is at least the distance
                squared. At low speed, halve the speed and the heat roughly halves while the time
                doubles; the product never drops below the square of how far you went. Going
                slowly shrinks the heat toward zero, but it never gets there for a walk that finishes,
                because zero heat takes infinite time, and a walk that takes forever never arrives.


                Theorem 1.9 (Heat against time). For a walker stepping forward with chance p and
                back with chance 1 − p, with 0 < p < 1, the entropy it hands to its surroundings
                                       p
                per tick, (2p − 1) ln 1− p , is zero at p = 21 and strictly positive otherwise. With speed
                                                                 1.6 Going faster gives off more heat   49


v = 2p − 1 in (0, 1) and distance N ≥ 0, the heat in units of kT, N ln 11+ v
                                                                         −v , times the
                       2
time N/v is at least N .

Proof. For p > 12 both factors are positive and for p < 12 both are negative, by
the monotonicity of the logarithm; at p = 21 the first factor is zero. For the floor,
ln(1 + v) ≥ 0 and ln(1 − v) ≤ −v since ln y ≤ y − 1, so ln 11−
                                                             +v ≥ v, and the product
                                                               v
is N 2 times that logarithm divided by v.
    That is the surroundings’ share of the entropy production. The whole of it adds
the change in the walker’s own spread, which on a line keeps growing but ever more
slowly, so per tick that share goes to zero and the long-run rate is the heat’s.
    The sharp floor is twice that. The difference ln 11−+v − 2v is zero at v = 0 and its
                                                          v
               2
derivative, 1−v2 − 2, is never negative on (0, 1), so the logarithm is at least 2v and
the product is at least 2N 2 . I state N 2 because the one-line bound gives it, and what
matters is the square, not the factor in front of it.
    The walker is the one case I prove, but it isn’t special, and the physicists have the
general form. Drag a bead held in a spring-like trap through water from one place to
another in a set time and the least work you can get away with is the drag times the
distance squared, divided by the time plus twice the drag over the stiffness, which
at long times is the drag times the distance squared over the time (Schmiedl and
Seifert, 2007, who worked out the best protocols for doing it in finite time). Change
any spread of chances into another in a set time and the entropy produced is at least
a fixed fraction of the square of how far apart the two spreads are, divided by the
time and by how mobile the states are: the diffusion, for a bead that drifts (Aurell,
Mejía-Monasterio and Muratore-Ginanneschi, 2011), and how busy the jumping
is, for states that jump (Shiraishi, Funo and Saito, 2018). Those are their results,
and I cite them as physics. Put them next to the step law and dissipation reads like
this in full. Every change a device makes to the spread of its states in a finite time
dissipates, merge or no merge, reversible or not; time sets how much, and only
infinite time makes it zero. All of that is for a device sitting in surroundings at some
temperature, and what it bounds is dissipation, entropy produced, not heat given off
step by step: a step that leaves the spread exactly as it was owes nothing on these
bounds, and the heat a single step gives off can be negative when the device’s own
entropy goes up. An idealised machine cut off from everything, frictionless billiard
balls bouncing their way through a computation (Edward Fredkin and Tommaso
Toffoli’s, 1982), could in principle run without dissipating at all; Bennett (2003)
wrote that such ballistic machines compute at constant velocity without dissipating
any energy, and that they must be kept isolated from heat baths and noise. Keeping
one on course against noise means correcting its errors, and whether that brings the
dissipation back I don’t settle here; in 2003 Bennett called the thermodynamics of
50   1 A distinction that stays


               error correction a subject that appears to be in its infancy. The bead of Jun, Gavrilov
               and Bechhoefer (2014) shows the other half. Put through the same moves as an
               erasure but with no tilt, so nothing is squashed, its work extrapolated to the slow
               limit came out at 0.05 ± 0.03 kT, within two error bars of zero: no floor under it,
               which is what the premise says. Keeping something costs, on top of that, either
               a merge, which under Landauer’s premise owes a floor of kT ln 2 per bit that no
               slowness removes, or a state the device has never used before. Taking a fresh state
               escapes the floor and never the dissipation of happening. And a finite set of states,
               where every state has a next one, forces the merge.
                   I also simulated the bead. Bérut, Arakelyan, Petrosyan, Ciliberto, Dillenschneider
               and Lutz (2012) erased one bit held by a glass bead in a laser double well, and found
               the heat falling toward Landauer’s number as they slowed the erasure, with the
               excess going like a constant over the time taken. I wrote their protocol as described,
               barrier down over a second, tilt ramped over the protocol time, tilt stopped, barrier
               up over a second, as overdamped Brownian motion in a quartic double well with
               their numbers, and added up the heat the way they do, the force times the bead’s
               displacement along each path. I set the tilt at each protocol time from a scan so
               that it erased about nine times in ten (between 88 and 92 times in a hundred across
               the six protocol times, two seconds to eighty; they took the smallest that erased
               ninety-five times in a hundred), and fitted the heat against the time. Averaged over
               every run, the fit’s floor is 0.56 kT. That sits above the floor for an erasure that comes
               off only about nine times in ten, ln 2 less the uncertainty left in the outcome, about
               0.37 kT, which is the formula the Bérut paper gives for an erasure that sometimes
               fails; it’s the honest floor for all the runs. Averaged over the successful erasures
               alone, the fit is 0.694 kT plus 3.64 kT · s divided by the time, and ln 2 is 0.693. The
               fit is good to about 0.015 kT, so the third decimal is luck, and ln 2 isn’t a floor for
               the successful runs taken alone. Their floor is lower, and it comes from Crooks’
               fluctuation theorem (1999): when the well starts and ends the same and the bead
               starts settled, a path’s chance under the protocol, divided by the chance of the same
               path run backward under the protocol run backward, is e to the work done on the
               bead along it, in units of kT. Add that up over the paths that end in the target well.
               The success rate times the mean of e−W/kT over the successes is the chance that the
               backward run starts in the target well, which is a half, and a mean of e−W/kT is at
               least e to minus the mean work. So the successful runs average at least kT ln(2p) of
               work, with p the success rate: ln 2 when every run succeeds, and about 0.59 kT at
               nine in ten. Picking out the runs that worked after the fact lets them come in under
               ln 2, and the slowest point, at eighty seconds, does, at 0.674 kT. The script adds up
               heat, which here sits about 0.05 kT under the work, because a successful bead ends a
               little higher in its well than it started, and every point still clears kT ln(2p) at its own
               success rate. The fit landing on ln 2 is only where it landed. The floor that holds for
                                                                   1.7 What the lab has measured   51


all the runs together is the one above. The script is scripts/bead_erasure_sim.py
in the repository, and it prints all of those numbers. My excess constant isn’t theirs,
which was 8.15; the shape is. There is nothing in that model but a particle, a well
moved by the protocol, noise, and a start in either well with even chances, and the
heat came down toward a floor as the erasure slowed, with the one-over-time excess
on top of it. The floor and heat against time show up together there, in a simulation
of their bead.

   Everything that has been measured agrees with the floor, stated for a symmetric
memory, and with heat against time at the measured rates, and nothing measured
has kept a reading with neither a merge nor a state never used before. The one
thing nobody has measured is the ceiling on fresh states, and it’s the one I lean on
least: every memory anyone can buy fills, and that needs no experiment.


1.8 Every scale pays the same way
One more question, and it’s the one that decides whether any of this is about the
world or only about my pictures. A state is a description. The dial on a lab bench is
a state, and so is each atom in it, and so is each atom together with the light it gave
off. Describe the same thing coarser or finer and you get different states. Does what
keeping takes change with the zoom?
    It doesn’t, and the reason fits in one picture. Draw the fine states, and draw a
fence around each group of them that counts as one coarse state. Say the coarse
picture merges: two coarse states step to one coarse state. Then, when the fine
states are finitely many, the fine step can’t keep them all apart either. Count them.
If the fine step sent different fine states to different fine states and none of them
stepped out of the fenced set, it would be a reshuffle of the fine states, with every
fine state landed on exactly once afterwards. But some fenced group is now landed
on by nothing, because the coarse step missed a coarse state (two coarse states went
to one, so on a finite set some coarse state is stepped to by nothing), and so nothing
lands on any fine state in that group. A reshuffle leaves no state out. So something
gave: the fine step merges too, or some fine state stepped out of the fenced set,
or the fenced set has no end. The three ways come back one level down, though
stepping out of the fenced set isn’t taking a fresh state; it’s where the coarse picture
stops tracking the fine one.


Theorem 1.10 (Every scale pays the same way). Let a fine machine have one rule
F on a set X of states, let A be a set of its states, and let a coarse description be a
map π from X to a set S of coarse states that takes A onto S, with a coarse rule f
on S such that π ( F ( x )) = f (π ( x )) for every x in A. If the coarse rule merges two
coarse states, then at least one of these holds: F merges two states of A; F takes
some state of A outside A; or some run of F from a state of A stays in A and never
comes back to a state it has visited.

Proof. Suppose the fine machine avoids all three ways out. It stays inside A, keeps
different states apart, and every run eventually visits a state it has visited before.
Follow one run to its first repeat. The two visits have the same state, so their
54   1 A distinction that stays


                predecessors must agree too: different predecessors are never allowed to land
                together. Walk backwards like that until the earlier visit reaches the start. The later
                visit has reached the same start. The run is a loop from the start, with no loose
                approach leading into it.
                    Now watch that loop through the coarse window. Every fine step gives the coarse
                step specified by f . When the fine state returns to its start, its picture returns too.
                Every coarse state has a fine state above it, because π takes A onto S. So every
                coarse state also lies on a loop.
                   That rules out a coarse merge. Suppose two different coarse starts had the same
                next state. Call the lengths of their loops L1 and L2 . Wait L1 L2 steps from the starts:
                that is a whole number of circuits for both loops, so each must be back at its own
                start. But after their first step they were together. The same rule cannot separate
                them afterwards, so at the end of that wait they are still together. Their starts must
                have been the same after all.
                   The coarse rule does merge, by hypothesis. The fine machine therefore cannot
                avoid all three alternatives. In the last alternative, every tick visits another state of
                A, so no finite collection can hold the run.
                   When I say a coarse description is exact about a set of fine states, I mean what
               the theorem asks: it follows the fine step on the set, and every coarse state describes
               some state in it. Put it next to the permanent flip. On a finite coarse picture, a
               reading that goes up and stays up is raised by a merge (the cell above, on three
               states; Theorem 3.1, two chapters on, in general). By this theorem, at every finer
               description that the coarse one is exact about, keeping that reading is again a merge,
               though not always where the reading rose, or a step off the described states, or a run
               that takes a fresh described state at every step. The dial and its light are the example.
               In the dial’s own picture, two blends of readings decay to one either-or, a merge
               (Section 18). In the picture of dial and light together, the step is one-to-one, and it’s
               the second case: the light starts blank and leaves carrying the copy, so the fine step
               leaves the set of states where the light is still blank. At the fine scale nothing merges;
               the step leaves the states the coarse picture describes. And the heat floor sits where
               the merge really is. Landauer’s premise charges the scale whose step merges states
               that were really possible; a description that merges only because it stopped looking
               at the light owes that floor nowhere, and owes a state never used before instead.


                1.9 What keeping takes, and where the toll comes in

                So that’s the whole of what keeping takes, set out before anybody writes a price on
                anything. The toll, which the next chapter states, is what keeping takes, written into
                a step. It’s the price of something being the case: a reading that goes from no to yes
                and stays is a distinction that stays, and a distinction that stays is a state the run has
                                                 1.9 What keeping takes, and where the toll comes in   55


used and can’t give back. Anything whose state includes distinctions it can’t give
back pays what the toll prices: the bead, the cell, the memory bit, a world with a
past. Give one a price list that obeys the toll and it’s a Thiele machine, and when the
cell could have held anything, Landauer’s premise puts a heat floor under that raise,
because on a finite cell the raise is a merge. The toll keeps its shape there, charged
in heat instead of units of cost. And what keeping takes, deterministic or noisy or
quantum, comes to this: in any real device every change that finishes dissipates,
more the faster it goes, which I prove for Bennett’s walker and cite the physicists for
wherever a device’s states jump or drift at random in surroundings at a temperature;
keeping something costs on top of that either a merge, with Landauer’s floor when
the merged states were really possible, or a state never used before; and a finite
machine, where every state has a next one, forces the merge. The step law, the
noisy steps and the unitary steps are proved, and the table above says how near the
laboratory has come to each; the heat is physics.
   That’s also why the rule sits on the raise and not on the merge. The toll charges
for what is kept whichever column pays for it, merge or fresh state. A price on
merges charges only the merge column, so it misses something kept by taking a
state never used before: the machine that keeps every history, the first way out two
chapters on, raises its reading at zero cost under it. And it charges merges that keep
nothing, like the reset that lowers a flag. The toll doesn’t ask that reset for a unit
of cost, and it still merges two states, so in a real device it owes Landauer’s floor
whenever the bit it lowers was really unknown; the ledger leaves that to physics,
the same as the dissipation of happening.
   Next comes the smallest model that keeps that cost on its own ledger: two boxes
on a sheet of paper, a tally, and one rule.
CHAPTER 2




A record and a toll

The last chapter found what keeping takes and kept no count of it. Now give it a
ledger. Take a record with two positions, no and yes, and build the smallest thing
that could carry a charge for its change, on paper, with a pencil. Write the charge
into its rules and see what follows. Keeping it this small is what lets you see which
part of the construction does which part of the work.
    The usual models charge a computation for two things: how long it runs and
how much space it uses. The bits it destroys have been counted too, as the opening
said, by Li and Vitányi and by Demaine and his coauthors. What this part charges is
something else: what the computation keeps and can’t take back. This part is about
that charge, which gets paid in a merge, carrying a heat floor when the merged
states were really possible, or by taking a state never used before, and which the
last chapter showed can’t be talked down to zero. The record built below is the
smallest thing that can carry the charge, and the tally next to it counts every time
the record goes up. Whether a machine has to charge it as a unit of cost, and on
which premises, is the next chapter.
    One thing needs saying about what a flag stands behind, because it stays out of
the picture a while. What I’m about to build prices vouching for anything at all: a
flag goes up, and the rule doesn’t ask what the flag is standing behind. A sorting of
a pile into groups, the kind of structure Part II starts from (Section 5), is the first
kind of claim I care about. It isn’t the only kind, and the book comes back to what
a flag stands behind in Section 8, and on a machine in Section 15, where a flag
stands on a checked claim. Until then nothing about the flag leans on groupings.
The floor in this section, the reason for it in the next, and the latch in Part II all work
whatever the reading is about, partition or no partition. When groupings come in,
in Section 8, it’s as a theorem: a reading that says a grouping has been checked
and committed sees the grouping only through its partition, and what it entitles is
exactly the groupings that refine it (Theorem 8.5). So the grouping gets a job, and
an exact one.
    But first the word, because I’ve got a new one and I don’t trust it either: record,
receipt, certificate, vouch. People have been making marks that other people are
supposed to rely on for a very long time, and I wanted to know what they thought
they were doing, and what it cost them, and whether any of them ever said the


                                   56
                                                                  2.1 Clay, seals, and seven witnesses   57


thing I need said. So here’s what I could reach, pushed on with you, and I’ll tell you
where the search ran out.


2.1 Clay, seals, and seven witnesses
Start a little over five thousand years ago, in the Near East, with people who counted
sheep with little clay tokens. To send a count across a distance without the courier
changing it, they put the tokens inside a hollow clay ball, pressed the shapes of the
tokens onto the outside while the clay was soft, and sealed it. The archaeologist
Denise Schmandt-Besserat has spent a career on these, and she puts the practice at
around 3300 BC; the ball is called a bulla. The push is one you can do with a cookie
tin, with a paper seal glued across the lid and rim. Let it dry, then try opening the
lid without tearing or disturbing the seal. The bare lid would come straight off; it
is the seal that makes this a test. A substitute seal could fool you, so this little trial
shows a disturbance, not an unforgeable history. In the clay ball, the outside shows
the count inside and opening the ball breaks it. That is the property the tin and seal
are trying to reproduce. The idea is a real one and it will show up again in a form
you won’t expect: a record is worth something only if it can’t be silently undone.
    Now law, which is where people get serious about who’s allowed to say what
happened. The book of Deuteronomy, chapter nineteen: nobody is convicted on the
word of one witness; it takes “two or three.” The Roman jurist Gaius, writing in the
second century, says a will the praetor will honour is one sealed by seven witnesses.
Why seven? Gaius doesn’t say. The legal historian Henry Maine, in 1861, had an
answer: the older Roman will was a mock sale, done in front of five witnesses, a
man holding the scales, and the buyer of the estate, seven people in all, and when
the ceremony fell away the seven seals kept the count. Maine’s is the only account
of it I found, so treat it as his. Gaius’s own text does show they kept those old
formalities around a will, and it isn’t hard to see why anyone would: one person can
lie, and a will moves a fortune, and the dead man can’t object. So the record isn’t
the paper; it’s the number of independent people who have put their own seal, their
own name, their own risk, next to the claim. Try it: write “paid five dollars, signed
A” on a napkin and ask a friend to forge it. It takes them ten seconds. Now require
two other people to initial it at the moment of payment and each keep a copy. Your
forger needs two accomplices or has to match two copies held in two other pockets.
The claim didn’t change, but what stands behind it did.
    Which brings me to seals, and the medieval historian Michael Clanchy, whose
book is called From Memory to Written Record. England between the Norman
Conquest and the early 1300s was learning to trust writing. Until then it had trusted
people who remembered. The lesson was painful: seals were forged, charters were
forged, and historians today have a whole craft of telling real charters from fake
58   2 A record and a toll


               ones because the fakes are so many. A seal is only as good as whoever holds the
               stamp. Keep that one too, because in 2011 a certificate authority called DigiNotar
               found out, at the cost of its existence, that a mathematically perfect signature is
               worth exactly what the custody of the key is worth, and intruders had taken control
               of the machines that signed. It is the same failure nine hundred years apart, and I
               find that oddly comforting.
                   And then the obvious next question: if seals could be forged, what caught the
               forgeries? It wasn’t the seals. The most famous forged record in European history
               is the Donation of Constantine, a document in which the emperor Constantine
               supposedly handed rule over Rome and the western empire to the Pope. It was most
               likely written in the eighth century, some four hundred years after Constantine died,
               and it was leaned on for centuries. Around 1440 a scholar named Lorenzo Valla
               took it apart by its Latin: the language belonged to a much later age, and it used
               words, “satraps” among them, that no Roman of Constantine’s day would have used
               for his officials. (Valla wasn’t even first. Nicholas of Cusa, a German churchman and
               philosopher who later became a cardinal, had already called it a forgery in 1433, in
               De concordantia catholica, a long book on how the Church and the empire ought to
               hang together. I know that from the reference works, and I haven’t read the book.
               Valla’s is the version people remember, which is a pattern that keeps turning up.)
               Look at what kind of check that was. The question wasn’t “is the stamp real.” It was
               “could these words have been written when they say they were.” A record can pass
               the first and fail the second, which is a hint that what I keep calling one thing, a
               record, is doing more than one job.


               2.2 Two columns and a stamp

               The one I’d never have guessed mattered is bookkeeping. Around 1300, the ledger
               of a Florentine company called Farolfi, kept at its branch in Provence, shows the
               earliest complete example anyone has found of a trick merchants were working out:
               write every transaction twice, once where the money came from and once where
               it went, and the two columns have to balance. The treasurers of the city of Genoa
               kept their ledger for 1340 that way, and accounting historians still count it among
               the most famous government account books of the Middle Ages kept in double entry.
               And in 1494 a friar named Luca Pacioli printed the method in a mathematics book,
               and it spread. The method is double-entry bookkeeping, and it’s easy to take it for
               just a tidy habit.
                   Do it for one day. Keep two columns of every dollar that moves, and total them
               at night. Now have a friend secretly change one entry in one column. The totals
               disagree; you catch it. Now have them change the matching entry in both columns.
               The totals agree, and you’ve caught nothing. Push on that and you’ve found what
                                                                 2.3 A demon, and the step that pays   59


double entry actually is: a check for slips, which a careful liar walks straight through.
Did Pacioli see that? I can only get at it secondhand. The scholar Forrester, in a paper
on the University of Strathclyde’s accounting-history pages, reads him as reporting
that in many places the books were taken to the local consul to be authenticated
before a single entry went in. The stamp is a witness again, from outside. The two
columns are the discipline; the stamp is the claim that someone other than you
will stand behind the fact that these are the books. No other set gets that stamp.
Keep both halves separate in your head, because one is a method and the other is a
commitment.
    And then I found the place where this got turned into a motto. The Royal Society,
founded in London in 1660 and still running, picked as its motto Nullius in verba:
take nobody’s word for it. (Where did they get it? From somebody’s words, naturally.
It’s half a line of the Roman poet Horace, from a verse letter to his patron, saying
he isn’t bound to swear by the words of any master. So the society that takes
nobody’s word for it took its motto from a poet and cut the line to fit. That’s not a
contradiction, and it’s a nice picture of the method: borrow what’s useful, say whose
it was, and don’t swear by it.) The historian Steven Shapin wrote a paper about
what that meant in practice, and the answer is more interesting than the slogan.
Robert Boyle, pumping the air out of a glass globe to see what happens to a candle
or a bird, had three problems: the machine, the report, and the witnesses. He solved
the third by having gentlemen present who’d sign their names, and the second by
writing the report so richly that a reader who wasn’t there could picture the scene
and count as a witness anyway. Shapin calls that virtual witnessing, and he notes,
dryly, that the air pump was very expensive, seventeenth-century big science. So
there was a cost; it just wasn’t a cost of declaring the fact. It was the cost of the
instrument and of getting enough people into the room. Hold on to that distinction,
because the rest of the book hangs on it.


2.3 A demon, and the step that pays

Now comes the strangest entry, and the one that gets closest. In 1867 the physicist
James Clerk Maxwell, in a letter to his friend the Scottish physicist Peter Guthrie Tait,
imagined a “very observant and neat-fingered being” sitting at a tiny door between
two halves of a box of gas, letting fast molecules through one way and slow ones
the other, so that one side heats up and the other cools with no work done, which is
supposed to be impossible. The being got called Maxwell’s demon, and physicists
have been arguing about it for a hundred and fifty years, which should tell you
something.
   In 1929 Leo Szilard, a young Hungarian physicist working in Berlin, cut the
demon’s box down to a single molecule, and that made information part of the
60   2 A record and a toll


               accounting. The tempting move, and the one Szilard’s own accounting made, is
               to put the whole heat floor on finding out which side the molecule is on. Bennett
               separated finding out from restoring the memory for another round: measuring
               onto a blank record can, in principle, be thermodynamically reversible, and resetting
               an unknown record is a different operation. That does not mean a real measuring
               device costs nothing to build or run. It says that learning and resetting do not carry
               the same unavoidable entropy cost, and I’m about to pick a step to charge, so I need
               that distinction before I do.
                   Bennett’s version of the rule, in a 2003 paper you can read, is that what must cost
               is “the erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths.” That is erasing,
               or taking two possible situations and making them one. And in the same paper he
               lists copying unknown data onto a blank place to write among “the most important
               logically reversible operations,” the kind he says can, at least in principle, be run
               thermodynamically reversibly. So, in the one place in all of this where a record is
               priced by physics, the unavoidable erasure charge belongs to forgetting the unknown
               record. Making a record on a blank place carries no such charge of its own. It does
               use up the blank place, which is a state the machine hasn’t used yet, and that place
               gets paid for in heat when it’s wiped to be used again. Read that twice, because it’s
               not what I expected either.
                   Making a record on a blank place is one operation. Landauer’s 1961 paper names
               another: set a bit to one whatever it held. If that bit is the whole state, down goes to
               up, up stays up, and two possible states become one. Landauer called this “restore
               to one.” On an uncertain input it removes information, and a heat bound then needs
               the thermodynamic premises.
                   A larger machine has more state than its flag. Two starts can both finish with
               the flag up while remaining different elsewhere. The next chapter proves that, on
               a finite machine whose reading is permanent, any instruction that raises it must
               merge some full states. It does not say the state whose flag just rose is one of that
               pair. Put one state outside the set that reads yes and two states inside it. Send the
               outside state to the first inside state, and send both inside states to the second. The
               flag rises for the outside state, but the two inside states are the ones that merge.
               These arrows describe alternative starts, not three things happening in one run.
                   That is the distinction the one-bit picture hides. The instruction has a collision
               somewhere, and the actual distribution of starting states determines whether that
               collision removes uncertainty. A known starting state loses none under the entropy
               premise, even when its flag rises (Theorem 3.17, next chapter). That isn’t a way
               around the heat floor: whoever knows the start is already holding the distinction,
               and the heat floor was paid in that knowing, or gets paid when that knowledge is
               wiped. The ledger can still charge the instruction under merge pricing. A ledger
               charge, information loss and a device’s heat are three quantities to keep apart.
                                                               2.3 A demon, and the step that pays   61


    I’ll put the rest of the lineage quickly, because it all points the same way. Regu-
lators who make brokers keep records on media that can’t be rewritten (the SEC
required exactly that, write once and read many, from 1997 until 2022, when it
allowed an audit trail as the other way to comply) are pricing the hardware. The
rule puts no charge on the act of writing. Haber and Stornetta in 1991, the times-
tamping that Bitcoin’s footnotes lead back to (Section 14 follows them), chained
time-stamped records together with hashes so that changing an old entry breaks
every entry after it (and Ralph Merkle’s hash tree, from his 1979 Stanford thesis on
secrecy and authentication, lets one short value vouch for a great many records);
try the dependency with five entries, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, adding each to the running
total: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. Keep that sheet and make another with the second entry
changed to 3. Its totals are 1, 4, 7, 11, 16. The change travels down the chain. Now
lower the third entry to 2, and the last total is 15 again. Simple addition can be
fooled by compensating changes. A cryptographic chain needs a stronger function,
and someone must retain a trusted value to compare against. This trial shows the
dependency between entries; it supplies neither that function’s security nor a price
on the record. Proof-of-work, which the computer scientists Cynthia Dwork and
Moni Naor proposed in 1992 to make junk mail expensive and which Bitcoin later
chained, is the one framing where a record genuinely costs, and what it charges for
is a search: how many tries it took to find a lucky number. An empty block costs
the same work as a full one. So the work prices the search. Proof-of-work charges
nothing extra for the moment anything becomes certified. Robert Floyd and Tony
Hoare, two computer scientists asking how you’d prove a program does what it’s
supposed to, attached claims to points in a program in 1967 and 1969 (“whenever
you get here, this is true”), and the claim is backed by a proof that’s paid for off
the machine. And the certificates of complexity theory, which go back to Stephen
Cook’s 1971 work on NP, are strings designed to be cheap to check: hand me the
certificate and I can confirm the claim quickly. Whether they’re also expensive to
find is the famous open question of the field, P versus NP, and nobody knows; what’s
settled is only the cheap half. That’s the opposite of a price on vouching, since the
whole design goal is that checking a claim costs nearly nothing. And from statistics,
a ledger that runs the other way: Dean Foster and Robert Stine’s alpha-investing
(2008) runs a long string of tests against a budget of allowed false alarms, where
every test spends some of the budget and every discovery, a rejection that stands,
pays some back. That’s the other way round from a price on vouching: the test pays,
and a discovery that stands gets paid.
62   2 A record and a toll


               2.4 What they all agree on, and who they rule out
               Lay them down, and this time what shows through is not one thing. It’s five different
               jobs that the word “record” has been doing, and I’d been letting one word carry all
               five. Most of them have a corpse next to them, and the corpses are different too.
                   Durability: the record can’t be silently undone. The bulla, the write-once disk,
               the hash chain and Bennett’s card that has to be wiped all do this job. The corpse
               is the editable log, and the company that kept its debts off the books: Enron hid
               its debt in side entities set up to keep it off the balance sheet, which is how the
               Justice Department described the scheme in 2002, and its auditor, Arthur Andersen,
               shredded the paper. Andersen was convicted for the shredding that year, and
               the Supreme Court threw the conviction out in 2005 over how the jury had been
               instructed; either way, the books concealed debts they should have shown. But
               notice that this job doesn’t need a witness at all. A copy will do: a hash chain
               nobody signed is still hard to change quietly, so long as somebody else holds the
               latest link, because a chain with no copy anywhere can be rewritten from end to
               end and recomputed, and nobody would know.
                   Authenticity: the record came from who it says it came from. Seals, the signature
               only a key-holder can make, and the consul’s stamp all do this one. The corpse is
               the forged charter and DigiNotar. This job is about custody of a stamp, and it’s a
               different job from durability; a perfectly authentic entry can still be erased, and a
               perfectly durable one can still be a forgery.
                   Evidence: enough independent people stand behind the claim that lying is
               expensive. Two witnesses, seven seals and Boyle’s gentlemen do this one. It rules
               out anonymous assertion, and it rules out “the universe keeps the receipt”, because
               information spread into the environment is not a record anyone can read or rely on.
               This one is about numbers of people and their risk. Paper has nothing to do with it.
                   Accounting: the record checks itself for slips. The two columns do this one. And
               one thing has to be kept straight: the second column is not an outside witness. It’s
               you, checking you. It catches a dropped digit. A careful liar gets past it, as you saw.
               It belongs on this list as its own job, separate from the seven seals.
                   Cheap checking: a record whose correctness can be confirmed for much less than
               it cost to make. Cook’s certificates, the signature and the hash do this one. This one
               isn’t universal, and I thought it was. Whether checking needs to be cheaper than
               making depends on who you’re worried about and how much a wrong record costs
               you; plenty of records are checked by redoing the whole thing, and that’s fine when
               the thing is small.
                   Now for the thing none of them says. Not one of these jobs is pricing the
               moment a record goes up and stays. Bennett prices merging and erasing, which that
               moment might or might not be. Proof-of-work prices a search the designer chose.
                                                     2.5 The smallest thing that could carry the charge   63


Bookkeeping prices a discipline. Witnesses and seals price showing up and guarding
the stamp. I looked, with everything I had, and that’s where it ran out. If there is a
cost charged for that moment itself, nobody in this lineage wrote it down, and that’s
either because it isn’t there or because the one person who did write it down is on a
shelf I never found. The literal one-bit reset already has a thermodynamic analysis:
Landauer’s restore to one. The question here is which premises force an instruction
that raises a record to merge full states, and which further premises put a price on
that loss. So I’m going to have to try it myself, on the smallest thing I can build, and
let you watch. And I’ll have to be honest about which of the five jobs the small thing
even attempts, because the answer is going to be none.


2.5 The smallest thing that could carry the charge

Take a sheet of paper. Draw two boxes and label them NO and YES. The two boxes
are the reading, a single yes-or-no question asked of the state, and I’m going to
be careful about what the question is, because after five thousand years of seals
and witnesses the word “vouch” is carrying a lot and this toy carries almost none
of it. The question is only: “has the designated flag been set.” It is not “is some
claim about a grouping true,” and it is not “did anyone check.” There is no claim in
this toy, no evidence, no checker, nobody standing behind anything. There is a flag.
Whether a flag can ever be made to mean that something was checked and can be
relied on is a real question, and it’s not this section’s; I’ll build toward it later, and
until then please read YES as “the flag is up” and nothing more. The state is which
box you’re in, and that’s the whole state, one bit. Then draw a line under the boxes
for tally marks. The marks sit outside the state. They’re the running total you keep
beside it as you play, the way you’d keep score beside a board game.
    Now give yourself three moves. STAY: you don’t move, and you make no mark.
WORK: you don’t move either (it’s a stand-in for every ordinary step a machine
takes), and you make no mark. VOUCH: from NO you move to YES; from YES
you stay in YES; either way you make one tally mark, because in this toy the price
belongs to the move’s name, and where you were standing doesn’t enter into it. Now
play. Start in NO, make any sequence of moves you like, and stop in YES. Count the
marks. Then try to reach YES with zero marks. You can’t, and you can see exactly
why: the only move that crosses from NO to YES is VOUCH, and VOUCH makes
a mark. Now erase the mark from VOUCH’s rule and play again. You reach YES
with no marks, every time. The entire content of what I’m about to call a rule is
this, and I want you to see how little it is before I dress it up: I’ve decided that the
move which crosses the line makes a mark. Nothing in the toy’s rules forces the
mark. VOUCH does merge, NO and YES both landing on YES, which is what the
last chapter says a kept raise on two states has to do; what nothing yet says is that
64   2 A record and a toll


               a merge has to cost a mark. Here it’s a choice, what the last chapter says keeping
               takes, written down as a rule. The next chapter is about when a machine has no
               choice.
                   Why tally marks, by the way? Because they’re about the oldest receipt there is.
               The real ones, the English treasury’s notched sticks split down the middle, get their
               own story in Part II (Section 6), fire and all. The tally on your paper is nothing like
               those. Nobody holds the other half. You keep it, beside the board, and you could
               rub a mark out and nobody would ever know. Hold on to that, because by the end
               of this section it’s the reason the toy does none of the five jobs a record does.
                   Here is the same toy, stated once, carefully, because this is the one place in the
               book where I state it exactly and everything later points back here. The point listed
               the five parts in a sentence; here they’re pinned down. The thing on your paper has
               five parts.
                   A set of states. (Here: NO and YES, and nothing else.)
                   A set of move names. (STAY, WORK, VOUCH.)
                   A step: for each state and each move name, where you land.
                   A cost for each move name: a whole number of tally marks, zero or more. (Zero,
               zero, one.)
                   A reading: for each state, yes or no.
                   Those five parts are the whole of it. Add the one rule below and I’ll call it a Thiele
               machine. And I want to be exact about what’s not in it. There’s no counter stored
               inside the state that’s forbidden from going down; the marks are the side tally from
               the board game, and the tally only ever grows because the costs are whole numbers,
               zero or more. (A machine could keep the total inside its state too; that’s an extra
               part beyond the five, and Section 6 builds it.) There’s no window, no observer who
               sees only part of the state; that’s a later question and it gets its own section. And
               the cost depends only on the move’s name; where you are when you make it doesn’t
               matter. That’s on purpose: the charge is on the attempt, so you pay for making
               the move, whatever it turns out to do. It’s also a real simplification, and where a
               result needs a price that depends on where you are, Section 7 says so and uses one.
               Last, the step gives every state and every move exactly one place to land. A choice
               becomes a move name, and a machine that has stopped steps to itself. A step that
               can land in several places by chance is a different picture, and the noisy steps in
               Section 1 take it up. One landing place for each state and move is what the step law
               there needs, and what the next chapter’s argument needs when it says a run either
               merges or takes a fresh state at every step. It also keeps a price per move name from
               charging exactly the raises: a move that raises the flag and has no next step once it’s
               up could cost one and never charge for anything else.
                   One rule, which I’ll call the toll. For every state and every move: if the reading
               is NO before the move and YES after it, the move’s cost is at least one. That’s the
                                                      2.5 The smallest thing that could carry the charge   65


whole rule. It says nothing about any other move. It says nothing about how big
a mark is in anything you could measure. One mark is one mark; what a mark is
worth, why the smallest charge is one (why not two, or a half?), and whether I had
any right to decide that, come next. The middle question has a short answer I’ll give
away now. What the next chapter forces, on its premises, is that a raise that stays up,
with only finitely many yes-states, merges two states, so any price on merges lands
on it. Costs here are whole numbers, which I chose so the ledger counts acts, and
the least whole number above nothing is one. The “at least one” comes from there.
    And one theorem, which is the only thing the toy actually proves, and you’ve
already proved it by playing. Take any run of moves that starts in a NO state and
ends in a YES state. Then the marks it made add up to at least one. The argument
in words is short enough that you can hold the whole thing. Walk the run move by
move, reading the box at each step. It read NO at the start and YES at the end, and
every move either leaves the reading alone or flips it, so at some move it went from
NO to YES. The toll says that move cost at least one. Every other move cost zero
or more. Add them up and the total is at least one. Notice what the argument did
not need. It didn’t need the reading to stay YES afterward; if a later move flipped
it back to NO and another flipped it to YES again, the toll charges twice, and the
argument still goes through. It didn’t need the machine to be finite. It didn’t need to
know what any move does besides what the reading says before and after. It needed
the toll, and two things the five parts already hand it: no cost is below zero, and the
reading has only two values, so a move that changes it from NO lands on YES. Give
the reading a third value, a “maybe” in between, and a run can get from NO to YES
through it without a single step the toll charges.
    That’s the whole theorem, and I’ll state it once more in the exact form, because
from here on the book carries two layers side by side: what I mean, in words, and
what’s stated and proved, in symbols you can hold me to. The symbols are few. N is
the whole numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on. S and I are just names for “the set of states”
and “the set of move names.” Writing step : S × I → S means “hand it a state and a
move name and it hands back a state.” A run is a list of move names, t = [i1 , . . . , in ],
played from a start s0 , one after another. The double arrow =⇒ reads “then”: the
thing on its left forces the thing on its right. For this first proof, keep your finger
on the run and stop at the first YES. The move immediately before that is the one
whose charge matters.

Definition 2.1 (Thiele machine). A Thiele machine consists of a set S of states, a
set I of move names, a step function step : S × I → S, a cost cost : I → N, and a
reading cert : S → {no, yes}, subject to one rule, the toll: for every state s and move
i,
              cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes =⇒ cost(i ) ≥ 1.
66   2 A record and a toll


               The run of t = [i1 , . . . , in ] from s0 ends at run(t, s0 ), the result of applying the steps
               in order, and its total cost is cost(t) = cost(i1 ) + · · · + cost(in ), with the empty run
               costing 0.

                  I write the yes-or-no reading as cert. It names the flag whose rise I am counting.
               What earns that flag its meaning will depend on the machine’s rules.
                  A word on the label before the first result. I call a result an observation when its
