               proof does little more than unfold the definitions, and in an axiomatic cost model
               that’s what the definitions are meant to do: the work is in choosing them, so the
               results that follow from them in a few lines are labelled that way and the theorems
               with more in them stand out.
               Observation 2.1 (The universal floor). In any Thiele machine, every run that starts
               at a state reading no and ends at a state reading yes has total cost at least 1: if
               cert(s0 ) = no and cert(run(t, s0 )) = yes, then cost(t) ≥ 1.
               Proof. Read the states of the run from left to right. The first reads no and the last
               reads yes, so there is a first state on this list that reads yes. It cannot be the starting
               state. The state immediately before it reads no: otherwise the chosen YES would
               not be the first. The move between them therefore costs at least one, by the toll.
                  Now add the charges for the whole run. That one charge is already at least one,
               and none of the other charges is negative. The total is at least one. The flag may
               come down later and go up again; that cannot remove the charge I have found.

               The tabletop and the stamp
               Put two boxes on the table. Each has tiles on top, and the tiles spell the same answer.
               On the side of one box the stamp is up. On the other it is down. Hang a camera
               directly above them. The photographs are identical.
                   Now hand me the photographs and ask which box was stamped. Take a better
               photograph. Enlarge it. Count every tile. None of that gets the side of the box into
               the picture. The difference is there, in the boxes. It has been left out of what you
               handed me.
                   That is the window I want to name. S is the set of full states of the boxes, and
               B is the set of tabletop pictures. The map π : S → B takes a full state and returns
               its picture. Every picture in B comes from a box; that is what onto says. Pick one
               picture, b, and gather every full state that gives that picture. That whole collection
               is the fibre above b, written π −1 (b).
                   Keep the whole collection in mind. The tiles can agree while the boxes differ in
               which checks ran, which earlier pages were certified, and what was kept when those
               pages were wiped. The fibre holds all the differences this camera leaves out. There
               can be two states in it, a million, or infinitely many.
                                                        2.5 The smallest thing that could carry the charge   67


   I started with one question: is the flag up? That gives me one yes-or-no reading
of the full state. A hundred different states can all answer yes. Reading that one
flag tells me where they stand on that one question; the other differences are still
there. Chapter 14 opens the gauge wider. It asks which checks passed and which
editions were certified, and counts how many states those answers require. Keep
independently chosen histories across arbitrarily many editions, all recoverable
above the same final picture, and the fibre has to be infinite. There is a proof of that
in Section 14.3.
   To see exactly what the tabletop can do by itself, give these boxes two kinds of
move. The tile moves are horizontal. They cost zero, leave the stamp alone, and
move the tiles according to what is on the tabletop. The stamp never reaches into
their gears. The stamp moves are vertical. They leave the tiles alone and can raise
the stamp or leave it where it is. Once raised, it stays raised. A raise pays the toll
already defined above.
   These are the rules of the sliced machine. They give me a computational view
that runs on its own and a record that survives beside it.

Definition 2.2 (Sliced Thiele machine). A sliced Thiele machine is a Thiele machine
with an onto view π : S → B and its move names split into horizontal moves IH and
vertical moves IV . Write r (s) = cert(s), with no < yes, and Fi (s) = step(s, i ). For
each i ∈ IH there is a map hi : B → B such that
             π ( Fi (s)) = hi (π (s)),    r ( Fi (s)) = r (s),     cost(i ) = 0.

For each v ∈ IV ,
                        π ( Fv (s)) = π (s),      r (s) ≤ r ( Fv (s)).
The toll remains: r (s) < r ( Fv (s)) implies cost(v) ≥ 1.

    The states can be counter configurations, tape configurations, or any other states
meeting these rules. The same horizontal argument works with a whole set of claims
as the record: every horizontal move preserves the set and evolves the picture using
only that picture. The number of possible records never enters that argument.
    Now give the two boxes the same horizontal moves. After one move the pictures
still agree. After two they still agree. Every next picture comes from the previous
picture and the move you named, and those agree at every step. Meanwhile one
stamp stays up and the other stays down. You can watch the tabletop for the whole
run and never see the difference you started with.
    Give somebody permission to read the stamp and choose a different tile move
because of it, and they can signal through the tiles. Here both boxes receive the
same moves. That is how I keep the question fixed while asking what the window
can reveal.
68   2 A record and a toll




               Theorem 2.2 (What the tabletop can tell). In a sliced Thiele machine, every hori-
               zontal word projects to the corresponding word of the maps hi on B, and preserves
               r. Two states with the same view and different records therefore keep the same view
               and different records after any common horizontal word. No function of the view
               alone can recover r on both states. A vertical move that changes r supplies such a
               pair: s and Fv (s).

               Proof. Start with two states showing the same picture. Give them the first horizontal
               move. Its rule chooses the next picture from the current picture alone, so the next
               pictures agree too. Neither record changes. You are back in the same situation,
               ready for the second move. Repeating this argument covers every move in the word,
               including a word with no moves. On each side the picture follows the corresponding
               hi , and the original record stays put.
                    A proposed reader of the picture now receives the same input from both states. It
               must give the same answer to that input, so it cannot return two different records
               correctly. Finally, a vertical move that changes the record gives you exactly such
               a pair: before and after, the picture agrees and the record differs. Those must be
               different full states.
                   The stamp remains in the full state through every one of those moves. The camera
               keeps missing it for exactly the same reason it missed it in the first photograph. In
               Part III a failed check can stop the gears. Hiding that stop while asking the picture to
               predict every later free move would also hide the difference between gears that turn
               and gears that cannot. Theorem 15.1 works through that obstruction; the live-state
               slice there keeps this boundary explicit.
                   The universal floor is about every Thiele machine, a system with the toll among
               its conditions, and about no system without it. One edge matters: the theorem does
               not assume that a YES state exists. If no state ever reads YES, no run meets the
               theorem’s hypothesis, so it’s true of every run and tells you nothing about any of
               them, which is a mathematician’s way of saying it’s true and useless. The toy on
               your paper has a YES box, so it isn’t useless there. It would be natural to assume the
               system has to have at least one NO state and one YES state; the statement has no
               such clause, and that’s on purpose, because a theorem that applies to no run is still
               a theorem and the toy is where you supply the runs.
                   The theorem also runs backwards, and that direction is one line. Suppose every
               run from a state reading no to a state reading yes costs at least one, whichever state
               you start from. A single move is a run of length one, so a move that takes no to yes
               costs at least one, which is the toll. The floor from every start and the toll are the
               same rule, and nobody has to choose between them. From one fixed start that reads
                                                               2.6 How the receipt earns its meaning   69


no, the floor asks for the toll only at the crossings you can reach without paying
anything; a crossing you can only reach by paying has already cost at least one by
the time you get there.
    And the bound of one is the smallest case of a count.
Observation 2.3 (One unit per crossing). In any Thiele machine, a run costs at least
the number of its steps that take the reading from no to yes, with no permanence
assumed. Conversely, a system in which every run costs at least its number of such steps
obeys the toll. And the bound is reached for every count: on the one-bit machine with a
set that costs one and a reset that costs nothing, setting and resetting n times from no
crosses n times and costs exactly n.
Proof. Each crossing step costs at least one by the toll, every other step costs at least
zero, and each step is counted once, so the total is at least the number of crossings.
Conversely, a single move that crosses is a run with one crossing, so it costs at least
one, which is the toll. On the one-bit machine, each set from no is a crossing costing
one and each reset costs nothing, so n rounds cost n and cross n times.
    And one more edge, because it’s the first thing to bite when you ask a machine
to stand behind more than one thing. The definition has one reading in it: one
question, one flag, and one crossing the toll charges. Once the flag is up, a second
claim has nowhere to go, because raising a flag that’s already up doesn’t move
anything. So a second claim needs a reading of its own, and a third claim a third:
one reading per claim, each with its own crossing. Part II builds that properly, as
a family of flags, one per threshold, with a step that raises any of them charged at
least one (Theorem 10.11). A step that raises three at once still owes at least one,
and nothing in the toll makes the charges add up flag by flag. Charges that add need
the composition assumptions for independent machines (Appendix F). The same
theorem has a count in it that is what finiteness takes. Picture the record as a row of
switches that only ever get turned on. Ten switches can change at most ten times in
one run, one switch per change, and then the row is full. (Across different runs the
row can end in any of its thousand and twenty-four settings; along any one run it
climbs through at most eleven.) A finite machine can keep only so many things up
for good in its whole life. That’s “you can’t keep all of it,” which Section 14 says of a
full trace, turned into a count.


2.6 How the receipt earns its meaning
Give the worker a whiteboard and a pen. Ask for an answer and a line underneath
saying “CHECKED = YES.” The worker can write both. So can somebody who copied
the answer and did no check at all. The extra line has told you nothing about which
happened.
70   2 A record and a toll


                   Follow that problem into the machine. If an unchecked run can reach the same
               accepting state as a checked run, there is nothing in that state that tells the two
               apart. To make the receipt carry the difference, the machine has to close the
               unchecked route. The worker can request the check; the worker cannot simply write
               its successful result into the accepting record. That restriction is what gives the
               record its force.
                   Put a variable called checked beside the answer and you have another place to
               write. The name does not give it authority. A program that can write yes there
               without doing the check can manufacture the same display as the program that
               earned it.
                   For an earned receipt, I want the machine’s rules to close that route. Every per-
               mitted program must go through the required check before it can reach acceptance.
               The program can ask for the check. It cannot give itself the successful verdict. That
               is the difference between carrying words about a check and enforcing what those
               words stand for.
                   So when somebody offers a simulation, showing me where its bits go is the
               beginning. Show me which instructions the simulated program can actually use,
               and prove that none of their allowed sequences can forge acceptance. Preserving
               that boundary is part of implementing this machine. A copy of the flag alone has
               not done it.
                   Now put the camera back over the tabletop. The same answer can sit above
               an accepting record or an unearned one. The record has to survive, and the rules
               governing access to it have to survive too. Those are the things I am asking the
               machine to keep.

               Look before the concrete covers it
               The inspector arrives after the concrete is poured. The question is about the rebar
               underneath. On one job it was sound. On the other it wasn’t. Give both jobs exactly
               the same finished appearance, and give the inspector only that appearance.
                  There is no amount of staring that tells those jobs apart. Searching for a sound
               arrangement that could have produced this surface doesn’t do it either. A sound
               arrangement was possible on the bad job too. What matters is which arrangement
               was there.
                  Write x for what was there, f ( x ) for what remains to be inspected, and P( x ) for
               the yes-or-no question about it. A good x+ and a bad x− leave the same f ( x ). The
               inspector receives one identical input and is supposed to give two different answers.
               Here is the whole obstruction.
                                                                 2.6 How the receipt earns its meaning   71




Theorem 2.4 (An erased distinction cannot answer its old question). Let f : X → Y
and P : X → {no, yes}. If f ( x+ ) = f ( x− ) but P( x+ ) = yes and P( x− ) = no, there
is no d : Y → {no, yes} with d( f ( x )) = P( x ) for every x. If P is available before the
loss, the enriched observation ( f ( x ), P( x )) does answer the question exactly and
distinguishes these two cases above their common view.

Proof. The proposed d would return both yes and no at f ( x+ ) = f ( x− ). The
enriched observation returns its second coordinate. Its two values are ( f ( x+ ), yes)
and ( f ( x− ), no): the first coordinates agree and the second coordinates differ, so
the enriched states remain distinct.
    While the rebar is exposed, you can inspect it and keep the answer. Or preserve
enough evidence to inspect later. Either way, something that distinguishes the good
case from the bad one has to survive. Wiping an unrelated detail causes no trouble.
Wiping the last difference your question depends on leaves the next inspector with
the same surface and two possible pasts.
    For one known question repeated along a run, the receipt can be very small. Start
a bit at yes and, at each check, replace it by the old answer AND the new answer.
It says exactly whether all checks so far passed. A later failure turns it down. The
permanent flag that says “some certification occurred” stays up. Put those gauges
beside each other and you can see why they answer different questions.

When the stamp merges two states
Draw two boxes with the same tiles: Unstamped and Stamped. Pressing the stamp
takes the first to Stamped. Pressing it on the second leaves that whole box exactly
where it is. Draw both arrows. They land in the same place.
   Call the press V. At a state s where it raises the record, s and V (s) are different. If
another press leaves the full state fixed, then V (V (s)) = V (s). Those two different
states have the same successor.
   Give the stamped box a hidden wheel that turns on every press. Now the picture
has more states in it. If every state reached after stamping still reads yes, and there
are only finitely many such states, a merge is forced somewhere along the continued
pressing. It can be later than the first press. Keep the entire move injective instead,
and the run has to keep finding distinct stamped states. Call that finite accepting
region H and the entering state u. The move sends all of H ∪ {u} into H. There
are | H | + 1 distinct sources and only | H | possible targets, so two sources share
a successor. The move preserves the working picture, so both sources and their
common successor lie in that same fibre.
72   2 A record and a toll


                    An internal ledger belongs in that full-state picture too. If each press increments
               it, two presses have different ledger values even when the stamp looks unchanged.
               Count those states with the others. The toll tells me what to charge for a raise; the
               next chapter gives the premises that connect charges to mergers. I want the arrows
               and the bill on the same page, with the rule connecting them where you can see it.
                    Notice also that it asks nothing about how strong the system is, in either direction.
               A system is Turing-complete when it can imitate a Turing machine, and no stronger
               than one when a Turing machine can imitate it. The theorem asks neither question.
               Whether the system is stronger than a Turing machine, weaker, or exactly as strong
               makes no difference to the floor. Bring the five parts, charge the toll on the crossing,
               and you’re in scope. The floor doesn’t check what you can compute, because it was
               never about what you can compute; it’s about what a move is allowed to do without
               costing anything.
                    That brings up the objection a theorist makes in about four seconds, so I’ll make
               it first. The toll is a floor, and a floor is easy to meet. Charge one unit for every move,
               whatever it does, and the toll holds for any reading you like, since every crossing is a
               move and every move costs one. So any computer with a step counter beside it, and
               any yes-or-no question at all about its state, is a Thiele machine, and a clock passes.
               Nothing about that is a loophole; it’s what the definition says, and it means the
               definition, on its own, doesn’t tie the cost to anything kept or certified. It only says a
               crossing can’t go unpriced. (It’s also why “a base that can compute anything plus a
               flag that obeys the toll” would be a cheap thing to call Thiele-complete, and why the
               definition that gets that name, at the end of Part II, asks for computing that costs
               nothing and a record that tells starts apart, which no clock meets; Section 10.8.)
               Three things later in the book tie the cost down. The first is that bar: computing
               that costs nothing, a charge of one, and a record that tells starts apart. The second is
               a ceiling: demand that a run’s total never exceed the number of times the flag went
               up. With a price that can depend on where the step starts, that and the floor leave
               exactly one way of charging, one unit per raise and nothing else (Sections 6 and 7).
               With a price per move name, as in my definition, no system whose flag ever rises
               meets both, because the raising move, played again from yes, which every move
               can be, raises nothing and still costs one. A clock fails the ceiling the first time it
               charges a step that raised nothing. The third is order, on any certified machine, and
               the example of Part III is one: there, from a clean start, the flag can’t go up unless a
               passing check of a claim came first, then a commitment to that same claim, and a
               clock can’t fake that, because it’s about which moves happened, and a clock only
               charges (Theorem 15.11).
                    There is also the matter of why the ledger doesn’t charge for heat. In any real
               device every step that changes something dissipates as it happens. A ledger that
               charged for that would charge every step that does anything, and that’s the clock
                                                                2.6 How the receipt earns its meaning   73


again: it can’t tell a run that kept something from a run that only ran. So the ledger
leaves the dissipation of happening to physics and counts one thing, the rise of a
reading that stays. A step that changes something and costs nothing still dissipates;
it just raises nothing the ledger prices.
    The other side of that is that nothing is in scope just for being a computation. A
Turing machine’s run isn’t an instance of this theorem because it’s a run. It becomes
one when somebody supplies all five parts for it, says which states read yes, and
proves the toll for that cost. Until then the theorem says nothing about it, and I
won’t pretend it does; that limit is the toll’s scope. What keeping takes has no scope
to supply, because every run of anything with one next state per state takes a fresh
state at every step, joins exactly one pair of its states into one, or goes round a loop
through its start and keeps nothing (Theorem 1.1). The reading this isn’t the state
I started in rises at the first step and stays up exactly on the runs that never come
back to their start, the first two kinds, and those pay, in states never used before or
in their one merge.
    That’s also where the hunch this book started from ended up, once I checked it:
the night a video about Flatland convinced me there was another axis, a direction
ordinary computing is blind to (the Afterword, Section 24, tells it). It isn’t a direction
an ordinary computer can’t reach. Hand a Turing machine a reading, charge the toll
on its crossing, and it’s in scope like anything else. The possibility was always there.
What the usual rules leave out is the price.
    The same goes for a system with no reading at all. If nothing in it answers “is
the flag up,” then nothing in it can say, from the inside, that anything is entitled to
be relied on. Whatever entitlement it ends up with gets carried in from outside, by
somebody who signs their name to it, and nothing in the system priced it. Smuggled
entitlement isn’t entitlement for the system, no matter whose name is on it. Be
careful which way that cuts, though. Whoever reads the signature can be perfectly
entitled on their own account; that’s what an auditor has, and it’s honest as long
as it’s called the auditor’s. It isn’t the system’s. On the example I build later, the
reason to believe its checker says yes only when the claim is true is exactly that
kind: a proof, done outside any record the machine keeps, and I’ll say so when I get
there (Section 15). What outside entitlement never is, is something the system itself
earned.
    There’s also a question I’ll only start on here: bolt two Thiele machines together,
and do you get one? Run them side by side, each move being a move of one or the
other, and add up the costs. It depends on the reading you give the pair. Take a
reading that can only go up when one of the parts’ readings goes up, like “either flag
is up” or “both are”: then any crossing of the pair is a crossing of a part, that part’s
toll charged it, and the pair obeys the toll. Take “the first flag is up and the second is
down,” and it doesn’t: that reading turns on when the second flag falls, and nothing
74   2 A record and a toll


               charges a fall. The first two readings are proved in Appendix F: read through “either
               flag is up” the pair is a Thiele machine whose floor is one. Read through “both are,”
               a run that starts with both flags down and ends with both up costs at least two, and
               two is reached when each part can raise its own flag for one. From a start with
               one flag already up, one raise is enough, so two is a floor for the clean start only.
               The third needs nothing beyond the one unpriced fall above. A related composite is
               proved too, a host machine running a guest, read through “the host’s own flag or its
               copy of the guest’s” (Theorem D.13). Whether every way of building one machine
               out of others keeps the toll is a bigger question, and Appendix F takes it as far as I
               could: some ways do, some provably don’t, and it says which.
                   So why bother with the toy at all? It isn’t because the lineage was looking for
               it. The bulla was after durability, the seven seals after evidence, the consul’s stamp
               after authenticity, the two columns after catching slips; none of them was trying
               to put a price on the moment a flag goes up, and I shouldn’t pretend they were.
               The reason is narrower. Everywhere in that lineage where somebody did locate a
               cost, but one, it sat on a step next to the flag. The flag itself went unpriced as a flag:
               Szilard on the measurement, Bennett on the wiping, proof-of-work on the search,
               Boyle on the instrument and the room, Foster and Stine on the test. One entry prices
               the crossing’s own shape, and I put it beside the toll on purpose: Landauer’s restore
               to one, the literal two-state version of the crossing, whose heat bound depends on
               the input uncertainty and the thermal premises. The flag’s job never came into it.
               The toy is the first thing I could build where the cost sits on the crossing itself, and
               it proves that if you price that step, the floor follows everywhere, for any machine
               with the five parts. That’s not an answer; it’s the question made exact enough to be
               wrong. And of the five jobs a record does, the toy attempts none, not even durability:
               the flag can be lowered by any move you care to write, and the cost that doesn’t go
               away is kept by you, the scorekeeper, beside the board. The machine keeps none of
               it. What the toy has is a scorekeeper’s receipt for the crossing. Whether the machine
               can be made to keep that receipt itself, where a step could reach in and change it, is
               Section 6’s question. Authenticity, evidence, accounting, cheap checking: none of
               them is in here, and I’ll say so again when it’s tempting to forget.
                   Let me say what I’ll owe you by the end. Whether the toll is a choice or a
               necessity: the next section, and I’ll tell you now that the answer surprised me. What
               a unit of cost is worth in anything physical: later, and only partly. What an observer
               who sees only a window can and cannot recover, including whether they can even
               tell which step paid: its own section. And whether the definition can be met by a
               machine that computes everything a Turing machine does, with its record earned
               and not declared, and what it costs to vouch for structure in one: Part III shows that
               with an example, and takes most of its length on it.
                                                           2.6 How the receipt earns its meaning   75


   For now you have a sheet of paper with two boxes, three moves, one rule that
writes what the last chapter says keeping takes into the step, and one theorem you
proved yourself in about a minute. Don’t let go of it. It’s the smallest version of
everything that follows, and if it’s wrong here, it’s wrong everywhere.
CHAPTER 3




Why the toll isn’t arbitrary

The first chapter of this part proved what keeping takes by counting states: a run
of one rule that raises a flag and keeps it up either lands two of its states on one
somewhere or never uses a state twice, so keeping is paid in a merge or by taking
states never used before; and in any real device every step that changes something
dissipates on top of that, by happening. The merge-or-fresh-state part needs no
premise beyond one next state for every state; the heat is physics, which I proved
for Bennett’s walker with Schnakenberg’s formula taken as the model, and cited for
devices whose states jump or drift at random in surroundings at a temperature. This
chapter counts the fresh states exactly, and asks what it takes to turn what keeping
pays into a unit on a ledger. The flag I built is one thing that stays; the result is
about anything that stays.
    The last chapter wrote what keeping takes into a toy as one rule, and in the toy
the move that raises the flag costs one because I said so. If that’s all it is, the ledger
is a long way of describing a preference, and you should treat it the way you’d treat
someone telling you their favourite colour is a law of nature. So this chapter is
me trying to find out whether a machine has to charge it. I’ll tell you the shape of
the answer up front, because I don’t want you reading forty paragraphs to find out
whether there’s a point. What keeping takes needs no “if” beyond a next state for
every state: on any machine, keeping something is paid in a merge or in states never
used before, and in any real device that comes on top of the dissipation of every
change, with time setting how much; that’s the paragraph above. Getting from what
keeping takes to my rule, one unit on the ledger for the step that raises the flag,
takes three “ifs”: there are finitely many states that read yes, so the fresh states run
out; the flag, once raised, stays up; and the ledger charges every move that forgets.
Then the move that raises the flag has to forget something, two of the states it acts
on landing on one, and pays. Forgetting is also the step Landauer’s principle, my
premise, puts a heat price on, when what’s forgotten wasn’t already known; when
somebody already knew, that knowing is where the heat went, and I’ll show you
that too. Each of the three “ifs” is a way out of the theorem, and I’m going to walk
through each one, because what’s on the other side of each is where the content is.
None of them is a way out of what keeping takes. Where the first fails, the machine
pays by taking states it has never used. Where the second fails, the flag comes back


                                   76
                                                              3.1 A closed room with no spare chair   77


down, so nothing is kept and there’s nothing to charge. Where the third fails, the
step still forgets, and only the ledger looks away.
    One more thing before the three ways out, and it comes first on purpose. Nothing
in the argument uses the word certify. It uses a reading that can go from no to yes
and never back. A fuse that has blown is one. So is a seal that has been broken, a
bit in write-once memory, a block a chain has finalized, a measurement somebody
wrote down and won’t take back. The argument below sends what keeping takes to
whichever of them you point at, and the latch chapter (Section 10) proves it doesn’t
matter which one you pick. Certification is the instance I build, for reasons I give
in Section 18 and don’t claim to have proved. So read this section as being about
anything that stays. The flag is only the one I keep on the table.


3.1 A closed room with no spare chair

Do this one with real objects, because the whole section rests on it and it’s about
ninety seconds of work. Draw a box on the table and call it the yes room. Put three
chairs inside the box and one chair outside, by the door. Four people, one per chair;
the people are the states your machine could be in, and the three inside are the ones
whose flag is already up. One move of the machine moves everybody at once: each
person stands up and goes to the chair the rule sends them to. There are two rules.
First, nobody inside the room may end up outside, because the flag, once up, stays
up. Second, the person by the door must end up inside, because this move is the
one that raises their flag.
    Now try to finish the move with one person in each chair.
    You can’t. Three people start inside and have to stay inside, so they take the three
inside chairs between them, with nobody left out, because nobody may leave. The
person from the door has to come in, there is no fourth chair inside, so somebody
has to share a chair, and two of the machine’s possible states have landed on one
state. Now use the chairs as a guessing game: secretly choose one starting chair,
apply the rule, and report only the finishing chair. If two starts are sent there, the
report cannot tell your partner which start you chose. Watching the people move
would tell them, but that would be keeping information outside the finishing chair,
and the chair alone has forgotten something.
    The whole argument is in that shared chair, and I want to name the piece of
mathematics that did the work, because it’s old and it’s not mine. If you put things
into fewer boxes than there are things, some box gets two. People call it the
pigeonhole principle; it’s the one from “The point,” where Jean Leurechon used
it in 1622 to argue that two people somewhere have the same number of hairs,
and the first name for it I could find came from Dirichlet, who used it in 1842
and later called it the drawer principle. It’s the kind of fact a child accepts and a
78   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                mathematician spends a career finding new uses for. Here the use is that a step
                which forgets nothing is a one-to-one shuffle, a one-to-one shuffle of a finite set of
                chairs lands on every chair, so the inside chairs are all taken by insiders and none
                is left for the newcomer. Finiteness, permanence and the flip are the three things
                that force a collision in the instruction’s map. The two starts that collide need not
                include the outsider: send the outsider to one inside chair and send two insiders
                to another. A run from a known outside chair can still have a uniquely identifiable
                start. The collision is a fact about the instruction over possible states.
                    The precise statement of the argument is a theorem a few lines down, and it
                needs one word first. “Injective” is the mathematician’s word for “forgets nothing”:
                a step is injective when two different starts always give two different ends. The
                theorem says exactly what the people and the chairs said and takes exactly the three
                premises: a duplicate-free list that names every state (finite), a reading that no step
                ever turns off (permanent), and one state that reads NO before the step and YES
                after it (the flip). There is no price in it anywhere; it is pure counting. I’ll come back
                to what counts as physics, but notice that nothing so far has been physics.
                    The exact words follow. For this whole section the setting is the five parts from
                Section 2 without the toll: states S, move names I, a step, a reading, and (later) a
                cost.

                Definition 3.1 (Finite, permanent, injective). The machine is finite when there is
                a list of states with no repeats that contains every state. The reading is permanent
                when no move ever turns it from yes back to no: for all s and i, cert(s) = yes implies
                cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A move i is injective (forgets nothing) when different starts
                give different ends: step( a, i ) = step(b, i ) implies a = b. A move that is not injective
                merges.



                Theorem 3.1 (A permanent flip merges). On a finite machine with a permanent
                reading, if cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes, then the move i merges.

                Proof. Suppose i were injective. Let C be the list of states that read yes: go down
                the list of every state and keep the ones that read yes. It has no repeats. (That is the
                only use of finiteness: all the proof needs is a duplicate-free list of the yes-states.)
                By permanence, used only for the move i, step(·, i ) sends every member of C into C.
                Being injective, it sends the members of C to members of C with no two landing on
                the same one, so its images are as many as C itself, and a list of that many distinct
                members of C is all of C. So the yes-state step(s, i ) equals step(c, i ) for some c in C,
                and injectivity gives s = c, so s reads yes. It reads no, and that is the contradiction,
                the same one the four people and the three inside chairs ran into.
                                                                3.1 A closed room with no spare chair   79


    A list with no repeats, as long as the set it draws from, contains the whole set.
Leave one member of the set out and you have packed the list into one place fewer
than it has members. That can’t be done: take away one occupied place and the
member sitting in it, and the list is still one too long for the places left, and it stays
one too long until there are no places left at all. This is the pigeonhole in the form
Leurechon would recognise.
    None of that is new. It has been sitting in two places for a long time, one in
physics and one in the theory of automata, and a physicist will recognise it on sight,
so I’ll start there. In 1876 Josef Loschmidt pointed out, against Ludwig Boltzmann’s
account of how a gas settles down, that the laws of mechanics run just as well
backwards: reverse every molecule’s velocity and the gas retraces its steps, so
mechanics alone can’t make entropy only ever climb. Twenty years on, in 1896, a
young assistant of Max Planck’s in Berlin pushed harder. He took Henri Poincaré’s
recurrence theorem of 1890, which says that in a system preserving a finite measure
of its accessible states, almost every starting state returns arbitrarily close to itself,
again and again, and used it to argue that nothing in such a system can climb
forever: give it time and it comes back down. The assistant was Ernst Zermelo,
the same Zermelo who’d put set theory on axioms twelve years later, axioms that
keep out the paradox that had sunk Frege’s foundations of arithmetic (Section 5
tells that one). Boltzmann answered the same year, not very politely, that the times
you’d have to wait for a return are so enormous that nobody would ever see one.
(Jos Uffink, who wrote the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on Boltzmann’s statistical
physics, calls that reply drenched in sarcasm and bitterness, and calls Zermelo’s own
paper a careful logical argument.)
    Now look back at the table. A step that forgets nothing, on a finite set, is a
reshuffle: it moves everybody around in loops, and every loop comes back to where
it started. A flag that goes up and stays up is exactly a quantity that climbs and
never comes back down. So a reshuffle can’t carry one, which is Zermelo’s objection
with the infinities taken out. On a finite set the loops are enough, and Poincaré’s
theorem isn’t needed. And the wait is at most as many steps as there are states,
nothing enormous. Zermelo was aiming it at the second law, and flags never came
into it. A quantum recurrence result came in 1957, when P. Bocchieri and A. Loinger
proved returns arbitrarily close to the initial state under their conditions on a closed
quantum system. That is a neighbouring recurrence argument, not this finite-state
proof: even a finite-dimensional quantum system has continuously many states.
Applying it to a physical record requires saying how that record is read and how
robustly it distinguishes nearby states.
    The second place stings more, because it’s in computer science, and somebody
got here first, again. Picture a finite machine that reads letters, one move per
letter. If every letter just reshuffles the states one for one, automata theorists call
80   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                it a permutation automaton, and the sets of inputs such machines can pick out
                are called group languages. Jean-Éric Pin’s 1992 paper on reversible automata,
                machines whose letters act as one-to-one maps, sorts out exactly which languages
                those machines recognise, and in that world this counting argument is folklore.
                The short version runs like this. Start at a state that reads no, and collect every
                input that ends at a yes. Because yes is permanent, adding letters to the end of a
                collected input keeps it collected. A group language with that property is either
                empty or everything, and everything would include the empty input, which ends
                where it started, at no. So it’s empty, no run of reshuffles raises the reading, and
                that’s Theorem 3.1 with the moves as letters. Pin’s paper is where I’d send you to
                check the automata side. It isn’t about flags or prices, and I’m not claiming it says
                anything about them.
                    There is a broader way to look at the same obstruction. Suppose every allowed
                move can be undone by another allowed sequence of moves. Start outside YES and
                try to enter it. Once inside, permanence says every allowed sequence keeps you
                there. But the undoing sequence must take you back outside. Those two demands
                cannot both hold.
                    On a finite set, a move that keeps all states apart is a reshuffle. Repeat that
                reshuffle enough times and every state comes home; all but the last repetition
                therefore undo one application. So the undoing sequence needed in that argument
                is available. Morgan Rogers studies systems of composable moves in his 2019 and
                2021 papers on toposes of monoid actions. That more general language gives this
                fact another home. Here the chairs and the undoing sequence already show why it
                holds.
                    Going quantum doesn’t get around the automata version either. Alex Brodsky and
                Nicholas Pippenger (2002) showed that a quantum finite automaton that measures
                only once, at the very end, accepts with bounded error exactly the group languages,
                the reshuffle kind. One that’s allowed to measure after every letter, and to stop on
                what it sees, does better: it accepts every piecewise testable language, and “has
                seen a b somewhere” is one of those. A measurement that can stop the machine is a
                record that stays, and it’s the extra thing that lets the bigger class in.
                    The third place is the closest, and it isn’t old at all. In 2023 Thomas Ouldridge
                and David Wolpert derived the thermodynamics of a finite automaton built the way
                real computers are: the same physical step run again and again, each time touching
                only the part of the machine that changes. They sorted languages into two kinds by
                the smallest automaton that recognises each one. If that automaton has a letter that
                sends two states to one, every automaton for the language has such a letter too, and
                on their derivation recognising the language on a device like that produces entropy,
                waste no cleverer design gets back, unless the inputs are so finely arranged that
                only one of the merged states ever actually turns up. If the smallest automaton only
                                                                 3.1 A closed room with no spare chair   81


reshuffles, they find the language can be recognised with no unavoidable entropy
production at all. One of their worked examples is the strings with no b in them,
which is my flag turned inside out: the runs that raise it are exactly the strings that
have seen a b. So the counting argument, a real price on it, and the case when you
already know which state you’re in are all in their paper, three years before this
book. Their price is derived from the physics of the device, and mine is assumed.
    There’s a fourth neighbour, and I’d call it a cousin, because it speaks another
language. Constructor theory is David Deutsch and Chiara Marletto’s programme for
stating physics as which transformations a device that runs in a cycle can and can’t
bring about, and in it a task is irreversible when it’s possible and its inverse isn’t.
Marletto’s version of thermodynamics (posted in 2016) leans on exactly that: tasks
that are possible while their transposes aren’t. Marletto, the physicist Vlatko Vedral
and coauthors (2022) made an irreversible task out of the quantum homogeniser, a
machine of reservoir qubits that interact by partial swaps, and ran it with photons.
Maria Violaris and Marletto (2022) then argued that the same machine, run in a
cycle, can turn a pure qubit into a mixed one and can never turn a mixed qubit
back into a pure one, even though every interaction in it is reversible, and that
this suggests erasure may cost something beyond Landauer’s bound. The counting
argument is a classical, finite, exact cousin of that sentence: a set of states a step can’t
leave, a task that’s possible, and no way back. Theirs is quantum and approximate
and aimed at physics’ price; mine is counted, and assumes its price. Deutsch and
Marletto’s paper on information (2015) has a neighbour of the counting argument in
its section 8.6: measuring one observable disturbs another irreducibly, and nothing
can undo the disturbance afterwards while the outcome stays in an information
variable. It’s a second, theory-independent way of saying that a record that stays
makes the step irreversible.
    So what I can claim here is narrower again, and I’d rather say exactly how. Even
the pricing form is, in physics and on their derivation, Ouldridge and Wolpert’s:
a merge the language can’t avoid costs entropy. A price assumed rather than
derived isn’t mine either: Li and Vitányi (1996) took a unit charge for every bit
irreversibly erased, with steps that can be undone priced at zero, as axioms of a
model of computation, and Demaine and his coauthors (2016) put a price on named
instructions that destroy bits, a unit for an AND or an overwrite. What I didn’t
find anywhere I looked is what a price on merging moves forces on a reading that
stays, charged on a ledger whether or not anybody’s physics is right (put a price on
merging and the flip has to pay it, which is the next subsection), and what I get out
of that: the toll, as a theorem about the ledger, the merge-or-revoke split for a single
move, the exact match between “forced to be priced” and “merges”, the squeeze
bound counted in whole units and its entropy form, a built machine walking out
through each of the three ways out, and every proof on the page. Those are the
82   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                forms I didn’t find stated anywhere I looked, and Appendix C sorts them the same
                way: the counting core classical and somebody else’s, the pricing form only partly
                mine. The core move is older than the computer, it had two homes before it got to
                mine, and its physical price had a third.

                Count the alternatives before putting a price on them
                Write N different starting configurations on cards and spread them across the bench.
                Run each through the same rule once. When several cards give the same full
                configuration, put them in one pile. Run the rule again and gather the new piles.
                Once cards agree on the full state, the same rule gives them the same next state too.
                   Count the different configurations after each tick. Call their set Qt and their
                number qt , with q0 = N and Qt+1 = F ( Qt ). The difference qt − qt+1 tells you how
                many alternatives disappeared on that tick. Four distinct configurations landing at
                one state lose three alternatives in one landing pile. Keep those two counts beside
                each other: three alternatives lost, one landing place.


                Theorem 3.2 (The alternatives balance exactly). For a total deterministic rule F
                and N distinct starts,
                                              T −1
                                              ∑ (qt − qt+1 ) + qT = N.
                                              t =0

                If all endpoints fit in K < N full states, a transition at some t < T identifies two
                different members of Qt . If all endpoints are one full state, the total loss is N − 1.

                Proof. An image has no more elements than its source, so every difference is non-
                negative. Add the differences: each intermediate qt cancels, leaving q0 − q T . If
                q T < N, at least one difference is positive; at that step a map from more states to
                fewer cannot be one-to-one. In particular, one final full state leaves a loss of N − 1
                alternatives.
                    Turn the cards over before counting them together. Two runs might show the
                same answer on the front and still carry different inputs on the back. Those are
                different full configurations. The count follows everything the machine kept.
                    Now put a price rule beside the piles. Let pt be the price at tick t, and require
                every landing pile to have at most 2 pt distinct sources. The number arriving is
                then at most 2 pt times the number of places they land: qt ≤ 2 pt qt+1 . Multiply that
                inequality through the run and you get
                                                     N ≤ 2∑ t < T p t q T .

                The rule connects the bill to how tightly the machine can pack the alternatives.
