landing places. An average of numbers no greater than log2 K cannot exceed log2 K.
For equality, put equal chance on every member of one pile of size K. There are
log2 K bits at the start and none at the single landing place.
    (2) An entropy price must cover that even preparation on every pile. A pile of
size n therefore requires cost c ≥ log2 n, or equivalently n ≤ 2c . That is the halving
rule: no landing place accepts more than 2c starts. Conversely, if the halving rule
holds, part (1), with K = 2c , says no preparation loses more than c bits. The same
price covers them all.
    (3) Now allow at most two starts. If they land separately, the move loses nothing.
If they land together, the halving rule reads 2 ≤ 2c , which asks for at least one
whole unit. This is exactly merge pricing. Nothing in that two-start argument needs
the rest of the machine to be finite.
    The chance calculation makes the same demand. Two possible starts hold at most
one bit, so a charge of one covers every spread over a merging pair. Equal chances
on that pair lose exactly one bit and force that charge. A single possible start, or two
108   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                that stay separate, lose zero. So restricting entropy pricing to at most two possible
                starts gives merge pricing too.
                   So merge pricing is weaker than full entropy pricing, though both force the
               one-unit toll under the permanence and finiteness premises. The prices are rules on
               moves. Reading one as physics takes Landauer’s premise for the actual spread and a
               stated exchange rate from bits or units of cost to heat.
                   Now for the case where the floor is zero. Take the coin under a cup: toss a fair
               coin under it without looking at how it lands, and let the rule be to set it heads up.
               You might have had tails; now you have heads; one bit of what you didn’t know is
               gone, and that’s the bit the principle charges for. Now lift the cup, see heads, put the
               cup back, and apply the rule again. Nothing you didn’t know changed, and no bit
               was lost. And the principle, applied to a state you already knew, demands nothing:
               the premise holds exactly when the heat is zero or more, which is to say it sets no
               positive floor. Setting a coin you know is tails to heads still dissipates when you do
               it in a finite time, as any change in a real device does (heat against time); setting
               one you know is heads changes nothing. What the premise gives up either way is
               a floor that survives going slowly. Whether the hand that sets the coin keeps one
               is a question about the hand, and I come to it below. And that isn’t a hole in what
               the premise charges. When you lifted the cup, which side was up got written down
               somewhere: in you. That’s a distinction that stays, kept by whoever knows, on a
               page that was blank before you looked, and the page gets paid for in heat when it’s
               wiped to be used again. The heat moved to the one who knows; it didn’t vanish.
               The entropy-loss bound depends on the preparation and on what the move does
               to it. Here “known” means a preparation concentrated on one logical state, or a
               conditional ensemble whose side information is explicitly included in the account.
               Merely telling a spectator which way the coin landed does not change an unchanged
               device’s heat. This is the generalized form of Landauer’s principle, worked out by
               Owen Maroney in 2009, in a paper he wrote at the Perimeter Institute in Canada (he
               has been a philosopher of physics at Oxford since 2011), and by Sagawa in 2014,
               and Landauer himself had the seed of it in 1961: for a row of bits all already ONE,
               he wrote, there’s no need to carry out any operation, so no entropy changes and no
               heat is given off, and resetting a row all ZERO to ONE involves no entropy change
               either, because neither row carries any information.


               Theorem 3.17 (A known state gets no heat floor from the premise). On a finite
               machine, if the spread puts all its chance on one state s, then any move removes
               zero bits, and Premise 3.5 for that move holds exactly when Q ≥ 0.
                                              3.7 The same bound, written in bits, and when it’s zero   109


Proof. A spread on one state has entropy 0, and so does its image, which is again on
one state. So ∆H = 0 and the premise reads Q ≥ 0.
    Be careful with that one, because it’s easy to overread. “The premise sets no heat
floor for a known state” does not mean a stamping machine run on a known-blank
sheet dissipates nothing. It dissipates every time the stamp actually comes down
in a finite time, known input or not, since the stamp changes the sheet: that’s heat
against time, proved here for Bennett’s walker (Theorem 1.9), found for a dragged
bead by Schmiedl and Seifert and for any classical jump process by Shiraishi, Funo
and Saito, and how much depends on the device’s physical implementation, its
control protocol and how fast it goes. What the theorem says is only that the premise
sets no floor there. The floor comes from what you didn’t know. That’s a sentence
about the premise’s floor, and the device is a separate matter. And notice that the
toll still charges the known-state stamp one unit, because the toll is a rule about the
move, and the move doesn’t know what the observer knows. That’s the worst-case
gap from the third way out showing up again, and it’s the price of having a rule a
machine can follow without asking who’s watching.
    The physics of all this has a standard review, the physicists Juan Parrondo, Jordan
Horowitz and Takahiro Sagawa’s “Thermodynamics of information” (2015), which
sets Landauer’s bound, its generalized form and the costs of measurement and
feedback side by side. And the gap between a device and the spread it runs on has a
physicist’s number on it. Artemy Kolchinsky and David Wolpert (2017) showed that
a fixed process built to dissipate as little as possible for one spread over its states
pays extra when it runs on another, and the extra is how much closer the process
brings the two spreads, measured in relative entropy; the extra was later named
mismatch cost. That’s the worst-case gap again, priced for an actual spread, where
the toll prices the move.
    Run a known input through a fixed device and a floor comes back, from the
device this time. Take K inputs the device sends to the same output, and spread your
chances evenly over them. The identity of Section 3 that ties Ladyman’s reading to
Sagawa’s says the average, over the K, of the entropy the device produces on each
one known equals the entropy it produces on the even spread, plus k B ln K. The
second law makes the entropy produced on the spread zero or more. So the average
is at least k B ln K, and the worst of the K is at least the average: on some one of
them the device produces at least k B ln K of entropy, which is at least k B T ln K of
dissipated work, however slowly it runs. Kolchinsky and Wolpert’s formula says,
under their conditions, which input pays: the one the device’s own best spread gave
the least chance. A device can make one input cheap only by making another dear.
Only a device chosen knowing the input gets it to nothing, and then the device is
where the knowing is kept. So the floor sits on the merging move, on its worst input,
110   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               whatever anyone knows, and that’s the shape of the toll. The bound on a device left
               to relax from a known start, in the next subsection, is one more floor of this kind.
                  There’s a second piece of fine print on Theorem 3.17, and it’s about who works
               the controls. The entropy-loss bound supplies no positive floor for a known input.
               Whether a device can approach that floor also depends on its controls: lower this
               barrier, tilt that well, raise the barrier again. Those operations have a timing and a
               physical implementation. The entropy calculation alone does not price either.
                  Paul Riechers, Alexander Boyd, Gregory Wimsatt and James Crutchfield (2020)
               analyse metastable memories under time-symmetric control: the prescribed control is
               the same played forwards or backwards, with the relevant time-reversal conventions.
               A symmetric clock pulse can meet that restriction; an arbitrary clocked pulse need
               not. For memory states unchanged by time reversal, their low-error result singles
               out the memory states that the desired logical map, applied twice, fails to bring back
               to where they started. They call those transitions nonreciprocal. With equal local-
               equilibrium free energies, the leading minimum-work term as the error allowance ε
               tends to zero is proportional to
                                                                           
                                            k B T ln(1/ε) Pr C (C (m)) ̸= m .
               The probability is over the initial memory states. This is a low-error scaling with
               physical premises, not an exact finite-error heat charge on every execution.
                  A permanent flip from no to yes is nonreciprocal at that no-state: a second
               application cannot return it to no. A known input at that state can then face the
               extra work cost in their restricted control setting, even though its initial logical
               entropy is zero. Their class also includes a three-state cycle, which merges nothing.
               The distinction is about the permitted controls as well as the logical map. It neither
               changes Theorem 3.17’s entropy calculation nor identifies the book’s abstract merge
               price with a universal physical heat floor.
                  A deterministic run from a known start has a known state at every step, so
               the premise sets no floor under any of its steps; each that changes something still
               dissipates when it happens in a finite time, and a fixed device keeps the floor above
               on each step that merges. One more limit, about which states collide. The counting
               guarantees a collision among the already-yes states together with the entering no-
               state. It does not guarantee that the entering state takes part in the collision. Take
               four states with only the first reading no, and a move that sends the first state to
               the second, the second to the third, and leaves the third and fourth where they are:
               the second and third both land on the third, and the first never shares with anyone.
               For an input distribution supported only on no-states, this counting argument alone
               forces no positive entropy loss. Whether other states in that support merge depends
               on the move. The operation-level ledger toll still follows under merge pricing.
                                                      3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   111


   What this section earns comes to this. A finite machine’s permanent flag-raising
instruction has two allowed starting states that land on one state. Prepare those two
with equal chances: that instruction removes one bit, and under the adopted physical
premise its mean heat is at least k B T ln 2. That is a worst-case preparation, not a
positive charge on every execution. A known start gives no positive entropy-loss
floor. It still dissipates whenever it runs in a finite time, and how much depends
on the device’s dynamics, controls and speed; a fixed device that merges K inputs
produces at least k B ln K of entropy on its worst one, however slowly it runs. The
ledger charges the merging move whatever the preparation, because merge pricing
says so. The counting proves a collision, the preparation determines the uncertainty
removed, and the physical premises connect that removal to heat.
   The general case is the one that shows you where the bits go. Split the bits
removed state by state. Each state x you might be in carries its chance p( x ) along
to where it lands, step( x, i ), and finds whatever other chance landed there too. If
nobody else landed there, its term is zero. If others did, its term is the difference
between how crowded its landing spot is and how much of the crowd it brought.


Theorem 3.18 (The bits removed, one term per state). On a finite machine, for any
move i and any chances p( x ) ≥ 0, with q the pushed spread,

                              ∑ p(x) log2 q(step(x, i)) − log2 p(x) .
                                                                    
         H ( p) − H (q) =
                               x: p( x )>0

Every term is zero or more, so a move never adds bits. If two different states x ̸= x ′ ,
both with positive chance, land on the same state, the sum is strictly positive.

Proof. Group the sum for H (q) by where things land: the chance q(y)
at a landing spot is the sum of the p( x ) that land there, so H (q) =
− ∑ x: p(x)>0 p( x ) log2 q(step( x, i )). Subtract from H ( p) term by term. Each
term is non-negative because the landing spot holds at least what x brought,
q(step( x, i )) ≥ p( x ), and the logarithm keeps order. If x and x ′ share a landing spot,
that spot holds at least p( x ) + p( x ′ ) > p( x ), so the term for x is strictly positive.


3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not

Let me total it: what have you earned the right to conclude, and where is there still
a way out?
   You’ve earned this first, and it needs no premise but one next state for every
state: on any machine run by one rule, finite or endless, a run that raises a reading
and keeps it up either merges two of its own states or never repeats one, and
112   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               on any machine at all a single move that raises a kept reading without merging
               anything has to send the kept states one-to-one into a part of themselves with a
               gap left over, which takes endlessly many of them. Either way it is a merge, or an
               endless supply of states never used before. You’ve earned this: on any machine with
               finitely many states, a move that raises a flag either forgets something or takes a
               flag down somewhere else. That is pure counting, with no physics and no premise
               beyond finiteness, and the half of it where nothing comes down is the pigeonhole
               on four states. You’ve earned this: on a finite machine, if a flag, once up, stays up,
               then raising it has a collision somewhere. If it raises several no-states at once, the
               yes-states together with those newcomers land on at least that many fewer spots
               than there are of them. This does not say that each newcomer shares its destination;
               this one is counting again. And you’ve earned this: if forgetting is charged for, the
               toll follows, and if forgetting is charged per halving, the size of the toll follows
               too; each of those derivations hands back a system with the five parts and the toll,
               so Section 2’s floor applies to it as it stands. This is the rule from Section 2, now
               derived, with every premise named, for any finite machine with a flag that stays up.
               In that section I only declared it.
                   Now for what you haven’t earned, which I list so you don’t assume it. You haven’t
               earned that forgetting costs anything in the world; that’s Landauer, it’s measured for
               beads and argued over for the general case, and in this book it’s an assumption with
               a name. And even granting it, Landauer’s entropy-loss bound demands no positive
               heat from a run whose state is known (the lifted cup of the coin example), so what
               the physics forces is a floor on a device that has to work whatever it’s holding. Any
               one run can come in under it, and when it does because somebody knows its state,
               that somebody is carrying the heat. You haven’t earned that any machine you’d
               actually want to build is of this kind, either, and there are two easy ways to miss.
               A machine that keeps its running total inside its own state, as a number with no
               ceiling, has infinitely many states, so the finite premise fails for it as a whole. And
               you can’t patch that by giving the total a ceiling. A total that only climbs, held in
               finite memory, eventually either stops at its top, and then two different histories
               leave the same top value, which is a merge, or rolls back over to zero, and then
               it doesn’t only climb. So any running total a finite machine keeps for itself has a
               horizon: it’s honest up to its width and no further. And a machine whose price list
               charges the step that raises the flag, but lets some other step merge two states at no
               cost, raises the flag honestly and still doesn’t charge for forgetting in general, so the
               merge-pricing premise fails for it. Either one puts a machine outside these theorems
               as stated, though a finite piece of it can still sit inside. The example I build later
               (Section 15) misses in both ways. It keeps counters with no ceiling, so it’s infinite
               outright, and some of its ordinary steps, counting a counter down among them,
               can land two different states on one at no charge on the ledger. So the counting,
                                                   3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   113


as stated, doesn’t reach it: it forces the toll only on machines with finitely many
yes-states that price every merge, and that example is neither. It doesn’t need the
counting, though: the moves that raise its flag merge states themselves, so the same
cost lands on them directly (Theorem 3.19).
    A finite piece can still sit inside, and the smallest one I could build where every
premise can be seen to hold is this. None of them is left as a hypothesis. It has four
slots times a flag, eight states, and three kinds of move: stamp (set the flag, go to
the next slot, cost one), jump to a chosen slot (cost two), next slot (cost zero). It’s
finite and permanent; the next-slot move forgets nothing; the stamp and the jump
merge; merges are priced, and priced per halving. So this section’s two conclusions
hold on it outright. The counting lemma underneath, that a duplicate-free list in
which no landing spot is hit by more than a set number of members has at most that
many times as many members as landing spots, is the plainer reading of the halving
price above. Merge pricing alone would take any price of at least one for the jump.
The jump’s price of two is what the halving price asks, since the jump squeezes four
states into one. One more fact about it: each move’s price is exactly the number of
halvings in its largest squeeze. A move that costs one has no spot hit by more than
two states, a move that costs two has none hit by more than four, and some spot is
hit by exactly that many (stamp squeezes at most two states into one, jump to a slot
squeezes four, and next-slot squeezes nothing).
    The example Part III builds runs this eight-state machine. Seen through a window
that shows only a line number, read modulo four as the slot, and a flag, a short
program of that machine, once a two-instruction setup has run, does what the
eight-state machine does, one move at a time, and pays exactly what the eight-state
machine charges (Section 15.14 has the construction and the exact statements).
The example as a whole prices its record layer and not every merge: some of its
zero-price steps merge states, and whatever those merges cost the hardware is off
the ledger, so the finite piece is a piece. The toll on the whole example comes from
the record layer (Theorem 3.19).
    Finiteness did one job in the counting. It forced the step that raises a permanent
flag to merge two states. On the machine of Part III no count over the whole machine
has to force that, because the merge is in plain view. Its record moves are the check,
the commitment and the raised flag that the opening’s lock puts in order, and it
names them CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY: COMMIT names a checked claim in
a slot called the channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. CERTIFY takes a state with
the flag down and the same state with the flag up to one place, since a flag that’s
already up just stays up. Its COMMIT overwrites the channel, so two states that
differ only in what the channel names land on one state. Part (1) of the theorem
below shows both. So any price list that charges every merge of that machine’s own
114   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               step charges the flag-raising step, with no premise that the machine is finite. It isn’t:
               its versions and its ledger grow without bound.
                   Finiteness is still there, in the smallest place it can be. Hold every part of the
               state but the flag fixed, and the flag has two readings, down and up. CERTIFY sends
               both to up, and it does the same to everything else from either, so the two states
               land together. That is the counting of Theorem 3.1 on a set of two. So the choice I
               made in the opening’s list isn’t the merge, and it isn’t the shape of CERTIFY. It’s that
               the step never reads the flag: the rest of the state moves by its own rule and the
               ledger adds the instruction’s price, whichever way the flag reads, so no instruction
               keeps a copy of the old reading, and any that raises the flag lands its two readings
               together. Make CERTIFY trap instead when the flag is already up, and the merge
               moves rather than goes away: the state it traps lands with the state that was trapped
               already, since a trapped machine only pays. That’s the halted state stepping to itself
               again, and it holds of every record move: any of the three that fails lands with the
               same state already trapped. The one way out of the flag’s merge is to write the old
               reading into a part of the state that grows, a list of every reading so far, say, and
               that is a state never used before, the other column. A ledger that adds more for a
               re-raise than for a raise doesn’t do it: the state with the flag up and the ledger a
               little lower lands where the raise lands, and the merge has only moved again.
                   That leaves the other miss, the unpriced merges. Clause (c) of certified Thiele-
               complete (Definition 15.7, in Part III) asks for base moves at zero, and a base move
               merges (DEC, counting a counter down, lands two states on one), so full merge
               pricing and clause (c) can’t both hold on that machine. They don’t have to. Split a
               state into its base part, which is what a two-counter machine would show (the line
               number and the two counters), and its record part, which is everything else: the
               versions (each counter’s count of how many times it has been written), the table
               of facts, the channel, the trap latch (which goes up when a record move fails, after
               which only the ledger moves), the ledger and the flag. Then price only the merges
               the record layer makes.

               Premise 3.7 (Record-layer merge pricing). A move that sends two different states
               with the same base part to one state costs at least one.

                   Part of where that line falls is forced. The line number has to be in the base
                part, or DEC, which can land two lines with the same counters on one, makes a
                record-layer merge at no cost; each counter has to be there, or its version, or DEC’s
                own merge gets charged; and the flag or the trap has to be outside it, or nothing
                charges CERTIFY. Where the versions, the table, the channel and the ledger sit
                moves nothing below.
                                                   3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   115


   The merges among base parts are the ordinary computer’s business, the ones any
two-counter machine makes, and whatever heat they cost is the ordinary computer’s
heat. The premise prices only merges between states with the same ordinary-
computer part. A step like DEC, which changes that part, can lose a version number
at no cost, and the premise doesn’t object. Merge pricing implies this premise, so it
asks less, and on the record distinctions it is still an assumed operation-level price;
identifying it with heat needs a physical model. And it is a price on this machine,
not a source of the toll on any machine. A certifying move whose effect on the
base read the flag, say one that moved a counter up when it raised the flag and left
the counter alone when the flag was up already, would raise the flag and send no
two states with the same base to one state, and the premise would have nothing to
charge at the raise. It would still merge: the state with the flag down and the state
with the flag up and that counter one higher land together, across two base parts,
where the premise doesn’t look. And on this machine its trap would still be charged
when it fails. The small machine’s record moves treat the base the same whichever
way the flag reads, which is why the premise does its job there, and the theorem
below is stated for that example and no other.


Theorem 3.19 (The toll on the example machine). For the small machine of
Section 15, with no finiteness premise: (1) CERTIFY merges, and so do COMMIT
and CHECK of every claim, and each joins two different states with the same line
and counters. (2) Every cost that satisfies merge pricing for that machine’s step
charges CERTIFY, every COMMIT and every CHECK at least one, and obeys the toll,
so the machine with that cost is a Thiele machine. (3) No INC, DEC or HALT sends
two different states with the same line and counters to one state. So the machine’s
own prices, base moves at zero and each record move at one, satisfy Premise 3.7,
they’re the least prices that do, and merge pricing fails for them. (4) Every cost
that satisfies Premise 3.7 obeys the toll, so the machine with that cost is a Thiele
machine.

Proof. (1) For CERTIFY, prepare two states identical except for the flag. Give both a
channel holding a commitment. One flag is down and one is up. CERTIFY raises
the first and leaves the second up. Both advance one line and add the same charge;
every other field agrees. They have become the same full state.
    For COMMIT, put the requested fact, at the counter’s current edition, in both
tables. Leave one channel empty and put that very commitment in the other.
COMMIT writes the same commitment into both channels and treats every other
field alike. Again the full successors agree.
116   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


                   For any CHECK, fill the fact table to its sixteen-entry limit. CHECK then fails,
               whatever claim it was asked to test. Compare that untrapped state with an otherwise
               identical state whose trap is already up. The first sets its trap; the second is already
               frozen. Neither changes the other core fields, and both pay the same charge. Their
               successors agree. In each construction the starting line and counters agree as well,
               so these are record-layer merges.
                   (2) A price on every merge charges each of those instructions at least one. Only
               CERTIFY can raise the certificate. Its merge therefore supplies the toll.
                   (3) Check the free instructions by asking whether two states with the same line
               and counters could become one. The table, channel, trap, ledger and certificate
               are left alone, so any difference in those fields survives. On a live state the shared
               line and counters choose the same instruction branch. A counter write adds one
               to its edition; different edition numbers stay different after the same addition.
               All unchanged editions stay different too. Hence no remaining field can hide a
               difference between those sources.
                   A trapped state stays exactly where it is under a free instruction. Two different
               trapped states therefore stay different. A live state remains live under these instruc-
               tions, so it cannot meet a trapped one. That exhausts the cases. The free instructions
               make no record-layer merge, and all three kinds of record instruction do. Charging
               the former zero and the latter one satisfies the premise and is the smallest such price
               list. Full merge pricing still fails: the zero-price DEC pair in Theorem 15.35 starts
               with different counters and lands together.
                   (4) Any record-layer merge price charges the CERTIFY pair from (1). Since no
               other instruction raises the flag, this gives the toll for every raise.
                   So this section reaches the example machine. On it the toll follows from record-
               layer merge pricing, and the example’s own price list, clause (c) included, satisfies
               that premise. This is a result about its ledger, not a heat bound. There’s a second
               way to settle the clash, which I note and didn’t take. Morita’s reversible two-counter
               machine, from the history earlier in this chapter, runs every step backwards and
               is still universal: with its input encoded, it computes anything a Turing machine
               can. Put the record layer on a base like that, with the base’s step taken as the
               program’s own step from line to line and the halt left with no next step, and every
               base step is one-to-one, and full merge pricing permits those base steps to cost zero.
               Choosing that schedule would meet clause (c); the lower-bound premise alone does
               not require zero charges. It wouldn’t meet clause (a) as I stated it, though. Clause
               (a) asks for a move for each two-counter instruction, acting from every live state,
               not a step for each line of one program, and DEC c j sends states on any two lines
               with the same counters, c above 0, to the same window, so whether it merges turns
               on the rest of the state and not on the program being reversible. That base wouldn’t
                                                    3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   117


be getting anything for nothing: what it doesn’t forget it keeps in its counters, which
is the column of states never used before, again. I haven’t built that machine.
    And you haven’t earned anything about what the flag means. The pigeonhole on
four states doesn’t know what it’s certifying. The cost is for raising a flag that stays
up. Whether raising that flag ever amounts to standing behind a structural fact, the
“vouching” I keep promising and keep not delivering, is a question for the certified
example in Part III, and here it has moved exactly this far: on a finite machine that
charges for every merge, if that flag stays up, it was paid for.
    One last thing, because it should nag at you. The toll is forced by the premises,
but the premises were chosen, and “permanent” in particular was chosen by me.
Why should a flag stay up? Why not let it come down, pay nothing, and be honest
about it? That’s a fair question, and merge or revoke is the start of an answer (the
three-card machine only showed that the converse of Corollary 3.9 fails): on a finite
machine that charges for every merge, a flag that goes up at zero cost is a flag the
same move takes back somewhere, and a record that can be silently taken back is
the thing the bulla and the hash chain and the write-once disk were all built against.
“Permanent” here is exactly that: the flag can’t be lowered. The toy in Section 2 has
it only because none of its three moves happens to lower the flag, and it does none
of a record’s five jobs; the lineage in that section, the bulla and the write-once disk,
was built around this one, durability; I chose it. Whether that was the right job to
pick out of the five is something you can argue with me about, and I’d want you to.
    And “permanent” is an idealization, which I should say before a physicist does. No
physical record lasts forever. A bit held behind an energy barrier leaks over it at some
rate, however slow, and a closed finite system comes back around, which is Zermelo’s
point from the counting (Theorem 1.6 is the finite form). The toll theorems in this
section, the ones that start from a flag that stays up, need permanence on every
state the machine can reach, including states a given run never visits, forever; on
states nothing reaches it never comes into it, and merge or revoke does without it.
Weaken that to “the flag stays up on the states that actually turn up, for as long as
anyone cares,” and merge-or-revoke tells you what goes wrong: the move could
take the flag down somewhere the machine could go and never does, and then it
isn’t forced to merge at all. A version of the toll stated in chances is the noisy steps
of Section 1: a step that squeezes nothing on average can’t raise a reading that stays,
and one that can strictly bunches the even spread. A version stated in time spans is
a different theorem, and what I have of it is below.
    One piece of it I can hand you, and the step law of Section 1 is its general form.
Take one move and repeat it from one start, forever. On a finite machine the states
that run passes through are finitely many, so it falls into a loop. If the move forgot
nothing on those states, it would be a reshuffle of them, and a reshuffle brings every
one of them back around, the start included, where the flag was down. So if the
118   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               flag goes up along that run and stays up from some point on, the move merges two
               states the run itself visits. The state they share is one the machine actually passes
               through. And it doesn’t touch the known-state point above: a merge among states
               the run visits still receives no positive lower bound from the entropy-loss premise
               when its state is known. The argument holds for any map on finitely many states
               iterated from a start whose flag is down, with the flag up at every step from some
               point on; no permanence premise is used.
                   Runs that mix different moves split two ways, and the answer is short enough to
               give here. If the moves are picked from outside, in any order at all, the answer is
               no. Take two states, one reading no and one reading yes. One move swaps them;
               the other does nothing. Run the swap once and then the do-nothing move forever:
               the flag goes up at the first step and stays up for good, and neither move merges
               anything anywhere. The swap would take the flag down from the yes-state if it ever
               ran there; on this run it never does, and that’s exactly the weakened permanence
               this paragraph is about. But if the machine is closed, picking its next move from its
               own state, the run is the orbit of one map, the step with whatever move the state
               picks, and the single-move argument applies to that map as it stands. Now say the
               moves come in a pattern that eventually repeats, one phrase of moves played over
               and over. Suppose the flag is down at some step after the repeating starts, and goes
               up and stays up after that. Count the repetitions from a step where the flag was
               down (start the phrase at that move if you have to) and run the same argument on
               the whole phrase treated as one move, at the states where each playing of it begins.
               It merges two of those states, both visited; follow the two through the phrase, and
               the first move where their paths meet merges two states the run visits at that move’s
               place in the pattern. So the answer is no for moves picked from outside, and yes for
               a closed machine, or for a repeating program once the flag is down somewhere after
               the repeating starts.
                   There is also a limited statement about how long a noisy record lasts, using a
               different quantity: total entropy production during relaxation. Take a device with
               no outside hand: a random process hopping among finitely many states at rates that
               never change, with a reverse for every hop and local detailed balance, able to get
               from any state to any other. Require at least one up-state and one down-state. Left
               to run, it settles into a long-run spread π. Measure each up or down stretch from
               its entrance, with entrances sampled in the stationary process, and call the mean
               lengths Tup and Tdown . Start the device in a known no-state s. The total entropy it
               produces over relaxation is at least ln(1 + Tup /Tdown ), in units of k B .
                   First compare the starting spread with the spread the device settles into. A state
               that is common at the start but rare in the settled spread is a large mismatch. For
               each state, take the ratio of those two chances, take its natural logarithm, and
                                                            3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   119


average using the starting chances. With p the starting spread, that number is
                                                                  p( x )
                           D ( p∥π ) =      ∑         p( x ) ln
                                                                  π (x)
                                                                         .
                                         x:p( x )>0

It is called relative entropy. Here every π ( x ) is positive, so the ratios are available.
The number is nonnegative: apply ln y ≤ y − 1 to π ( x )/p( x ), multiply by p( x ), and
add. The right side is at most zero, since the included π chances total at most one
and the p chances total exactly one. Negating that comparison gives D ( p∥π ) ≥ 0.
    For a known start s, all the starting chance is at s. There is only one term:
D = ln(1/π (s)) = − ln π (s). A state with settled chance one tenth therefore starts
with mismatch ln 10. Since s is a no-state, its settled chance cannot exceed the total
chance of all no-states. Its mismatch is at least − ln π (no).
    The physical step in the argument is the fixed-rate entropy-production split of
Massimiliano Esposito and Christian Van den Broeck (2010). In that setting the total
entropy produced is at least the decrease in this relative entropy. Once the spread
has settled to π, the relative entropy left is zero. So the initial mismatch supplies
the lower bound for the whole relaxation.
    Now read the same number from the record of up and down stretches. In a long
settled run, each entry into YES is followed by an exit; apart from the two ends of
the record, there are equally many up-stretches and down-stretches. Total time up
is the number of up-stretches times their mean length, and likewise for time down.
Dividing gives
                                   π (up)        Tup
                                          =           .
                                   π (no)      Tdown
The two chances add to one. If the ratio on the right is r, the no-share is 1/(1 + r ),
and its negative logarithm is ln(1 + r ). That gives the stated bound. The settling and
mean-length arguments below justify passing from a long record to these limiting
quantities.
    For a large up-to-down ratio, doubling that ratio raises this lower bound by about
k B ln 2. Making both stretches longer by the same factor leaves it unchanged. Across
a family of devices whose ratio tends to infinity, the bound diverges; no single
finite irreducible device in this class keeps its flag up forever. This is a relaxation
bound, not a heat charge on each flip. It uses neither a thermodynamic reverse-path
construction nor time-symmetric control, so it does not identify the quantities in
those other results. It also leaves the known-input case of the deterministic entropy-
loss bound where it was: this noisy evolution and its total entropy production are a
different question. The entropy is added up over one whole relaxation, from the
known no-state s until the device has settled, and local detailed balance is what
ties it to heat exchanged with the reservoirs. Total entropy production includes the
120   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               change in the device’s entropy too; it is not heat alone. It also isn’t the permanence
               of the finite-state theorems on a noisy device: on this device the flag comes back
               down, and Tup and Tdown are average stretches.
                   The core of it for a chain that ticks, worked out, runs as follows in the case where
               the long-run spread π gives every state a positive chance and satisfies detailed
               balance: in the long run as much weight flows from x to y in one step as from y
               to x, π ( x ) P( x, y) = π (y) P(y, x ), where P( x, y) is the chance of stepping from x
               to y. Count the entropy produced in one step as the change in the device’s own
               entropy plus what goes out to the surroundings, which for a hop from x to y is
               ln( P( x, y)/P(y, x )). Detailed balance turns that ratio into π (y)/π ( x ), and the sum
               collapses: the entropy produced in one step is exactly the drop in relative entropy to
               π. It’s never negative, because a step that leaves π where it is can’t make any other
               spread harder to tell from π (that’s the data-processing inequality, a standard fact of
               information theory). Add the steps up and the sum telescopes. A known start s has
               relative entropy − ln π (s), so the entropy produced in the first T steps is − ln π (s)
               minus the relative entropy left at step T: it never exceeds − ln π (s), and it reaches it
               in the limit exactly when that remainder goes to zero. Next, − ln π (s) ≥ − ln π (no),
               because s is one of the no-states and so carries at most their total chance. The flow
               from the no-states to the yes-states equals the flow back, because in the long run the
               weight on the yes-states doesn’t change, so what flows in equals what flows out. Last,
               take each mean stretch as its mass over that flow; then Tup /Tdown = π (up)/π (no),
               and since the two chances add to one, − ln π (no) = ln(1 + Tup /Tdown ).
                   Try the stretches with a bag of ten counters: nine marked YES and one NO.
               Draw, record the answer, replace the counter and mix again. Each draw gives
               YES with chance 9/10, whatever the last answer was. A YES stretch ends on the
               next draw with chance 1/10, so its mean length is ten draws: the mean L obeys
               L = 1 + (9/10) L. A NO stretch similarly averages 10/9 draws. Their ratio is nine,
               just like the ratio of YES to NO counters. In a long record, count all the YES entries
               and divide by the number of YES stretches; that is the measured mean stretch length.
               Divide both counts by the total number of draws and you have mass divided by flow.
                   For this rule the long-run flow from NO to YES is (1/10)(9/10) = 9/100 per
               draw, and the reverse flow is the same. A start known to be NO has relative entropy
               − ln(1/10) = ln 10 against the long-run spread; after one draw the spread is already
               1/10, 9/10, so none of that relative entropy remains. This bag shows the probability
               accounting. The entropy-production interpretation still needs the stated physical
               model; shaking counters in a bag does not measure that heat.
                   Two things need establishing for a general device: that it actually settles, and
               that “mean stretch length” means what it sounds like. I’ll say what each says, and
               why it holds.
                                                      3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   121


    Settling comes first. A chain doesn’t have to settle. It can get stuck in a corner, or
cycle round forever. What rules that out here is a condition named for Wolfgang
Doeblin, a German-born French mathematician, son of the novelist Alfred Döblin,
who took his doctorate at the Sorbonne in 1938 for work on chains like this one and
died in June 1940, at twenty-five. In words: from wherever the device is, its next
step lands on each state with at least some fixed fraction δ of that state’s long-run
chance. No state is ever out of reach in one step, and none is favoured so heavily
that the others starve. Under that condition each step shrinks the distance between
where the device is and where it’s going by the factor 1 − δ (the distance here is the
total of the differences in chance, state by state). To see why, split each step in two:
with chance δ, forget where the device was and draw a fresh state from π; otherwise,
move by whatever is left over, and the condition is exactly what makes the leftover
a genuine set of chances. The fresh draw puts the device’s spread and π in the same
place, so only the other share, 1 − δ, can keep them apart, and no step pushes two
spreads further apart than they were. So the distance dies off geometrically and the
spread converges to π at every state. The payoff for the bound is that the entropy
produced from the known start stays under − ln π (s), and it also gets there: after T
steps it falls short by at most (4/πmin )(1 − δ)2T , where πmin is the smallest long-run
chance of any state. The shortfall is the relative entropy left, and ln y ≤ y − 1 once
more puts that under the sum of ( p( x ) − π ( x ))2 /π ( x ), which is at most the square
of the distance over πmin ; the distance starts at no more than 2 and shrinks by 1 − δ
a step. So − ln π (s) is the exact total entropy production of the whole relaxation, in
units of k B , and the bound − ln π (s) is reached.
    For rates satisfying detailed balance with π, the same equality holds when the
device hops at random moments, with no clock ticking. Write out how fast the
relative entropy to π changes and pair each hop with its reverse. Detailed balance
makes each pair’s share minus (the flow one way minus the flow back) times the
logarithm of their ratio, and that is exactly the pair’s share of the rate entropy is
produced; a difference times the logarithm of the same ratio is never negative. So at
every instant the relative entropy falls at exactly the rate entropy is being produced,
and that rate is never negative; add the rate up between two times and you get
exactly the drop in relative entropy between them. For settling, Doeblin’s condition
becomes a condition on rates: the rate of hopping from any state x to any state y
is at least c times π (y), for some fixed c > 0. Split the rates in two again: a part
that, at rate c, forgets where the device was and redraws it from π, and the rest,
which still satisfies detailed balance. The production rate adds over the two parts,
because with detailed balance it’s the rates times quantities that don’t depend on
the rates. The rest produces nothing negative, and the redraw part alone produces
at least c times the relative entropy still left. So relative entropy falls at least as fast
as e−ct . One wrinkle needs its own line. A known start puts all its weight on one
122   3 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary


               state and none anywhere else, and the logarithms in the relative entropy go bad at
               zero. The relative entropy is still continuous at the starting instant, because each of
               its terms has the form u ln(u/π ), and u ln u goes to zero as u does. So adding up
               the production from the start out to infinity gives exactly − ln π (s).
                   I should say what Doeblin’s condition costs. It asks for every hop to be possible
               directly, in one step or at a positive rate. A device whose states reach each other
               only through other states can still settle, and the standard theory of these chains
               says when: always, for a device that hops at random moments and can get from any
               state to any other; and for a chain that ticks, as long as it also doesn’t march round a
               cycle. Those devices meet the condition for some fixed stretch of time or number of
               steps instead of one, and the same argument runs on blocks of that length, because
               the relative entropy never goes up in between.
                   Then come the stretches. The bound used the fact that the long-run chances of
               up and down stand in the ratio of the mean stretch lengths, and I took the mean
               length of a stretch with the flag up to be the long-run weight of the up-states divided
               by the flow into them. For a chain that ticks, that’s right for the following reason.
               Start each stretch the way the flow starts them, count the steps until the chain leaves
               the up-states, and the average is exactly π (up) over the flow. Look at the long-run
               weight that has been up at each of the last k + 1 ticks. It splits in two: the part
               whose stretch began exactly k ticks ago, which is the flow times the chance that a
               fresh stretch lasts more than k ticks, and the part that was up one tick earlier still.
               Add those splits from k = 0 up to some K and the sum telescopes: π (up) is the flow
               times the sum of those chances, plus the weight that has been up for more than K
               ticks. The sum of the chances that a stretch lasts more than k is its mean length.
               Doeblin’s condition makes the leftover die: from any up-state the next step lands in
               the down-states with chance at least δ π (down), so the weight that has stayed up
               for K ticks is at most (1 − δ π (down))K .
                   With the stretches measured in seconds, when the device hops at random mo-
               ments, it comes out the same, by a different route. Ask, for each up-state, how
               long on average the device takes to leave the up-states from there. Call that its
               leaving time. The leaving times are finite: from every up-state the device hops
               into the down-states at a total rate of at least c π (down), so the chance a stretch
               is still running at time t falls at least as fast as e−c π (down) t , and no leaving time is
               more than one over c π (down). And they obey one plain rule, which you get by
               asking what happens in the first instant: from any up-state, the rate out of it times
               its leaving time, minus the rates into the other up-states times their leaving times,
               comes to exactly one (per second times seconds is a pure number). Average the
               leaving times over the way the flow starts stretches, multiply by the flow, and the
               rule plus the balance of the steady spread (as much weight flows into each state as
               out of it) rearrange the sum into exactly π (up), so in seconds too the mean stretch
                                                  3.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not   123


is its mass over the flow. Both of the bound’s premises are proved now, in steps and
in seconds, under Doeblin’s condition.
    One chapter remains in this part, and it’s about a different way out entirely.
Forgetting has had its chapter; the question after that is whether finding out costs,
because the demon’s whole trick was that it knew which way the molecule was
going, and I owe you a straight answer on what knowing costs.
CHAPTER 4




Learning borrows, committing
pays

I ended the last chapter owing you an answer about knowing. What keeping takes so
far sits on forgetting: under merge pricing, a finite machine’s permanent flag-raising
instruction was paid for because it merges two states somewhere. But there’s a thing
that looks like the opposite of forgetting and feels like it ought to cost at least as
much, probably more, and that is finding out. Every time a machine rules out a
possibility, it knows more than it did. If forgetting a bit costs, does learning one cost
too? I had a strong feeling about this, and you probably have it too, so I’ll say it first:
learning is the expensive part. Most physicists had that feeling as well, for a long
time. It’s why the demon took a hundred and fifteen years to exorcise, or didn’t.
“Exorcise” is the word the people who think it worked like to use. John Earman and
John Norton, the doubters from the last chapter, called their two-part paper on it
“Exorcist XIV: The Wrath of Maxwell’s Demon,” and I read that Roman numeral as a
joke about how many times the demon has been declared gone. So hold the word
loosely. This section is me finding out where the feeling goes wrong, and where it’s
right. I’ll give the answer up front. Looking, like every change a real device makes,
dissipates when it happens. But it doesn’t have to merge anything, so it owes no
floor, and a ledger that charges merges can charge it nothing. What it does use up
is a blank page to write on. Learning borrows that page. Wiping the page to use it
again is a merge, and that’s where the floor gets paid. Committing, making a record
nobody can hand back, is paying for good. I’m going to tell you the version where
the exorcism worked, Charles Bennett’s, because it’s the version that says where the
heat goes, and the third way out in the last chapter, the one Landauer’s premise is
there to close, stays open behind it.


4.1 Somebody got there first, goddamn it

I’d been sitting on this idea that committing, making a result stay so it can’t be
handed back, is what pays, and learning, writing on a blank page you could hand
back, only borrows, and I thought: this one’s mine, I finally had an original thought.
Then I found Carlo Rovelli’s 2024 paper, “The Thermodynamic Cost of Choosing.”


                                   124
                                                                   4.2 A small being at a small door   125


I hadn’t. Somebody got there first, goddamn it: a real physicist, with a real paper,
saying that making a choice that sticks dissipates at least the energy Landauer
charges for erasing a bit. He even quotes a German saying, Wahl ist Leiden, to choose
is to suffer, and at that point what are you going to do but laugh.
    And then, taking him apart properly, it got good, because on its face he contradicts
Bennett. Bennett says measuring owes no floor; Rovelli says any measurement costs.
So which is it? Look at what Rovelli calls a choice. A coin in the air hasn’t chosen
anything; it has to hit the ground and stop. And then comes the sentence I’d put
on my wall: “stabilization must be irreversible, otherwise it is not stabilization.”
Bennett’s floorless measurement is one that could still be undone; that’s why it owes
no floor. It only borrows the page. Rovelli’s choice is one that’s been made to stay;
that’s why it costs. The way I read them, they’re standing on opposite sides of the
same line: learning, which borrows, on Bennett’s side; committing, which pays, on
Rovelli’s. (Bennett’s demon still pays in the end, when it wipes the page.) Neither of
them puts it that way, so push on it. But if it holds, it’s the best sign I’ve got that the
line I’m drawing between finding something out and making it stay isn’t something
I made up.
    Push on it with his paper open and it gives in four places, which I go through at
the end of this chapter, once the demon has been built. So the two-sides-of-one-line
picture is my reading, not his, and the piece of it that’s really his is the one sentence
about stabilizing. That sentence I’ll still put on my wall.
    So he’s my closest neighbour, and the difference between us is exact. His is
physics: a dissipation bound, at least kT ln 2 at the temperature of the recording
parts, with no outside heat bath, for a choice that sticks. Mine is a rule in a model
of computation: a charge in the machine’s own count, on the step that flips a
permanent reading on, with no temperature anywhere in it. It’s the same instinct in
a different place, and I’ll take it, because it’s annoying to be second but worse to
be alone and wrong. And he’s the closest only on choosing. On copying there’s an
older neighbour, in the chemistry of copying molecules, and the end of this chapter
gets to it.


4.2 A small being at a small door

You met Maxwell’s demon briefly in Section 2. It gets a whole section here, because
the step it seemed to pay for and the step it actually pays for are what this section is
about.
    In December 1867 James Clerk Maxwell, who had published his equations for
electricity and magnetism two years before, in 1865, and to my mind had as good a
claim as anyone to being the most important physicist alive, wrote a letter to his
friend Peter Tait describing a problem he couldn’t get rid of. Take a box of gas at one
126   4 Learning borrows, committing pays


               temperature, with a wall down the middle and a tiny door in the wall. Now imagine,
               he said, a “very observant and neat-fingered being” sitting at the door, who can see
               individual molecules coming. When a fast one approaches from the left, it opens
               the door and lets it through. When a slow one approaches from the right, same.
               Otherwise it keeps the door shut. It never pushes anything; it only opens and closes
               a frictionless door at the right moments. After a while the right side is hot and the
               left side is cold, and you’ve got a temperature difference you could run an engine
               off, made out of nothing but looking. That’s supposed to be impossible; it’s the thing
               the second law of thermodynamics says can’t happen, and the second law is the law
               physicists are least willing to give up. Arthur Eddington, the English astronomer,
               wrote in a 1928 book of popular lectures that a theory found to contradict it has
               nothing for it but to collapse in deepest humiliation, and nobody has had to test that
               yet.
                   Maxwell put it in his textbook in 1871, and it got named Maxwell’s demon,
               though not by Maxwell. William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, called it a demon
               in Nature in 1874, and Maxwell, in an undated note to Tait headed “Concerning
               Demons,” tried to take the name back: “Call him no more a demon but a valve . . . ”
               Nobody listened, which is probably for the best, because “Maxwell’s valve” would
               not have lasted a century. But keep his correction, because it’s exactly right and it’s
               the whole problem: the being does no work. It opens and shuts a door. So physicists
               spent the next century trying to find where the being was cheating. I want you to
               feel the pull of the obvious answer, because I felt it and so did most of them: the
               being has to see the molecules, seeing costs, and the case is closed. In 1929 Leo
               Szilard built a one-molecule version of the box and did the arithmetic, and said
               the second law survives if finding out which side the molecule is on costs at least
               as much entropy as the being gains. In 1951 the French physicist Léon Brillouin
               made it concrete: to see a molecule you have to bounce light off it, and the way the
               philosopher of physics Jeffrey Bub sums up the result, finding out that way costs
               at least k ln 2 of entropy for every bit, which is kT ln 2 of heat, Landauer’s number
               before Landauer, and there was your charge on looking. For thirty years that was
               the answer. Information costs because getting it costs.
                   That’s a price on one way of looking, and it doesn’t show that every possible way
               of making a record has to pay it. A device can burn energy without that being a law.
                   Szilard is worth one more minute, for a reason that has nothing to do with the
               demon. Four years after the one-molecule engine, in September 1933, by his own
               later telling, he was waiting at a traffic light on Southampton Row in London, having
               just read a newspaper report in which Ernest Rutherford, the physicist who had
               announced the atomic nucleus in 1911, called the hope of getting power out of
               atoms moonshine, and as the light changed it occurred to him that an element which
               gave off two neutrons when it swallowed one could keep a reaction going by itself.
                                                           4.3 Bennett moves where the heat is paid   127


That’s the nuclear chain reaction, thought up crossing a street. It’s his memory of
himself, and Richard Rhodes’s history of the bomb opens with it, in a first chapter
called “Moonshine,” which is where most people meet it, so hold it as the man’s own
story, not a record made at the time. Does it change anything about the demon? No.
What it adds is a picture of the man: the same mind looked at one molecule in 1929
and one neutron in 1933, and both times the question was what a single small step
forces downstream.


4.3 Bennett moves where the heat is paid

In 1982 Charles Bennett, who’d already shown in 1973 that computation can be
done without forgetting if it keeps its whole history and pays by taking states it
has never used instead, took the demon apart one step at a time. The being looks
at a molecule and writes down which side it’s on. Is writing that down a merge?
Picture the being’s notepad, which starts blank. After looking, the notepad says
“left” or “right.” There are two possible worlds before the look (molecule left, pad
blank; molecule right, pad blank) and two possible worlds after it (left, “left”; right,
“right”), so nothing merged: two went in, two came out, and you can read the before
off the after. Copying what you see onto a blank page forgets nothing, and a step
that forgets nothing owes no floor under Landauer’s premise. It still dissipates when
it happens, like any change a real device makes, and going slowly shrinks that as
far as you have patience for. But it did use something up: the blank page. Before
the look, the pad was blank and ready; after it, the pad is full. Brillouin had priced
one particular way of looking (bouncing light) and took it as the price of getting
information at all. Bennett gave a way of looking that, on his account, doesn’t pay
that price. It borrows a page instead.
    So where is the heat floor? The being has one notepad and a lot of molecules.
After the first molecule the page is full, and to do the next one it has to wipe the
page. Wiping takes two possible worlds (pad says “left”; pad says “right”) to one
(pad blank), and that’s the merge, the step with no way back. The demon pays
every cycle, and what it pays for is clearing the page so it can see again, and the
amount it pays is at least what it gained, and the second law sleeps soundly. It’s
the rule from his 2003 notes that I quoted in Section 2: erasing and merging carry
the unavoidable charge, and copying onto a blank place to write doesn’t. The look
borrows the page, and the wipe pays the page back, with the floor’s worth of heat.
And the blank page the being started with was itself a distinction somebody paid
to set, because writing a blank is a write, and Section 1 showed what a write on a
finite cell is: a merge.
    Section 2 separated making a record from resetting it. Now you can see exactly
which step pays, and why the other one was tempting, because looking feels like
128   4 Learning borrows, committing pays


               the active part, the thing the being does, while wiping feels like housekeeping. The
               housekeeping is where the floor gets paid. If there’s one sentence in this section I’d
               want you to carry out of it, it’s that one, and the idea in it is Bennett’s.


               4.4 Two different things called “narrowing”
               Here is what I had to get straight in my own head before any of this made sense,
               and I’ll give it to you as a picture because that’s how I eventually got it.
                   Draw the machine’s possible states as a row of dots. Now draw a second row
               above it: the dots that you, standing outside, still think it might be in. Those are two
               different rows: the first is a fact about the machine, and the second is a fact about
               you, about what you’ve seen and what you’ve ruled out. Both rows can shrink, but
               they shrink for different reasons, and only one of them costs.
                   The machine’s row shrinks when two of its states land on the same state, which
               is a merge, and a merge is what the price charges. Under the halving rule from
               Section 3, a run can’t shrink the machine’s own row by more halvings than it paid
               for. That’s the theorem just below, and it’s that section’s halving price run forward
               along a whole program, where that section took it one step at a time. There is no
               new idea in it, only the same counting of states.
                   To state it exactly, write ⌈log2 n⌉ for the index-bit count of n: the smallest
               whole number k with 2k ≥ n, the fewest yes-or-no questions that can guarantee
               identification among n things when arbitrary binary splits are allowed. It is 0 at
               n = 1, and 0 at n = 0 too, since 20 ≥ 0; the definition covers empty lists, where the
               logarithm of zero isn’t a number. Wherever I write an ordinary logarithm without
               the rounding, its argument is positive. For a run t and a list D of starting states,
               let imgt ( D ) be the set of states the run can end in, starting from somewhere in D,
               and write |imgt ( D )| for how many there are (in Section 3 the symbol for one move
               already meant the count; here I need the set and its size both). Let cost(t) be the
               run’s total cost.


               Theorem 4.1 (The machine’s own narrowing is priced). If the cost satisfies the
               halving price (Premise 3.4), then for every run t and every list D of starting states
               with no repeats,
                | D | ≤ 2cost(t) · |imgt ( D )|,   so    ⌈log2 | D |⌉ ≤ cost(t) + ⌈log2 |imgt ( D )|⌉.

               Proof. After each move, gather the states still possible and count each different state
               once. If the first move costs c1 , the halving rule says the original count is at most
               2c1 times this new count. If the next move costs c2 , the new count is at most 2c2
                                                          4.4 Two different things called “narrowing”   129


times the count after that. Put the inequalities together: the original count is at
most 2c1 2c2 times the count after two moves.
   Carry on to the end. The factors multiply, their exponents add, and the added
prices are exactly cost(t). The last collection is imgt ( D ), giving the first inequality.
An empty run contributes no factor and leaves the collection unchanged, so it fits
too.
   For the rounded count, let k bits suffice to number all the endpoints. There are
then at most 2k endpoints, and the first inequality gives at most 2cost(t)+k starts.
That many bits therefore suffice for the starts. This also covers an empty starting
collection, whose stipulated index-bit count is zero, without taking a logarithm of
zero.
   Rounding throws some information away. Four starts and three endpoints both
need two index bits, so the rounded comparison alone permits zero cost. The
unrounded comparison still sees that four is more than three and forces a positive
charge.
   The run itself is the witness; nothing else is handed in. That will matter in
Section 8, and I’ll say why at the end of this section.
   Your row shrinks when you see something that some of your candidates couldn’t
have shown you, and you cross those candidates off. Nothing happened to the
machine. It didn’t merge anything; it didn’t know you were watching; it would have
done the same thing with nobody there. The physicist Edwin Jaynes had a name
for mixing these up, and I think it’s one of the most useful names in all of science:
the mind projection fallacy, treating what you know about a thing as if it were a
property of the thing. Your list of candidates is in your head, and the machine’s
row is in the machine. The halving price is about the machine’s row, and crossing a
candidate off yours doesn’t move it.
   And here I have to be fair to Jaynes, because he’d argue with where I just took
his phrase. In a 1965 paper on Gibbs’s and Boltzmann’s entropies he wrote that
entropy is “an anthropomorphic concept” (a phrase he credited to the physicist
Eugene Wigner), and by that he meant a property of the particular experiments you
or I choose to do on a physical system. On his account the system alone doesn’t
carry it. So for Jaynes the second law is about what’s known too, and the line I’d
have liked to draw, that the second law has opinions about the machine and none
about you, is exactly the line he’d refuse. Who’s right is one of the oldest fights in
statistical physics, Jaynes’s reading against Boltzmann’s, and I can’t settle it and
don’t have to. The spreads in Section 3’s entropy theorems are spreads over the
states the device might be in when the step runs, and every theorem there holds
whether you read those chances as ignorance or as physics; “the floor comes from
what you didn’t know” is the same sentence in either reading, with “you” being
130   4 Learning borrows, committing pays


               whoever built the spread. What I need from the fallacy is only this: the two rows
               are different rows, and only one of them is the machine’s.


               4.5 The demon on a sheet of paper
              Build it, because the whole claim is four dots and two arrows and you should see it
              merge or not merge with your own eyes.
                   The machine has a hidden bit (think of it as the molecule’s side) and a display
              (the notepad). It has four states, written as pairs, hidden bit then display: 00, 01,
              10, 11. It has two moves.
                   MEASURE copies the hidden bit onto the display, by adding it in the way that a
              light switch adds: if the hidden bit is 1, flip the display; if it’s 0, leave it. Draw the
              arrows: 00 goes to 00, 01 goes to 01, 10 goes to 11, and 11 goes to 10. Look at the
              arrowheads: every state has exactly one arrow landing on it, so nothing merged and
              MEASURE forgets nothing. Look at the two states where the display starts blank: 00
              goes to 00 and 10 goes to 11, which is the copy onto a blank page, (hidden, blank)
              to (hidden, hidden), and it’s the use that matters here. And the light switch isn’t
              one way of copying among several. A MEASURE that merges nothing, copies onto a
              blank display and leaves the hidden bit where it was has nowhere else to send 01
              and 11: each has one landing left on its own side.
                   WIPE sets the display to 0 whatever it held. 00 goes to 00; 01 goes to 00 as well.
              10 goes to 10; 11 goes to 10 as well. Two arrows land on 00 and two on 10, which
              is a merge, twice over. Under any price that charges per halving, WIPE costs at least
              one, while MEASURE is allowed to cost zero. Zero on the price list isn’t zero spent:
              a real MEASURE dissipates when it happens, like any change, and it uses up the
              blank display. What it doesn’t do is merge, so it owes no floor.
                   Now be the observer. You can see the display and not the hidden bit. What you’re
              shown, the display here, is what I’ll call a window: the part of the state an outside
              observer gets to see. Section 7 is about windows in general; here the window is
              just the display. The display starts blank, so your list of candidates is {00, 10}: two
              possibilities, one bit you don’t know. The machine runs MEASURE and you look at
              the display. If it shows 1, the only candidate that could have produced it is 10, and
              if it shows 0, only 00, so your list went from two to one and you learned the hidden
              bit. The machine’s price for that move, on a list that charges merges, is zero, and
              what it spent was the blank display. Its own row of possible states went from {00,
              10} to {00, 11}, still two; nothing it could have been got merged with anything else.
              You narrowed and it didn’t. That’s the measuring half of Bennett’s argument on four
              dots, and WIPE’s charge is the wiping half. So the demon just broke something: one
              bit gained, nothing charged. The thing it broke, written out so you can see exactly
              where the crack runs, is this: for every list of starting candidates, every run, and
                                                                 4.5 The demon on a sheet of paper   131


every actual start in the list, the index bits the observer gains (log2 of the candidates
before minus log2 of the candidates after, both rounded up) are at most what the
run was charged. On four dots that sentence is false.

Definition 4.1 (What an observer knows). Fix a window w from states to what can
be seen. Given a list Ω of candidate starting states, a run t, and the actual start
s0 ∈ Ω, the observer’s knowledge K (Ω, t, s0 ) is the list of candidates s ∈ Ω whose
run shows the same thing through the window at every step as the actual run does.
   If that definition looks familiar, it should. It’s the standard way logicians of
knowledge set it up: what you know is whatever holds of every case you can’t tell
apart from the actual one, given everything you’ve seen (Fagin, Halpern, Moses
and Vardi’s Reasoning About Knowledge, 1995, builds a whole subject on it, runs
and observations included). And it’s the logically omniscient kind, the kind where
knowing some facts means knowing everything that follows from them, at no extra
cost (Section 14 comes back to that flaw). I’m using it on purpose, flaw and all.
This section is about learning, and learning in that sense is exactly the thing that
doesn’t have to merge. Settling, making a result stay so it can’t be handed back, is
the separate act with a price, and nothing in this definition settles anything.


Theorem 4.2 (An observer can learn with no merge). There is a four-state machine
(the demon), a window (the display), a cost satisfying the halving price, a run of cost
0, and candidates with |Ω| = 2, for which |K (Ω, t, s0 )| = 1. So the claim “for every
Ω with no repeats, every t, and every s0 in Ω: ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ − ⌈log2 |K (Ω, t, s0 )|⌉ ≤
cost(t)” is false for that machine and that cost. In the same machine, every cost
satisfying the halving price charges WIPE at least one.

Proof. The machine and run are the four dots above: MEASURE is a bijection, so cost
0 satisfies the halving price; the observer’s two candidates show different displays
after MEASURE; WIPE sends two pairs of states to one each, so the halving price
needs its cost ≥ 1.
   The demon is the picture, and the smallest case is smaller than it. The claim as
written already fails on a machine with two states that the window tells apart and
every move priced at zero, because the observer’s very first look tells the two apart,
and it never fails on a machine with one state. That’s why the interesting version is
learning after the first look, which is where the three states of Theorem 4.3 come in.
And WIPE’s price needs less than the halving rule: merge pricing alone charges it at
least one.
132   4 Learning borrows, committing pays


                   There is one thing to be exact about. The halving rule is a floor: it says merges
               cost at least this much, and it doesn’t say anything costs zero. So the theorem
               exhibits one price schedule that meets the halving rule and charges MEASURE
               nothing. A different schedule could meet the rule and still charge MEASURE;
               nothing in counting forbids overcharging. The claim is that learning is not forced to
               cost a unit. That’s what “borrows” in the section’s title means: the look takes a page
               and pays nothing, and the unit, like the floor, comes due at the wipe.
                   The physicists had this freedom on the books long before me. Paul Fahn (1996),
               doing the entropy accounting of Szilard’s one-molecule engine step by step, argued
               for a symmetry between the measuring step and the erasing step: on his account,
               which of the two you charge is partly a choice of bookkeeping, and the total is
               what’s fixed. Sagawa and Ueda (2009) derived a bound on that total, with the
               split depending on the memory. So, on their accounts, “a schedule could charge
               MEASURE instead” is a known freedom in how the books are kept, and I didn’t find
               a loophole. The other reading is very much alive too. Ruth Kastner (2025) argues
