the machine of Part III the chain stops at the first step, the checker’s own proof, by
choice; Section 15 says why.
    The engineering version of this was already built, in 1996 and 1997. The
computer scientist George Necula, then at Carnegie Mellon, called it proof-carrying
code: when you ship a program to a host that doesn’t trust you, you ship a proof
with it that the program obeys the host’s safety rules, and the host checks the proof
that arrived before running anything: not your reputation, and not “a proof exists
somewhere,” but the one in the box. A quarter century earlier Stephen Cook’s
certificates had the same bones, from Section 2: a claim comes with a witness that’s
cheap to check, and the checker checks that witness. And the Scottish philosopher
David Hume, in 1748, arguing about miracles in his Enquiry Concerning Human
Understanding, laid out the thing the receipt replaces. He weighed testimony against
evidence, and wrote that “a wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the
evidence.” The way I read him, the whole of his argument is a method for how
much to trust a witness when you have no receipt. The move in this book is to stop
weighing. A claim on the record is either backed by its object and its paid event,
or it’s testimony from outside, and a run that leans on testimony hasn’t earned it
itself. It can inherit it, but only as far as the copy it leans on is genuine, which is
Section 7’s problem of a record shown from outside.
    Robert Brandom, a philosopher at the University of Pittsburgh, built a whole
account of language on two words this book leans on, commitment and entitlement,
and his Making It Explicit (1994) is where I’d send anyone who suspects I invented
the pair. In his picture, as I read it and as his reviewers describe it, people talking
keep score on each other: what each speaker is committed to, what they’ve put
themselves on the hook for, and what each is entitled to, what they’re licensed to
claim. You can be committed without being entitled (a reckless assertion), many
claims count as entitled by default until someone challenges them, and entitlement
can be borrowed: I can claim a thing on your say-so and defer to you when I’m
challenged. Lay mine beside his and the differences are the content. His score is
kept by the other people in the room; here it’s a reading in the state. His entitlement
often comes by default; here it’s an event that has to happen and is charged. And
his deferral is my testimony, which I’ve just let back in on a leash: borrowed
entitlement is only as good as the copy is genuine. The leash has an older formal
cousin, the jurisdiction rule of Burrows, Abadi and Needham’s logic of authentication
208   8 Structural entitlement


               (Section 7), where you take a statement on an authority’s word only if you already
               believe the authority has jurisdiction over it. It came first, presented in 1989 and
               printed in 1990, years ahead of Brandom’s book of 1994, and its words are believes
               and jurisdiction where his are commitment and entitlement.
                   There’s a whole field that would want a word here too, the logic of belief revision,
               which asks how a reasonable mind should change what it believes when something
               new comes in. Its nearest neighbours are worth naming, and I couldn’t keep them
               apart until I put them back on the table with the cups. Your friend believes the coin
               is under cup one. They can learn something that doesn’t clash with that, say cup two
               is empty, and just add it. They can lift cup one, find nothing, and have to change
               their mind about a table nobody touched. Or you can tell them you moved the coin.
               The last two felt alike to me at first, but they aren’t: in one the friend was wrong,
               and in the other the friend was right, and then the table changed.
                   Krister Segerberg, a Swedish logician at Uppsala, built a logic of irrevocable
               revision in 1998: accepting something so that it can’t be given up, which is the
               firmness question taken to its end. Isaac Levi, a philosopher at Columbia who spent
               a career on how beliefs get fixed and unfixed, split adding a belief into a deliberate
               kind and a routine kind (I cite his 1991 book; the split goes back to his 1980 one).
               Deliberate is reasoning your way there. Routine is where you take on whatever a
               procedure you committed to in advance hands you, the way you’d accept a reading
               off a thermometer you’ve already decided to trust, or what’s under a cup when you
               lift it. What I think the split rests on is when the trust goes in: once, before the
               data comes. A passing CHECK, the test move of the small machine in Section 15, is
               routine in exactly that sense, with a checker proved honest once, outside every run.
                   Neil Tennant, a logician at Ohio State, and Gösta Grahne, a computer scientist
               trained at Helsinki, I first filed as two separate complaints. They’re one move
               made from opposite sides. The target is the best-known impossibility in that field,
               the Swedish philosopher Peter Gärdenfors’s 1986 theorem that a natural rule for
               conditionals, the one his paper calls the Ramsey test, can’t live with rational revision.
               Tennant argued in 2008 that it goes through only by treating some additions as
               revisions: the friend who learned cup two was empty gets counted as having changed
               their mind. Grahne, working on updates and counterfactuals, argued in 1998 that
               Gärdenfors’s theorem bites only revising, so the friend whose coin was moved is out
               of its reach. Side by side, they squeeze the theorem from both ends into one case:
               being wrong about a table nobody touched.
                   The line this book leans on hardest is between two kinds of change. Revising is
               changing what you believe about a world that stayed put. Updating is changing it
               because the world moved. Two computer scientists, Hirofumi Katsuno and Alberto
               Mendelzon, drew that line for knowledge bases in a 1991 paper on the difference
               between updating a knowledge base and revising it; database researchers had
                                                                          8.3 The shape, said once   209


been working on updates with incomplete information since the mid-1980s, Arthur
Keller and Marianne Winslett among them. Grahne’s result stands on it. And look
at what the friend sees: an empty cup one is the same empty cup whether they
misremembered or you moved the coin. The evidence alone can’t tell revising from
updating; that’s a fibre. What tells them apart is a count of how often the cups were
touched. The machine in Part III keeps that count as an edition number for each
thing, and its version rule treats every write as an update: a write moves the edition
number, so every fact about the old edition stops counting for the new one.
    And Alexandru Baltag, Bryan Renne and Sonja Smets, three logicians at Am-
sterdam, gave a logic in 2014 that keeps apart three things Gettier’s cases blur:
justified belief, explicit knowledge and conclusive evidence. The friend who watched
has justified belief; the friend who lifted the cup has conclusive evidence. Explicit
knowledge I read as knowing with the justification written out beside it, the way the
record keeps its check, and I’m less sure of that one. Put them together and they say
something exact about this book’s record. A record that’s never wrong and never
corrected would be a dogmatist’s dream if its sentences were about the present, but
they aren’t: each says a property held of a thing at one edition, and that sentence
stays true after the edition number moves on. The record can be infallible and never
corrected only because its sentences are edition-stamped. Strip the stamps, and the
first write would turn it into a liar that can’t take anything back.
    Push on that and it gives twice. The record is Segerberg’s irrevocable acceptance
every time, with no revising in it. If a check was dishonest, the only fix that fits a
record like this is a second record on top saying “withdrawn,” the way a revocation
list works, so the infallibility leans on the checker, proved once, outside. And the
record is never wrong partly because it only talks about past editions. Whoever
reads it wants now, and getting from “held at that edition” to “holds now” crosses
every update since. The record doesn’t make that step for you.
    That leaves the logicians who taught the logic of knowing to count, whom
Section 14 names again in passing. This time I take them properly, and I want to
see what each price rests on. Ho Ngoc Duc, in 1997, gave the logic of knowing
an operator for “true after some train of thought”: an agent doesn’t know every
consequence of what it knows now. It can come to know any of them by taking
steps of reasoning. I took that at first for the thing I was after, until I saw which way
it points. His operator points forward, at what the agent could come to know. A
record points back, at what was checked. His operator and a record are one arrow,
read from opposite ends. And Sergei Artemov and Roman Kuznets, in 2014, turned
logical omniscience into a question of cost: a logic escapes it when every valid claim
that something is known comes with a proof whose size is bounded by a polynomial
in the size of the claim. The usual modal logics of knowledge can’t pass that test
unless NP equals coNP, which most people would bet against, and justification logic
210   8 Structural entitlement


               passes it for knowledge stated together with its justification, because the size of the
               justification pays for the search. That last clause took me a few reads. What I think
               it means is Cook’s certificate from the proof-carrying-code paragraph above: put the
               justification inside the claim, and the hard part, finding it, was paid before the claim
               was written. Their price rests on an open bet, and it’s a price on looking, which is a
               price of a sort. Steps and a price are both there, then, in their own form. What I
               still don’t find in them is the one I care about: a single act that closes a question for
               good and is charged as that act. Their steps are steps of reasoning, and their price is
               on finding a proof. Neither is on settling. I couldn’t get past the journal’s paywall
               to Artemov and Kuznets’s paper, so my account of it comes from how other people
               describe it.
                   Push on mine the same way and it gives. A check is one of Duc’s trains of thought,
               so my act is the last step of his train, where the walking stops. What I’ve added is a
               direction and a charge on stopping. Where the charge sits follows from one choice:
               I want it to bind every program the machine runs, and a charge that does that has
               to sit inside the step, since a program can skip any charge kept where it can write.
                   There are three things entitlement is not. It isn’t permission: an access control
               system says who may write to what, and that’s granted from outside and says nothing
               about truth; a process with permission to write the note still has no entitlement.
               It isn’t “it’s true, so I can use it”: that’s the cups. And it isn’t “sound by luck”: a
               shortcut that gives the right answer because the inputs happened to cooperate is the
               stopped clock. The count below has one condition aimed at it, and I’ll tell you what
               the condition says and how much it actually catches.


               8.4 What narrowing costs: count the rivals

               Now I need the number, because a book about what keeping costs has to say how
               much, and the idea fits in a game you can play with three playing cards. Shuffle
               cards marked 1, 2, 3 face down. Sort them using only questions of the form “is this
               one bigger than that one?”, and count the questions. There are six orders the cards
               could be in. Each question has two answers, so after one question you’ve split the
               six into at most two piles, after two questions at most four, and you need to get
               down to one. Four is less than six, so two questions can’t always do it, and three
               can, and you can draw the tree of questions on paper and see it: six leaves, three
               deep. The number of questions you need is at least the base-two logarithm of the
               number of possibilities you started with, rounded up: that’s log2 of 6, which is a
               bit under 3, rounded to 3. Donald Knuth, a computer scientist at Stanford, gives
               this, in the volume on sorting of his The Art of Computer Programming, as the lower
               bound for all comparison sorting, and the shape of the argument is just: a tree f
               questions deep has at most 2 f leaves, so it can’t tell apart more than 2 f cases.
                                                         8.4 What narrowing costs: count the rivals   211


    And then the obvious next question: is the floor always the price? Try five cards.
There are 120 orders, log2 of 120 is a bit under 7, so you need at least seven
questions, and seven is enough, though not by the obvious method. Finding the
way is a good evening with a deck of cards (Knuth has it, under the name merge
insertion, from the mathematicians Lester Ford and Selmer Johnson in 1959). Now
take twelve cards. They can be in 479,001,600 orders, log2 of that is about 28.8,
so the count says at least 29. Ford and Johnson’s method takes 30, and in 1965
Mark Wells, a mathematician at Los Alamos who built a programming language for
exactly this kind of combinatorial search, showed by a computer search that nothing
does better: twelve cards need 30. The floor was 29 and the price is 30, so the count
is a floor and only a floor; it never promises the floor can be reached, and the bound
later in this section has to be read exactly the same way.
    Ralph Hartley, an electronics researcher at Bell Labs, writing in the Bell System
Technical Journal in 1928, before Shannon, measured information exactly this way:
the logarithm of the number of possibilities, no probabilities, just a count. I use that
measure here, and I’ll say plainly it’s Hartley’s. Shannon’s would need a distribution
over the list, and there isn’t one; there’s just the list’s length.
    The same count works with something you can hold. Put three coins under three
cups. Each coin is heads or tails, so there are eight possible rows under the cups.
Someone hands you two answers: heads under the first cup, tails under the second.
Lift the first cup and compare, and a matching answer leaves four possible rows. Lift
the second and compare, and a match leaves two. The last coin can still be either
way. The list really shrank: eight, four, two. Nothing in that count needed a claim
about which way the last coin faces.
    This is a parlour game, and an old one. In A Christmas Carol, in 1843, Scrooge’s
nephew Fred plays a game called Yes and No at his Christmas party: he thinks
of something, and everybody else asks questions he may only answer yes or no.
He’s thinking of an animal, a disagreeable, savage one that growls and grunts and
lives in London, and the answer is Uncle Scrooge. Most people know the game as
twenty questions, and twenty is a good number for it: a balanced question splits
the remaining field in half, and twenty such questions can guarantee identification
among 220 = 1,048,576 possibilities. A lucky answer to “is it this one?” can finish
immediately; the count is about handling every possible answer. Push on that,
though. The halving only happens because Fred answers truthfully about what’s
actually in his head. Lie once and the count still shrinks; it shrinks around the wrong
animal. The cups showed the same thing: the four and the two are real because
you lifted the cup and compared. Being told what was under it wouldn’t have made
them real.
    Now put it on a run. Say a run comes with a list of states that are “still on the
table,” the candidates, and a shorter list, with some ruled out. Call the first the prior
212   8 Structural entitlement


               and the second the posterior, and I want you to hear those as a list you could print.
               They aren’t “the space of possible worlds.” Picture the ruling-out as observations,
               each observation that ruled something out being one branch point in a tree like the
               card tree. The bound says that if that tree is no deeper than the number of paid
               steps the run took, and the tree has enough leaves to cover the narrowing in a way
               I’ll spell out in a moment, then the counter rose by at least log2 of the prior’s length,
               rounded up, minus log2 of the posterior’s length, rounded up. Put another way, the
               counter rose by at least one unit for each of the index bits the list lost, where the
               index bits of a list are the yes/no questions it takes to point at one entry of it, the
               card count again.
                    “Paid step” needs its own sentence. It means a step the price list charges at least
               one for. In a Thiele machine the toll guarantees that every crossing of the reading is
               one; a price list may put a floor under more steps than that (a look, a send, a check),
               and the count takes every paid step there is. The tree is a bare shape, branches
               and leaves with nothing written on them, and “no deeper than the number of paid
               steps” is a count along the run that happened, not a walk down the tree. A paid step
               doesn’t have to have asked any question at all.
                    Notice, too, what the bound does and doesn’t say about the run. It takes the two
               lists, the tree and the covering as given. It doesn’t say the run produced the posterior
               from the prior; nothing in it reads the lists off the run. What it says is that, given
               lists, a tree and a covering that someone supplies, the paid steps of the run cover
               the rounded drop in list length. Here Section 4’s warning comes due: watching can
               narrow without costing anything, so the payment can’t be dug out of the narrowing.
               It goes in as a premise, the tree’s depth against the paid steps, and I’ll keep calling it
               one. Later in this section the run makes the posterior itself, from a prior and the
               tests it passed (Theorem 8.4), and then the premise is a share each test keeps.


               8.5 What “narrower” buys: a stronger test
               Before the count, one link that’s pure logic, and Plato’s third account is the whole
               of it. Take a list of candidates and an observation, a function that says what each
               candidate looks like from outside. The list’s membership test accepts an observation
               when some candidate on the list shows it. Shrink the list, and the test can only get
               pickier: anything the short list’s test accepts, the long list’s accepts too. The word
               for that, and it runs backward from English, is stronger: the stronger test is the one
               that lets fewer things through.
                   Pickier, though, isn’t the same as strictly pickier, and the cards show the gap. Take
               all six orders as the prior, and as the posterior the three where card 1 sits left of card
               2: 1-2-3, 1-3-2 and 3-1-2. First observation: “is 1 left of 2?” Every survivor says yes,
               and the removed 2-1-3 says no, so the prior’s test accepts yes and no, the posterior’s
                                                                             8.6 The count, exactly   213


only yes, and the posterior’s test is strictly stronger. Second observation, same two
lists: “is the first card a 3?” Now 3-1-2 says yes and the other two survivors say no,
and among the removed orders 3-2-1 says yes and 2-1-3 says no. Both tests accept
yes and no, so they have the same strength, even though three orders are gone.
What made the difference is a removed candidate whose observation no survivor
shares. Such a candidate is Plato’s mark, the thing that sets this case apart from
everything it could be confused with, turned into a function. Narrow the list and
keep one distinguishing removed candidate, and the test is strictly stronger; narrow
it without one, and the test may not have moved at all.


8.6 The count, exactly
I’ll set out the words and then the count, for any system with Section 6’s counter. A
list is a finite list of candidates, repeats allowed, and |Ω| is the length of the list Ω,
repeats counted. ⌈log2 x ⌉ is the base-two logarithm of x rounded up: the smallest
k ∈ N with 2k ≥ x. At x = 0 it is 0, since 20 ≥ 0. And a −̇ b is subtraction on whole
numbers that stops at zero, so 3 −̇ 5 = 0.

Definition 8.2 (Decision tree). A decision tree is a leaf, or a branch with two subtrees.
Its depth is 0 for a leaf and one more than the deeper subtree for a branch; its leaf
count L( T ) is 1 for a leaf and the sum of the two counts for a branch. Nothing is
written on a tree: no question, no answer, no candidate.



Lemma 8.1 (A tree is no wider than two to its depth). For every decision tree T,
L( T ) ≤ 2depth(T ) , and so ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ ≤ depth( T ).

Proof. Start at the root. At the first level there can be at most two places, at the
second at most four, and each further level at most doubles the places available. To
count leaves that stop early as well, extend each such leaf with branches until all
tips reach the tree’s greatest depth. This only adds leaves. At depth d the filled-out
tree has 2d tips, so the original tree has at most that many leaves. For depth zero
there is just the root, which is one leaf.
   Thus d bits are enough to number all the leaves. The least number of bits that
will do, ⌈log2 L( T )⌉, cannot be greater than d.
    Nothing about any machine is in the definition or the lemma. They’re about trees,
a leaf or a branch, and nothing else.
214   8 Structural entitlement




               Theorem 8.2 (Paid narrowing, counted). Take a system with a counter µ and a price
               list c that obey conservation (Theorem 6.2): each step raises µ by exactly its charge.
               Let Ω and Ω′ be lists with |Ω′ | > 0, let T be a decision tree with |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |
               (the tree covers the narrowing), and let t be a run from s ending at s′ in which at
               least depth( T ) steps are charged at least one each. Then
                                 ′
                  |Ω| ≤ 2µ(s )−µ(s) · |Ω′ |,          so      ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ µ(s′ ) − µ(s).

               Proof. Count the bill first. There are at least as many paid steps as levels in the tree.
               Each paid step adds at least one and every other charge is nonnegative. The total
               bill is therefore at least the tree’s depth. Conservation says that bill is exactly the
               counter’s rise, µ(s′ ) − µ(s).
                   Now count the room the tree supplies. It has at most two to its depth leaves. The
               covering premise allows at most |Ω′ | prior entries per leaf, so
                                                                                 ′
                                     |Ω| ≤ L( T )|Ω′ | ≤ 2depth(T ) |Ω′ | ≤ 2µ(s )−µ(s) |Ω′ |.
               That is the first bound.
                  For the bit version, let k = ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉. The posterior has at most 2k entries.
                                                                                ′
               Insert that count in the first bound: the prior has at most 2µ(s )−µ(s)+k entries. So
               numbering its entries needs no more than the counter’s rise plus k bits. Subtracting
               the posterior’s k bits gives the claimed bound; if the subtraction would go negative,
               the stipulated subtraction stops at zero. An empty prior already has bit count zero
               and satisfies the same conclusion.
                   Two arguments are stuck together in that proof, and they come apart. The tree
               half (the covering and the lemma) bounds the index bits by the sum of the charges
               of the run, on any price list at all. Conservation is only what turns that sum into the
               counter’s rise. So the form in terms of cost, with the sum of the charges in place of
               the counter, holds in any Thiele machine, and it’s part (3) of Theorem 8.3 below.
               The shape of the bound shows in what’s missing from the hypotheses: anything
               tying the lists to the run.
                   There are three honest pieces of small print, all of them visible in the statement.
               Both logarithms round up separately, and the subtraction stops at zero, so when the
               prior and the posterior round up to the same number of index bits (four candidates
               narrowed to three, say) the rounded bound says nothing, though the first form of the
               theorem charges the run one unit: one leaf can’t cover four candidates with three.
               The lists are plain lists, repeats allowed, so “index bits” is a difference of rounded list
               lengths with repeats counted; a list can get shorter by dropping a duplicate without
               losing a single candidate, and “a candidate was ruled out” and “the list got shorter”
                                                                          8.6 The count, exactly   215


are two different claims. And the difference isn’t the number of questions anyone
asked.
    The covering condition, |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |, is the nearest thing the count has to
an anti-stopped-clock clause, and I have to be exact about how near. Picture each
survivor standing for a little crowd of the prior’s candidates, a crowd no bigger than
the tree has leaves. The condition says the crowds can hold the whole prior between
them: share the prior’s candidates out among them and none overflows. That limits
how much can be deleted per leaf you paid for, but it doesn’t say why anything was
deleted. So the condition rules out deleting too much for the tree you’ve paid for,
and it doesn’t rule out deleting for no reason. A run can satisfy every hypothesis
of the count and have ruled nothing out on purpose; the count prices the size of
the drop and says nothing about the honesty of it. And the covering can’t just be
dropped. On the small machine of Part III (Section 15), whose record moves CHECK,
COMMIT and CERTIFY cost one each, take the sixteen starts with A at 0 through 15,
and the run CHECK “A ≥ 15,” COMMIT, CERTIFY from the start with A at 15. One
yes-or-no question with a big constant in it narrows sixteen candidates to one, four
index bits, and the run has three paid steps, a ledger of three. A tree no deeper than
three has at most eight leaves, and eight times one survivor is less than sixteen, so
the covering fails, and without it the bound would say 4 ≤ 3. More candidates only
widen the gap: 2n starts and the constant 2n − 1 give n index bits for the same cost
of three (Section 15.14, Proposition 15.39).
    A side trip is worth taking here, because it looks like it breaks the count and
doesn’t. Two information theorists, Rudolf Ahlswede and Gunter Dueck (1989),
noticed that asking “is it this one?” is a different job from asking “which one is it?”
If each receiver only wants to know whether the message is theirs, a noisy channel
used n times can serve a number of receivers that grows like two raised to two to
the nC, with C the channel’s capacity, where naming the message only gets you
two to the nC. The task is called identification, and on its face it says checking
can be exponentially cheaper than naming. But their tests are allowed to say yes
wrongly once in a while. Make the yes sound, a test that never says yes to the wrong
message, which is the only kind of check this book lets raise a record, and the double
exponential collapses. The argument is two lines of pigeonhole. Each receiver’s test,
to be any use, says yes on some output its own message can produce, and soundness
means no other message can produce that output; so those outputs are all different,
one per receiver, and there can’t be more receivers than outputs, |Y |n for an output
alphabet Y. That bound is single exponential, the same order as naming. So for a
check that never lies, the card count is the right scale after all, and the cheap trick
needs a check that can be fooled.
216   8 Structural entitlement


               8.7 What you’ve got
               A paid flag is not a true claim; Section 7 left it at “a paid flag is a paid flag,” and
               Section 9 will say it flatly. What a paid flag with an object and a checked relation
               behind it gives you is entitlement: anyone auditing the run may treat the claim as
               established, and can point at the event where that became legitimate. (Nothing
               in the five parts makes the system itself read the flag; I said that above and I’m
               saying it again because it’s the sentence most likely to get lost.) Entitlement costs
               at least the index bits of narrowing it commits to, given lists, a tree and a covering
               somebody supplies, and given a run that paid for the tree’s depth. The cups say why
               entitlement and truth are different. Plato says what the checked relation has to do,
               which is to distinguish. Necula says how to build it. Hartley says what to count.
                   Put the three pieces on one hypothesis list (narrow the list with a test that
               separates, find the paid event, count the charges against a tree the run paid for) and
               you get a single statement, structural entitlement, once over any Thiele machine
               and once, under the longer name structural entitlement represented, for every
               certified Thiele-complete machine, the small machine included (Theorem 15.36).
               The machine version asks the same things with two changes: the run starts clean
               instead of merely at no, and the paid steps are the run’s own record moves, CHECK,
               COMMIT and CERTIFY, at a cost of exactly one each. The first one reads as follows.


               Theorem 8.3 (Structural entitlement, over any Thiele machine). Take a Thiele
               machine (Definition 2.1), a state s that reads no, and a run t from s that ends in a
               state that reads yes. Take a type of candidates, a type of observations with an exact
               equality test, an observation obs of each candidate, and a decoder d that turns a run
               into an observation (what its record shows). Take lists Ω and Ω′ of candidates and
               a decision tree T such that: (H1) Ω′ strictly narrows Ω: every member of Ω′ is in Ω,
               and some member of Ω isn’t in Ω′ ; (H2) some dropped candidate w, in Ω and not
               in Ω′ , shows an observation different from every survivor’s; (H3) the decoded run
               d(t) is shown by some survivor; (H4) |Ω′ | > 0 and |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |; (H5) at least
               depth( T ) steps of the run are charged at least one each. Then (1) the membership
               test of Ω′ is strictly stronger than the membership test of Ω; (2) some step of the
               run took the reading from no to yes, and that step was charged at least one; and (3)
               the sum of the charges of the run’s steps is at least ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉.

               Proof. (1) is the cards’ argument: the dropped w shows something no survivor
               shows, so the posterior test says no where the prior test says yes, and every survivor
               was in the prior, so nothing the posterior accepts is refused by the prior. (2) The run
               starts at no and ends at yes, so at some step the reading goes from no to yes, and
               the toll charges that step at least one. (3) is the proof of Theorem 8.2 with the sum
                                                                                8.7 What you’ve got   217


of the charges in place of the counter’s rise: the covering and Lemma 8.1 bound the
index bits by depth( T ), and the sum of the charges is at least the number of steps
charged at least one. On a system that obeys conservation the sum of the charges is
the counter’s rise.
    Theorem 8.2 is the same count with the counter’s rise, so for a system that obeys
conservation it’s the special case. Three things in the hypotheses feed nothing, and
I’m naming them here so you don’t have to find them: (H3) isn’t used by any of the
three conclusions; from (H1) only the inclusion is used, and the gap goes unused;
and in (H2) the words “not in Ω′ ” go unused, since a candidate whose observation
differs from every survivor’s can’t be a survivor itself. And (H4)’s |Ω′ | > 0 is used
in that proof but can be dropped too: the covering forces it once the prior has a
member.
    A statement like that is true by packaging: it takes the hypotheses in and hands
the conclusions back, and the right word for it is a checklist, a checklist for leaning
on a claim. It discovers nothing about leaning. The version in which the run itself
does the narrowing, Theorem 8.4, comes later in this section.
    And a checklist isn’t nothing. On 30 October 1935, at Wright Field, northeast of
Dayton, Ohio, the Army was evaluating Boeing’s new four-engine bomber, the Model
299. Shortly after take-off it plunged back onto the field and caught fire; that’s how
the wire report of that day has it, and the later histories add that it pitched up and
stalled first, which is what elevators locked in a raised position would do. Two men
died of their injuries, the Army’s pilot, Major Ployer Hill, and Boeing’s chief test pilot,
Leslie Tower. The airplane was fine. The crew had left the gust locks on, a locking
mechanism worked from inside the cockpit that holds the control surfaces still while
the plane sits on the ground. There’s a famous line that a newspaper called it too
much airplane for one man to fly. I couldn’t find that line in any paper from 1935;
the earliest place I could find it is a New Yorker article from December 2007 by Atul
Gawande, a surgeon who writes about how people get complicated work right, and
he names no newspaper, so take it as a lead. What I can find is what came after. The
answer was a card: a list of things to check, in order, every time, and the crews of
the airplane worked through written checklists for each phase of flight. The most
careful history of it I found is by Walter Boyne, a retired Air Force colonel and a
former director of the National Air and Space Museum. By his account it wasn’t
the first written routine for a pilot; those go back before the First World War. And
it’s this crash, he says, that made the checklist the way a crew flew. The airplane
went on to be the B-17. Nothing on that card was a discovery. Every item on it was
something the pilots already knew. What the card did was make sure none of it
got left out when it mattered. Putting entitlement’s hypotheses on one list does the
218   8 Structural entitlement


               same: it finds nothing new about leaning on a claim, and it makes the hypotheses
               impossible to drop quietly.


               8.8 When the run does the narrowing
               Theorem 8.3 takes the lists in. In the version below, the run makes the posterior,
               and the count stops being an item on the list and becomes a consequence. That
               version needs one thing a bare Thiele machine doesn’t have: which steps are tests,
               and what each asks. So a reading names them. For each instruction it gives either
               nothing or a yes-or-no question about the state the run is in when it gets there, and
               a test step passes when its question says yes there. The candidates are states the run
               could have started from. A passed test is asked of a candidate by running the same
               moves from the candidate up to that step and asking the same question there. The
               posterior is the candidates that pass every test the run passed, asked that way, in the
               order the run asked them.


               Theorem 8.4 (Structural entitlement, with the narrowing made by the run). Take
               a Thiele machine and a reading that names its test steps, every test step charged
               at least one. Take a state s that reads no, a run t from s that ends in a state that
               reads yes, and a list Ω of candidate starts that contains s. Let Ω′ be the posterior t
               makes from Ω, and let bi and ai be the numbers of candidates standing just before
               and just after the ith test t passed. Then (1) Ω′ sits inside Ω and contains s; (2)
               every candidate of Ω that isn’t in Ω′ fails, asked that way, a test t passed; (3)
               |Ω| · ∏i ai = |Ω′ | · ∏i bi ; (4) if every test t passed keeps at least a 2−k share of the
               candidates standing before it, bi ≤ 2k ai , then ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ is at most
               k times the number of tests t passed, that number is at most the number of steps
               charged at least one, and the index bits are at most k times the sum of the charges;
               and (5) some step of t took the reading from no to yes and was charged at least one.

               Proof. (1) Start with the prior list. Each passed test only removes candidates; it
               never inserts one. The actual start s passes every test used to filter the list, because
               these are precisely the tests the actual run passed. So s remains throughout, and the
               final list is a nonempty part of the original.
                   (2) Follow any candidate that is absent at the end. It was present at first, so there
               is a first test at which it disappears. The filter removes it only when its version of
               that test says no while the actual run’s says yes. That test is the required witness.
                   (3) Write the list lengths on the bench: q0 before any passed test, q1 after the
               first, through qn after the last. Here q0 = |Ω| and qn = |Ω′ |. Every before-count bi
               is qi−1 and every after-count ai is qi . The left product in the statement is therefore
                                                              8.9 A grouping, checked and committed   219


q0 q1 · · · qn ; the right product has the same factors with qn placed first. They are
equal, including when there are no tests and both products are empty products,
equal to one.
    (4) At the first test the share premise gives q0 ≤ 2k q1 . At the second it gives
q1 ≤ 2k q2 . Substitute one into the other, and continue. After n tests, q0 ≤ 2kn qn . If
j bits number the final candidates, then qn ≤ 2 j , so kn + j bits suffice to number the
original ones. The rounded bit drop is at most kn. Each of the n passed tests is a
separate paid step, and each adds at least one to the nonnegative bill. Thus n is
at most the number of paid steps and at most the total charge, giving the two cost
comparisons.
    (5) Read the actual run from its initial no until its first yes. The preceding reading
was no, so that step raised it. The toll charges that step at least one.
    Part (3) is the exact count: take base-two logarithms and log2 |Ω| − log2 |Ω′ | is
the sum, over the tests the run passed, of log2 (bi /ai ), the bits each one took. Part (2)
answers the complaint I made about the covering, that it doesn’t say why anything
was deleted: here everything deleted was deleted by a test the run passed and paid
for. Two premises stay, the prior list and the share, a bound k fixed before the run on
what one test can take. Every run meets some bound, its own biggest test’s, so what
the share adds is fixing it in advance, and that is needed. On the small machine
one CHECK of “A ≥ 15,” asked of sixteen candidates, keeps one, a 2−4 share, and
narrows by 4 index bits on a run of 3 record moves (Proposition 15.39); with k = 1
part (4) would say 4 ≤ 3. The same statement on every certified Thiele-complete
machine, where the tests are the CHECK moves and the charges are counted by the
ledger, is Theorem 15.38.


8.9 A grouping, checked and committed

Section 5 ended on buckets, and the toll of Part I never needed them: it prices any
yes-or-no reading. In this subsection the word in this section’s title gets attached to
a partition in a theorem. Take a pile, a finite list of items, and a grouping, a bucket
label for each item. Its partition is “same label,” and the classes of that relation are a
partition in the sense of Definition 5.1. The data is a key for each item, drawn from
any type with at least two values (a grouping’s own labels can serve as a key), and a
grouping is sound for a key when any two items it puts in one bucket have the same
key. The grouping says “these belong together,” and the key says whether they do.
One grouping refines another when every bucket of the first sits inside a bucket of
the second.
   Put two red buttons and two blue buttons on the table, numbered 1 through
4, with 1 and 2 red. Let the key be colour. Circles round {1, 2} and {3, 4} give a
sound grouping: every pair inside a circle has the same colour. Split the red circle
220   8 Structural entitlement


               into two singletons and it stays sound; splitting cannot introduce a mismatched pair.
               Join 1 and 3 instead and it fails. Changing the circles’ names from A and B to North
               and South changes none of these checks. That is why the reading below uses the
               partition, not the spelling of its labels.
                  Now comes the rule for the record. Put a tick beside a grouping only after
               comparing the colours within each circle. Copy that ticked grouping onto a separate
               commitment card, then place the card in a record envelope; charge one tally for
               each of those three acts. Change a button’s colour between the check and the copy,
               and the old tick must no longer authorize the copy. The machine’s SET rule below
               does that by clearing the current table and channel. A record already kept remains
               about the old colours, which it keeps with the grouping.
                  Here is one example machine that meets the model, the smallest I know that
               makes a record from a checked claim. It is an illustration; the theorem above holds
               of any Thiele machine. The bucket machine holds a key, a table of checked groupings,
               a channel, a record, a trap latch and a ledger. SET costs nothing; it replaces the key
               and throws away the table and the channel, which were checked against the old key.
               CHECK g costs one and passes when g is sound for the current key, and, when it
               passes, writes g in the table. COMMIT g costs one and passes when the table holds
               a grouping with the same partition as g, and puts g in the channel. CERTIFY costs
               one and passes when the channel holds a grouping; if the record is still down it
               then keeps that grouping with the current key, the key a grouping with its partition
               was checked against, and a record already kept is left as it is. A CHECK, COMMIT
               or CERTIFY that fails traps, and a trapped machine only pays. The reading for a
               grouping g is: the record holds a grouping with g’s partition. In words, that reading
               says “this grouping has been checked and committed.”


               Theorem 8.5 (A committed grouping entitles exactly its refinements). (1) The
               classes of “same label” under any grouping form a partition. (2) Two groupings with
               the same partition of the pile have the same reading at every state of the bucket
               machine. (3) For groupings g and h of the pile, soundness of g for a key gives
               soundness of h for that key, for every key, exactly when h refines g. (4) On every run
               from a clean state (table and channel empty, record down), if the reading for g is up,
               the record holds a grouping and a key for which g is sound, and so is every grouping
               that refines g; and for every grouping h that doesn’t refine g there is a key for which
               g is sound and h isn’t. (5) The bucket machine obeys the toll, and a run from a clean
               state that ends with the record up has raised the ledger by at least three.
                                                           8.9 A grouping, checked and committed   221


Proof. (1) Every item has its own label, exchanging two items does not change
whether their labels agree, and two agreements through a third label give agreement
with each other. Thus “same label” has the three sameness rules, and its classes form
the partition already constructed in Theorem 5.1.
    (2) The reading asks which items were put together, not what the buckets were
called. Replacing one grouping by another with exactly the same buckets therefore
changes no answer to that reading.
    (3) If h only cuts g’s buckets smaller, every pair h keeps together was already
together under g. Soundness of g gives that pair equal keys, so h is sound too. If h
does anything else, it puts some two items together that g kept in separate buckets.
Give every item in the first item’s g-bucket one key value and every other item a
second key value. Each g-bucket has a single key, so g is sound. The chosen h-bucket
contains both key values, so h is not. This is why the key type needs two values.
    (4) Follow the table, channel and record through the commands. They begin
empty. CHECK inserts only a grouping it has found sound for the current key.
COMMIT takes the partition of a grouping already in that table, so the selected
grouping is sound for the same key. CERTIFY keeps that grouping and that key
together; later commands do not replace an existing record. SET changes the
key but empties both the table and the channel, so no old unchecked carry-over
remains there. A failed command traps instead of inserting an unsound grouping,
and trapped commands leave those fields alone. These are all the ways those
fields change. Their promised soundness therefore survives every command of any
run from the clean start. Apply (3) to the grouping and key in the record: every
refinement is sound, and every non-refinement has the counterexample key just
constructed.
    (5) Only CERTIFY raises the record, and its price is one, giving the toll. A
successful CERTIFY needs a grouping in the channel. From an empty channel only a
successful COMMIT could have supplied it. From an empty table that COMMIT in
turn needs a successful CHECK. These are three distinct earlier acts in order, each
charged one. The run’s nonnegative bill is at least three.
    So “structural” has a theorem under it. The reading sees a grouping only through
its partition, which is item (2). If the recorded circles are sound, so is any way of
cutting them smaller, whatever the key is. A grouping that isn’t a cutting-smaller can
still happen to be sound for this key (paint all four buttons red and every grouping
is sound), but nothing in the record promises it: for some key it fails. Item (3) and
item (4) say exactly that much, and that’s all the record buys. It’s the three parts
of entitlement from the start of this section in their smallest case: the object is the
grouping, the checked relation is soundness for the key, and the paid event is the
CERTIFY, on top of a CHECK and a COMMIT at a cost of one each. What it doesn’t
222   8 Structural entitlement


               do is make a later move act on the record. The only move that reads it is CERTIFY,
               and only to leave a kept grouping alone. Like everything in this section, it says what
               someone auditing the run may conclude.
                  Before the machine of Part III, I owe you the word the toll is named after, the
               “insight” in “No Free Insight” (Section 4), because I’ve been using it as if it meant
               one thing.
CHAPTER 9




What insight is

I named the rule in this book “No Free Insight,” and the name ran ahead of any
careful account of what insight is. The book has been narrowing it ever since: not
learning (Section 4), not looking, not copying. Part I already says where to look:
learning borrows and committing pays, so the part of insight a toll can price is the
part that stays. It’s time to say what that is, and to say it in a way that someone who
studies actual insight, in actual heads, wouldn’t laugh at. So who are those people,
and what did they find? I’ll go through what I ran into and push on each piece as I
go. Where a story reached me secondhand, I treat it as a lead to check.


9.1 Sultan and the sticks
In 1913 the psychologist Wolfgang Köhler went to Tenerife to run a research station
with a colony of chimpanzees, and the First World War then kept him there until
1920, five years longer than planned, with the chimpanzees to watch. The famous
one is Sultan. Food is outside the cage, out of reach; two sticks are inside, each
too short, but one fits into the end of the other. Sultan tries each stick, fails, sulks,
plays with the sticks, and then, by Köhler’s account, at a moment you can see, joins
them and reaches the food. Köhler’s words were Einsicht and einsichtig, which came
into English as “insight,” and the whole school of psychology he belonged to, the
Gestalt school, said that’s what thinking is: a restructuring, the moment two sticks
stop being two sticks and become one tool. Stacking up tries until one works was,
for them, something else. Karl Duncker gave the human version, in German in 1935
and in English in 1945, five years after he died at thirty-seven; he’d spent his last
years working with Köhler at Swarthmore. You can set it up yourself: a candle, a
box of tacks, matches, and the task of fixing the candle to the wall. Almost nobody
sees that the box is a shelf, until they do. And then he found that if you hand people
the box empty, with the tacks poured out beside it, they solve it far more readily.
The objects were the same; what changed was which relation among them was on
the table.
   I like both of these for the same reason: the insight didn’t add an object. Sultan
had both sticks the whole time. The box was there the whole time. What arrived
was a relation, which is to say a piece of structure in Section 5’s sense, and the


                                                  223
224   9 What insight is


               arrival was sudden. Hold that, because the thing the toll prices also arrives in one
               step, and at its best it’s also a relation.


               9.2 It isn’t a feeling
               But there’s a finding I’d hand anyone who thinks insight is a feeling, and it comes
               from someone who measured it. In the 1980s the psychologist Janet Metcalfe asked
               people to solve problems while rating, every fifteen seconds, how “warm” they felt,
               how close to the answer. On ordinary problems, algebra for instance, the warmth
               climbs steadily and peaks at the answer, which is what you’d expect. On insight
               problems, riddles of the candle-box kind, the warmth stays flat, flat, flat, and then
               the answer arrives, and if anything the people who felt warmest beforehand were
               more likely to be wrong. She put that last finding in the title of a 1986 paper:
               premonitions of insight predict impending error. The feeling of being close is not a
               gauge of being close. Try it yourself: write a number from one to seven every fifteen
               seconds while doing a long sum, then while doing a riddle, and compare the curves.
                   And the most famous insight story there is fits Metcalfe uncomfortably well.
               Archimedes, a mathematician who died in 212 BC, asked by Hiero, the king of
               Syracuse, whether a goldsmith had cheated him on a crown, gets into a bath, sees
               the water rise, and runs home naked shouting “eureka,” I’ve found it. That comes
               from Vitruvius, a Roman writer on architecture, writing about two centuries later. Is
               it true? Galileo Galilei, then a young Italian mathematician, at twenty-two, in 1586,
               took it as known that Archimedes caught the goldsmith. What he didn’t buy was the
               method. Water spilling over the side, as Vitruvius tells it, was to him “a crude thing,
               far from scientific precision,” and he guessed some writer had set down a rumour.
               So he wrote a little tract, La Bilancetta, proposing a balance weighed in air and in
               water instead, which he thought was probably what Archimedes actually did, since
               it rests on Archimedes’s own results. Whether there was ever a bath, or a shout,
               nobody can check now. What survives is a story two centuries late, wrapped around
               a real man and probably a real problem. Notice what the legend kept: the bath, the
               shout, the running home naked, which is to say the feeling. What it left shaky is the
               part that would count as the check, the test that could have caught the goldsmith.
               The bit everybody remembers is the bit that tells you least.
                   So any account of insight that keys on the sensation, the “aha,” is keyed to
               something that the data says is unreliable. Whatever insight is, it isn’t the feeling of
               having it. That’s a relief, because a system of states and moves doesn’t have feelings,
               and a word that only meant a feeling would be cheating if I hung it on one. The
               version this book can price has to be keyed to an event, and the question is which.
                                                      9.3 What happens when a computation learns   225


9.3 What happens when a computation learns
I’ll lay out the split first, then say what the toll does with each part, and then say
who decided the split. Keep Section 2’s sheet of paper in front of you: the NO box,
the YES box, the tally line, and the three moves STAY, WORK and VOUCH.
     The first thing: raw observation. Something comes in and gets written down. A
counter ticks. Nothing is claimed about what it means, nothing is marked as resting
on it, and the reading doesn’t move because of it. Later moves can read what it
wrote, but that reading is a move of its own. The demon’s pad in Section 4 was raw
observation, and raw observation is what the statistician Dennis Lindley measured
in 1956 as the information provided by an experiment, the words of his title, and
defined as the expected drop in your uncertainty: a real quantity, and a quantity
about what was seen. It can cost nothing on the ledger. The toll says nothing at all
about a move that doesn’t cross from NO to YES, so a price list may charge it zero:
on the paper, STAY and WORK cost nothing, and Section 4’s watcher narrowed a
whole row of candidates without paying anything. “Can” is the word that matters.
A price list is allowed to charge for looking anyway. And in the physical world a
look takes something too: copied onto a blank page it merges nothing and owes no
floor under Landauer’s premise, but it still dissipates when it happens, in any real
device, and it uses up the page, which means taking states the machine hasn’t used,
borrowed until the page is wiped (Section 4).
     Lindley’s measure has a back story, and it runs through Bletchley Park. I. J. Good,
who was Alan Turing’s main statistical assistant at Bletchley Park in 1941, wrote in
1979 that Turing had worked out the expected weight of evidence an experiment
would give, to judge one of the codebreaking procedures before running it, and so
partly anticipated Lindley by about fifteen years, in work that stayed secret. Turing
measured evidence in bans, logarithms to base ten, with a tenth of one called a
deciban, and the name came from the town of Banbury, where tens of thousands of
the sheets used in that procedure were printed. It’s the same base-ten unit other
people call the hartley, after the Hartley from the last section. And Good adds that
Turing didn’t know the logarithm he was using had already appeared in 1878, in a
paper by Charles Sanders Peirce, the same Peirce from Section 5, who’d called it the
weight of evidence. Peirce is as far back as Good takes it. It changes nothing in the
argument, but it shows how well trodden this first kind of thing is. For a century and
a half careful people have measured what an observation tells you, and every one of
those measures is about what was seen. The toll leaves that side of the line alone.
     The second thing: the raise. Some move turns the reading from NO to YES, and
that move is where the toll applies. In any system with the five parts that obeys
the toll, that move costs at least one, and every run that starts at NO and ends at
YES pays at least one somewhere along the way, which is Section 2’s universal floor.
226   9 What insight is


              What’s being charged for, at its best, is exactly the Gestalt thing, a relation committed
              to: one tool, claimed, out of two sticks. I say “at its best” because Section 2 was
              careful about what YES means: the flag is up, and nothing more. A crossing that
              writes down which relation it’s committing to carries Sultan’s tool with it. A bare
              crossing, VOUCH on the paper, commits to no relation at all, and it pays exactly the
              same.
                   The third thing isn’t a kind of event. It’s an observation about the price: it’s
              flat, whatever is certified. Say the YES state also shows something striking, a deep
              relation, a result nobody could have guessed, Sultan’s two sticks become one tool.
              The toll charges the crossing at least one. It doesn’t charge the striking crossing
              more, because the floor’s proof never looks at anything but the reading before and
              after. On the paper, VOUCH from NO makes one mark whether you were thinking
              of Duncker’s box or of lunch. Meaning is not cost; the depth of what’s certified adds
              meaning, and it doesn’t add a unit.
                   The candle box has a footnote that says the same thing from the other side. In
              1962 the psychologist Sam Glucksberg ran Duncker’s problem with money on it:
              some people were told they could win five or twenty dollars depending on how
              fast they solved it. With the tacks in the box, the people chasing the money did
              worse than the people who weren’t. With the box empty the problem was easier for
              everybody, and the accounts I’ve read don’t agree on what the money did there, so
              I’ll leave that half alone. Paying more didn’t buy the insight, and on the hard version
              it got in the way. That’s a fact about heads. It says nothing about records, and I
              won’t push it further than that. But it makes a nice parallel to the paper. On the
              paper a deeper crossing isn’t charged more, and in Glucksberg’s room a bigger prize
              didn’t bring the crossing sooner. In neither place does the price measure the depth.
                   I’ll state them exactly now, for any Thiele machine (Definition 2.1). A run is still
              just a list of moves, carried out in the order written. The question is which of those
              moves crosses from no to yes, and what that crossing lets you conclude about the
              total charge.

               Definition 9.1 (Raise, non-raising move). In a Thiele machine, a step from state s by
               move i is a raise when it turns the reading on: cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes.
               A move i is a non-raising move when no step by it, from any state, is a raise. Raw
               observation, the first thing above, is one kind.

               Remark 9.1 (What the toll prices, and what it doesn’t). All three read straight off
               Definition 2.1 and Observation 2.1, with Section 2’s board as the example. (1) The
               toll puts no bound on the cost of a non-raising move; on Section 2’s board STAY and
               WORK are non-raising moves and cost 0. (2) Every raise is charged at least 1, by the
               toll, and every run from a state reading no to one reading yes has total cost at least
                                  9.4 Test, then commit, and nothing forces the second to follow the first   227


1, by the universal floor. (3) The price is flat: the floor’s proof uses nothing about the
end state but its reading, so it gives the same floor of 1 whatever else the end state
shows. A higher floor needs more hypotheses than the toll, and those hypotheses do
the work. A system that wants to charge more for a deeper certification has to write
that into its price list, move by move; the toll doesn’t do it for anyone.
   So the account comes down to two facts and a warning: looking can stay off the
ledger, turning the reading on can’t, and the toll alone does not charge more for a
remarkable claim, though another pricing rule or an additional requirement could.
   Who decided the split? The costs alone didn’t. The toll prices exactly one thing,
the crossing. A price list is allowed to put a floor under more moves than that (a
look, a send, a check) and allowed to leave other moves at zero, so the sorting into
non-raising moves and raises is by whether the reading moves, and that sorting is
this book’s. The part that’s forced is the floor under the crossing, once you grant a
reading that stays up, finitely many states that read yes, and a price on every merge;
Section 3 is the argument; anything a price list charges beyond that is a choice,
and any concrete machine owes you its whole table so you can see which choices it
made.


9.4 Test, then commit, and nothing forces the second to follow the first

The philosopher Karl Popper said a theory earns its standing by being exposed: you
make a conjecture, you try to kill it, and what survives a real attempt counts for
something, where “real” means the test could have failed. His word for that earned
credit is corroboration. I lean on that idea all through this book (Section 14 gives it
its full due), and this subsection shows where a Thiele machine has a version of it
and where that version is weaker than Popper, which I have to say plainly.
    Add a fourth move to the paper: CHECK. It looks at something (a sum, a coin
under a cup, a formula against a row of values), and it can come out pass or fail,
and it doesn’t move the box. Charge it whatever you like; charging it on the attempt,
pass or fail, fits Popper, because what made his test count was that it was really run
and could have failed. CHECK is the test, and it’s a non-raising move in the sense
above, because it never turns the reading on. VOUCH is the commit. So the honest
protocol is two moves: test, then commit, and the costs are separate, one for the
checking work and one for the crossing.
    But nothing in the five parts makes the second move wait for the first. The step
is handed the current state and a move name; the toll looks only at whether the
reading crossed. Play VOUCH from NO with no CHECK anywhere before it, and you
land in YES and make one mark, the same box and the same mark as the player who
checked first. The two tally lines differ by exactly what the CHECK was charged,
228   9 What insight is


               and if you charged it nothing they don’t differ at all. The mark for the crossing is the
               same mark either way. The receipt says a commitment was paid for; it does not say
               the commitment was earned. Popper’s corroboration needs the test; the toll doesn’t.
                   You can build a system that makes the commit wait. Let CHECK leave a mark in
               the state when it passes, and write the step so VOUCH only crosses when that mark
               is there. Making VOUCH wait like that is a design, written into the step function,
               and it’s a perfectly good one. Nothing in the five parts or the toll asks for it. The
               gap between the word and the bare system is real, and I’m leaving it in plain sight:
               the toll prices the commit, and whether the commit was preceded by a test is a fact
               about the run, or about a design somebody chose. The five parts don’t guarantee it.

               Remark 9.2 (Nothing makes the crossing wait). Read off Definition 2.1. The toll
               constrains cost(i ) for moves that cross, and nothing else; the step function is any
               function of the current state and the move. So a Thiele machine may have a move
               that crosses from a state no check has touched, and the toll still holds. On Section 2’s
               board extended with CHECK, the run [VOUCH] from NO crosses with one mark, and
               [CHECK, VOUCH] crosses with one mark for the crossing plus whatever CHECK was
               charged, one mark in all if CHECK is priced at zero. Making a crossing depend on
               an earlier check is a condition on the step function, which a particular system can
               impose and the definition does not.


               9.5 What the word means

               Insight, in the sense this book prices, is a distinction made to stay: a move that flips
               a reading from off to on, for good, and that move costs at least one, in any system
               with the toll, whatever the reading is about and whatever its depth. At its best the
               reading is a relation committed to, a claim checked and closed; a bare crossing that
               commits to nothing pays the same, and the toll doesn’t tell the two apart. Part III’s
               certified machine is one way to make sure a crossing is the first kind. There are
               three boundaries, each from a different place. From Metcalfe: it isn’t a feeling, and
               a system’s version has to be an event. From the proof: the price is flat; a shallow
               commit and a deep one both cost at least one, and cost is not depth. A system can
               pay heavily to check a trivial claim, and Duncker’s box, a real insight, is still one
               small commit. And from the two-move protocol: a paid flag proves nothing on its
               own. Price and correctness are separate books.
                   Which leaves a suspicion I’d have in your place. Everything so far has been one
               reading on one sheet of paper, with a rule I chose and a count I bolted on. Is the
               shape of that record something I picked, or is it what any base-driven record has
               to look like, on any machine at all? The next section answers it: take any machine
               that steps, bolt a record onto it, and see what shape it’s forced into. How a concrete
                                                                   9.5 What the word means   229


machine hangs actual claims on its parts, a checked property of one counter at one
edition, and where those sit in the state, comes in Part III (Section 15).
CHAPTER 10




Records over any base: the latch

The blank cell comes back here, over any machine: a reading that goes from no to
yes because the machine did something, and stays. For the whole book so far I’ve
been building up a thing with a flag and a counter, and you’d be right to suspect that
the whole apparatus is special pleading for one machine, the one I keep promising
to build. So this section answers the suspicion with no particular machine in it at
all, and sees what’s left. Take any machine that steps deterministically: a Turing
machine, a register machine (a few numbered boxes that each hold a whole number,
and a program that adds, subtracts and jumps), a lambda calculus (Alonzo Church’s
way of computing by nothing but plugging expressions into expressions; Section 13
builds one), anything. Call it the base. Now bolt a record onto it, under rules I’ll
state, and ask: what can the record be?
    The answer is one shape, and I’ll show you the shape first because it’s a thing
you can build from a cup and a die.


10.1 A cup and a die

Put a cup upside down on the table. The rule is that the first time a coin lands in
front of it, you turn it right side up. There is no rule for turning it back over. Now
roll a die, and put a coin down on every six. Roll twenty times. If a six appears, the
cup turns over on the first one and stays turned over. Write down which roll did it.
That number is where the record happened, and the cup afterward is the record. If
no six appears, the cup stays down; a reachable event need not occur on every trial.
    For the deterministic base in the theorem, write the rolls down first and replay
them. The base state is the fixed list and a finger pointing to its next entry; a step
moves the finger one place, regardless of the cup. The event asks whether that entry
is six. Nothing about the cup changes which entry comes next.
    The cup is a latch. Electrical engineers have had the circuit since 1918, when two
British physicists teaching engineering in London, William Eccles, a radio pioneer,
and Frank Jordan, applied for a patent on a two-valve arrangement that holds
whichever state you last put it in; it became the flip-flop, and the registers and
caches in the device you’re reading this on descend from it. Cut its reset wire and
what’s left has one input, “set,” and the rule new state = old state or set: once set, it
stays set. The cup is that circuit: a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off.

                                  230
                                                              10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   231


     (Eccles and Jordan didn’t call it a flip-flop. Their 1919 paper calls it a trigger
relay. Where the newer, sillier name came from I can’t source, so I’ll leave it at that.)
     Is a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off only a picture, or did anybody ever build
one on purpose? Somebody did, and for a reason that’s very close to this book’s. In
the mid-1950s Wen Tsing Chow, an engineer at the Arma division of the American
Bosch Arma Corporation in Garden City, New York, was asked by the United States
Air Force, in the accounts of his career I could find, for a more flexible and secure
way to hold the fixed numbers, the targeting constants, inside the guidance computer
of the Atlas missile. What he and his Arma colleague William Henrich patented
(filed in 1957, granted in 1962, under the plain title “Storage matrix”) was a grid
with a connection at every crossing, where you set the numbers by taking out the
connections you didn’t want, physically or by burning them out with too much
current. The word burn is right there in the patent, and people still say they burn a
chip. The descendants are called programmable read-only memories, PROMs, and
a fuse blown in one stays blown: there’s no current you can send to grow it back.
The grid was a whole memory built out of cups with no reset wire, made because
somebody wanted numbers nobody could quietly change later. That doesn’t prove
anything here, because the theorem below doesn’t care what a cup is made of. But
it’s good to know the shape wasn’t invented for a sheet of paper. Somebody needed
it, for stakes a good deal higher than a die.
     Now the claim, stated loosely and then exactly: every base-driven record, over any
base, is a cup with no reset wire, turned by some event the base passes through.


10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean
The content is in the definition, and I’ll give you all five rules, because the theorem
is only as strong as they are.
    A machine extends a base when there’s a map from the bigger machine’s states
down to the base’s, and that map starts in the base’s start states, reaches every one of
them, moves in step with the base (one step up top is one step down below, through
the map), and agrees about halting. The bigger machine may carry as much hidden
state as it likes beyond the base, and that’s what the words “any base” are about:
the base doesn’t get to see the extension, and the extension doesn’t get to change
what the base does.
    The extension carries a record, a yes/no reading, and a ledger, a counter. It’s
a base-driven record when five things hold. One: the record’s next value depends
only on the base’s current state and the record’s current value. (I’ll call this driven
by the computation. It says the record answers to what the machine is doing. A
clock on the wall or someone’s hand doesn’t get a say.) Two: the ledger never
goes down (Section 6). Three: the step that turns the record on costs at least one;
232   10 Records over any base: the latch


               that’s the toll (Section 2). Four: once on, the record stays on; that’s permanence
               (Section 3). Distributed-systems people have a name for a predicate like that. The
               computer scientists K. Mani Chandy and Leslie Lamport, in their 1985 paper on
               taking a consistent snapshot of a distributed system, called a property stable when
               once it holds it holds forever after, and stable properties are the ones a snapshot can
               be trusted to detect. Five: some run from a start state actually reaches a step that
               turns the record on; otherwise the record is decoration.
                   I’ll write the rules out exactly. On/off is true/false, ∨ is “or” (on when either side
               is on), and nextk is k steps.

               Definition 10.1 (Base, record-carrying machine, cover). A base B is a set of states
               with a step function nextB , a set of starting states, and a halting predicate. A record-
               carrying machine M is a set of states with a step function next M , a set of starting
               states, a record rec from states to Booleans, a ledger µ from states to whole numbers,
               and a halting predicate. The cost of a step is cost(m) = µ(next M (m)) −̇ µ(m). A
               cover of B by M is a map π from states of M to states of B that sends starting states
               to starting states, has every starting state of B as the image of some starting state
               of M, commutes with the steps, π (next M (m)) = nextB (π (m)), and agrees about
               halting: m halts exactly when π (m) does.


               Definition 10.2 (Base-driven record, latch). M with cover π is a base-driven record
               over B when (R1, driven by the computation) there is one function f such that, for
               every state m, rec(next M (m)) = f (π (m), rec(m)); for every state m, (R2, ledger)
               µ(m) ≤ µ(next M (m)); (R3, toll) if rec(m) is off and rec(next M (m)) is on, then
               cost(m) ≥ 1; (R4, permanence) if rec(m) is on, so is rec(next M (m)); and (R5, a
               reachable write) some starting state m0 and some k have rec(nextkM (m0 )) off and
               rec(nextkM+1 (m0 )) on. An event is a function h from base states to Booleans, and its
               latch is the step (b, r ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b)). M factors as the latch of h when, for
               every state m (reachable or not),

                      (π (next M (m)), rec(next M (m))) = (nextB (π (m)), rec(m) ∨ h(π (m))).
                  The theorem says that under those rules the base state and the record move
               exactly as a latch: the record switches on at the first base state where some event
               holds, if it started off, and never goes off, and the event is read off the extension’s
               own rule by asking it what it does when the record is off (stated exactly below).
               The theorem is about what the base and the record do together. The hidden state
               the extension carries can’t push the record anywhere (R1) doesn’t allow, since the
               record’s next value is a function of the base state and the record’s own value. The
               theorem doesn’t say the whole extension is a bare latch machine, and it doesn’t
               make hidden state show up anywhere in particular: an extension can carry a field
                                                              10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   233


that touches neither the record nor the ledger. And the event is pinned down only
on base states that some state with the record off covers; on a base state with no
such state above it, f (b, off) is whatever (R1)’s function says, and nothing in a run
ever consults it.
    I promised the content was in the definition, and the proof bears that out: it is
a short case split on whether the record is already on, and it uses only two of the
five rules, “driven by the computation” and “permanent.” The ledger, the toll, and
the reachable-write clauses play no part in it. A latch is what you get from “answers
only to the base” plus “never comes back down” alone. The other three rules matter
for the converse: for any base and any event the base can reach, the latch of that
event, priced at one unit per write, is a base-driven record. The event can be one
that holds everywhere, and then its latch is up after one step from every start and
tells no two starts apart. It’s still a latch and still base-driven: the converse doesn’t
ask the record to distinguish anything. A record that starts off and tells two starts
apart at some step has to latch an event that has held along one run by then and
not yet along the other, and the latch tells them apart for as long as that stays so.
Put the two together and base-driven records are exactly latches: one shape, and no
others, over any base.
Observation 10.1 (The record is a latch). Let B be any base, π a cover of B by
M, and suppose M’s record is driven by the computation (R1), through a function
f , and permanent (R4). Then M factors as the latch of the event h(b) = f (b, off).
