In particular every base-driven record factors that way; (R2), (R3) and (R5) are not
hypotheses.
Proof. Ask the extension what it would do with the record off above each base state
b. Call its answer h(b). Rule (R1) lets you ask that as one function of b: no other
hidden field is allowed to change the answer.
   Now take an actual state. If its record is off, (R1) gives exactly that answer h(b)
for the next record. If its record is already on, permanence keeps it on, whatever
h(b) says. Together those two cases say “keep an existing on, otherwise use h(b),”
which is r ∨ h(b).
   The cover already says that the base part takes its own next step. Put that base
step beside the record rule just obtained and I have the stated latch equation. No
charge or starting condition entered the argument.
   The latch’s nearest neighbours are in verification, and they’re old. The computer
scientists Martín Abadi and Leslie Lamport, then at Digital’s research lab in Palo
Alto, added history variables to specifications in 1991: extra state that records what
has happened and never steers the system, used to prove that one specification
implements another. A history variable that only ever turns on is the cup. Temporal
logic has the same record as an operator. In the past-time temporal logic that Orna
234   10 Records over any base: the latch


               Lichtenstein, Amir Pnueli and Lenore Zuck set out in 1985, “once h” holds now
               exactly when h has held at some point so far, and a runtime monitor keeps it in one
               bit with the update r ′ = r ∨ h. Klaus Havelund and Grigore Roşu, two computer
               scientists working on runtime verification, synthesized monitors of exactly that
               kind for safety properties written in that logic in 2002. That update is the latch of
               Definition 10.2, word for word. The observation adds the other direction: a record
               driven by the computation that never comes down can’t be anything else.
                   One thing about that proof deserves a second look, because it cuts both ways: it
               never asks what the base is. The cover decides that: whatever the map sends down
               is base, and the record’s rule is allowed to read all of it; whatever stays up top is
               extension, and (R1) keeps the record’s rule from reading it. Draw the line low, so
               the base is only the computation’s own working state, and (R1) is a real demand.
               Draw it high, put every table and every refusal bit into the base, and (R1) is easy
               to meet, and the latch shape comes out exactly the same. So the theorem holds
               wherever you draw the line, and that’s exactly why it can’t tell you where a record’s
               meaning lives. The meaning lives in what the event h reads, and that’s in the base
               by construction. On the small machine of Part III (Section 15), the checks that give
               the flag its meaning sit in the base its cover picks out. So when that machine arrives,
               ask it first which parts it puts above the line.



               Theorem 10.2 (Every reachable latch is a base-driven record). Let B be any base
               and h any event. Let Latchh have states (b, r, x ), starting states (b, off, 0) with b
               starting in B, step (b, r, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b), x + δ) with δ = 1 when r is off
               and h(b) is on and δ = 0 otherwise, record r, ledger x, halting as b halts, and cover
               (b, r, x ) 7→ b. Suppose some starting b0 and some k bring Latchh from (b0 , off, 0), in
               k steps, to a state whose record is still off and whose base state satisfies h. Then
               Latchh is a base-driven record over B.

               Proof. The construction keeps a base state, a flag and a tally. Looking only at the
               base state gives the promised cover: a start lies over the chosen base start, every
               base start has such a flag-down, tally-zero start above it, and each step advances the
               base exactly once. Halting is read from that same base state.
                   The next flag consults only the present flag and the base event, giving (R1). The
               tally adds either zero or one and never falls, giving (R2). If the flag rises, it was off
               and the event held, exactly the case that adds one, giving (R3). An on flag stays on
               under the displayed rule, giving (R4). Finally the supplied run reaches a state with
               the flag still off and the event true. Its next step raises the flag, giving the reachable
               write (R5).
                                                               10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   235


   Whenever a base run reaches the event at all, use its first such visit. Before that
visit the flag remains off, so this is the supplied kind of run.
   What about a base that never merges, a reversible one? It can carry a record,
and the next theorem says exactly what it pays. Keep every earlier record value in a
history beside the latch, one more entry on every step, and the whole step merges
nothing either. But that history needs a fresh slot at every step, forever, so the
machine never comes back to a state it has been in, which puts it in the fresh-state
column. On a finite state space there aren’t fresh states to go on taking forever, and
a permanent record can’t be written by a step that merges nothing at all. A step that
merges nothing is called injective: no two states go to the same next state. Keep
the old readings on a strip, newest first. If the strip reads [off, off] and the current
reading is on, the next strip reads [on, off, off]. The notation r :: H below means
exactly that: put the old reading r at the front of the old strip H.


Theorem 10.3 (Records on reversible machines). (1) Let B be a base whose step
is injective. The machine with states (b, r, H, x ), step (b, r, H, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨
h(b), r :: H, x + δ) (δ as in Theorem 10.2), starting states with r off, H empty and
x = 0, has an injective step, never visits the same state twice on a run (the history
gets one entry longer on every step), and under the supposition of Theorem 10.2 it
is a base-driven record over B. (2) With finitely many states reading on, a single
injective step with a permanent reading never turns that reading from off to on.

Proof. (1) Suppose two full states have the same successor. Can you recover what
they were? Their successor base states agree. The base keeps different sources apart,
so their earlier base states agreed too. Their new history strips also agree. The first
entry of each strip is the old record, so the old records agree; removing that first
entry leaves the old histories, which therefore agree as well.
    Those equal old base states and records determine the same charge δ. Subtract it
from the equal new tallies and the old tallies agree. Every part of the two earlier
full states agrees, so they were the same state. The step is one-to-one.
    On a run the strip grows by one entry every tick. A full state cannot recur, because
its strip would have to have two different lengths. Carrying that strip changes neither
the base nor the flag nor the tally rules checked in the preceding construction, so
all five base-driven record conditions still hold under the supplied reachable-event
premise.
    (2) Suppose instead there are only K on-states and an off-state enters them.
Permanence sends all K on-states into that same collection, and the entrant lands
there too. A one-to-one step would have to put K + 1 different sources into K places.
236   10 Records over any base: the latch


               It cannot. Hence a permanent reading with finitely many on-states cannot rise under
               a one-to-one step.
                   So a base that never merges can carry a record without merging anywhere only
               by paying in fresh states: once the record is up, the run never comes back to a state
               it has been in (Proposition 3.5). A history that grows by one entry every step is one
               way to supply them, and a base that never repeats a state, a counter, supplies them
               already. A machine with finitely many states hasn’t got fresh states to go on taking,
               so it can’t carry one without merging: on a finite machine an instruction that first
               raises a permanent reading must merge some possible states. The entering state
               need not belong to the colliding pair; Section 3 prices the instruction under merge
               pricing.
                   Process-calculus people ran into the same thing from the other side. Vincent
               Danos and Jean Krivine, two theoretical computer scientists in Paris, wanted to pin
               down what a transaction is. In 2004 they had built a reversible version of CCS,
               Robin Milner’s calculus of processes that talk to each other, where every step can
               be rolled back, and in 2005 they modelled a transaction in it as a process that
               wanders freely through everything that can be undone until it performs an action
               declared irreversible, which is the commit. The way I read it, they start from steps
               that all come undone and ask what has to be added before anything sticks, and
               the theorem above starts from a record and asks what the step under it must be.
               In their calculus, as in the theorem, a permanent effect needs a step with no way
               back, and the calculus has to say which steps those are. The word I tripped on was
               declared. Theirs are labelled. Mine, I thought, are picked out by counting, since on a
               finite machine the first write merges whatever anyone calls it. Push on that and it
               gives. I choose the event h, and on a base that grows its history forever the write
               merges nothing, because it pays in fresh states instead (Theorem 10.3), so there my
               permanence is declared too.
                   There’s an arrow of time in that theorem, and I should say where it came from,
               because I put it there by hand. Every starting state has the record off. That’s the
               only reason a raised record means the event happened: it was down at the start,
               and only h lifts it. Turn the cup up before the first roll and it tells you nothing
               about the die. So the clean start is an assumed ready state, a past hypothesis in
               miniature. The past hypothesis is David Albert’s name for an assumed low-entropy
               beginning of the universe, which several of the accounts below lean records on.
               Whether every trusted record leans on it is their argument, and I’m not settling it.
               Nothing in this book derives one; every theorem here that reads a raised record as
               news that the event happened assumes its small version and starts from there. The
               latch observation doesn’t need it, and that’s why on its own it can’t say the event
               happened.
                                                             10.2 What “base-driven” has to mean   237


    When I went looking for who else had found the arrow hiding in the start, I got
five papers that read like five unrelated answers. They lined up once I asked each
one the same thing: what does the cup being down at the start rest on? There are
two places to put it. You can put it at the beginning, as a fact about how things
started. Or you can put it in the structure of what causes what. David Wolpert,
then a physicist at Los Alamos and the same Wolpert as the free-lunch theorem
(Appendix C), sorted memory systems in 1992, and one of his kinds works only
because it begins in a prepared state set up by a process that runs one way, which is
how it leans on the second law. That’s the cup put down by somebody before the
game, at the first place. Wolpert and Jens Kipper, a philosopher at Rochester, put in
2024 that sorting on a formal footing, and they say plainly that they have no formal
proof this kind can only remember the past. I trust them more for that sentence.
What I think they’re saying is that a prepared start buys you a memory, and getting
its direction too takes something they can’t yet prove.
    Aram Ebtekar, an independent researcher in Vancouver, and Marcus Hutter, who
works on the theory of general artificial intelligence at Google DeepMind and the
Australian National University, built in 2024 a reversible toy world, imposed a past
hypothesis on it, coarse-grained it, and got records of the past and none of the
future. As I read their route, the clean start doesn’t go straight to the records. It
goes through a causal structure first, and the arrows come out of that. Thomas
Blanchard, a philosopher of science at Cologne, got in 2024 the same lopsidedness
of knowledge out of the causal Markov condition, a condition on causal structure.
So Blanchard starts at the second place, which is the middle of Ebtekar and Hutter’s
road. That took me a while to see, because one is a toy world and the other is
philosophy of causation. They go from the start to causes to records; he goes from
causes to records. The fit is my reading, and it’s mine to defend. And Carlo Rovelli,
two years before his paper on the cost of choosing from Section 4, studied traces in
“Memory and entropy” (2022) and concluded that a memory turns low entropy into
available information. He’s at the first place, and he says what the beginning gets
spent on. Read against the latch, that’s the blank the record uses up: the flag can
say yes once because it started at no.
    So does the latch explain why records point backwards? It doesn’t, and I’ll say
that plainly so it doesn’t look like it does. The step runs forwards and the runs start
clean, and a theorem built on those two can only hand the arrow back. Push further
and it gives in a second place. The history that grows forever looked like a way
around the clean start. It starts empty, so it leans on the same blank. Under a step
that forgets nothing, on a finite set, no permanent record can ever be written, past
or future, which is Zermelo again. On the map the book sits at the first place, with
Wolpert and Rovelli, and it sits there by assumption. Ebtekar and Hutter at least
238   10 Records over any base: the latch


               imposed their start on a world with its own dynamics and watched what came out.
               I wrote mine into the definition.
                   Constructor theory, which Section 3 brings in as a neighbour of the counting
               argument, has a paper on time (Deutsch and Marletto, 2025) saying that laws stated
               as which transformations a device can and can’t bring about can’t mention time at
               all, so duration has to come from relations between physical systems, clocks, that
               have their own dynamics. What I think they’re saying is that whenever you want a
               duration you point at a second system and count what it did. This book is in that
               position by construction. The step count is the only time in it, and it comes from

               The base is my clock, and I assumed it.
                   Physicists have built this latch on paper too, in quantum mechanics, and it
               behaves the way the last theorem says. The question that sorted them for me is
               where the cup puts what it forgets, since a closed quantum system with separate
               energy levels comes back (Bocchieri and Loinger, Section 3) and the theorem left
               only two ways to pay for a record that stays: fresh states, which here mean a history
               that never ends, or a merge. Klaus Hepp, a mathematical physicist at ETH Zurich,
               wanted a measuring device inside quantum mechanics itself, and studied in 1972 a

               model (I know Hepp’s paper only from accounts of it), and John Bell (1975) took it
               apart: the record is exactly definite only for an infinitely long chain, which is the
               fresh-state column above, a history that never ends, in quantum clothes. Jonathan
               Halliwell, a theoretical physicist at Imperial College London, used in 1999 a two-

               back by a large environment, which is a latch with the environment holding the
               history. His abstract calls it effectively irreversible, and I like that he puts the word
               effectively right there where you can see it. And Murray Gell-Mann, the physicist
               who named the quark, and James Hartle, of the University of California at Santa
               Barbara, gave in 1995 the property a name inside their framework of decoherent
               histories: the permanence of the past, past alternatives that stay settled as the story
               is extended into the future. They name (R4) for whole histories and leave the cup to
               others. So Hepp’s chain, as Bell read it, is exact and infinite, and Halliwell’s detector
               is finite and only effectively permanent. Mine is finite, exact and permanent at once,
               and it gets there by letting the first write merge. Push on that and it gives: I never
               say where the merged state goes. Hepp’s chain had to be infinite. Halliwell had to

put his in an environment. Mine just goes, and the toll writes a unit in a counter.
That’s fine in a model of computation, and it’s exactly where this stops being physics.


10.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp
A theorem with two hypotheses should have two counterexamples, one for each
hypothesis dropped, and it does, and they’re the two ways a record goes wrong in
the world.
    Drop permanence. Take a base that just counts, and a record that flips at every
step: on, off, on, off. It’s driven by the computation; it’s not permanent; and it’s not
a latch of any event. Such a record is a toggle, a piece of working state. A record you
can revoke is working state wearing a record’s clothes, and if a revocation has to stick,
that’s a second latch (“revoked”), which is how certificate revocation lists actually
work: you add an entry; you never delete the certificate. Alin Tomescu, a computer
scientist then at MIT, and his coauthors (2019) built append-only authenticated
sets and dictionaries for transparency logs, and revocation fits that shape exactly:
a revocation goes in once and stays. The pair lemma (stated below) covers two
latches that can each read the other; do it with two cups where the second only
turns over on an even roll if the first is already up, and you’ll see the second can
never turn before the first.
    Dialogue theorists built a version of that two-latch rule for arguments. Give each
speaker a row of cups, one for every claim they’ve made. Everybody I read in this
field is answering two questions about those cups: whose hand turns them, and can
they come back down. C. L. Hamblin, an Australian philosopher and logician who
also came up with reverse Polish notation for early computers, wrote Fallacies (1970),
and it has a chapter on formal dialectic where each speaker has a commitment store, a
list of what they’re on the hook for, and the rules of the dialogue update it, while the
speaker doesn’t. I know that chapter from other people’s accounts of it. Hamblin’s
store is an answer to the first question, and it’s (R1) for arguments: the cup answers
to what happened in the dialogue, and the speaker’s hand is kept off it. Henry
Prakken, who works on AI and law at Utrecht, built in 2005 dialogue games for
argumentation on stores like that and made commitments sticky: a claim can be
retracted only when it has been challenged, and claims and backtracking carry a
price. He also floats a convention that once a player has retracted a proposition,
that player can’t take it on again, which is a revocation that stays revoked, the way
an entry on a revocation list does. Prakken’s rules are an answer to the second
question, and it took me a second pass to see that they’re two answers: a cup can
come down, and coming down costs, and once it has, the taking-back is itself a cup
that stays up. Erik Krabbe, an argumentation theorist at Groningen, names in 2001
the awkward part of that: retraction is frowned on, and yet resolving a dispute takes
240   10 Records over any base: the latch


               somebody retracting a doubt or a point of view, so the rules have to say when taking
               a commitment back is allowed. As I read him, he’s standing between the two ends
               of the second question. A store that never gives can’t settle a dispute, and a store
               that gives whenever it’s asked isn’t a store. The part of all that I’d keep is Hamblin’s,
               that the store belongs to the rules and doesn’t belong to the speaker. Take the pen
               away from the program. And this book answers Krabbe with a price: a take-back is
               a second cup, “revoked,” and turning it costs at least one like any other write, so a
               retraction is allowed, permanent and paid for, which is Prakken’s convention with
               the toll attached. Where mine gives is his first condition. He lets a claim come down
               only when it’s been challenged, and nothing in my latch asks why the second cup
               turned. The pair lemma lets the second cup’s event read the base and the first cup,
               and nothing in it requires a challenge to be there.
                   The same field has a notion that looks a lot like earning. In the abstract argumen-
               tation of Phan Minh Dung, a computer scientist at the Asian Institute of Technology
               in Bangkok (1995), arguments attack one another, and the grounded semantics starts
               from the arguments nobody attacks and keeps adding the ones they defend. Look at
               how it’s built: things go in and never come out, which is a row of cups turned one
               at a time. Pietro Baroni and Massimiliano Giacomin, at Brescia, introduced in 2007,
               and Martin Caminada, then at Aberdeen, revisited in 2014, strong admissibility: a
               set is strongly admissible when every argument in it is defended by others in the
               set that don’t lean back on it, so the support bottoms out. Strong admissibility is
               the argumentation form of an earned claim. Above the bottom, nothing in it is
               in by default, which puts it at the far end from Burge’s default on the testimony
               map in Section 7. Caminada argues it plays a vital part in the dialogue games that
               decide grounded acceptance. I’ve read Caminada’s paper; Dung’s and Baroni and
               Giacomin’s I know through what later papers say about them. Notice the bottom,
               though. An argument nobody attacks gets in on a check that can’t fail, and this book
               says a check that can’t fail establishes nothing (Section 14). Now turn that on my
               own cups, because it lands. My first write needs only that h holds, and what h reads
               sits in the base, where the latch theorem doesn’t look. I charge a unit for it, and a
               unit is a price, not a check. So my earned records bottom out the way Dung’s do, in
               something let in without an argument, and the one difference is that mine pays to
               get in. Whether a machine’s earned record certifies exactly the strongly admissible
               sets is the kind of statement I’d have to prove before I said it, and I haven’t.
                   A record that’s allowed to change its mind isn’t lawless, though; it’s somebody
               else’s subject. Count how many times the cup may be turned. Once, from down
               to up, is the latch. More than once and you’re somewhere else, and the people
               who went there sort it two ways: by how many turns are allowed, and by how long
               the game runs. The philosopher Hilary Putnam, then at MIT, and E. Mark Gold,
               a computer scientist at a research lab in Santa Monica, in back-to-back papers in
                                               10.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp   241


1965, looked at questions a machine answers by guessing and revising, where the
answer is whatever the guesses finally settle on. Putnam’s paper says outright that
you’re never sure you have the correct answer. That stopped me the first time. What
kind of answer can’t you ever be sure you have? The way I came to read it: the
cup’s position at any moment is the current guess, the answer is where it ends up,
and nobody watching can tell when it’s done moving. Yuri Ershov, a logician in
Novosibirsk, sorted those in 1968 by how many revisions they’re allowed (that’s
how his hierarchy is described; I haven’t read his paper). Allow one, from no to yes,
and you get exactly the sets a program can list. That level is in a modern account of
the hierarchy by Rod Downey, Carl Jockusch, Timothy McNicholl and Paul Schupp,
four computability theorists, and you don’t need their word for it. If a program lists
the set, guess no for every number and flip the guess to yes when the number shows
up on the list. Going back, if every guess flips at most once, from no to yes, run all
the guessing side by side and write a number down the moment its guess says yes.
Those listable sets are what a permanent record raised by a search catches. Allow
two, three, and so on, and every extra change buys new sets: the rungs of the ladder
are all different. A record that can come back down lives on that ladder. Now put
Putnam’s worry on my cup, because it lands. On the bottom rung a yes is final the
moment it appears, and a no never is, since down means not yet. A single cup of
mine can certify that something happened and can never certify that it didn’t; a
final no would take a second cup, turned by finding a reason, and that’s the pair of
latches again. That’s what the bottom rung costs, and I’d rather name it. This book
stays on the bottom rung; I’m pointing at the ladder, and I’m not climbing it.
    The ladder doesn’t stop at finite time, and the people who followed it past infinity
have names for the two kinds of record I just described. A definition that only ever
adds, stage after stage, and keeps everything it has at each limit, is an inductive
definition (the long treatment is a 1974 chapter by Wayne Richter and Peter Aczel,
two recursion theorists). It’s the latch run through the infinite, a cup that goes up at
some stage and is still up at every stage after. Let it take things back, and keep what
stays put from some stage on, and you have what John Burgess, a philosopher and
logician at Princeton, called in 1986 quasi-inductive definitions, which he met in the
revision theories of truth that grew up beside the logician Saul Kripke’s 1975 theory
of truth, which builds up the true sentences in stages. Burgess’s paper measures how
complicated the truths of those theories get. I’ve read its abstract, but not the place
where he names them. What took me a few reads is that Burgess’s rule at a limit
is Putnam and Gold’s rule, keep whatever the guesses settled on, applied at every
limit stage along the way. That’s my reading of how the two fit. If it’s right, the split
between a cup that only goes up and a cup that settles is the same split at finite
time and past it: a permanent record is the first kind, and a toggle that’s allowed to
settle is the second. Joel Hamkins and Andy Lewis, two set theorists, let a Turing
242   10 Records over any base: the latch


               machine keep running through the ordinals in 2000. At a limit a cell keeps its value
               if it settled, and reads 1 if it kept flipping back and forth forever, and the trick they
               use again and again is the toggle: flash a flag on and off every time a guess changes,
               and at the limit the flag is on exactly when the guess changed infinitely often. A flag
               that can come back down is how that machine learns what no finite run could tell it.
               A permanent one can’t do that trick, because at a limit a cell that only ever goes up
               just stays up. So past infinity the toggle is the clever one: a latch tells you a thing
               happened at least once, and their flashing flag tells you it happened infinitely often.
               I threw the toggle out a few paragraphs back anyway, and I’d do it again, because
               before the limit its reading can’t be relied on, and nobody using a machine of mine
               gets to wait for a limit. One finite-time fact belongs beside it, so nobody concludes
               too much from permanence. Hao Wang, a logician then at Oxford, described in
               1957 a machine whose only write is to mark a square and which can never erase
               one, and it computes everything a Turing machine does. Permanence of a machine’s
               own memory costs it no computing power, given an endless tape: each mark goes
               on a square nobody marked before, which is the fresh-state column again. What
               the book prices is a permanent reading raised by a step that has to work whether
               or not the reading is already up, which is a different thing. So the cost I named a
               paragraph ago is a cost in what a reading can claim, and computing power doesn’t
               pay it.
                    Drop “driven by the computation.” Take a base that counts, and a record that
               switches on at the fifth tick of a hidden clock, whatever the base is doing. It’s
               permanent, and the computation doesn’t drive it; such a record is a timestamp. A
               timestamp is not evidence: it says when and doesn’t say what happened, and a record
               switched by an outside party or a clock records that party or that clock and leaves
               the computation out. Try it with the recorded die list. Keep a second tally hidden
               beside it, and turn the cup when that tally reads five before a move; then advance
               both the tally and the finger on the list. Run two trials from the same list entry with
               the cup down, but start the hidden tally at five in one trial and zero in the other.
               The next cup values disagree although everything the base shows agrees, which is
               the failure of being driven by the base. If the tally always starts synchronized with
               the list position, the position can predict the cup; the distinction matters below.
                    The two examples do exactly what I said they do: the toggle is driven, isn’t
               permanent and isn’t a latch; the timestamp is permanent and isn’t driven. That each
               also keeps the other rules (the ledger is the step count, the first switch-on costs one,
               a run reaches it) is true by inspection.
                    Permanent but undriven is a timestamp, driven but impermanent is a toggle,
               and a record is the thing that’s both. Undriven, for the timestamp, means that
               along the runs that actually happen the base state doesn’t fix when the record turns;
               Lemma 10.7 below says why that’s the condition, and what (R1) as written adds to
                                                   10.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the timestamp   243


it. That’s the whole discrimination, and I think it’s the most useful single sentence
in this book for looking at systems other than the one I build, which is why it’s here.
    I’ll now state the pair lemma and the two counterexamples exactly. The base for
both counterexamples is the counter: states are whole numbers, the step adds one,
every state is a starting state, and nothing halts. Two more bits of shorthand: ¬r is r
flipped, and a statement in square brackets, like [k = 5], reads on when it’s true and
off when it isn’t.


Lemma 10.4 (Two records are two latches). Let c1 , c2 be two records on
M, with cover π onto a base B, such that: there is one function F with
(c1 (next M (m)), c2 (next M (m))) = F (π (m), c1 (m), c2 (m)); the ledger never goes
down; a step that turns either record on costs at least one; and each record is
permanent. Then there are h1 , h2 with c1 (next M (m)) = c1 (m) ∨ h1 (π (m), c2 (m))
and c2 (next M (m)) = c2 (m) ∨ h2 (π (m), c1 (m)) for every m.

Proof. Hold the second record fixed and ask what the joint rule does to the first when
the first is off. Call that answer h1 (b, r2 ); it is the first component of F (b, off, r2 ). At
any actual state whose first record is off, that is its next value. At any state whose
first record is on, permanence keeps it on. Thus its rule is r1 ∨ h1 (b, r2 ).
    Now hold the first record fixed and ask the corresponding question with the
second off. The answer is h2 (b, r1 ), the second component of F (b, r1 , off). The same
off/on argument gives r2 ∨ h2 (b, r1 ). The records may affect each other’s raising
condition, but neither can undo an on once it is there.



Lemma 10.5 (The toggle). Let the toggle have states (n, r ), step (n, r ) 7→ (n +
1, ¬r ), every state starting, record r, ledger n, cover (n, r ) 7→ n onto the counter. It
is driven by the computation, with f (b, r ) = ¬r; it is not permanent; and it factors
as the latch of no event.

Proof. At (0, on) the next record is off, which breaks permanence; and any latch
gives on ∨ h(0) = on there.



Lemma 10.6 (The timestamp). Let the timestamp have states (b, k, r ), step
(b, k, r ) 7→ (b + 1, k + 1, r ∨ [k = 5]), every state starting, record r, ledger b, cover
(b, k, r ) 7→ b onto the counter. It is permanent and not driven by the computation.
244   10 Records over any base: the latch


               Proof. Permanence: on ∨ x is on. Not driven: the states (0, 5, off) and (0, 0, off)
               have the same base state and the same record, and their next records are on and off,
               so no f of the base state and the record can give both.
                   “Driven” is a condition on every state. The timestamp makes every state a starting
               state, so the two states the proof compares are both ones a run can begin at, even
               though a timestamp started at (0, 0, off) would never reach (0, 5, off).
                   That last sentence does more work than it looks, so I’ll state it as a lemma. Start
               the same timestamp in sync, at (b, b, off) only. On every state its runs reach, the
               hidden count equals the base, and the timestamp is exactly the latch of [b = 5].
               (R1) still rejects it, because (R1) asks about every state, and (0, 5, off) is a state,
               though no run from a synchronised start reaches it. So (R1) as written separates the
               timestamp from a latch partly by how the cover is drawn and through states nobody
               visits. The separation I mean is the one on reachable states: the timestamp with
               every state a start fails (R1) even when only states some run reaches are counted,
               since two starting states sit over the same base state with the same record and
               disagree about the next one. And the latch theorem holds in that reachable form
               too.


               Lemma 10.7 (The timestamp, on the states runs reach). Say M’s record is driven on
               reachable states when (R1) holds for every state reached from a starting state in some
               number of steps. (1) If M’s record is driven on reachable states and permanent, then
               on every reachable state M steps as the latch of some event. (2) The timestamp of
               Lemma 10.6 isn’t driven on reachable states. (3) The timestamp started in sync, with
               starting states (b, b, off) and the same step, record, ledger and cover, is permanent,
               isn’t driven by the computation, is driven on reachable states, and on every reachable
               state steps as the latch of [b = 5].

               Proof. (1) is the proof of Observation 10.1, run on reachable states only. (2) The
               states (0, 5, off) and (0, 0, off) are starting states, reached in no steps, and the proof
               of Lemma 10.6 applies to them. (3) From (b, b, off) every step adds one to both
               counts, so a reachable state has k = b and its next record is r ∨ [b = 5]. Over every
               state, (R1) fails at the same pair as in Lemma 10.6.
                   So “permanent but undriven is a timestamp” is a sentence about the timestamp
               with every state a start, over the cover that hides its count, and it holds there in the
               strong form: undriven on the very states its runs pass through. A timestamp started
               in step with its base is a latch on the runs it has, and (R1) throws it out only because
               (R1) also looks at states those runs never reach.
                          10.4 Is there only one such machine? No: one structure, two unforced choices.   245


10.4 Is there only one such machine? No: one structure, two unforced choices.
I have to take apart the sentence “there’s only one way to carry a record,” because
three different things get squeezed into it.
    The first claim asks: given the toll and a fixed price list, is there one way to
keep the books, starting at zero and adding each move’s price? Yes, on every state
reachable from the start; that’s Section 6’s initiality, and it assumes the price list.
    The second claim asks: is every base-driven record over a base the same machine,
charges and all? No, and the counterexample is embarrassing in its simplicity. Take
any base-driven record, give it a new ledger that adds each step’s old cost and one
unit more, whatever the step is, and then walk the five rules. The record still answers
only to the base and its own value (R1); the cost never touches it. The ledger still
never goes down (R2); it climbs faster, if anything. The step that turns the record
on still costs at least one (R3), because the toll is a floor and a surcharge only raises
the price. Once on, the record stays on (R4), and the same run still reaches the
write (R5). So the surcharged machine is base-driven, and it isn’t the machine you
started with: wherever the original sat still at no charge, the surcharged one pays
one unit a step for sitting still. Do it with the cup and the die, and charge one unit
for every roll, six or not. The cup turns over on the same roll as before, so you’ve
changed the cost and nothing about the record. A machine that charges for CPU
time is base-driven and isn’t the one that doesn’t. The new ledger has to sit beside
the old state and not be read off it. A step’s cost is the ledger after less the ledger
before, so a ledger read off the state charges nothing for a step that leaves the state
where it was, such as a halted machine stepping to itself, or for any step on a loop
(Section 6). The surcharge is paid in fresh ledger values, the way every counter that
climbs is paid for.
    But the surcharged machine isn’t a different structure, since it has the same
record, steps and halting with a different price list. So the claim worth keeping
is sameness up to the price schedule: compare two machines by their record, their
halting and their steps, through their maps down to the base, and don’t compare
charges. Once you fix which event the record is, the cost stops mattering; a flat
surcharge, or any surcharge that depends on the current state, sits on the same
structure. The price list is the first unforced choice. The walk above is the whole
argument, and it works over an arbitrary base, with any surcharge that depends on
the current state: the surcharged machine is base-driven, has the same latch event,
steps along with the original on record, halting and base, and pays each step’s cost
plus the surcharge.
    And then there’s the second unforced choice, and this one still surprises me:
which event is the record? Nothing in the five rules picks it, beyond (R5)’s demand
that it hold somewhere a run reaches; on a base whose runs pass through only one
246   10 Records over any base: the latch


               state that leaves one record, and the choice opens as soon as a run passes two states
               an event can tell apart. The converse above already says so, if you read it twice:
               for any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit per
               write, is a base-driven record. Do it with the die. One cup turns over on the first six,
               and another turns over on the first one. Both are cups with no reset wire; both are
               base-driven. Roll a one first, and until a six turns up the two cups disagree about
               whether anything has been recorded. So which permanent reading counts as the
               record is a second thing nobody forces on you. The price list is one unforced choice
               and the event is the other, and that second choice is the question Section 18 is about:
               what, if anything, makes certification the event worth recording. “The ledger passed
               one” is an event only if the chosen base includes enough information to decide it.
               An extension-only ledger is hidden from a base event, just as the hidden clock was.
               The unforced choice is among functions of the chosen base.


               Corollary 10.8 (The event is an unforced choice). Let B be any base and h1 , h2 two
               events, each meeting the supposition of Theorem 10.2. Then Latchh1 and Latchh2
               are both base-driven records over B. If some run from a start of B reaches a base
               state b with h1 (b) on and h2 (b) off, and h2 holds nowhere earlier on that run, then
               after the step from b the same run has the first record on and the second off.

               Proof. That both are base-driven is Theorem 10.2 applied twice. Along that run the
               second record is still off when it reaches b, since h2 hasn’t held, and the latch’s own
               rule keeps it off, off ∨ h2 (b); the first is on after that step, whatever it was before,
               since h1 (b) is on.
                   Now let the cup wobble. Say whatever turns it over sometimes does and some-
               times doesn’t, with odds you could write on a card. Does fixing the price list fix
               the odds? No, and the counterexample is two cups with the same price tag and
               differently loaded coins. I’ll set it up carefully. Let a record be a single bit that moves
               at random: from each value, a list of weighted next values, every weight positive,
               never empty, never leaving on once on, and with the write from off to on charged at
               least one. Call such a record a permanent probabilistic record. Call two such records
               the same schedule when the same moves are possible and every move is charged the
               same, and the same in probability when the weighted lists give every move the same
               odds.


               Theorem 10.9 (The schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities). (1) There are two
               permanent probabilistic records with the same schedule that are not the same in
                                     10.5 Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about   247


probability. (2) There is a permanent probabilistic record that no deterministic latch
on its current value describes.

Proof. (1) From off, one record moves to off or on with weights 1 and 1, the other
with weights 1 and 2; from on, both stay on with weight 1; both charge 1 for the
write. Same possible moves, same charges, different weights. (2) The first record
moves from off both to off and to on, while a latch r ∨ h(r ) gives one value.
    These are finite-weight models on one bit with no base underneath; they say
nothing about any particular machine.
    The third claim asks: is there one state space, up to renaming, that every base-
driven record-carrier has to have? No, because the extension may carry any hidden
field it likes, so two carriers over one base can have state spaces of different sizes,
and nothing needs them to match.


10.5 Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about
The theorem is stated for any base, so let me put it on three models of computation
that other people built: a small Turing machine (any program); a register machine
of the kind the computer scientists Stephen Cook (of the certificates) and Robert
Reckhow described in 1973, with unit-cost indirect addressing (any program); and
a lambda calculus (call-by-value, meaning an argument is worked out before it’s
plugged in, and made deterministic by letting a term with no step left to take step
to itself). On each, the latch form holds, by the one generic theorem applied to
that base (the bases are defined below). So a register machine with a base-driven
record is a register machine plus a cup, and so is a lambda calculus. (There’s one
more instance, the machine I build later, where a particular flag is shown to be a
base-driven record and the same theorem makes it a latch, in Section 15.)
   I’ll give the three bases explicitly. A base needs a state, a next-state function, a
set of starting states and a halting predicate; the latch theorem asks for nothing else
about its instruction vocabulary.

Definition 10.3 (Three concrete bases). The tape base has a finite Boolean list t, a
head index h, a program counter q and a natural-number cost field. Reading beyond
the list returns false. Writing at h extends the list with false cells if needed, then
changes that cell. Moving right increments h and extends the list through the new
head position. Moving left decrements a positive h; at h = 0, it prepends a false cell
and keeps the head at zero. A fixed finite program contains these instructions:
248   10 Records over any base: the latch


                Instruction                               Next state
                Write a bit                               Perform the write and advance q by one.
                Move left or right                        Perform the move and advance q by one.
                Branch to j                               Set q := j if the current cell is true;
                                                          otherwise advance q by one.
                Halt                                      Leave the entire state unchanged.
                ClaimTapeIsZero with a label ℓ            Advance q by one and do nothing else.


                  An out-of-range program fetch is Halt. Every state is allowed as a starting state,
               and halting means the fetched instruction is Halt. The cost field is preserved by
               every instruction in this base. In particular, its ClaimTapeIsZero instruction neither
               erases the tape nor charges the cost field; neither the name nor the label supplies
               any semantics.
                  The random-access base has a register function X : N → N and a program
               counter q. For a fixed finite program its instructions are:

                Instruction                               Next state
                Constant (i, c)                           Set X (i ) := c.
                Add (i, j, k)                             Set X (i ) := X ( j) + X (k).
                Subtract (i, j, k)                        Set X (i ) := max(0, X ( j) − X (k)).
                Indirect load (i, j)                      Set X (i ) := X ( X ( j)).
                Indirect store (i, j)                     Set X ( X (i )) := X ( j).
                Positive branch ( j, a)                   Set q := a if X ( j) > 0; otherwise advance q
                                                          by one.
                Jump to a                                 Set q := a.
                Halt                                      Leave the entire state unchanged.


                   Each register-writing instruction advances q by one; its operands are evaluated
               in the old state, and all other registers are preserved. A fetch outside the program
               also leaves the state unchanged. Starting states have q = 0 and arbitrary register
               contents. A state is halted when it fetches Halt or is outside the program. Unit cost
               here counts instructions. It has nothing to do with the record’s ledger.
                   For the indirect instructions, draw boxes 1, 2 and 3 and put 2, 7 and 0 in them.
               Indirect load (3, 1) first reads the 2 in box 1, uses it as an address, and copies box
               2’s 7 into box 3. Now put 9 in box 3 and execute indirect store (1, 3): the 2 in box 1
               tells it where to put the 9, so box 2 changes and box 1 stays 2. An address is being
               read from a box; it is not necessarily the box’s own number.
                                     10.5 Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about   249


   The lambda base uses the terms and weak call-by-value rule defined in Defi-
nition 13.3. To compute its next state, first try to reduce the function part of an
application. If that part cannot step and is an abstraction, either substitute an
argument that is already an abstraction or take a step in the argument. If neither
applies, the term cannot step. Variables and abstractions cannot step by themselves,
and there is no reduction under an abstraction. The base leaves a term unchanged
when it cannot step and calls precisely those terms halted. Every term is allowed as
a starting state, including open terms.
    So all three are bases in the sense of Definition 10.1, and the latch theorem
applies to each. It says nothing else about them, nothing about what they can
compute or how fast.
    There’s also a relation defined between bases, weak base equivalence: two bases
are equivalent when some correspondence covers their start states both ways, related
states agree on an observation and on halting, and one step on one side is matched
by some number of steps, possibly zero, on the other. That “some number of steps”
is the stuttering idea Leslie Lamport (the same Lamport as Section 6’s message
counters) put forward in 1983: a fine-grained machine and a coarse one shouldn’t
count as different because one takes three ticks to do what the other does in one.
The relation carries no cost; a machine that multiplies huge numbers in one step
and a Turing machine differ in price. The relation never looks at price, so on what it
does look at they can match. It’s proved to be an equivalence relation, and the latch
form is preserved across it.
    Draw a coarse machine 0 → 1, with 1 halted, and a finer one a → b → c, with
c halted. Let a and b both show 0 and c show 1; halted states stay where they are.
Relate 0 to both a and b, and 1 to c. The fine move a → b changes nothing visible,
so the coarse machine matches it by taking no step. Its move b → c matches 0 → 1.
Starting from a, the coarse move is matched by two fine steps. “Possibly zero” allows
this; the relation is about matching observations and halting, not matching the
number of ticks or their cost.
    There is a limit to that statement. The “preserved across it” proof throws away its
equivalence hypothesis; the latch holds on every base regardless, so the preservation
is true for a boring reason. And nowhere in this book are two of the bases actually
related by this relation. The relation is defined, it’s an equivalence, and it is not
used to connect the Turing machine to the register machine to the lambda calculus,
or any of them to the machine of Section 15. It would be easy to read that list as if
it did. The honest sentence is the one that’s proved: each base, separately, carries a
latch.
250   10 Records over any base: the latch


               Definition 10.4 (Weak base equivalence). Bases B1 and B2 , with observations o1
               and o2 into one common set, are weakly equivalent when some relation R relates
               every starting state of each to some starting state of the other, and any related x,
               y have o1 ( x ) = o2 (y), the same halting, some n ≥ 0 with R(nextB1 ( x ), nextnB2 (y)),
               and some n ≥ 0 with R(nextnB1 ( x ), nextB2 (y)).



               Theorem 10.10 (Outside bases, and the relation). (1) Weak base equivalence is
               reflexive, symmetric and transitive. (2) If two bases are weakly equivalent, Observa-
               tion 10.1 holds over one exactly when it holds over the other. (3) Observation 10.1
               holds over each of the three bases in Definition 10.3, for every fixed program where
               the base has one.

               Proof. (1) A base matches itself by pairing each state with itself and matching one
               step with one step. Reverse any matching between two bases and it gives a matching
               in the other direction.
                   For three bases, pair a state of the first with a state of the third whenever some
               middle state matches both. A start on either outside has a middle start beside it, and
               that middle start has a start on the far side. Observations and halting agree across
               the first pair and then across the second, so they agree across the outside pair too.
                   Follow one step on the first base. Its match supplies a finite sequence of middle
               steps. Match the first of those steps on the third base, then the second from where
               that match ended, and continue. Joining the finite sequences gives a match for the
               original step. If the middle sequence is empty, take no step on the third base. Do the
               same in the other direction for a step on the third base. This checks both stepping
               requirements and proves transitivity.
                  (2) The latch argument uses only a base step and the stated record rules. It
               therefore holds over both bases, whether or not they are matched. (3) Each of the
               three displayed constructions supplies that step, its starts and its halting reading.
               The same latch argument applies separately to each.


               10.6 Records with more than two values

               A cup has two positions, and some records have more: a counter of how many
               checks passed, or a level that only rises. The same reasoning goes through one
               threshold at a time. For each value a, “the record has reached a” is a yes/no reading,
               and each of those readings is a latch. What doesn’t go through is squeezing the
               whole record into one cup. “Rises” needs one word of explanation: the values come
                                                            10.6 Records with more than two values   251


with an order ≤, “is at or below,” which needn’t compare every pair (that’s what
makes it a partial order), and [ a ≤ x ] is the yes/no reading “x has reached a.
    For example, keep separate records that an experiment was repeated and that
its calculation was checked. “Repeated only” and “calculation checked only” are
different places; neither includes the other. “Both” is above each. In this order,
moving up means retaining what was already done and possibly adding another act.
The order also has three rules: a place includes itself, inclusion carries through an
intermediate place, and two places including each other are the same place. Those
are the rules the proof below uses.”

Definition 10.5 (A growing record). Let the record take values in a set A with
a partial order ≤ decided by a Boolean test. A record ρ on M, with cover π
onto a base B, is a base-driven growing record when: there is one function f with
ρ(next M (m)) = f (π (m), ρ(m)); it grows, ρ(m) ≤ ρ(next M (m)); the ledger never
goes down and every step that changes ρ costs at least one; and some run from a
starting state reaches a step that changes it.



Theorem 10.11 (Growing records are families of latches). (1) For every base-driven
growing record there is an h with

                [ a ≤ ρ(next M (m))] = [ a ≤ ρ(m)] ∨ h( a, π (m), ρ(m))
for every value a and state m: each threshold is a latch, whose event may read
the current value. (2) The thresholds determine the value: if [ a ≤ x ] = [ a ≤ y]
for every a, then x = y. (3) For a growing record, charging every change is the
same as charging every threshold that switches on. (4) One latch is not enough:
a three-valued record that climbs 0 → 1 → 2 over a one-state base, each climb
charged one, is base-driven, and no single Boolean latch with a decoding from the
base state and the latch reproduces it. (5) A chain of distinct k-bit words, each
word’s set bits contained in the next one’s, has at most k + 1 members.

Proof. (1) Fix a threshold a. If the old record has already reached it, growth keeps
it reached. If it has not, the cup rises exactly when the next record f (b, x ) reaches
it. Define the event to say both things: “not reached at x, reached at f (b, x ),” or
h( a, b, x ) = [ a ̸≤ x ] ∧ [ a ≤ f (b, x )]. Keeping an existing yes and otherwise using
that event gives the stated latch equation.
    (2) Suppose x and y give the same answer at every threshold. Ask the threshold
named x itself. The record x has reached it, so y must have reached it too: x ≤ y.
Ask the threshold named y and get y ≤ x. The order’s third rule says those two
records are the same.
252   10 Records over any base: the latch


                   (3) If the value stays put, every threshold gives the same answer before and after.
               If it grows from x to a different y, look at the threshold y. It is reached afterwards.
               It was not reached before: y ≤ x, together with growth x ≤ y, would force x = y.
               Thus some threshold switches on exactly when the record changes. Charging those
               steps is the same requirement in either wording.
                   (4) Keep the base at its sole state and let the record move from zero to one, then
               two, then stay at two. Add one to the tally at each climb. The record rule consults
               only its present value, keeps it growing and pays for both changes, so it meets the
               requirements. A single flag over that unchanging base offers a decoder only two
               inputs, flag down and flag up. It cannot reproduce the three different record values
               just visited.
                   (5) Lay the distinct bit words out in their increasing order. At each move to the
               next word, at least one bit that was zero must become one; no one may become
               zero. Across the whole chain there are only k bits available for those changes. There
               are therefore at most k moves between distinct words, or k + 1 words including the
               first.
                  I have two cautions about that. In (1) each threshold’s event may read the
               record’s current value, so the events aren’t all functions of the base alone. And (3)
               charges a step when it switches some threshold on: a step that switches on three
               thresholds at once owes at least one, and nothing here makes the charges add up
               per threshold.
                  The order need not be finite; (5) is the finite-memory bound.


               10.7 What leaving the base open buys you
               The reason this section exists is to answer the suspicion I started with. The record
               isn’t special pleading for one machine. Over any base that steps deterministically,
               under rules you can read, a record that answers to the computation and never comes
               down is a latch on an event, and the proof doesn’t care what the base is. What a
               particular machine adds on top of the latch is a choice of price list and a choice of
               event, and both are choices. That is why the permanent-flip theorem in Section 3
               never needed the word certify: it forces a merge in whatever stays. The surcharged
               cup shows the first: the cost can change and the record not notice. The two cups on
               one die show the second: the rules are happy with either event. Any machine that
               meets the model will have to make both choices, and whether its choice of event is
               the right one is a question I’ll get to (Section 18), and won’t claim to have settled.
               Before that, a record can have more than two positions. Earlier in this section a
               record that rises got cut into one cup per threshold; the next section asks how much
               of the rest of the book survives once a record has more places to be than up and
               down.
                                                                   10.8 What it takes to be complete   253


10.8 What it takes to be complete
The latch left two choices open, the price list and the event. A machine I can hold up
against everything else has to make both, and a name for “this machine computes,
and its record keeps something” has to ask for more than the toll does. The toll
alone is a low bar. A machine that charges one for every step it takes is a clock
bolted to a computer, and it obeys the toll for any record at all: every raise costs
at least one because every move does. And a machine whose record never goes up
obeys it too, because a toll on a raise that never happens is never broken. Neither
one keeps anything a computation made, and a name both of them get without
trying isn’t saying much.
    I’ll give the names now, all of them, once, with the reason for each, and they work
the way Turing’s do. The Thiele Machine, with capitals, is the model: a computer
with a reading that can go from no to yes, a ledger, and the toll. A Thiele machine,
lower case, is any particular system that fits the model, the way one rule table is a
Turing machine. That bar is low on purpose, and a clock clears it. Thiele-complete,
defined next, is the bar worth meeting, the way Turing-complete is: a machine
that computes anything, with its record kept apart from its computing and able to
tell starts apart. Part III adds one stricter bar, certified Thiele-complete, for a record
that, from a clean start, goes up only on a claim that was checked, committed and
certified. And Appendix D names a universal Thiele machine: one machine that runs
the others, the way Turing’s universal machine runs every Turing machine. Those
are all of them: the model, the systems that obey it, the ones that compute and keep,
the ones whose keeping is earned, and the one that runs them.
    The bar comes in four clauses, and nothing in it mentions what the record is
about.

Definition 10.6 (Thiele-complete). A machine with the five parts is Thiele-complete
when it can be read through an interface that hands over three things: a universal
base, a split of its moves into computing moves and marks, and a ledger, a whole num-
ber for each state. A universal base is a way of reading each state as a configuration
of a machine that runs every program (I use Minsky’s two counters, Section 15.2), a
class of live states, a computing move for each of that machine’s instructions that
does to the configuration exactly what the instruction does from every live state
and keeps it live, and, for each start, a live loaded state showing that start. The
interface has to meet four clauses. (A) Computing can’t reach the record, and the
record stays. No computing move changes the record, and a record that’s up stays
up under every move. (B) Starts are blank. Every loaded state has the record down.
(C) Computing costs nothing, marks cost one. Computing moves cost 0, every other
move costs exactly 1, and each move adds its cost to the ledger. (D) The record tells
254   10 Records over any base: the latch


               starts apart. Some run, the same list of moves, ends with the record up from one
               loaded state and down from another.
                   Read the clauses as four plain sentences, with the universal base underneath
               them: the machine computes anything a Turing machine can. (A) The computing
               never touches what’s kept, and what’s kept stays. (B) Nothing is kept before the
               run starts. (C) The ledger counts the marks, and only the marks. (D) What’s kept
               depends on where you started: there’s a run whose record says something about its
               start.
                   (D) is the clause where distinction comes in, and it’s a low bar: a mark that reads
               one bit of the input meets it. What it excludes is a record that ignores the start. A
               record that goes up on every run from every start keeps a before and an after, and
               nothing about where the run began. (D) doesn’t ask that every raise tell starts apart;
               it asks that the machine can. A machine may have a mark that raises the record
               from any state at all; it pays one for it, like every raise, and (D) is still met by some
               other run. Which runs a machine wants its record to tell apart is its own choice, and
               Part III makes one.
                   The name echoes Turing-complete, but this is a specification a machine meets,
               not a class closed under simulation: a machine is held up against it through an
               interface, and changing the unit of price drops a machine out.


               Theorem 10.12 (What every Thiele-complete machine has). Let a machine be
               Thiele-complete through an interface. (1) It obeys the toll, and the move that raises
               its record is a mark, never a computing move, and costs exactly one. (2) Along any
               run, the ledger rises by exactly the number of marks in it. (3) From any state with
               the record down, every run that ends with the record up raises the ledger by at least
               1. (4) Some run from some loaded state raises the record. (5) Every move costs 0
               or 1, and some move costs 0. (6) Its base runs every two-counter program step for
               step from every live state, and halting from a loaded state matches halting from the
               configuration it shows.

               Proof. (1) If a computing move raised the record it would change it, against (A);
               so the raising move is a mark, and a mark costs one by (C). (2) is (C) added up
               along the run. (3) Somewhere along the run the record goes from down to up,
               and that move is a mark, by (1), so it adds one. (4) is (D), and by (B) the record
               started down. (5) Every move is a computing move or a mark, and the universal
               base supplies computing moves. (6) is the universal base, one instruction at a time,
               from a loaded state that is live and shows its start.
                                                                   10.8 What it takes to be complete   255


    The floor is one, and one is reached: the lift below gives a machine whose record
goes up after a single mark.
Observation 10.13 (A clock is a Thiele machine and isn’t Thiele-complete). Take the
two-counter machine, let every move cost 1, and take as the record any yes/no question
about its configuration; or a flag that switches on, and stays on, the first time a chosen
test of the configuration says yes. It obeys the toll and has a two-counter machine inside
it, and it isn’t Thiele-complete. No machine whose every move costs at least 1 is.
Proof. A Thiele-complete machine has a move priced 0, by Theorem 10.12(5), and
this one has none.
    A two-counter base priced 0 with a record that’s down at every state obeys the
toll and meets (A), (B) and (C), and isn’t Thiele-complete either: (D) asks for a run
that raises the record.


Theorem 10.14 (Each of the four clauses is needed). For each clause there’s a
machine that meets the other three through some interface and is Thiele-complete
through none. Two of them are built on the two counters with two marks, one that
raises the record when A is 0 and one that always raises it, and a ledger beside them
that each move adds its cost to. (A) fails: that machine, and one more move, priced
0, that puts the record back down. (B) fails: the two counters, every move priced 0,
with a record that no move ever changes, up at the starts where A is 0 and down
elsewhere. (C) fails: the two counters with two marks, every move priced 1. (D)
fails: the two counters, every move priced 0, with a record that’s always down.

Proof. Each machine meets the three by construction. The first fails (A) through
every interface, because a move lowers the record, so the record doesn’t stay. The
second: every one of its moves costs 0, so (C) makes every move a computing move
under any interface; then by (A) no run changes the record, and with every start
blank by (B) no run raises it, so (D) fails. The third has no move priced 0, so it fails
by Observation 10.13. The fourth never raises its record.



Theorem 10.15 (The record can’t be read off the window). Let a machine be
Thiele-complete through an interface. (1) Every configuration is shown, at no cost,
with the record down, by one computing move from some loaded state. (2) Some
loaded state has two runs that end on the same window, one with the record up and
one with it down, and their ledgers differ by at least 1. (3) So no rule that reads
only the window says, at the end of every run from every loaded state, whether the
record is up, and none says what the ledger reads.
256   10 Records over any base: the latch


               Proof. (1) From the loaded state (1, x + 1, y), the computing move “DEC A to line
               p” shows ( p, x, y), costs nothing by (C), and leaves the record down by (A) and (B).
               (2) Take the run (D) gives, from the loaded state where it raises the record. Its end
               shows some configuration. From the same loaded state, computing moves alone
               reach any configuration at all: count each counter down to zero, count it up to the
               value wanted, and jump to the line wanted. That run ends on the same window,
               and it’s all computing, so by (A) and (B) its record is still down and by (C) its ledger
               hasn’t moved, while the first run’s ledger went up by at least one, at its raise. (3)
               A rule that reads the window gives one answer for one window, and (2) has one
               window with two answers.
                  Part III proves the same blindness for its certified machines (Observation 15.32),
               with a gap of three, because a certified raise costs three. Here the gap is one, and
               one is reached.


               Theorem 10.16 (Every universal base becomes Thiele-complete). Take any machine
               with a universal base and any events on its states, and add a record, a ledger and,
               for each event, a mark that costs one and raises the record exactly when the event
               holds; computing moves cost nothing and leave the record alone, and every move
               adds its cost to the ledger. If some run of computing moves makes some event
               hold from one loaded state and not from another, the result is Thiele-complete, its
               computing is the original machine’s step for step, and its record goes up after a
               single mark from any state where the event already holds.

               Proof. (A): computing moves are the original’s and don’t touch the record, and a
               mark only adds to it. (B): the record starts down. (C): by construction. (D): run the
               moves that make the event hold from one loaded state and not the other, then the
               event’s mark. Step for step: a computing move acts on the original part and nothing
               else. And a mark from a state where its event holds puts the record up.
                   One mark on “A is at least 1” always works: the starts with A at 0 and at
               1 already differ on it, so that mark alone, run from each, tells them apart. So
               Thiele-complete isn’t a property only a special machine has. Any model with a
               universal base becomes Thiele-complete by adding marks, and needs no claims and
               no checker to do it; a model that simulates the two counters some other way does
               so once its moves are grouped into ones that carry out a counter instruction each
               (Theorem E.6). Two kinds of base don’t lift, whatever the events: one whose moves
               don’t depend on the state it’s in, and one whose moves lead from each state to only
               finitely many next states. A universal base needs, from one state, a move at no cost
               to every line of a program, and that’s infinitely many places to go.
                                                                   10.8 What it takes to be complete   257


   Some Thiele-complete machine runs every Thiele machine a program can de-
scribe. Appendix D defines a universal Thiele machine and builds hosts that run
any machine a program can describe, in order, carrying its reading as a latch and
matching its ledger up to a surcharge of at most three, with every computing step
done by counter moves on the host and every rise of the host’s record placed by its
program. None of that needs certification: the presented host’s own program, read
on a host with no claims, no checker and no table of facts, and one paid mark that
raises the record when a register is at least 1, meets the definition too.
   The rest of the book holds machines to this bar. Part III gives one example that
clears it, and then asks for the stricter certified bar: that from a clean start its record
go up only on a claim that was checked, by a checker proved to mean it, and then
committed, and that some claim’s check can come out either way. Asking that is a
choice of what the record answers to, the second of the latch’s two open choices,
made one way, with clean starts and three priced acts added (Theorem 15.23).
CHAPTER 11




The whole direction

I have a hunch I can’t fully back up, and Part III tells where it came from (Section 14):
established doesn’t feel like a switch to me. It feels like a direction with lines drawn
across it, and the switch is just the first line. The one piece of that I can settle is that
a single switch isn’t enough once there are three or more stages. I settle it in this
section, and find out how much of the rest survives being pushed on.
    A row of cells that only ever go from blank to written is a direction: you can tell
how far along it a state is, and nothing walks it back. The cup of Section 10 has two
positions. Everything the book has proved about the toll so far (the universal floor,
the merges, the squeeze, the windows) was proved for a cup. The question for this
section is blunt: if the record has more places to be than up and down, how many
of those results come along, and which ones break?


11.1 A row of cups
Get four cups and a pencil. Write five stages of an experiment on a strip of paper,
left to right: proposed, set up, run, read, recorded. Agree to do them in that order.
Put an upside-down cup between each pair of neighbours. The first means “the
setup happened,” the second “the run happened,” the third “the result was read,”
the fourth “the result was recorded.” As you complete a stage, turn over its cup.
Cups only ever get turned right side up; none has a reset wire. These are records
of completed acts. A fourth cup up does not make a false conclusion true, and a
different experiment may need a different order.
    Two things to notice with the cups in front of you. Each cup by itself is exactly
the cup of Section 10: it reads yes or no, and once yes it stays yes. And four cups
were enough for five stages. Try it with three, and you’ll find you can’t: three cups
that only ever turn up, in order, give you at most four different arrangements along
the way. I’ll prove both of those in a minute, and the proof is about as short as the
experiment.
    Now a harder strip. Some checks don’t line up. One person repeats the experi-
ment; another independently works through the calculation. Neither act includes
the other. Draw a diamond: neither at the bottom, experiment repeated on the left,
calculation checked on the right, both at the top. There are two ways up, and the
middle points don’t compare, which is what a partial order allows. Put a cup on

                                   258
                                                                       11.2 The order, said exactly   259


each point except the bottom, one for the repeat, one for the calculation, one for
both. Each cup is still a latch. The three cups tell you which acts have happened.
They do not decide whether the experimental model or the calculation’s premises
were appropriate.
   Whatever the shape of the strip, a straight line of stages or a diamond or some-
thing with a hundred points, I’ll call the set of places the record can be the direction,
and each question “has the record reached at least this place?” a line across it. One
line is one cup.


11.2 The order, said exactly

The strip and the diamond each come with an order you can see by looking: whether
one place is at or below another. Said exactly, the order is a test. For any two places
x and y it answers “is x at or below y?” with yes or no, and I write a yes as x ≤ y.
The test has to obey two rules: every place is at or below itself, and if x ≤ y and
y ≤ z then x ≤ z. An order that obeys just those two is called a preorder. If it also
obeys a third rule, that x ≤ y and y ≤ x together force x = y, it’s a partial order,
and that third rule is called antisymmetry. The two-point order, no below yes, is the
cup. The whole numbers in their usual order are a straight strip that never ends.
    The cups say the same thing in their own terms. For a place a, the cup for a asks
“has the record reached at least a?”, so with the record at x it’s up exactly when
a ≤ x, and I write its answer as [ a ≤ x ]. In the row of cups I said the cups together
tell you which place the record is at. On the strip and the diamond you can check
that with your eyes, and part (2) of Theorem 10.11 already proved it whenever the
order is partial, though I hadn’t asked what in that proof was doing the work. My
first guess was that it held for every order.
    Why bother with the bare preorder at all, when every strip on the table is a
partial order? I bothered because I wanted to see what the third rule was doing,
