and the way to see what a rule does is to take it away. Take a preorder with two
places, call them left and right, where each is at or below the other. There are two
cups, one asking “at least left?” and one asking “at least right?”, and both are up at
left and both are up at right. Look at the table and you can’t say where the record
is. Now build a record that swaps between left and right on every single step and
charges nothing. Every rule I’m about to state is satisfied. The record never drops
below anywhere it was, because each place is at or below the other. No cup ever
moves, so the toll in the next subsection has nothing to charge. The record moved
on every step and nothing on the table noticed.
260   11 The whole direction




              Theorem 11.1 (The cups fix the place, and only with antisymmetry). (1) In a
              partial order, if two places x and y leave the same cups up, [ a ≤ x ] = [ a ≤ y] for
              every a, then x = y. (2) In a preorder that isn’t a partial order this can fail: there’s a
              preorder with two different places that leave the same cups up, and a record over it,
              driven by the computation and growing in that preorder, that changes on every step
              while no cup moves.

              Proof. (1) Look at the cup for x. It’s up when the record is at x, since x is at or below
              itself, so it’s up at y too, and that says x ≤ y. The cup for y gives y ≤ x the same
              way. Antisymmetry gives x = y. (2) Left and right above, with the record swapping
              every step.
                  So in a partial order the cups are the place, and in the preorder I built they aren’t.
              That second half holds in every preorder that isn’t partial, by one line: if x ≤ y and
              y ≤ x with x ̸= y, then a cup that’s up at either one is up at the other, by transitivity.
              So the cups fix the place if and only if the order is partial. My first guess was right
              on every strip I could draw, and it was right because of a rule I hadn’t noticed I was
              leaning on. On a bare preorder, putting two places on the same rung tells the toll
              not to care about moves between them, and it doesn’t. I don’t think that’s a defect;
              it’s the order telling you what you agreed to count.


               11.3 The toll, over the whole direction

              One cup had one rule: the step that turns it right side up pays. Now there’s a row of
              cups, or a diamond of them, and a single step can turn over several at once. The
              rule I’d guess first turns out to be the right one: a step that turns over any cup pays
              at least one. A step that turns over three cups at once still only has to pay one. The
              rule asks whether a step turned something over. It doesn’t ask how many.
                  That rule buys the same thing one cup bought. Take any run, and suppose some
              cup is up at the end that was down at the start. Somewhere along the run a step
              turned that cup over, and that step paid. So the run paid at least one. Count the
              same way and you get more: the run paid at least once for every step that turned
              anything over.
                  Now look at what that argument didn’t use. It didn’t care whether the cups sat in
              a row or a diamond or something with a hundred points. It didn’t care how many
              there were. It didn’t even use the fact that cups never get turned back down. If
              something could knock a cup back over, the argument still works, because all it
              needs is the one step where that cup went up.
                                                                        11.4 One line isn’t enough   261


   To say it exactly I want to translate it into places. The cup at a place a is up
exactly when the record is at or above a. Say a step takes the record from x to y.
The cup at y is up afterwards, since y is at or above itself, and it was down before
exactly when y isn’t at or below x. And if y is at or below x, any cup that’s up at y
was already up at x. So a step turns over some cup exactly when it lands somewhere
that isn’t at or below where it started. The same reasoning says a run ends with
some cup up that was down at the start exactly when it ends somewhere that isn’t
at or below where it started.


Theorem 11.2 (The toll over any direction). Take a machine whose record is a
place in any preorder, and say a step turns a cup over when it takes the record from x
to a place that isn’t at or below x. (1) Every step that turns a cup over costs at least
one exactly when every run, from whatever state it starts, that ends somewhere
not at or below its start costs at least one. (2) When that holds, a run costs at
least the number of its steps that turn a cup over. (3) It holds exactly when every
cup, on its own, obeys the toll of Section 10: for every place a, a step that turns
the cup at a from down to up costs at least one. The universal floor of Section 2
(Observation 2.1) is (1) with one cup.

Proof. (1) and (2) are the walk above. For the other half of (1), a run of one step
that turns a cup over ends somewhere not at or below its start. (3) is the translation
above.
   When the cups only ever go up, as on the strip and the diamond, a step that turns
a cup over is just a step up.
   That surprised me a little, because I’d filed the floor away as a fact about one bit,
and nothing in it was about one bit. It was about one cup going up, and anything
you build out of cups has that.


11.4 One line isn’t enough

Now comes the payoff I promised at the start of this section. Could a cleverer single
cup do the job of all four, with one latch and some decoding that reads the record’s
place off the latch and whatever the machine shows? Section 10 already ruled that
out in the smallest case: over a machine with one visible state, a record that climbs
through three places can’t be produced by one latch and a decoding, because one
latch and one visible state make two outcomes and the record has three.
   So try a second guess, closer to the cup’s own rule. The cup’s rule was “new
value is old value or the event.” The obvious rule for a whole row is “new place is
old place joined with the event’s place,” where joining two places means going to
262   11 The whole direction


              the lowest place at or above both. On the row, the event names a place, and you
              turn up every cup as far as that place. To see it break, take the strip 0 < 1 < 2, a
              cup at 1 and a cup at 2, over a machine with one visible state, so the event has to be
              one fixed place. Let the record jump from 0 straight to 2, turning up both cups in
              one step, and stay put at 1 and at 2. From 0 the event has to turn up both cups, so
              the fixed place is 2. From 1 the same event would turn up the second cup as well,
              and the record stays at 1.
                  What works is giving every cup its own event, and letting the event for a cup
              look at where the record already is. Theorem 10.11 said exactly that, and this is
              why it had to say it. That leaves the question of how many cups. In the row of cups
              I asked you to try five stages with three and said you couldn’t. Theorem 10.11 (5)
              already bounded the chain from above. The count behind that bound comes again
              below, with the matching example added, and with an arrangement of k cups read
              as a k-bit word, a one for every cup that’s up.


              Theorem 11.3 (Lines a direction needs). (1) A list of different arrangements of k
              cups, each keeping up every cup the one before had up (a chain of different k-bit
              words in which each word’s set bits are among the next word’s), has at most k + 1
              members, and for every k there’s such a chain with exactly k + 1. So a straight strip
              of n + 1 stages needs exactly n cups. (2) Over a machine with one visible state, take
              the record on the strip 0 < 1 < 2 that jumps from 0 to 2 and stays put at 1 and at 2.
              It grows and is driven by the computation, and no rule of the form “join the record
              with a fixed place” reproduces its steps.

               Proof. (1) Going from one arrangement to the next, which is a different one, turns
               up at least one more cup, and there are k cups, so there are at most k steps and k + 1
               arrangements. For the matching chain, take no cups up, then the first, then the first
               two, and so on, packed to the left: that’s the row of cups. (2) Joining 0 with a fixed
               place g gives g, and from 0 the step has to give 2, so g is 2. Joining 1 with 2 gives 2,
               and from 1 the step has to stay at 1.
                 So five stages need four cups, and neither one nor three will do it, as long as the
              cups only turn up. An ordinary binary counter holds a thousand stages in ten bits,
              because its bits go down as well as up, and the theorem says nothing against that.
              The switch isn’t wrong: it’s the first line, and a straight strip with more than two
              places needs more of them, exactly one fewer than it has stages. A direction that
              branches needs at least as many cups as the steps in its longest strict climb, and at
              least as many as it takes to tell its places apart, the rounded-up logarithm of how
              many there are. Put three places above a bottom, none of them above another: the
              longest climb is one step, and one cup can’t tell four places apart, so it takes two,
                                                                11.5 Why crossing a line has to cost   263


and two do it, though not two lines: one cup that goes up at the first and the third,
and one that goes up at the second and the third. It can need more than both. Take
two places each below two others: one step of climb, four places, and two cups still
won’t do, because both upper places would have to keep up every cup either lower
one has up, and two cups allow at most one arrangement like that besides the lower
places’ own.
    People got here before me, and from a direction I didn’t expect, which was
programming for many processors at once. Lindsey Kuper and Ryan Newton’s LVars
(2013), “lattice-based data structures for deterministic parallelism” in their own
title, are memory cells whose value only climbs in an order, where a read can’t ask
for the value and can only ask whether it has climbed past a threshold. That’s a
cup. Writers running side by side can push the value up in different orders, and
a threshold once passed stays passed. Their deterministic behaviour also depends
on which reads and updates the language permits. Permanence alone would not
do it: a program allowed to ask whether the cup is up yet could still see another
writer’s timing. Amin Timany and Lars Birkedal (2021), coming at it from proofs
about programs, show, as I read their paper, that any preorder at all can be carried
as monotone ghost state in a program logic. That’s the closest thing I’ve found to
somebody else arriving at the decomposition into lines.
    The two rest on the same thing, a value that only climbs and a question that
only asks whether it’s past a point, and they use it for opposite jobs. In an LVar the
threshold read steers the program. Ghost state, as far as I understand the term,
lives in the proof, and the running program never reads it. Here the record is never
allowed to steer the base computation, so that particular restriction sits closer to the
ghost state. Push on that and it gives a little: Section 5’s glance, the whole reason to
keep a record, is a read. What keeps me on that side is that a glance worth trusting
gives the answer the long way would have given. Their purposes aren’t mine, but
the shape is theirs first. What I can’t find in either is a price on crossing a line.


11.5 Why crossing a line has to cost
Part I showed that the cup’s toll isn’t an arbitrary rule. It’s forced by three premises,
and the argument that ties them together was the pigeonhole: on a machine with
finitely many states, the move that raises a record that goes up and stays up has
to land two possible states on one state (Theorem 3.1), and a step that lands two
states on one is a step that forgets which one it came from. Does that survive the
whole row of cups? Mostly, and the parts that don’t survive are the interesting ones.
    The counting needs a flag, because what it counts is the collection of states with
that flag up, and now there are many cups, each one a yes-or-no reading that could
serve as the flag, so the first job is to pick one. My first guess was the cup for the
264   11 The whole direction


              place where the record starts. That goes nowhere: the starting state already has
              that cup up, so it’s already in the collection, and there’s no state coming in from
              outside. The cup that works is the one the step turns over, the cup for the place
              where the record lands. It’s up after the step, since a place is at or above itself, and
              it was down before, which is what turning a cup over means. So the collection is
              every state with that landing cup up, and the state the step starts from is the one
              coming in from outside. If the move keeps every state in the collection inside it and
              never lands two states on one, the states already inside use up every state in the
              collection between them, and there’s none left for the newcomer. So one of two
              things happened. Either two states landed on one, or some state that was in the
              collection got moved out, which means its landing cup went back down. I’ll call that
              second thing a revocation.


              Theorem 11.4 (Turning a cup over merges). On a machine with a record in any
              preorder, where each place has finitely many states with its cup up: (1) if a move
              turns a cup over at some state and lands the record at a place a, then either the
              move merges two states, or there’s a state with the cup at a up that the same move
              takes to a state with the cup at a down, which is a revocation; (2) if the record only
              grows, so that no cup ever goes back down, the move merges; (3) if the record only
              grows, the toll holds exactly when every move that turns a cup over at some state,
              and merges, costs at least one, so merge pricing gives the toll.

              Proof. (1) Gather every state with the cup at a up. There are finitely many. If the
              move keeps each of them there and is injective, it maps that collection into itself
              without two landing on one, so it hits all of them, including the state it sends the
              starting state to; injectivity then says the starting state was in the collection already,
              and it wasn’t, because its cup at a was down. So either some state in the collection
              has its cup at a knocked down, or the move isn’t injective. (2) Growth rules out the
              knocking down. (3) If the toll holds, every move that turns a cup over somewhere
              pays, merging or not. The other way, a move that turns a cup over merges by (2), so
              the hypothesis charges it.
                  It’s the old counting argument again, run once for every cup.
                  Each premise there can be knocked out, and I wanted to see each one go, because
               a premise you’ve never seen fail is one you don’t understand yet.
                  Knock out finiteness. Take the whole numbers as the states, which gives a row
               of cups that never ends, and let the record be the state itself, one more on every
               step, at no charge. Every step turns up one more cup. The step never merges
               anything: different numbers go to different numbers. Merge pricing holds, because
               there are no merges to price, and the toll fails on every single step. The counting
                                                              11.5 Why crossing a line has to cost   265


broke at the one place it needed the collection to be finite. Every state moved one
along, and there was always another state to move to. That’s Charles Bennett’s
1973 construction in miniature: a machine that keeps its whole history never has
to forget, so it never has to merge. It hasn’t got out of paying. Every step lands it
on a state it has never used, and that’s the fresh-state column. The toll fails here
because merge pricing only charges merges and this machine pays by taking a state
it has never used, which that price list doesn’t charge. Take the infinity away and
the supply of fresh states goes with it.
    Knock out growth. Take a two-state machine whose record flips back and forth
between two places, so a cup goes up on one step and gets knocked back down on
the next. The two states just swap with each other, so nothing merges, and the price
list is honest about merges. The step that turns the cup up pays nothing. It takes the
other branch of (1) and revokes: the state that had the cup up gets moved to where
it’s down.
    Knock out the price on merges. A two-state machine that stamps every state
with yes turns the cup up wherever it was down, merges at the stamp, and charges
nothing. Of course the toll fails; nobody asked the merge to pay.


Theorem 11.5 (Each premise does work). (1) There’s a machine with infinitely
many states, a growing record and an honest merge price on which every step
turns a cup over and the toll fails. (2) There’s a two-state machine with an honest
merge price whose record doesn’t grow, which turns a cup over and fails the toll.
(3) There’s a two-state machine with a growing record whose merges aren’t priced,
which fails the toll.

Proof. The three machines above, in order.
   So the toll over a whole direction rests on exactly the three things the cup’s toll
rested on: finitely many states with each cup up, a record that doesn’t come down,
and merges that pay. Nothing extra got smuggled in when one cup became a row,
and nothing the one cup needed got left behind.
   I’d half expected the diamond to need something new, some extra rule for the
two middle cups that don’t compare. It didn’t. Every cup gets its own collection of
states, and the argument on each is the old one.
CHAPTER 12




The shadow, exactly

Section 7 put the machine behind a window and asked what an outsider could tell.
It found that two states can look the same through the window and differ in what
matters, and that a price computed from the window can’t be exact if the window
has a collision (Observation 7.2). That was for one cup. With a whole row of cups
in hand I can ask the sharper version of the same question, which is also the one I
actually care about. Take the ordinary machine, the one with no cups and no ledger,
and let it look at itself. What’s the shape of everything it can’t see, and what does
the toll cost in terms of that shape?


12.1 The ordinary machine is a shadow
Take any machine with a record and a ledger, and sweep both off the table, the
cups and the counter. What’s left is a machine that steps the same way and knows
nothing about either, provided the step’s effect on everything else never depends on
the cups or the counter: sweeping them off has to commute with the step. A system
whose control reads its record or its ledger has no shadow in this sense. Where the
premise holds, call what’s left the shadow. Over any one state of the shadow there’s
a pile of full states, all casting that same shadow and differing only in their record
and their ledger. Section 7 already called the pile over a point the fibre over it. The
shadow is one particular window, the one that shows everything except the cups
and the ledger.
   The shadow has its own fibres, and every move has piles of its own too: the states
a move sends to one landing spot. I’ll call those the move’s landing piles. A fibre is
everything that looks the same before anybody moves. A landing pile is everything
that ends up in the same spot after one move. Keep the two kinds apart, because
the whole section turns on how they meet.


12.2 Pricing from the shadow

First the window question, over a whole row. A window price charges each step from
what the window shows before and after it. It meets the floor if it charges at least
one for every step that turns a cup over, and it’s exact if it also charges nothing for


                                 266
                                                                     12.2 Pricing from the shadow   267


any step that turns no cup over. A collision is two steps that look the same through
the window, where one turns a cup over and the other doesn’t.
    With one cup, the fix in Section 7 was to put the cup in the window. So my first
guess for a row was that the window has to show some of the cups. Try the smallest
version: a record in the whole numbers, and a window that shows only the first
cup, the one that asks “at least one?” Let the record rise on some steps and hold
still on others. Once it’s past one, that cup is up before and after both kinds of step,
so a step that turned over a cup further along looks exactly like a step that turned
over nothing, and the two make a collision. So then, I thought, the window has to
show every cup. That’s wrong too, from the other side. Take a record in the whole
numbers with two moves, one that adds one and one that leaves it alone, and a
window that shows only whether the record is even, which on the row is whether an
even number of cups are up. You can’t read the record off that window, and no flat
charge is exact, since some steps turn a cup over and some don’t. But the evenness
changes on exactly the steps that turn a cup over, so charging one exactly when the
evenness changed is exact.


Theorem 12.1 (Window prices over a direction). (1) If the window has a collision,
every window price that meets the floor charges at least one for some step that turns
no cup over, so no window price is exact. (2) An exact window price exists exactly
when the window has no collision; on a machine with finitely many states and
moves, whose views can be told apart by a yes-or-no test, it can also be computed.
(3) Along any run, a window price that meets the floor charges at least the number
of steps that turn no cup over but look, through the window, like a step that does.
Some window price meets the floor and, among the steps that turn no cup over,
charges one on exactly those, so that number is the least overcharge; when it can be
decided, for each pair of views, whether some step showing them turns a cup over,
that price can be computed. (4) A window can price exactly without showing where
the record is: there’s a record in the whole numbers with a move that raises it and a
move that leaves it alone, and a window that shows only whether the record is even;
the evenness changes exactly on the rises, no charge that is the same for every step
is exact, and charging one exactly when the evenness changes is exact, although no
rule reads the record off the window. (5) There’s a record in the whole numbers
and a window that shows only the one cup “at least one,” and that window has a
collision.

Proof. (1) The two colliding steps get the same charge. The floor makes it at least
one because of the step that turns a cup over, and the other step pays it too. (2)
Without a collision, “does some step that looks like this turn a cup over?” is a
268   12 The shadow, exactly


              question about what the window shows; charge one exactly when the answer is yes.
              On a finite machine you can answer it for every pair of views. (3) A step that turns
              no cup over but looks like one that does gets that step’s charge, which is at least
              one by (1)’s argument; add along the run. For the other half, charge one exactly
              when the answer to (2)’s question is yes, which needs that question to be decidable,
              and count the overcharge. (4) A rise changes the evenness and the other move
              doesn’t, so the window sees exactly the steps that turn a cup over; a flat charge
              either charges nothing for a rise or charges something for a step that turns nothing
              over; and 0 and 2 look the same through the window. (5) The first cup, as above.
                 Item (4) changed how I think about this. I’d assumed a window had to see the
              cups to price them. It doesn’t; it has to see them move. A window that cannot tell
              you your exact place, but detects every rise and every pause, can charge the right
              amount every time.


              12.3 What a priced move destroys

              Now the fibres. Part I showed that the move raising a permanent flag on a finite
              machine lands two possible states on one state, and Theorem 11.4 showed the same
              for a step that turns any cup over, once the cups only go up. Which two? It matters
              a great deal. If they’re in different shadow fibres, then the ordinary machine lost
              a distinction too; the record may also differ between them. If they’re in the same
              fibre, the ordinary machine lost nothing, and what got destroyed was only ever off
              the table: two states that cast one shadow, told apart by their cups or their ledger,
              crushed into one.
                  My first guess was that it’s always the second kind, because the cups are where
              everything happens. It isn’t always. It depends on whether the ordinary machine
              forgets anything on its own.


              Theorem 12.2 (The toll prices a collapse inside a fibre). On a machine with finitely
              many states and a growing record: (1) a move that turns a cup over somewhere
              sends two different states to one landing spot; (2) if the shadow exists, so that
              sweeping commutes with the step, and the shadow’s step for that move forgets
              nothing, sending different shadow states to different shadow states, then those two
              states are in the same shadow fibre, and every landing pile of the move lies inside
              one fibre; (3) without that premise it can fail: there’s a two-state machine whose
              two states sit in different fibres and whose shadow step forgets, so the merge at
              the step that turns the cup over lands two states from different fibres and no fibre
              loses a point. (4) The halving price, which says a move of cost c shrinks any finite
                                                         12.4 How much gets destroyed, on average   269


collection of states by at most a factor of 2c , holds exactly when every landing pile
has at most 2c states, on a machine of any size.

Proof. (1) is the counting argument of Theorem 11.4, with growth. (2) If two states
land on one spot, their shadows land on one shadow spot, and the shadow’s step
tells shadows apart, so the two states cast the same shadow to begin with. (3) The
stamp of Theorem 11.5, with the record’s value also shown in the visible part, so
each state is its own shadow: both states land on yes, and so do their shadows. (4)
is the worst pile-up of Premise 3.4. Any 2c + 1 states of one landing pile would be a
collection that lands on a single spot, which the premise caps at 2c , so no pile has
more; and any finite collection is at most the number of spots it lands on times the
biggest pile. Neither half needs the machine to be finite.
   So on a machine with finitely many states and a record that only grows, when the
ordinary machine forgets nothing, the toll is a price on crushing a fibre: on taking
two states that cast one shadow, which only what’s off the table told apart, and
making them one. The last of those premises is the one I just showed you failing.


12.4 How much gets destroyed, on average
The halving price is a worst case, because it prices the largest landing pile a move
can have. The next question is the average one: if I don’t know which state the
machine was in, cups and all, but I have some spread of chances over the states,
how much do I lose, on average, about which state it was, once I know where it
landed? Shannon’s conditional entropy measures exactly that (Section 3 built the
entropy from scratch, so I won’t do it again here), and I’ll write it in bits.


Theorem 12.3 (The halving price in bits bounds the average loss). Take any spread
of non-negative weights over the states, uniform or not, with finite total weight, on a
machine of any size. (1) If every landing pile has at most N states, with N ≥ 1, the
weighted conditional entropy of the state given its landing spot is at most the total
weight times log2 N bits. (2) So on a machine with the halving price, that weighted
information loss is at most its cost in bits times the total weight, even when the
spread’s own entropy is infinite. For a probability distribution, the total weight is
one and the average loss is at most the cost. (3) If a landing pile has 2c states, the
uniform probability distribution on it loses exactly c bits and attains that bound.

Proof. Look at one landing spot. Suppose the sources that land there carry total
weight w > 0. Divide each source’s weight by w. Those shares now add to one:
they describe the uncertainty about the source once you know this landing spot.
270   12 The shadow, exactly


              There are at most N possible sources. The logarithm argument in Section 3 says
              the uncertainty is greatest when those possibilities have equal shares, and is then
              at most log2 N bits. Multiply by w to put this pile back into the whole spread. Its
              contribution is at most w log2 N. A pile with zero weight contributes nothing.
                 Add the contributions. The pile weights add to the original total weight, so
              the same log2 N multiplies that total. Under the halving price, N = 2cost , whose
              base-two logarithm is exactly the cost.
                  Infinitely many piles cause no subtraction of one infinite entropy from another.
              I am adding the nonnegative uncertainties inside the piles. Every finite collection
              contributes at most its weight times the bound, and its weight is at most the total.
              Taking the largest value approached by those finite sums keeps the same bound.
                  Finally put all probability on one pile of 2c sources, equally shared. Before landing
              there are 2c equally possible origins; afterwards the landing spot distinguishes none
              of them. The uncertainty left about the origin is log2 (2c ) = c bits. That attains the
              bound.
                  Where does it stop? My first guess was one place, a landing pile with infinitely
              many states, and that the average would blow up there right along with the worst
              case. That’s half right, and the half that’s wrong surprised me. No finite charge
              satisfying the halving price can price a move that sends infinitely many states to one
              spot. The weaker merge price could still charge one, since it does not measure the
              pile’s size. But the average depends on the spread. Put weight 12 on the first state, 14
              on the next, 18 on the next, and so on, and the information lost by crushing the pile
              never reaches 2 bits, however many of its states you count. Under that spread, a
              two-bit information budget covers the average, though no finite budget covers the
              worst case. So I went looking for a spread that does blow up, and it took a nastier
                                                        k                         1
              one: blocks of states, block k holding 22 states and a share (k+1)(   k +2)
                                                                                          of the weight,
              which adds up to one. Under that spread the loss grows past every bound, and no
              finite information budget covers that average loss.
                  You can generate the first spread by tossing a fair coin until the first head. Zero
              tails names state 0, one tail names state 1, and so on. State j has chance 2−( j+1) , and
              identifying that outcome takes j + 1 toss-results, so its entropy term is ( j + 1)/2 j+1 .
              Add these by counting each possible toss position: the first is reached with chance
              1, the second with chance 1/2, the third with chance 1/4, and so on. The total
              is 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + · · · = 2; every finite partial sum of the state terms is smaller.
              Resetting all those outcomes to one box can lose only those two bits on average,
              despite having infinitely many possible starts.
                  For the block spread, split each block’s weight equally among its states. The block
              weights sum to one because 1/((k + 1)(k + 2)) = 1/(k + 1) − 1/(k + 2). Within
                                     k
              block k, there are 22 equally likely choices, so just identifying a state within that
                                                                          12.5 What the shadow is   271


block contributes 2k /((k + 1)(k + 2)) to the average bits. Those contributions grow
without bound as k grows, and forgetting which block it was only adds to the loss.
And no finite worst-case price can handle an infinite pile: for any proposed cost c,
select 2c + 1 different states in it. They all land together, violating the halving rule’s
maximum of 2c .


Theorem 12.4 (An infinite pile). (1) A move that sends infinitely many states to
one spot isn’t priced by the halving price at any finite cost. (2) Under the halving
spread 2−( j+1) , crushing the pile loses exactly 2 bits, and counted over its first n
states, less than 2 for every n. (3) Under the block spread, the information lost
grows past every bound, so no finite bit budget covers it.

Proof. The three computations above.
    And heat? Part I already said where the line is, and it’s the same line here.
Landauer’s principle, that crushing c bits’ worth of possibilities gives off at least
c kT ln 2 of heat on average, is a premise from physics, and a contested one (Sec-
tion 3). Nothing in this section proves anything about heat. What the counting does
give is that, under that premise, on a machine with the halving price, a move’s cost
priced at kT ln 2 per unit, times the weight of the piles, is always enough to cover
the minimum the premise would demand, for every spread of finite total weight.
If the premise falls, that sentence falls with it, and every theorem above it stands,
because none of them used it.


12.5 What the shadow is
Put the two sections together and you get the shape I’ve been circling since the
Flatland night (the night a video about Flatland gave me the hunch behind this book;
Section 24 tells it). The ordinary machine is the shadow of a machine with a row of
cups beside it. Over every shadow state there’s a whole fibre, a pile of states that
differ only in their cups and their ledger, and the ordinary machine can’t tell them
apart, on a machine whose step never looks at the cups. On a machine that obeys
the toll, a step that turns a cup over costs, whichever cup it is and however many it
turns, and on a machine with finitely many states whose record only grows, when
the ordinary machine forgets nothing, what that cost pays for is exactly crushing
two states of one fibre into one. A window can charge the right cost without seeing
the cups, if it sees them move. And on a machine with the halving price, where each
unit of cost pays for at most one halving, the cost in bits, times the weight of the
spread, is never less than what got crushed on average.
272   12 The shadow, exactly


                  What I haven’t shown is that any of this is out there in the world, that nature
              keeps a direction like this over its own shadows. That’s a belief of mine, and nothing
              in this book proves it. What I’ve shown, and you can check, comes with its premises
              showing. A machine whose record is driven by the computation and climbs a partial
              order is a row of cups, one latch for every line. If it also has finitely many states,
              never lets the record come down, and prices its merges, it has to pay this way. And
              when its ordinary machine forgets nothing, what it pays for is exactly this. It’s less
              than the Flatland night promised me. It’s also the part of it that held when I pushed.


              12.6 Shortcuts

              There’s a question every machine with a record runs into once its programs can
              be handed their own code. A cup is worth turning over because something later
              glances at it and doesn’t have to work the thing out again, the way Section 5’s glance
              reads a block’s bucket off the table without applying the rule from scratch. Call any
              move like that a shortcut, and call it sound when it gives the answer the long way
              would have given. (That gloss is about cost, leaning on what was done so nothing
              is redone, and the wall I’m about to show you doesn’t look at cost at all; the next
              section says exactly what it does look at.) So can a machine like that decide, from
              inside, whether its own shortcuts are sound? That question runs into a wall, the
              same wall Kurt Gödel and Alan Turing hit, and I have to show you that it’s there
              before I show you anything that pretends to be on the other side of it.
CHAPTER 13




The diagonal

In Section 5 I said you’d watch the same move get made again and again as the
book went on: somebody says “everything is X,” it’s true enough to do real work
with, and then somebody draws the diagonal. I owe you the diagonal itself now,
because Sections 10 to 12 just handed a record, and a whole direction of them, to
any system that steps, and the next thing anyone wants from a system with a record
is for it to tell sound shortcuts from unsound ones by itself. Before I let anything
claim that, I have to show you the wall every such claim runs into, and then show
you exactly where a system with a record stands relative to the wall. It doesn’t stand
on the far side, because nobody’s on the far side. A record keeps a distinction and
pays for it. What it can’t do is the judging: no machine that can hand a program
its own code, and can run the flip of a verdict as one of its own programs, can sort
all its programs, from inside, by a question about what they do that some pass and
some fail. So the record carries a commitment, and somebody still has to make it.


13.1 Five names and a table

Do this first, with a pencil, because the whole family of arguments is this one trick
and you should own it. Write five friends’ names down the left of a page. Next
to each name, write a five-digit string of zeros and ones, anything you like. Now
build a new string: its first digit is the opposite of the first digit of the first row; its
second digit is the opposite of the second digit of the second row; and so on down
the diagonal. Look at what you’ve made. It differs from row one in position one,
from row two in position two, from every row at that row’s own position. So it’s
nobody’s string, and your table of five missed something.
    With five rows and five digits that’s a cute fact. Georg Cantor, a mathematician
working out how to compare infinite sets, made the point in 1891 that it works for
any list, however long, even infinite: hand me a complete list of all infinite strings
of two symbols, I’ll walk the diagonal flipping as I go, and I’ll hand you back a string
that’s on no row. So there is no complete list. There are more such strings than
there are places on any list, and that’s where “some infinities are bigger than others”
comes from. (He wrote the two symbols as m and w, where I’d write 0 and 1, and
that paper wasn’t even his first proof of the fact. The first was in 1874, by a harder


                                                    273
274   13 The diagonal


              road through the real numbers, and in 1891 he called the new one much simpler.
              The diagonal was him finding the easy way.)
                 Now look at what the argument did, because it’s going to do the same thing
              again and again, in new clothes, and I want you to recognise it each time. (Not
              every name below is a flipped diagonal in the table sense. Kleene’s theorem is the
              tool that makes the diagonal buildable, Rice’s is the general form, the one from Ken
              Thompson, who built the original Unix operating system at Bell Labs, is an attack
              that uses the same trick, and the last, Lawvere’s, is the theorem that makes them all
              one.) There was a table: rows are the things being listed, columns are questions,
              each cell says “does row i do column j.” There was the diagonal: the cells where
              a thing is asked about itself. There was a flip: something with no fixed point, like
              turning yes into no, applied along the diagonal. And the thing that got refuted was
              the assumed object, the complete list. Nothing outside the assumption was touched.
              Hold on to those four: a table, a diagonal, a flip, and the assumption eating itself.


              13.2 The same move, again and again

              Russell, 1902, from Section 5: the collection of all collections that don’t contain
              themselves. It’s Cantor’s flipped diagonal with “contains” as the table, and Russell
              said as much, in The Principles of Mathematics in 1903. He got there, he wrote, by
              running Cantor’s argument on a supposed collection of everything, which ought to
              be the biggest collection there is. What got refuted was the assumed object, the
              collection of everything, and Zermelo’s fix was to stop assuming it. I promised in
              Section 5 that I’d come back to this here. Every reading in this book is a yes or no
              question on the states of one machine, a collection cut out of a collection I was
              already given, and never a sort of everything. When Part I asked for one state that
              codes every question about the states (Section 1), the same flip refuted it.
                   Jules Richard, a French mathematician who taught at the lycées of Tours, Dijon
              and Châteauroux, took his doctorate in Paris in 1901 and wrote mostly on geometry.
              In 1905, in a short note, a letter to the editor of a French science review, he
              observed: some phrases (his were in French) define real numbers (“the ratio of a
              circle’s circumference to its diameter”); there are only countably many phrases, so
              list the numbers they define in order; run Cantor’s diagonal down their decimal
              expansions and you get a real number no phrase defines, except that you just defined
              it, in the phrase that describes the diagonal. The lesson I take from that one is the
              lesson this whole section turns on: keep apart the language a system talks in and
              the language you use to talk about it. Mix them and the diagonal bites you.
                   Richard’s paradox has a cousin small enough to do at the table, and it comes
              with a footnote I can’t resist. Russell, the first to put it in print, in 1906, credited
              it to G. G. Berry, a junior librarian at the Bodleian Library in Oxford. The paradox
                                                              13.2 The same move, again and again   275


has outlived empires, and it came from the library desk. In the version in Principia
Mathematica it’s about syllables. Take the phrase “the least integer not nameable
in fewer than nineteen syllables.” There are only so many phrases shorter than
nineteen syllables, so they name only so many numbers, so some least number is
left over, and the phrase picks it out. Now count the phrase: the, least, in-te-ger,
not, name-a-ble, in, few-er, than, nine-teen, syl-la-bles, and it comes to eighteen.
In eighteen syllables it has named the number that can’t be named in fewer than
nineteen. It’s the same lesson as Richard’s, in a smaller coat: “nameable” is a word
about the language, used inside the language, and that’s where the bite is.
    Kurt Gödel, 1931, with an improvement in 1936 by Barkley Rosser, a logician
who had studied under Alonzo Church at Princeton and whose trick lets the theorem
assume only that the system is consistent: the big one, and I’ll say exactly what it
says, because every word of it is carrying weight. Take any consistent formal system
with a mechanically checkable list of axioms that can do a bit of arithmetic. Then
there are sentences it can neither prove nor refute. The engine is a lemma that lets
you build, for any property you can write down, a sentence that the system proves
equivalent to that property holding of the sentence’s own code number. Apply it
to “not provable” and you get a sentence equivalent, inside the system, to its own
unprovability. The table is the sentences listed by code, the diagonal is a sentence
about its own code, and the flip turns provable into not-provable. The Stanford
Encyclopedia stresses two cautions, and I’ll repeat them. The sentence doesn’t
literally “say” anything about itself. It’s provably equivalent to a claim about its code,
which is less mystical and more exact. And the theorem doesn’t say the sentence is
unknowable. It says this one system can’t settle it.
    And how did the world take it? Mostly, at first, it didn’t. Gödel, twenty-four years
old, announced the first theorem during a round-table discussion on the last day
of a conference in Königsberg in September 1930, and by the account of Solomon
Feferman, one of the editors of Gödel’s collected works, the room met it with general
incomprehension, except for one man. John von Neumann pulled Gödel aside to
talk about it, kept thinking about it, and a couple of months later saw that the
argument gave something more: a consistent system of this kind can’t prove its own
consistency. He wrote to Gödel with it in a letter dated 20 November 1930. Gödel
had already got there. His paper had reached the journal three days earlier, with
that second theorem announced in it, and von Neumann left the credit with Gödel.
It’s the “somebody got there first” shape from Section 4, with one difference: here
the man who got there second was von Neumann.
    Alan Turing, 1936. I’d always taken it that Turing proved the halting problem
undecidable, and here I had to go and look. The set theorist Joel David Hamkins and
his coauthor Theodor Nenu went back to the 1936 paper and report that the word
“halting,” the modern statement, and the self-referential proof everyone teaches are
276   13 The diagonal


              all, strictly speaking, absent from it. What Turing proved undecidable were two
              other questions about his machines (whether a machine prints infinitely many digits;
              whether it ever prints a given symbol). The second is equivalent to halting and the
              first is strictly harder. So their answer cuts both ways, and they say so: Turing never
              stated the halting problem, and he essentially proved it, because his second question
              is a short translation away from it. The name came later. Martin Davis seems to have
              been the first to write “halting problem,” in a book of 1958, and Stephen Kleene had
              already stated the problem, without that name, in his 1952 textbook Introduction to
              Metamathematics. The textbook version is still right as mathematics, and it fits on
              two index cards. Card A is the Checker: hand it any program card and it announces
              “halts” or “runs forever.” Card B is the Contrarian: “Hand me to the Checker. If
              it says I halt, run forever. If it says I run forever, stop.” Hand B to A, and either
              answer is wrong, so there’s no Checker. The table is programs against programs, the
              diagonal is a program run on itself, and the flip turns halt into loop.
                  Stephen Kleene, 1938, the logician whose textbook I just mentioned, and this is
              the one that turns the paradox into a tool, so slow down. Everything above needs
              the self-referring object to exist: Gödel’s sentence has to be buildable, the Contrarian
              has to be able to “hand me to the Checker.” Kleene’s second recursion theorem
              says: for any transformation of programs you can compute, there’s a program that
              behaves exactly as if it had been handed its own source code. Any program may
              be written as though it already had a copy of itself in hand. He stated it almost in
              passing, in a paper on something else, and proved it in the last two lines of one
              of its sections. I have that count from Yiannis Moschovakis, a logician at UCLA
              and Athens who wrote a 2009 paper on it, expanded in the Bulletin of Symbolic
              Logic in 2010, called “Kleene’s Amazing Second Recursion Theorem,” and he calls
              it a little gem. It’s the reason “programs that print their own source” exist in every
              ordinary programming language: one that can compute whatever a Turing machine
              can and can build, from a program and an input, a program that runs the first on
              that input (they’re called quines, after a philosopher I’ll come to in a moment; try
              “Print the following twice, the second time in quotes: ‘Print the following twice,
              the second time in quotes:’ ” and obey it). Self-reference in computation isn’t a
              paradox but a construction. The paradoxes happened only when someone assumed
              an unrestricted collection or language; the theorem happens when you build the
              self-referrer honestly.
                  And where does the word quine come from? The philosopher didn’t coin it
              himself. Douglas Hofstadter coined it in 1979, in Gödel, Escher, Bach, in honour of
              Willard Van Orman Quine, who had made a long study of self-reference that works
              indirectly. Quine left a sentence you can take apart at the table, from a 1962 essay
              on paradox, and in full it reads: “yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation”
              yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation. Do what it says. Take the part in
                                                             13.2 The same move, again and again   277


quotation marks, put a quoted copy of it in front of itself, and look at what you’ve
built: it’s the whole sentence, word for word. So the sentence says that it itself is
false. It’s the liar paradox, but look at how it got there: no “this sentence” anywhere,
no pointing at itself, just an instruction to quote and copy, the same move as the
print-twice instruction above. Quoting and copying is Kleene’s trick in plain English,
and it’s why the paradox and the tool look so alike. The paradox is what you get
when the copy asserts something about its own truth. The tool is what you get when
the copy just does something.
    Henry Rice, 1953, whom you met briefly in Section 7: the general form. Any
property that depends only on what a program does, whatever its text, and that’s
true of some programs and false of others, has no algorithm that decides it for all
programs. “Does this program halt” is one such property. “Does this program ever
output 7” is another. “Does this program contain an if-statement” isn’t, because
that’s about the text. One standard proof goes straight through Kleene.
    And the one that’s actually an attack: Ken Thompson, in his Turing Award lecture,
published in 1984. Build a compiler that, when it compiles the login program, plants
a back door, and when it compiles a compiler, plants both habits into that one too.
Then delete the trick from the source. The compiled compiler still carries it, and
recompiling a clean source with the poisoned binary re-plants it, forever. Reading
the source never reveals it. A locksmith teaches an apprentice to cut a spare for
every town-hall key and to teach that to every apprentice they train, and never to
write it in the manual; years later the manual is spotless and every locksmith in
town cuts the spare. Thompson’s compiler is the recursion theorem with a knife in
it, and his moral was that you can’t trust code you didn’t write entirely yourself.
    And Thompson wasn’t first either, and he said so. Pull on the lecture’s acknowl-
edgment the way Section 14 pulls on Bitcoin’s footnotes: he writes that he first read
of the possibility in an Air Force critique of the security of an early implementation
of Multics, a time-sharing system from the 1960s, and that he couldn’t find a more
specific reference to it, and he asks anyone who can to send him one. The critique is
Paul Karger and Roger Schell’s 1974 security evaluation of Multics, which already
described a trap door planted in a compiler that, because the compiler is written in
its own language, keeps itself alive. So the knife was in the drawer ten years before
the lecture was printed. Then comes the obvious next question, whether there’s
any way out or whether “trust no binary you didn’t build” is the bottom. There’s
a partial answer, and it took a while. David A. Wheeler, in a 2005 paper and a
2009 dissertation at George Mason University, worked out diverse double-compiling:
compile the suspect compiler’s source with a second, independently made compiler,
use the result to compile that source again, and compare the output bit for bit with
the suspect binary. If they match, the binary really is what its source says, unless
both compilers were poisoned in the same way. The trust doesn’t vanish but moves,
278   13 The diagonal


              from one compiler to the claim that two unrelated ones weren’t rigged together.
              Every stopping point in this book has that shape. You don’t reach the bottom, but
              you do reach a place where you can say exactly what you’re trusting.
                  Bill Lawvere, in 1969, proved a fixed-point theorem that, as I read it, makes all
              of these one theorem in disguise: if a set can be mapped onto all the functions from
              itself to some target, then every function on the target has a fixed point; so if the
              target has a function with no fixed point (a flip), no such covering exists. Cantor,
              Russell, Gödel and halting all come out as instances of one shape. Noson Yanofsky
              retold it in 2003 without the category theory. I mention it because “it’s the same
              wall” is a claim I make below, and I want you to know it’s fair at the level of proof
              shape, and that every instance has its own boundary of who counts as a decider, and
              that boundary is exactly where most overclaims live.


              13.3 Applying the diagonal
              Before applying the diagonal to a system with a record, identify who the proposed
              decider is and what it must decide. Four familiar applications show why those
              details matter.
                  “Gödel shows minds aren’t machines.” John Lucas, a philosopher who spent
              thirty-six years as a fellow of Merton College, Oxford, argued it in 1961, in a paper
              called “Minds, Machines and Gödel.” Roger Penrose, the Oxford mathematical
              physicist who later shared a Nobel prize for his work on how black holes form,
              revived it twice, in two books, The Emperor’s New Mind in 1989 and Shadows of
              the Mind in 1994. I’m sure of who argued it and when. Whether they’re right is
              the question, and the standard replies, as far as I can tell, have held up: the Gödel
              sentence is true only if the system is consistent, so a human who “sees” its truth has
              to know the system is consistent, which is the hard part; and nobody can build the
              Gödel sentence of a system they can’t specify, so humans might be machines too
              complicated to diagonalise. The theorem has a conditional in it and the argument
              drops the conditional.
                  And the part that’s easy to miss is that Gödel himself didn’t go as far as Lucas.
              In a lecture on the day after Christmas in 1951, at a meeting of the American
              Mathematical Society at Brown University, he drew from his own theorems only an
              either-or. Either the human mind, even inside pure mathematics, infinitely surpasses
              the powers of any finite machine, or there are problems about whole numbers, of
              a certain simple kind, that no proof the human mind can conceive will ever settle.
              Feferman, writing about that lecture, says Gödel privately believed the first half and
              still stated only the disjunction, because he didn’t have a knock-down argument
              against the machine side. Gödel wrote soon afterward that he meant to publish the
              lecture, and never did; the text sat among his papers until after his death. So the
                                                                   13.4 Now point it at the record   279


man whose theorem gets quoted for “minds aren’t machines” stated an either-or and
left the deciding to whoever came next. The conditional is there again, kept by the
person with the most right to drop it.
    “Undecidable means unknowable.” Two senses share the word: a problem with
no single algorithm correct on every instance, and a sentence independent of one
particular system. Neither means nobody can know a given answer. Any single
instance is decidable, trivially: for any one program, one of “say yes” and “say no” is
right. What’s ruled out is one inside procedure that’s right on every case.
    “Everything interesting is undecidable.” Rice is about behavioural properties over
all programs. It says nothing against checking the text, nothing against deciding for
specific programs, nothing against analyses allowed to say “I don’t know,” nothing
against finite-state model checking or type checking. Real compilers and analysers
live with Rice by being sound but incomplete, and what limits them in practice is
mostly cost. The diagonal shapes them; it doesn’t stop them.
    “Self-reference is a paradox.” It’s a theorem with a construction, as Kleene, the
quines and Thompson show.


13.4 Now point it at the record
The question Section 12 left open can be asked with nothing in it but what Parts I
and II have built. A system steps; a record rides along and latches on an event
(Section 10); when the event is a certification, Section 8 said the reading, with
its object and its paid event behind it, is what lets an auditor treat a claim as
established, and for a claim that a shortcut is sound, that’s what makes the shortcut
admissible. Can a system like that have, as one of its own programs, a procedure that
correctly decides, for every program, “does this program admit a sound shortcut”? A
procedure like that would be autopilot: hand it any program and it says yes or no,
and it’s always right.
    The exact statement is narrower than the question in plain words, so I’ll give it
before the proof. In the theorem, “admits a shortcut” is any property of programs
with two features: two programs that behave alike agree on it, and there’s one
program that has it and one that doesn’t. Those two features are all the argument
gets to look at. The diagonal doesn’t see soundness. Each system that wants the
wall picks its own property, and whether that property lines up with being entitled
to soundness in Section 8’s sense is a separate fact about that system, checked one
system at a time if it’s checked at all. A procedure that returns soundness records for
some programs, or only for restricted inputs, or with outside evidence, is not what
the wall rules out.
    So in the theorem “shortcut” is a label. The plain-words gloss at the end of
Section 12, leaning on a record so the thing isn’t worked out again, is about how a
280   13 The diagonal


              program gets its answer, and how is exactly what extensionality throws away: the
              theorem only gets to see what programs do, and it treats any two that do the same
              as one. A question like “is there a cheaper program that gives the same answers?”
              isn’t the theorem’s question, and a wall for it would need a different theorem. The
              nearest thing I know of is Manuel Blum’s speedup theorem, from 1967, and it
              goes somewhere stranger: there are computable functions with no fastest program
              at all, where every program for the function has another that’s faster on all but
              finitely many inputs. Blum’s theorem is a fact about cost, not a wall about deciding,
              and nothing in this book proves anything in that territory. Each use of the wall
              also names its sameness. In the substrate theorem it’s the substrate’s own ≃; on
              L it’s what a term computes; on the host of the small machine Part III builds, in
              Appendix D.4, it’s the partial function a program computes (Theorem D.20). A
              particular notion of shortcut gets the wall only after someone proves it behaves alike
              on programs that are the same in the sense in use, and holds of one program and
              fails of another.
                  The answer is no, under premises. The proof is the two index cards, and I’ll give
              you the premises because they’re the whole content. Suppose there were such a
              decider, one that says yes exactly when a program admits a shortcut. Build the flip:
              “if the decider says yes about me, behave like a program that admits no shortcut;
              if it says no, behave like one that does.” If the system has a recursion theorem (a
              program can be handed its own code), and if that flip is one of the transformations
              the system can carry out, and if “admits a shortcut” depends only on behaviour (two
              programs that behave the same agree on it), and if there’s at least one program each
              way, then there’s a program that behaves exactly like its own flip, and whatever
              the decider says about it is wrong. Both cases close in a line each. This rules out a
              decider that says yes if and only if a program admits a shortcut, for any substrate
              with those parts. (A substrate here is the mathematical structure just described:
              programs, a run that may fail to give back a state, a counter with a step relation it
              never goes down along, an encoding of programs as data, a notion of “representable”
              transformation, and the recursion theorem for those. It says nothing about what
              the states are made of. A small instance is the nat family below.) It’s Rice’s trick
              one floor over, and I should be careful with that. Rice stated his theorem for classes
              of recursively enumerable sets, the sets a program can list, and it’s usually taught
              now for the functions Turing machines compute. This wall is the same diagonal
              with different premises: it carries its own recursion theorem and its own list of
              representable transformations, and it picks the property. So it isn’t a corollary of Rice
              as Rice stated it, and it doesn’t show that any property is harder or easier to decide
              than classical halting. And I want you to have one thing about its proof: it never
              touches the counter, the toll, or the step relation. It uses the recursion theorem,
              representability of the flip, the two witnesses, and extensionality, and nothing else.
                                                                  13.4 Now point it at the record   281


   I’ll set out the setting and the wall now, with every word pinned down so you
can poke at it.

Definition 13.1 (Substrate). A substrate has a type of states, a type Prog of pro-
grams, and a run map that takes a program and a state and either gives back a state
or gives nothing. It has a counter µ on states and a step relation along which µ
never decreases; an encoding enc of programs as states with a decoder dec such
that dec(enc( p)) = p; and a predicate Rep on maps f : Prog → Prog, the transfor-
mations the substrate counts as its own. Two programs are equivalent, p ≃ q, when
run( p, s) = run(q, s) for every state s. The last condition is the recursion theorem:
for every f with Rep( f ) there is a program p with p ≃ f ( p).


Definition 13.2 (Shortcut predicate). A shortcut predicate on a substrate is a prop-
erty A of programs with two programs y and n such that A(y) holds, A(n) fails,
and A is extensional: p ≃ q implies A( p) ⇐⇒ A(q). For a Boolean function d on
programs, its flip is f d ( p) = n if d( p) is true and f d ( p) = y if d( p) is false.



Theorem 13.1 (No inside decider). Let a substrate carry a shortcut predicate A
with witnesses y and n. Then for every Boolean function d on programs with Rep( f d )
there is a program p with p ≃ f d ( p), and d( p) = true ⇐⇒ A( p) fails at that p. So
no such d is right about A on every program.

Proof. Hand the proposed judge d to the flip construction. The flip is an allowed
program transformation, so the recursion theorem supplies a program p that behaves
exactly as its own flip tells it to behave. Now ask the judge about that particular
program.
   If the judge says yes, the flip sends p to the no-example n. Thus p and n behave
alike. The question depends only on behaviour, and n fails it, so p fails it too. The
judge’s yes is wrong.
   If the judge says no, the flip sends p to the yes-example y. Now p and y behave
alike. Since y passes, p passes too. The judge’s no is wrong. Those are its only
answers.
   I used the recursion theorem to obtain this one self-matching program, the two
examples to give the flip somewhere to go, and the rule that alike behaviour gets the
same verdict. The counter, the step relation and the encoding played no part. Any
setting supplying that same fixed point for the flip gives the same contradiction.
282   13 The diagonal


                  So what’s ruled out is a d that says true exactly when A holds, and whose flip the
              substrate can represent. Every part I named is a premise, and the theorem covers
              every substrate that supplies them all.
                  So the wall is there. The part I have to be honest about is who counts as a decider.
              The theorem rules out a decider whose flip the substrate can itself represent. It says
              nothing about a decider standing outside, and an outside decider can exist for the
              very same property, correct on every program. The line between inside and outside
              is the boundary of the sentence, and the boundary is Richard’s lesson: the language
              you talk about a system in is a different language from the one it talks in. You’ll see
              it in miniature in a minute, on the nat family, with a pencil.
                  Two forms of the wall live in this section, and they’re honest in different ways.
                  The first is the nat family, a tiny substrate built so that program two is the
              Contrarian for a given candidate decider d, and for every d, d is wrong about
              program two. It’s a family, one instance per d, and its recursion theorem holds by
              construction. It’s the index cards made formal and nothing more.


              Theorem 13.2 (The nat family). Fix any Boolean function d on N. Let the substrate
              Nd have programs and states N; program 0 returns 1, program 1 returns 0, program
              2 returns 0 if d(2) is true and 1 if it is false, whatever the input state, and every
              other program gives nothing; each program is encoded as itself; µ is constantly 0, so
              any step relation will do; Rep( f ) holds when f ( p) = 1 for every p with d( p) true
              and f ( p) = 0 for every other p; and A( p) holds when program p returns 1 on input
              0. Then it is not the case that d( p) = true ⇐⇒ A( p) for every p.

              Proof. The recursion theorem of Nd holds with the fixed witness 2: for a repre-
              sentable f , f (2) is 1 or 0 according to d(2), and program 2 returns exactly what
              that program returns. The witnesses for A are 0 and 1, and A is extensional because
              it reads only what a program returns. The flip of d is representable by the definition
              of Rep, so Theorem 13.1 applies to d itself. Directly: A(2) holds exactly when d(2)
              is false.
                  Now push on it once more, because the nat family shows the outside decider in
              three lines, and you can do them yourself. Stand outside Nd , knowing d. Write down
              a new decider e: say yes on program 0, say “not d(2)” on program 2, and say no on
              everything else. Check it against A. Program 0 returns 1, so A(0) holds and e says
              yes. Program 1 returns 0, so A(1) fails and e says no. Program 2 returns 1 exactly
              when d(2) is false, and that’s what e says. Every other program gives nothing, so A
              fails and e says no. So e is right about every program. Does that break the wall? It
              doesn’t, and the reason is the part that matters: in Nd a flip is representable only if it
              says 1 exactly where d says yes, so the flip of e is representable only if e and d agree
                                                                   13.4 Now point it at the record   283


everywhere, and they disagree at program 2. The correct decider exists; its flip just
isn’t one of the substrate’s own moves. (It’s three lines and a pencil, and you just did
it.) One and the same property is undecidable from inside and decided cleanly from
outside, at the same time. That’s not a paradox, because it’s two different people
asking.
    The second form is the one where the recursion theorem is proved from the
reduction rules rather than assumed. It’s on L, the weak call-by-value lambda
calculus that Yannick Forster and Gert Smolka presented in 2017 as a model of
computation, and which a group at Saarland has since used as the seed of a
whole library of undecidable problems. Here L is built from its reduction rules.
The recursion theorem is proved, Rice’s theorem follows, halting follows, and the
diagonal is reproved in the shape of the substrate theorem, for any property of
programs that depends only on what they compute and that holds of one program
and fails of another. The statement mentions no shortcut. So on L the result is the
diagonal for one fixed model, and I don’t plug L into the substrate theorem, for this
reason: a substrate’s run map has to answer, with a state or with nothing, and for L
that map is the halting function itself, which no term of L computes. Using it would
take something from outside L, and L is in this book as the model where nothing
is taken from outside. So on L I run the argument again from scratch instead of
applying the general one. Both are true; they’re different sentences.
    I’ll say what that string of words means, because L is the strangest thing in this
book that computes, and the smallest. The lambda calculus is Alonzo Church’s, from
the 1930s, and it’s a programming language with one idea in it: functions. A term is
one of three things: a variable; a function, written λ followed by its body, the body
saying what to do with whatever you hand it; or one term applied to another, written
side by side. Running a program is one move, over and over: when a function meets
an argument, put the argument into the body where the variable was. The lambda
calculus has no numbers, no memory, no instructions, and in 1937 Turing published
a proof that it computes exactly what his machines compute. “Weak call-by-value” is
two house rules about the order of moves: an argument is run down to a finished
function (a value) before it’s put in, and nothing runs inside a function that hasn’t
been handed anything yet. Variables are written as numbers counting how many
λs back they were bound (a trick of Nicolaas de Bruijn; it means two variables can
never get mixed up by sharing a name), and a term is closed when every variable
in it is bound inside it, so it leans on nothing outside. Last, to hand a program to a
program, L needs a way to write any term as data, the way a program’s source is
a string you can pass around. The one used here is the Scott encoding, named for
Dana Scott, a student of Church’s who went on to build mathematical models of the
lambda calculus itself. As far as I can trace it, the encoding first appeared in lecture
notes of his from Berkeley in 1962 that he never published, as a way to write data;
284   13 The diagonal


              Torben Mogensen carried it over to lambda terms themselves in 1992, and that’s the
              form used here. All you need about it is that every term t gets one code, written ⌜t⌝,
              and the code is itself a closed value. Two tools get built on top of that in the proof:
              a quoting term Q that takes the code of a term to the code of that code (a program
              that prints its own source needs exactly this move), and a fixed-point combinator, a
              term that lets a function call itself, which is how Q works its way through a code of
              any size.
                  Do two of these on paper before I give you the general rule. Write I = λx.x: its
              instruction is “return whatever you were handed.” Hand I its own card and you
              get I I → I, and it stops. Now write D = λx.x x: “make two copies of what you
              were handed and apply the first to the second.” Hand it its own card. Putting D in
              for both copies of x gives D D → D D. You’re back at exactly the same instruction
              and argument, so the rule never finishes. Both arguments were already functions,
              so neither example sneaks any work under a function that hasn’t been handed
              anything.
                  The variable numbers are what keep the copying from getting confused. In
              λx.λy.x, the last x points past the nearest λ (the one for y) to the one before it, so
              its number is 1; in λx.λy.y the last variable has number 0. Rename x and y however
              you like and neither recipe changes. The codes below are a way of putting a whole
              recipe on a card that another recipe can read.

              Definition 13.3 (L, as built here). A term of L is a variable (a de Bruijn number),
              an application s t, or an abstraction λs; the values are the abstractions. One step
              is weak call-by-value, left to right: (λb) v steps to b with v substituted when v is a
              value, a step inside the left part of an application is a step of the application, and
              so is a step inside the right part once the left part is a value. A term s evaluates to
              v when s reaches v in some number of steps and v is a value; p ≡ q when p and q
              evaluate to the same values. Every term t has a code ⌜t⌝, its Scott encoding, which
              is a closed value. A map f on terms is L-computable when some closed value s has
              s ⌜ p⌝ ≡ f ( p) for every p. A term D decides a property P of terms when, for every p,
              D ⌜ p⌝ reaches λλ.1 (true) if P( p) holds and λλ.0 (false) if it fails. P is extensional
              when p ≡ q and P( p) give P(q).



              Theorem 13.3 (Recursion, Rice and halting for L). (1) For every closed value s
              there is a closed term t that reaches s ⌜t⌝; so every L-computable f has a term p
              with p ≡ f ( p). (2) Let P be extensional, with P(y) and not P(n) for closed terms
              y and n. Then no closed term decides P. (3) No closed term decides halting, the
              property of evaluating to some value.
                                                                   13.4 Now point it at the record   285


Proof. (1) First build a program that can assemble the code of the very application I
am about to run. The quoting program Q takes a term’s code and returns the code
of that code. Appendix J gives its construction and follows it through the three kinds
of term. The program mkapp takes two codes and joins them into the code of an
application.
    Make A do this when handed a code x: quote x, put that quoted code beside x
using mkapp, and hand the result to s. Written out,

                             A = λx. s (mkapp x ( Q x )).
Now run A on its own code, and call that whole application t: t = A ⌜ A⌝. The
first step puts ⌜ A⌝ where x stood. Quoting it supplies the code of ⌜ A⌝; joining the
two codes supplies the code of A ⌜ A⌝. That is the code of t itself. The computation
therefore reaches s ⌜t⌝, as promised. All the pieces were closed, so t is closed too. If
s computes f , the resulting behaviour is exactly f (t).
    (2) Suppose a closed program D decides P. Build another program that asks D
about the code it receives, then runs the no-example n after yes and the yes-example
y after no. In this language you must keep the two branches wrapped as functions
until the answer chooses one; otherwise call-by-value would try to run them before
choosing. The following term does that:

                            λx. D x (λ_. n) (λ_. y) (λz.z).

The final identity function is the harmless argument that opens the selected wrapper.
Thus a true answer runs n, and a false answer runs y.
   Apply part (1) to this program, obtaining its self-matching t. If P(t) holds, the
judge says true and t behaves like n, where P fails. If P(t) fails, the judge says false
and t behaves like y, where P holds. Either answer contradicts the requirement that
alike behaviour has the same verdict. No such D exists.
