   (3) Halting depends only on which values a term reaches. The identity λz.z is
already a value. The term (λx. x x )(λx. x x ) takes a step back to itself each time,
and is never a value. These supply the yes-example and no-example for part (2), so
halting has no closed decider either.
   The construction in that proof isn’t mine, and the credit belongs right here.
Forster and Smolka’s L development of 2017 has the Scott encoding of terms,
a closed quoting term with exactly this specification, the code of a term to the
code of its code, and a fixed point built the same way: their t is C ⌜C⌝ with
C = λx. s ( A x ( Q x )), so their C is my A, and their A, which builds the code of an
application, is my mkapp. They say they follow the proof in the Dutch logician Henk
Barendregt’s textbook on the lambda calculus (1984), where statement (1) is the
full lambda calculus’s second fixed-point theorem, and part (2) is what they call
286   13 The diagonal


              Scott’s theorem. The term construction is given in Appendix J; the route is theirs,
              and Barendregt’s before them.
                  So I’ve given the wall on paper, on a family built to fit it, and on one outside
              model. The machine built in Part III (Section 15) fills in this same shape: on its
              host machine, the one the universal program of Appendix D.1 runs on, which has a
              counter for every whole number, programs are numbers, Kleene’s recursion theorem
              is a theorem, and so is Rice’s, and the fixed point can be taken to agree on what the
              program computes and also on the ledger and the flag at the end of every run where
              they stop (Appendix D.4).
                  The table below lines up the picture all of that fills in against Turing’s, one column
              per axis.

               Time axis                                   Structural axis
               counts: steps                               counts: µ
               asks: does it halt?                         asks: does it admit the shortcut?
               the wall: no Turing machine decides halting the wall: no decider whose flip is
                                                           representable, under a recursion theorem


                 Read the table as two uses of one diagonal, each under its own premises, and
              as saying nothing more than that. The structural wall never uses µ; the µ entry
              only says what that axis counts. The nat result is a family indexed by the candidate
              decider, and L’s results are about one fixed model and properties that mention
              no shortcut. Neither hands you a second fixed undecidable problem, and neither
              separates Turing degrees: a property can sit behind the wall from inside and be
              decided cleanly from outside, as the pencil argument on Nd showed. And “admits
              the shortcut” in the right-hand column is the theorem’s sense, any behavioural
              property with a yes and a no. “Has a cheaper way to the same answer” is a second
              question, and the column has no wall for it.


              13.5 Where the diagonal applies
              The three versions put the candidate procedure in different places. In the general
              substrate argument, the substrate must represent the candidate’s flip. In the natural-
              number family, each candidate d supplies the substrate whose predicate defeats
              it. In L, the candidate is a closed term and the question is a nontrivial extensional
              property of closed terms. The reduction rules and recursion argument give Rice’s
              theorem there.
                                                                      13.6 What this does to the book   287


   The pencil calculation on Nd is useful precisely because it is outside that substrate.
To run the diagonal inside, I need the representability and recursion conditions
stated in the theorem.


13.6 What this does to the book
It does two things. It keeps me honest: nothing in what follows claims that a system
with a record can check its own shortcuts on autopilot, because that’s a wall, the
same wall, and I showed you the bricks. And it tells you what a record can do,
which is the thing Part II has been about since the counter: it can carry a shortcut
with its receipt, so that the question “was this earned” is answered by an event you
can point at. No decider has to exist for that, which is lucky, because on a system
with a recursion theorem no inside one can. The diagonal says such a system can’t
automate the judgement from inside, for any behavioural property with a yes and a
no. The latch says you can record the commitment. Those are different jobs, and a
record does the second.
     The diagonal has a famous cousin that looks as if it ought to bite a record too, so
let me walk right up to it. Gödel’s second theorem says a consistent system strong
enough for arithmetic can’t prove its own consistency, and Martin Löb, a logician
answering another logician’s question, sharpened that in 1955: if such a system
proves “if this is provable, it’s true,” it already proves the thing itself. So can a record
vouch for itself, and does Löb stop it? My first guess was that Löb stops it, since a
record looked like a system talking about itself. I landed somewhere else, and mostly
it’s a relief. Hold two things side by side: “there’s a receipt for this somewhere,” and
the receipt in your hand. Löb’s theorem is about provability, the bare claim that
some proof exists, the receipt somewhere. A record of the kind this book keeps is
the receipt in your hand, and it’s a different thing: an event, a check of some claim
that passed, a commitment to it, and a certificate, at a definite step of the run. It
doesn’t say which claim or which step, as the two runs near the end of Section 15,
under “Reading the instruction rules”, show; it says the event happened. Sergei
Artemov, a logician who comes back in Section 14, drew exactly that line in 2001,
between implicit provability (“there is a proof”) and explicit evidence (“this is a
proof”). As I read him, for explicit evidence the reflection step “if this is a proof of F,
then F” is harmless, while for the bare “there is a proof” it’s what Gödel and Löb
forbid. The reason, in my words, is that a receipt in your hand is one you can look
at, and a receipt somewhere is one you take on the system’s own word. A record sits
on the explicit side.
     Push on that and it gives, because a receipt is only as good as whoever wrote it.
Its trust rests on the checker meaning what it says, and that gets settled once, from
outside the machine. That’s where I chose to stop this machine’s chain of reasons.
288   13 The diagonal


              Gödel’s second theorem does not forbid a machine from checking a proof about a
              checker. What it limits is a system’s ability to prove its own consistency, when the
              system is strong enough to do arithmetic and its axioms can be listed by a machine.
              Eliezer Yudkowsky and Marcello Herreshoff’s 2013 draft on agents that trust their
              own rewrites describes a related problem, the Löbian obstacle: how an agent can
              justify trust in a successor’s proofs. That’s a cousin of this question, and it doesn’t
              settle it, and it doesn’t make my design the only one possible. So I didn’t get rid of
              the receipt somewhere. I moved it out of the machine and handed it to whoever
              reads the record.
                   One more thing follows from the same picture, by a short argument. Can a record
              rest on itself, the way the sentence “this sentence is certified” would like to? It can’t
              if it’s earned and permanent. The check behind the certificate that put the record up
              happened while the record was still down, because the record goes up only after that
              check passes, and once up it never comes back down, so it goes up only once. So
              no claim whose truth needs the record already up can be the claim the record went
              up on. (A later certificate, with the record already up, can stand on such a claim; it
              raises nothing.) Saul Kripke’s 1975 theory of truth calls a sentence like that, one that
              only ever leans on itself, ungrounded, and earned records are grounded in his sense:
              every one bottoms out in a check that didn’t lean on it. Caspar Oesterheld’s 2019
              work on programs that cooperate by simulating each other needed a grounding step
              of the same kind to stop an infinite regress. I haven’t written this argument out
              anywhere else; the claim is exactly what this paragraph says, and it’s short enough
              to check by hand.
                   I want to draw one last distinction, because the two are easy to conflate and
              conflating them is the easiest way to misread this book. There’s a second wall,
              nothing to do with the diagonal. It’s Section 7’s kind of wall, a window with a
              colliding pair in it. Two states that differ in their certification reading can look
              identical through a window that doesn’t show that reading, the stamp inside the
              closed drawer and the drawer opened and shut, and then no function of the window
              recovers the reading (Theorem 7.1: a decoder has to give one answer on everything
              the window lumps together). This wall comes from missing information. Nothing
              about it is undecidable; it holds for finite things with nothing to compute; and it
              sits beside Rice. None of Rice is underneath it. The property the diagonal uses (any
              behavioural property of programs with a yes and a no) is a different kind of thing
              from the reading the window hides, and nothing here says the two are the same. So
              there are two walls, on two different axes. The diagonal is about what no inside
              procedure can decide. The window is about what no outside observer can see. I’ll
              need both, and I’ll try not to call one by the other’s name again. The machine I build
              later has a colliding pair of exactly that kind (Theorem 15.17).

Established
290


          Part III is step four, the sharpest case. A record that a claim was checked and
      closed is a distinction that stays, so it pays what Part I found keeping takes, and it’s
      the case where you can point at the kept 0 and at what it cost. It starts with what
      established means, and why two computers with the same bits can differ in it. Then
      it builds the smallest example I could find that meets the definition: an ordinary
      computer of two counters, with a record layer on top whose flag is the blank cell, six
      kinds of instruction in all. Read through its window, the line and the two counters,
      it’s the ordinary computer again, run by its moves for the instructions and blind
      to the record and the ledger: the record layer is the part the slice forgets, and the
      appendix proves that every computer with a move for each two-counter instruction
      is the slice of a certified Thiele-complete machine (Theorem E.4). The step that
      raises the flag is the write of a 0, a merge in the record layer, and that’s why it’s
      charged; the order the step enforces, check, then commit, then certify, is what makes
      this record’s raise mean a claim held. That’s what I mean by certification, and it’s
      the layer this part adds to the bar Part II set. Then how far the example reaches,
      the real systems that already put a price on a write, the thesis about which kept
      distinction is worth paying for, and what the example’s counter has to do with heat.
      Those claims are about the model; the example is where you can check them line by
      line. The ordinary computer’s own steps merge too (counting a counter down lands
      two states on one), and like every step that changes something they dissipate when
      they happen; the ledger leaves them alone.
CHAPTER 14




What established means

Parts I and II were about any kept distinction at all. This chapter picks one: the
distinction between an answer that was checked and the same answer that wasn’t.
It’s the case the first pages of the book called the sharpest, and it’s sharp because
the two answers are the same bits, and everything that differs is in what was kept.


14.1 Two computers that end up the same

You met these two computers in one paragraph at the start of the book. Now I’ll
take them slowly: what an ordinary computer does about what Part I found keeping
takes, and why that matters to anybody who isn’t a physicist.
    Put two computers on a table. Hand each of them the same list of a thousand
numbers.
    The first one sorts it. It compares, swaps, walks the list again and again until
nothing is out of order. Then it does one more thing: it walks the whole list front to
back and checks that every number is no bigger than the one after it. That check
could have failed. It passes. Then it tidies up after itself, wipes its scratch work,
and leaves the sorted list in memory. (That check compares neighbours, so what it
settles is that the output is in order. That the output holds your thousand numbers
and no others is a second claim, and it would take a second check comparing the
output with the input. When I say sorted below, I mean in order.)
    The second one never looks at your list. Somebody typed the sorted version into
it earlier, same thousand numbers, same order, and it puts them in memory.
    Now wait until both are done and look inside. The bits in memory are the same,
and so are the bits on the screen. Set it up right, which you can, and it’s the same
everything, down to the last bit. The first compared the entries and checked their
order. The second loaded the same answer without doing either. The list is in order
in both; the difference is what each run did with it. Wheel them out on a cart, swap
them, wheel them back, and ask me which is which. I can’t tell you, and you can’t
tell me. And the part that bugs me most is that, built the ordinary way, neither
machine can tell you either.
    Sure, while they ran they were different. One did thousands of comparisons, the
other did a copy. But the runs are over and the runs are gone, and nobody was being
sloppy. Ordinary computers are built to forget how their bits got there, on purpose.

                                                 291
292   14 What established means


              That’s Landauer’s sentence about standardizing signals, from the start of the book,
              and why he said it gives off heat.
                   Who cares? Anybody who’s been handed a sheet that says “all tests passed.”
              Anybody who’s looked at an inspection sticker on a windshield: the sticker looks the
              same whether somebody checked the brakes or somebody sold the sticker. An audit,
              a proof, a ledger, an AI that sounds very sure of itself: every one of them is a pile
              of bits that could have come out of either computer, and the question that matters
              is the one the bits can’t answer. Did something establish this, or did it just print it?
              I’ll come back to every one of those later in this chapter and say which of them this
              book actually helps with, and I’ll warn you now that it’s fewer than you’d hope.
                   I’m going to call the first run’s relation to that answer established: it checked the
              order of this list. The second run has the answer without that relation. The list’s
              order is there either way. What can a machine keep of the difference between the
              runs? The rest of this chapter takes that question apart.
                   It belongs in a book about a 0 because a record that the check ran would be a
              distinction that stays, a 0 in some cell that says “checked.” These two computers
              did not keep that record. A machine that does keep it gives you something more to
              inspect.


              14.2 Look harder

              The obvious answer is: just look harder. Don’t look at the end, look at everything.
              So make the computers as lookable as computers get. Scale them up to the size of
              a warehouse, every wire a lamp that’s lit or dark, every switch something you can
              walk up to and touch. Nothing is hidden in a chip too small to see. Put both of them
              side by side and walk the floor.
                  While they run, sure, you’d see the difference. One has a whole wing lighting
              up, comparing and swapping, and the other just copies. But they finish, and the
              comparing wing goes dark. Now walk the floor and look at every single lamp.
              The sorted list is spelled out in lit and dark lamps in both, the same pattern, and
              everything else is dark in both, because both cleaned up.
                  There is no lamp anywhere that says “a check ran here and passed.” It isn’t
              hidden, and it isn’t encrypted; it just isn’t there. You can see everything there is,
              and the thing I’m after isn’t one of the things there is. Looking harder doesn’t help,
              because the problem isn’t that you can’t see enough. It’s that nothing was kept.
                  The shape I want you to carry through the rest is that the problem was never
              visibility; it’s keeping.
                                                                            14.3 So keep the trace   293


14.3 So keep the trace
Then the fix is obvious, isn’t it? Don’t let the run go. Keep the trace: every
comparison, every swap, the check and its answer, written down as it happens.
Wheel the computers out on the cart and back, read the traces, and you’ll know
which one sorted. Problem solved?
    It’s the right instinct, and it gets most of the way to this book. But take it apart,
because “just keep the trace” has three things wrong with it, and each one is a piece
of what comes later.
    First, a trace is bits, and bits can be typed in. Whoever typed the sorted list into
the second machine can type a trace in too: “compared, swapped, checked, passed,”
a few thousand lines of it, every one of them plausible. A trace written by a program
is something the program produced, and the machine running the program doesn’t
care whether it’s true. So keeping the trace doesn’t answer the question; it moves it.
Did something establish this trace, or did it just print it?
    Second, the way out of that is to take the pen away from the program. Don’t let
the program write its own trace. Have something underneath it write the trace, one
step at a time, as the steps actually happen, so nothing a program does can add a
line that didn’t happen or erase one that did. Airplanes do a version of this. Flight
recorders go back to a prototype David Warren built in Melbourne in the 1950s.
He was an Australian scientist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories, working
on jet fuel, and after a string of unexplained airliner crashes he wanted a box that
would hold the instrument readings and the voices in the cockpit for whoever came
looking afterwards; I know his story from museum and encyclopedia accounts, and I
haven’t read his own report. The recorders that came out of that idea are fed by the
aircraft’s own instruments. Nobody’s account of events goes into them. And they’re
built to survive the crash, so the investigators don’t have to depend on anyone’s
memory of what happened. The flight recorder has the right shape, and that shape
isn’t mine. Later in this chapter it gets its name from computer security, a reference
monitor, and I’ll say outright that a machine built that way would be doing what
this book describes. What the book adds is narrower than a rulebook for everything
underneath. It’s about the records that go up and never come back down: what that
something has to keep for good, and what keeping it takes.
    Third, you can’t keep all of it. A full trace grows with every step and never
stops growing, and a machine with finite memory runs out. Even the flight recorder
doesn’t keep everything. The cockpit voice recorder is a loop. I went looking for how
long the loop is, and it has kept growing: for decades it held the last thirty minutes,
an American rule in 2008 raised that to at least two hours, and the international
rules ask big airliners built since 2021 to carry twenty-five hours. Whatever the
294   14 What established means


              length, everything older gets recorded over. Every real machine that keeps a trace
              keeps a window of it, or a fingerprint of it, and forgets the content.
                  The fingerprint is the sharpest reply, so take it seriously. Fold every new line of
              the trace into a fixed-size scramble of everything before it, and you’ve got a hash
              chain. The timestamps of Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, two cryptographers at
              Bellcore whose story comes later in this chapter, work that way; so do the audit logs
              the cryptographers Bruce Schneier and John Kelsey designed in 1999; and so do
              the measurement registers in the security chip a lot of computers carry, the TPM.
              A running program can only extend those registers, folding a new measurement
              in. It can’t write a value of its own into them, and the ones that matter here start
              over only at the next reboot. That really does keep something about the whole
              trace in a few dozen bytes. But look at what it keeps: it keeps a binding, and the
              content isn’t in it. To read the history you still need the trace stored somewhere,
              and the fingerprint only tells you whether a copy somebody hands you is the one
              that went in. The binding holds only because nobody knows how to find two traces
              with the same fingerprint, which is a bet on how hard a search is. No law of nature
              backs it. That part isn’t only my opinion. The computer scientists Moni Naor and
              Guy Rothblum proved a sharp version of it in 2005, and they even call the thing
              a fingerprint: keep a small private fingerprint of a big file somebody else stores,
              check the file by reading only a little of it, and against an opponent with unlimited
              computing the size of the fingerprint times the amount you read has to be on the
              order of the whole file. Do even slightly better than that against an opponent with
              limited computing, and you’ve shown that one-way functions exist, which is the
              hardness bet in its barest form. Their setting is a stored file. A growing trace is a
              different setting, but it’s the same bet, with its terms written down. And squeezing
              traces that keep growing into a fixed number of bits has to land many traces on
              one fingerprint, and that’s a merge, hidden behind how hard it is to find which
              traces land on the same fingerprint. It’s the same merge as in the example of Part I
              (Section 3) where four people have to sit in three chairs. Fingerprints are great, but
              they’re not a way out of forgetting; they’re a very clever way of forgetting.
                  So the real question was never “save everything.” The real question is: what’s the
              smallest thing worth keeping for good, and what does keeping it take? The answer
              this book ends up with is the commitment, in the database’s sense, a question closed,
              and the trace drops away. (The cryptographer’s sealed envelope also goes by the
              name commitment. It’s a different thing, and both come up later.) What’s kept for
              good isn’t every comparison the sort made, just the one fact that a check of this very
              claim passed and the question got closed. And the part that matters most is that
              keeping even that one fact for good takes something on every machine. It’s paid by
              forgetting something somewhere else or by taking fresh states the machine never
                                                                           14.3 So keep the trace   295


gets back, and on a finite machine the fresh states run out, so it’s the forgetting.
That’s Part I’s counting of states again, and Part I counted the fresh states.
    So the premise was never that computers can’t keep records. They keep records
all day. It’s that nothing in the rules of an ordinary computer makes the record paid
for, permanent, or earned, and those three come in at different places, so I’ll say
where. Paid for is the model’s one rule: in the Thiele Machine, the step that raises
the record has to cost something. Permanent is a premise, the one Part I’s counting
of states needs, and one of the conditions Part II puts on a record. Earned, meaning
a check of this very claim passed first, isn’t in the model’s core at all. It’s what the
step of the small machine in the next chapter enforces, proved for that machine
and every program on it run from a clean start. One more word rides along with
permanent, and it’ll come up when I line my record up against other people’s: dated.
A record that goes up and stays up went up at one particular step of the run and not
another, even though the record doesn’t write down which step. So dated, in this
book, means it has a place in the run’s history. Carrying a timestamp is something
else, and my record doesn’t do it. A machine that charges one for every step it takes
meets the first rule, and the charging does nothing toward the others, and I’ll keep
pointing that out.

Open the gauge wider
Go back to the Sorter. It checked the order of the list. Now ask it another question:
did it also check that none of the original numbers went missing? The list on the
screen can be the same whether that second check happened or not. One lamp
saying “checked” will not tell me which work was done.
    Put a sheet beside the scratchpad, with a named box for each check. Order gets
a box. Membership gets a box. Each other check you want to remember gets its
own. When I come back, I want to know which boxes were ticked. If two runs tick
different boxes and leave the same working value, the full machine has to leave me
something that tells them apart. That is more of the fibre above the same tabletop
picture, brought within the question.
    Here are the moves. WRITE puts a value b on the scratchpad and starts a fresh
sheet, even if I write the same value again. CHECK i tests its named predicate Pi
and records its name when it passes. A failed check changes nothing in this monitor.
IDLE leaves both scratchpad and sheet alone. The reader can see the working value
and ask about every check name: did it pass since the last WRITE? The sheet must
answer yes when it did and no when it didn’t.
    Take a finite list of named checks, and let m(b) count the ones whose predicates
are true at b. Each of those can be run or left unrun. The truths themselves may
overlap; it is my choice to perform each check that is independent. Four true
296   14 What established means


              predicates give sixteen possible ticked sheets above the same value. The general
              count follows in the same way.


              Theorem 14.1 (Exactly how many current sheets). For a finite nonempty working
              set B and this WRITE/CHECK/IDLE interface, an exact host needs at least 2m(b)
              reachable full states above each b. The minimum total reachable state count is

                                                    ∑ 2m ( b ) .
                                                   b∈ B

              Proof. Hold the working value fixed and start with two named checks that would
              pass there. Run neither, the first alone, the second alone, or both. The working
              value is the same in all four cases. The required answers are not. In particular, the
              first-only case and the second-only case cannot finish at the same full state: ask
              whether the first check ran, and that one state would have to answer both yes and
              no.
                   Each further check that would pass doubles the choices. For every sheet you
              already had, you can leave its new box blank or run that check and tick it. Starting
              from one empty sheet, m(b) such choices give 2m(b) sheets. Every sheet is reachable:
              WRITE the value b, then perform exactly the checks whose boxes it ticks. Any
              two different sheets disagree at some named box, so they need different full states.
              States showing different working values are also different. Add the required states
              for each value to get the displayed sum.
                   Now build a machine with exactly that many states. A state consists of the
              working value and its ticked sheet. Include every sheet that ticks only checks true at
              that value. WRITE replaces the value and clears the sheet. CHECK ticks its own box
              if its predicate is true, and otherwise leaves the sheet alone. IDLE changes nothing.
              These rules never produce a forbidden sheet.
                   Start with the empty sheet. After a WRITE it is empty again, exactly as the task
              requires. After a successful CHECK it has precisely that success added; a repeated
              success changes nothing further. A failed CHECK adds nothing, and IDLE adds
              nothing. If the sheet described the history correctly before a command, it therefore
              describes it correctly afterward. Following any finite list of commands proves the
              promised answers. The WRITE-and-check runs above reach every state I included.
              The lower count is attained.
                 Try it with just one box. The workspace holds false or true, and CHECK asks
              whether it is true. The whole monitor fits in three states: false, true-unchecked,
              true-checked. WRITE false goes to the first. WRITE true goes to the second. CHECK
              moves the second to the third and leaves the other two alone. IDLE leaves all three
              alone. Start at false. WRITE true reaches true-unchecked, and then CHECK reaches
                                                                          14.3 So keep the trace   297


true-checked; all three states are reachable. Now take any word of instructions. A
WRITE makes the verdict false and starts a new sheet, even if it writes the same
value. A CHECK on false leaves the verdict false; a CHECK on either true state
makes or keeps the verdict true. IDLE preserves it. These are all the cases, and each
matches exactly what happened since the last WRITE. Applying that argument after
each instruction proves the promise for every finite word. In particular, the first
arrival at true-checked must use CHECK: neither WRITE nor IDLE can enter it from
another state.
   The two true states also show you the merger. CHECK sends true-unchecked
and true-checked to the same next state, right above the same working value. A
larger implementation can move that merger later: let CHECK enter a finite region
of accepting states in the fibre and keep it there, and some two distinct states must
share a CHECK successor. WRITE can still clear the current sheet. Permanence under
that one check and permanence under every instruction are different promises.
Call that finite accepting region H and the entering state u. The move sends all of
H ∪ {u} into H. There are | H | + 1 distinct sources and only | H | possible targets,
so two sources share a successor. The move preserves the working picture, so both
sources and their common successor lie in that same fibre.

Keep the old receipts when the page is wiped
Now wipe the scratchpad and use it again. I still want the receipt for the first page.
Then use it a third time. I want that receipt too. Think of carbon copies filed before
each sheet goes in the bin. On the tabletop, you can be back where you started. In
the file, you have a past you didn’t have before.
   On each of n editions, give me the choice to certify it or leave it uncertified.
Bring every choice back to the same final working picture b. Then ask the machine
about any edition I name. It has to answer whether that edition was certified. Two
histories that disagree on that answer need two different full states, however alike
their tabletops look. There are 2n possible yes-or-no lists to distinguish.


Theorem 14.2 (Room for independently retained editions). Under those realization
and exact-query requirements, the fibre above b contains at least 2n reachable states.
If one fixed host meets the requirements for every finite n at that same b, no finite
set covers its reachable fibre.

Proof. Two different lists of length n differ at an edition. Equal endpoints could
not answer that edition’s query differently, so the endpoints are distinct. A putative
finite cover of size K fails once 2n > K. Every endpoint being counted has the same
working view b.
298   14 What established means


                  You can build the witness directly. Keep a Boolean workspace, the answers for
              the completed editions, and the current stage of CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY.
              On a true workspace, run the chain for an edition you choose to certify, or skip it for
              one you don’t. Then WRITE true to start the next edition. Every choice brings you
              back to the same true workspace and a fresh current stage. Open the file and the
              choices are still there, in exactly the places you made them.
                  Put the whole machine on the table. There is the current page, holding false
              or true. There is a marker beside it, with four positions: raw, checked, committed,
              published. And there is a numbered file of yes-or-no answers for pages already put
              away. Start with a true page, the marker at raw, and an empty file.
                  CHECK can move the marker from raw to checked, but only if the page says
              true. COMMIT can move it from checked to committed. CERTIFY can move it from
              committed to published. Press any of those buttons at another stage and it leaves the
              arrangement alone. IDLE always leaves it alone. Those are all the ways to move the
              marker without replacing the page, so there is no shortcut from raw to published.
                  WRITE does three things, in this order. It files yes if the marker is at published
              and no otherwise. It puts the requested value on the page. Then it returns the
              marker to raw. The answer goes into the file before the marker is reset, and no
              command alters an answer already filed.
                  Check what that means after any command. CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY
              move the current page through exactly the named stages; they do not touch earlier
              pages’ answers. IDLE leaves both alone. WRITE closes the current page with the
              answer its stage warrants, then opens a raw page. Start with no earlier pages and
              follow those rules one command at a time: the file always answers the completed-
              page questions correctly, and the marker gives the current page’s stage.
                  To file a yes, run CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY, then WRITE true. To file a no, use
              WRITE true alone. Either choice leaves a true page with the marker at raw, ready
              for the next choice. After n choices the page and marker are identical in every run,
              while the file holds exactly the n answers chosen. Every yes-or-no list is possible,
              and different lists are different full states.
                  Keep asking for another edition, with the same freedom of choice and the same
              right to read back every answer. Whatever finite number of full states you offer
              above b, a long enough history outruns it. The tabletop can keep coming back to
              one picture. The machine that keeps all those choices cannot fit its reachable fibre
              into a finite set. That is where the infinity comes from.
                  The old yes-or-no gauge still has a job. Ask whether the file contains any
              certification at all and it becomes a permanent lamp: once yes, always yes. Ask
              whether today’s sheet is certified and wiping that sheet starts the answer over. The
              small native machine in the next chapter has the permanent lamp. I will look behind
              it at the whole native state, then count which publication histories even that larger
                                                                 14.4 Computed, stored, established   299


view leaves out. That camera sees more than the working value here; the next count
will name its fibre just as explicitly.


14.4 Computed, stored, established
Three words get used like they’re one.
    Computed is about the steps. The first machine computed the sorted list. The
second didn’t.
    Stored is about the bits. Both machines stored it.
    Established is neither, and that’s the whole problem. It isn’t the steps, because
they’re gone. It isn’t the bits, because they’re identical. It’s something like this: the
first machine has a right to lean on “this list is sorted,” because it ran a test that
could have failed, the test passed, the test was about this very list, and then the
question got closed. The second machine has the same sentence and no right to it.
That’s a true fact about the two of them, and it’s written down nowhere, in either
one. (Whose right, strictly? A machine doesn’t lean on anything, any more than a
filing cabinet does. It’s the right of whoever reads the first machine to lean on what
it says, and the machine is where the grounds for that right would have to be kept.
“The machine has a right” is shorter, so I’ll keep saying it, and now you know what
it’s short for.)
    I’ll hold four words still from here on. A check is the test, the thing that could say
no. A commit is the closing, the question shut for good, about that edition of that
thing. The record is whatever stays behind to say so. And established, in the sense a
machine can carry, is all three, about one thing. The first machine had the check
and the closing and kept no record of either, which is the problem above. Where
the closing and the record are one act, as in a database’s commit, writing the record
is the closing. The small machine keeps them apart, a commitment the next one
replaces and a certificate that stays. The book cashes this working sense at three
depths: a paid closing in the bare model; an object with a checked relation and a
paid event, in Part II (Section 8); and the whole chain on the small machine, in the
next chapter. Each place says which one it means.
    That raises a fair question: what if the second machine, handed the typed-in
list, runs the check on it? Then it has what the first machine had, and if it closes
the question and keeps the record, it has established that the list is sorted. It didn’t
do the sorting and it doesn’t need to. The line I’m drawing is between checked
and unchecked. Whether the list was computed or copied doesn’t enter into it, and
“without doing either” up there was about the copier that never looked. So whatever
this book ends up counting, it isn’t how hard anybody worked.
300   14 What established means


                 People say “a right to lean on it” about a lot of things that turn out to be vibes, so
              I had to find out whether this one was anything. I went looking, and I’ll go through
              what I ran into.


              14.5 The clerk who forgets everything
              The picture of a computer I used in Section 5 is a person with a pencil, a strip of
              paper and a short list of rules. So I went back to the source, Alan Turing’s 1936
              paper, to see how far he actually takes it.
                  He takes it a long way. Back then a “computer” was a job, a human doing sums
              by hand, and Turing modelled that person. He’s careful with the person’s mind:
              whatever the clerk knows, beyond a handful of states, has to go down on the paper.
              Then he goes all the way. He imagines the clerk getting up, walking off, forgetting
              everything, and coming back later. To pick up where he left off, the clerk leaves
              himself “a note of instructions,” and Turing says that note is the clerk’s state of mind,
              as far as the computation is concerned. Marks on paper and a note are the whole
              state.
                  My two computers are sitting right inside that. Suppose the clerk didn’t write
              the note. Somebody slipped it under the door, in the right form, with the right
              instructions. He comes back, reads it, carries on, and every mark he makes from
              then on is exactly what he’d have made if he’d written it himself. Turing’s model
              can’t tell the clerk who did the work from the clerk who was handed a note saying
              he did. It was never asked to. Turing wanted something you could check without
              crawling into anybody’s head, and a note on a desk is about as checkable as it gets.
              That’s why the paper still works ninety years later. It’s also why there’s no place in it
              for the thing I’m after.
                  So the founding picture of computing is a man who leaves his desk, forgets
              everything he was doing, and trusts a sticky note. I relate to him deeply.
                  And now the question nobody needs answered to follow the argument, which is
              exactly the kind I can’t leave alone: who were those clerks? They were real people.
              In the late 1800s the Harvard Observatory hired rooms full of women to do the
              arithmetic of the sky, cataloguing stars by hand for a fraction of a man’s wage, and
              some of them made discoveries of their own, Henrietta Leavitt’s way of telling how
              far away a star is among them. (I took the wages and the discoveries from Dava
              Sobel’s history of those women, and from the historians at the American Institute of
              Physics, who put the men’s hourly pay at nearly five times the women’s.) Rooms
              like that ran artillery tables in both world wars; that part I took from David Alan
              Grier’s history of human computers. So when Turing modelled “the computer,” he
              was modelling somebody’s actual afternoon. That doesn’t change the argument a
              bit. It changes the picture, though, for me anyway: the sticky note was always a
                                                            14.6 Information doesn’t have it either   301


person trusting another person’s work, and the question of whether the work behind
it was really done is older than any machine.


14.6 Information doesn’t have it either
My next guess was information: one machine got some, the other didn’t. That one
died fast. Claude Shannon, who turned information into a number in 1948, says
on his first page that the meaning of a message is “irrelevant to the engineering
problem.” His number measures how many messages you could have sent. What
the one you sent did is outside it, which is exactly right for building telephone lines
and exactly no help to me. The same message out of the same set gets the same
number, for both computers. He’d give them the same number if one of them got hit
by lightning and came out right by luck.
    Fine, forget the set and look at the one message. In the 1960s three people, sepa-
rately, worked out how to measure the information in one string: Ray Solomonoff,
an American who was after a theory of guessing what comes next from what came
before; Andrei Kolmogorov, the great Soviet mathematician; and Gregory Chaitin, an
Argentine-American mathematician who later worked at IBM. Their measure is the
length of the shortest program that prints the string. The same two computers hold
the same string and get the same number. And then there’s the thing in that theory
I keep going back to and standing on, to see if it creaks. Running a program can’t
add this kind of information. What comes out can’t hold more than what went in
plus the program, give or take a little. Leonid Levin, who studied under Kolmogorov
in Moscow and later left the Soviet Union to teach at Boston University, proved a
general version of this, and he has a one-liner for it that’s too good not to repeat:
you can torture an uninformed witness all you want, you won’t get information
about the crime.
    That means, as far as information goes, sorting your list told you nothing. The
sorted list holds nothing that “your list, plus the word sort” didn’t already hold.
    Logic says the same thing in a different coat. The standard logic of knowing, the
one the Finnish philosopher Jaakko Hintikka worked out in 1962, has a property
people call logical omniscience: if you know some facts, you automatically know
everything that follows from them. So by that logic, once you knew every number
on your list, you already knew whether it was sorted. Hintikka flagged the problem
himself, in the same book, and people have been trying to fix it since. The fixes read
like a pile until I asked each one the same thing: when it lets you write known next
to “sorted,” what does it make you write in the margin? Hintikka’s margin is empty.
Each fix writes one thing there.
    The fix that comes closest to me is from 1995, by Sergei Artemov, a logician
at the City University of New York who studied under that same Kolmogorov (the
302   14 What established means


              1995 report came out of Cornell). He wanted a logic that could name the proof
              itself. What I think he’s saying: you only get to know a thing if you’ve built an actual
              justification for it, and the justification rides along with the claim. That’s a reason
              traveling with the claim, which is almost a record, but only almost, because it’s a
              way of writing things down and reasoning about them, and nothing in his margin
              says the reason was ever run, or when. People have taught it to count, too: Ho
              Ngoc Duc, a logician at Leipzig, in 1997, made knowing take reasoning steps, and
              Artemov and Roman Kuznets, a logician then at Bern, in 2014, asked how big a
              justification can get before knowing by it stops being feasible (Part II weighed both
              properly, in Section 8). I took those for rivals at first. As I read them now, Duc
              counts the steps the knower takes and Artemov and Kuznets weigh what you’d hand
              somebody to check it, one distance from two ends. It has a computational side, too:
              Francisco Bavera and Eduardo Bonelli, two Argentine computer scientists who work
              on what programming languages mean, in 2018 turned justification logic into a
              lambda calculus whose terms carry, and can inspect, the history of the computation
              that made them, and Samuel Bucheli, Meghdad Ghari and Thomas Studer, three
              logicians, Studer the head of the logic group at Bern, put justifications on a time
              line in 2017, where they persist and change.
                  Line that up against the margin this book wants: earned, paid for, permanent,
              dated. Artemov’s reason is nearly earned, the steps and the sizes are prices, the time
              line is a date. Their time line keeps its dates. Mine is dated only in the execution
              history: the raise happened at a definite step, and the record doesn’t keep the step
              number. What none of it has is the closing of a question as a step with a price. Their
              prices are on reasoning, and the Bern justifications change, the one thing a closed
              question doesn’t do. Push on mine, though, and it gives twice. Artemov’s margin
              holds the reason itself, and mine only says a check passed. And their prices grow
              with how hard the thing was to know. This book charges the step that raises the
              record, and how long the checking took never enters it, so for a measure of effort,
              read theirs.
                  So the two most careful accounts I could find, one about bits and one about
              knowing, say the same thing: the sort added nothing.
                  And yet you know something after the sort that you didn’t before. You can read
              the smallest number off the first slot. You can stop worrying. Something happened,
              and that’s the clue, the first solid thing I’ve got: whatever established is, it isn’t new
              bits. It’s the same bits, settled: a question sorted into yes and no, with yes made to
              stay. It’s the 0 again, about a claim.
                                                                      14.7 The guy who got closest   303


14.7 The guy who got closest
Somebody had that clue before me, and on that clue he’s the closest neighbour I’ve
found, so he gets the most space and the hardest push.
   Bennett again, the one from Part I’s counting of states and the demon, wrote a
paper in 1988 that starts where I just ended up: information isn’t the same as value.
His example is an almanac of where the moon and planets will be every day for
a hundred years. It has no more information than the equations it was calculated
from, but it saves you doing the calculating. So the value is the work. He called the
amount of work a thing carries its depth.
   Was this my idea, already done, by a guy at IBM? The only way to find out was
to find where it parts from mine, because if I couldn’t find that place I’d just be
renaming his idea. And it’s one word: plausibly. Depth is the amount of work a
thing was plausibly made with. Bennett says straight out that you can’t know how a
message actually came to be; for all you know it came from flipping coins. Depth is
read off the finished thing, the way a fossil’s age is read off the fossil.
   Bring the two computers back. The sorted list in the first one has some depth.
The identical list in the second has exactly the same depth, because depth looks at
the list and nothing else. A photocopy of a deep thing is just as deep. Depth tells
you what work a plausible way of making the thing would take. It’s not a record
that this machine did it, and it’s not a receipt for what doing it cost.
   So Bennett’s standing right next to the line, on the other side of it, and as far as I
can tell he got his own question right. He asked how much work a thing embodies.
I’m asking who has the right to lean on it and what they paid to get there. His
answer lives in the object. Mine, if I’ve got one, has to live in the machine.


14.8 Statues that walk off

If it isn’t in the information, maybe it’s in the knowing, so I went and read the
philosophers. And there it was again: people had been arguing about the difference
between having the right answer and knowing it for a couple thousand years.
    Plato’s version is a joke about statues. There was a story that the sculptor
Daedalus made statues so lifelike they’d walk off if you didn’t tie them down. Plato
says true opinions are like that: they wander off, and they’re not worth much
until you tie them down with the reason why. Once they’re tied down, they’re
knowledge, and they stay put. Knowledge tied to a reason, and knowledge that
stays: of everybody I’d have bet on to hand me that shape, Plato wasn’t on the list.
    Then in 1963 Edmund Gettier, whose trap Part II played with cups (Section 8),
broke the tidy version in three pages. Smith and Jones are up for the same job.
Smith has good reason to think Jones will get it, and he’s counted the coins in
304   14 What established means


              Jones’s pocket: ten. So Smith figures, with good reason, that the man who’ll get
              the job has ten coins in his pocket. Then Smith gets the job, and, unknown to him,
              Smith also has ten coins in his pocket. Smith had a belief that was true and backed
              by a reason, and it still wasn’t knowledge. He was right by luck, because his reason
              was about the wrong pocket.
                  Gettier’s case is the push that matters for a machine. Checking one pocket and
              committing to a claim about another is right by luck. So whatever a machine
              commits to, the check underneath has to be about this very claim, and I’d better say
              exactly what that means, because it carries a lot of weight later.
                  A check is about this very claim when four things hold. It tests the same property
              the commit names. A cousin of that property won’t do. It tests that property on the
              same thing the commit names, and the thing next to it won’t do either. Nothing has
              written to that thing between the check and the commit, so it’s still the same edition
              the check looked at. And the check is honest: it says yes when the property is true
              and no when it isn’t, on every value it could ever be handed, this one and all the
              others. Break the first three and you’re Smith with his ten coins. Break the fourth
              and the check is just a rubber stamp. The next chapter builds a machine whose step
              won’t let a commit through unless the first three hold, and whose checks come with
              a proof of the fourth.
                  Two notes on those four, because they matter later. The fourth asks for more
              than it needs. To rule out luck, a check only has to never say yes when the property
              is false; saying yes every time it’s true is a bonus. And the third is a very old bug in
              computing wearing Gettier’s coat. Security people call it time-of-check-to-time-of-
              use: check a file, use it, and something swaps the file in between (Matt Bishop and
              Michael Dilger, two computer security researchers at the University of California,
              Davis, wrote up how to hunt for it in 1996). Databases guard against the same
              thing by making sure, just before a commit, that nothing they read has been written
              since; H. T. Kung and John Robinson, two computer scientists at Carnegie-Mellon,
              called that optimistic concurrency control in 1981. A philosopher’s pocket and a
              sysadmin’s race condition are the same bug. One limit, said now: a machine can
              only promise “nothing has written to that thing” about its own memory; for brake
              pads or a voter roll the third condition becomes a premise about whoever measured
              (Section 17).
                  At this point I went further than this chapter needs, because the obvious next
              question is: does anything fix Gettier? People tried for years. The first patch is “no
              false steps in the reasoning”: Smith’s mistake was believing Jones would get the job,
              so rule that out. Then a philosopher named Alvin Goldman came back with barns,
              and he credits the barns to Carl Ginet, another philosopher working on what it takes
              to know something. You’re driving through a county that, unknown to you, is full of
              fake barns, just painted fronts propped up to look like the real thing. You look at
                                                                 14.9 What “could have failed” means   305


the one real barn in the county and think “that’s a barn.” It’s true, you believe it,
you have a good reason, your own eyes, and there’s no false step anywhere. And
still you were lucky: if you’d glanced at the next one over you’d have believed the
same thing and been wrong. Every patch gets a new barn, and as far as I can tell
the arguing hasn’t stopped. That tells me something I’ll keep: whether a check was
good isn’t only about this one case. It’s about what the check would have done on
the cases next door. Hold on to that, because it’s the next section.


14.9 What “could have failed” means

I keep saying the first machine’s test could have failed. Take that apart, because it’s
the piece everything else hangs off.
    The machine is deterministic. Given your list, the check was always going to pass.
So in what sense could it have failed? By “could have failed” I mean this: hand
the checking stage an out-of-order candidate output and it says no. I do not mean
hand the whole sorter an unsorted input; putting that input in order is its job. The
relevant counterfactual is a defective candidate reaching the checker. An ordinary
unsorted input reaching the sorter isn’t it. Chance has nothing to do with it. The
copier that never checks has no corresponding rejection.
    A check is a question asked of every possible input, and it splits them into two
piles: the ones it says yes to and the ones it says no to. “Could have failed” just
means the no pile isn’t empty. A check that says yes to everything has an empty
no pile, and it distinguishes no inputs, however long it runs and however official
it looks. It can still be sound, when its property holds of everything, and then it’s
sound and tells you nothing you didn’t have. A philosopher, Robert Nozick, made a
version of this a condition for knowing, in 1981: you know a thing only if, had it
been false, you wouldn’t believe it.
    “Could have failed” describes the procedure, about what the check would have
done on other lists. It isn’t a fact about the end state at all. Look at the first machine’s
memory when it’s done: a sorted list. Nothing in those bits says “and whatever made
me would have caught a mistake.” The warehouse comes back here, every lamp
visible and none of them saying it. The one thing that makes the first machine’s
answer worth more is exactly the kind of thing those bits can’t hold: the copier
ends with the same bits, and neither machine kept anything else. An end state can
hold more than the answer, and the only way a machine can own this is to write
something down at the moment the check passes, and to have that something mean
what it says. More than anything else in this chapter, that’s why I ended up needing
a record. A better answer wouldn’t have done it. Even then the record only carries
half of it. It can say a check ran on an edition and passed. That the check would
have said no on a bad list is a fact about the checker, and that half rides on a proof
306   14 What established means


              about the checker; on this machine that proof sits outside, and whoever reads the
              record reads and accepts it. Where that kind of chain of reasons stops is the swamp
              of the philosopher Karl Popper, a little further down.
                  One more thing that tripped me up and then didn’t. Rig a check to pass only on
              your one list. Is that cheating? No. It’s a perfectly honest check of a different claim,
              “this is that exact list,” and it has a big no pile: every other list. It establishes exactly
              that and nothing more. What a check establishes is whatever it’s honest about.
                  Put that next to the empty no pile and the two fit together: a check establishes
              what it’s honest about, and a check with an empty no pile is honest only about what
              you already had. One thing I’ll say plainly now, so it doesn’t ambush you in the next
              chapter: the example I build there doesn’t police this. Its step makes sure a commit
              was checked first, about the same thing, by a checker proved honest. It doesn’t stop
              you asking a question that can’t come out no, like “is this number at least zero.”
              Ask one and the whole chain runs, it costs three, and nothing is established but the
              chain. The certificate I show off there asks one that can fail.


              14.10 Settled, whether it’s true or not
              Then I ran into Charles Sanders Peirce again, the one from Section 5, in an 1877
              essay called “The Fixation of Belief.” He was asking what inquiry is for, and his
              answer named the thing I’d been running together without noticing. The point of
              inquiry, he says, is to get out of doubt and settle on a belief. And when someone
              objects that surely what people want is a true belief, he answers like a guy who’s
              watched a lot of arguments end: “as soon as a firm belief is reached we are entirely
              satisfied, whether the belief be true or false.”
                  That’s funny, and then it isn’t, because he’s right. Settling and being right are two
              different events. A question can be closed on a wrong answer, and once it’s closed it
              acts closed. Peirce cares a lot about which ways of settling hold up (science wins,
              for him, because it has to answer to something outside any one person), but the
              settling itself, the question snapping shut, is there every time, and it never comes
              with a guarantee.
                  Karl Popper came at it from the other side. He was a philosopher from Vienna
              asking what separates science from everything else, and in his 1934 book, the one
              that came into English as The Logic of Scientific Discovery, he says every test has to
              stop somewhere, at some statement somebody decides to accept, and nothing in
              the evidence forces you to stop there instead of one step further. You stop when
              you’re satisfied. His picture is a jury: the verdict is a decision about what happened,
              and the jury deciding it doesn’t make it true. Science, for him, is a building on piles
              driven into a swamp, and the piles stop where somebody’s satisfied they’ll hold.
              They never reach firm ground.
                                                              14.10 Settled, whether it’s true or not   307


    A real jury has a problem Popper doesn’t mention, because a real jury is twelve
people. Lewis Kornhauser and Lawrence Sager, two law professors writing in the
Yale Law Journal, noticed in 1986 that a court that votes by majority on each premise
of a case and also on the verdict can end up contradicting itself: every judge is
consistent, and the court isn’t. Christian List and Philip Pettit, two philosophers
writing in Economics and Philosophy, turned that in 2002 into a theorem. No way of
combining people’s yes-or-no judgments on connected questions meets a short list of
conditions that each look harmless on their own and always hands back a consistent,
complete group judgment. A group’s settling is a rule’s settling, and which rule you
pick decides which of the honest settlings sticks. Try the problem with three ballots
and a rule that a payment is due only if a contract was signed and a deadline was
missed. One voter says yes to both, one says signed but not missed, and one says
missed but not signed. Each voter applies the rule consistently. Count separately: a
majority says signed, a majority says missed, and a majority says no payment. You
can point to the disagreement on the paper without blaming any one voter’s logic.
I haven’t tried to put a group on the machine, and that’s where I’d expect the first
wall to be.
    Popper’s swamp sent me further down, because it’s the oldest problem in the
book and it doesn’t have a bottom. Ask why you believe something and you get a
reason. Ask why you believe the reason and you get another one. Sextus Empiricus,
a skeptic and doctor who lived probably in the second or third century and whose
whole method was holding off judgment, wrote down the ancient version, credited
to someone called Agrippa, and in 1968 the German philosopher Hans Albert, who
with Popper led the school called critical rationalism, gave it a name with a joke in
it: the Münchhausen trilemma, after the baron who claimed he pulled himself out of
a swamp by his own hair. Every chain of reasons does one of three things. It goes on
forever. It loops back on itself. Or it stops somewhere, because somebody decided it
stops. People have argued for a very long time about which of the three to live with.
So “when do I actually know, and when am I done checking?” doesn’t get a clean
answer from anybody. What you can do is be honest about where you stopped and
why. That’s a lot of what the rest of this book is: every place it stops is written down,
with its name on it, so you can decide whether you’d have stopped there too.
    Lay Peirce and Popper on top of each other and what shows through is that the
check is one act and the stopping is another. The check can run as long as you like
and it never makes you stop; at some point something decides, and the deciding is
its own event. That’s the second machine’s whole trick: it skipped the check and
kept the answer.
    And a logician said the part I didn’t expect a logician to say. Per Martin-Löf, a
Swedish logician, says a proof is an act, and once it’s done it’s done. His words,
from lectures he gave in Siena in 1983: “a proof is, not an object, but an act . . .
308   14 What established means


              Only secondarily, and irrevocably, does it become the act that has been performed.”
              That took me a few reads, and the tenses unlocked it: first the act being done, then,
              for good, the act that has been done. You could say that’s true of everything that
              ever happened, and I’d grant it, but it’s the two computers again: the first machine’s
              check happened, irrevocably, and the machine right now carries no trace of it. The
              past can’t be undone. The record of it can be lost, unless something keeps one. That
              gap is where this book lives.
                 Then the intuitionists got there first, which by now I should’ve expected. The
              Dutch mathematician L. E. J. Brouwer, who held that a mathematical truth is some-
              thing a mind makes evident, argued from 1948 on about an idealised mathematician
              working in stages, the creating subject. The people after him only came clear to me
              once I sorted them by three words: the act, the object, and the trace the act leaves
              behind, which Martin-Löf’s sentence has no room for. The logician Georg Kreisel
              (1967), Austrian-born and then at Stanford, wrote it down as a formula: the subject
              has evidence for A at stage n. That’s a trace, something you can come back and
              ask about after the act is over. Anne Troelstra (1969), a Dutch logician who studied
              under Brouwer’s student Arend Heyting and became one of the leading authorities
              on intuitionism, added that the subject never forgets what it has made evident, so
              the trace never fades. That’s how Mark van Atten (2018), a philosopher in Paris
              who has spent years on Brouwer, credits it; the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on
              intuitionism lists the never-forgets axiom among Kreisel’s own, and I haven’t settled
              which is right. Van Atten, going through the whole history, reads the formula as “by
              stage n the Creating Subject has made A evident.” Look at the tense. Has made is
              Martin-Löf’s “the act that has been performed,” reached from the other end. And
              look at what that carries. It’s tied to a stage; at any stage you can ask whether it’s
              happened yet; it never goes away; and it’s never wrong. Van Atten even says the
              subject can’t just accept a proof handed to it from outside: it has to go through the
              steps and rebuild the evidence itself, which is the copier who runs the check. And
              then there’s Göran Sundholm, a philosopher of logic at Leiden. He has long kept a
              proof as an act apart from a proof as an object (1998), and, as I understand his work,
              apart from its trace as well. In a 2014 paper he worked through how Brouwer’s
              theory of the creating subject sits beside the thesis that every effective procedure is
              a program, which is the side this book’s machines live on. I know that second paper
              only by what it sets out to do, so I lean on it lightly.
                 Set their trace beside my record and the columns nearly all fill: their stage is my
              dated, their never forgetting my permanent, their never wrong my earned. Their
              stage is written into the trace, though, and my dated is only a step in the run that
              the record doesn’t keep. The empty one is the price, and I think I see why. A mind
              with unlimited memory pays for never forgetting by taking states it has never used,
              and an idealised mind has endless fresh states to take, so nobody charges it for
                                                                               14.11 Not a switch   309


that. On a finite machine the fresh states run out, and writing a record that stays
up forces the instruction to merge some states. Charging for that merge is a further
premise. The forcing is Part I’s counting of used and fresh states, and the charging is
the price rule Part I sets. So it’s the closest thing to my established that I’ve found.
The formula is around sixty years old, and the idea under it, Brouwer’s creating
subject, is older than that. Push on my side from theirs, though, and it gives twice.
Van Atten’s subject won’t take a proof from outside, and my machine takes exactly
one: its checker is trusted on a proof about the checker that somebody did outside
every run. And their evidence is never wrong because, for Brouwer, made evident
is what true means. Mine is right only as far as that checker is honest. Where they
differ, the difference is honest: their subject is an idealised mind with unlimited
time and memory, and mine is a machine with a finite table that establishes only the
claims its program checks.


14.11 Not a switch

So far I’ve been talking about established as if it were a light switch: on or off, the
first computer on and the second one off. That bothered me the whole time I was
writing it, and for a while I couldn’t say why. It felt too small, the way a word can be
technically right and still not cover what you’re pointing at. I don’t trust that feeling
on its own, because I’ve had it plenty of times about things that turned out to be
nothing. So I went looking for something outside my own head that would either
give the feeling something to stand on or show me I was imagining it.
    I didn’t know what I was looking for, at first, beyond a rough shape: two things
that look exactly the same and differ in how far something about them has been
settled. So I started collecting anything that seemed to have that shape, and most
of what I collected fell apart as soon as I looked at it closely. How each one fell
apart taught me more than the thing itself did, so I’ll go through them in the order it
happened. Every story below is the version I could piece together from the records I
could reach, and where I couldn’t reach a record I’ll say so. Check me.
    The first batch was all hidden things. A pea under one of three cups. A tree, whose
age you can’t see from the outside. A forged painting that looks right until somebody
tests the paint. A glass of gas, where the thermometer shows one temperature and
underneath there are uncountably many arrangements of molecules that would all
show the same reading. Plato’s prisoners in the cave, who see shadows on a wall.
The things casting them stay behind their backs (Section 7 tells their story). Every
one of these looked promising for about a minute. Then I noticed they all fail the
same way: look harder and the hidden thing shows up. Lift the cup. Cut the trunk
and count the rings. Run the paint test. Look at the molecules, at least in principle.
Turn around in the cave. In each case the hidden part is a fact about the object that
310   14 What established means


              better eyes could find. That isn’t what the two computers have. You can see every
              lamp in the warehouse and not find the check.
                  That failure gave me the first real tool I had, and it’s a crude one. Give an
              observer perfect vision of the visible thing, as much detail as they want, and ask
              whether they could read the difference off it. If they could, it’s something hidden,
              and that’s not what I’m after. If they couldn’t, it might be. I should say how much
              weight that test holds. It’s a judgment, and I’m the one making it, so it’s a way of
              sorting my own examples, not a verdict. If you find a case it sorts wrongly, that tells
              me something about the test and about me.
                  The second batch got past that test and failed a different way. A clock face reads
              three o’clock and doesn’t show how many days have gone by; no amount of staring
              at the face tells you. And a computer can keep a complete history of what it did. It’s
              Bennett’s 1973 machine from Part I’s counting of states, and the story is better than
              I let on there. Landauer had argued in 1961 that real computers throw information
              away all the time, and Bennett, his younger colleague, asked whether they had to.
              His answer, in a 1973 paper, was no. A machine can write down every step it takes,
              copy out its answer, and then run itself backward, retracing its steps and wiping the
              history as it goes, until it holds only the input and the answer and has never thrown
              anything away. It takes a forward run, a copy of the answer and a backward run,
              with scratch space for the history. Bennett thanks Landauer at the end for raising
              the question in the first place, which I like: the man whose principle says forgetting
              gives off heat is the one who asked whether you could get out of it. The history
              it keeps along the way is real extra information, sitting out where anyone could
              read it, so it isn’t a hidden fact of the first batch’s kind. Keeping it and unwinding
              it throws nothing away, so by Landauer’s own reckoning there’s no floor under its
              heat: run it slowly and the heat comes down as near nothing as you like, though
              never to nothing for a run that finishes, which Part I proved for Bennett’s own model
              (Theorem 1.9). What it spends besides is fresh states, the scratch space the history
              sits in. And it can be run back down. Neither of those two, the keeping that merges
              nothing and the running back down, fits what happened to the first computer, which
              did something that can’t be undone and paid for it. If the standing I’m after could
              be put up and taken back down with nothing kept and no floor either way, it would
              just be bookkeeping. So that batch taught me what else I needed: something that
              only moves one way, and costs something to move.
                  The third batch came closer and still didn’t quite fit. In 1782 James Six, a
              Canterbury man from a family of silk weavers who had taken up watching the
              weather, described a thermometer for the Royal Society. He wanted the coldest
              moment of every night, and he’d found that with an ordinary thermometer you had
              to be looking at it when it happened, because, in his words, “if it be not immediately
              noticed, it can never after be known.” His fix was two little steel markers in the tube
                                                                                14.11 Not a switch   311


that the column pushes up and that stay where they’re left. The markers make a
record that only moves one way. Then he spoils it, for my purposes, in the same
paper: every evening he wrote the numbers down and slid the markers back with a
magnet, “without a touch.” A record anybody can reset with a magnet is not the
thing I’m after, and Six would have been the first to say he wasn’t the first to build
one; his paper lists the thermometers that came before his.
    Since 1996, starting with oral polio vaccine, vials of vaccine bought through
UNICEF have carried a small sticker, a square inside a circle. The square darkens as
the vial takes on heat, and the darkening doesn’t undo when the vial cools. When
the square matches the circle, the vaccine shouldn’t be used. It only moves one way,
and it can’t be reset. But it’s chemistry. The reaction in the square is chosen to run
about as fast as the vaccine itself spoils, so the sticker is really reading the vaccine’s
own condition by a proxy. Nobody ran a check; the heat did.
    Closer still: the International Vocabulary of Metrology, the reference book that
measurement laboratories work from, says a result is traceable only if it “can be
related to a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each
contributing to the measurement uncertainty.” That’s a lot like what I want, a
standing earned by checks, step by step. The same document adds that traceability
“does not ensure . . . that there is an absence of mistakes,” which is the true-versus-
established split written into an international standard. And the top of the chain
wasn’t fixed either. When the official copies of the kilogram were compared with
the prototype in 1889, 1946 and around 1991, they had drifted apart by tens
of micrograms over the century, and nobody can say which one moved, because
the prototype was the kilogram. In 2019 the kilogram was redefined by fixing a
constant of nature, Planck’s constant, instead. A chain like that can also lapse: if the
calibrations stop, new results stop being traceable. The standing has to be kept up,
which my record doesn’t.
    The rules of chess have the shape too. The current Laws of Chess of FIDE, the
international chess federation, say in Article 9.2.3 that two positions are the same
only if “the same player has the move, pieces of the same kind and colour occupy
