the same squares and the possible moves of all the pieces of both players are the
same,” and they spell out that a king that could still castle and one that can’t are in
different positions, even on an identical board. That passes the perfect-vision test.
And the official text says why it passes: the castling right changes which moves are
legal. So the hidden part steers the game: it decides what can happen next. In the
example machine, the flag never steers. It never touches the ordinary computing at
all. The table and the trap that give the flag its meaning do steer, and Section 15
says where that line falls. Each of these got something right and missed something
else.
312   14 What established means


                  The one that fit best, and I want to say clearly that it only fit best among the ones
              I found, was the standing of a mathematical statement. I’ll go through how it went
              for one statement, as far as I could follow it.
                  In 1611 Johannes Kepler, the emperor’s mathematician in Prague, owed his
              friend and patron Johann Matthäus Wackher von Wackenfels a New Year’s present
              and, he said, had nothing to give. Wackher, Kepler wrote, loved nothing, for the
              games you can play with the word, so Kepler wrote him a little pamphlet about the
              nearest thing to nothing he could find, a snowflake, which had landed on his coat
              as he crossed a bridge. Why six corners? Kepler couldn’t say in the end. But along
              the way he stacked equal balls in his head and asserted that one way of stacking
              them, the way grocers stack oranges, packs them so tightly that, in the 1966 English
              translation, “in no other arrangement could more pellets be stuffed into the same
              container.” He didn’t prove it. He said it.
                  Then the sentence sat. In 1831 Carl Friedrich Gauss, reviewing somebody else’s
              book on a piece of number theory, proved what amounts to the special case of
              stackings laid out on a regular grid. In 1900 David Hilbert put the general question
              of packing equal spheres on his famous list of problems for the new century, without
              mentioning Kepler. In 1953 the Hungarian geometer László Fejes Tóth showed how
              the whole thing might be cut down to a problem with finitely many numbers in
              it, and a decade later he guessed that computers might one day finish it. Thomas
              Hales, a mathematician then at the University of Michigan, started on it in earnest
              in 1994, and in August 1998 he and his student Samuel Ferguson announced a
              proof that leaned on a great deal of computer work. The Annals of Mathematics
              gave the paper to a panel of twelve referees, led by Gábor Fejes Tóth, László’s son.
              They ran seminars on it for years. A journalist, George Szpiro, later reported that by
              July 2002 they were 99 percent certain it was right; I couldn’t find those words in
              anything the referees wrote themselves. What Szpiro printed in Nature in 2003 was
              the editor’s letter as Hales reported it: the referees had “not been able to certify the
              correctness of the proof, and will not be able to certify it in the future, because they
              have run out of energy . . . ” The Annals printed the human part in 2005, and the
              whole proof appeared in 2006. Hales started the Flyspeck project in 2003 to supply
              a fully explicit derivation of the entire argument. It was finished on 10 August 2014.
                  Lay those dates out on the table and look at what moved. The sentence never
              changed. Hilbert’s version of the question didn’t even name the man who first said
              it. Whether it’s true never changed, as far as anyone can tell. What changed was
              how far it had been established, and it changed in stages, each one paid for by
              somebody’s work: a guess, a special case, a place on a list, a plan, an announcement,
              a panel’s reported ninety-nine percent and their exhaustion, a printing, a machine
              check. A perfect reader of the sentence can’t see which stage it’s at. And it only ever
              moved one way.
                                                                               14.11 Not a switch   313


    Then I tried to break that one too, because by this point I’d watched a lot of
good-looking examples fall over, and there’s an obvious place to push. Standing can
fall. In 1852 a student named Francis Guthrie, colouring a map of the counties of
England, noticed that four colours always seemed to be enough to keep neighbouring
counties different. The question passed to his old teacher Augustus De Morgan,
who wrote to the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton that a student had
asked him for “a reason for a fact which I did not know was a fact,” and that he
didn’t know it yet either. In 1879 Alfred Kempe, a barrister who did mathematics on
the side and sang counter-tenor, published a proof, and his description of finding
it is wonderful: “After a somewhat arduous search, I have succeeded, suddenly, as
might be expected, in hitting upon the weak point . . . ” The journal’s associate editor,
William Story, added a note saying Kempe had “substantially proved” the theorem,
and tightened the counting part of the argument. Eleven years later Percy Heawood,
a lecturer at Durham who by one account brought his dog to his lectures, showed
that one step of what he called “the now apparently recognised proof” doesn’t work.
Kempe swaps colours along two chains at once, and swapping the first can spoil the
second.
    So standing can fall, and I went back and forth on what that does to my picture.
Where I’ve landed for now: the check that got Kempe’s proof accepted, Story’s note,
went through the counting and never examined the double swap. A check that
never looked at a step can’t have said no to that step. In the sense of the previous
few pages, the part that fell was never earned in the first place. I’m aware that’s
a convenient reading for me, and I’m wary of convenient readings, especially my
own. Take it as where I ended up. It isn’t a settled answer. It is, though, the reason
the example machine in the next chapter only lets its record go up after a passing,
sound check and a matching commitment.
    And then came the part I didn’t expect. The four-colour statement was true all
along. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken, two mathematicians at the University
of Illinois, proved it in 1976 with a computer, and the proof was met with suspicion
for years; a cleaner version came in the 1990s; and in 2005 Georges Gonthier, a
computer scientist at Microsoft Research in Cambridge, finished a proof of the whole
thing checked by a small proof-checking program. So this one statement stayed true
the entire time while its standing went up in 1879, came down in 1890, went up
again in 1976 against a lot of doubt, and went up further in 2005. The fall wasn’t
a fall of the truth. It was a fall of how far the truth had been established, and it
was the right fall to have, because what had been established was less than anyone
thought.
    Laying all of that out together is what changed my picture. If there are stages,
then at each one there’s a line, and the line has two sides: not this far yet, and
at least this far. Each line amounts to its own yes-or-no question. But choose the
314   14 What established means


              question carefully. “Do I still trust this proof?” can turn back to no, as Kempe’s did.
              “Did I carry out this particular check?” asks about a completed act. Cross out the
              acceptance and the act still happened. To keep that answer, the machine has to keep
              a record of it and have no move that knocks the record down. A check that could
              have failed doesn’t give you that by itself. Maybe the switch wasn’t wrong. Maybe it
              was just incomplete, the first of many lines, and the real shape is a direction with
              lines drawn across it. I’ve gone around many times on whether the lines create the
              direction or the direction comes first and the lines are just places where you cut
              it, and on whether yes and no are even different from each other until something
              draws the line between them. I don’t have an answer to that. The one part I could
              actually settle is that a single switch isn’t enough once there are three or more stages,
              and Part II proved it (Section 11). Everything else in this paragraph is me thinking
              out loud.
                  Flatland, where this hunch started (Section 24), turned out to belong in the
              first batch. It’s a novel Edwin Abbott published in 1884, narrated by a square
              who lives in a flat, two-dimensional world (Section 7 says more about him and it).
              When a sphere passes through the flat world, the narrator sees a line whose ends
              fade wrong and whose length keeps changing, and only when he feels it does he
              find a circle, a perfect one. Then the sphere tells him it will rise, and he watches
              it dwindle to a point and vanish, and come back larger and larger. The hidden
              direction leaks into his view, faintly, and a sharp enough flat observer could in
              principle work out where the sphere is. In this machine two states can sit at different
              places along the established direction and agree on every bit of the ordinary machine
              (Theorem 15.17). That may be exactly why the ordinary machine can’t see it. It may
              also be why, if the direction is worth having, someone has to build it in on purpose
              and keep it on purpose. Keeping it is paid for; Part I’s counting of states says so.
              What’s still open is what has to be kept, and that’s what the rest of this chapter is for.
                  Those readings helped me separate the jobs. A Thiele machine keeps a distinction
              about a claim. Its step determines how that distinction is established, its record
              keeps it through later work, and its schedule counts the charge. The next few
              sections put those jobs in computing’s own words; the next chapter builds one
              example.


              14.12 Computing already had a word for it
              Computing already has a word for this and uses it every day. Anyone who’s used a
              database has seen it: COMMIT.
                 A database does a pile of tentative work, and then there’s one moment, the
              commit, written to a log, after which the change counts. Jim Gray, who more or less
              built the theory behind that, opens his 1981 paper on it by saying the idea comes
                                                        14.12 Computing already had a word for it   315


from contract law, and his example is a wedding. People negotiate, somebody asks,
two people say “I do,” and from then on it’s binding. If it was a mistake, you don’t
erase it. You do another transaction to fix it, the way a bad contract gets a second
contract. Nobody reaches for a time machine.
    The wedding was a philosopher’s example first. The Oxford philosopher J. L.
Austin, lecturing in 1955, said “I do” makes a marriage. It doesn’t describe one, and
sayings like that aren’t true or false. They can misfire (the wrong person says it,
a step gets skipped). They can’t be false. A commit works exactly the same way.
Writing the commit record doesn’t report that a question got closed. Writing it is the
closing. And a commit can’t be false. It can misfire: committed without the check,
committed about the wrong pocket. Those two misfires are Gettier and Peirce again,
coming in from a third direction. Then somebody else reads the record, and for
them it stops being a performance and turns into a report: “this was checked and
closed.” A report can be false. On the small machine of the next chapter it can’t be,
about the machine’s own history: if its flag is up from a clean start, some claim was
checked and closed, and that claim held of that edition when it was checked. That’s
how this book ties a commit to the truth, on that machine and the ones built on it,
and it took a proof to do it.
    Robin Milner, building a proof checker in the 1970s, ran out of memory, so he
decided to keep only the finished theorems and throw the proofs away, like a teacher
rubbing out the blackboard to make room. The obvious worry is forgery: if the
proofs are gone, what stops someone just writing a theorem down? His answer was
beautiful. Theorems got their own type in the programming language, and the only
way to make one was through the rules of logic. You couldn’t forge one because the
language wouldn’t let you build it any other way. He named that language ML, for
Meta Language. I wanted to call my machine the meta machine. I’m choosing to
treat that as a coincidence. Calling it a sign would be more my style, so this is more
restraint than I usually manage.
    Bitcoin is the loud modern version. Its records can’t be changed without redoing
all the work that came after them, and a computer that drops off the network and
comes back trusts the longest chain as the story of what happened while it was
gone. The returning computer is Turing’s clerk again, coming back to a note. The
difference is that the clerk’s note costs next to nothing to forge and Bitcoin’s costs
a mountain of work. It’s the clearest case I know of somebody making a settled
fact expensive to fake, and they got there by paying for a search. The settling itself
carries no price.
    Making a settled fact expensive to fake is a different job from the one this book’s
price does, the unit of cost it charges for raising a record. Bitcoin makes it tempting
to read the toll of Section 2 as a deterrent, so I’d rather say this here. One unit
of cost deters nobody. Bitcoin’s work is tied to something scarce, electricity and
316   14 What established means


              hardware; a unit of cost in this book is tied to nothing. Eric Budish, an economist at
              the University of Chicago, built a model in 2025 of what that tie has to cost. As I
              read him, for Bitcoin’s kind of trust to hold, the honest work has to stay expensive at
              every moment compared with what an attacker could win, and the expense grows
              in step with the value being protected. A flat charge of one unit can’t do that job,
              and it isn’t trying to. It’s a count, not a lock, as the start of the book put it: the lock
              is the order rule, check, then commit, then certify, and it would work at a price of
              zero. The price is there because nothing is kept for free: Part I’s counting of states
              shows that a machine with finitely many states that prices its merges can’t avoid
              it. Scaring anybody off has nothing to do with it. The machines I actually build
              have counters with no top, endless fresh states, so Part I’s counting of states doesn’t
              reach them whole. It reaches the flag: CERTIFY sends its two readings to one, the
              same counting run on a set of two. The charge comes from pricing that merge in
              the record’s own part of the state, a premise I choose (Theorem 3.19), and the size
              of the charge is my choice too (Section 15 says why).
                  And Bitcoin wasn’t first. Pull on its footnotes: three of the eight references in the
              paper that started it point to Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, who in 1991 worked
              out how to stamp a document with a time nobody could fake later, by chaining each
              stamp to the ones before it. A company built on their idea, Surety, printed a short
              fingerprint of its chain in the classified ads of the New York Times once a week from
              1995, and it was still doing it in 2018. I found that in a piece the journalist Daniel
              Oberhaus wrote that year, which says the ad runs under “Notices & Lost and Found.”
              Think about that for a second. To make a record nobody could quietly rewrite, they
              put it somewhere a million people would keep a copy of without even meaning to.
              A physicist named Wojciech Zurek has spent decades arguing that the world does
              the same thing with a measurement, copying the result into so many places that
              nobody can take it back. I’ll get to him properly later in this part (Section 18).
                  There are more fences like these: logs that can’t quietly change, certificates you
              can check. Later in this part, Section 17 takes five of them apart. I lean on all of
              them. They work. I want that said plainly, because the next thing isn’t “they’re
              broken.”
                  The next thing is where they sit. The database’s commit is bits in a log, kept by
              a database program, on a machine whose own step will overwrite those bits the
              moment some instruction says to. Milner’s guarantee is a type checker; it holds
              inside programs written in his language and nowhere else. Bitcoin is a protocol
              on ordinary computers that will do whatever they’re told. Every one of them is a
              program or a rule, on top of a machine that can’t tell my two computers apart. The
              machine underneath keeps nothing and charges nothing for what got settled.
                  The obvious comeback: so put the rule one level lower, in the operating system, or
              what security people call a reference monitor, the small always-on piece everything
                                                                     14.13 What settling looks like   317


has to pass through. Yes, exactly that: a monitor that wouldn’t let any program raise
its record without paying would be doing the thing I’m talking about. In this book’s
words it would be implementing the model, and I’d count that as agreement. What I
care about isn’t who builds the fence. It’s what the fence has to obey, wherever it’s
built, and whether that’s forced or just a good idea.
    That comeback has a history, and it’s older than me by a lot. In 1972 James
P. Anderson’s planning study for the US Air Force described a reference monitor:
a piece every access has to pass through, that can’t be tampered with, and small
enough to check. In 2000 Fred Schneider, a computer scientist at Cornell, argued
that a monitor that only watches a run as it goes can enforce only rules whose
breaking shows up at some finite point, the kind computer scientists call safety rules.
“No certificate without an earlier passing check and a commit” is one of those. And
in 2015 Arthur Azevedo de Amorim, a computer scientist then at the University
of Pennsylvania, and six coauthors built monitors that check a rule at every single
instruction, and proved them correct. So putting a rule under every program, so
nothing can get around it, is their move. I didn’t invent it. What I’m putting under
that move is narrower: a record that has to be paid for, on the small machine one
that has to be earned, and a reason, from counting, why a finite machine that prices
its merges can’t make the price of a record that never comes down zero.


14.13 What settling looks like
The chapter on what structure is (Section 5) ends with a pile of things sorted into
buckets. Settling a question is that, plus one more thing, and it’s the 0 from the start
of the book at a bigger size.
    Picture every state the machine could be in as a field of dots. A yes-or-no question
about the state splits the field into two parts: yes and no. That split is a sorting, the
smallest one there is. And remember the no pile: if one of the parts is empty, there’s
no sorting at all, just a field. Now the extra thing that makes it a settlement: once
the machine is in the yes part, no step it can take leads back out. The door opens one
way. A settled question is a sorting plus a door that only swings in.
    At its best, what goes through the door is a relation: these numbers are in this
order, these two things belong together. Sultan, the chimpanzee of Section 9, fitted
two short sticks into one long one and reached the food. Nothing new got added to
the cage. Two sticks became one tool. That’s what I’d want the door to be for.
    But the door doesn’t care, and this is the honest edge of the whole picture. Hook
the door to a check that says yes to everything and the machine walks through even
when the claim is false. The question is settled either way, true or false, like Peirce
said. A door that only swings one way tells you a question was closed. It doesn’t tell
318   14 What established means


              you it was closed right. Price and correctness are two different books, and I keep
              both, separately.
                  One more edge, the one Gray’s wedding already hinted at. What stays shut for
              good is that the question got closed, about that edition of that thing. Whether the
              claim is still true is another matter. Change the list after the commit and the record
              still says, truthfully, that the old edition was checked and closed. And if the claim
              turns out bad, the fix is another act on top, a second record that says “withdrawn.”
              The first one never quietly comes back down. So “entitled to lean on it right now” is
              three things at once: closed, not withdrawn since, and the thing unchanged.


              14.14 What the Thiele Machine is
              So I’ll set out what I built, and which parts I was pushed into and which parts I
              chose, because you should know which is which.
                  You’ve had the model since the start of the book: five parts (states, moves, a
              step, a price on each move in whole units, and a yes-or-no reading), one rule, the
              toll, and a counter and a window when a result needs them. You can’t buy it in a
              box. It isn’t a device, a CPU or an instruction set; those are things you build to carry
              it, and the next chapter builds one, as small as I could make it. It counts what a
              computation makes the case, and this chapter’s case is the sharpest one: the reading
              is a record that says whether something’s been established, and the toll is what the
              first page of the book said about records, nothing becomes something for free. The
              event it accounts for happens on any computer, whether anybody keeps track of it
              or not, and the record exists only if something keeps it. The window earns its place
              here too, because the two computers already showed you the problem: the usual
              window, the bits, can’t see the record.
                  A unit of cost isn’t a joule or a dollar; whether it’s worth anything physical is
              Landauer’s assumption, named, and nowhere else. And one unit is just the floor:
              Part I shows that if you charge one unit per halving, a step that squeezes a lot
              together pays at least the logarithm of the squeeze, roughly how many times it
              halves the number of states it can tell apart. Don’t read that backwards, though.
              One unit isn’t one halving. A single state flipping into a big set of states that already
              read yes, with every state in play equally likely, squeezes things together only a little,
              much less than a halving, and the whole-number count rounds that up to one. Read
              in the worst case over what the machine might be holding, the same flip can remove
              a full bit; Section 3 has both readings.
                  What “new model of computation” means here. The Thiele Machine takes distinc-
              tions I choose and writes them into the state, the step and the price. In the case
              on the table that means which thing a check was about, which edition of it the
              check saw, and which later act gets to lean on it. A record keeps some of that. A
                                                                14.14 What the Thiele Machine is   319


window decides how much of it somebody looking in can get back. Change what’s
kept, or what the window shows, and you change which questions the end state can
answer. The machine underneath does the computing. The record adds no function
it couldn’t already compute.
    Which leaves a fair question hanging: if it computes nothing new, does it even
get to call itself a model of computation? It does, for the reason the start of the
book gave: the random-access machine computes exactly what Turing’s does, the
cell-probe and input-output models leave the computing between the moves they
count out of the count, and each is worth having for what it counts. So are the
energy-aware random-access machines of Demaine and his coauthors (2016), which
count the bits destroyed. Add one more to that family, the bulk-synchronous parallel
model of Leslie Valiant, a computer scientist at Harvard (1990), which charges for
rounds of communication between processors. Closest in kind are Blum’s axioms,
also from the start of the book, which constrain every cost the way the toll constrains
every price list on the model. The Thiele Machine’s own axis is what a run made
the case, and what that cost. Part II laid the toll over a register machine of Cook
and Reckhow’s kind, and over a Turing machine and a lambda calculus, and none of
them computes one function more afterward (Section 10). What each of them gains
is a record and a cost.
    The opening split what I found from what I assumed and what I chose, and the
choice that matters most here is the first on its last list: the count goes inside the
step.
    About the name. I named it after myself, on purpose. Half of that is a joke and
half of it is a stake in the ground. Turing got a machine, so here’s mine. The longer
story, meta machines and all, is in the afterword, “How I got here” (Section 24).
    The names are the ones Section 10.8 set out, and they work the way Turing’s
do. A clock is enough to make something a Thiele machine. It isn’t Thiele-complete,
because it charges for computing, and neither is a machine whose record never
goes up. The small machine of the next chapter is held to a higher bar, certified
Thiele-complete: on top of all that, from a clean start the record goes up only after a
passing check of a claim, by a checker proved to mean what the claim says, then
a commitment to that same claim, then a certificate, one unit each; and some
claim’s check, commitment and certificate raise the record from some starts and not
from others, exactly where the claim holds. A universal Thiele machine runs any
machine of a stated class as a guest, with every computing step done by its own
counter moves and every rise placed by its program; a certified one also earns each
guest’s record again. The end of this chapter pins every one of these words down
(Section 14.18).

to. And no outside window that only shows the list can tell you which is which; the

    Now, how literally should you take that table? It’s a picture of the chain, and
the chain is what’s proved. The small machine’s own checks are three questions
about one counter: is it zero, is it even, is it at least some number. What its proofs
need from the questions is a checker proved to say yes exactly when the answer is
yes, and an exact test for telling two questions apart. That’s enough for “sorted”: a
version of the machine that takes any questions with checkers like that proves the
same chain once for all of them, and with a list packed into one counter it certifies
a sorted list for a cost of three and refuses an unsorted one forever (Section 15).
Without a proved checker for “sorted,” the chain would be honest about a counter
and only by convention about your list, which is Gettier’s pocket again, one level
down.
    And a lamp for whom? The record is bits too. It’s a lamp on the machine, for
anybody walking that warehouse. Hand somebody a printout of it across a desk and
you’re back at the sticker on the windshield: they have to trust whoever hands it
over, or have some way to check the box that says it ran. That crossing is a different
problem with its own tools, signatures, attestation and proofs a stranger can check,
and this book doesn’t solve it. Section 7 says what those tools rest on, and the
small machine’s record, like any record kept in a machine’s state, carries nobody’s
signature. What the step changes is the question, from “did it run?” to “do I trust
the box that says it ran?” That’s a smaller question, but it isn’t no question.
    So, back to the list from the start of this chapter: the test sheet, the sticker,
the audit, the ledger, the proof, the confident AI. I’ll give the straight answer on
which of those this helps. The sticker is a question of whether a piece of paper is
genuine, and nothing here touches it. The “all tests passed” sheet fits only if the
test is a checker proved to mean what it says, in the machine’s own language; a set
of tests that can miss a bug certifies “this procedure said yes,” which is true and
smaller. An audit and a ledger get the test sheet’s answer: kept by a program on an
ordinary computer, they’re bits the program wrote, and they fit only where the step
underneath keeps the record and refuses to raise it without the check. A proof is
one example: checking its steps is a procedure that can reject them. Whether its
statement says what you meant is still yours to read. The AI that talks as if it’s sure
of itself isn’t addressed at all. Section 22, under “Outward consequences,” says how
little of the outside world I’ve reached.
    Now comes the honest half. Take away the small machine’s rules and keep only
the bare toll, and the copier has an easier move: pay one unit, flip the record to
yes, and that’s the whole move. The toll is satisfied and the receipt is real, but it’s
322   14 What established means


              a receipt for nothing. The bare toll prices the closing of the door, and the check
              behind it goes unpriced.


              14.16 What putting it in the step buys
              The hardest objection is one I’d rather make myself. You defined a flag and a charge,
              then proved the charge gets paid when the flag goes up. That’s your definitions
              agreeing with each other.
                  On the bare model, that’s fair, and the copier’s receipt for nothing is the proof.
              What makes the record mean established is the small machine’s step, which won’t
              let a commit through unless a check of that very claim passed, meeting the first
              three of the four conditions from Gettier’s pocket, with the fourth, an honest checker,
              proved about the checker separately. And what it proves isn’t about one program:
              on every list of instructions anybody can write, starting clean, if the record is up,
              then somewhere earlier a check of some claim, about some edition, passed; then
              a commit of that same claim; then the certificate; with nothing touching the thing
              between the check and the commit.
                  So a raised flag, from a clean start, tells you some claim went through a passing
              check, a commitment to it about the same edition, and a certificate. That piece
              of history is what the flag keeps, and only that. The channel names the latest
              commitment that got through, which needn’t be the one the flag first went up on,
              and in general you can’t read off the end state which claim was certified at that first
              rise, or when. And the flag doesn’t say the claim still holds, at the certificate or at
              the end, because the counter can change after the commitment.
                  That “every” is the whole answer to what the step buys. A log kept by a program
              gives you a fact about that program: if the program’s right, the log’s right. The
              database’s guarantee holds for work that goes through the database. A rule in the
              step gives you a fact about every program the machine can run, the buggy ones
              and the hostile ones too, because there’s no way to run anything on it that isn’t a
              string of its steps. What moving the rule down a level changes is not what can be
              computed but which programs the guarantee covers: this one becomes every one.
              And the tie between a check and the thing it checked gets a job: the step reads it,
              and refuses a commitment when it no longer fits, so the structure is doing something
              in the machine instead of sitting in a note beside it.
                  There are two limits on that “every,” and I’ll say them now so you don’t have
              to find them later. First, it’s every program, not every everything. The guarantee
              covers any list of instructions, run from a clean start, one step at a time, on a step
              that does what its definition says. Hostile programs are inside it. A hostile start (a
              table of facts nobody checked, a reset), hostile hardware (a soldering iron on the
              flag’s bit, a second writer the step can’t see) or a hostile reader isn’t; Section 22 lists
                                                        14.17 The record, the checker and the host   323


the whole fence. The guarantee has the same shape as the database’s, true if the
layer underneath is faithful, with a much bigger class of programs inside it.
    Second, the flag and the ledger on their own are what people who verify programs
call ghost state: erase them and every program computes exactly what it did before
(Section 6 has where that idea comes from). What isn’t ghost on the small machine
is the table of checked facts, which the step reads and refuses on, at run time, for
every program. And the move of putting a rule under every program isn’t mine
either. It’s the reference monitor’s, and its history is a few sections back.


14.17 The record, the checker and the host

Take the flag and ledger off the small machine’s drawing. The core follows the same
steps: neither field tells it what to do next. Put them back and you can read whether
certification occurred and what the instruction schedule charged. That is the passive
record’s job. The latch argument in Section 10 gives its form over any fixed base
when the record is driven by that base and never comes down.
    The checker has another job. CHECK of “A ≥ m” tests the counter in one
instruction; a program using only the two counter moves would have to work
through their operations. A step comparison therefore starts with the instructions
each machine is given. Every checker built in this book is a program. The abstract
certified interface also admits a supplied checker, so its computational power includes
whatever that checker can do: supply a halting oracle and CHECK can answer halting
questions. The effective implementations here use effective checks.
    Now put a guest program inside the host. A guest that can write any value into
its own “checked” variable can write YES without checking. The host I build gives
the guest three entry points instead: CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. Its step rule
controls those entry points for every allowed guest program. The fact table and
channel determine whether the next act is permitted; the flag and ledger record the
result. An ordinary universal machine can implement these rules. The work is in
preserving them through every guest instruction.
    The universal program in Appendix D.1 does that work with the small machine’s
six instruction kinds on a host with more counters. It fetches a guest instruction,
decodes it, and carries it out. At matching points the guest and host ledgers agree.
The host halts exactly when the guest halts, keeps the guest’s answer in its counters,
and raises its own flag exactly when the guest raises its flag, through its own earned
chain. Its guests are the small machine’s programs from clean starts, with Minsky’s
encoding supplying their universal computation. Appendix D.3 gives a simpler
picture with a guest-step operation supplied directly; the instruction-by-instruction
construction shows how to build it.
324   14 What established means


                  Add a one-unit PAY instruction and the host can also follow a computably pre-
              sented Thiele machine: its selected moves, transitions, prices and total yes-or-no
              reading are all given by programs. Appendix D.2 constructs that interpreter. Starting
              with the guest’s reading at no, the host follows its ledger with at most two extra units
              at the raise. Starting with the guest already at yes, the clean host must establish
              its own flag immediately and spends three. The same clean-start three-act count
              explains the surcharge when the guest certifies with a whole ledger below three.


              14.18 Two layers, and the names

              The layers, once. The core definition (Definition 2.1) is a Thiele machine: states,
              moves, a step, a cost for each move, a yes-or-no reading, and the toll. Everything
              else is added on top, and each theorem names what it adds. First come extra
              structures and requirements: a ledger that sums the costs, a window, permanence of
              the reading, a price on merges. Then an earned implementation, the small machine
              of the next chapter, with a checker proved sound and a provenance theorem. Then
              two interfaces any machine can be read through: Thiele-complete, about computing
              and a record that tells starts apart, and certified Thiele-complete, which adds the
              earned chain. Then a universal interpreter for a stated class of guests. The bare
              definition doesn’t ask the step to be computable, so when I say the record adds no
              computing power, I mean relative to a fixed base.
                  Substrate versus scaffolding. Two layers run through the book, and confusing
              them makes the theorems quietly stop meaning what they say. The substrate is the
              shape: a kind of state and a rule for stepping. Different theorems ask that shape
              for different extra pieces, and the pieces aren’t the same. The universal floor (the
              “pays something” result of Section 2) asks for a yes-or-no reading and the toll on it.
              The counter’s uniqueness (only one count fits a chosen start and price list) asks for a
              starting value and a schedule of increments; Section 6 gives the argument, a short
              induction that works for any system with those two pieces, and on the small machine
              of the next chapter the ledger is the sum of the charges by theorem (Section 15).
              The diagonal asks for a recursion theorem for the transformations the substrate can
              express, and needs no toll and no encoding at all. “Substrate-level” doesn’t mean
              one fixed set of parts that every theorem shares. A theorem only gets to use the
              parts it asks for. Ask it what it needs and it’ll tell you, and whatever else is lying
              around the workshop isn’t the theorem’s. So each result is stated over exactly the
              extension it uses. The substrate with the extension a theorem names is what I mean
              by the model, and the name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. The scaffolding is
              everything that holds the shape up so you can touch it, and when I say my machine,
              the small machine, the machine I build or the build, this is what I mean: the machine
              of the next chapter, with its two counters and their versions, its table of checked
                                                                    14.18 Two layers, and the names   325


facts, its channel, trap, ledger and flag, its six instruction kinds and their prices, the
host with a register for every whole number, and the universal programs that run on
that host (Appendix D.1). The build fills in several extensions at once and borrows,
for any one theorem, only the extension that theorem names. Let that line blur and
a theorem stated over one extension starts reading as if it carried premises it never
uses. “Substrate” never means the build, and it never means the side of a simulation
doing the stepping; for that I say “the machine doing the stepping,” as against “the
program it runs.”
    So the book keeps the two apart: Parts I and II were about any system with
the pieces each result names, and their pictures were small worked instances you
could hold (two boxes on a sheet of paper, chairs in a room, a row of dots). The
example machine wasn’t one of them; where they said something about it, they
pointed ahead, and the next chapter builds it. Every Part II claim that has a machine
instance gets that instance there (Section 15.14) or in Appendix D.1, with its own
theorem, and Part II said so in one sentence at most. When the origin story (the
afterword, Section 24) says the shape “was the substrate the entire time,” it means
this layer, the model’s shape. It doesn’t mean any piece of the build. The same goes
for two more of its words. When it says “the machine” about the thing it named
the Thiele Machine, or calls that thing a meta machine, it means the model; “my
machine” is the build of the next chapter. And when it lists what the model asks for
(a state, a step, a record, a ledger, a window), read the ledger and the window as
two of the extra pieces: a result asks for them only if it uses them.
    The build is one piece of scaffolding, and I’d rather you know up front that it is
one instance, chosen to be small enough to inspect. Section 15 builds the smallest
honest machine I could: two counters, six instructions, a table of checked facts,
a ledger and a flag. Earned commitments are proved there (a flag raised from
a clean start was checked, then committed, then certified, on the same edition,
with nothing touching that thing between the check and the commit), and so is
universality, through Minsky’s two-counter machines and his halting result, through
the counter constructions of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and their coauthors, set
out in Appendix K. Then one fixed program, on a host made of the same kinds of
instruction with more counters, runs every program of it, and with one paid move
added, every computably presented Thiele machine (Appendix D.1). None of that is
the model. It shows the model fits in six instruction kinds.
    The names again, with every part of the certified one pinned down, because I’ll
hold to them for the rest of the book. A Thiele machine is any particular system that
fits the model’s core definition, its five parts and its toll (Definition 2.1); the toys on
paper in Part I count, and so does the small machine, with its toll proved. Thiele-
complete (Definition 10.6) says nothing about what the record is about. Certified
Thiele-complete asks for four things of its own (Definition 15.7), and it is exactly
326   14 What established means


              Thiele-complete with clean loads, the earned record and a claim that can fail added
              (Theorem 15.23). The first of the four is a universal base whose moves can’t touch
              the record, and a record that stays up once it’s up. The second is a record that,
              from a clean start, rises only after a passing check of a claim, then a commitment
              to that same claim with nothing it’s about changed in between, then a certificate,
              with the checker proved to mean what it says. Over a language fixed first, the claims

              makes the claim true in its sense; every instance in this book is stated that way
              (Theorem 15.26). The third is exact prices: one unit for each of those three acts
              and nothing for anything else. And the fourth is a claim whose check, commit and
              certificate raise the record from a loaded start exactly when the claim holds there,
              with the claim holding at some loaded starts and failing at others. Every clock-style
              machine fails the definition, because it charges for computing, whatever its record,
              and every machine that meets the definition hides its record and its ledger from its
              own window, both by theorem. That’s about an observer who sees only where a
              run ended; one who also has the program and the start can work both out. None
              of the four clauses is there for decoration: for each one there’s a machine that
              meets the other three and fails it, each of them a Thiele machine with a two-counter
              machine inside that no interface makes certified Thiele-complete (Theorem 15.29).
              The small machine meets it, and so does the same machine over any properties
              with an exact test for telling two of them apart and a checker proved to say yes
              exactly when the property holds, as long as one of them can come out both ways,
              sorted lists included. A universal Thiele machine is one fixed machine running one
              fixed program that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with every step of
              the guest’s computing done by the host’s own counter moves and every rise of its
              record put where its program put it; a certified one also earns each guest’s record
              again by its own check, commit and certificate. Nothing is left to the guest’s good
              manners. Appendix D.1 builds one, U: a fixed program in the small machine’s own
              six kinds of instruction, on a host with more counters, with no step of any guest
              built in. Its guests are the small machine’s programs, so every computation runs
              on it under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine, and it matches each
              guest’s halting, answer, flag and ledger exactly, raising its own flag by its own check,
              commit and certificate. Then UP , the same program with one more handler for a
              paid move that does nothing else, takes as its guests every computably presented
              Thiele machine, one whose next move (picked by a driver), step, prices and reading
              are computed by programs, with the reading decided on every state. It matches the
              guest’s halting, raises its own flag on its own earned chain exactly when the guest’s
              reading has said yes, and keeps the guest’s prices to within a surcharge of at most
              two when the guest’s reading starts at no, which no program on that host, run from
              a clean start, can avoid in general. And a computer that runs the small machine,
                                                                    14.18 Two layers, and the names   327


your laptop say, isn’t the small machine. Read through the emulator’s prices and flag
it’s a Thiele machine, a finite one, like the toys of Part I, but it isn’t Thiele-complete,
because its counters stop somewhere and a universal base needs every configuration.
It implements the small machine, inside bounds, the way a laptop implements a
Turing machine. Push on that comparison, because it’s loose, and the looseness is
the point. Does a laptop implement a Turing machine? Not exactly. Turing’s tape
never runs out, and a laptop’s memory does; strictly, a laptop is a very large machine
with finitely many states, and it behaves like a Turing machine only on computations
that fit. Nobody minds, because the bound is known and most computations people
care about fit inside it. That’s the same deal any device running the small machine
gets: its counters stop somewhere, and the theorems speak only for runs that fit.
The bounds aren’t fine print. They’re the whole difference between implementing a
model and being one.
    How much can a difference in width matter? There’s a famous answer, and
it’s worth the detour. On 4 June 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket lifted off and
broke apart about forty seconds after its engines lit. The inquiry board, chaired by
the mathematician Jacques-Louis Lions, traced it to one conversion in the inertial
reference software: a sixty-four-bit floating-point number, an alignment value called
BH that’s tied to horizontal speed, squeezed into a sixteen-bit signed integer. On
Ariane 4, where the software came from, that value could never get big enough to
overflow, because of how that rocket flew in its first forty seconds. Ariane 5 flew
differently. The value got too big, the backup unit failed on it, the main unit failed
the same way one cycle of its software later, seventy-two thousandths of a second,
and the function doing the converting didn’t even serve a purpose once the rocket
had lifted off; it was kept for commonality with the old rocket. The board’s report
says the assumption that made the conversion safe had been agreed on and then,
not on purpose, kept out of sight of any outside review. A width premise that holds
on one machine is a fact about how that machine gets used. The code doesn’t carry
it, and yet it travels with the code without anybody noticing. The only defence I
know is the dull one: write the premise into every statement that needs it, where
the next person will trip over it.
CHAPTER 15




A smallest example machine

The chapters before this one never built a machine you could program. They said
“any states, any steps,” and whenever a picture was needed, a board or some chairs
or a cup stood in. Now I have to build a machine, and the first question is about
the one I built before it. I built a big one first, on the way here (the Afterword,
Section 24, tells that story), with dozens of instructions, some picked for reasons
and some picked because I had to pick something, and theorems held of it. What
does that show? That the model works, or that I’m good at stacking instructions
until the proofs go through? A big machine is a wonderful place to hide a mistake.
It’s a garage so full of stuff that you could lose a car in it.
    So the example machine in this book is a small one. I want the state and every
way of changing it where you can inspect them. There are six instruction kinds, and
you can follow how a check stays tied to an object, how a change makes it stale,
and how the next move uses that relation. Each kind takes operands, a counter or a
property or a line to jump to, so there are unboundedly many instructions. It’s one
way of building the model, not the only one, and the theorems will say which facts
hang on these particular choices. “Smallest,” in the title, is me telling you how I
built it: by throwing things out until nothing more would go. I haven’t got a proof
that nothing smaller works, and I’m not claiming one.


15.1 What the model asks for, and the example that meets it
The model asks only for states, moves, a step, a price on each move and a yes-or-no
reading, with the toll. Before any of its parts, I’ll give the example that meets it in
three sentences. It’s an ordinary computer, two counters and a jump, with a record
layer on top. The flag in the record layer is the blank cell, and raising it is the write
of a 0, a merge in the record layer (flag down and flag up land on the same state),
which is why the step that raises it is charged once merges in that layer are priced
(Theorem 3.19, in Part I). And the order rule, check, then commit, then certify, is
what makes a raised flag mean something.
   Parts I and II define the model by five parts and one rule. The example meets
them by adding a record, a flag that reads no or yes and, once yes, stays, which on a
machine is the blank cell’s 0. Here yes means “certified,” because that’s the event I
picked (Section 18, later in this part, asks whether anything outside the rules picks

                                  328
                                          15.1 What the model asks for, and the example that meets it   329


it out). It adds a toll: the step that raises the flag costs something (Section 2). And
it adds a ledger, the running total of those costs, a whole number that only climbs
(Section 6). And Section 10 proved the thing this whole chapter stands on: over any
base at all, a base-driven record is a latch, a bit that switches on at an event the base
decides and never switches off (Observation 10.1). The record watches the base. It
doesn’t compute anything the base couldn’t compute without it.
    Push on that for a second, because it cuts the job in half. If the record adds
no computing power, then all the computing power comes from the base, and the
question “how small can the machine be” splits into two questions that don’t touch
each other. For the base: what’s the smallest thing that can compute everything
there is to compute? For the record: what’s the smallest set of pieces that makes the
flag mean something?
    There’s one honest asterisk on “don’t touch,” because the machine below makes
it matter. What’s blind is the flag and the ledger: the base never reads either of
them. But the pieces that make the flag mean something (a table of checked facts, a
slot for a commitment, a trap that stops a refused run) have to sit where the step
can read them, which is in the base, and they do steer the run: a failed check stops
a program dead. The latch theorem holds wherever you draw the line between base
and record, which is exactly why it can’t tell you where the meaning lives. On this
machine the meaning lives on the base side of that line, in the bookkeeping, and the
flag on top reports it. That line has to sit at the core: the step reads the table, the
channel and the trap, so a map that hid any of them wouldn’t move in step. The
record-layer merge of Part I draws a lower line, with only the line number and the
two counters below it, and what the premise charges moves with that line. Drawn
there, all three record acts merge in the record’s part and the premise charges each
of them; drawn at the core, it charges only CERTIFY.
    The record question, the second of those two, is the one Part II left to the machine,
on purpose. Section 9 said that testing a claim and committing to it are two different
acts, and that nothing in the five parts of the model makes the second wait for the
first. Read Section 2’s definition again with that in mind: a machine where you pay
one unit and raise the flag over nothing in particular obeys every rule in it. That
machine is honest about the price and silent about what was bought: it’s a receipt
for nothing. The toll alone can’t fix that, because the toll is a rule about cost, and
“was this earned” is a question about order: did a check happen, of this claim, before
the commitment, with nothing changing underneath in between?
    This machine is my attempt to make the order part of the machine, in the smallest
place I could find to do it. I’ll show you the pieces, then the proofs, then the places
it falls short, which there are, and which I’d rather you hear from me.
330   15 A smallest example machine


              The blown fuse cannot be hidden from every future move
              Blow the fuse and pull the lever. Nothing moves. Replace the fuse, start from the
              same counter values, and that lever can turn the gears. The fuse decides what the
              next pull does, whether the camera can see it or not.
                 That is what a failed CHECK does here. It traps the core, and every free instruction
              then leaves the whole state alone. Suppose I hide the failed check from the camera
              and still demand that the next picture depend only on the present picture and the
              free move. The live and trapped pictures agree. The camera’s rule must give them
              the same next picture. Since the trapped box stays still, the projected live box has to
              stay still too.


              Theorem 15.1 (A globally check-silent native shadow is static). Let π be any
              projection from native full states, with any target type. Suppose every CHECK
              preserves π, and each zero-cost instruction i has an autonomous projected rule hi ,
              so π (exec(s, i )) = hi (π (s)) for every state. Then hi (π (s)) = π (s) for every s, i. If π
              is onto, each hi is identity everywhere. The conclusion also holds on the reachable
              states from a fixed start when those same laws hold throughout that reachable
              domain.

              Proof. Stand at any native state s and read counter A. Ask CHECK whether that
              counter is at least one greater than the number just read. It is not, so this check
              leaves a trapped state t. In symbols, the chosen question is A ≥ A(s) + 1.
                 By the proposed silence rule, the failed check has not changed the picture:
              π (t) = π (s). Now choose any free instruction i. At the trapped state it changes
              nothing at all. The camera’s rule hi must therefore leave that picture alone. But it is
              also the picture of s, and hi receives only the picture, not a choice between the two
              boxes. It must leave s’s picture alone too. Written as one chain,

                               hi (π (s)) = hi (π (t)) = π (exec(t, i )) = π (t) = π (s).

                  You could begin at any s and choose any free i, so every free projected move is
              still on the whole image. If every base picture occurs, that is the whole base. I did
              choose a different failing question for different counter values; the premise allows
              every CHECK at every state, so it allows each of those choices. Finally, if s was
              reached from the fixed start, append this CHECK to that run to reach t. Both boxes
              remain inside the reachable domain, and the same argument applies there.
                 The fuse belongs with the gears that read it. The certificate and ledger can sit
              beside them unread. The later slice follows the computing moves while the machine
                                                                          15.2 Where the counters come from   331


is live; a failed check takes it out of that working domain. That is where the line
goes on this machine. 3


15.2 Where the counters come from
The base first, and the base isn’t mine. It’s Marvin Minsky’s. In a 1961 paper in the
Annals of Mathematics, and then in his 1967 book Computation: Finite and Infinite
Machines, Minsky studied a machine so bare it’s almost a joke. Picture a few bins of
pebbles and a numbered list of instructions. There are only two kinds of instruction:
put a pebble in bin c and go to the next line; or take a pebble out of bin c if there’s
one to take, and go one way if there was and another way if the bin was empty.
There’s nothing else: no memory but the bins, no tape, no arithmetic beyond plus
one and minus one. When the line you’re on has no instruction, the machine stops.
    What Minsky proved is that two bins are enough to compute anything a Turing
machine can compute, as long as you’re willing to pack the input in a strange way.
The trick is to keep many numbers inside one number, as the powers of different
primes (2x 3y 5z holds three numbers in one), and to do arithmetic on the exponents
by multiplying and dividing with the second bin as scratch space. Packing numbers
that way can turn a modest input into an enormous pile of pebbles, handled one at
a time, so it’s no way to build a fast machine. It’s a way to settle a question: with
that packing, the two bins can do every Turing computation. What the bins give me
here is a base whose ordinary moves you can see all of. Each of the earlier results
says which properties of a base it needs, and Appendix E carries the earned layer
over to other bases once you’ve named what they have to supply.
    Who cares? Minsky did, because the question then was where the edge of
computation sits and how little machinery reaches it. You should, because it means
the base of this chapter’s machine hides nothing: if it can compute everything with
plus one, minus one and a jump, then nothing about the record can be smuggling
computing power in through some instruction I made fancy. For this construction
I use Minsky’s two-counter halting result and the counter constructions of Forster,
Larchey-Wendling and their coauthors. Appendix K sets out the reduction; the
step-for-step connection to this machine is the part I have to establish.
    And the pebbles aren’t only my picture. They were somebody’s actual machine,
the same year. In one issue of the Canadian Mathematical Bulletin, September 1961,
Z. A. Melzak, a mathematician at the University of British Columbia, described a
computer made of distinguishable holes and an unlimited supply of pebbles, with
one three-place operation, and a few pages later Joachim Lambek, a mathematician
   3 A view that exposes refusal, or a machine with a different failure rule, would supply a different

interface. The obstruction concerns the native failure semantics and a globally CHECK-silent autonomous
projection.
332   15 A smallest example machine


              at McGill University, trimmed it to two moves: put a pebble in hole X; take one
              out of hole X if there’s one to take. He called it an infinite abacus, and early on
              he writes “Our method is probably not new,” which is a hard sentence to beat. He
              also tells anybody who distrusts infinity not to worry about all those holes, since
              any one computation only ever uses finitely many of them. Is that two inventions
              or one? Lambek says his was a modification of Melzak’s, so call it one and a half,
              with Minsky’s as a separate find the same year. And then Lambek went somewhere
              you wouldn’t guess: in 1986, with Philip Scott, a logician who had come to McGill
              to work with him and later taught at the University of Ottawa, he wrote a book
              whose first part, as the publisher describes it, shows that typed lambda calculi and
              a certain kind of category are essentially the same thing. He went from pebbles to
              category theory in one career, twenty-five years end to end. Does any of it change
              the argument? No. The machine uses Minsky’s version and Minsky’s name. But a
              bare machine that several people reach for in the same year looks like a shape that
              was sitting there. It doesn’t look much like anybody’s invention.
                  The title of Minsky’s 1961 paper is the clue I can’t leave alone. It’s about “Post’s
              problem of tag.” Who’s Post, and what’s tag? Emil Post was a logician, a fresh PhD
              from Columbia, who in 1921, on a fellowship at Princeton, was playing with about
              the simplest rewriting game there is. Take a word of 0s and 1s. Look at its first
              letter, chop the first three letters off the front, and stick something on the end: 00
              if the letter you looked at was 0, 1101 if it was 1. Repeat, and stop when fewer
              than three letters are left. Try it at the table. Start from 1000: you get 01101, then
              0100, then 000, then 00, and it stops. Start from 100: you get 1101, 11101, 011101,
              10100, 001101, and then 10100 again, and it goes round forever. Post wanted a rule
              that tells you, for every starting word, which of those happens. He worked at it for
              months and later called it hopeless, and as far as I can tell it still is: a hundred years
              on, nobody knows whether that one little game, with that one rule, can be decided.
              Stephen Wolfram, the physicist who built Mathematica, wrote a 2021 article on
              it that tells the Princeton story, and it’s where I’d start. In his 1961 paper Minsky
              proved that tag games in general can compute anything, which is why Post’s name is
              on it. It didn’t settle Post’s own game. And the chase goes one step further. In 2008
              Liesbeth De Mol, a historian and philosopher of computing who wrote her doctoral
              work on tag systems, turned the famous 3n + 1 problem (halve an even number,
              triple an odd one and add one, and ask whether you always get down to 1) into a
              small tag game of the same kind. So is Post’s game secretly as hard as everything, or
              just stubborn? I can’t tell you, and as far as the published work goes, nobody can
              yet.
                  None of that changes the machine below. It changes the picture. The two-counter
              machine came out of a hunt for the smallest thing that can’t be predicted, and the
              smallest things are exactly where the open questions are still sitting.
                                                          15.3 The example machine, piece by piece   333


   There’s one word clash to settle before it bites. Minsky’s machine is usually called
a counter machine, and its bins are counters. Section 6 also had a counter: the ledger
µ, the number that only climbs. It’s the same word for two completely different
things, and I’d love to say I set that up on purpose. In this chapter, counter means
one of Minsky’s two bins, called A and B, and the climbing total is always the ledger
µ.


15.3 The example machine, piece by piece
I’ll go through the whole state a piece at a time, in words first.
• Two counters, A and B. Each holds a whole number, with no upper limit.
• A version for each counter, also a whole number with no limit. It starts at 0 and
  goes up by one every time its counter is written. Think of it as the counter’s
  edition number: a new value is a new edition.
• A line number, which instruction comes next, counting from 1 (more on that
  choice just below).
• A fact table: a list of facts. A fact is three things stuck together: a property, a
  counter, and a version. “A is even, as of edition 3” is a fact. The table has room
  for sixteen. Why sixteen? It’s a pick, with no derivation behind it, and what the
  pick gives up is set out in the subsection near the end of this chapter on what the
  machine doesn’t do.
• A channel: either empty, or holding one fact. This is where a commitment sits.
• A trap: one bit, down at the start. When it goes up, the machine has refused
  something, and it stays up.
    Counting lines from 1 looks like the least interesting choice in the chapter, and
it’s one of the oldest arguments in programming, with a famous referee. Edsger
Dijkstra was a Dutch computer scientist, one of the generation that founded the
field, and for over forty years he mailed numbered notes to a few dozen colleagues.
In 1982 he wrote one of them, EWD 831, titled “Why numbering should start at
zero.” His case goes through ranges first. Of the four ways to write “2 up to 12” with
less-than signs, he picks the one that takes the bottom in and leaves the top out,
2 ≤ i < 13: two ranges that meet end to end then share one number written once,
and the length is just the top minus the bottom. Start a sequence of N things at zero
and it’s 0 ≤ i < N, and each thing’s number is how many things came before it. He
reports that programmers on the language Mesa, which allowed all four conventions,
found the other three a steady source of clumsiness and mistakes, and he points
out that FORTRAN starts at one. Does that settle it? It settles which convention is
tidier, by an argument you can check. It doesn’t settle which convention somebody
334   15 A smallest example machine


              else’s work used, and that’s the catch: the two-counter machine used by Forster,
              Larchey-Wendling and coauthors numbers its lines from 1, and so does this machine,
              because matching it line for line is worth more here than tidiness. Is zero the right
              place to start counting? Dijkstra’s title says it is, and I can’t tell you more than that.
              What his note carries is an argument about which way makes fewer mistakes. That
              part you can check for yourself, and it’s the more useful thing to have.
                  Everything in that list is the core, the part the base moves. Outside the core sit
              the two pieces from the model: the ledger µ and the flag. The machine never reads
              either of them to decide what to do next. I’m not asking you to take that on trust:
              it’s how the step is written, and it shows up as a theorem below.
                  The properties a fact can name come from a tiny fixed language with three words:
              is zero; is even; and is at least n, for any whole number n you like. Each one comes
              in two forms. There’s the checker, a little program that computes yes or no: compare
              with 0, look at the last bit, compare with n. And there’s the meaning, the plain
              arithmetic statement the checker is supposed to be checking: the number is 0; the
              number is two times something; n is less than or equal to the number. Why both?
              Because a checker is code, and code can be wrong in ways that look right, and
              “the checker says yes” is only worth anything once somebody has proved it says yes
              exactly when the meaning is true. That proof is one line per property, and it’s the
              first block below.
                  Why can a machine check a claim at all? Because a claim with a precise meaning
              is something you evaluate: plug in the values and turn the crank. George Boole
              worked out in 1847 that you can do arithmetic on claims this way, treating “and”
              like multiplication and “or” like a kind of addition. Why multiplication? Try it at
              the table. Write 1 for true and 0 for false, and multiply: one times one is one, and
              anything times zero is zero. That’s “and” to the letter. Then comes the stranger thing
              Boole noticed. Say “x and x” and you’ve said nothing new; it’s just x. In numbers
              that’s x × x = x, and he made it a law of his system, and it’s a law ordinary numbers
              mostly break. Which numbers equal their own square? Two times two is four, no. A
              half times a half is a quarter, no. Zero, yes. One, yes. That’s the whole list. So when
              Boole wrote his bigger book in 1854, The Laws of Thought, he asked you to imagine
              an algebra whose letters take the values 0 and 1 and nothing else. Every checker on
              this machine answers in that algebra.
                  And the 1847 book has a backstory worth a detour, which I found in the Stanford
              Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on Boole. Boole was largely self-taught and spent
              about fifteen years as a schoolmaster, and what pulled him back to logic, early in
              1847, was a loud public quarrel between Augustus De Morgan and the Scottish
              philosopher Sir William Hamilton over who had first thought of a small technical
              idea in the old logic of syllogisms. Two well-known men fighting over credit, and a
              schoolmaster watching from the side picks up the subject and writes the little book
                                                         15.3 The example machine, piece by piece   335


this paragraph is about. Few people remember what the quarrel was over. Every
checker in this chapter runs on what the bystander wrote.
    Then push on it, because Boole’s “or” isn’t quite the one a checker uses. His plus
only made sense for things that can’t both hold at once, so “x or y” with both of them
true had no meaning in his system. William Stanley Jevons, an English economist
who also worked on logic, read “or” as “either or both,” which gives “x or x is x,”
the same trick as before. He wrote to Boole in 1863 saying plus ought to work that
way, and in 1864 he put it in a book called Pure Logic. Boole wouldn’t have it, since
it broke the tie to ordinary algebra his whole system stood on. The “or” in every
programming language I know is the inclusive one Jevons argued for. Does that
change anything about the checker? No; the crank turns the same way. It changes
the picture: the “or” a checker uses is the one the man who invented the algebra
turned down.
    Hanging a checked claim on a point in a computation is an old move too. Tony
Hoare, in 1969, built a whole way of reasoning about programs out of it: attach a
claim to a point in a program (“whenever execution reaches here, this is true”), and
reason forward from claim to claim. Robert Floyd had done it two years earlier on
flowcharts. Their claims were checked on paper by the person writing the proof.
This machine’s version is a property of one counter at one edition, checked by a step
while it runs.
    And is two years earlier the bottom? Not even close, and the next step down is a
paper this book already leaned on. In June 1949, at a Cambridge conference held
for the new EDSAC computer, Alan Turing gave a talk three pages long, “Checking
a large routine,” the same note the counter chapter used for stopping (Section 6).
Stopping was the second half of it. The first half is this move, twenty years before
Hoare: the programmer should make “definite assertions which can be checked
individually,” and the correctness of the whole should follow from them. His example
program computes a factorial using nothing but addition, and his picture for why
you’d bother is one you can do on the back of an envelope. Add up a long column
of four-digit numbers and hand someone only the total, and they have to redo the
whole sum at one sitting, because the carries tie every column to the one before
it. Hand them the total of each column as well, and the job falls apart into small
checks they can do one at a time. Each column total is a claim hung on a point in
the middle of the work, so the person checking never has to hold all of it at once.
The paper got its due mostly later: in 1984 two computer scientists, F. L. Morris of
Syracuse University and C. B. Jones of Manchester University, who had worked on it
together at Oxford, republished it, with its misprints corrected, as an early program
proof by Alan Turing. Theirs is the text I read, and the column of numbers is Turing’s
own example in it. Does any of that change the machine? No. It changes the date
336   15 A smallest example machine


              on the idea, and it tells you something I like: the first person to ask how you’d check
              a program put the claims in the middle of it. He didn’t save them for the end.
                 The machine has six instruction kinds.

                Instruction           What it does, when the trap is Cost
                                      down
                INC c                 Adds one to counter c, adds one      0

                  The first two are Minsky’s machine, and HALT lets a program say it’s done. It says
              it by doing nothing: HALT leaves the state where it is. If it put the trap up instead,
              it would land a live state on its trapped twin, a merge in the record’s part, and the
              record-layer merge would charge it. The last three are the record’s, and they read
              as a chain: you can only certify with a commitment in the channel, you can only
              commit to a fact in the table, and the only way into the table is a check that passed.
              The chain has three links, and each one costs.
                  One of what? One unit of µ, the same unit as Section 2’s toll. Why one? Why
              would ten be worse? Because one is the least each of these three acts can cost once
                                                         15.3 The example machine, piece by piece   337


a merge in the record’s own part of the state is priced, as the end of this paragraph
says, and Section 3 is where that pricing comes from. The argument for a whole
finite machine doesn’t reach this one: these counters have no top, and some of the
base moves merge states at a price of zero. What does reach it is the record-layer
merge named at the start of this chapter (Theorem 3.19, in Part I), which gives
the toll once you’ve agreed to price a merge in the record’s own part of the state.
Agreeing to that is my choice. Once I have, one unit on each of the three acts isn’t:
COMMIT and CERTIFY merge when they pass, and all three merge when they fail,
because a failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else, so the failed state lands
where the same state with the trap already up lands. What I pick is one rather than
more.
    The whole numbers have a history of their own. In 1888 the German mathe-
matician Richard Dedekind published a little book whose title asks what numbers
are and what they’re for, and in 1889 the Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano
published a booklet, written in Latin, that set out the axioms for the whole numbers
in the form people still teach: there’s a first number, and every number has a next
one, and a few rules about how “next” behaves. I had the two of them down as
working independently. I went looking, and the Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry on
Dedekind says Peano acknowledged Dedekind’s priority, which is why the axioms
often go by both names. (Peano’s booklet is also where the sign ∈ that you met in
Section 5 comes from: he wrote it as a Greek epsilon, for the Latin est, “is.”) Start
from zero and take “the next one” three times, and you have three. Once prices are
whole numbers, one is the smallest price that isn’t nothing.
    The zeros matter just as much: computing costs nothing on this ledger. Plus one,
minus one and jumping around cost zero, though in a real device each of them still
dissipates when it happens. Only the three acts that make a claim cost, and each of
them costs whether it passes or traps. Failing is not a discount.
    The version rule. Some numbers show why versions exist. Start with A = 4,
version 0. CHECK is even A passes, and the table gets the fact (even, A, 0). Now INC
A: A becomes 5, and its version becomes 1. Now COMMIT is even A. The machine
looks for (even, A, 1), the claim about the current edition. The table only has (even,
A, 0). There’s no match, so the machine traps. The old fact is still sitting in the
table, still true about edition 0, and completely useless for committing to anything
