about edition 1. A fact is about one edition of one counter, and an edition never
comes back, because versions only go up and never wrap. The version rule is the
whole trick against stale evidence: you can’t check a number, change it, and then
commit to the check. And the never-wrap part isn’t a convenience. INC A, then DEC
A back to the same line, puts the line and both counters exactly where they were, at
no cost, and once record-layer merges are priced neither move may join two states
that agree on those. If the record had only finitely many settings over one line and
338   15 A smallest example machine


              one pair of counters, enough round trips would bring the whole state back to where
              a CHECK left it, with A touched in between and its COMMIT still passing. So an
              edition has to be able to grow without end.
                  What the version rule stops is the time-of-check-to-time-of-use bug from Sec-
              tion 14, the file checked and then swapped, and the database answer to it is Kung
              and Robinson’s: at commit time, check that nothing you read was written in the
              meantime, and back out if something was. The version rule is that check, done by
              the step, on one counter. It also shows where the guarantee ends. It works because
              one step does every write and every write bumps a version. A second writer that
              changed a counter without bumping its version, a second processor or a device
              writing memory on its own, would walk right around it, and none of the theorems
              below are about a machine with one of those.
                  Processor designers put a cousin of this check in silicon. Jensen, Hagensen and
              Broughton, at Lawrence Livermore in 1987, described a pair of instructions now
              called load-linked and store-conditional: the load reads a word and the processor
              starts watching it, and the store goes through only if nothing has written that word
              since; otherwise it fails and the program tries again. It’s tempting to say CHECK
              is the load and COMMIT is the conditional store, and it’s wrong in two places.
              COMMIT doesn’t write the counter it checked, and the thing doing the watching,
              the fact, sits in a table the step keeps. No single processor holds it. The hardware
              version does cover the second writer, because the watching happens on the memory
              everyone shares, which is exactly the case the version rule leaves out.
                  The real kinship is older, and it’s somewhere else. Picture the table and the
              counters shared by many processors, with CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY each
              done as one indivisible step. Maurice Herlihy (1991), a computer scientist who has
              spent his career on how many processors can share memory safely, ranked shared
              objects by how many processors each one can bring to agree on a single value with
              nobody ever waiting on anybody. Test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and
              reports what was there, brings exactly two. A sticky bit, the idea of Serge Plotkin
              (1989), a Stanford computer scientist working on distributed algorithms, is a cell the
              first writer jams for good, with the first writer’s value, and everyone after can read
              it; it brings any number. I guessed that the shared object would sit at the top with
              the sticky bit, because a write that kills every fact about a counter, together with a
              commitment other processors can see, looks like a way to build one. Ranking the
              object takes its operations, what each one returns, which steps are indivisible, how
              it starts and which processes run it, and then a proof that every processor decides,
              they all decide the same value, the value is one somebody proposed, and nobody
              waits. That proof goes through with every instruction one indivisible step and the
              whole state readable, and it puts the object at the top. The reason is the order of the
              fact table. Start it clean, with counter A at zero and the trap down. Each processor
                                                         15.3 The example machine, piece by piece   339


CHECKs a property that holds of A at zero, Zero to propose 0 and Even to propose
1, then reads the table and decides the bit of its oldest fact. Nobody touches A, so
the first CHECK of the run passes. The table never loses an entry or reorders the
ones it has, and a CHECK that finds it full trips the trap, after which nothing moves,
so the first CHECK of the run fixes the oldest fact for good. Every processor that
decides decides that bit, the bit is somebody’s proposal, and each one decides after
two of its own steps whatever the others do. The version rule and the commitment
play no part. The trap alone doesn’t do it: it records that something trapped, and it
doesn’t hand everyone the first writer’s value.
    Now take the version rule away, let failures change nothing, keep only the
properties “at least n” so that a checked property only ever turns true, drop the
decrement, and make the fact table (with no room limit), the commitments and
the flag sets and latches that only grow. I guessed that then the object drops to the
bottom rung, the level of plain memory, which is the shared-memory face of what
the database researchers Joseph Hellerstein and Peter Alvaro (2020), at Berkeley
and Santa Cruz, call CALM, where monotone means nobody has to coordinate. That
guess is proved too, by Herlihy’s own kind of argument. Let the updates return
nothing and let the whole state be readable. If at every state, of any two updates,
one leaves the state alone, or the two commute, or one overwrites the other, then no
protocol brings two processors to agreement with nobody waiting. To see why, give
one processor 0 and the other 1. At the start the answer isn’t settled, since either
one running alone has to decide its own bit. Nobody waits, so it can’t stay unsettled
forever, and there’s a last unsettled state: whichever processor moves next settles
it, one way if it’s the first and the other way if it’s the second. Look at those two
moves. If one is a read, or an update that leaves the state alone, the other processor
can’t tell whether it happened, and running alone it decides the same bit either
way. If the two commute, both orders end on the same state with both processors
in the same place. If one overwrites the other, the overwriter running alone can’t
tell whether the other move happened first. Each case contradicts the two ways the
answer was settled. The monotone object, with registers beside it, has that property.
An update that fails changes nothing. Two updates that both succeed still succeed in
either order, because an instruction that would succeed still succeeds after anything
else has run, and adding to sets and to counters gives the same result in either order.
Two of the conditions do real work there. The table needs no room limit: a full table
that turns away the latecomer is a first-writer-wins cell again, and that’s back at the
top. And the ledger: it changes neither result as long as a failed act in the variant
isn’t charged, or nobody reads the ledger. Charge a failed CHECK where everyone
can read the total, and one processor INCs while the other CHECKs at least 1; the
total and the table then tell each of them which act came first, and that’s enough
340   15 A smallest example machine


              for two to agree. Neither idea is mine: the top is Plotkin’s and the bottom is the
              monotone fact that field already knows.
                  Process-calculus people have a statement of the same split. Johannes Åman
              Pohjola and Joachim Parrow, computer scientists at Uppsala University (Parrow
              is one of the inventors of the pi-calculus, a mathematical model of processes that
              talk over channels), in 2016 proved that no model whose parallel composition is
              monotonic, where a neighbouring process can never stop a step, has a consensus
              process. One of their examples of a model that does is test-and-set. Test-and-set isn’t
              a sticky bit: in Herlihy’s ranking it brings two processors to agree, and a sticky bit
              brings any number.
                  Their setting is small enough to go through here whole. A model is any set of
              processes with a step relation and a way to compose two processes that doesn’t care
              about order or grouping. Composition is monotonic when whatever a process can
              reach alone, it can still reach with anything set beside it. A consensus process is one
              where any number of copies, run together, can end up agreeing on either of two
              outcomes; once a run has one outcome it can never show the other; and an outcome,
              once reached, survives having more copies, run any way you like, set beside it. Their
              theorem goes through in a few lines: run half the copies to one outcome and the
              other half to the other. If neither half can block the other, the whole crowd can
              reach the pair of end states set side by side, and since each outcome survives the
              company, both outcomes hold there, which is forbidden. Then the machine goes
              into it. A process is a shared machine state with a crowd of threads, each proposing
              a bit. Composing two processes pools their threads, each thread keeping whatever it
              has already decided, and settles the shared state like this: if one side is still at the
              fresh start, the composite takes the other side’s state; if both have already moved,
              the composite is jammed, a state where no thread can take a step. That composition
              doesn’t care about order or grouping: a fresh start is neutral, and any two moved
              states jam whichever way round you put them. One thread proposing each bit is
              a consensus process in exactly their sense, for the outcomes “some thread decided
              0” and “some thread decided 1”: copies started fresh can reach either outcome and
              never both, because the first passing check fixes the oldest fact and every later thread
              reads the same one; and an outcome survives company, because pooled threads
              keep their decisions. So by their theorem the composition isn’t monotonic, and
              the small machine sits on their non-monotonic side. That verdict is cheap, though:
              a composition that jams any two moved states makes every shared-state machine
              non-monotonic, so the encoding puts it there, not the fact table. What does the
              work in the run, making every thread read the same outcome, is the order of the
              fact table, the same as above; a store that refuses a stale commit for good, as the
              version rule does, refuses in the same spirit. The shared-memory version of their
              split is the pair of results above: the small machine’s object reaches agreement for
                                                          15.3 The example machine, piece by piece   341


any number of processors, and the monotone variant, with its table unbounded and
no charge for failing that anyone can see, doesn’t reach it even for two.
    Security people know the pattern by a third name. A check that blesses a value,
and a write that takes the blessing away, is close kin to dynamic taint tracking,
where a label rides along with the data and a sanitizing step changes it; the labels go
back to the computer-security researcher Dorothy Denning’s 1976 lattice model of
how information is allowed to flow. How much a monitor like that has to remember
is a studied question too: Chamseddine Talhi, Nadia Tawbi and Mourad Debbabi
(2008), three security researchers at universities in Quebec, worked out which rules
a monitor can still enforce when its memory is bounded. The version rule is one
small, specific member of that family, done by the step.
    Notice what isn’t a write. DEC on a counter that’s already 0 doesn’t change the
counter, so it doesn’t change the version. It’s a test that happens to move the line
number.
    The fact table. Facts go in and never come out. Nothing erases them and nothing
overwrites them. When the table is full, a seventeenth CHECK traps rather than
pushing an old fact out to make room. That choice has a downside, and I’ll set it out
in the subsection on what this machine doesn’t do.
    Traps. Any failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else in the core; the
ledger still takes the instruction’s cost. Once it’s up, every instruction leaves the
core alone. A stored program stops at a trap. But I also prove things about any list
of instructions, programs or otherwise, because an adversary doesn’t have to run
my programs; they can feed the machine whatever they want. For those lists, an
instruction after a trap is still charged its cost, and still changes nothing. That trap
keeps nothing of what tripped it, and the record-layer merge charges it for that. A
trap that counted its refusals would keep the two apart, and then a CHECK would
merge nothing and the premise would charge it nothing.
    The exact version comes next.

Definition 15.1 (Properties, checker, meaning). A property is one of: Zero, Even,
or Ge(n) for a whole number n. The checker eval( p, v) computes yes or no: v = 0
by equality, evenness by the parity function, n ≤ v by comparison. The meaning
holds( p, v) is the arithmetic statement: v = 0; there is an m with v = 2m; n ≤ v.



Lemma 15.2 (The checker says what it means). For every property p and every
whole number v, eval( p, v) = yes if and only if holds( p, v).
342   15 A smallest example machine


              Proof. Ask whether the number is zero: the equality test says yes at zero and no at
              every other number. Ask whether it is at least n: the comparison says yes precisely
              when n is no larger than it. Those two tests already answer the arithmetic questions
              they name.
                 For evenness, the checker says yes at zero, no at one, and adding two leaves its
              answer unchanged. Take any whole number and remove pairs until fewer than two
              remain. If none remain, the number was two times the number of pairs removed,
              and the checker gives zero’s answer, yes. If one remains, it was two times that many
              pairs plus one, and the checker gives one’s answer, no. Thus yes means exactly
              v = 2m for some whole number m. These are all three properties in the language.


              Definition 15.2 (Core, state, claim, start). A core k holds two counters A, B and
              their versions (whole numbers), a line number, a fact table (a list of facts, a fact
              being a triple of a property, a counter and a version), a channel (empty or one fact),
              and a trap bit. Write val(k, c) and ver(k, c) for counter c’s value and version. A state
              s is a core, written core(s), with a ledger µ(s) and a flag cert(s). The claim p of c in
              k is the fact ( p, c, ver(k, c)). The table’s room is 16. The start start( a, b) has counters
              a and b, versions 0, line 1, an empty table, an empty channel, the trap down, µ = 0
              and the flag down. A state is clean when its table and channel are empty and its flag
              is down.


              Definition 15.3 (Instructions, costs, the step). The instructions are INC c, DEC c j,
              HALT, CHECK p c, COMMIT p c and CERTIFY, with effects on a core with the trap
              down as in the table above. Passing any check, commitment or certification requires
              the trap to be down. With that condition, CHECK passes when eval( p, val(k, c)) =
              yes and the table holds fewer than 16 facts, COMMIT passes when the claim p of
              c is in the table, and CERTIFY passes when the channel holds a fact; a failing one
              sets the trap and changes nothing else. On a core with the trap up, every instruction
              changes nothing. Costs: CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost 1, the rest 0. One step
              on a state is
                                                                                                  
                   exec(s, i ) = cexec(core(s), i ), µ(s) + cost(i ), cert(s) ∨ fires(core(s), i ) ,

              where cexec is the core’s step and fires(k, i ) is yes exactly when i is CERTIFY and
              passes at k. For any list t of instructions (a trace), run(t, s) applies them in order
              and cost(t) adds their costs. A program is a list of instructions numbered from 1; a
              program run fetches the instruction at the line number and executes it, and stops
              when the trap is up, the line holds HALT, or the line holds nothing.
                 Read the step line slowly, because the rest of the chapter leans on its shape. The
              core moves by its own rule and nothing else. The ledger adds the cost. The flag
                                                           15.3 The example machine, piece by piece   343


becomes “it was up, or this is a CERTIFY that passed.” The core’s move doesn’t
mention µ or the flag anywhere. The base is blind to the record by construction.
    The shortest worked run there is uses the program CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is
zero A; CERTIFY. Start at start(0, b), for any b. Line 1: A is 0, the checker says yes,
the table is empty so there’s room, and the fact (zero, A, 0) goes in. µ = 1. Line 2:
the claim about A’s current edition is (zero, A, 0), and it’s right there, so it goes into
the channel, and µ = 2. Line 3: the channel holds a fact, the flag goes up. µ = 3.
Line 4 has no instruction, so the program stops. The run ends with three paid acts,
in order, a flag that’s up, and a channel that names the last earned commitment,
which here is (zero, A, 0).
    Now start the same program at start(5, b). Line 1: A is 5, the checker says no,
the trap goes up, µ = 1, and the program stops right there. The flag is down, and
you can run it as long as you like: it stays down. That second run is the point of the
first. The same three instructions certify from some starts and refuse from others,
because the check could have failed, and from most starts it does. A check like that
has a no pile, which is the only kind Section 14 counts as establishing anything.
    Could I have picked an even dumber claim? I could: CHECK at least 0 A passes
on every number there is, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the flag for
3 from every start. The step doesn’t ask whether the question was worth asking,
and it shouldn’t. Worth is a count over the rivals a run narrows (Section 8), and a
step that sees one state has no list of rivals to count. What the step checks is order,
aboutness and that the checker tells the truth. What a check that can’t fail is worth,
the entitlement count says exactly: zero bits, for a cost of three. The price is for
standing behind the claim. What the claim bought is a separate number, one the
step doesn’t compute, and I keep the two apart. It’s on the list at the end of the
chapter.
    Others walked into the same line from communication. Three theoretical com-
puter scientists, Oded Goldreich, Brendan Juba and Madhu Sudan (2012), built a
theory of communication with a partner you may not understand, in which getting
a message across counts only as a way to reach a goal, and the central notion is
sensing: being able to tell, from what you see, whether you’re making progress. They
ask two things of it. It has to be safe: with any partner in the class, when there’s no
progress it keeps saying so, so it can’t report a lasting success that didn’t happen.
And it has to be viable: with a partner who could help if you spoke its language, the
right way of speaking gets a yes from it within a known time, and keeps getting one.
Either half alone is cheap. A sensor that always says no is safe, and one that always
says yes is viable. Their main result, as I read it, is that the two together, with the
ways of speaking listed one after another, are enough for one strategy that reaches
the goal with every such partner. Their theorem, in their setting, is a check that can
344   15 A smallest example machine


              fail and never lies, standing in front of a verdict you can’t take back, and it’s the
              same shape.


              15.4 It computes everything two counters can
              First the base, because if the base can’t compute, nothing else here matters. Put the
              ordinary two-counter program beside this machine’s program. Replace each “add
              one” by this machine’s INC, and each “subtract if possible and jump” by its DEC,
              keeping the named counter and jump destination. That is all the translation does.
                 Now cover the facts, versions, channel, flag and ledger with a sheet. Leave the
              two counters and line number visible. I want to show that the visible part follows the
              original program exactly. The hidden versions may change, but these instructions
              cannot raise the trap, so the sheet never hides a new refusal that would stop the
              comparison. Here are the two programs and the window written precisely.

              Definition 15.4 (Two-counter program, compile, window). A two-counter program
              M is a list of instructions, each either MINC c or MDEC c j. A configuration is a
              triple (line, a, b). One step of M: if the line holds no instruction, M has stopped;
              MINC adds one to c and goes to the next line; MDEC subtracts one from c and goes
              to line j if c is above 0, and goes to the next line if c is 0. mrun(n, M, x ) is n steps
              from x, staying put once stopped. The compile of M replaces each MINC c by INC c
              and each MDEC c j by DEC c j. The window of a core k is the triple (line number,
              val(k, A), val(k, B)).



              Theorem 15.3 (Step for step). For every two-counter program M and every core
              k with the trap down: M has stopped at window(k) if and only if the program
              compile( M ) has halted at k; and if M steps from window(k ) to y, then one program
              step of compile( M ) from k lands on a core with window y and the trap still down.
              So for every n, n program steps of compile( M ) from k land on a core whose window
              is mrun(n, M, window(k)), with the trap down.

              Proof. Look up the instruction at the line. If there is none, both sides stop. If
              it’s MINC c, the compiled INC c adds one to c and goes to the next line, which is
              exactly the window’s move (the version also moves, but the window doesn’t show
              versions). If it’s MDEC c j, split on whether c is 0, and both sides do the same
              thing in each case. Neither instruction can trap. After that move the windows agree
              again and the trap is still down. Those are exactly the conditions I began with, so
              the next instruction can be compared in the same way. Repeat until the chosen n
                                                        15.4 It computes everything two counters can   345


steps have been counted; if either side stops earlier, both stay put for the remaining
comparisons.



Theorem 15.4 (Halting matches). For every two-counter program M and whole
numbers a, b: M stops after some number of steps from (1, a, b) if and only if the
program compile( M ) halts after some number of program steps from start( a, b).

Proof. The start has window (1, a, b) and its trap is down. Apply Theorem 15.3
after any number n of steps: the two configurations still have the same window, the
trap is still down, and one is stopped exactly when the other is halted. The same n
witnesses termination in either direction.
     Now comes the part that isn’t mine. Two-counter universality is Minsky’s, and
the constructions of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and their coauthors connect it to
several other models. The counter convention matters: DEC at zero goes on to
the next instruction; otherwise it takes one off and jumps, the convention used
in Andrej Dudenhefner’s certified decision procedures for two-counter machines
(2022). Appendix K builds the route from a tape to counters, packs finitely many
counters into two, and gives the halting diagonal. The remaining step here is to
match that two-counter machine to this machine’s INC/DEC fragment, instruction
for instruction.
     I want to be exact about what “undecidable” means in the theorem below, because
it’s stated as a connection between two problems. Suppose you had a procedure that
answered the halting question for this machine. Then you could write a program
that lists, one by one, every single-tape Turing machine that doesn’t halt. No such
list can exist: the ones that do halt can already be listed (just run them all, a step at
a time, and call out each one as it stops), and with both lists running side by side
you’d have a halting decider. So the theorem says: a decider here would give you
that impossible list.


Theorem 15.5 (Halting is undecidable for this machine). The two-counter machine
with the instruction convention just stated agrees with the INC/DEC fragment: its
step, its stop, and its termination match those of the compiled program, so its
halting problem at ( M, a, b) has a positive answer if and only if compile( M ) halts
from start( a, b). Consequently, the question “does program P halt from start( a, b)?”
is undecidable in the following reduction sense: a decider for it would make the
complement of single-tape binary Turing machine halting enumerable.
346   15 A smallest example machine


              Proof. The agreement is a case split on the counter-machine instruction at the
              current line, and then induction along the run, ending in Theorem 15.4. Composing
              a proposed decider for the compiled program with the compile map would decide
              two-counter halting. The tape-to-counter reduction in Appendix K would then
              decide single-tape binary halting and so list its complement, as claimed.
                 What that buys is that the base of this machine is a universal machine in Minsky’s
              sense, and that no algorithm can predict in general what it’ll do. What it doesn’t
              buy is a fast machine, or one where your input arrives conveniently. The counters
              start holding a and b, given directly; there’s no encoding layer in this construction.
              Minsky’s prime-power packing is how you’d get from “any Turing machine” to “two
              counters,” and I use that construction as it stands (Appendix K.3 sets it out).
                 Is “given directly” just a convenience, or does it bite? It bites, and somebody
              found exactly where. In 1972 Rich Schroeppel, then at the MIT AI Lab, wrote a
              ten-page memo titled “A Two Counter Machine Cannot Calculate 2 N .” He spells out
              the convention first: a counter machine computing a function starts with n in one
              counter and zero in the others. Then he gives a proof that a two-counter machine
              started that way can’t compute 2n . That’s his theorem, and I don’t reprove it. What
              I prove is a cousin, in Appendix D.4 (Theorem D.23): no program multiplies every
              input by one large constant fixed by the program’s length. So the packing Minsky
              needs is precisely the thing two plain counters can’t do for themselves. Hand the
              small machine its inputs straight and there are functions of them it can’t compute;
              hand it the inputs already packed and it computes anything a Turing machine can.
              That’s no contradiction with the undecidability above, which ranges over every
              program and every starting pair, packed ones included. The base hides nothing; it
              just needs its input pre-chewed, and the chewing is somebody else’s.


              15.5 It’s a Thiele machine, and the flag is a latch

              Now it’s the record’s turn. There are three facts to state first, and all of them read
              straight off the step line.


              Theorem 15.6 (Ledger, toll, permanence). For every state s and instruction i,
              µ(exec(s, i )) = µ(s) + cost(i ), and for every trace t, µ(run(t, s)) = µ(s) + cost(t).
              If cert(s) is down and cert(exec(s, i )) is up, then i is CERTIFY, it passes at core(s),
              and cost(i ) ≥ 1. If cert(s) is up, so is cert(exec(s, i )).

              Proof. Each instruction adds its listed charge to the ledger. Start at µ(s): after the
              first instruction its charge has been added, after the second both charges have been
                                                   15.5 It’s a Thiele machine, and the flag is a latch   347


added, and every further instruction adds its own. An empty list adds nothing. Thus
any finite trace leaves exactly the starting ledger plus the sum of the charges.
    The flag has two ways to be up afterwards: it was already up, or this instruction
successfully certified. If it was down before and up afterwards, only the second way
is available. The instruction must be CERTIFY, its check of the channel must pass,
and its listed charge is one. If the flag was already up, the first way keeps it up
regardless of the next instruction.
   The middle clause of those three is Section 2’s toll, for this machine, which means
this machine is one of the things Section 2 was about, and Section 2’s universal floor
applies to it without my lifting a finger.


Theorem 15.7 (The small machine is a Thiele machine). The states, the instructions,
the step exec, the cost and the flag, with the toll of Theorem 15.6, form a Thiele
machine (Definition 2.1). So the universal floor (Observation 2.1) holds here: if
cert(s0 ) is down and cert(run(t, s0 )) is up, then cost(t) ≥ 1.

Proof. Take the state and instruction sets of Definitions 15.2 and 15.3, their step and
cost, and the flag as the reading. These provide the five components of Definition 2.1.
Theorem 15.6 supplies its one required rule. Applying Observation 2.1 gives the
claimed bound.
   Section 10 comes next. Section 10 said: take any base, and any record that
answers only to the base and never comes back down, and the record is a latch.
This machine has a base: a program together with a core, stepping by the program
step. And it has a record, the flag, with the ledger riding along. So the question is
whether it’s a base-driven extension in Section 10’s five-rule sense (Definition 10.2),
and if it is, Section 10 does the rest.


Theorem 15.8 (The flag is a latch of the base). Let the base have states (program,
core), stepping by the program step, starting at start( a, b)’s core for any a, b, and
halting when the program has halted. Map each (program, state) to (program, core).
Then the machine, run as a closed machine on (program, state), is a base-driven
record over that base, and so its flag factors as the latch (Observation 10.1) of the
event “the next instruction is a CERTIFY that passes.”

Proof. First the cover (Definition 10.1): the map sends starts onto starts, it commutes
with the step because the core’s move never reads µ or the flag, and whether the
program has halted is read off the core. Then the rules of Definition 10.2 one at a
348   15 A smallest example machine


              time. Driven by the computation: the next flag is the old flag or “the next instruction
              is a passing CERTIFY,” which is a function of the base state and the old flag (that’s
              the step line). Ledger: µ only adds. Toll: Theorem 15.6. Permanence: Theorem 15.6.
              A reachable write: the three-line program of the worked run raises the flag from a
              start. Section 10’s theorem then gives the factorization.
                  So far there’s nothing new. The toll, the floor and the latch are things Parts I and
              II already promised about any machine of this kind. The next subsection is the part
              neither of them could give.

              The lamp and the claims it does not name
              The lamp is on. Which claim turned it on? Did another claim get certified afterwards?
              Look at the lamp as long as you like. It still gives you one answer.
                 Put a file beside it. Every time CERTIFY succeeds, copy the fact from its channel
              into the file: the predicate, the counter it concerns, and that counter’s edition. Call
              the set of filed facts R. Publishing the same fact again leaves the same set. A later
              write can change the counters while the old receipt stays filed under its old edition.
                 Run this record alongside the native state. The native instructions keep doing
              exactly what they did before. Forget the file and you recover their run. Open the file
              and you can ask which claims were actually published.


              Theorem 15.9 (The native lamp is the archive’s Boolean reading). From a clean
              start with an empty added archive, after every finite native instruction word,
                                         cert(s) = true    ⇐⇒      R ̸= ∅.

              Membership in R means exactly that this fact was emitted by a successful CERTIFY
              earlier in that word. Already recorded facts persist, and zero-cost instructions cannot
              add a fact.

              Proof. Start with the empty archive and the flag down. Inspect the next instruction.
              A successful CERTIFY inserts its channel fact into R and raises the flag. Whether
              or not that fact was already present, the resulting set is nonempty and the flag is
              up. Every other case leaves both the archive and the flag alone, including failed or
              trapped instructions. This includes every horizontal move. It follows, one instruction
              at a time, that a fact belongs to R exactly when some earlier successful CERTIFY
              published it, that no later move removes it, and that the flag is up exactly when R is
              nonempty. Forgetting R leaves the native updates untouched, so it also recovers the
              native run.
                                                                    15.6 Commitments are earned   349


    The lamp tells you whether that file is empty. The file tells you what is in it.
Below, I will make 65,535 different nonempty files leave the entire native machine in
one identical state. Before that, follow how a fact earns its place: CHECK establishes
it in the table, COMMIT selects it, and a successful CERTIFY publishes it. Each step
has a job.


15.6 Commitments are earned
The shape comes first, before the words. Pick any run from a clean start, any list of
instructions at all, chosen by somebody who’d love to cheat. Look at the moment
a COMMIT would pass. Then, somewhere earlier in that run, there’s a CHECK of
exactly the same claim that passed and paid, at the same edition of the counter, and
between that CHECK and now, nothing touched the counter. That holds on every
list of instructions anybody can write, not “probably” and not only “on the programs
I wrote.”
    To say “nothing touched it” exactly takes one word.

Definition 15.5 (Untouched). A list of instructions mid, run from a state s, leaves
counter c untouched when, for every way of splitting mid as t1 , then i, then t2 ,
executing i at the core reached by running t1 from s leaves both ver(·, c) and val(·, c)
as they were.



Theorem 15.10 (A commitment was checked first). Let s0 be clean and pre any
trace after which COMMIT p c would pass. Then pre splits as pre1 , then CHECK p c,
then mid, where: the CHECK passes at the core reached by pre1 ; CHECK p c and
COMMIT p c each cost 1; c’s version after pre1 equals its version after pre; and mid,
run from just after the CHECK, leaves c untouched.

Proof. COMMIT passes, so the claim ( p, c, ver(c)) for the current version is in the
table. By the no-forging invariant (Theorem 15.14 below), that fact was written by
a passing CHECK p c at some point pre1 , with the version c had then; since it’s the
current version too, the two versions are equal. Versions never go down, and any
instruction that changes a counter’s value also raises its version, so an instruction in
mid that touched c would have left c’s version higher at the end than at the CHECK.
It isn’t. So nothing in mid touched c.
350   15 A smallest example machine




              Theorem 15.11 (A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified). Let s0
              be clean and t any trace with cert(run(t, s0 )) up. Then for some p and c, t is

                        pre1 , CHECK p c, mid1 , COMMIT p c, mid2 , CERTIFY, post,
              where the CHECK passes at its state, the COMMIT passes at its state, the CERTIFY
              passes at its state, c has the same version at the CHECK as at the COMMIT, and
              mid1 leaves c untouched. And when the CERTIFY runs, the channel holds exactly
              the claim that COMMIT made: the fact (p, c, c’s version at the CHECK). CERTIFY
              takes no operand; this is what ties it to the claim.

              Proof. The flag starts down, so some first instruction raised it, and by Theorem 15.6
              it’s a passing CERTIFY. A CERTIFY passes only with a fact in the channel, the channel
              starts empty, and only a passing COMMIT puts a fact there, so some earlier COMMIT
              p c passed. Take the last one before the CERTIFY: the fact in the channel is the one
              it wrote. Theorem 15.10 at that COMMIT gives the CHECK, the equal version, and
              the untouched stretch, and the equal version makes the committed fact (p, c, c’s
              version at the CHECK).
                  The failure side comes next, so you can see the refusals are clean, with nothing
              left half-done:


              Theorem 15.12 (Unearned steps trap and change no claim). If COMMIT p c would
              not pass at a core k, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the channel and the
              table as they were. If CERTIFY would not pass at a state s, executing it puts the trap
              up and leaves the flag as it was.

              Proof. If the trap is already up, the core is unchanged and its trap remains up.
              Otherwise, the failed COMMIT takes the failure branch of the instruction table: set
              the trap, leave every other core field alone. A failed CERTIFY takes the same branch,
              and its fires value is false. The flag update is then its old value or false, which leaves
              it unchanged. The instruction’s charge still applies to the ledger.
                 If that rings a bell, it should. It’s Milner’s move from Section 14: in LCF a
              theorem is a value that only the rules of the logic can build, so nobody can just
              print one (Milner and two colleagues on his Edinburgh project, Michael Gordon and
              Christopher Wadsworth, wrote the system up in 1979, and Gordon, who went on to
              build the HOL prover at Cambridge, told its history in 2000). Here the thing nobody
                                                                    15.6 Commitments are earned   351


can print is one bit, and what guards it is one step rule. Milner’s guard was a type
checker. Same architecture, much lower down.
    A provenance theorem is also an itemised receipt, and the itemised receipt has
a history that’s exactly this gap. James Ritty ran a saloon in Dayton, Ohio, and
believed some of his staff were pocketing money. On a steamboat trip to Europe in
1878 he watched a mechanism that counted the turns of the ship’s propeller, and
wondered whether something like it could count the money instead. In 1879 he and
his brother John patented a “Cash Register and Indicator,” and they sold a version
under the wonderful name Ritty’s Incorruptible Cashier. The first model was this
book’s counter (Section 6) with brass on it: press a key, the amount goes onto a
dial showing the day’s running total. There was no drawer and no paper. At closing
time you hold the dial up against the cash. And that’s all a total can do. It tells you
that the money is short. It can’t tell you which sale went missing or who rang it
up. The paper came later. The patents passed to other owners, first a Cincinnati
salesman named Jacob Eckert, and in 1884 to John H. Patterson, who renamed the
business the National Cash Register Company, and the story told about that company
is that it added a paper roll: one copy kept for the shop’s own books, one handed to
the customer. That last part I only have from histories of the company and of the
machine, so hold it the way you’d hold any company’s story about itself. The order
is right either way: first a total that can tell you something’s wrong, then a list that
tells you where. The ledger µ is the dial. Theorem 15.11 is the list: which CHECK,
of which claim, about which edition, before which COMMIT. The theorem supplies
that list about the run. The machine doesn’t keep it as data anyone can read back
from the end state, and nothing in the theorem gives a procedure for rebuilding it
from there. A fact in the table holds a property, a counter and a version number.
That’s neither the counter’s value back then nor a log of what happened in between.
    Read Theorem 15.11 once more for what it doesn’t say. Between the CHECK and
the COMMIT, the counter is untouched. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY,
it isn’t promised anything. You can check A is even, commit to it, add one to A,
and then certify. The flag goes up, and what it stands on is a commitment about
the edition that was current when you committed. The certificate is historical: it
says “this was checked and committed about this edition,” and it says nothing about
whether that’s still true. I think that’s the right meaning for a certificate (a birth
certificate doesn’t expire when the baby grows), but it’s a meaning, and you should
know which one you’re getting. So a certificate doesn’t say the claim holds at the
CERTIFY, and it doesn’t say the claim holds at the end of the run. A CERTIFY that
rechecked the version would give a different guarantee. That’s a possible extension,
and the historical theorem doesn’t need it.
352   15 A smallest example machine


              15.7 What a passing check means
              Provenance says a CHECK happened. It doesn’t yet say the CHECK was right, and
              that’s a separate question with a separate proof. A machine could have a perfectly
              ordered chain of check, commit, certify, all standing on a checker that says yes to
              everything. So what does a fact in the table actually tell you about the counter?


              Theorem 15.13 (Checker soundness). Let s0 be clean and t any trace, and let k
              be the core of run(t, s0 ). For every fact ( p, c, v) in k’s table with v = ver(k, c), the
              property holds of the counter’s current value: holds( p, val(k, c)). In particular, if
              COMMIT p c would pass at k, then holds( p, val(k, c)).

              Proof. Carry one sentence through every instruction: every fact in the table has a
              version no higher than its counter’s, and if its version equals its counter’s, its property
              holds of its counter’s value. A clean start has an empty table, so the sentence holds
              there. A passing CHECK adds a fact at the current version, and the checker said
              yes, so by Lemma 15.2 the property holds. A write raises one counter’s version, so
              every old fact about that counter falls strictly behind and the second half no longer
              applies to it. Nothing else changes a value or a version. The sentence holds after
              every instruction, so it holds at the end. The part about COMMIT is the case where
              the claim is in the table at the current version.
                  So, on a run from a clean start, a live fact means exactly that one of three
              arithmetic properties holds of one counter’s current value. It doesn’t mean “the
              program is correct,” and it doesn’t mean “the number is interesting”; it means the
              property holds of the value, now. That’s all “checked” means on this machine, and
              it’s enough to be true. Three events stay separate here. The property holding of the
              value is one. A CHECK passing is another: a CHECK of a property that holds still
              doesn’t pass when the table is full or the trap is already up. A certification is a third,
              and it needs a COMMIT and a CERTIFY after the CHECK. So a CHECK that didn’t
              pass says its property is false only when the trap was down and the table had room
              before it.
                  So who checked the checker? Nothing on the record did. From a clean start, the
              record carries the run’s half of the story: a CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same
              claim about the same edition, then a CERTIFY. The other half, that the checker says
              yes exactly when the property holds, isn’t in any run. It’s Lemma 15.2, a proof
              about the little program the step calls, priced by nothing on the ledger. So a claim
              established here stands on two legs: a fact about this run, carried by the record, and
              a fact about the checker, carried by a proof that whoever reads the record has to
              accept. That’s the Münchhausen trilemma from Section 14 taking its third horn on
                                                                  15.7 What a passing check means   353


purpose: the chain of reasons stops at a proof, named and on the page, where you
can decide whether you’d have stopped there too. And the entitlement it gives is the
reader’s. The machine doesn’t know anything. It keeps the order.
    The question in that paragraph is older than any checker, and its most famous
wording isn’t about what you’d guess. “Who will guard the guardians?” gets
quoted about governments and police and the people checking mathematical proofs.
Where’s it from? Plato’s Republic has the worry, sort of: in Book III (at 403e),
Glaucon, Plato’s older brother and one of the people Socrates is talking with, says
it would be absurd for a guardian to need a guardian, which is close in words and
opposite in mood, a man calling the question silly. The Latin, quis custodiet ipsos
custodes, is from the Roman satirist Juvenal’s sixth satire, and it’s a joke about a
husband. His friends tell him to bolt his wife in and set guards on her; the line
asks who’ll watch the guards, since she’ll start with them. And it gets better. In
1899 an Oxford undergraduate, E. O. Winstedt, found extra lines of that satire in
a medieval manuscript in the Bodleian Library, lines the other copies lack, partly
overlapping the familiar ones, and the famous question sits in that tangle. Scholars
have argued ever since about whether those lines are Juvenal’s at all. So the most
quoted sentence about trusting the checker comes with a doubtful source of its own.
Does that change anything here? It doesn’t. The answer used here is simple: you
never get rid of the last guard, you make the last guard small enough to watch
yourself. Lemma 15.2 is one line per property. Euclid had the instinct: five postulates
you can hold in your head, and everything else meant to follow from them.
    That split, a fixed checker proved sound from outside and a process that only
gets to act when the checker says yes, has a name in the writing on self-improving
programs. The AI researcher Jürgen Schmidhuber, at the IDSIA lab in Lugano,
described a Gödel machine (2003) that rewrites its own code only after its built-in
proof searcher has proved the rewrite useful, and Benja Fallenstein and Nate Soares
(2015), researchers at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, survey
agents that reason about their successors through formal proofs a fixed checker
accepts. Same architecture, aimed at a different question: they want to know when
a machine may trust a smarter version of itself, and this machine only wants to
know whether a flag was earned. Keeping the checker’s proof outside the machine
is my design choice. The nearest theorem, in Section 13, is narrower: no procedure
whose flip the substrate can represent decides, for every program, a property that
depends only on behaviour and holds of one program and fails of another. It doesn’t
say a machine can’t check a proof about a checker, or verify a restricted part of itself.
    Soundness rules out a lying checker. It doesn’t rule out a pointless question:
at least 0 has a perfectly sound checker and an empty no pile, as the worked run
showed.
354   15 A smallest example machine


                 Program checking has a theory of its own, and its founding paper asks for a
              checker that could have said no. The computer scientists Manuel Blum and Sampath
              Kannan (1989; journal version 1995) defined a checker for a computational problem:
              given a program and an input, it may run the program as it likes, and it must say
              “correct” with high probability when the program is right everywhere and “buggy”
              with high probability when its answer on that input is wrong. A checker that always
              says “correct” isn’t one. Here the checker is fixed, deterministic and proved sound
              once, and the part of their demand that survives is the fourth clause of certified
              Thiele-complete (Definition 15.7 below): some claim whose check can fail.


              15.8 Nothing gets forged
              The proof of Theorem 15.10 leaned on an invariant I promised to show you, and this
              subsection shows it. The fear it answers: could some clever sequence of instructions
              get a fact into the table without a CHECK writing it? Could a DEC with a funny
              jump target do it, or a COMMIT after a trap, or something I didn’t think of? I answer
              it one instruction at a time, which is the only way I trust myself to answer it.

              Definition 15.6 (Earned fact; no forgery). After a trace t from s0 , a fact f = ( p, c, v)
              is earned when t is pre, then CHECK p c, then mid, where the CHECK passes at the
              core reached by pre, f is exactly the claim p of c at that core, and, if f is live at the
              end (v equals c’s version after t), mid leaves c untouched. The trace has no forgery
              when every fact in the table after it is earned.



              Theorem 15.14 (No forging). For every core k, instruction i and fact f in the table
              after executing i at k: either f was already in k’s table, or i is CHECK of f ’s property
              and counter, it passes at k, and f is the claim it writes. Consequently, if a trace has
              no forgery, so does that trace followed by any one instruction; and from every clean
              start, every trace has no forgery.

              Proof. Inspect who can write to the table. INC and DEC change counters, versions
              and the line; they leave the table alone. HALT leaves it alone. COMMIT reads it and
              may write the channel, but cannot write the table. CERTIFY reads the channel and
              cannot write the table either. CHECK is the only remaining instruction. On failure it
              adds nothing; on success it adds exactly the property, counter and present edition it
              just checked. A trapped instruction changes no core field. That exhausts the ways a
              fact could appear after one instruction.
                 Now suppose the table’s old entries already have their promised histories. A new
              entry gets its history from the passing CHECK just performed. For an old entry, that
                                                                        15.8 Nothing gets forged   355


earlier CHECK still happened. If the entry is live after the new instruction, its saved
edition equals the counter’s edition now. The counter’s edition never goes down.
It therefore could not have risen away from the saved edition and then returned.
In particular, it was already live before this instruction and the instruction did not
change the edition or the value. Its untouched stretch extends by this one step. If the
entry is stale, only its earlier passing CHECK is required, and that history remains.
    At a clean start there are no entries to forge. The argument preserves that promise
after the first instruction, after the next, and after each further instruction in any
finite trace.
   The closest earlier result is in capability hardware, and it’s much bigger. The
computer scientists Jack Dennis and Earl Van Horn, at MIT, introduced capabilities in
1966: tokens a process has to hold to touch an object, which it can pass on and can’t
forge. CHERI, a capability extension of real instruction sets built at the University
of Cambridge and SRI International, rests on that idea, and in 2020 Kyndylan
Nienhuis and twelve coauthors proved, for the whole CHERI-MIPS instruction set,
that arbitrary code given some capabilities can’t increase them as it runs (up to any
change of protection domain). Their result says nothing gets forged across a full
instruction set. Theorem 15.14 is the same shape, one instruction at a time, for six
instruction kinds and a table of checked facts.

The actual counter covers every added fact
Put the table beside the bill. Every passing CHECK writes one more entry and adds
one to the ledger. A failed CHECK writes no entry. COMMIT and CERTIFY can add
to the bill without adding a table entry. Walk down the run one instruction at a time:
the table can never grow faster than the bill.


Theorem 15.15 (The native bill bounds the table). For every clean run, whether
driven by a finite instruction word or by the stored-program step for a finite number
of ticks,
                                   len(facts) ≤ µ.

More generally, table growth is exactly the number of passing CHECKs, and is at
most the increase in the ledger from any starting state.

Proof. A passing CHECK adds one entry and one unit to the bill. A false CHECK,
a full-table CHECK or a trapped CHECK adds no entry but still adds one unit.
COMMIT and CERTIFY add one unit and no entry. INC, DEC and HALT add neither.
No instruction removes an entry.
356   15 A smallest example machine


                  Place a mark beside each passing CHECK in the run. The final table has exactly
              one more entry for every mark. Each mark also accounts for one unit on the bill;
              unmarked instructions can add further units, never take them away. So table growth
              is exactly the number of marks and at most the ledger’s increase. This works from
              any starting state.
                  At a clean start the table is empty. The initial ledger is a nonnegative whole
              number, so the table length is at most the final ledger. At the specified loaded starts
              the ledger begins at zero as well. For a stored program, every running tick executes
              one of the six instructions just counted, and every stopped tick leaves both table and
              bill alone. The same count therefore applies to any finite number of ticks.
                  One passing CHECK from a clean start gives one entry and a bill of one. Repeat
              a passing check and its duplicate entry counts as another line in the table. The
              tally follows what was written there. COMMIT and CERTIFY can then make the bill
              larger while the number of lines stays put.


              15.9 A full table traps
              The table has room for sixteen facts and evicts none of them, so there are two halves
              to prove: nothing ever leaves, and nothing ever overflows.


              Theorem 15.16 (Bounded table, no eviction). Every instruction keeps every fact
              already in the table. If the table holds 16 or more facts, CHECK p c puts the trap
              up and leaves the table as it was. If the table holds at most 16 facts, it still holds at
              most 16 after any instruction.

              Proof. With a raised trap no instruction changes the table. With the trap down, only
              CHECK can change it, and a successful CHECK adds one fact without removing an
              entry. Success requires a previous length strictly below 16, so the new length is at
              most 16. At length 16 or greater that branch is unavailable: CHECK raises the trap
              and preserves the table. Every other instruction preserves it as well.
                  Why trap? Why not make room? Because “making room” means deciding which
              fact dies, and a fact that can die is a fact whose absence you have to explain later.
              A table that only grows keeps every checked fact available to read back, and the
              shared-memory result above leans on exactly that, since its oldest fact can never
              move. Provenance doesn’t: a table that dropped its oldest fact to make room would
              still hold only facts a CHECK wrote. What the choice gives up is real, though, and
              it’s in the subsection near the end of this chapter on what the machine doesn’t do.
                                                            15.10 The window can’t see the record   357


15.10 The window can’t see the record
Section 7 was about windows: a view of a state that shows some of it, and the
theorem that a window which shows the same before-and-after pair for a raise and
a non-raise cannot price both exactly (Observation 7.2). The two runs below are the
smallest pair I could build where the window is Minsky’s view of the machine (line
number and the two counters) and the record is everything else.
    Run two traces from start(0, 0). The earned run is CHECK is zero A; COMMIT
is zero A; CERTIFY. The idle run is DEC A 0, three times. In the idle run, A is 0
every time, so each DEC just goes to the next line and writes nothing. Both runs
end on line 4, with A = 0 and B = 0, both versions 0. Through the window they’re
identical. One of them has paid 3, holds a fact, could commit again, and has its flag
up. The other has paid nothing, holds nothing, can’t commit, and its flag is down.
They’re like two photographs that show the same picture and are of different people.


Theorem 15.17 (Same window, different record). The earned run and the idle run
from start(0, 0) end at cores with the same window and the same versions of A and
B, and with different ledgers, different flags, different tables, and different answers
to “would COMMIT is zero A pass.”

Proof. In the earned run, CHECK adds (Zero, A, 0), COMMIT puts that fact in the
channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. The ledger is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. No counter
is written. In the idle run each DEC sees zero, so it advances the line without
writing a counter or raising a version. Its three costs are zero and it adds no fact or
commitment. So both final windows are (4, 0, 0) with versions (0, 0). The earned
table contains the current zero claim and the idle table is empty, giving the stated
difference in whether another COMMIT would pass, as well as in the ledger and
flag.



Theorem 15.18 (No window oracle). There is no function g from windows to whole
numbers with g(window) = µ at the end of every trace from start(0, 0). Likewise
there is no function from windows to yes or no that gives the flag at the end of every
such trace, and none that gives whether COMMIT is zero A would pass.

Proof. Such a g would have to give both 3 and 0 on the one window the two runs
of Theorem 15.17 share. The same for the flag and the commit right.
  The record lives off the window, and that’s Section 7’s shape, made of pebbles.
Anybody who only watches the counters and the line number, which is everything
358   15 A smallest example machine


              Minsky’s machine is, can’t tell you what was paid, what was committed, or whether
              the flag is up, and the reason isn’t that they looked carelessly; it’s that none of it is
              there to see.
                 Two things the same in everything you look at and still two things: philosophy
              has an old fight about exactly that, and it’s worth a detour, because it tells you which
              side of the fight these theorems stand on. Leibniz said that for real things it can’t
              happen. There are no two individuals indiscernible from each other, he wrote in
              1716 to Samuel Clarke, the English philosopher and theologian who was taking
              Newton’s side against him in an exchange of letters, and he told a story to go with it.
              A clever gentleman of his acquaintance, talking with him in front of the Electress
              Sophia of Hanover, Leibniz’s friend and patron, in the garden at Herrenhausen she
              had helped lay out, thought he could find two leaves perfectly alike. She dared him
              to. He “ran all over the Garden a long time” looking, and it was “to no purpose.”
              You can run his search tonight with a handful of anything, leaves or coins or grains
              of rice: look hard enough and every pair differs somewhere. Then in 1952 Max
              Black, a Russian-born philosopher teaching at Cornell, pushed back with a universe
              you can’t build at the table. Nothing in it but two iron spheres, the same size, the
              same colour, the same everything, some distance apart. Name a difference between
              them. There isn’t one, and there are still two of them. People have argued about
              Black’s spheres ever since, and I’m not going to settle it.
                 I don’t have to, because Leibniz’s claim is about every property a thing has. The
              theorems above are about three: the line and the two counters. The two runs aren’t
              indiscernible in his sense at all: one has a fact in its table and its flag up, and the
              other doesn’t. They’re indiscernible to a window, which is a much cheaper thing,
              and it’s the thing that matters for a machine, because an observer of a machine only
              ever gets a window. Leibniz’s gentleman would always find his difference if he could
              look at everything. It doesn’t help him if all he’s allowed to look at is three things
              about each leaf.
                 There’s a horse in this, too, if you squint. In Germany in the early 1900s a
              mathematics teacher named Wilhelm von Osten showed off a horse called Clever
              Hans, who answered arithmetic questions by tapping a hoof, and got them right, in
              front of crowds. Hans gave the same answers out as a horse that could count, and
              that’s the idle run’s matching window. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst stopped
              looking at the answers and started changing the conditions, and published what he
              found in 1907. Put blinders on Hans, or have him asked by someone who didn’t
              know the answer, and the arithmetic fell apart. Hans was reading the questioner:
              tiny, unintended movements of the head and body as the hoof reached the right
              number. That’s the probe. Pfungst didn’t argue with the answers. He asked a
              question the answers couldn’t fake, one that needed the real thing to be there, the
              way a COMMIT needs a checked fact to be in the table: run COMMIT is zero A after
                                                             15.10 The window can’t see the record   359


each of the two runs, and one passes and the other traps (Theorem 15.17). And
the part of the story I like best: nobody was lying. Von Osten was never persuaded
by Pfungst and kept showing his horse. A matching window doesn’t need a cheat
behind it, which is why you want a probe. An accusation is the wrong tool for it.

The rebar example, on the actual counters
Put a one in counter A, leave B at zero, and give the machine these four instructions:

          CHECK ( A ≥ 1);      COMMIT ( A ≥ 1);       CERTIFY;     DEC A 5.
The check passes. The claim gets committed and certified. Then DEC takes the one
away. Look at the counters now: zero and zero. The value that passed the check has
gone.
   Start again with both counters zero and give the same instructions. This time
the first check fails and the machine traps. The zero stays where it was. Look at the
counters at the end: zero and zero again. One run has its certificate up; the other
has it down.


Theorem 15.19 (Same final counters and bill, different certification). For those
two clean starts and that word, both final counter pairs are (0, 0) and both ledgers
are 3. The first certificate is true and the second false. No function of just the final
counter pair can recover which of those starts passed the check.

Proof. For the start A = 1, B = 0, CHECK sees 1 ≥ 1, writes the edition-zero fact,
advances the line from 1 to 2 and makes the ledger 1. COMMIT finds that live fact,
puts it in the channel, advances to line 3 and makes the ledger 2. CERTIFY sees the
occupied channel, raises the flag, advances to line 4 and makes the ledger 3. DEC
sees a positive A, changes it to zero, advances to line 5 and raises A’s version from
0 to 1. Its price is zero. The final counters are (0, 0) and the flag is up.
    For the start A = 0, B = 0, the first CHECK fails. It sets the trap, leaves the
line at 1, leaves the table empty and charges one. The external word still supplies
COMMIT and CERTIFY: on a trapped state they change no core field and cannot
raise the flag, but each adds its unit to the ledger. DEC then changes nothing and
charges zero. The final counters are again (0, 0), both versions stay zero and the
flag is down. Both ledgers are 3. A function of the common counter pair would have
to return both flag values, which is impossible.
   The counters show the same surface. The record keeps the difference. Open the
rest of the box and the trap, version and line number tell different parts of the story
too: one run reached DEC, while the other stopped at the check.
360   15 A smallest example machine


                 Ask the successful run to CHECK A ≥ 1 once more. It fails; A is zero now. The
              old certificate stays up because the earlier certification still happened. That receipt
              keeps its past even while the workspace goes on to something else.

              One clipboard, 65,535 different publication histories
              Open the whole native box this time. Read the counters, versions, table, channel,
              line number, trap, ledger and lamp. I can make all of them agree while the files of
              published claims differ in 65,535 ways.
                 Start clean at A = 16, B = 0. CHECK the sixteen claims A ≥ 0, . . . , A ≥ 15.
              Every one passes on edition zero. The clipboard now has sixteen entries. The line
              number is 17, the bill is 16, and the certificate is still down. I can choose which of
              those checked claims to publish.
                 Visit the claims in order. At each one, choose between these blocks:
                             publish it:           COMMIT claim; CERTIFY,
                             leave it unpublished: COMMIT claim; COMMIT claim.
              Count the steps in either block: two. Count the charge: two. Look at the channel
              when it finishes: the same claim. The counters and table stayed put. Once one
              publication has raised the lamp, that lamp stays up whichever later blocks you
              choose. The predicates overlap logically; it is the choice to publish each checked
              claim that is independent.


              Theorem 15.20 (The exact native publication-history fibre). In the extension re-
              taining the set of published claim/edition facts, exactly 65,535 different nonempty
              sets can lie above one reachable native endpoint. This is the maximum over clean
              native runs with cert true. Sixteen additional fixed binary bits suffice to encode the
              set relative to the native table, and fifteen do not suffice in the worst case.

              Proof. First prepare the table. After the first j checks, for 0 ≤ j ≤ 16, its entries are
              exactly A ≥ 0, . . . , A ≥ j − 1, in that order and all on edition zero. The line is 1 + j,
              the ledger is j, the counters and versions are unchanged, the trap is down and the
              flag is down. This holds at j = 0. If j < 16, there is still room and 16 ≥ j, so the
              next CHECK appends precisely the next fact, advances one line and charges one.
              That proves the preparation claim through j = 16.
                 Now process the sixteen facts in order. Each COMMIT finds its fact in the
              unchanged table at the current edition. Either block ends with that fact in the
              channel, advances two lines and charges two. The publishing block additionally
              raises the flag and inserts that fact into the archive; the other block changes neither.
              Inducting on the number j of blocks gives line 17 + 2j, ledger 16 + 2j, and exactly
                                                                15.10 The window can’t see the record   361


the chosen subset of the first j facts in the archive. The flag is up if and only if at least
one publishing block has occurred. None of the blocks changes counters, versions,
table order or trap. At j = 16 every nonempty choice therefore has the same native
endpoint: A = 16, B = 0, versions zero, line 49, ledger 48, trap down, flag up, and
channel ( A ≥ 15, A, 0). Its archive is precisely its chosen subset. There are two
independent choices at each of sixteen positions, hence 216 subsets; excluding the
empty one leaves 65,535 different archives above that endpoint.
    For the upper bound, keep two invariants together: every published fact is in
the table, and every occupied channel names a fact in the table. Both hold at a
clean start. CHECK only appends to the table. A successful COMMIT selects an entry
already there. CERTIFY publishes only its occupied channel. Writes can make a fact
stale or clear a channel, but they never remove table entries; failed and trapped
instructions do not introduce a new channel fact or publication. Thus both invariants
survive every instruction, including later writes. Every final archive is a subset of
the final table.
    If that table has d distinct entries, it has at most 2d − 1 nonempty subsets. The
table has at most sixteen entries, so d ≤ 16 and 2d − 1 ≤ 65,535. An explicit code
puts beside each table entry one bit saying whether it belongs to the archive, and
pads with zeros to sixteen positions. Duplicate entries receive matching bits. Read
back the entries with bit one and you recover the set. Equal codes therefore give
equal archives, and an archive above a flag-up state uses a nonzero code. Finally,
fifteen fixed bits have only 215 = 32,768 values, fewer than the exhibited 65,535
archives; sixteen bits have 65,536 values and the code just given suffices.
    Put sixteen checkboxes beside the clipboard’s sixteen lines. A tick says that line’s
claim was published at least once. The table already names the claims and editions;
the extra marks say which ones made it into the publication file. The lamp gives
the same yes for every nonempty selection. Open the checkboxes and all 65,535
selections come apart. Each tick answers whether that claim was published at least
once. Order and repeated publications leave these answers unchanged.
    In Chapter 14 the camera showed the working value. Here I let it see the entire
native machine and still found histories it could not recover. The map here forgets
the added publication file; its fibre contains those different files above one native
endpoint.
    The sixteen-line clipboard eventually fills. Even sixteen repeated checks of one
fact fill it, and the next CHECK traps. The unlimited-edition machine has a larger
obligation: keep accepting independent publication choices across every finite
number of editions and keep them recoverable at the same working picture. Its fibre
has to keep growing. That is the count from Chapter 14, with its own camera and
its own task.
362   15 A smallest example machine


              15.11 The exact price is three
              Section 2 said a raised flag costs at least one. On this machine that’s true and too
              modest. A raised flag needs a CERTIFY, a CERTIFY needs a COMMIT, a COMMIT
              needs a CHECK, and each of those is its own instruction costing one. So a raised
              flag costs at least three. One of what: three units of µ, one per paid act, each one
              the least price a record-layer merge allows. And three is the number of links in the
              chain, not a guess that happens to hold.
              Observation 15.21 (The minimum price of a certificate). If s0 is clean and
              cert(run(t, s0 )) is up, then cost(t) ≥ 3 and µ(run(t, s0 )) ≥ µ(s0 ) + 3. For programs:
              if the flag is up after n program steps from start( a, b), then µ ≥ 3 there.
              Proof. Theorem 15.11 finds a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different
              places in t, each costing 1, and every other instruction costs at least 0. The ledger
              statement is Theorem 15.6. A program run is the run of the instructions it actually
              executes, so the program form follows.
                  The three is three independent units, one for each part of a clean start. A flag
              that is down buys the first: a run that raises it costs at least one. An empty channel
              buys the second: with the flag down and the channel empty, a run that raises the
              flag costs at least two. An empty table buys the third, and that is the theorem above.
              Leave out any one part and its floor fails, and a cheaper certificate is there: with the
              flag already up it costs 0, with a commitment already in the channel 1, and with
              a live fact already in the table 2. Every run from a state that ends with the flag
              up costs at least three exactly when the flag is down and one of two things holds:
              the trap is up, or the channel is empty and every fact in the table is about an older
              version of its counter. And three is paid exactly from every clean start whose trap is
              down.


              Theorem 15.22 (Three is tight). For all whole numbers a and b, run the program
              CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero A; CERTIFY for 4 program steps from start( a, b).
              If a = 0, it ends with the flag up and µ = 3 exactly. If a ̸= 0, it ends with the flag
              down and the trap up, and for every n, n program steps from start( a, b) leave the
              flag down.

              Proof. If a = 0, the checker for Zero says yes at 0, so the first instruction adds
              (Zero, A, 0) to the empty table and charges 1. No counter changes, so the second
              instruction finds that same fact, puts it in the channel and charges 1. The third finds
              the channel occupied, raises the flag and charges 1. The line is now 4, beyond the
              three-instruction program, and the fourth program step adds no charge. The final
              ledger is exactly 3. If a ̸= 0, the checker says no, so the first instruction sets the trap
                                                                 15.12 What it takes to be certified   363


and leaves the flag down. A program run takes no step once the trap is up, so every
later program step leaves the state, flag included, exactly where it is.
   Theorem 15.22 is the worked run from early in this chapter, now holding from
every start.
   The version whose check can’t fail, CHECK at least 0 A; COMMIT at least 0 A;
CERTIFY, certifies from every start for exactly 3. So the floor of three is reachable
from every loaded start, and that’s the machine declining to police trivial checks.
On that program the check distinguishes no inputs.
   The floor is 3, and a run whose check could have failed pays exactly 3, so 3 is the
price. The bound has no slack in it.
   Don’t mistake that 3 for a measure of how hard a claim is to certify. It’s the
same 3 for every claim, easy or hard, because only the three acts that make a
claim are priced and the counters work out whatever the check needs at no charge
on the ledger. A cost of certifying that grows with the claim would have to price
the checking itself, and that’s a different question with its own literature. Four
theoretical computer scientists, Guy Blanc, Caleb Koch, Jane Lange and Li-Yang
Tan (2022), studied one version of it under the name the query complexity of
certification: how many questions an algorithm has to ask a black-box function to
hand back a small certificate for its answer. Their count moves with the function.
Mine doesn’t move at all.
   And that’s every piece of the machine, standing on six instruction kinds: a base
that computes everything two counters can, a ledger that’s exact, a toll the universal
floor applies to, a flag that’s a latch of the base, a window that can’t see the record,
and, from a clean start, a commitment that can’t happen unless a check of the same
claim, on the same edition, came first and was right.


15.12 What it takes to be certified

Section 10.8 set the bar worth meeting, Thiele-complete, and it says nothing about
what the record is about. A clock fails it, and so does a machine whose record never
goes up. The small machine clears it (Theorems 15.31 and 15.23(2) below), and it
does more: from a clean start, its flag goes up only on top of a check of a claim, by a
checker proved to mean what the claim says, then a commitment to the same claim
with nothing changed underneath, then a certificate. A Thiele-complete machine
can raise its record with one mark that goes up from any state at all, a receipt for
nothing (Section 14). A certified one can’t. The second definition is the first one
