              the one pebble in A. They are at the same line with the same B, and they stop at
              the same moment if they stop at all, though A ≥ m holds of one start and not the
              other. (2) Run the ladder from A = a. Each of the first min( a, m) moves takes a
              pebble off A and jumps two lines on. If a ≥ m that’s all m moves, ending on line
              2m + 1. If a < m, the run reaches line 2a + 1 after a moves and from there goes on
              one line per move (a DEC falling through, then an INC), so after m moves it’s on
              line a + m + 1, below 2m + 1. It’s all DEC and INC, so it costs 0. (3) is the price
              table: CHECK (A ≥ m) passes exactly when A ≥ m, a failing CHECK traps and the
              flag stays down, and the three moves cost three. (4) is the same price table with one
              instruction: a passing CHECK goes on to line 2 and a failing one traps and leaves
              the line at 1. (5) is arithmetic on (1) to (4).
                  Try m = 3 with A = 2. The ladder takes a pebble on line 1 and jumps to line
              3, takes the second and jumps to line 5, then finds A empty and falls through to
              line 6, the INC: after three moves it sits on line 6, not 7. With A = 3 the third DEC
              succeeds and the run is on line 7. Two moves in, both runs are on line 5 with B
              untouched, which is (1).
                  So the paid route to a certificate wins when 3 + 3λ < m, and the paid route to a
              bare answer wins when 1 + λ < m. The exchange rate is sharper than a comparison
                                                               15.15 Reading the instruction rules   389


of two programs I happened to write would give: the unpaid side is a floor under
every program of INC and DEC there is, so no choice of program comes into it, and
the paid side doesn’t move with m at all. The bound has limits. It’s for programs that
make no record move, INC and DEC with HALT or falling off the end as stopping.
It doesn’t cover every certified Thiele-complete machine, because the definition
doesn’t forbid a base move that changes a counter by more than one pebble, and
such a machine is a different machine, one the bound doesn’t speak for. And the
two routes put their answers in different places, the unpaid one in the line number
and the paid one in the flag; this compares two ways to answer one question, not
two certifications. Zero cost isn’t zero heat, either: every move on either route is an
event, and the moves are what λ prices.


15.15 Reading the instruction rules

The instruction rules settle some concrete questions about running this machine.
Follow them through a check, a zero decrement and a trapped trace.
• The check price is flat. CHECK costs 1 whether it’s asking “is this 0” or “is
  this at least a billion.” The property language is fixed and each property is one
  evaluation, so “pays for its work” here means that flat price, the same however
  hard the question was. A machine that charged by the difficulty of the check
  would be a different machine, and I haven’t built it.
• DEC on zero isn’t a write. It doesn’t change the counter, so it doesn’t change
  the version. That’s the right call for versions (nothing changed), but it means
  DEC on zero is a way to move the line number that adds nothing to the ledger
  and leaves no trace in the record. The idle run in the subsection on the window,
  earlier in this chapter, uses exactly that.
• After a trap, a trace still pays. On programs, a trap stops the run. On arbitrary
  traces, instructions after a trap are each charged their cost and none of them
  changes the core. That isn’t a separate choice. A price belongs to the instruction,
  the same from every state (Definition 2.1), so a CERTIFY on a trapped machine
  costs what every CERTIFY costs, and clause (c) of Definition 15.7 has the ledger
  add it; Theorem 15.6 has no exceptions for that reason. The choice is one level
  up, in putting the price on the instruction and not on the instruction at a state,
  and what it brings with it is that a trapped machine is still charged for instructions
  that change nothing.
• “Checked” means what the property language can say. On this machine that’s
  is zero, is even and is at least n, and a live fact means one of those holds of one
  counter’s current value. It doesn’t mean the program is correct, or that anything
  follows from the property, or that the property was worth checking. So can a
390   15 A smallest example machine


                 proved machine of this kind check “sorted,” the claim the sorter-and-copier table
                 of Section 14 runs on? It can, through an encoding. A copy of this machine,
                 instruction for instruction, with its property language left open, has provenance,
                 checker soundness, no forging and the floor of three proved once for every
                 property language that comes with an exact equality test and a checker proved
                 equal to its meaning. Give it “the list this counter encodes is sorted” as a property
                 and it certifies a sorted list for three and refuses an unsorted one forever. The
                 instruction rules are those already given, with the chosen property language in
                 place of the three original properties. For sorted lists, decode 0 as the empty
                 list and 2h (2t + 1) as the list with head h and tail decoded from t, the list code
                 of Theorem 15.31. Every positive code has t smaller than itself, so decoding
                 terminates. The checker returns yes on an empty list or singleton, and on a, b, . . .
                 exactly when a ≤ b and it returns yes on b, . . .. Induction on the list proves
                 that this is exactly adjacent nondecreasing order. The provenance proof uses
                 only equality of properties, and soundness only that the checker’s yes means the
                 property holds, so the same instruction-by-instruction argument applies. What
                 makes that a check of the list is the proof that the checker means sortedness.
                 Without that proof, “sorted” would be a number some unconstrained code wrote
                 into a counter, and the record would be honest about the counter and silent
                 about the list.
               • The certificate is historical. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, the counter
                 can change, and the flag still goes up. The flag says a claim was checked and
                 committed about an edition. It says nothing about whether the claim is still true.
               • One latch, and a channel that moves on. The flag records that an earned chain
                 happened, once. After that it stays up, and later CERTIFYs change nothing. The
                 channel is the part that names a fact: with the flag up from a clean start, it names
                 a fact that some earlier passing COMMIT committed. But a later commitment
                 replaces it, so at the end it names the last earned commitment, which needn’t
                 be the one the flag rose on. Two runs from start(0, 0) show it, worked from
                 the instruction table. First run: CHECK is zero A; CHECK is zero B; COMMIT
                 is zero A; CERTIFY; COMMIT is zero B. Second run: the same five instructions
                 with the last two swapped, so COMMIT is zero B comes before CERTIFY. Both
                 end in the same state: both counters 0 at version 0, both facts in the table, the
                 channel holding (zero, B, 0), the trap down, a ledger of five and the flag up. In
                 the first run the flag rose at step four, on the commitment about A. In the second
                 it rose at step five, on the commitment about B. So the flag is an ever-certified
                 latch: it says an earned chain happened at some step, and the end state doesn’t
                 say which claim or which step. A receipt naming the claim the flag first rose
                 on would need that claim kept where nothing can overwrite it; a receipt with
                                                              15.15 Reading the instruction rules   391


  a time on it would also need the step number kept; and several certifications
  that each last would need a record richer than one flag. The publication file
  constructed earlier in this chapter keeps the set of claims certified at least once.
  That extension shows exactly what the native state left out. It still does not record
  which certification came first or at what step; those questions would need their
  own retained answers.
• Sixteen checks per run, ever. Facts never leave and the table holds sixteen, so a
  run gets at most sixteen passing CHECKs in its whole life, and the seventeenth
  traps. A certificate needs only one, so this costs nothing for the theorems, but
  it’s a hard wall for any program that wants to keep checking forever, and it’s this
  machine’s small version of “you can’t keep all of it” from Section 14. A CHECK
  that repeats a claim already in the table, same property, same counter, same
  edition, passes again and takes another entry. So the wall is sixteen passing
  CHECKs, and sixteen different claims is a different count. Removing duplicates,
  evicting old facts or collecting dead ones would each be a different design, and
  each would need its own invariants proved.
• The clean start matters. Provenance, soundness, no forging and the price of
  three are all stated from a clean start. Hand the machine a table pre-loaded with
  facts nobody checked, and of course none of that follows. The theorems are about
  what the machine produces. What you smuggle in at the door is outside them.
  The door is narrower than clean for some of them: a commitment’s provenance
  and checker soundness use only the table, and hold from any start whose table
  holds nothing but facts about older editions; the empty channel and the lowered
  flag come in for the flag’s provenance and the price of three. Spell the door out
  once: the theorems cover any list of instructions anybody can issue, from a clean
  start, on a step that runs as written, with nothing else writing to the machine.
  They say nothing about whoever sets or restores the start, about a reset, about a
  device that misbehaves, or about whoever carries the flag’s value to you.
• The universal programs have stated guests. U (Appendix D.1) runs every
  one of this machine’s programs from every clean start start( x, y), with halting,
  answers, flag and ledger matched (the flag over the whole run, the ledger at
  matching points). UP (Appendix D.2) runs every computably presented Thiele
  machine, with its reading decided by a program, its record carried as a latch, and
  its ledger matched to within a surcharge of at most two when its reading starts
  at no, and of three when it starts at yes. When the guest certifies with a ledger
  below three, no program on that host, run from a clean start, matches its ledger
  exactly. A machine outside that class, with a reading no program decides, isn’t
  covered by either. The simpler host with the built-in guest step (Appendix D.3)
392   15 A smallest example machine


                  pays one per guest step whatever the step was, so its ledger is at least the guest’s
                  and usually more; U’s is exact, and UP ’s is exact up to the surcharge.
               • Encoding and running time. The universality result takes its inputs already
                 packed into the counters. Getting there from an arbitrary Turing machine goes
                 through Minsky’s exponential packing (Appendix K), and that packing is what
                 it takes to reach the two-counter base this way. Carrying the record to another
                 base has its own conditions, in Appendix E, and anyone who wanted this to run
                 fast would have to start the analysis over.
               • The step charges for the act, not for what the claim is worth. CHECK at least
                 0 passes on every value, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the flag for
                 three from any fresh loaded start (the note after Theorem 15.22), and that’s by
                 design. The step checks order, aboutness and an honest checker. What a claim is
                 worth is the entitlement count of Section 8, a number computed over the rivals a
                 run narrows. A step sees one state, so it cannot compute that count. A check that
                 cannot fail narrows nothing and costs three, and the book keeps both numbers,
                 apart.
               • The toll on this machine comes from the record layer, with no finiteness
                 premise on the whole machine. Section 3’s counting of states forces a toll on
                 a finite machine that prices every merge. This machine is neither. Its counters
                 have no ceiling, as a universal base has to have, and its editions can’t have one
                 either (the version rule says why), so it’s infinite. And, by design, its unpriced
                 instructions merge states: take a core at line ℓ with c at 1 and version w, and a
                 core at line j − 1 with c at 0 and version w + 1, everything else alike, and DEC c
                 j sends both to line j with c at 0 and version w + 1, at a price of zero. A price
                 of zero doesn’t mean the hardware pays nothing. Every one of those moves is
                 an event, and whatever the hardware pays for it, heat for happening and, under
                 Landauer’s premise, a floor for each merge of states that were really possible,
                 is off the ledger. The ledger leaves those merges out on purpose. It counts the
                 keeping in the record, not what computing spends. Computing doesn’t have to
                 merge; a reversible base computes by paying in fresh states. On this machine
                 full merge pricing would charge DEC, an ordinary step, and clause (c) asks for
                 computing to cost nothing. Pricing the dissipation of happening would be worse.
                 Every step that changes something on a real device dissipates, so that ledger
                 charges every step, and that’s the clock of Observation 15.27: its total says how
                 long it ran and nothing about what it kept. So merge pricing on this machine
                 applies to the record layer only: a move that sends two different states with the
                 same line and counters to one state costs at least one. This machine’s own prices
                 meet it. The endless counters would allow a raise that merges nothing, and the
                 flag doesn’t take it: CERTIFY lands a state with the flag down and the same state
                                                               15.16 What this chapter adds up to   393


   with the flag up on one state, a merge of exactly that kind, in plain view. So every
   price list that meets the premise charges the flag-raising step at least one, with no
   finiteness premise, and through the trap it charges every CHECK and COMMIT at
   least one too, so a certificate from a clean start costs at least three on every such
   list (Theorem 3.19). That’s a price I assume for losing distinctions in the record,
   and assuming it is all it is. Turning it into heat takes the physical conditions of
   Section 3; a unit on a ledger isn’t heat on its own. The exact price of one, the
   least the premise allows on each of the three acts, is still a design choice.


15.16 What this chapter adds up to

So this chapter has one machine, and it isn’t the model. It’s a Thiele machine in
the opening’s sense, a Thiele machine with the toll proved (Theorem 15.7), and
its toll charges the blank cell’s 0: raising its flag is a merge in its record layer
(Theorem 3.19). It’s Thiele-complete, the sense no clock meets (Section 10.8),
and certified Thiele-complete, in the sense of Definition 15.7 (Theorem 15.31): it
computes whatever a Turing machine can, under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside
the machine, its computing adds nothing to the ledger and can’t touch the record,
and, from a clean start, its record is earned.
    If you ever find yourself wondering whether a property of this machine is the
model’s or just the machine’s, hold it up against Section 2’s definition of a Thiele
machine, the latch of Section 10, the four clauses of Thiele-complete, and the four
of certified Thiele-complete. What follows from those holds of every machine that
meets them; the rest (a table of sixteen facts, three properties) is this machine’s
choice. The flat price of one is clause (c), and at least one of it is what the record-
layer premise asks of each act on this machine. There are six instruction kinds, and
a seventh, PAY, for a host that has to charge somebody else’s prices (Appendix D.2).
If the model needs more than the five parts and the toll, this is where it will show.
CHAPTER 16




How far it reaches

The small machine earns its flag, and pays for it, on its own programs. Everything
in this chapter asks how far that carries. Every statement in it is proved, and the
runs are reported as runs. I give each statement here and leave the constructions to
the appendices, because they’re about the reach of the case, not the case.
    Other machines as guests. One fixed program, U, written in the small machine’s
own six kinds of instruction on a host with more counters, runs every program of
the small machine as a guest, from every clean start. It fetches, decodes and carries
out each guest instruction itself, the way Turing’s universal machine does; nothing
in the host means “run one guest step.” It halts exactly when its guest halts, with
the guest’s answer in its counters; its flag goes up during its run exactly when the
guest’s goes up during the guest’s, by its own check, its own commitment and its
own certificate; and its ledger equals the guest’s at every point where the two runs
match. The host is certified Thiele-complete, and whether U halts is undecidable.
Add one move, PAY, that costs one and does nothing else, and the same kind of
program, UP , runs every Thiele machine whose next move, step, prices and reading
are computed by programs that always answer: it halts when the guest’s run stops,
its flag goes up exactly when the guest’s reading is yes at some state of its run, on
a chain whose check is the guest’s own reading, and its ledger is the guest’s prices
plus a surcharge of at most two at the raise when the guest’s reading starts at no,
and exactly three when it starts at yes, a surcharge that no program on that host,
run from a clean start, can always avoid. Appendix D has both, with their proofs.
    Other models of computation. Lay the toll over a register machine, a Turing
machine (with one move for each whole program, not one for each row of one fixed
table, which provably can’t serve as a base) or the lambda calculus and none of
them computes one function more; what each gains is a record and a cost. What
carries over from any base, what never does, and why the small machine uses two
counters, are in Appendix E.
    Machines from parts. Wired side by side, end to end, or one inside the other, a
Thiele machine stays a Thiele machine, and the tolls add the way money adds. What
breaks, breaks for reasons you could name in advance: a single flag for two claims
costs two claims’ worth, a clock is still a clock, a shared value without a version can’t




                                  394
                                                                                        395


be trusted, and a hand-off that costs nothing can’t be allowed to carry a certificate
(Appendix F).
    Running it. The machine is built twice, once from the definitions and once by
hand, and the two are compared after every step; U and UP have run on guests
small enough to finish; a compiler from a small programming language to the host
is proved correct stage by stage, and Ackermann’s function at (3, 5) comes out of
nothing but INC and DEC (Appendix G).
    A check worth earning. A flag is only as interesting as the claim under it. The
CHSH game, the two-player game behind Bell’s theorem, gives a claim whose check
is a piece of real mathematics: an integer test on the game’s tally whose passing
implies Tsirelson’s bound, earned on the host by the same check, commit and certify
(Appendix H). It’s there to show the toll charges the same however deep the check
behind it is.
CHAPTER 17




Five small models

So far there’s been a toll, a counter, two kinds of wall and a latch, every one of them
shown on paper, on cups and cards and dice I made up, and then a small machine to
run them on. That is the model on paper and on one small example. It’s time to go
and look at what people actually do. I picked five systems that keep records other
people rely on, with real money or real security behind them, and asked each the
pricing question from the paper models: is there a price on the moment the record is
written? The question isn’t about the work around the write; it’s about the write,
the moment the 0 goes on the page and stays. I’ll tell you the answer first, because
it’s a single sentence and it surprised me: of the five specifications, read through the
transcriptions I made of them, only one takes a fee at the moment of the write, and
that one has a leak at exactly the place Section 6 said a counter leaks, where it goes
down.
     “Price” needs one meaning for all five, or the answer is whatever I want it to be,
so I’ll fix it here, and every system below gets classified by it. A specification prices
an event when it attaches one of three costs to it. A fee: something taken at the
event itself, whatever happens afterward. A bond: value put at risk by the event
and lost only if some later event happens, a contradiction, say. A budget: a finite
allowance the event draws down, so that only so many such events can ever happen.
A wall isn’t a price under this definition. Nobody pays a hash; reversing one is just
infeasible. Neither is work a protocol needs and never charges for. The table at the
end of the section has a column for each of the three kinds, and what it shows is a
finding about the five, because the definition came first.
     Three things are easy to blur in a section like this, so I’ll name them now and
keep them apart all the way through. There’s the real specification: the document
real money and real security run on. There’s my transcription: one mechanism
copied out of that document into a mathematical model, small enough to examine.
And for some of the five there’s a wrapper: a tiny abstract model that takes one
premise as given and says what follows from it. A claim proved at one level isn’t a
claim at the level above it. Near the end I’ll walk one system, gas, through all three,
so you can see exactly where each claim stops.
     For each system I isolate the mechanism the question concerns: a fragment with
its own states and operations, transcribed from the system’s specification where one


                                  396
                                                17.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back   397


was available. I will put that mechanism on the page, state the guarantee it carries,
and show how the argument follows its rules.


17.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back
Ethereum and chains like it decide which blocks are final by having validators,
people who’ve locked up money (their stake), vote on checkpoints: blocks picked out
at regular numbered rounds called epochs. A vote isn’t for one checkpoint. It’s a link
from a checkpoint the validator already trusts, the source, to a later one, the target,
and every chain starts from one first block, its genesis, which counts as trusted from
the start. In the design Vitalik Buterin and Virgil Griffith published in 2017, called
Casper, a checkpoint is justified when validators holding two thirds of the stake vote
a link to it from a justified source, and finalized when it is justified and a two-thirds
link runs from it to its direct child. The record is “this checkpoint is final.”
    Two rules carry the price: don’t vote for two different targets in the same epoch,
and don’t cast a vote whose span, source to target, surrounds the span of another of
your votes. Break either and your deposit can be destroyed, which is called slashing.
The theorem they prove, called accountable safety, says that if two conflicting
checkpoints are ever both finalized, at least a third of the stake broke a rule and can
be slashed. So the price is on reversal, on making the record contradict itself. The
write itself, finalizing, takes no fee: honest validators finalize all day and nobody
loses anything. In the terms from the start of the section, Casper’s price is a bond.
The deposit stands behind every vote, the finalizing votes included, and it’s taken
only from a validator whose own votes contradict each other, which is what making
the record contradict itself takes from a third of the stake.
    Do it with three validators of equal stake. Draw genesis at epoch 0, two competing
children at epoch 1, and one child of each at epoch 2. Let A and B vote both links on
the left branch, from genesis to its first child and from that child to the next. Let B
and C do the same on the right. Each link has two of the three votes. Both epoch-1
blocks are justified and have the required link to their child, so both finalize. B voted
for different targets at the same epoch, which makes B the third that gets slashed,
while A and C are clean. That’s what a fork costs and who pays, and Theorem 17.2
below has exactly this instance, so the theorem’s premise isn’t vacuous: forks of that
kind can be built, and the theorem fires on them.
    The fragment is a reconstruction of the published casper-proofs argument from
Runtime Verification and the University of Texas at Austin, based on Yoichi Hirai’s
proof, with validator sets and quorum intersection as a premise. A quorum is a set
of validators big enough to act, here two thirds of the stake, and quorum intersection
is the arithmetic of the three-validator example: two thirds plus two thirds is four
thirds, so any two quorums share at least a third. The fragment takes the overlap as
398   17 Five small models


              given; it doesn’t do that arithmetic. It has no deposits, no rewards, no fork choice
              (the rule for picking a branch to build on), and no connection to anything else in this
              book. A finalization fork implies that a set of validators the size of that overlap, at
              least a third of the stake, is slashed. And a one-validator chain finalizes and nobody’s
              slashed, which is the “write costs no stake” sentence, proved here in a degenerate
              setting.
                 The fragment is small enough to read in one sitting, and every name below is
              from the transcription.

              Definition 17.1 (Casper setting and votes). A setting has a type of validators, a
              type of block hashes with a parent relation and a genesis hash, and two classes of
              validator sets, the “two-thirds” sets Q1 and the “one-third” sets Q2 . It carries two
              premises: quorum intersection, for any two sets in Q1 some set in Q2 lies inside
              both; and at most one parent per hash. A state says, for each validator, target hash h,
              target epoch t and source epoch u, whether that validator voted the link (h, t, u). A
              link from p at epoch u to h at epoch t is justified by q when q ∈ Q1 , every member of
              q voted (h, t, u), h is the (t − u)-th descendant of p, and t > u. Genesis is justified
              at epoch 0, and a block reached from a justified block by a justified link landing
              at epoch t is justified at t. Block h is finalized at epoch v with child c when c is a
              child of h, h is justified at v, and the link from h at v to c at v + 1 is justified. A
              finalization fork is two finalized blocks h1 ̸= h2 , neither an ancestor of the other. A
              validator is slashed when it voted two different targets with the same target epoch (a
              double vote), or voted links (h1 , t1 , u1 ) and (h2 , t2 , u2 ) with t1 > t2 and u2 > u1 (a
              surround vote). The state is quorum-slashed when some set in Q2 consists of slashed
              validators.



              Theorem 17.1 (Accountable safety). In every setting, every state with a finalization
              fork is quorum-slashed.

              Proof. Let the fork be h1 finalized at v1 and h2 at v2 . If v1 = v2 , the epoch is above
              0, since genesis is the only block justified at 0, so the links that justified h1 and
              h2 there are each voted by a set in Q1 ; quorum intersection gives a set in Q2 that
              voted both, and their targets h1 and h2 differ. That set double-voted. If v1 ̸= v2 , say
              v1 < v2 , walk down the chain of justified links that justifies h2 . Every block on that
              chain is an ancestor of h2 , so none descends from h1 . (So v1 > 0: the only block
              justified at epoch 0 is genesis, an ancestor of every justified block.) Some link in
              the chain starts at or below v1 and lands above v1 . If it lands at v1 + 1, it and the
              finalization link of h1 have distinct targets at that epoch, and the intersection set
              double-voted. If it starts at v1 , its source is a justified block at v1 other than h1 , and
                                                  17.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back   399


the links that justified those two blocks give a double vote the same way. Otherwise
it starts below v1 and lands above v1 + 1, so it surrounds the finalization link of h1 ,
and the intersection set made a surround vote.
   Everything the fragment promises stands on the overlap, and with the overlap
taken away it promises nothing. The one parent is in the setting because the original
proof uses it, and the proof above never does.


Theorem 17.2 (The premise can hold, and the write costs no stake). (1) In the
three-validator setting where each validator has stake 1, Q1 is the sets of stake at
least two thirds and Q2 the sets of at least one third, the state where A and B vote
one branch and B and C the other has a finalization fork; B is slashed, A and C
are not, and { B} is in Q2 . (2) In the one-validator chain setting, one vote finalizes
genesis and no validator is slashed.

Proof. Both are computations on fixed finite data. In (1) every link carries two of
the three votes, so stake two thirds, so both epoch-1 blocks are justified and each has
a justified link to its child at epoch 2: both are finalized, and as siblings neither is an
ancestor of the other. B voted two different targets at epoch 1, which is the double
vote; A’s and C’s votes are one link at epoch 1 from source 0 and one at epoch 2
from source 1, which neither double-vote nor surround. In (2) the one validator’s
vote from genesis at 0 to its child at 1 is a justified link, so genesis is finalized, and a
single vote can neither double-vote nor surround.
    For the record itself, one thing that means is that finality is revocable at a price,
the price is named, and a final block can hold a false statement.
    The obvious next question is whether the 2017 design is what Ethereum actually
runs. The answer is partly, and the paper’s own title is the clue. It’s called Casper the
Friendly Finality Gadget, and its first sentence says it’s a finality system that overlays
a chain still choosing its blocks by proof of work, so it’s a gadget, bolted on top. In
2020 a larger group, Buterin among them, wrote up Gasper, which joins Casper’s
finality to a fork-choice rule called LMD GHOST, and on 15 September 2022, in the
switch people called the Merge, Ethereum stopped choosing blocks by proof of work
at all and went over to proof of stake. So the checkpoints and the two slashing rules
above are one part of a system that holds real money today, and the transcription
is of that part’s safety proof as the 2017 design states it. Everything between the
two, the fork choice and the rest of the running protocol, is the gap between my
transcription and the running system, which I walk through near the end of this
section with a photocopied recipe and a kitchen. None of that moves the price:
400   17 Five small models


               finalizing still costs an honest validator no stake, and what costs is contradicting
               yourself.


               17.2 Gas: the one that charges a fee at the write
              Every operation on Ethereum costs gas, paid in ether by whoever sent the transaction.
              The yellow paper, Ethereum’s formal specification, gives the reason in one line: every
              computation is fee-bearing so the network can’t be abused and halting questions are
              sidestepped. The record I care about is a nonzero slot in the shared storage, which
              every full node in the world (every computer keeping its own complete copy of the
              chain) has to keep until it’s cleared. Clearing a slot is allowed, and the refund rules
              below exist to reward it.
                  Writing a fresh storage slot from zero to nonzero costs twenty thousand gas, by
              the table in the paper’s appendix, plus twenty-one hundred for touching a cold slot,
              one the transaction hasn’t touched yet (after the first touch it’s warm). As I read it,
              the point is to discourage storage growth, since storage grows every node’s database.
              That charge is a fee on the write, at the moment of the write, and it’s the only fee in
              the five. Gas has a budget too, in the sense from the start of the section: every block
              has a gas limit, and the gas its transactions use can’t exceed it, so only so many
              writes fit in a block.
                  Where does a number like twenty-one hundred come from? Somebody picked
              it, so the obvious next question is who, and why, and the answer has a date on it.
              In September 2016, just as Ethereum’s developers were gathering in Shanghai for
              Devcon 2, their developer conference (the third one, since they started counting
              at zero), attackers started filling blocks with an operation that was cheap in gas
              and expensive in fact: it sent every node off to read data from its disk, and nodes
              fell behind the chain. The first repair, a fork that October called Tangerine Whistle,
              raised the prices of the operations the attack had leaned on. The cold-slot charge
              came later, in a proposal by Vitalik Buterin and Martin Swende called EIP-2929,
              switched on in the Berlin upgrade of April 2021, and the motivation it gives is still
              those 2016 attacks. So twenty-one hundred isn’t a law of nature or a measurement
              of anything deep. It’s a scar: a price set after somebody found the place where the
              old price was wrong. That doesn’t change the argument; the write is still priced at
              the moment of the write. It does change how I read the rest of that table: some of
              its numbers, at least, are somebody’s answer to “what did this cost last time,” which
              is a record of a different kind.
                  Now for the leak, which is Section 6’s leak. Set a slot and then clear it in the same
              transaction and you get a refund. Count it through: first write twenty-two thousand
              one hundred; clearing it costs a hundred and credits a refund of nineteen thousand
              nine hundred; net, twenty-three hundred. The other half is that if you leave it set,
                                                    17.2 Gas: the one that charges a fee at the write   401


you pay at least twenty thousand. The write is priced, and the revoked write nearly
isn’t. But I have to add what the fragment leaves out, because twenty-three hundred
on its own misleads: the realized refund is capped at one fifth of the gas the whole
transaction used (that’s the 2021 change from Section 6, the one that ended the
refund-hoarding token’s advantage). So a real set-then-clear pays a lot more than
twenty-three hundred. As for how much more, the cap is a fifth of everything the
transaction used, and that includes the twenty-one thousand every transaction pays
just for existing. Take a transaction that does nothing but set and clear the slot, and
count only that base and the two stores (the instructions that load their arguments
add about a dozen more): it uses 43,200 gas, so the cap is 8,640, so it pays 34,560,
which is 13,560 on top of the base. (Look at the slot alone and forget the base, which
the rule doesn’t do, and you’d get 17,760.) Either way it’s far above twenty-three
hundred. The counter-level net is twenty-three hundred, and what the transaction
pays is not.
    The arithmetic below is the way the specification has it, so you can redo it with a
pencil.

Definition 17.2 (One slot in one transaction). A slot run records the slot’s value at
the start of the transaction (original), its current value, whether it has been touched
(warm), the gas charged so far, and the refund counter. A store of a new value
charges 2100 if the slot is cold, plus 20000 if the slot still holds its original value,
the new value differs, and the original is 0 (2900 if the original is nonzero), and
otherwise 100. If the value is unchanged, the refund does not change. Otherwise
add together these applicable adjustments: add 4800 when the original and current
values are nonzero and the new value is zero; subtract 4800 when the original is
nonzero and the current value is zero; and, when the new value restores the original,
add 19900 if that original is zero, or 2800 if it is nonzero. Store the new current
value, mark the slot warm, and keep the original value unchanged. The run starts
fresh: original and current 0, cold, gas and refund 0. The net charge is gas minus
refund.



Theorem 17.3 (Pricing the persistent write and the revoked one). (1) For every list
of stores from a slot whose original and current values are 0, warm or cold, with
gas and refund 0, if the slot ends nonzero then the net charge is at least 20000, and
from a fresh slot, which is cold, at least 22100. (2) Storing 1 then 0 leaves the slot
at 0 with net charge 2300; storing 1 alone has net charge 22100.
402   17 Five small models


              Proof. (1) Keep two lines on the sheet: “current value zero: net at least zero,” and
              “current value nonzero: net at least 20000.” The starting slot meets the first line. I
              will check that every store leaves it meeting whichever line describes its new value.
              The original value remains zero throughout, so there are only four changes to check.
              Zero to zero adds 100 to net; zero to nonzero adds 20000; nonzero to nonzero adds
              100; and nonzero to zero adds 100 − 19900 = −19800. The last case starts with
              net at least 20000 and so ends at least 200, still nonnegative. So every store leaves
              the appropriate line true. Carry the two-line test through the list of stores: if the
              final value is nonzero, the net charge is at least 20000. A cold access adds another
              2100, once, on the first store. Keep that extra charge in a separate column; later
              updates are exactly the ones just checked and do not depend on the accumulated
              total. A nonempty run from a cold slot therefore pays that 2100 on top of the
              bound, giving at least 20000 + 2100 when it ends nonzero. (2) Direct computation:
              2100 + 20000 = 22100 for the first store, 100 for the second, refund 19900, and
              22200 − 19900 = 2300.
                  The fragment covers one slot in one transaction, with the gas and refund arith-
              metic copied out of the Ethereum execution specification’s storage instruction and
              gas table, at a named commit. It has no stack, no call context, no other slots, and no
              refund cap, the one-fifth rule applied at the end of a transaction.
                  Then comes the wrapper, which is a different kind of object, and the walk near
              the end is about exactly that difference. It’s a gas schedule in the abstract: any states,
              any steps, a cost per step, a yes/no commitment flag, and a charge predicate saying
              which steps get charged. It formalises no EVM (the Ethereum virtual machine) at
              all. It is Section 7’s result with the whole-run ceiling, the one that pins the amount
              as well as which steps pay, under a new name. Its two halves are worth reading
              separately. Leave one committing step uncharged, and a one-step run commits at no
              charge, so the floor fails outright; one missed commit is enough. Charge one step
              that doesn’t commit, and the schedule charges more than the number of commits
              on that one-step run, so the ceiling fails. And the class isn’t empty: in any system,
              the price that charges one exactly on a step that raises the flag and nothing on any
              other meets both halves (Section 7’s step price).
                  The wrapper itself is the cleanest thing in this section and has the least Ethereum
              in it.

               Definition 17.3 (A gas schedule). A gas schedule has states, instructions, a step,
               a cost c(s, i ) ∈ N that may depend on the state, a Boolean commitment flag on
               states, and a Boolean charge predicate χ(s, i ), with two premises: a charged step
               costs at least 1, and an uncharged step costs 0. A step commits when it takes the flag
               from false to true. For a run t from s, let c(t) be its total cost and n(t) its number of
               committing steps. The schedule has the floor when c(t) ≥ n(t) for every run, and
                                           17.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past   403


no overcharge when c(t) ≤ n(t) for every run. It has unit pricing when c(s, i ) = 1 if
χ(s, i ) and 0 otherwise.



Theorem 17.4 (Gas schedule exactness). For every gas schedule: it has the floor
and no overcharge if and only if χ(s, i ) holds exactly when the step from s by i
commits, and it has unit pricing. Moreover, (1) if some committing step from an
uncommitted state is uncharged, that one-step run costs 0 and the schedule fails the
floor; (2) if some charged step does not commit, the schedule overcharges.

Proof. The equivalence is Section 7’s characterization with the whole-run ceiling,
under another name. From right to left, each step’s cost is 1 on a committing step
and 0 otherwise, so a run’s cost counts its commitments. From left to right, apply
the floor and no overcharge to one-step runs: a committing step must cost at least 1,
so it is charged; a charged step costs at least 1 and may not exceed its commitment
count, so it commits and costs exactly 1. Parts (1) and (2) are those one-step runs
read the other way.
   Gas prices storage growth and computation. It says nothing about whether what’s
stored is true.


17.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past
A trusted platform module, the small chip on most laptop motherboards, keeps a
handful of registers that can only be extended: the new value is a hash of the old
value together with a digest (a short hash) of whatever software just loaded. You
can’t set them; you can only fold more in. A quote is the chip signing those register
values together with a number the asker chose, a nonce, so the asker knows the
quote is fresh. Intel’s SGX does the equivalent for an enclave, a walled-off region a
program runs in. The record is the extended register.
   What does the specification price on the registers? Nothing: no fee, no bond,
no budget. Reversal isn’t expensive, it’s infeasible: you’d have to invert a hash or
steal a key. Expensive against infeasible is the difference between a price and a
wall, and it’s easy to blur, which is why the definition at the start of the section
leaves walls out. What stands behind a cost can come in three currencies. It can be
economic, a fee or a deposit the protocol takes (Casper and gas are here). It can be
cryptographic, a reversal made infeasible by a hardness assumption, which makes it
a wall with no exact price on it (attestation and transparency are here). Or it can be
physical, energy spent or hardware worn, which none of these five specifications
charges as a fee or a bond; the nearest thing is the chip’s write budget, below. And
404   17 Five small models


              the record’s permanence is only as long as the register lives: a platform’s registers
              are cleared when it resets, so the permanence is per boot.
                  Why the registers, then, when something that lasts would make a better record?
              Because the quote is what a remote asker reads, and the registers are what it signs.
              The same chip has longer-lived records, and they’re closer to the latch than anything
              else in this section. Version 2.0 of its specification has storage slots of a kind it calls a
              bit field, changed only by a command that ORs new bits into the old value: a bit can
              be set and never cleared, which is r ∨ h from Section 10, on a laptop motherboard.
              It has counters that can only be incremented, and a counter’s first increment starts
              it at the largest value any counter on that chip has ever held, so deleting one and
              making a new one can’t wind it back. And those slots are rationed. Bryan Parno and
              his coauthors, building a system called Memoir in 2011, noted that the specification
              of the day only required a counter to be able to tick once every five seconds, and
              that the chip’s storage was expected to survive about a hundred thousand writes
              in its whole life, so writing once a second would wear it out in under twenty-eight
              hours. Memoir writes to it twice per boot. The permanent record, then, is finite and
              rationed: it has a budget, in exactly the sense from the start of the section, and it
              sits on these slots and counters; the registers the quote signs have none. On the bit
              field it’s the budget of Theorem 10.11’s chain of k-bit words, which can only climb
              k times. Phones and small controllers go one floor further down, to fuses like the
              PROMs in Section 10: a version number kept as a row of fuses, one more blown at
              each security update, and boot code that refuses anything older. An industry guide
              on it, Rob Smart’s 2021 explainer for PSA Certified, a security certification scheme
              for chips and devices, tells designers to make sure there are enough fuse bits to last
              the number of updates expected over the device’s lifetime, which is part (5) of that
              same theorem, written as a design rule.
                  What all of this is for is rollback. Memoir’s example is a password checker restored
              to an old saved state to undo a user’s password change, and in 2017 a system called
              ROTE did the same job for Intel’s enclaves by having several machines vouch for
              each other’s counters, with the stated result that the only way left to break it is to
              reset every one of them to its start. In 2016 Raoul Strackx and Frank Piessens’s
              Ariadne got that job down to flipping a single bit of non-volatile memory per state
              update, which they call the theoretical lower limit. Notice who the attacker is in
              every one of these: whoever gets to put an old state back. A bad program doesn’t
              come into it. A record kept by the step can’t see that attacker. Every guarantee the
              small machine gives about a record’s earned history (Section 15) is stated from a
              clean start; put back a state the machine really reached and each one still holds
              of it, through the run that reached it first, and none of them can say that nothing
              came after it. The per-step toll still holds after a restore; it just can’t tell you what
              happened before it.
                                           17.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past   405


    Replicated services put the same kind of record somewhere else: inside each
replica, where a replica that’s been taken over still can’t make it say two different
things. Byung-Gon Chun and coauthors’ attested append-only memory (A2M, 2007)
is a log a replica can only add to; Dave Levin and coauthors’ TrInc (2009) shrinks
that to a trusted counter; MinBFT (Giuliana Veronese and coauthors, 2013) uses
a trusted counter to reach agreement with 2 f + 1 replicas when f of them can lie,
where the usual count is 3 f + 1; and Damysus (Jérémie Decouchant, David Kozhaya,
Vincent Rahli and Jiangshan Yu, 2022) has a small trusted service, the Checker,
that keeps a monotonic counter of where the protocol is. Allen Clement, Flavio
Junqueira, Aniket Kate and Rodrigo Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what
such a record buys, and as I read their result it’s a good warning for this book. On
its own, stopping a replica from saying two different things doesn’t lower the 3 f + 1
bound in an asynchronous network at all. Add signatures that a third party can
check, and it turns any protocol that survives crashes into one that survives liars,
with no extra replicas. The way I read it, a record helps the others only as far as
they can check what it says, which is Section 7’s point from the other side.
    There’s a fourth currency under those three, the logical kind, and it’s the one
every permanent record on a finite chip pays in: Section 3’s counting of used and
fresh states applies to any of these records. With only finitely many states holding
the record on, a step that switches it on somewhere, and never switches it off
anywhere, forgets something. Forgetting alone doesn’t single out a record write:
any step that overwrites a field able to hold two values forgets something too. What
singles it out is where the forgetting lands. Take the states the record already reads
yes on, together with the one the step switches on. The step sends every one of
them to a yes state, and it can’t keep them apart, so what it destroys is a distinction
on the record’s own yes side: two states it already vouched for, or the state it just
raised and one that was up already. Any overwrite merges states somewhere; a
permanent write is forced to merge them on that side. That needs no premise about
money, keys or heat. The economic, cryptographic and physical payments each
need a premise of their own about their kind (a fee rule, a hardness assumption,
Landauer’s principle), and they hold exactly where that premise holds.


Theorem 17.5 (A permanent write forgets on its own yes side). For any states S,
instructions I, step and Boolean reading: suppose a duplicate-free list names every
state, the instruction i never turns the reading from on to off, and i turns it on at
some state s. Then the step by i is not injective. More: the step by i sends every
state that reads on, and s, to a state that reads on, and it is not injective even on
those states.
406   17 Five small models


                   Count the on-states and call their number K. The list of all states is finite, so this
               count is finite too. The instruction keeps each of those K sources on, and it also
               sends the additional off-state s to on. That gives K + 1 distinct sources with only K
               on-states available as landing places. Two sources must land together. Both came
               from the stated collection, so the failure to keep sources apart already occurs there.
               Permanence of any other instruction was never needed.
                   What the quote can do is say what was measured. It can’t say the measured
               code is correct, and it can’t say anything about runtime state that was never folded
               in. A correctly measured buggy program attests beautifully. The fragment proves
               that exact limit: one register, a hash about which nothing is assumed, a quote as a
               pair, and no function of the quote decides a runtime flag the quote ignores, which
               is Section 7’s cube again. And a second small result shows that a sign-and-verify
               interface alone gives no authenticity (a scheme where verify always says yes passes
               the interface), so a cryptographic premise has to be added; the fragment doesn’t
               model signatures, formats, or a freshness check (the nonce is just a field the verifier
               fixes).
                   The same limit, turned outward, is the honest edge of the four conditions of
               Section 14. Every one of them is about a thing the machine holds: same property,
               same thing, same edition, honest check. For a claim about the world (the oven is
               hot, the parcel arrived) there’s no edition the machine controls. Whatever reads
               the world is a window onto it, and “nothing changed between the check and the
               commit” stops being something a step can enforce and becomes a premise about the
               sensor. So a record can establish claims about the machine’s own state, and claims
               about the world only through named premises about whatever measured them. A
               correctly recorded sensor reading certifies the sensor.

              Definition 17.4 (Platform and quote). Fix any functions H : N × N → N (the
              extend hash) and δ : N → N (the digest); nothing is assumed about either. A
              platform is a measurement log (a list of numbers) and a Boolean runtime flag.
              Its register is the log folded from 0 by H. The quote with nonce n is the pair
              (δ(register), n).



              Theorem 17.6 (The quote cannot attest unmeasured state). For every nonce n
              there is no function D from quotes to Booleans with D (quoten ( P)) = flag( P) for
              every platform P.

               Proof. Take two platforms with the empty log, one flagged true and one false. Their
               quotes are equal, since the quote never reads the flag, so D would have to return
               both values on one input.
                                                      17.4 Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced   407


    Anything that depends only on δ(register), the quote can answer; that’s what it’s
for. And the second result is the one I mentioned: a “signature” scheme whose check
always says yes fits the sign-and-verify interface perfectly and accepts a signature
no key ever made, so the interface on its own promises nothing.


17.4 Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced

The certificates that make your browser show a padlock are issued by hundreds
of authorities, and a bad or compromised one can issue a certificate for a domain
it shouldn’t. Certificate Transparency makes authorities submit every certificate
to public append-only logs built as Merkle trees, so that anyone can check that a
certificate was logged and that the log never rewrote its past. It was specified in
RFC 6962 in 2013 and revised as RFC 9162 in 2021. I went looking for which one
the running logs follow, and it’s still 6962: Mozilla’s reference for web developers
says browser implementations are based on 6962, and as late as November 2025
Chrome’s team was only proposing to drop its rule that every certificate carry a
timestamp from at least one 6962 log. The fragment I transcribe is 9162’s. A Merkle
tree is Section 2’s hash chain folded into a tree: hash each certificate (those are
the leaves), hash the leaf hashes in pairs, hash those in pairs, and so on up to one
root hash. To prove one leaf is in, the log hands you only the few hashes sitting
beside the climb from that leaf to the root, the path, and you redo the climb yourself.
A second check, consistency, shows that a bigger tree is a smaller one with leaves
added on the end and nothing rewritten. The record is a leaf in the tree.
    The data structure has a history of its own in security. The computer scientists
Scott Crosby and Dan Wallach, at Rice University, built tamper-evident logs on the
same kind of tree in 2009, with a proof that an entry is in the log and a proof that a
later version of the log extends an earlier one, each a logarithmic number of hashes;
a logger that rewrites its past gets caught by the second.
    The RFC prices nothing, and it says in its first section that logs let interested
parties detect misissuance afterward. They don’t prevent it. And a log that shows
different views to different people (a split view) can defeat the auditing, so logs are
still trusted parties. What it buys is visibility.
    Which raises the obvious question: if the specification prices nothing, why does
any authority bother logging? Nothing in the RFC makes it. The answer is a browser.
Chrome’s team set the rule, enforced from Chrome 68 in July 2018, that every
certificate issued after 30 April 2018 had to meet its transparency policy, and a
publicly trusted certificate that doesn’t is simply not trusted by Chrome: the visitor
gets a full-page warning in front of the site. So there is a price after all, though it
isn’t anywhere in the specification: it lives in one vendor’s browser, and it’s the price
of being shown to that browser’s users at all. Is that the bottom? Not quite, because
408   17 Five small models


              it means the strongest lever on this record is a policy one company can change,
              which is a fact about who holds the stamp. The tree has nothing to do with it. That
              policy changes nothing in the table at the end of this section, which asks what each
              specification prices. But it’s worth keeping two sentences apart: “the specification
              prices nothing” and “nothing is priced.”
                  Do the inclusion proof by hand. Lay out seven cards d0 through d6 . Join
              neighbours with paper brackets: a = ν(d0 , d1 ), b = ν(d2 , d3 ) and c = ν(d4 , d5 ).
              The last card stands alone. Next join a to b, giving L = ν( a, b), and c to d6 , giving
              R = ν(c, d6 ). The root is ν( L, R). Here ν means “put these two expressions, in this
              order, inside one labelled bracket.” Equal symbolic hashes must have exactly the
              same bracket structure.
                  To check d3 , keep only that card and the three siblings d2 , a, R. Combine d2 on
              its left to recover b, then a on the left to recover L, then R on the right to recover the
              root. You never needed to open the cards inside a or R. Those three siblings are the
              inclusion path. The hashes here are brackets, not numbers, so what you just checked
              is how the tree is put together; a real log uses short hashes, and “two different
              trees can’t give the same root” is then a separate promise from the cryptography.
              Nothing in this fragment signs anything, no auditors talk to each other, and no log
              misbehaves.

              Definition 17.5 (Inclusion check, RFC 9162 section 2.1.3.2). Given a leaf index
              m, a tree size N, a leaf hash, a root hash and a path, the check rejects unless
              m < N. Otherwise start counters f = m, s = N − 1 and an accumulated hash r
              equal to the leaf hash. For each path element p, reject if s = 0. If f is odd or f = s,
              replace r by ν( p, r ); in this branch, while f is positive and even, halve both counters
              with rounding down. In the other branch replace r by ν(r, p). After either branch
              halve both counters once more. At the end accept exactly when s = 0 and r is
              the claimed root. A symbolic hash makes a leaf hash ℓ( x ) and a node hash ν( a, b)
              distinct constructors: two hashes are equal only when their entire constructions
              agree.
                  The consistency check used here takes old and new sizes M, N, roots u, v and a
              path, and rejects unless 0 < M < N. If M is a power of two, prepend u to the path.
              Reject an empty resulting path; otherwise its first element seeds two accumulated
              hashes rold , rnew . Start f = M − 1, s = N − 1, and halve both while f is odd.
              Process each remaining path element p: reject if s = 0; when f is odd or f = s, put
              p on the left of both accumulated hashes and halve both counters while f is positive
              and even; otherwise leave rold alone and put p on the right of rnew . After either
              branch halve both counters once. Accept exactly when s = 0, rold = u and rnew = v.
              All halvings round down.
                                                     17.5 Proof-carrying code: no price, no permanence   409




Theorem 17.7 (The RFC’s own examples pass). With the symbolic hash, in the
RFC’s seven-leaf tree with leaves d0 , . . . , d6 (writing dk also for its leaf hash ℓ(dk )),
the inclusion check accepts leaf 3 with path [d2 , ν(d0 , d1 ), ν(ν(d4 , d5 ), d6 )], and
likewise leaves 0, 4 and 6 with their paths; the consistency check from size 4 to size
7 accepts. For every input with m = N, the inclusion check rejects.

Proof. Use the brackets a, b, c, L, R built above. For leaf 3, the counters start at
(3, 6): put d2 on the left, leaving (1, 3); put a on the left, leaving (0, 1); put R on
the right, leaving (0, 0) and root ν( L, R). Leaf 0 has path [d1 , b, R] and three right
combinations. Leaf 4 has path [d5 , d6 , L]: right, right, left. Leaf 6 has path [c, L]: left,
then left; its first branch shifts (6, 6) to (3, 3) before the ordinary halving, which
accounts for the unpaired last leaf. Each reconstructs the same root. For consistency
from 4 to 7, the old root is L and the supplied path is [ R]. Prepending L seeds both
hashes with L; shifting the initial (3, 6) gives (0, 1), so the sole remaining element
leaves the old root alone and makes the new root ν( L, R), with final counters (0, 0).
The boundary case m = N fails the first test m < N.
    And the append-only part of the fragment is as plain as it sounds: the history is a
list, and adding to the end of a list leaves every old entry where it was.


17.5 Proof-carrying code: no price, no permanence
Necula’s idea, from Section 8, is to ship untrusted code with a proof that it obeys
the host’s policy; the host computes what would need to be true and checks the
proof with a small checker. The record is the checked proof, and it’s held only for
the moment of loading. It isn’t priced: checking is cheap by design, which is the
whole point, and the producer paid to build the proof off the host. It isn’t permanent
either, since nothing’s written. The fragment is a three-instruction memory-bounds
language with the policy “every address is below the limit”: the checker accepts
exactly when the condition holds, and a certificate implies the condition. One
example sits on top of that, a computation you can do in your head: a program that
reads address two under a limit of two is rejected. The fragment isn’t the paper’s
real case study, and nothing connects it to anything else in this book. And it has a
limit: a program that writes garbage to address zero passes if zero is below the limit.
The proof is of the stated policy and nothing else.
   And what was the paper’s real case study, the one my fragment isn’t? It was
network packet filters, the little programs an operating system runs on incoming
network traffic to decide which program gets to see which packet. They run inside
the kernel, the most trusted part of the system, and they have to be fast, so they’re
410   17 Five small models


              exactly the code you’d most like to take from a stranger and least like to trust. In
              the 1996 paper that first set out the idea, Necula and Peter Lee wrote several filters
              by hand in the assembly language of a DEC Alpha, shipped each with its proof, and
              reported a one-time cost of 1 to 3 milliseconds to check the proof, after which the
              filter ran with no checks at all. Those milliseconds put a number on “checking is
              cheap by design”. What the paper reports changes nothing about my fragment,
              which still isn’t that case study, and it doesn’t add a price: the milliseconds are the
              checker’s work, and nothing is being written down for them to be a toll on.

               Definition 17.6 (The bounds fragment). Instructions are READ a, WRITE a v, and
               HALT. For a memory limit L, the policy allows READ a and WRITE a v when a < L,
               and always allows HALT. The verification condition of a program is that the policy
               allows every instruction in it. A certificate is a list of per-instruction policy facts, one
               for each instruction in order. The checker tests the policy on each instruction and
               returns the conjunction.



              Theorem 17.8 (The checker is the verification condition). For every limit L and
              program P: the checker accepts P exactly when the verification condition holds; any
              certificate for P gives the verification condition; and with L = 2 the checker rejects
              READ 2 followed by HALT.

              Proof. Lay the instructions in a row. For each READ or WRITE, compare its address
              with L; put yes beneath it exactly when the address is smaller. Put yes beneath HALT
              without asking about an address. The checker accepts exactly when every mark in
              that row is yes. The verification condition asks for exactly those same per-instruction
              facts. An empty row has no failing instruction, and extending the row preserves
              acceptance precisely when the new instruction also passes. This covers programs of
              every finite length.
                 A certificate supplies one policy fact at each place in the same row. Reading
              them in order gives every fact the verification condition asks for, so it implies that
              condition too.
                 With limit two, the first instruction READ 2 asks whether 2 < 2. It does not.
              The later HALT is allowed, but cannot undo that failed comparison, so the checker
              rejects the two-instruction program.


               17.6 One example, three levels
               Before I lay all five side by side, let me walk one of them up and down the three
               levels from the start of the section, because every claim in here lives at exactly one
                                                                     17.6 One example, three levels   411


level and it’s easy to let a claim slide up a floor without noticing. I’ll take gas, since
it’s the one place all three line up. Think of a restaurant’s real recipe, my photocopy
of one page of it, and a cookbook chapter on what any recipe has to contain. I can
check my photocopy line by line. That tells you nothing about what the kitchen
cooks tonight.
    Start with the real specification. Ethereum’s execution specification says, in a
document that runs real money, what a storage write costs, what clearing it refunds,
and how the refund is capped at the end of the transaction. None of what I proved
is at this level. What the network actually charges is whatever the clients people run
actually compute, and the evidence for that is the clients and the chain. This book
has none of it.
    Next comes the transcription. I copied one mechanism out of that document,
one slot in one transaction, gas and refund arithmetic only, at a named commit
(Definition 17.2, Theorem 17.3). What the result tells you: if the storage rule is
what I copied, then leaving a fresh slot set costs at least twenty thousand, and
set-then-clear nets twenty-three hundred at the counter. What it can’t tell you:
anything about the refund cap (not copied, which is why what a real set-then-clear
pays came out so different from the counter earlier), the stack, calls, other slots, or
whether any client implements the rule as written. The boundary of the claim is the
edge of the copy.
    Last comes the wrapper. The gas schedule of Definition 17.3 isn’t Ethereum. It’s
any system with steps, a cost per step and a yes/no commitment flag, plus one thing
stipulated: a charge predicate, with the premise that a charged step costs at least one
and an uncharged one costs zero. That premise is the whole of what the wrapper
adds, and it’s added by hand; no specification supplies it. Given it, the theorem says
every run costs exactly its number of commits, never letting a commit go unbilled,
never billing one twice and never billing a non-commit, exactly when the charge
predicate is the commit predicate at unit price. What that tells you is what exact
pricing would have to look like, in any system. It doesn’t say Ethereum meets it,
and Ethereum doesn’t: real gas bills computation that commits nothing, which the
transcription shows in numbers. So the wrapper prices a definition, the transcription
prices a copied rule, and neither prices the chain.
    The other four sit on the same three levels, and only one more wrapper is spelled
out in this section. Casper’s transcription is the accountable-safety proof above; its
wrapper is a small gadget with the stake at risk handed in. A finalize step that risks
nothing turns the record on at no charge, which breaks Section 2’s toll, and one
that risks at least one unit has a floor. It records exposure to loss (no collateral is
destroyed in it), has no Casper checkpoints in it at all, and is priced by stipulation,
the same way the gas wrapper is. Attestation, transparency and proof-carrying code
have transcriptions that prove what their verifiers do and no price theorem, because
412   17 Five small models


              no specification of theirs puts a price on the verdict. Their wrappers, which I don’t
              spell out here, are Section 7’s verifier argument told in each system’s vocabulary,
              with a colliding pair behind each one, and that argument is all they carry here.
                 The book’s rule is that every claim gets a way to break it, so I’ll say how to knock
              down the four claims with the most weight on them. For the gas transcription: a list
              of stores from a fresh slot that ends nonzero with net charge under 22100. For the
              gas wrapper: a schedule in which every run costs exactly its number of commits,
              whose charge predicate still differs from the commit predicate at some step. For
              the finality gadget: a finalizing trace from unfinalized to finalized whose charged
              stake is zero while the gadget claims a floor. For the attestation fragment: a verifier
              reading only the quote’s fields that decides a runtime flag the quote ignores.

   Each row proves what its own transcription says, and no more. To read a row
