         Part III followed one example machine from its first step to the host running a
      guest. Bring those pieces back to the bench. The holding count says what the arrows
      must do. The price rule says what goes on the ledger. The window says which of
      those distinctions a reader receives. The earned chain says how the flag got there.
CHAPTER 20




The claims and their conditions

Start with a box holding an answer. I need to know which full states count as
holding it, which moves keep it there, and whether the box has finitely many such
states. Those choices make the counting argument possible. Add a price on merging
and the same count gives a charge. Give a reader only the tabletop picture and there
is another question: how much of that event reaches the reader?
    Here I put the connections in one place. The statements and their proofs stay in
the chapters where I built them; this is a way to follow what each piece contributes
to the next.


20.1 Keeping a distinction
One next state. Follow one deterministic rule from a start. Until the first repeated
state, every visit is new. At the first repeat, either you have returned to the start,
or two different predecessors have reached the same state. From then on the rule
repeats the same successors. Those are the three columns of the step law (Section 1).
A choice between several successors would change the argument at precisely the
point where you follow the next arrow.
     A finite place to hold the answer. Suppose a move keeps every YES state at YES
and brings a NO state in. With K YES states, those states and the entrant give K + 1
sources landing in K places. Two arrows meet. The entering arrow need not be one
of them: a chain can run through the held states before meeting a fixed endpoint.
Section 3 gives the general count and its attaining constructions.
     Each part of that picture matters. An endless strip can keep moving to a different
YES state forever. A two-state toggle keeps the arrows one-to-one by turning YES
back to NO. A finite permanent holder has neither route available. For a single rule,
if its entered holding run were to repeat while remaining one-to-one, cancelling the
equal successors backwards would identify the unfinished entrant with a held state.
That is why the one-to-one alternative needs a fresh configuration at every later tick.
     Section 1 also follows finite noisy and unitary systems using their own preserva-
tion conditions. For a table of chances, both row and column sums enter the count.
For a unitary map, preservation of inner products supplies it. For the zoom argument,
keep track of the full states behind the coarse picture. The finite collection being


                                                 441
442   20 The claims and their conditions


               counted must remain closed under the step; otherwise the next tick can move into a
               state the count left out.


               20.2 Putting a price beside the arrows
               A graph tells you which states meet. A price schedule tells you what a move costs.
               The finite holding count and a rule charging merging moves together force a charge
               on a permanent raise. Once the one-step toll is part of the machine, every run from
               NO to YES includes a charged crossing; adding nonnegative costs gives the universal
               floor (Section 2).
                  There are two useful schedules to keep separate. Charge by instruction name and
               repeating that instruction has the same price even after the flag is up. Charge by the
               source state and the schedule can ask whether this particular step raises the flag.
               The floor together with a ceiling of one unit per raise selects the latter charge, one
               for a raise and zero otherwise. When the same instruction performs the raise and
               the later idle, this state-sensitive policy lets the raise pay once and the idle stay free.
                  The three-card example makes the choice visible. Call the states blank, once and
               twice; once and twice read YES. A move sending once to twice and fixing blank and
               twice merges two states without raising the reading. A merge price charges it. A
               raise price leaves it free. The chosen reading and the chosen schedule specify which
               question the ledger answers.
                  With a halving allowance on each move, the list of possible starts can shrink only
               as far as the accumulated allowance permits. The entropy form additionally counts
               a supplied probability distribution. A physical heat reading uses Landauer’s premise
               for the device and process being described. These are the successive inputs to the
               arguments in Sections 3 and 4.
                  The four-state demon shows the distinction between learning and wiping. MEA-
               SURE copies onto a blank page reversibly; applied again it can return that page.
               WIPE sends different page contents to the same blank state. The first operation uses
               the prepared page; the second merges the alternatives. The price rule can therefore
               charge them differently.


               20.3 What reaches the reader

               Put a raising step and a quiet step behind a window that shows the same before-
               and-after pictures for both. Any price computed only from those pictures gives the
               same answer for both. It cannot both charge the raise and leave the quiet step free.
               Let the window show the raise and that ambiguity disappears (Section 7).
                  The same argument applies to a question about an earlier value. If a good and a
               bad value leave the same complete retained observation, a reader of that observation
                                                           20.4 The concrete machine and its guests   443


has one input for two required answers. Inspect the value while it is live and retain
an adequate answer, or retain the distinctions the later questions will need. Which
questions are allowed determines how much must survive.
    A permanent base-driven record has the latch form: it switches on at the first
occurrence of an event and stays on (Section 10). A toggle changes that task by
allowing the record to fall; a hidden clock changes what drives it. For an ordered
growing record, threshold readings give the row of cups in Section 11. A chain with
k cups can have at most k + 1 different arrangements if cups only turn up.
    Entitlement adds a particular claim and the evidence permitting a later step to
use it. Its index count uses a covering tree whose depth the paid steps cover. The
uncovered narrowing example in Section 8 shows why that connection belongs
in the statement: narrowing a candidate list alone supplies no such bound on the
ledger.


20.4 The concrete machine and its guests

From a clean start, only CERTIFY raises the flag, only a successful COMMIT supplies
its channel, and only a successful CHECK supplies the matching fact. The counter’s
edition must still match at commitment. Following those entry points backwards
gives the earned chain and its minimum charge of three (Section 15). A claim such
as “this counter is at least zero” passes everywhere and still uses the same three acts.
The flag records their occurrence; the claim says what they established.
    The ledger starts at zero and each step adds its scheduled price. Induction on the
run then gives both its total and its uniqueness: two ledgers following that same
start and schedule agree before the first step and still agree after each addition
(Section 6).
    The universal program follows a guest through matching points, preserving
its halting, flag and ledger guarantees (Appendix D.1). The presented-machine
interpreter extends this to guests with computable transitions, prices and readings,
with the surcharge stated in Appendix D.2. Each interpreter earns its own flag
through the host’s instructions.
    The computational slice. The lift in Appendix E gives a universal base a check
language, room for a fact, a channel and the earned operations. While the lift is live,
base moves follow the base and the panel leaves its working value alone. A failed
check can trap the lift. Later free moves then freeze, so keeping that failure globally
invisible would also hide the change in subsequent computation. The live-state
clause is what connects this lift to its stated slice.
    The Thiele-complete interfaces specify free base moves and a record that sep-
arates runs with the same working observation. The clock and silent-machine
examples show what each requirement contributes; the four independence wit-
444   20 The claims and their conditions


               nesses separate the clauses. Interface and instruction choice also explain why the
               one-rule presentation and its macro version have different coverage.
                  Independent components compose by interleaving their moves. Each move
               changes its own component, so the pair’s cost is the sum of the two component costs.
               Keep each component’s own move order fixed and every interleaving has the same
               final state. Nesting instead follows a guest through a host map; the record-order
               condition carries the guest’s crossings into the host’s accounting (Appendix F).


               20.5 The diagonal and the worked models

               The diagonal argument supplies the contradiction inside a substrate that can repre-
               sent the candidate’s flip and has the stated recursion property. Its fixed point makes
               the proposed decision disagree with itself. An outside calculation of the natural-
               number example does not supply an inside program for that substrate. Section 13
               and the appendices state the input conventions separately for the natural-number
               family, L, the counter programs and the host.
                   The protocol examples in Section 17 isolate particular mechanisms: finality, a
               charge on commitment, an attestation window, an inclusion proof and a bounds
               check. Their statements follow the operations in those fragments. The pointer thesis
               then asks why certification is the event to choose. It proposes a connection to records
               copied and relied on by independent parties. The counting and window arguments
               apply to any record meeting their premises; the thesis supplies the proposed reason
               for this choice.
                   The game checks in Appendix H give another worked construction. Four fixed bits
               yield the classical bound by the displayed sign calculation. The matrix arguments
               relate contraction, positive semidefiniteness and the score bound. The integer
               checker implements its specified test on tallies with every pair sampled. Its earned
               chain connects a raised flag to that test. The pinned-matrix test and the completion
               test ask different questions: the appendix’s all-ones and PR-box examples make the
               difference visible.
                   Those connections are what the book has built: a count, a schedule, an ob-
               servation and an earned record, with instructions carrying them through actual
               runs.

CHAPTER 21




The claim ledger

This section lists everything this book claims, one line each, with what kind of
claim it is and where it lives. “Proved” means proved under the premises printed
in that section, and nothing more. If a line here ever says more than its section
does, the section is right and the line is wrong. “Directly from the rules” means the
claim can be read off the stated operations by checking their cases. “Directly from
the interface” means its requirements already include the claimed behavior. These
claims are true, but carry almost nothing beyond what those definitions already say.
If you’re counting results, count those differently. I mark them so they don’t pad the
list, and where they’re stated in the book they carry the label observation, with three
exceptions: Theorem 15.6, part (3) of Theorem D.8, and the parts of Theorem E.4
its line names.
    Ledger is a good word for it, and it’s older than bookkeeping. Around 1400 a
ledger was a book that lay permanently in one place, a big church breviary, say, from
the old verb leggen, to lay; the account-book sense turns up in the 1500s. Staying
put is the job here too. The home sections are long and they wander, and this is the
one place where every claim lies still, so you can come back and find it where you
left it.


21.1 Claims about the model

The model comes first. Every line in this table is about any system that has the
pieces the line names: a state and a step, plus whatever the result asks for, a reading
and the toll, a counter and a price list, a window, programs. None of them is about
my machine, except the lines that run these results on it, which say so. The table
runs over several pages, in reading order, except that a line running a result on the
small machine sits beside the result it runs.
   There’s a way to use it that takes five minutes. Pick the sentence in this book you
trust least. Find its line. Read the Kind column before anything else. Then go to the
home section and check that the line says no more than the section does. If it says
more, you’ve found my mistake, and the end of this section says what I’d like done
about it.

21.2 Claims about the machine
Part III built one small machine, with the hosts that run it in an appendix, and
the ledger keeps them apart from the model. The machine is the small one of
Section 15, two counters and six instruction kinds, where commitments are earned
and universality is proved, with the definition of certified Thiele-complete that every
machine can be held against, the universal program U on a host made of the same
instruction kinds, and the priced program UP that runs every computably presented
Thiele machine. Every line in the next tables is about those machines, or about every
machine meeting that definition, or about the physics section that closes Part III and
the game check in Appendix H, or about the hosts, bases, models, parts and tools
the appendices build around them, and nothing else, under the premises printed in
its section.

               21.3 What I propose

              What ties all of those results together is a proposal, and it’s mine: put the relations a
              computation carries, and what keeping them takes, into the state and the step. The
              items below spell that out, along with one narrower bet inside it, the pointer thesis
              about certification. Every one of them reaches past the theorems, and none of them
              adds to the physics, which stays in the premises the book names and the results it
              cites.
               • That the axis belongs in the step (Section 22, Section 23).
               • That the usual account of a computation is a shadow of the step, for machines
                 whose control never reads their record (Section 12). For a computer with a
                 move for each two-counter instruction, under the record layer of Appendix E,
                 part of that is proved: the computer is a slice of a certified Thiele-complete
                 machine, what’s left with the layer forgotten, and it can’t see the record or the
                 ledger (Theorem E.4). That layer’s control reads its trap, so the slice follows the
                                                                             21.3 What I propose   487


   computer only while the trap is down. The proposal is the rest: that this is how
   to see computation in general. The small machine’s control does read its own
   record layer: a commitment that finds no fact traps. So for it the claim is about
   its ordinary computer, not the whole machine.
• Within the record construction, that certification is the event selected by the
  reliance criterion of the pointer thesis (Section 18).
• That this is a structural account of computation, with a cost model as one part of
  it (Section 22).
• That the toll is the right thing to price. The alternatives are a wall or a penalty
  for contradiction (Section 17, Section 23).
    And there are three things this book doesn’t settle, each with what would settle
it. Whether Landauer’s critics are right, which would leave every theorem standing
and one premise unowned by the world: that takes measurements of real devices
(Section 3). Whether certification really is the pointer event: that takes a way to tie
the definitions to the systems the thesis is about, and Section 18 sets out the three
comparisons needed. And whether there’s a smaller start than a partition: that takes
a ruler someone can state and a smaller structure measured by it (Section 5).
    That’s the whole ledger. If you find a claim in this book that isn’t on it, or a line
that says more than its home does, that’s my mistake, and I’d want to hear about it.
CHAPTER 22




Scope

The definition asks for states, moves, readings and charges. To use a result elsewhere,
put that other system beside the drawing and match the pieces. Which states carry
the record? Which operation establishes it? What does the reader see, and what
does the price count?
   The following comparisons work through those questions for heat, computation
and the choice of record. They show which further connections an application needs.
   Physical interpretation of the counter. Choose a start and a price schedule and the
ledger is determined on reachable states. To read it as a physical quantity, specify
which states carry information and how the scheduled charge relates to dissipation,
under physical premises that hold together. The permanent-certificate theorems
supply the first for an abstract finite machine with a permanent reading. The two
premises are shown able to hold together whenever every counted step costs at
least one, and for a one-bit reset. The small machine’s unpriced steps merge states
and are charged nothing, so its ledger is not a heat meter for computing: whatever
those merges cost the hardware is off the ledger, and the two premises hold together
for the record steps only (Section 19); and the calorimeter protocol shows that
population dynamics don’t fix the energy scale. No joule value attaches to one unit
of cost without thermal and device premises (Section 3, Section 19). Once you pick
the start and the price list, the number is forced by arithmetic, and it isn’t energy.
What I’d need before it could be is the list at the top of this paragraph.
   Class separation. The witnesses show specific windows losing specific fields. They
don’t stop a conventional simulator from keeping those fields in its encoding. No
separation of standard complexity classes follows from the collisions (Section 7,
Section 15). I’ll be blunt about why I’m careful here. Whether P equals NP is
one of the seven problems the Clay Mathematics Institute put a million dollars on,
at a meeting in Paris in May 2000. One of the seven has been solved since, the
Poincaré conjecture, by the mathematician Grigori Perelman, who posted the proof
as preprints in 2002 and 2003. P versus NP hasn’t. If a two-state collision on my
machine settled it, I’d be owed a million dollars. Nobody owes me anything. A
window that loses a field is a fact about that window. A complexity class is a fact
about what every possible program can do within a budget, and nothing in these
collisions reaches that far.


                                 488
                                                                                          489


   Trace initiality, and what it doesn’t settle. The universal property of the trace
fold is about evaluating lists of instructions: pick where a target starts, and there’s
exactly one way to fold a list into it (Section 6). The counter’s uniqueness assumes a
schedule. Rise-only pricing assumes an event, and a reference count that says what
charging too much means (Section 7). Those results make the construction precise.
None of them shows that the schedule I chose, or the event I chose, is physically
necessary.
   Other observables. Certification is one worked example. A family of other
observations could turn up other structural laws, but each would need its own
events, its own evidence, and its own cost rules, justified on their own terms. The
window and oracle results are about what specific maps keep, and nothing more.
   Program predicates versus state observations. The state-level collision (Section 7’s
wall) and the program-level diagonal (Section 13’s wall) live in different domains.
Linking them would take a theorem of its own. The nat family and L (Section 13)
keep their explicit quantifiers and representability premises.
   Entitlement bounds. The count is handed its tree and its covering, along with
the payment condition. It doesn’t dig the tree out of an arbitrary run, and it isn’t
a Shannon bound on every trace (Section 8). On every certified Thiele-complete
machine the payment is the record moves, each costing exactly one, and a floor
that takes no tree exists when the questions are the run’s own CHECKs; but its
answers are taken at the rivals as they start, a branch that costs nothing can still
narrow, the lists, tree and fibres are supplied except in the worked members, and
the covering can’t be dropped. The search through n bits is capped at 16 questions
by the machine’s fact table, and the time tax is a lower bound for programs of INC
and DEC only. Nothing here extends it to every certified Thiele-complete machine
(Section 15.14).
   Quantum behaviour. The fixed-matrix equivalence is about one completion with
zero marginals and zero within-party moments. The elliptope lets the within-party
moments move, at the level of correlators. A completion of the correlators is realised
by actual measurements, by the construction in Appendix I. A full behaviour, with
each room’s own odds prescribed as well, asks for more, and the construction doesn’t
deliver those extra probabilities. A sound check isn’t complete for those bigger sets,
and the elliptope decider is mathematics on the page, not a part of the small machine
(Appendix H).
   The record axis. The proved structural result is: a permanent record driven by a
base computation is a latch on an event; on a finite machine its write merges states;
and the named windows don’t recover it. Certification is one instance. No theorem
selects it as the unique event every system must record (Section 10, Section 18).
A finite monotone multi-valued record decomposes into threshold latches. One
Boolean latch can’t hold it. Revocation, including revocation priced from the other
490   22 Scope


             side as in Casper, lies outside the permanent-record axis; a price on revocation
             doesn’t transfer to a price on the write (Section 17). Probabilistic records don’t
             inherit the uniqueness result either. Two honest random records can have the same
             branches and the same charges and still give those branches different weights, one
             choosing evenly and one two to one, so the schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities.
             And no single deterministic latch explains a record that can branch both ways from
             the same observation. Weak base equivalence is defined and is an equivalence; no
             two of the three bases of Definition 10.3, and none of them and the small machine,
             are related by it in this book, and the latch form holds on each separately, so it
             doesn’t tell them apart (Section 10). Records that can come back down lie outside
             all of this: they’re limit computability’s, and Section 10 points at Ershov’s ladder.
                 Who it’s safe against. Every guarantee about the record is about programs: any
             list of instructions, run from a clean start on a step that does what its definition says,
             one writer stepping at a time. That covers the buggy program and the hostile one. It
             doesn’t cover whoever sets the start (a snapshot put back, a table loaded with facts
             nobody checked), a reset or a power cycle, whoever picks the program, the wire
             that carries the report, someone who flips the flag with a probe, the tools that built
             the step, or a second writer that changes a counter without bumping its edition.
             Those are the operator, the device and the tool chain, and they’re outside this fence.
             A record read by someone who didn’t watch it being made is only as good as their
             reason to believe the box that shows it. The ways across that I know of, a quote over
             measured state and a proof that travels on its own, are in Section 7 and Section 17,
             and this book builds neither. What the guarantee gives inside the fence is safety: no
             program forges the chain. Availability is a different promise, and it isn’t given. A
             hostile program can put the trap up or fill the table, and after that nothing useful
             gets done. The mathematical machine uses whole numbers, which never overflow,
             so versions and the ledger grow without bound. A build with fixed-width counters,
             versions or ledger has to stop before any of them wraps, failing safe with the trap up,
             because a wrapped version could make an old fact look live again and a wrapped
             ledger would fall. Starting, restoring, resetting and that overflow stop belong to the
             implementation, and none of them is proved here.
                 The diagonal on the machine. What’s proved for the small machine’s programs is
             that halting is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.5, for them and for
             the universal program (Section 15; for the universal program, Appendix D.1). L has
             its recursion theorem, Rice and halting by proof (Section 13). On the host machine,
             the one with a counter for every number, Rice’s theorem holds for properties that
             depend on everything a program ends with (every register, the table, the channel,
             the trap, the ledger and the flag; the line number and the versions are left out), for
             programs run on an input in register 1; s-m-n holds with no premise on register
             2; and Kleene’s recursion theorem holds for the transformations a host program
                                                                                           491


carries out on numbers, with a fixed point that agrees with its image on stopping,
register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of facts and whether the
channel is empty; for some of these transformations no fixed point agrees on every
register. On the two-counter machine itself Rice’s theorem is proved on every input,
with facts compared by what they’re about, their versions left out of the comparison;
Kleene’s is proved with inputs written as powers of two and refuted with plain inputs
(Appendix D.4).
    The five models. Each is a fragment transcribed from a specification, with a named
theorem and a named limit: the Casper transcription has no deposits or fork choice;
the gas fragment omits the refund cap; the attestation fragment has no signatures;
the transparency verifier covers control flow and leaves collision resistance out; the
proof-carrying checker is a three-instruction memory-bounds language. None is a
claim about the real system beyond its fragment (Section 17).
    The machine. Part III has one small machine, with the hosts that run it in an
appendix, and this paragraph is its fence. The small machine of Section 15 (two
counters, six instruction kinds) is where commitments are earned: from a clean
start, a raised flag went through a passing check, a commitment and a certification
of the same claim, nothing is forged, and the cheapest such run adds exactly three
to the ledger, a price reached by a check that could have failed (the step doesn’t
police trivial checks: a check that can’t fail certifies for three too). It’s also where
universality is proved, by matching Minsky’s two-counter machines step for step
and using the halting reduction of Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors. It’s
certified Thiele-complete under a definition every clock-style machine fails, and every
machine meeting that definition hides its record and ledger from its own window.
The universal Thiele machine for the small machine’s programs (Definition D.1)
is a host with the small machine’s instruction kinds and more counters, running
one fixed program, U, with no guest step built in: it runs every program of the
small machine from every clean start start( x, y), halts when the guest halts, raises
its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate if and only if the guest’s flag
rises somewhere in the guest’s run, and keeps a ledger equal to the guest’s at every
matching point. With one paid move added, one fixed program, UP , runs every
computably presented Thiele machine: its step, prices and reading computed by
programs, the reading decided on every state, the run fixed by a driver. The host
halts when the guest stops, its flag is the latch of the guest’s reading, raised on its
own earned chain whose claim is that reading, and its ledger is the guest’s plus a
surcharge of at most two when the reading starts at no, a surcharge no program on
that host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest certifies with its whole
ledger below three. A machine whose reading no program decides is outside. A
simpler host with a guest step built in runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror
of the guest’s flag; its ledger only covers the guest’s. The small machine’s check price
492   22 Scope


             is flat, its fact table holds sixteen, and its certificate is historical (Section 15 lists the
             rest).
                 The comparison machines. The bases I put the latch on are fragments too. The
             register machine of Section 10 is the one with indirect addressing in Definition 10.3,
             and Theorem 10.10 is about it. The reversible result (Theorem 10.3) covers any
             base whose step is injective, and on a finite state space says only that no injective
             step raises a permanent reading. None is a theorem about real memories or full
             reversible languages. The cost-semantics results are local correspondences, short of
             full cost-framework embeddings: the trace’s cost is a writer cost and a grade, and
             the toll is the potential method with one potential (Section 6). Nobody’s whole type
             system gets embedded either.
                 Outward consequences. I looked for results about real systems that would need the
             record axis. What’s proved are the five fragments of Section 17, each a transcription
             with its own named limit, and none is a theorem about the deployed system. Stronger
             candidates would need protocol or hardware semantics I haven’t formalised, and
             I’ve proved nothing about them. So none of this yields a new outside result that
             both needs the record axis and is ready to use.
                 Where each result lives. Every deterministic machine, finite or endless: the step
             law, a merge or fresh states for a kept reading, and the endless supply of fresh
             states a raise of a kept reading with no merge needs. Every system that follows
             the toll, whatever its states: the floor, at most as many certifications as cost, and
             the potential-method reading. Every machine with finitely many yes-states whose
             price covers merges: the toll for permanent records. Every machine, finite or not:
             which instructions every price that covers merges must charge, namely the merging
             ones. Every machine paying per halving, finite or not: the machine’s own narrowing
             bound. Every machine extending a base with a driven, permanent record: the
             latch. Every window through which a certifying and a non-certifying step look
             alike: no exact price from the window. Every machine meeting the definition of
             Thiele-complete: a move that costs nothing, a cost of at least one on any run from a
             state with the record down that ends with it up, and a final window that doesn’t
             determine the record or the ledger. Every machine meeting the definition of certified
             Thiele-complete: a move that costs nothing, a cost of at least three on any run from a
             clean state that ends certified, and a final window that doesn’t determine the record
             or the ledger. Every box with a universal base: a slice of its lift with the window
             claims and room for a fact, blind to the flag and the ledger. Every Thiele-complete
             machine: its moves that cost nothing are the same through every interface, and its
             window is a slice onto two counters. Every machine run as one rule: no universal
             base, no slice, and a Thiele machine only as a clock or with a reading that never rises.
             Any eight counts: the integer check and its PSD bridge, which are mathematics.
                                                                                             493


This machine only: its six instruction kinds and their prices, its sixteen slots, its own
colliding pair, and the encodings its universal programs use.
    Models and processes. For a model of computation written down as states, a step
and a reading that stays, what keeping takes is a theorem about the model, not a
thesis. The thesis in the Conclusion is only the tie from a physical process to such
a description. Here’s how far the theorems reach, and where they stop. A step
that gives every state one next state, on any number of states: a run that raises a
reading and keeps it up merges two of its own states or never visits a state twice
(Proposition 3.5), and with finitely many states reading yes the move that raises it
merges (Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.4). That takes in a Turing machine or a counter
machine stepping by its program, and a cellular automaton stepping its whole grid
at once. A model that halts has no next state at its halt, and slips past with no
merge; give the halt a next state and the run is one rule again, so keeping the answer
merges or takes fresh states, and with the halted state stepping to itself the step
onto it is a merge (Theorem 1.2). Steps by chance on finitely many states: one
whose chances into each state add to one, which is what keeping the even spread
takes, never enters a finite set nothing leaves from a state outside it (Theorem 1.7).
A unitary step that keeps a finite-dimensional part of the space keeps the part at
right angles to it, so a state at right angles to the kept part stays at right angles
(Theorem 1.8).
    A model whose step may offer several next states, or none, comes in too: a
nondeterministic machine, a lambda term reduced at whichever redex you like,
a rewriting system, a proof system read as derivations made one rule at a time.
Nothing earlier in the book is stated for such steps, so here are the two arguments.
The first is the pigeonhole of Proposition 3.4 on one choice of next state, and the
second is the walk back of Proposition 3.5, stopped at the raise. First, suppose only
finitely many states read yes, none of them can step to a state reading no, each has
at least one next state, and some state reading no can step to one of them. Pick one
next state for each yes-state, and the outside state’s step into the yes-states: that’s
one more step than there are yes-states, each leaving a different state and landing
on a yes-state, so two land on the same one, and two different states share a next
state. That needs the yes-states finite; Hilbert’s hotel, everybody moving up one,
keeps a reading with no two states sharing a next state. Second, along any one run,
however its choices fall, take the step where a reading goes up, and suppose it stays
up for the rest of that run. If the run is in one state at two times after the raise, step
both times back together. They can’t stay equal past the raise, because the state at
the raise reads no and every later one reads yes, so at the first pair that differs, two
different states of that very run step onto one. So after the raise the run merges or
never repeats a state, on any number of states. Before the raise it can come back to
a state and then leave it for good with no merge, which one rule can’t do. A normal
494   22 Scope


             form, with no next state, is the halt again: a reading kept by stopping is kept with
             no merge, as Theorem 1.2 says. For such steps the first argument says little by itself:
             in the lambda calculus every term N is one step from two different terms, (λx.x ) N
             and (λz.N ) M with z not free in N, so two states sharing a next state is no news
             there, and the second argument is the one that carries weight. And when a step
             can branch, a shared next state doesn’t by itself bunch the crowd up, since a branch
             spreads it out again; with chances on the steps and finitely many states, the count
             that does is Theorem 1.7.
                 Where they stop. Steps in continuous time have no next state to count, and
             nothing here covers them. Steps by chance where endlessly many states read yes,
             and unitary steps whose kept part has endlessly many dimensions, get none of the
             finite results above, and the bilateral shift keeps a reading with no merge, a fresh
             state every step. What still reaches them is the run: a unitary step is one rule, so
             its runs are Proposition 3.5’s, and one run of steps by chance is a run the second
             argument covers. And a truth isn’t a process at all: that a statement is provable is a
             fact with no step in it, and the theorems are about a run that derives it. What they
             give is the merge or the fresh states. The heat stays Landauer’s premise.
                 What I’m proposing beyond that. A way of describing computation in which the
             relations a computation carries live in the state, what each move does to them lives
             in the step, and a price list is one part of the description, not an afterthought. The
             permanent record is the one case I took apart all the way. The pointer thesis asks
             whether certifying is the thing that deserves that record in the systems it talks about,
             and it can be wrong without touching the latch or the window arguments, which
             never use it.
                 Underneath that is a question about which distinctions a description of a compu-
             tation ought to keep. The constructions show particular ways of keeping some, and
             what follows once you do, under premises I’ve printed. What that’s worth depends
             on what you need the description to answer. A program log with a proof about its
             updates may recover the required distinctions. A host can instead enforce those
             updates through every guest program. A system may prevent an act with a wall,
             penalise it afterwards, or charge it at the step. Comparing those choices means
             following what each one guarantees for the task.
CHAPTER 23




Conclusion

Put the blank cell, the triangle, the cups and the two computers back on the table.
The cell went from nothing to a 0 and stayed, and that was an event that had to be
paid for. Turning the triangle preserves relations you can check with your fingers.
Turning a cup records an act; a row of cups can distinguish stages that one cup
cannot. The two computers can leave the same answer while differing in what they
did to reach it. In each case I had to say what the things were, which moves were
allowed, which relations survived, and what my way of looking could tell apart.
    Part I started at the bottom, with the cell. On any machine run by one rule, every
step lands on a fresh state, merges two into one, or goes round a loop, and a run
that raises a reading that stays either merges somewhere or never repeats a state,
so it’s paid in a merge or in fresh states, on top of the dissipation of every change
a real device makes, more the faster it goes. The counting needs nothing but one
rule and a reading that stays. A single 0 written on a blank cell is already a merge,
and every zoom pays the same way. Then the model got an exact form: five parts,
one rule, one theorem you proved at the table, what keeping takes written into a
step. Then the rule stopped being only my preference. With finitely many yes-states
and a flag that stays up, the fresh states run out, every move that raises the flag
merges, and under the merge-pricing rule the toll follows. The collision belongs
to the instruction, over the states it’s allowed to act on; the state that just came in
needn’t be one of the two that collide. Turning that into heat takes a spread over
inputs and Landauer’s premise on top, its critics named; from a start somebody
already knows, the premise puts no floor under it, because the distinction was kept,
and paid for, in the knowing; the step still dissipates when it happens. The toll is a
derivation under three premises you can refuse one at a time, each with the machine
that walks past it built; what keeping takes, underneath it, isn’t. Learning borrows:
copying onto a blank page merges nothing, the copy can be handed back, and the
page is paid for when it’s wiped. Committing makes a record that can’t be handed
back, so it pays. That’s as far as physics goes in this book, and I’ve tried to keep it
exactly that far.
    Part II gave the triangle and the cups their words: structure is relations among
things, kept under the changes you choose, carried by whatever stuff happens to
be there, relative to a frame. A partition turned out to be the smallest sorting by


                                                 495
496   23 Conclusion


              the ruler I picked, and a cell that goes from blank to 0 and stays is that smallest
              sorting, one yes-or-no question, kept. And making a grouping, keeping it, checking
              it and standing behind it came apart into four different acts. So the question became
              how an account of computation could carry what keeping the cell’s 0 takes, and the
              difference between those acts, in its step.
                  The rest of Part II was the logic, and what it earned comes next, in the order
              it was earned. The counter is arithmetic once the schedule is chosen. A window
              in which a raising step and a quiet one look the same can’t price the raise exactly,
              by a fact about functions far older than the machine. Entitlement is defined as
              an object, a checked relation, and a paid event; given lists, a tree and a covering
              somebody supplies, a run that paid a charged step for every level of the tree has
              paid for the index bits it commits to (that count doesn’t show a run has to pay them,
              the run doesn’t recover the tree, the lists count repeats, and the index bits aren’t the
              questions anybody asked); when the run makes the narrowing itself, every candidate
              dropped was dropped by a test the run paid for, and the index bits are at most k
              times the cost when each test keeps a 2−k share; on every certified Thiele-complete
              machine the same count, for a run from a clean start, is a theorem about its record
              moves, with the earned chain inside the run, and the count can’t do without the
              covering; and it is a license to lean on a claim. It doesn’t prove the claim true.
              Insight, in the sense the toll prices, is a distinction made to stay. A feeling doesn’t
              count. Its floor is flat: at least one, however deep. The claim behind the flag is
              something a check could have refused, and in the bare model nothing makes the
              commit wait for the check. Over any base, a base-driven record is a latch, with two
              unforced choices, the event and the price list; “only one substrate” is false and “one
              structure, many price lists” is true once the event is fixed. No procedure whose flip
              the substrate itself can represent decides the shortcut predicate, given a recursion
              theorem, by the same diagonal that broke Frege’s floor, and the machine’s answer is
              to record the commitment. It leaves the judgement unautomated.
                  Part III built an example that meets the definition. The small machine’s state
              ties a checked claim to an edition of a counter, and its step uses the tie: change the
              counter and the old check no longer lets you commit. So from a clean start a raised
              flag needs a passing check, a commitment about the same edition and a certificate,
              in that order. A cost of three is enough, and no such run pays less. Those are facts
              about the example, the check that can’t fail included, and its two-counter base is
              universal under Minsky’s packing.
                  The universal programs ask whether those relations survive somebody else’s
              machine doing the work. On the host with more counters, U runs the small
              machine’s programs from clean starts, halts when they halt with their answers, earns
              its own flag exactly when the guest raises one, and matches the ledger wherever the
              two line up. With PAY added, UP runs every computably presented Thiele machine,
                                                                                            497


latches the guest’s reading through its own earned chain, and carries the guest’s
ledger to within the stated surcharge: at most two at the raise when the reading
starts at no. The theorems say which states match; the appendix on running it
(Appendix G) says how long this particular build takes to get there, which is a long
time.
    Then I changed the base and joined machines up, to see what carried over. The
panel bolts onto any box with a universal base, with the boxes it won’t fit named
(Appendix E). Two machines side by side need both records kept; one total loses
which side did the work. Hand-offs and nested runs each come with conditions
of their own (Appendix F). Every one of those constructions makes you say which
relation survives the change and which is lost, and that saying is the work.
    Then came a check worth earning, the two-player game with an integer test
whose pass forces Tsirelson’s bound for the tally it’s handed. Of five record disciplines
I modelled in fragments, one charges a fee at the write, and which event to record
is a thesis, with its refutations listed. And then came what the counter has to do
with physics, which is less than the name Landauer might suggest. Two facts about
the machine sit where they belong. Its unpriced steps merge states, because that’s
what forgetting scratch work is; whatever those merges cost the hardware is off the
ledger, so the toll on this machine comes from the record layer’s merge premise,
with no finiteness premise on the whole machine; the only finiteness in it is the
flag’s two readings. And a check that cannot fail still certifies for three, because the
step charges for the act, and the entitlement count says what the claim bought.
    Part IV brings those pieces together (Section 20). A finite permanent holder has
to merge; the named price rule puts that merger on a ledger; a window determines
which part of it a reader can recover. The example machine then supplies the earned
path from a passing check to commitment and certification. Each argument has its
place in that chain, and the constructions show how to carry it out.
    Four contributions bring that chain into focus, each alongside the earlier work
it builds on. First, the toll isn’t only my preference: on a finite machine a reading
nothing turns off can only be turned on by a step that merges states, so if merges
are priced, raising it costs (Theorem 3.1, Observation 3.3); and on any machine
a raise that merges nothing needs endlessly many yes-states, so it pays in fresh
states instead (Proposition 3.4). The counting under it is the finite cousin of the
recurrence argument Zermelo threw at Boltzmann in 1896, and the abstract merge
price is motivated by Landauer’s reset example. Identifying that price with heat
needs the further premises stated in Part I. Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) had
already put a physical price on that merge for finite automata, and Li and Vitányi
(1996) had already assumed a unit price on each irreversibly erased bit in a model
of computation, and Demaine and his coauthors (2016) a price on instructions that
destroy bits, so what’s here is the toll such a price forces on a reading that stays.
498   23 Conclusion


              Second, a window that shows a raising step and a quiet one the same can’t price
              the raise exactly (Observation 7.2); that a price computed from what a window
              shows can’t tell apart two steps the window shows the same is elementary, and
              what’s here is the pricing form. Third, a record driven by the computation that
              never switches off is a latch on one event, over any base (Observation 10.1); latches
              and history variables are old, and the theorem covers only records that never come
              down. Beside it, built rather than new, sit the definition of Thiele-complete, which
              any universal base meets once marks are added (Section 10.8), and the slice under
              it: a computer with a move for each two-counter instruction is what’s left of a
              certified Thiele-complete machine with its record layer forgotten, blind to the record
              and the ledger, and every Thiele-complete machine leaves one through its window
              (Theorem E.4). That forgetting a layer gives the runs back, where the step doesn’t
              read it, is the ghost-code erasure of Section 6; what’s here is that the forgotten
              layer still earns its record, and that what’s left can’t see it. It’s a theorem about
              boxes with a universal base, and it uses no equivalence between models; the one
              that carries a box to the other models is imported (Theorem E.6). Fourth, a record
              that’s priced, and on the small machine earned (Theorem 15.11), under the move of
              guaranteeing something about every program. That move isn’t mine at all. It’s the
              reference monitor’s (Anderson, 1972), made precise for monitors that watch a run
              (Schneider, 2000), and proved for monitors checked at every instruction (Azevedo
              de Amorim and coauthors, 2015). What I put together under it is built, and its
              idea isn’t new: the check bound to the edition it looked at, the toll charged on top,
              and universal programs that carry both to every program of the small machine and
              to every computably presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag as they go.
              Appendix C sorts all four with sources.
                  And there are two things I’d point at if you asked how far the proofs reach.
              Neither is a fifth new thing.
                  In the game: an integer check on eight counts forces a five-by-five matrix to be
              positive semidefinite, and from there the Tsirelson bound follows, and the chain
              never once reaches for physics. There’s no Hilbert space in it, no operators, no
              observables. The route through the matrix is the first rung of a ladder Navascués,
              Pironio and Acín built in 2007. None of that route is mine, and the semidefinite road
              to Tsirelson’s bound is older than that. What’s here is the check that runs in whole
              numbers, and the proved link from “the check passed” to the bound. It’s algebra
              you can follow line by line. It’s algebra and nothing more, because nothing in the
              definitions or the argument ties the counts or the matrix to any physical device. And
              on the small machine’s host a raised flag can stand on that check: from a clean
              start a raised flag contains a passing CHECK of the packed counts, a COMMIT and
              a CERTIFY, and the check passes exactly when every pair was sampled and the
              five-by-five is positive semidefinite (Appendix H).
                                                                                            499


    In the model: the diagonal rules out a correct decider whenever its flip can be
expressed inside the substrate and the substrate supplies the fixed point; in L the
fixed point is proved from the reduction rules and the diagonal is Rice’s theorem.
On the small machine’s host, Kleene’s recursion theorem and Rice’s theorem are
proved for its own programs, so the wall stands there by proof, with its premise
a theorem: no host program decides a property of what a program computes that
some program has and some lacks; such a property is undecidable in the reduction
sense of Theorem 15.5 (Appendix D.4).
    There are things this book doesn’t settle, by my count. It doesn’t settle whether
the toll is the right thing to price; the five real systems mostly built a wall or a
penalty for contradiction. It doesn’t settle whether certification is the pointer event.
And it doesn’t settle whether Landauer’s critics are right, which would leave every
theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world. And the question I’d
most like someone to take from me: is there a smaller start than a partition, by a
ruler they can state? I said in Section 5 it would change this book, and it would.
    One more claim ties the counting to the world, the way Church and Turing’s
ties computing to it, and I’ll state it as what it is, a thesis, the Thiele thesis: every
physical process that computes with final answers has an exact description as a
machine run by one rule, with a next state for every state, computably presented (its
states written as whole numbers, and its step, its reading and its start for each input
computed by programs that halt on every input), on which the answer is a reading
that no run from any input ever turns off, on inputs accepted and rejected alike.
No proof settles it, because “a physical process that computes” isn’t a mathematical
object. A model of computation is one, and for a model written down as states, a
step and a reading that stays, what keeping takes needs no thesis: it’s a theorem, and
Section 22 says how far it reaches. The thesis is about what a physical computation
pays for what it keeps, which is Part I, and not a claim that its description run by one
rule, with its program loaded, is a Thiele machine: by Theorem E.4(4) that one-rule
description is one only as a clock or with a reading that never rises. Whether the
computer underneath is a Thiele machine depends on the moves it offers before a
program is chosen, and with the program in the state a reading is a record, not a
simulated bit, exactly when it never comes down from any state (Observation E.5).
So the thesis is about physical processes and the one-rule descriptions of them. The
Thiele Machine is the model that prices what such a description keeps; the thesis
does not say a physical process is one. What is proved sits on either side of the
thesis. On one side, Part I applies to every such description on the states its inputs
reach, where the answer never comes down: a run that raises it merges two of its
own states or never visits a state twice (Proposition 3.5). On the other, seen only
through which inputs it accepts, the thesis says exactly that every set a physical
process accepts with final answers is one a Turing machine can list, which is the
500   23 Conclusion


              physical Church-Turing thesis for final answers. One way, run the description from
              every input, a step at a time across all of them, and list an input the first time its
              reading says yes; no run turns its answer off, so a yes seen once is the answer. The
              other way, a set a Turing machine lists is accepted by the machine that searches
              the list for its input and then steps from its halted configuration to itself, with the
              reading “halted,” which nothing turns off. Nothing about how the keeping is paid
              survives that view: the same search held at its halt by a step to itself, which merges,
              or by a counter that goes on ticking, which takes fresh states, accepts the same
              inputs. And “final” has to cover the rejected inputs too. A machine that starts at no,
              reads yes while program n is still running and falls to no for good if it halts reads
              yes for good on exactly the programs that never halt, and no Turing machine lists
              those, since one that did, run beside the search for a halt, would decide halting.
                  And then there are the two computers of Section 14, the sorter and the copier,
              holding the same list. Walk the warehouse again. The list is in order on both. On
              the machine with the earned layer, a different part of the state tells you whether a
              check happened and a matching commitment followed it, and the rules keep that
              tied to the edition that was checked. Put your hand over that part of the machine
              and the difference between the two computers vanishes from where you’re standing.
              Change the counter and you can watch the old check go stale. Those are different
              operations with different consequences, and you can follow each one with your
              finger.
                  Carry a report out of the warehouse and you’ve got another question: what
              connects the report to the machine? The flag on its own doesn’t answer it. A
              window, a copy, a second machine and a reader each bring relations of their own,
              and the constructions in this book ask, one at a time, which of those relations hold.
              That’s how the example gets past the lamp: by what survives a change of view, a
              change of state, or a change of machine.
                  At the bottom of the Thiele Machine is one cell going from blank to 0, and the
              claim that nothing gets to be the case for free. Built on that cell, the machine is
              structure held as state, acted on by a step, with an account of the changes and a view
              that may keep or lose their distinctions. What I’m arguing is that those relations are
              part of computation itself, and not something you bolt on afterwards. The record
              and its toll are the part of that I’ve worked all the way through, and there this much
              is proved: a computer with a move for each two-counter instruction is a slice of a
              certified Thiele-complete machine, what’s left when the record layer is forgotten,
              blind to what was kept and what it cost, and every Thiele-complete machine has
              such a slice (Theorem E.4). Run as one rule, a machine has no universal base and
              no slice, and is a Thiele machine only as a clock or with a reading that never rises.
              The small machine and its interpreters are things you can take apart. Each theorem
              answers a stated question under stated premises. Put the computation, the record
                                                                                    501


and its account on the same drawing, and you can follow what changes, what stays,
and what the next reader has to work with.
CHAPTER 24




Afterword: how I got here

What I am is curious, past the point of good sense.
   I pick a thing up and cannot set it down until I have turned it over enough times
to see how it holds together, and this time it did not let go.
   I am not a programmer and I was never formally taught any of this.
   I was not trying to build a new model of computation.
   I would not have known what one was if it bit me.
   I was trying to build a 3D renderer.
   There was no plan behind it.
   Just a pull to make something real with my own hands, and the kind of stubborn-
ness that will not let a thing go until it stands up on its own.
   I have worked on it in off hours every day since.
   Once I started digging in, two things came clear fast. I knew nothing about
computers, and the field was already saturated, every obvious road paved and
crowded. So I needed an angle nobody else was standing on, and the angle I had
wasn’t a strategy. It was just the only way my head works. I did not know what
compositional meant. I had never heard of category theory. I called the thing I was
building digital DNA, because that is what it felt like in my hands, and I thought
about it in the only language I had: gravity pipes and directions and vectors, things
that were linear and somehow not linear at the same time, structure that flowed
and joined and came apart without my owning one proper word for any of it. I built
a custom rendering pipeline out of those intuitions, by feel, throwing out pieces that
did not sit right even when I could not have told you the rule they were breaking.
And then, the way I always do, I went looking for what I was actually doing, and
found out it already had a name. An old one. A deep one. What I had been reaching
for in the dark was composition. It was category theory, a whole field I had never
once heard of, sitting there describing the exact shapes I had been shoving around.
The moment that landed, the rendering pipeline stopped being a rendering pipeline
and started turning into a categorical engine, and I started swallowing the real
theory as fast as I could find the words for things I had already built.
   I took it one concept at a time, and I would not move to the next until I could
watch the current one actually run. Category. Object. Morphism. Functor. Monoidal
product. It came together in pieces and never in chapters, the way a picture resolves


                                 502
                                                                                           503


out of static. The Yoneda lemma (a result buried deep in category theory) was the
piece that made the rest snap into place.
    Then within weeks I found out the engine I had built to draw pictures was
general enough to run a physics simulation on the exact same primitives, without my
rewriting any of it. I wrote Newton’s laws as a program in it, half expecting nothing,
and it ran. I want to be careful about what that was and what it was not, because
this is exactly the kind of thing that gets misread. It was not me deriving physics, and
I am not claiming the machine explains gravity. It was the compositional structure
being general enough to express a physics simulation the same way it had expressed
a renderer, and that generality is what told me the structure was the point and the
pixels never were. Somewhere in those weeks I crossed from debugging why one
pixel would not show up to understanding that I had quietly built a categorical
computing engine, and that the rendering had only ever been the first thing I aimed
it at. The pixel did eventually show up, for what it is worth.
    I kept going, because by then I could not not keep going. The night the engine
first ran a program declaratively, meaning I told it what should happen and let it
work out the how without my spelling out each step, I told my wife, Julie, I thought
I was onto something. She said okay.
    Then I hit a wall, and it is the wall this whole document is about. Every tool I
had for settling questions about what I’d built could settle the small ones and fell
over on the exact ones I needed answered, which left me staring down an infinite
hallway of guess-and-test with no proof waiting at the end of it, ever. One night, not
even working, I was watching a video about Flatland, the old story about a creature
living in two dimensions who cannot so much as picture a third. And it landed on
me sideways, all at once, the way the real ones always do. I said it out loud: I get it
now. There is another axis. Classical computation only ever sees what it can read
and write off its own surface, and there is a whole direction it is blind to. It isn’t
broken. It was just never built with an eye that points that way. That’s how it landed
that night, and it didn’t survive in that form: the direction turned out to be one
an ordinary computer can reach, and what the usual rules leave out is the price
(Section 2.6 says where the axis ended up). The two computers in Section 14 are my
attempt to show you that blindness with something you can hold. That same night
I gave the idea a name: the Thiele Machine. The name began as a working title
and became the name of the model. It carries the larger claim plainly: the machine
treats structural state as part of computation.
    What survived the whole trip from there to here is not the renderer. Not one
piece of it, and good riddance. What survived was a single commitment I made
early and never once let anyone talk me out of: structure is the state itself, the
actual thing the machine runs on. It is no metaphor laid over some realer state
underneath. Category theory was the first language I found for that structure. It is
504   24 Afterword: how I got here


              not what the model is. The model asks for a state, a step, a record, a ledger, and a
              window, and category theory appears nowhere in that list. The morphisms in that
              first engine, the night they first composed correctly at two in the morning, were
              objects that remembered where they came from; the records in the small machine I
              ended up with remember where they came from too, and you can walk up to one
              and challenge it. The receipt grew teeth. But the shape itself never moved. The
              shape was the substrate the entire time, and everything else, every renderer and
              every proof, was me slowly learning to see what I had already built. By the shape I
              mean structure held as state. Not category theory. Category theory was just the first
              language I had for it.
                  Every step pulled back to show another layer underneath that I had not known
              was there, and I mean that plainly: I did not know what a Turing machine was when
              I started, I did not know most of the words in this document existed. I learned each
              one the same way, by walking face-first into a wall that needed it and not being let
              past until I had it. The needing always came first. The learning came after, dragged
              along behind the needing because it had no say in the matter.
                  Large language models were my hands the whole way through, and I want
              the division of labor exact, because it is the thing people most want to get wrong
              about work like this. The hands had nothing like this to draw on: no reference
              implementation, no prior project to point at. The ideas, the architecture, the
              direction, the demand that the thing be true: those are mine, all of them, no asterisk.
              The symbol-pushing, the code and the formal derivations, the models produced. So I
              read every statement. A derivation can settle an empty question, and I had to refuse
              that too. However the symbols got onto the page, the argument on it is checkable
              by reading, and it would be exactly as right or as wrong if a million monkeys had
              typed it. The monkeys could not have refused.
                  A word on what I actually do, because it runs under everything after it. I do
              not write code or math by hand. I do not pick constants. I do not grind through
              derivations. I have never written a line of code on paper or in a notepad in my life.
              What I do is see, and direct, and refuse. When I take hold of an idea it does not stay
              a point. It opens up. It becomes a shape I can blow up and turn over and take apart,
              lay across another shape to find where the two of them touch, run forward and then
              back to where it started, zoom into until it is the only thing in the world and pull
              back until it is one dot in a field of other dots, and the whole time it stays wired to
              everything I have ever connected it to, the right connections and the wrong ones
              both, all of them live at once. I am not reading that field neutrally, the way a search
              would. The thing doing the looking is me, the whole of me, my gut and my mood
              and my stubbornness picking what lights up and which way I move through it, and
              that is the part you cannot lift out without turning me back into a search engine. So
              I see where a thing has to fit, the shape it is obligated to have, usually well before I
                                                                                            505


could write it down in a single symbol. Then the model gives me the symbols, and I
refuse anything whose argument does not hold or does not match the shape I am
holding. That refusal is the one thing in this entire document that is mine and only
mine: the demand that it be true, and the throwing-out of everything that wasn’t.
    I am telling you all of this because it’s the engine. I did not come up through
anywhere that hands you a foundation and says trust us, this part is settled. No
professors, no colleagues, no field full of authority to lean back on when a claim got
heavy. From the outside that is a deficit. From the inside it is the whole reason any
of this is solid: when I meet a claim I either find the proof or I do not believe it, and
that goes double for my own, because my own are the ones I most want to wave
through. It is how I am built. It is the only way I know to hold a thing and actually
trust that I am holding it.
    So everything in here gets built from the ground up. It isn’t a courtesy to you. I
build it because I do not believe I understand a thing until I have built it with my
own hands, watched it stand up on its own, and tried to knock it over. I built this
document the exact way I built the machine, brick by brick, refusing each brick until
it held weight. That includes the parts you already knew cold before you opened
this. I did not skip them for you, and I could not skip them for me.
    The vocabulary I had to go look up to do any of this sits at the back of the book,
so the argument comes first. If a word stops you, it is there. If you already know this
material, you never have to open it. But if you catch something in the basics that is
wrong, I want to know, and I mean that as a real ask. It isn’t politeness. Nothing in
here is correct just because I wrote it. Especially the parts I wrote.
    On the name. I wanted to call it the meta machine. Then, in October 2021,
Facebook renamed its company Meta: a company taking a term for self-reference as
its name and draining the word of meaning in the same motion. So I went one level
up, where this machine already lives. The most meta move available, for a machine
that runs on meta-level reasoning, was to put my own name on the cover and take
the word back. That’s the whole of it, a meta move on a meta machine. It happens
to be my dad’s name too, and my wife’s now. So I asked them before I did it. They
said go ahead.
APPENDIX A




Things I had to learn first

I came in with none of the formal fields this work turned out to need. By the time
the argument had taken shape I’d needed enough of half a dozen of them that I had
to put down somewhere what those fields had words for. This appendix is that place.
None of it is the argument; it’s what I needed to be able to make it. Everything
below is what I understood after I went and read about it; I’m not claiming to teach
you these subjects, and if you already know a part, skip it.


A.1 Bits, bytes, and what a CPU sees

A bit is one digit that’s either zero or one, the smallest fact a machine can hold.
Everything else is bits stacked up. Eight of them make a byte, which lands you any
number from 0 to 255, and the first thing that genuinely surprised me is that the
same byte is also a letter: a convention called ASCII simply agrees to call 65 the
letter A, 48 the digit 0, 32 a space. Nothing in the byte knows which it is. The
meaning is a convention laid on top.
    You can see the convention’s seams with a pencil. Write 65 in binary: 1000001.
Knock off the first two digits and what’s left, 00001, is 1, and A is the first letter. B is
66, which ends in 00010, two. Now lower case: a is 97, which is 1100001, the same
pattern with one more bit switched on, the one worth 32. Every capital and its small
letter differ in exactly that bit, and that’s on purpose. The first version of the code,
in 1963, had no lower case at all; when lower case arrived, in the 1967 revision,
it was placed so the two cases differ by one bit, which made matching them, and
building keyboards and printers, simpler. Nothing in the byte knows it’s a letter, but
somebody made the letters easy for a circuit to tell apart.
    Everything in this subsection is about real CPUs. None of it belongs to the abstract
model, which has a kind of state and a step rule and nothing about widths or slots,
and the small machine of Section 15 needs very little of it: its two counters have no
width at all, and hold any whole number.
    A word is a chunk of bits the CPU treats as one unit, in 2026 usually 64 bits (0 to
about 18 quintillion) on a desktop or server and 32 (0 to about 4 billion) on many
small devices. The abstract model doesn’t care which width.
    A register is a named storage slot inside the CPU that holds one word, the fastest
place to read or write. Memory is a longer list of word-sized slots accessed by index,

                                   506
                                                              A.2 The notation the formal parts use   507


the address. The program counter is one specific register that tracks where in the
program the machine is; after every instruction it moves on to the next instruction
unless the instruction says jump. On the small machine it’s called the line number.
A stack pointer is a register pointing at the top of a region used for nested calls. A
port is a named channel for talking to the outside world.
   Modular arithmetic means counting wraps around: counting modulo 16, the
numbers run 0 to 15, and 17 wraps to 1. Bitwise operations work on the bits of a
value one position at a time: AND is 1 only when both bits are, OR when either is,
XOR (exclusive or) exactly when they differ. A logical shift moves bits left or right:
for unsigned values it multiplies or divides by a power of two, discarding overflow
on a fixed-width left shift and rounding down on a right shift. Popcount is the count
of one-bits in a value. Hexadecimal is base 16, digits 0 to 9 then A to F, written with
a 0x prefix: 0xFF is 255.
   A trap, on a CPU, transfers control to a handler; the interrupted program may
later resume. It can report an error or request a service. On the small machine a
trap is one bit that goes up when an instruction refuses, and then the core stops
moving. An ISA, instruction set architecture, is the list of every instruction a CPU
recognises, each identified by an opcode, a numeric tag the CPU decodes. The small
machine’s has six. The abstract model has none; it has a step rule.


A.2 The notation the formal parts use
I don’t think in these symbols, and I had to learn to read them. The natural numbers
are 0, 1, 2, and so on, written with a double-struck N; the integers add the negatives;
the reals are the whole number line. A function from a set A to a set B is written
with an arrow. For a finite set, vertical bars around it mean its size; for a number, its
absolute value. A big sigma is a sum over every member of a set. A delta before a
quantity means the change in it. An upside-down A means “for every”; a backwards
E means “there exists.” A double arrow is implication; a double-headed one is “if
and only if.” A small circle between two functions is composition, apply the right one
first. Angle brackets mean one of three things, and the sentence around them says
which: a pair of numbers packed into one, ⟨m, n⟩ (Appendix D.1); a dot product of
two vectors; or, around a random quantity, its long-run average, which I picked up
from the Bell-test papers. The circled times ⊗ in the quantum derivation combines
two systems: A ⊗ B acts as A on the first and B on the second; Appendix I gives
its entries. The integer check itself uses neither it nor any quantum system. A
superscript T on a matrix is its transpose, rows and columns swapped, and I with a
subscript n is the identity matrix.
508   A Things I had to learn first


               A.3 Category theory beyond the sketch
               Section 5 sketches objects, arrows, composition, identities, associativity, and the
               identity laws. Beyond that: a functor is a structure-preserving map from one
               category to another, sending objects to objects and arrows to arrows while respecting
               composition and identities; think of it as a translation rule between two worlds
               of structure. An embedding is a functor that throws nothing away, and faithful is
               the precise version for arrows: two distinct arrows between the same two objects
               never land on one. Conservative is the version for inverses: if the image of an arrow
               has an inverse, the arrow already had one, so the functor can’t manufacture an
               isomorphism (an arrow with an inverse) that wasn’t there. The two properties are
               different, and neither gives the other. Read the natural numbers under addition as
               a category with one object and an arrow for each number, and the same for the
               integers. The inclusion of the first into the second is faithful, since distinct naturals
