    Everything in the right column is stated with its premises in the body of the book,
and everything in the middle column is cited where it’s used. The table is the short
form. The long form is the rest of this appendix, which takes each row, says what
was already known with sources, and says what kind of addition each one is. Very
little of the right column is a new result. Most of it is things built, new proofs of
known things, and known pieces put together under one question.
    A few more labels I went and looked up are neighbours. Some of them also sit in
the table above, and one, the reference monitor, is the move the small machine’s
step makes. I list them so you can see why I don’t think the toll is one of them under
a new name. Each is a claim inviting correction.
• Linear logic (Girard 1987) treats an assumption as a resource that gets used up.
  It constrains what a program, or a proof, may consume. The toll constrains the
  model’s step function instead. It’s the same instinct at a different layer.
• Foundational proof-carrying code (Appel 2001) checks safety proofs against the
  smallest trusted base it can: a logic plus the machine’s semantics. Here no proof
  rides along with the program. The step rule writes the receipts as the run goes.
• Session types (Honda 1993) constrain how programs talk to each other so the
  conversation can’t go off script. The toll is about what one computation has paid
  to establish, which is a different problem.
• No Free Lunch (Wolpert and Macready 1997): averaged over every problem,
  whatever an optimiser gains on some problems it gives back on others. That’s an
528   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


                  average over a whole problem space, and the edge is paid for elsewhere. The toll
                  charges one step in one run, with no refund anywhere.
               • Kolmogorov complexity (Kolmogorov 1965): the description complexity of a
                 string is the length of the shortest program that prints it, relative to a fixed
                 description language. That’s a property of a finished string, with no steps and no
                 moment of paying. The toll is a law about a step.
               • Irreversibility cost and information distance (Zurek 1989; Bennett, Gács, Li,
                 Vitányi and Zurek 1998; Li and Vitányi 1996): the fewest bits a reversible
                 machine must take in and erase irreversibly to turn a string x into a string y,
                 about C ( x | y) + C (y | x ), where C ( x | y) is the length of the shortest program
                 that prints x given y; and Kolchinsky and Wolpert’s thermodynamic complexity
                 of a Turing machine’s outputs (2020). These tie algorithmic information to steps
                 and erasures, and they price a transformation between strings, or an output, in
                 erased bits. The toll prices the rise of a chosen reading.
               • Cook and Levin (Cook 1971; Levin 1973): checking can be cheap while finding
                 looks expensive, and whether finding is really harder is the open P-versus-NP
                 question, a gap in how difficulty grows with size. The toll puts a fixed floor under
                 the one step that commits, however easy or hard the finding was.
               • The thermodynamic cost of choosing (Rovelli 2024): settling a binary choice at
                 temperature T dissipates at least kT ln 2, with no outside heat bath. That’s the
                 closest thing to the toll itself I’ve found, because it charges a commitment. An
                 object or an average isn’t what it prices. But it’s physics, indexed to a temperature,
                 and its choice is unpredictable, a branching, and stable only for a while, where
                 the toll prices a deterministic no-to-yes transition. On my side, finitely many
                 yes-states and permanence are what force the raising move to merge states. The
                 toll charges the commitment in a model of computation, with no temperature in
                 it. It’s the closest neighbour, and it’s still a different thing.
               • Persistent copies (Ouldridge and ten Wolde 2017; Ouldridge, Govern and ten
                 Wolde 2017): making a copy that stays correlated with its original after the
                 two come apart has a thermodynamic floor. The nearest physics I’ve found to
                 “learning borrows, committing pays.” It’s heat for a correlation, in chemistry; the
                 toll is a count in a model of computation.
               • Thermodynamics of finite automata (Ouldridge and Wolpert 2023): if the smallest
                 automaton for a language has a letter that sends two states to one, recognising
                 that language on a device that repeats one local step produces entropy, and if
                 the smallest automaton only reshuffles, recognition carries no such floor. That’s
                 Part I’s counting of states with a physical price on it, and one of their worked
                 examples is the latch’s language turned inside out. It’s the closest neighbour of
                                                                                         529


  all to the road the toll is derived on; Section 3 says exactly what’s left over for
  me.
• CerCo, the Certified Complexity project of Amadio and coauthors, builds a verified
  C compiler that carries the object code’s execution cost back up to annotations
  on the source. There the cost decorates the program and survives compilation.
  Here it lives in the model’s step rule.
• Reference monitors and execution monitors (Anderson 1972; Schneider 2000;
  Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors 2015). A small piece every action passes
  through, enforcing a rule on every program. Schneider argued that a monitor
  watching a run can enforce only rules whose breaking shows up at a finite point,
  and “no certificate without an earlier passing check and commit” is one of those;
  the micro-policies check a tag rule at every instruction, proved correct. That’s the
  move the small machine’s step makes, so this one isn’t a neighbour at all: the
  small machine’s step is a monitor of this kind. What’s added is the edition-bound
  check-then-commit with a paid, permanent record on top, and the derivation
  of why the payment can’t be zero. Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett and Fred
  Schneider (2006) went on to sort which rules monitors, program rewriters and
  static checkers can each enforce, and they differ, which is one reason this book
  doesn’t claim that every enforcement mechanism is a Thiele machine underneath.
• Trusted components in replicated services (Chun and coauthors 2007; Levin and
  coauthors 2009; Veronese and coauthors 2013; Decouchant and coauthors 2022;
  Clement, Junqueira, Kate and Rodrigues 2012): a small record inside each replica
  that a replica taken over still can’t make say two things, with a proof of exactly
  what that buys. The record is theirs. The toll isn’t in their picture.
• Ghost state (Owicki and Gries 1976; Filliâtre, Gondelman and Paskevich 2014):
  variables added for a proof that can be erased without changing what the program
  computes. The flag and the counter are ghost in that sense. The small machine’s
  table of checked facts isn’t, because the step reads it and refuses on it, for every
  program. The slice of Appendix E is that erasure on the lift, while its trap is
  down, with two things on top: the erased layer still earns its record, and what’s
  left can’t read the record or the ledger (Theorem E.4).
• Verifiable computation and proof-carrying data (Parno, Howell, Gentry and
  Raykova 2013; Chiesa and Tromer 2010): a short proof, checkable by a stranger,
  that a computation’s output is right. That establishes the claim for the stranger,
  and anyone with the inputs can make one, the copier included. The record here
  is about one machine’s own history. A proof like that is one way to carry the local
  record out of the box.
• Commitments and entitlements (Brandom 1994): talk as score-keeping, tracking
  who is committed to what and who is entitled to it. Brandom’s entitlements can
530   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


                  be defeated and can be passed on by testimony. Here entitlement is priced, step
                  by step, and a copy carries it only as far as the copy is genuine. The words are
                  the same and the machinery is different.
               • Correspondence assertions (Woo and Lam 1993; Gordon and Jeffrey 2003). In
                 protocol verification, “this end event must be preceded by a begin event for the
                 same thing” is a correspondence assertion, and a type system can prove a protocol
                 keeps it against any opponent. “No certificate without an earlier commit, and
                 no commit without an earlier check of the same claim” has that shape. Theirs is
                 proved about programs by typing. Mine is enforced by the step, which is the LCF
                 comparison again, at the level of single instructions.
               • Monotonic parallel composition (Åman Pohjola and Parrow 2016) and persistence
                 in the pi-calculus (Palamidessi, Saraswat, Valencia and Victor 2006). Åman
                 Pohjola and Parrow separate models where a neighbouring process can never
                 stop a step from models that can solve consensus, and test-and-set, an instruction
                 that writes a cell and reports what was there, is on the consensus side. Palamidessi
                 and coauthors compare messages that are used up with messages that stay, and
                 the end of their study is a reduction from Minsky machines. The small machine,
                 put into Åman Pohjola and Parrow’s setting with threads pooled on one shared
                 state (two states that have both moved jam), has a consensus process in their
                 sense, so it lands on their non-monotonic side; their theorem and that placing
                 are argued in a few lines in Section 15. The comparison with Palamidessi and
                 coauthors’ persistence stays a comparison.
               • Constructor theory (Deutsch and Marletto 2015; Marletto 2016; Marletto, Vedral
                 and coauthors 2022; Violaris and Marletto 2022): physics as which tasks a device
                 that runs in a cycle can do, with irreversible meaning possible while the inverse
                 isn’t. It’s the nearest physics I know to “committing costs” stated for a cycling
                 device. It’s quantum and approximate, and Part I’s counting of states is classical,
                 finite and exact (Section 3).
               • Accountability and fault detection (Haeberlen and Kuznetsov 2009; Küsters,
                 Truderung and Vogt 2010; Treitz and Künnemann 2026): when an outside party
                 can tell who misbehaved. Their windows are this book’s windows, and the trust
                 they leave over, an honest log or a trusted step, is left over here too (Section 7).
               • Transferability (Easwaran 2009): a deductive proof lets you learn from someone
                 you don’t trust because you can check every step, and a probabilistic proof doesn’t.
                 That’s the argument for carrying the object and re-running the check (Section 7).
                   And then the silly question that list raises, which I’m going to chase anyway: why
               is an optimisation theorem named after lunch? Wolpert and Macready borrowed
               an old saying, “there ain’t no such thing as a free lunch,” and the saying is older
                                                   C.1 Every step is a fresh state, a merge, or a loop   531


than almost everyone who gets credit for it. American saloons in the 1800s put out
a free lunch for anyone who bought a drink, and the drink paid for the lunch. A
Washington newspaper was already saying in 1909 that somebody has to pay for a
free lunch; a newspaper fable by Walter Morrow had the whole line in 1938; a book
by Pierre Dos Utt already had the squeezed form, TANSTAAFL, as its title in 1949;
Robert Heinlein’s 1966 novel The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress made that squeezed form
famous; and the economist Milton Friedman put the saying on the cover of his 1975
book of essays on public policy. I’d have credited Heinlein or Friedman. As far as
anything I could find goes, neither coined it. That’s Stigler’s law again, at lunch,
and it matters here because No Free Insight is named like a cousin of the saying,
and the family resemblance misleads in one way. The saloon’s lunch was paid for
somewhere else, in the price of the beer, and that’s Wolpert and Macready’s shape:
a gain here, handed back over there. The toll isn’t that. On the ledger nothing gets
paid somewhere else: the step that raises the flag pays, on the spot. A blank tape is
the saloon’s shape, paid for before the run by whoever wiped it; the toll is the step
that won’t hide its share that way.


C.1 Every step is a fresh state, a merge, or a loop
Known: the step law is the first-return argument every textbook on dynamics makes,
and under it sits the pigeonhole. A one-to-one move that raises a reading and
keeps it is Hilbert’s hotel, everybody moving up a room so that a room is left empty
(Hilbert’s lecture course of 1924–25, made famous by Gamow in 1947), and a
collection that can be matched one-to-one with a part of itself that leaves something
out is exactly what Dedekind (1888) called infinite. Recurrence for reversible finite
machines is Poincaré’s (1890) and Zermelo’s (1896) in its finite form. The noisy
steps are the fact that a doubly stochastic chain has no closed class it can enter
from outside, with Gibbs’s inequality for the entropy gap; the unitary steps are that
a unitary preserving a finite-dimensional subspace preserves its complement; the
bilateral shift is the standard example of what goes wrong without finite dimension.
Heat against time is Bennett’s Brownian computer (1982) with Schnakenberg’s
formula for the entropy a biased walk hands its surroundings; that any change of
a device’s states finished in a finite time dissipates, shrinking toward zero only as
the time grows without bound, is finite-time stochastic thermodynamics (Schmiedl
and Seifert, 2007; Shiraishi, Funo and Saito, 2018); and the trade of space for time
by recomputing is Bennett’s (1989). The measurements are Bérut and coauthors’
(2012), Jun, Gavrilov and Bechhoefer’s (2014), Hong and coauthors’ (2016) and
Gaudenzi and coauthors’ (2018). Mine: the reading, that the write of a 0 on a cell is
a merge and the toll is the price of something being the case; putting those old facts
side by side as one law with three columns (a fresh state, a merge, a loop that makes
532   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               nothing new) and no fourth, for deterministic, noisy and quantum steps alike; the
               merge-or-fresh-state dichotomy for a reading that stays up, with no finiteness in it;
               and the exact count of states for a bounded memory, M ≥ 1 + ( T + 1)( N − 1), with
               a building that reaches it (Section 3, Section 1); and that a merge seen in a coarse
               description forces, in any finer description it’s exact about, a fine merge, a fine
               step out of the set, or infinitely many fine states (Theorem 1.10). Kind: synthesis
               and a reading, with the count of states and the every-scale theorem as small exact
               lemmas. The mathematics is old. What I’d defend is the arrangement: endless
               memory, history-keeping and reversible machines aren’t a way out of what keeping
               takes, they’re the fresh-state column, which dodges only the floor a merge adds and
               never the dissipation of a step happening; and finiteness is what takes that column
               away.


               C.2 The universal floor and the potential method
               Known: the potential method of amortized analysis, a function on states whose drop
               bounds the cost of a run, is Tarjan’s (1985). Later developments include Nipkow’s
               accounts (2015 and 2019) and Charguéraud and Pottier’s time credits (2019). It
               has been built into type systems for automatic resource analysis (from Hofmann
               and Jost, 2003, and Hoffmann and coauthors, 2011, onward), and recast in cost-
               aware type theories (Niu, Sterling, Grodin and Harper, 2022). Mine: choosing
               the potential that is one when a designated reading says no and zero when it says
               yes, so that “the crossing costs” (the toll) and “every run that crosses paid” (the
               floor) are the potential method’s two halves (Section 6), and its count, one unit per
               crossing (Observation 2.3), the same sum read crossing by crossing. Kind: a known
               technique, used with one particular potential. The choice is the reading, and it’s
               the point: it makes “was certified” something the account must carry. The numbers
               come with it. A potential that reads only the reading has to drop by exactly one
               from no to yes, or its inequality says something other than the toll on a machine of
               two states and one move; so it’s one at no and zero at yes, up to a constant added
               to both. The theorem is not new mathematics. If it looks clever, that’s Tarjan’s
               cleverness; my part was picking which reading to plug in.
                  Go back to Tarjan’s paper and there’s a sentence that sits right on the line this
               book draws. He opens with the dictionary (to amortize is to put money aside at
               intervals, as in a sinking fund) and then gives two views of the method. In the
               banker’s view the computer is coin-operated, and each operation is handed credits
               to spend or save; in the physicist’s view, which he credits to Daniel Sleator, every
               state has a potential and you count its changes. Then he stops to say that the credits
               are only an accounting device: the programs that actually run contain no mention
               of credits or debits. That’s exactly right for what he wanted, a bound proved about
                                       C.3 The toll from finiteness, permanence, and a price on merges   533


a program from outside. It’s also exactly the gap. In his method the coins live in the
proof. The one move I chose was to put them in the step, where no program takes
a step without it being counted. The arithmetic is the same, and only the place is
different.


C.3 The toll from finiteness, permanence, and a price on merges

Known: that steps which merge states (no single-valued inverse) are what Landauer’s
principle charges for is Landauer’s (1961), sharpened by Bennett (1973, 1982, 2003;
the words “the erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths” are from
the 2003 abstract); generalizations and the dependence on the input distribution are
Maroney’s (2009), Sagawa’s (2014), Wolpert’s; the critique is Earman and Norton’s
and Norton’s. Write-once memory is an old topic in coding theory (Rivest and Shamir,
1982), where the question is reuse, and what it takes is counted in cells, which in
this book’s words is paying in fresh states; heat and prices never come up, and Chris
Heegard (1985) worked out the capacity of permanent memory with noise, again
a question of how much fits. Statisticians priced permanence on finite memory in
their own currency: in Hellman and Cover’s analysis of hypothesis testing with finite
memory (1970), a machine that settles its answer by falling into states it never leaves
does worse than one that doesn’t, so a decision held for good costs memory states.
Heat never enters their analysis. And the counting under the theorem is older than
any of that, twice over. Theorem 3.1 is the finite, discrete cousin of the recurrence
argument Zermelo, using Poincaré’s theorem of 1890, turned on Boltzmann in 1896,
here aimed at a reading. Zermelo aimed it at entropy, and Bocchieri and Loinger
gave the quantum recurrence in 1957. In automata form it is classical: a finite
machine whose moves are all one-to-one reshuffles recognises only group languages,
and the inputs that raise a permanent reading form a language that is never one of
those unless it is empty (Pin’s 1992 paper on reversible automata is the reference
I’d check; automata theorists treat the step as folklore), and going quantum doesn’t
change it (Brodsky and Pippenger, 2002: quantum finite automata that measure
once, at the end, accept with bounded error exactly the group languages). The
closest of all is recent. Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) give a proof that if the smallest
automaton for a language has a step that merges states, every automaton for it
does, and argue that recognising it on a device that repeats one local step carries an
entropy floor, while a language whose smallest automaton only reshuffles carries no
such floor; one of their worked examples is the strings with no b, the complement
of the latch’s language. That’s the core with a physical price already on it. And the
logarithm in the heat floor matches the absolute-irreversibility bound of Murashita,
Funo and Ueda (2014), which Manzano, Kardeş, Roldán and Wolpert (2024) carried
over to computation. The logarithms coincide for the stated counts. This does not
534   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               supply a physical reverse process: absolute irreversibility needs forward and reverse
               path probabilities that the logical map alone does not specify. Constructor theory
               states a cousin of the same core for devices that run in a cycle: Marletto, Vedral
               and coauthors (2022) and Violaris and Marletto (2022) built an irreversible task
               out of the quantum homogeniser and argued that erasure may dissipate more than
               Landauer’s bound. Section 3 tells all of it. The price isn’t mine: Li and Vitányi priced
               each erased bit (1996), and Demaine and his coauthors priced named instructions
               that destroy bits (2016). Mine is what a flat price of at least one on every merging
               move does to a reading that stays: it turns “the flip merges” into “the flip costs” on
               any machine with finitely many states reading yes, whether or not anybody’s physics
               is right, and gives the toll (Observation 3.3); what comes with that form, namely
               the characterisation of the moves every merge-pricing schedule must charge (the
               merging moves, so the core again in pricing words), the merge-or-revoke dichotomy
               for a single move, the squeeze and entropy forms for a permanent flip, and a built
               counterexample for each premise (Section 3). The counterexample for finiteness is
               the endless strip, the machine that keeps every history, and it says what the premise
               is for: the strip raises its reading with no merge by taking a fresh state at every step,
               so a price list that charges merges and nothing else lets it certify at a cost of zero.
               That’s a price list that charges nothing for the fresh states, not a machine that got
               out of paying, and its steps still dissipate as they happen. Kind: the core is classical,
               and somebody else’s: Zermelo’s in physics, folklore in automata theory, with Pin’s
               paper as the place to check it. The pricing form isn’t wholly mine either: priced in
               entropy, for automata, it’s Ouldridge and Wolpert’s. They derive the price from the
               physics. An assumed price is older than mine too: Li and Vitányi (1996) took a unit
               charge per irreversibly erased bit, with reversible steps priced at zero, as axioms of
               a model of computation, and Demaine and his coauthors (2016) put that charge on
               named instructions of the random-access machine. What’s mine is the toll derived
               from a price on merging moves for a reading that stays, its single-move and counted
               forms, and the counterexamples. The physics is a named premise and is Landauer’s.
               Searches: the core turned up in the places just named, and its physical price in
               Ouldridge and Wolpert; I didn’t find the derived toll stated anywhere I looked, and
               nobody’s search covers a whole field, mine least of all.


               C.4 Learning borrows, committing pays
               Known: that a measurement can be made without merging anything, so that
               Landauer’s premise sets it no floor, and that the floor lands when the demon wipes
               its notes to look again, is Bennett’s resolution of Maxwell’s demon (1982), with the
               quantitative trade-off by Sagawa and Ueda (2009); that the entropy can be split
               between measuring and erasing in more than one way is Fahn’s (1996), and that
                                                                       C.5 The counter as a receipt   535


the work an erasure takes depends on what the eraser already knows is del Rio
and colleagues’ (2011). The closest physics I found to the line between learning
and committing is Ouldridge and ten Wolde’s fundamental costs of persistent copies
(2017; with Govern, 2017), copies that stay correlated with their originals after the
two come apart; theirs is heat for a correlation in chemistry, and Section 4 says how
it differs. The sharp chemical form, that a persistent copy grown at equilibrium
carries no information about its template, is Poulton, ten Wolde and Ouldridge’s
(2019). Mine: the four-state demon, where copying a hidden bit onto a display
known to be blank merges nothing and wiping the display merges two pairs of states;
the second copy that hands the display back blank while the original is still there;
the three-state ring and the two-state impossibility (Section 4); and the certainty
bound (Theorem 4.5), which splits the uncertainty about the start into the part a
run destroyed, paid for in units of cost, and the part the end state still holds. That
split is Shannon’s chain rule (1948), and bounds of this kind on the actual spread
are Maroney’s (2009) and Sagawa’s (2014); mine is reading it on the ledger, about
what an observer saw. Kind: finite models and one bookkeeping identity illustrating
a known physical point inside my ledger, and not a new physical claim. Bennett did
the hard part in 1982. My four dots put the line where you can work it through
yourself: the copy owes no floor and can cost nothing, but it still takes something.
Like any step that happens, it dissipates as it happens, less the slower it goes. And
it uses up a blank page, which is a fresh state; while the original is still there it
can hand the page back, so learning borrows. The page’s floor gets paid when it’s
wiped for reuse, and a blank page was itself a distinction somebody paid to set.
Committing makes the record permanent, so there’s nothing to hand back, and with
finitely many states it has to merge.


C.5 The counter as a receipt
Known: one-way counters that give order and termination are old: Turing’s 1949
note on checking a large routine, Floyd’s ranking functions (1967), Lamport’s clocks
(1978). Carrying a run’s cost beside its result is the writer cost of Danner, Licata and
Ramyaa (2015) and of Danner and Licata (2022), and the graded effect semantics
of Katsumata (2014), with a working-language version in Orchard, Liepelt and
Eades (2019). The receipt side of time credits is Mével, Jourdan and Pottier’s
(2019): in their extension of the Iris logic every step uses up a credit and produces a
receipt, receipts prove lower bounds, and enough of them prove that a counter can’t
overflow in any feasible time, which is the closest published neighbour of a total
that only climbs. Mine: putting three properties side by side (the total only climbs,
it equals the sum of the charges on every path including the failures, and it is the
only such total, on the states a run from the start reaches, for a given price list), the
536   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               argument for any system with a counter and a price list, and the sum proved from
               the small machine’s own step (Section 6, Section 15). Kind: synthesis; the abstract
               statements are proved for any system with a counter and a price list, and on the
               small machine the sum is proved too. Against the graded frameworks the answer is
               split: the counter is their writer exactly, and their type systems, bounding relations
               and before-the-run checking of grades are not embedded, because the grade here
               is written by the step during the run (Section 6). For the well-graded, loop-free
               programs defined in Section 6, on runs that do not trap, the counter’s rise equals
               the fixed grade. The loop built there costs its input value, so no fixed whole number
               is its exact grade on every input; an input-dependent grade is exact. The arguments
               are given there. Cost-aware type theories such as calf allow grades that depend on
               the inputs.


               C.6 Windows that can’t price what they hide
              Known: a function of an observation is constant on the observation’s fibres; that’s
              elementary, and the systems version of it is Moore’s distinguishing experiments
              (1956), Kalman’s observability (1960), and the completeness question of abstract
              interpretation (Cousot and Cousot, 1977; Giacobazzi, Ranzato and Scozzari, 2000);
              in control theory it is diagnosability and opacity of discrete-event systems (Sampath
              and coauthors, 1995; Saboori and Hadjicostis, 2007), where a collision is a hidden
              event no observer can diagnose without delay; in economics it is the hard-evidence
              view of mechanism design (Green and Laffont, 1986; Bull and Watson, 2007), where
              what a mechanism can tell apart is limited by the evidence on offer; and its sharp
              form for fingerprints is Naor and Rothblum’s lower bound for checking a stored file
              (2005); in distributed systems it is Haeberlen and Kuznetsov’s (2009), that only
              omission and commission faults can be detected from outside, and in philosophy it
              is Easwaran’s transferability (2009). Mine: stating the pricing version (no window
              price is exact across a collision), exhibiting a colliding pair for the small machine’s
              window, and the theorem that every certified Thiele-complete machine has two runs
              from one clean start that end looking the same through the window its base shows,
              one certified and one not (Section 7, Section 15). Kind: an elementary observation
              about what a window hides, plus specific facts about the machine and the definition.


               C.7 Structural entitlement and its bound

               Known: decision-tree counting bounds (a tree that tells N cases apart has depth at
               least log2 N); certifying algorithms that hand over checkable certificates (McConnell,
               Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer, 2011); proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997); the
               gap between justified true belief and knowledge (Gettier, 1963). Mine: the definition
                                                                     C.8 The record axis is a latch   537


of entitlement as an object, a checked relation, and a paid event on the record, and
the count that, given lists, a tree and a covering, a run that paid for the tree’s depth
pays at least the index bits it commits to (Section 8). Kind: synthesis; the counting
idea is standard, the assembly and its vocabulary are this work’s, the pricing policy
is assumed (nothing derives it), and the count is proved in its cost form over any
Thiele machine, and for the record moves of every certified Thiele-complete machine
on a run from a clean start, with the earned chain in the run, a floor that takes the
run’s own checks in place of a tree, and a counterexample showing the covering
can’t be dropped (Section 15.14); and in a form where the run makes the posterior
from a prior, every drop is made by a check the run passed, and the index bits are at
most k times the cost when each passing check keeps a 2−k share, a hypothesis the
same counterexample shows is needed (Theorems 8.4 and 15.38).


C.8 The record axis is a latch
Known: monotone, write-once state is old: the latch (Eccles and Jordan, patent
filed 1918, paper 1919), sticky bits (Plotkin, 1989), grow-only state in replicated
data types (Shapiro and coauthors), history variables and stuttering in refinement
(Abadi and Lamport, 1991), append-only authenticated sets for transparency logs,
which fit revocation as a once-only event (Tomescu and coauthors, 2019), and, in
program logic, monotonic state, where a property witnessed once on state that only
moves forward can be recalled at any later point, with a soundness proof and a
working home in F⋆ (Ahman, Fournet, Hriţcu, Maillard, Rastogi and Swamy, 2018):
the type-theory name for a record that stays up. Past the finite case, inductive and
quasi-inductive definitions (Richter and Aczel, 1974; Burgess, 1986) and the flag
trick of infinite time Turing machines (Hamkins and Lewis, 2000) are the transfinite
versions of a record that only grows and a toggle, and Danos and Krivine’s (2004)
reversible calculus needs an action declared irreversible in order to commit. Mine:
the exact statement that a record driven by the computation that never switches
off is, over any base, a latch on one event, with its converse and a counterexample
for each of the two conditions, and the argument that base-driven records agree
up to the price list while the stronger uniqueness fails (Section 10). Kind: a small
structural lemma, I think not stated before in this form (I found no prior statement
in the searches I ran), built from old notions. The proofs show why the record must
latch and why its price list remains a separate choice.


C.9 The diagonal and L
Known: Kleene’s recursion theorem and Rice’s theorem; Lawvere’s fixed-point form
(1969) and Yanofsky’s retelling (2003); later detailed developments of recursion
538   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               theorems and Rice (Norrish, 2011; Carneiro; Forster, Kunze, Smolka and coauthors,
               including L itself, 2017, and their library of undecidability results). Mine: the
               diagonal stated once over any substrate that supplies a recursion theorem; and Rice
               and halting proved again for L from its reduction rules (Section 13); and Rice’s and
               Kleene’s theorems proved for the small machine’s host, with Rice’s on every input
               of the two-counter machine itself, Kleene’s there with inputs written as powers of
               two, and Kleene’s refuted for plain inputs (Appendix D.4). Kind: new proofs of
               known theorems of computability, for particular machines. The theorems hold for
               any model with universality and s-m-n, and the work is in building those for each
               machine; the refutation on plain inputs is a small fact about two counters, resting
               on Schroeppel’s.


               C.10 An example machine that meets the definition

              Known: two-counter machines and the undecidability of their halting are Minsky’s
              (1961, 1967), developed further by Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors (2019,
              2020). The guarantee about every program is older than any of this, and it isn’t mine
              either. It’s the reference monitor (Anderson, 1972): a check that sits in the path of
              every operation, so no program gets around it. Schneider (2000) worked out what
              a monitor that watches a run can enforce: only safety properties, the kind a bad run
              breaks at some finite moment, and “no CERTIFY without an earlier earned COMMIT”
              is one of those. Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors (2015) verified monitors that
              check tags at every instruction. The shape of “earned,” a certificate nothing can
              make except through the rules, is Milner’s LCF, where a theorem is a value only
              the logic’s rules can build (Gordon, Milner and Wadsworth, 1979; Gordon, 2000);
              the small machine is that architecture at the level of single instructions. “No certify
              without an earlier commit” is also a correspondence assertion in the sense of Woo
              and Lam (1993), which Gordon and Jeffrey (2003) check with a type system, and a
              store of commitments that the rules of a dialogue keep, each speaker’s updated by
              the rules as the moves are made, is Hamblin’s (1970, chapter 8, on formal dialectic);
              the difference from all three is again that here the step enforces it. A check that
              blesses a value and a write that takes the blessing away is close kin to dynamic
              taint tracking, whose labels go back to Denning’s lattice model of information flow
              (1976), with the blessing itself, controlled endorsement, given a type system and a
              security theorem by Cecchetti, Myers and Arden (2017), and what a monitor can
              enforce with bounded memory is Talhi, Tawbi and Debbabi’s question (2008). A
              small monotone record inside each replica of a replicated service is A2M (Chun
              and coauthors, 2007), TrInc (Levin and coauthors, 2009), MinBFT (Veronese and
              coauthors, 2013) and Damysus (Decouchant and coauthors, 2022), and Clement,
              Junqueira, Kate and Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what such a record
                             C.11 Thiele-complete and certified Thiele-complete, defined so a clock fails   539


buys and what it doesn’t. The signature route to the same goal, which needs no
trusted step, is IA-CCF (Shamis and coauthors, 2021): replicas sign and log their
protocol messages in the ledger, so blame lands on individual members however
many of them misbehave. And “check once, issue a capability the system trusts, rely
on it later” is built and deployed in Garg and Pfenning’s proof-carrying file system
(2010), whose logic lets a policy’s consequences change with time and state, and
in Sirer and coauthors’ logical attestation for the Nexus operating system (2011),
unforgeable statements about programs used as credentials; those are the closest
systems I’ve found to check, commit, certify. Mine: one worked example, a machine
of six instruction kinds on two counters, proved to meet the definition so that the
definition is not empty, with a version for each counter, a bounded fact table and
a channel; its theorems that, from a clean start, a committed fact was checked
first about the same edition, that nothing is forged, that nothing is evicted, that
with the flag up from a clean start the channel names a fact an earlier passing
COMMIT committed, and a later commit can replace it, as a two-commit run shows,
and that a run from a clean start to a raised flag adds at least three to the ledger,
with three reached by a run whose check could have failed (the step doesn’t police
trivial checks, so one that can’t fail costs three too); the same theorems for any
property language with an exact equality test whose checker is proved to say yes
exactly when the claim holds, a sorted list read out of a counter included; and the
step-for-step match with the two-counter machine, so halting is undecidable for it
(Section 15). Kind: an instance of monitor enforcement with two things on top that
I didn’t find put together where I looked: the check is bound to the edition of the
thing it checked, and a toll is paid for the commitment. The first of those alone is
old: checking at commit time that nothing you read has changed since is optimistic
concurrency control (Kung and Robinson, 1981), and each counter’s version here is
that scheme’s version number. What I didn’t find is that check put together with a
toll. The universality and the undecidability are borrowed, and the other properties
are short consequences of the step rule. Whether the design is new I can’t say, and I
make no claim beyond the proofs.


C.11 Thiele-complete and certified Thiele-complete, defined so a clock fails

Known: Turing completeness, and the observation every theorist makes in four
seconds, that a toll alone is cheap: a machine that charges for every step pays
any toll. Enforcement mechanisms have been compared and sorted before, and
they aren’t one notion seen several ways: James Morris (1973) separated access
limitation from authentication in programming languages, and Kevin Hamlen, Greg
Morrisett and Fred Schneider (2006) classified which policies execution monitors,
program rewriters and static analysis can each enforce, and they differ; Wai Wong
540   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


              (1995), on a neighbouring track, recorded and checked HOL proofs so a theorem
              could carry its derivation. Mine: a definition of Thiele-complete with four clauses
              that say nothing about what the record is about (computing that runs every program,
              costs nothing and can’t touch the record, while every other move costs one; a record
              that stays; blank starts; and some run whose record tells two starts apart), with the
              proofs that a clock and a silent machine fail it, that each clause is needed, that every
              universal base becomes one by adding marks, and that every machine meeting it
              hides its record and ledger from its own window (Section 10.8); and a definition
              of certified Thiele-complete with four clauses (a universal base that can’t touch
              the record and a record that stays up once it’s up, an earned record, exact prices,
              nothing for the base and one for each of the three record acts, and some claim whose
              check can fail), the proofs that every clock-style machine and a paid latch and a
              silent machine fail it while the small machine, the same machine over any property
              language with an exact equality test, a checker proved to say yes exactly when the
              property holds and a property that holds of one number and fails of another, and
              the universal program’s host meet it, that the four clauses are independent, each
              failed by some machine with a two-counter machine inside that meets the other
              three (Theorem 15.29), and the theorem that every machine meeting it hides its
              record and ledger from its own window (Section 15), with the theorem that it is
              exactly Thiele-complete with clean starts, the earned chain and a claim that could
              have failed added (Theorem 15.23). Kind: definitions with short consequences. The
              window theorem is the fibre fact of item 6 plus one observation, that a universal
              base prints any window at no cost on the ledger. I’m not claiming the definition is
              the only reasonable one, or that LCF kernels, reference monitors and proof-carrying
              code are all certified Thiele-complete machines in disguise; Hamlen, Morrisett and
              Schneider’s sorting says such mechanisms genuinely differ, and the book doesn’t
              have a theorem showing the definition holds up across such differences.

C.14 The universal host for the example

Known: Turing’s universal machine (1936), which runs any machine given as data,
and the universal register machines that run two-counter programs. Keeping a guest
and the code running beside it out of each other’s state is what a virtual machine
monitor promises (Popek and Goldberg, 1974). Compiling computable functions
into counter machines is Forster, Larchey-Wendling and coauthors’ work. Mine: one
fixed program, U, written in the small machine’s own six kinds of instruction on a
host with a register for every whole number, with no guest step built in, that runs
every program of the small machine from every clean start start( x, y), halts exactly
when its guest does, raises its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate
if and only if the guest’s rises somewhere in its run, and keeps a ledger equal to
the guest’s at every matching point; its host machine is certified Thiele-complete,
and whether U halts on a loaded guest is undecidable (Appendix D.1). Two small
facts force its shape, and they’re stated there: reading a counter above 0 into the
program’s control flow on this machine writes it, and a finite program can’t keep
the guest’s facts on a copy of the guest’s counter, by the pigeonhole. Beside it, a
simpler host with a built-in guest step runs guests by construction and keeps a
mirror of the guest’s flag, with the mirror, isolation and earned-chain theorems.
Code that shares unprotected memory with a record can overwrite it, and ordinary
computers isolate memory and enforce rules with monitors too, so what I claim
is narrower: the simulation and the record guarantee proved for this one fixed
program U. Kind: an implementation, with its proofs, of a design whose shape
is Turing’s universal machine, with the record and the toll carried through. The
universality is borrowed from the small machine and from Minsky. And the same
program with one paid move added, UP , runs every computably presented Thiele
machine, with its halting matched, its reading carried as a latch on the host’s own
earned flag whose claim is that reading, and its ledger to within a surcharge of
at most two when the reading starts at no (exactly three when it starts at yes),
which no program on the host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest
certifies with its whole ledger below three (Appendix D.2); the counter-compilation
542   C What’s mine, and what isn’t


               construction is given in Appendix K. Kind for that part: an implementation with its
               proofs again. That a universal machine runs any computable machine is Turing’s;
               what’s carried through here is the record, earned again, and the prices, exact up to
               the surcharge, and I didn’t find that put together where I looked. In the words of
               Definition D.1, U is a universal Thiele machine for the small machine’s programs
               with no surcharge, and UP is one for every computably presented Thiele machine
               with a surcharge of at most two when the guest’s reading starts at no and three
               when it starts at yes.

              Known: that positive semidefiniteness of a correlation matrix gives the Tsirelson

C.16 What that adds up to
Read straight down the list. The mathematics underneath this book is mostly known,
and some of it is very old. The question organizing this book is what it costs
for a distinction to come into being and stay, written into the step of a model of
computation, with certification, a record that a claim was checked, as its sharpest
case, and what’s mine in the answer isn’t one result. It’s four, and I name them the
same way wherever they come up. The toll derived from finiteness, permanence and
a price on merges (item 3; the counting is classical, the finite cousin of Zermelo’s
recurrence objection and folklore about permutation automata, and Ouldridge and
Wolpert already priced it in entropy for automata, so what’s mine is the toll a price on
merging moves gives for a reading that stays, after Li and Vitányi’s price per erased
bit and Demaine and his coauthors’ price on instructions, and the price is an abstract
premise motivated by Landauer’s reset). The pricing form of the window fact (item
6; the fact itself is elementary). The latch form of a record that never comes down
(item 8; latches and history variables are old). And a record that’s priced, and on the
small machine earned, under the reference monitor’s every-program move (items
10, 11 and 14; the move is Anderson’s, Schneider’s and the micro-policy authors’,
and what’s added is the check bound to its edition, the toll on top, a definition of
Thiele-complete that a clock fails, over any base and any event, a certified refinement
the small machine meets, and universal programs that carry the check and the toll
to every small-machine program and to every computably presented Thiele machine,
earning their own flag). Under all four sits item 1, which is old mathematics read
one way: every step of every machine run by one rule takes a fresh state, merges, or
goes round a loop, a merge in a coarse description is, in every finer description it is
exact about, a fine merge, a fine step out of the set, or endlessly many fresh states,
any step that changes something in a real device dissipates besides, and finiteness is
what takes the fresh states away. The first is a ledger form of a core that’s classical
and already priced in physics; the second and third are small exact statements I
didn’t find stated where I looked; the fourth is built, with its proofs on the page,
and its idea isn’t new. The general statements are proved for every machine that
meets the definition; the small machine and the programs that run on it are the
worked instance that shows the definition can be met. Around it is my best attempt
at saying which is which, which you should check as hard as anything else in here.
If someone shows me item 3’s ledger form, the pricing form in item 6, or item 8
stated earlier, I’ll move it up the list.
APPENDIX D




The universal machines

This appendix carries the two universal programs of Section 16 in full: U, which
runs every program of the small machine, and UP , which runs every computably
presented Thiele machine, with the simpler host that has the guest step built in, the
diagonal on the small machine’s programs, and exactly what the universal machines
cover.


D.1 One machine that runs them all
The small machine raises its flag only by checking, committing and certifying, and it
pays for that. The next question is whether one machine can stand in for a whole
class of machines, the way Turing’s universal machine stands in for every Turing
machine. What I mean by that is a universal Thiele machine: one fixed machine
running one fixed program that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with
every step of the guest’s computing done by the host’s own counter moves and every
rise of the host’s record put where the host’s program put it. No program running
on the host has to keep a convention for it. In full:

Definition D.1 (Universal Thiele machine). Fix a class C of Thiele machines, each
with its runs from given start states. A universal Thiele machine for C is a Thiele
machine H, the host, with one program P fixed for the whole class, a way to load
any guest M in C with any start s0 into a start state of H, and a way to read a guest’s
state off the host’s registers, such that: (1) H is Thiele-complete (Definition 10.6),
and its computing moves are its counter moves; (2) the run of P from the loaded
state halts exactly when M’s run from s0 stops, and then shows the observable part
of M’s last state, as the class names it, its reading kept as a latch, and its ledger up
to the surcharge; (3) the run passes, in order, through host states that show the
observable part of M’s states along its run, at which the host’s record equals M’s
reading kept as a latch and the host’s ledger equals M’s ledger plus a surcharge,
never negative and bounded by a number fixed for the class; (4) the rise is the
program’s: each record move either traps or raises the record exactly when the line
it sits on is one P marks as raising, from every untrapped state, so nothing the move
reads decides it; (5) H is a register host: its counter moves are INC, DEC and HALT
on registers, its record moves leave the registers alone and go to the next line or

                                 544
                                                                D.1 One machine that runs them all   545


trap, and which move comes next depends only on the line and whether the trap
is up; (6) each guest is loaded with the record down, no trap, a fixed line and the
guest written into the registers, and the guest’s state is read off the registers in a
coding fixed with the class, before any guest is named. A certified universal Thiele
machine also has its host certified Thiele-complete with clean loads, and its record,
whenever it’s up, standing on the host’s own check of the guest’s own justification,
as the class supplies it.

    For U the guest’s justification is its chain claim; for UP , the guest’s reading at a
state of the run. For U the observable part I’ve proved it matches with all six clauses
is the guest’s two counters, and in order it matches everything but the guest’s version
numbers, which no run of the guest can show; for UP it’s the whole state.
    The guest lives only in the loaded state; the machine and the program are fixed
before any guest is named. For U the surcharge is zero; for UP it is at most two
when the guest’s reading starts at no, and exactly three when it starts at yes, so
three bounds it over the whole class. Both are certified universal Thiele machines,
by the theorems of this appendix put together: each meets the six clauses, each host
is certified Thiele-complete with clean loads, and each one’s flag stands on its own
check of the guest’s justification.
    The two that UP adds once a guest’s record is up is, at worst, the price of
certification, not of universality. A certified host raises its record from a clean load
only after three marks, so on a guest whose whole ledger is one when its reading
first says yes it falls two behind at least. A host without certification can keep up
exactly: on a host with registers, INC, DEC, HALT, a paid move TICK that always
raises the record, a paid move PAY that never does, and a paid move MARK that
raises it when register 0 is at least 1, which no program below runs and which
Thiele-complete needs, since without it no run’s record depends on where it started,
the program “count register 0 down to zero; TICK; HALT” runs the guests that count
a pile down to zero and then raise their reading at a cost of one, each from its own
pile, with surcharge zero. A guest whose reading is already yes at its start costs any
host loaded with its record down at least one, and one is reached. And from a start
at no one host keeps up exactly on the whole class: UP ’s compiler on that host, with
the three-act chain at the first yes replaced by one TICK and the rest of that move’s
price paid in PAYs. The toll on the guest makes that move cost at least one, so the
TICK always fits inside it, and the host’s ledger is the guest’s at every matching point.
On a host without certification the surcharge is zero from no and one from yes, and
neither can be lowered. (And PAY is needed on such a host: a guest that pays while
its reading is down makes the host run a record move that doesn’t raise, which is
what PAY is.)
546   D The universal machines


                  Each clause stops something. For clauses (1), (4) and (5) there’s a host that
              meets the others and fails it; (2) and (3) together stop a host that ignores its guest;
              (6) I state in words below. Clause (1) stops a host that raises its record early and
              lowers it again before anyone looks. Clause (4) stops a mark that reads the registers,
              or a copy of the guest kept outside them, and raises when the guest would: the same
              move on the same line would raise from one state and not from another. Clause
              (5) stops a host with a move that takes one step of the guest. In the one I built
              that move costs nothing on the guest’s unpriced instructions and traps on its paid
              ones; costing nothing, it would have to be a counter move, and a counter move
              never traps. Make such a move cost one instead and it’s a record move, which has to
              leave the registers alone, so it can’t move the guest’s counters, which (6) puts there.
              Clause (5) also stops a move costing nothing that fetches, decodes and carries out a
              guest instruction on the registers, because that move adds one to one register from
              one state and to another register from another, which no single INC or DEC does.
              Clause (6) makes the guest come in through the registers. It’s the one clause I’ve
              stated in words without a theorem that it discriminates: a reading of the registers
              that adds part of the guest back in isn’t excluded by anything I’ve proved. What
              stops a host that ignores its guest is (2) and (3), on any class whose guests differ in
              when they halt or what they record, which a universal class does. What the clauses
              allow is exact too. By (1), (4) and (5), the line, the registers, the record and the
              ledger of a run before any trap depend only on the line, registers, record and ledger
              it was loaded with: each counter move acts on those alone, each record move leaves
              the registers and moves the line, and its effect on the record is fixed by its line. So a
              host may carry anything else along, even a copy of the guest that its counter moves
              step, and what it carries along that way can’t touch anything the host shows. One
              route I haven’t closed: a move that traps may read anything, and stopping the run is
              all it can do. UP never traps on its class, so for it the route is shut. For U it’s shut too:
              U is loaded with every version at 0 and an empty table and channel, so whatever
              a trapping move of U reads was written by the run itself, from the registers it was
              loaded with. For a host in general it stays open.
                  None of this needs certification. UP ’s own program, read on a host with no
              claims, no checker, no table and no channel but with that MARK, with CHECK,
              COMMIT and PAY read as PAY and CERTIFY as TICK, meets (1) to (6) with the same
              surcharge: UP never traps on its class, and while nothing traps the two hosts agree,
              step for step, on the line, the registers, the record and the ledger. Certification adds
              the tie to the guest’s own justification, and it needs (4) as much as anything: a host
              that carries out a hidden copy’s own check, commit and certificate meets the tie and
              fails only (4) and (5).
                  And I want it the hard way. The easy way is to give the host a move that means
              “take one step of the guest,” and then “it runs any guest” is true because I wrote it
                                                                D.1 One machine that runs them all   547


that way. There’s a host like that two subsections on, after the two programs, and
it’s useful as a picture. It isn’t Turing’s kind of universal. Turing’s universal machine
has no instruction for “do what the machine on the tape would do.” It has the same
kind of instructions every other Turing machine has, and one fixed table, and the
table does the reading and the deciding and the carrying out. The bar here is the
same, and clauses (4) and (5) make it exact: one fixed program, every computing
step a counter move, every rise where the program put it, and anything else the host
carries unable to touch what it shows.
    Turing’s own explanation is worth having in your head, because the program
below copies its shape. In the 1936 paper the universal machine’s tape starts with
the machine to imitate, written out as a string of letters, its standard description, and
after it the imitated machine’s complete configurations, one after another: where its
head is, what state it’s in, what’s on its tape. To take one step, the universal machine
finds the last configuration, looks through the description line by line, comparing,
until it finds the line for that state and that symbol, and then writes out the next
configuration the way that line says. Then it goes back and does it again. It leaves
marks on squares so it doesn’t lose its place. Every bit of that is ordinary instructions
on an ordinary tape, and nothing in its table knows any particular machine.
    Turing’s universal program came first on paper, and one that people actually
came to use arrived through the side door. John McCarthy, who had started the
artificial intelligence project at MIT with Minsky, was writing up his new language
Lisp around 1960 and wanted to show it was neater than Turing machines, so he
wrote a universal function for it, eval, the language describing how to evaluate itself,
and argued it was shorter and easier to follow than a universal Turing machine. In
his own history of Lisp, that was for the paper, a thing to read; the notation for
writing programs as data was made up for the paper with no thought of using it in
practice. Then Steve Russell (S. R. Russell in McCarthy’s account), a programmer
on that MIT project, noticed that eval could serve as an interpreter and coded it
by hand, and there was a running language with an interpreter that nobody had
planned. McCarthy adds that the surprise froze some decisions he’d made “rather
lightheartedly” for the paper. So the trick has a habit: written to be read, it ends up
being run. The program below goes the other way round, on purpose. It’s written to
run, and the proofs show that what runs is what the page says.
    The host. The program runs on a machine with the small machine’s instructions
and the small machine’s prices: INC, DEC, HALT costing nothing, and CHECK,
COMMIT, CERTIFY costing one each, with the same table of sixteen facts, the same
channel, trap, ledger and flag. One change: it has a counter for every whole number,
each with its own version, where the small machine had two. There’s no new
kind of instruction and no new price. Take away the table, the channel and the
flag and what’s left is old: a machine with as many registers as it needs, adding
548   D The universal machines


              one, taking one away and jumping on zero, is the unlimited register machine of
              John Shepherdson and H. E. Sturgis, two logicians who proved in 1963 that such
              machines compute every partial recursive function.

              Definition D.2 (The host machine). The host machine is the machine of Defini-
              tion 15.3 with one change: it has a counter, with its version, for every whole number
              r (a register), and INC r, DEC r j, CHECK p r and COMMIT p r name one register
              each. Its property language has one property, Slot. Write ⟨m, n⟩ for the number
              (2n + 1) · 2m ; every positive number is ⟨m, n⟩ for exactly one pair, and 0 is no pair.
              Number the small machine’s properties Zero 7→ 0, Even 7→ 1, Ge(n) 7→ n + 2.
              The checker of Slot says yes at a value x exactly when x = ⟨m, v⟩ and the small
              machine’s checker says yes to the property numbered m at v; its meaning is the
              same with holds in place of the checker.

                  There’s one place the guest’s machine shows up in the host. The host’s single
              property knows how to read the small machine’s three-word property language:
              “this number is the pair (property, value) and the property holds of the value.” It
              doesn’t know the small machine’s step. Knowing the language and not the step is
              the counter version of Turing’s universal machine knowing the alphabet its guests
              write in.
                  Two facts that force the design. Why more counters? The answer is two facts,
              and the program looks the way it does because of them.
                  The first is about reading. On this machine a program that wants a counter’s
              value in its own control flow has to take pebbles out (DEC) and put them back (INC),
              and every INC, and every DEC on a counter above 0, is a write, so the counter’s
              version goes up. A fact is about one version, so a read done that way kills every
              live fact about the counter. Not every look is a write: CHECK reads a value without
              writing it, a DEC on 0 changes no version, and a fresh CHECK after such a read can
              make a new live fact. But the guest’s counters are exactly the ones the host has to
              read by taking pebbles out, again and again, to decide which way a DEC jumps and
              to work out a property’s answer, and each of those reads kills whatever fact was
              kept there. So the host can’t keep the guest’s facts on the copies it reads, and a copy
              it only writes is what the second fact rules out.
                  The second says that even if reading wrote nothing, a fixed program couldn’t keep
              them by sending each guest property to one of a fixed, finite list of host properties
              and checking it on the same register the guest’s fact is about. The theorem below
              rules out that and nothing more, and the pigeonhole is what rules it out.
                                                               D.1 One machine that runs them all   549




Theorem D.1 (No host fact on an exact copy of the guest’s counter). Take any host
property language with an exact equality test and any checker, a finite list Q of host
properties, and any translation of the small machine’s properties into members of
Q whose host check passes whenever the guest’s check passes on the same number.
Then there are n ̸= m, with Ge(n) and Ge(m) translated to the same host property,
such that the guest program CHECK Ge(n) A; COMMIT Ge(m) A traps within two
steps from every start, while on every host state with the trap down and room in
its table, and some register holding a number at least n, the translated CHECK and
COMMIT on that register both pass and put the committed claim in the channel.

Proof. A fixed program mentions finitely many properties, so Q is finite, and the
translation sends the infinitely many Ge(0), Ge(1), . . . into it: two of them land on
the same member. The guest’s COMMIT asks for Ge(m), and its table can only hold
Ge(n), so it traps (or its CHECK already trapped). The host sees one property twice:
its CHECK passes, since the guest’s would, and its COMMIT finds exactly what that
CHECK wrote.
    So the host keeps the guest’s facts somewhere else: in slots, extra registers
used for nothing but holding facts, one per checked fact, each holding the pair
(property number, value) that the guest checked. The pigeonhole doesn’t bite a slot,
because the property lives in the slot’s number. The instruction doesn’t have to carry
it: CHECK Slot on a slot asks about whatever pair is sitting there, and there are
infinitely many pairs. A slot’s number changes only when the program is moving a
fact into it. And when the guest writes the counter a fact was about, the program
gives every slot about that counter a nudge, one INC and one DEC, which leaves the
number alone and pushes the version up, so the host’s facts go stale at exactly the
moment the guest’s do.
    Do one slot by hand. The property “even” has number 1. Checking it on value 4
puts ⟨1, 4⟩ = (2 · 4 + 1)21 = 18 in a separate slot. To read that pair, halve 18 until
what’s left is odd: one halving gives 9, so the property number is 1; subtract one
from 9 and halve to recover value 4. The host checks that property of that value. A
second register, the mirror, holds 2: the property number plus one. COMMIT can
read this second register while leaving the checked slot untouched.
    When the guest changes the counter that fact concerned, nudge the slot 18 →
19 → 18 and set the mirror to zero. The number is back where it was, but the
version went up twice, so the host’s old fact about that slot is stale. Putting a number
back doesn’t put an old check back. The mirror is what tells the search to leave that
slot alone, and if the search tried it anyway, the version rule would refuse it.
550   D The universal machines


                  The program. I’ll describe U the way Turing would, one register at a time and
              then one job at a time. Registers 0 and 1 hold the guest’s A and B. Register 2
              holds the guest’s whole program as one number: each instruction gets a number
              (an opcode paired with its operands, INC as 0, DEC as 1, HALT as 2, CHECK as 3,
              COMMIT as 4, CERTIFY as 5), and the list of them is packed with ⟨·, ·⟩, the empty
              list as 0. Register 3 is the guest’s line. Registers 4 to 13 are scratch. Registers 14 and
              15 count how many CHECKs on A and on B have passed. Registers 16 to 47 are
              mirrors, sixteen for each guest counter, and registers 48 to 79 are the slots, sixteen
              for each guest counter. The guest’s table holds sixteen facts in total, across both
              counters, and all sixteen can be about one counter, so the host gives each counter
              room for all of them. The reservation is the host’s, and the guest’s own capacity
              stays sixteen in all. Register 80 is a dead end that’s never written.
                  Each guest step goes like this. At line 1 the program copies the program number
              and the guest’s line into scratch, putting the originals back as it goes, because
              copying a counter on this machine means emptying it into two others and refilling
              it. If the guest’s line is 0, or past the end of the program, it stops. Otherwise it peels
              instructions off the front of the copy, one per line, until it holds the one at the guest’s
              line, and splits that into opcode and operands. Then a chain of DECs on the opcode
              sends it to one of six handlers.
               • INC c: INC the guest’s counter c, nudge every slot about c and zero its mirrors,
                 add one to the guest’s line, back to line 1.
               • DEC c j: DEC the guest’s counter c. If it was 0, add one to the guest’s line. If it
                 wasn’t, nudge every slot about c, zero its mirrors, and set the guest’s line to j.
                 Back to line 1.
               • HALT: stop.
               • CHECK p c: let k be the count of passed CHECKs on c. If k is below 16, build
                 ⟨number of p, value of c⟩ in slot k of c, run CHECK Slot on that slot, set its mirror
                 to the number of p plus one, add one to the count and to the guest’s line, and go
                 back to line 1. If k is 16, run CHECK Slot on the dead end, which holds 0, which
                 is no pair, so it traps, just as the guest’s seventeenth CHECK does.
               • COMMIT p c: look through the sixteen mirrors of c for one equal to the number
                 of p plus one. At the first match, run COMMIT Slot on that slot. With no match,
                 run COMMIT Slot on the dead end, which traps.
               • CERTIFY: run CERTIFY, add one to the guest’s line, back to line 1.
                 Why the mirrors? COMMIT has to find the slot holding the claim, and it can’t
              read the slot to find out, because reading would make the fact stale. So beside
              every slot sits a mirror the program is allowed to read: the property’s number plus
              one while the slot’s fact is live, 0 once the guest has written the counter. If a guest
                                                               D.1 One machine that runs them all   551


CHECK fails its property, the host’s CHECK on the slot fails too, since the slot holds
exactly the pair the guest checked. If the guest table is full across both counters, the
host’s own sixteen-entry table is full as well, even when this counter’s slot count is
below sixteen; its CHECK then traps for lack of room. So both kinds of refusal come
through.
   Count what costs anything. Fetching, unpacking, copying, nudging and branching
are all INC and DEC, and all cost nothing, as computing does on the small machine.
The only paid instructions are the CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY sites, and each
guest CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY makes the program run exactly one of them.
So the host’s ledger lands on the guest’s, unit for unit. And when the guest’s flag
goes up, the host’s goes up by the host’s own CERTIFY, standing on the host’s own
COMMIT and CHECK on a slot. The host isn’t copying a bit; it runs the same chain
on its own registers.

Definition D.3 (The program U, and loading a guest). U is the fixed list of 3728
host instructions specified by the block expansions in Appendix L, starting at line
1 and mentioning registers 0 to 80; exactly 69 of them cost anything. For a guest
program P and a start ( x, y), the loaded host hload( P, x, y) has register 0 at x,
register 1 at y, register 2 at the number of P, register 3 at 1 and every other register
at 0, every version 0, line 1, an empty table and channel, the trap down, ledger
0 and flag down. Write grun(m) for m program steps of P from start( x, y), and
hrun(n) for n program steps of U from hload( P, x, y).



Theorem D.2 (U keeps pace with its guest). For every guest program P, start ( x, y)
and number of guest steps m, there’s a number of host steps n such that one of
two things holds. Either the host is back at line 1 with m ≤ n and related to the
guest: registers 0 and 1 hold the guest’s A and B, register 3 holds the guest’s line,
the guest’s trap is down, the two ledgers are equal, the two flags are equal, and the
host’s table and channel hold, fact for fact, slot facts matching the guest’s facts and
channel. Or both have stopped, with the same counters, the same trap, the same
ledger, the same flag, and matching tables and channels. And from any related pair
where the guest hasn’t stopped, one guest step is matched by at least one host step
that lands related again, or with both stopped.

Proof. The one-step part is a case for each thing the guest can do at its line: stop;
INC; DEC, taken or not; CHECK, passing, failing, or with a full table; COMMIT,
found or not; CERTIFY, passing or not. The block invariants and the case analysis
in Appendix L show where each matching stretch lands. The relation carries the
bookkeeping that makes the next case go through: each count register equals the
552   D The universal machines


              number of slots in use for its counter, each slot in use holds (property number,
              checked value), a slot’s fact is current exactly when the matching guest fact is, a live
              slot’s mirror is the property’s number plus one and a stale one’s is 0, and unused
              slots, unused mirrors and the dead end are 0. At loading, the counters and guest
              line have their specified starting values, and both tables and channels are empty,
              so the matching conditions hold before any step. Now take one guest instruction.
              The matching stretch just described ends either at the next matching point or with
              both machines stopped. In the first case its slot and mirror conditions are exactly
              what the following instruction needs, so you can do the next stretch. Repeat this for
              the first m guest steps. Each running stretch takes at least one host step; if neither
              machine has stopped, the accumulated host count is therefore at least m. If they stop
              earlier, both remain stopped with the matching final fields. That gives the whole-run
              statement for every m.



              Theorem D.3 (Halting and answers match). For every P, x and y, the guest’s run
              of P from start( x, y) halts if and only if U’s run from hload( P, x, y) halts. And
              whenever the guest has halted at step m and U at step n, the host’s registers 0 and 1
              hold the guest’s A and B, and the two traps, the two ledgers and the two flags are
              equal.

              Proof. Theorem D.2: a halted guest is matched by a stopped host, and a host that
              has stopped can’t be back at line 1 with the guest still running, because line 1 isn’t
              a stop. A halted machine stays halted, so the two halting points carry the same
              values.



              Theorem D.4 (The host’s flag is the guest’s, and its ledger is exact). (1) The guest’s
              flag is up at some step of its run if and only if the host’s flag is up at some step of
              U’s run. (2) For every m there’s an n at which the two are related, with m ≤ n, or
              both stopped, with µ(hrun(n)) = µ(grun(m)). And for every n there’s an m with
              µ(grun(m)) ≤ µ(hrun(n)) ≤ µ(grun(m + 1)): in between matching points, the
              host’s ledger never gets ahead of the guest’s next step.

              Proof. (1) Flags are equal at matching points and never come down. (2) Ledgers
              are equal at matching points; inside the stretch of U that runs one guest instruction,
              at most the one paid site of that instruction runs, so the host’s ledger sits between
              the guest’s before and after it.
                                                               D.1 One machine that runs them all   553


    Equal ledgers at the matching points are a third sense of “exact,” and the plainest
of the three (Section 15 names all three): two ledgers holding one number.


Theorem D.5 (The host earns its own flag). If the host’s flag is up after n steps of
U from hload( P, x, y), then the instructions U executed contain, in order, a passing
CHECK Slot on a slot, then a passing COMMIT Slot on the same slot, with the slot
untouched and its version unchanged in between, then a passing CERTIFY; the slot
held ⟨number of p, v⟩ at the CHECK, with holds( p, v). And the guest’s own run from
start( x, y) contains a passing CHECK p c, then, with c untouched and its version
unchanged, a passing COMMIT p c, then a passing CERTIFY, with c holding v at its
CHECK.

Proof. By Theorem D.4 the guest’s flag rises too; find the guest step where it rises, a
passing CERTIFY, and the related host point just before it. The guest’s channel there
names a fact, and the relation says the host’s channel names the matching slot fact.
The host’s own flag rises at its own first passing CERTIFY, and nothing paid runs
between the related point and that CERTIFY, so the host’s channel hasn’t moved: it
names that slot fact. The host machine’s version of Theorem 15.11 gives the host’s
