CHECK and COMMIT on that slot. The record kept with the slot says what pair it
held and when, and the checker’s meaning gives holds( p, v). The same theorem
on the guest’s run, up to the step where its flag rose, gives the guest’s chain on the
same p and c, and the record says c held v at its CHECK.



Theorem D.6 (The host is certified Thiele-complete, and U’s halting is undecidable).
(1) The host machine, with Slot as its property and one move per instruction, is
certified Thiele-complete (Definition 15.7), and certified Thiele-complete over its
own claim language, whose claims are “Slot holds of register r,” whose meanings
are written without the host’s checker, and whose “unchanged” is “same value and
same version of register r”; and U’s run from hload( P, x, y) is a run of it. (2) Read
as a Thiele machine it obeys the universal floor; a run of U that raises the host’s flag
costs at least 3 there. The system built from its certified Thiele-completeness agrees
with it step for step and cost for cost, so the same run costs at least 3 on that one
too, and the universal floor of 1 holds there directly. (3) U halts from hload( P, x, y)
exactly when P halts from start( x, y), so the question “does U halt from this loaded
host?” is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.5.
554   D The universal machines


              Proof. (1) The base is registers 0 and 1, run by INC and DEC; the claims are “Slot
              holds of register r”; the rest is the host machine’s own versions of the small machine’s
              theorems, and for non-vacuity, register 0 loaded with 1, which is ⟨0, 0⟩, the pair
              of Zero and 0, against register 0 loaded with 0, which is no pair. Over the claim
              language the interface is the same one, with the meanings handed over by the
              language. (2) is Theorem 15.31(4) and Theorem D.5. (3) is Theorem D.3, and
              the loading map reduces the small machine’s halting question, undecidable by
              Theorem 15.5, to this one.
                 Put it together, plainly. One fixed program, 3728 instructions of the small
              machine’s six kinds, with no guest step built into anything, runs every program of
              the small machine from every clean start start( x, y). It halts exactly when its guest
              halts, with the guest’s answer in its first two registers. Its flag goes up at some
              step of its run exactly when the guest’s goes up at some step of the guest’s run,
              by its own check, its own commit and its own certificate. Its ledger is the guest’s,
              unit for unit, wherever the two line up. And the machine it runs on is certified
              Thiele-complete. Since the small machine runs every two-counter program, through
              those guests U runs every computation, under Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside
              the machine. That’s a universal Thiele machine for the small machine’s programs,
              and the definition allows any other host that meets it; the next subsection carries it
              to every computably presented Thiele machine whose reading a program decides on
              every state.
                 There’s fine print, and it comes before you take that anywhere. The guests start
              clean, from start( x, y); the whole-run theorems are about loaded hosts, and only
              the one-step theorem is about any related pair. The host’s property reads the small
              machine’s three-word language, so a guest with a different property language needs
              a different host property; the host of the next subsection has one, a single property
              that reads a universal claim language. Sixteen slots per counter is the guest’s whole
              table size, reserved for each counter in case every fact is about that one. And it’s
              slow: for every guest step it unpacks the program number from the front again,
              and it copies a number one pebble at a time. That’s where the running time in
              Appendix G comes from. The theorems above say nothing about time; they match
              states and ledgers at the points where the two line up.
                 Enforcement in the step is the reference monitor’s move from Section 14, An-
              derson’s 1972 move: one mechanism everything has to pass through. What’s put
              together here is a priced, earned record under that move, carried to every guest by
              one fixed program. The move itself is Anderson’s. Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett
              and Fred Schneider (2006) worked out, in their model, which policies mechanisms
              like that can enforce at all, and their paper is where I’d go to see why enforcing a
              property of every run escapes the Rice-style walls that deciding one runs into.
D.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided, priced in whole units, carried as a latch
                                                                                                                  555

    Why make such a fuss about proofs that walk every case? Because the first
universal machine had bugs. It’s the machine in Turing’s 1936 paper, and nobody
gets to call Turing careless. In 1947 Emil Post, in an appendix to a paper on a
problem of Thue, pointed out that the construction leaned on a convention it hadn’t
earned, and he patched a small defect in how the universal machine writes out
each complete configuration. Around the same time Donald Davies, who joined
the National Physical Laboratory in 1947, where Turing was designing a computer,
worked through the universal machine’s tables and found more mistakes, much to
Turing’s annoyance, as the accounts of Davies’s life have it. (It’s the same Davies who
later named the packet in packet switching.) His corrections were finally printed
in a collection edited by Jack Copeland, a philosopher and historian of computing
who runs an archive of Turing’s papers, The Essential Turing, in 2004. They may be
some of the first bugs ever written, in a program for a computer that didn’t exist
yet. That’s a lovely claim, and I haven’t been able to confirm it, so take it as a lead.
What it changes here: a universal machine is exactly the kind of construction where
a careful person leaves a hole, U has 3728 lines for a hole to hide in, and each case
of its simulation argument has to hold. The definitions are on the page so you can
examine what those cases establish.


D.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided,
    priced in whole units, carried as a latch
U runs the small machine’s programs, and through them every computation, under
Minsky’s 2n encoding, done outside the machine. But a Thiele machine from
somewhere else has its own states, its own moves, its own prices and its own
reading, and running it through the two-counter encoding keeps its computation
and nothing else. So the question Turing’s machine raises for this book is the bigger
one. Take any Thiele machine whose workings can be computed. Is there one fixed
program that runs every such machine as a guest, keeping its halting, raising its own
flag exactly when the guest’s reading would rise, on an earned chain of its own, and
keeping a ledger equal to the guest’s own prices, with the host’s flat ones nowhere
in it? There is, within limits I’ll list, and this subsection gives it.
    First the class, said plainly. A computably presented Thiele machine is a Thiele
machine in Section 2’s sense (states, moves, a step, a price for each move, a yes/no
reading, and the toll: a move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one)
together with a driver that picks the next move from the current state or says stop,
and a way of writing states and moves as whole numbers. “Computably” means four
little programs, written in the plainest language of computable functions there is,
the one built from zero, plus one, picking an argument, composing, recursion and
search: one computes the driver, one the step, one the price, and one the reading,
556   D The universal machines


              and each of the four halts on every input: the driver with a move or stop, the step
              with a state, the price with a whole number, and the reading with yes or no. Run
              from a start s0 , the driver’s moves give one run. Its ledger after n moves is the sum
              of their prices, and its latch after n moves says whether the reading has been yes at
              any state so far.
                  The host gets one thing the small machine doesn’t have: a paid move that certifies
              nothing. On the small machine every charge comes from a CHECK, a COMMIT or a
              CERTIFY, and those can charge without raising the flag: one passing CHECK and six
              COMMITs of the same claim cost seven. But every passing CHECK takes one of the
              table’s sixteen entries for good, every COMMIT rewrites the channel, and a failing
              CHECK traps. So the host machine gets a seventh instruction kind, PAY: it costs one,
              goes to the next line, and changes nothing else; it never raises the flag, takes no
              table entry and leaves the channel alone. That’s why the compiler uses it.
                  How far the small machine gets without it is proved, and the count is short. Take
              a run that never traps and ends with the flag down. No CERTIFY ran in it, since
              a passing one raises the flag and a failing one traps. Every CHECK in it passed,
              since a failing one traps, and each passing CHECK filled one of the table’s sixteen
              entries, so there were at most sixteen. Every COMMIT in it committed a claim the
              table holds, and the table holds at most sixteen, so at most sixteen COMMITs can
              be of claims the run hadn’t committed before. Sixteen and sixteen make 32, and
              the only way past it is a COMMIT of a claim already committed earlier in the run.
              A claim names its counter’s version, and the version changes at every write, so a
              repeat needs its counter left alone since the earlier COMMIT. A guest that writes
              both counters between any two of its payments can’t do that, and it can’t commit
              at all, since a COMMIT needs its counter left alone since its CHECK, so it runs out
              of ways to pay after sixteen. Without that limit, 32 is reached: sixteen rounds of
              CHECK at least 0 A; COMMIT at least 0 A; INC A pay 32 with no trap and the flag
              down. A guest that writes both counters at every move of the machine it simulates
              needs a fresh CHECK for each move it pays for, so it can pay for at most sixteen of
              them. A simulated machine that charges more often than that has to be paid for
              somewhere, and PAY is where. The 32 isn’t a ceiling on either machine: a program
              that checks one fact about a counter it never writes can commit that fact again and
              again, at a cost of one each, with the flag down and no trap, because the counter’s
              version never changes. On the small machine that leaves one counter to compute
              with while it repeats, which is too few (Theorem E.7); the host has a counter for
              every whole number, so on it the repeats cost the computing nothing. A program
              written for the host’s registers doesn’t need PAY: it checks one true fact once, about
              a register it never writes, and pays every later unit by committing that fact again.
              Those commits overwrite the channel, so at the move where the reading first says
              yes it runs the chain’s CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY back to back and pays the rest
D.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided, priced in whole units, carried as a latch
                                                                                                                  557

of that move after the CERTIFY. UP can do without it on its class, and PAY is what it
needs beyond the class. UP names no register above 80 and its guest can’t name a
host register, so two sit untouched. Pay the first unit by raising one of them to 1,
which reads “zero holds at 0,” and checking it; pay every later unit by committing
that fact again, which passes because the register’s version never moves. A compiled
guest runs its chain back to back and pays after it, so the chain’s own commitment
is what its certificate finds, and its one check leaves the table at two facts. Every
payment costs one, the surcharge is unchanged, and the host is the register host
with no seventh instruction. Outside the class the trick fails: a guest that pays twice
and then certifies with nothing committed traps, and this host, with the pay-fact
sitting in its channel, would raise its flag instead. PAY leaves the channel alone, and
that is what those guests need. On a host without certification PAY is a necessity:
a guest that pays while its reading is down makes the host run a paid move that
doesn’t raise its record.
    Read as a Thiele-complete machine, the host needs no filing at all: PAY is a mark
that never raises the record. The definition of certified Thiele-complete sorts every
paid move into CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY, so PAY has to be filed under one of
them, and it’s filed as a CHECK of the empty claim, a claim that never holds. The
filing is for the interface. It isn’t what PAY does on the machine: a CHECK that fails
on this machine traps, and PAY goes on to the next line. With PAY filed that way
the host stays certified Thiele-complete, and certified Thiele-complete over its own
claim language, in which the empty claim holds of no state. PAY costs exactly one,
as clause (c) asks of a CHECK; its check never passes, so it can’t stand in a chain;
and it leaves the table, the channel and the flag alone, so it can’t add to a chain or
raise the flag either. For the same reason the floor of three for a flag raised from a
clean start still holds with PAY present: the flag still needs a CHECK, a COMMIT and
a CERTIFY.
    The program is U with one more handler: a seventh branch on the guest’s opcode,
for PAY, that runs the host’s own PAY once. Call it UP ; it’s 3735 instructions, with
70 paid sites, the 69 of U plus the PAY. The guest it runs is a program of the small
machine with PAY added, and that guest is where the presented machine goes. Its
four programs are compiled into two counters, by the packing Minsky used, using
the translations of Appendix K from computable functions to counter programs; the
guest keeps the presented machine’s state coded in its counter B, takes one of its
moves by running the compiled driver and step, runs the compiled reading on the
new state, and pays the move’s price in PAYs; the first time the reading says yes, it
checks, commits and certifies, and those three paid instructions count toward that
move’s price. The host’s one property is fixed too: a claim is either one of the small
machine’s three words about a number, or “run reading program r on the coded state
v,” and the host’s checker evaluates that with one fixed routine for every presented
558   D The universal machines


              machine there is. So nothing in UP knows any particular presented machine. The
              machine arrives as data, the way Turing’s guests arrived on the tape.
                  A fixed checker that runs whatever program it’s handed and always answers
              needs saying how, so here is the routine. A claim of the second kind carries a number
              r. The checker decodes r as a counter-machine routine: its instructions, where they
              sit, which register holds the answer, which register holds the fuel, and how many
              registers to load. If r doesn’t decode to a routine, the answer is no. Otherwise the
              checker loads the routine’s registers from v, reads a fuel number f out of v too (the
              fuel register’s entry in v’s prime factorisation), runs the routine for at most f steps,
              and says yes exactly when by then the routine has left its code with 1 in its answer
              register. Every input gets an answer within f steps, so the checker is total, and what
              it means is that bounded run: yes if and only if the routine halts within the fuel
              the value carries, with answer 1. That’s how it stays clear of the diagonal. A total
              evaluator E that agreed with every total yes-or-no program on that program’s code
              alone would let g(n) = ¬ E(n, n) contradict itself at its own code, as long as E is
              itself computable. This checker never evaluates a program on its code alone: the
              fuel comes with the claim’s value. The guest compiled from M runs M’s reading
              routine itself and puts at least the step count it took into the fuel register, and at
              such a value the checker says yes if and only if the reading says yes.
                  For the fuel rule, take a routine containing just one instruction: increment an
              answer register initially holding 0, then leave its one-line code. Give it fuel 0 and
              the check says no: it has not completed. Give it fuel 1 and the check says yes: it
              has left the code with answer 1. The first no did not mean the routine would never
              answer yes. It meant “not within this allowance.” You can run that distinction with
              a pebble and one instruction card. The real checker does the same job for any list of
              instructions, with the allowance handed in alongside the claim.


              Theorem D.7 (One host runs every computably presented Thiele machine). Let
              M be a computably presented Thiele machine, so that a driver picks its next move
              (one run per start), a program decides its reading on every state, and its prices are
              whole numbers; and let s0 be a start state. Load UP with the guest compiled from
              M’s presentation and s0 coded in. What the host carries of M’s reading is its latch.
              Then: (1) UP halts exactly when M’s run stops. (2) For every n such that M hasn’t
              stopped before move n, there’s a host time t at which the host’s register for the
              guest’s counter B decodes to M’s state after n moves, the host’s ledger is M’s ledger
              after n moves plus a surcharge, and the host’s flag is M’s latch after n moves; and
              if M stops at n, such a t has UP halted as well. (3) The host’s flag is up at some
              time exactly when M’s reading is yes at some state of its run. (4) If the host’s flag is
              up at time t, the host’s own instructions up to t contain a passing CHECK on a slot,
D.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided, priced in whole units, carried as a latch
                                                                                                                  559

then a passing COMMIT on the same slot with the slot untouched in between, then
a passing CERTIFY; and the slot held the claim “reading program r says yes of v” for
M’s own reading program r, that claim holds, and v decodes to a state of M’s run
where the reading is yes.

Proof. Two layers, each proved on its own. The bottom layer is the compiler: for
every presented machine, its guest program’s run passes through points that code
M’s states in order, with the guest’s ledger equal to M’s ledger plus the surcharge
and the guest’s flag equal to M’s latch, and the guest’s own flag stands on an earned
chain whose claim is M’s reading program applied to the coded state where the
reading first said yes. Here is why. The guest keeps a few registers packed into its
counters the way Minsky packed them: the coded state, a latch bit, the price still
owed, and a register that counts the reading’s steps. It starts at the reading with
nothing owed, and goes round one loop. Run the compiled reading on the coded
state, counting its steps. If it says yes and the latch bit is 0, run CHECK, COMMIT
and CERTIFY on the claim “reading program r says yes of v,” v being the packed
registers with the step count as fuel, set the latch bit, and take three off what’s owed,
stopping at zero. Pay what’s owed in PAYs. Run the compiled driver, and halt if it
says stop. Otherwise run the compiled step and price for the move it picked, put
the new coded state and that price in place, and go round again. Everything but
the PAYs and the one chain is INC and DEC, at no cost. So at the point just after
the PAYs and before the driver runs, once n moves have been made, the coded state
is M’s state after n moves, the latch bit is M’s latch, and the ledger is M’s ledger,
except that the move where the latch bit was set was paid with the chain’s three
and the larger of c − 3 and 0 in PAYs instead of its price c (or, if the reading is yes at
s0 , the start was charged the chain’s three). The CHECK passes, because the fuel is
the reading’s own step count, and at such a value the fixed checker says what the
reading says; the COMMIT finds that fact, since nothing wrote B in between; and
the latch bit lets the chain run once. The top layer is UP , proved the way U was in
the previous theorems, with the PAY case added: it keeps pace with any guest of
this kind, halting and flag matched, ledger equal at matching points, and its flag
earned on a slot. Compose the two. The earned part takes one more step: the host’s
chain gives a guest CHECK that passed, and a guest run that ends with its flag up
has exactly one passing CHECK, the compiler’s CHECK of the reading on counter
B. So the guest CHECK the host’s chain points to is that one, and its claim is M’s
reading at the first state where it said yes.
   There are two things the theorem doesn’t say. First, the host’s flag is M’s latch.
If M’s reading says yes at some state and no at a later one, the host’s flag stays
up, so it says the reading was yes somewhere in the run, and it doesn’t say the
reading is yes now. Second, what the host re-establishes is the reading: the claim
560   D The universal machines


              it checked is “M’s reading program says yes of this coded state,” and that’s all. A
              bare Thiele machine needn’t tie its reading to anything true about sorting, proofs
              or the world outside. If M’s reading is meant to say a list is sorted, that it does is
              a separate correctness theorem about the reading, and the host doesn’t supply it.
              The two universal programs also keep their own guests: U runs the small machine’s
              programs over its three words about numbers, and UP runs computably presented
              machines over the universal claim language.
                  The surcharge comes next, because that’s where the ledger stops being exact,
              and below three units it can’t be helped. The host raises its flag the only way the
              host machine allows, by a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY, and those cost three.
              If M’s first move that turns its reading to yes costs at least three, the host pays the
              difference in PAYs and nothing more is owed. If it costs less, the host pays three
              there anyway, which is the larger of three and the move’s price. The surcharge
              starts at that move: while M’s latch is down it’s zero, so a run that never certifies is
              matched exactly. Whether anything could do better depends on what M paid before.
              When M’s whole ledger at the raise is below three, no program on the host machine
              can match it, since a raised host flag costs three from a clean start. When M’s ledger
              at the raise is three or more, this compiler isn’t always the cheapest. Take a guest
              whose first move costs two and leaves its reading at no, and whose second costs one
              and turns it to yes. This compiler carries it at 2 and then 5, against the guest’s 2
              and 3. A program that looks ahead carries it exactly: inside the first move’s price of
              two it works out the guest’s state two moves on, puts it on B, runs the CHECK and
              the COMMIT of the reading’s claim about it, and puts the guest’s state back; inside
              the second move’s price of one it runs the CERTIFY, which needs only a fact in the
              channel, and nothing has committed since. Its totals are 2 and 3, and its flag stands
              on the guest’s reading at the first state where it said yes. Part (1) of the theorem
              below bounds this compiler, and part (3) is the only lower bound proved.
                  Keep two tally lines for a guest whose first three moves each cost one and whose
              reading first says yes after the third. The guest’s totals are 1, 2, 3. This compiler
              pays one PAY on each of the first two moves, then its three-act chain: the host
              totals are 1, 2, 5. The excess is two, added once. If the third move instead costs
              four, the host runs the chain and one PAY there; both totals then read 6. These are
              counts of charged instructions, not counts of all the work needed to decode the
              guest. Stopping at zero throws away what the chain paid beyond the move’s price.
              A compiler that kept it as credit against the moves after the raise would bring the
              surcharge back to zero once the guest had paid three from the raising move on, and
              a guest whose reading starts at yes would be matched exactly from its third unit of
              cost on. I keep the simpler rule, and every surcharge stated below is this compiler’s.
D.2 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host: driven, decided, priced in whole units, carried as a latch
                                                                                                                  561




Theorem D.8 (Exact, within two, and no better). Let M, s0 and the loaded host be
as in Theorem D.7, and let M’s reading be no at s0 . (1) For every n before M stops
there’s a host time at which the state is decoded and the flag matched as before,
and the host’s ledger is M’s ledger after n moves while M’s latch is down, and that
plus the larger of 3 − c and 0 once it’s up, where c is the price of the move that first
turned M’s reading to yes; so the surcharge is at most two. (2) If moreover every
move that first turns M’s reading to yes costs at least three, the surcharge is zero
and the host’s ledger equals M’s exactly at those times. (3) If M’s latch is up after n
moves while its ledger is below three, then no run of the host machine from a clean
start, under any program at all, ends with its flag equal to that latch and its ledger
raised by exactly M’s ledger. (4) If instead M’s reading is yes at s0 , then at the host
time matching each move n before M stops, the host’s ledger is M’s ledger after n
moves plus exactly three.

Proof. (1) and (2): the guest pays M’s prices in PAYs, a unit at a time, except at the
move where M’s reading first says yes. There it has to run its CHECK, COMMIT
and CERTIFY, three units, and it makes up the rest of the move’s price in PAYs, so it
pays the larger of the price c and three. The price is at least one, because the move
raised a reading (the toll), so the excess is at most two, and none when c ≥ 3. (3):
a raised flag on the host machine costs at least three from a clean start, whatever
the program, and M’s ledger is less. (4): the guest finds the reading yes before M
has made a move, runs its CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY there, three units on top
of a ledger of nothing, and from then on its flag is up, so the reading never first says
yes again and every move’s price is paid in PAYs, exactly.
   Part (3) is an observation in the sense of Section 2: it reads off Observation 15.21,
which holds on the host machine with PAY for the reason given above. Part (4) is
the same three paid at once: if the reading is already yes at the start, the host has
to raise its flag before M has paid anything, and at that point no program can do
better, since M’s ledger there is nothing. After it the three stay on only because this
compiler doesn’t count them against M’s later prices.
   And one machine is carried all the way, by proof, so the class isn’t empty. Its
states are whole numbers, its one move adds one and costs three, its driver always
picks that move, and its reading is “at least three.” The driver returns the fixed
move; the step adds one; the price returns three; and the reading compares the state
with three. The counter constructions in Appendix K implement all four. Loaded
into UP from 0, the host never halts, its flag goes up, at the host time matching
move n its ledger is exactly 3n and its flag is up exactly when n ≥ 3, and the raised
flag stands on a host chain whose slot claims the machine’s own reading of a state
562   D The universal machines


              at least three. That follows from the two theorems above: the reading is no at 0,
              and the one move that turns it to yes, from 2 to 3, costs three, so part (2) of the
              surcharge theorem makes the ledger exact.
                  Now the limits, each of which is in the statement, said plainly.
               • Readings that are decided. The reading’s program has to answer yes or no on
                 every state. A reading a program could only confirm, waiting forever on the no
                 cases, isn’t covered, and neither is a reading no program computes at all.
               • One run per start. The driver picks the move, so the guest is deterministic. A
                 machine whose next move is somebody’s unforced choice gets in only with that
                 choice written into its driver.
               • The record is the latch. The host’s flag is up once M’s reading has been yes at
                 any state of the run, which is exactly the latch of Section 10. A reading that goes
                 yes and then back to no is carried as “it was yes once.”
               • The ledger is exact up to the surcharge. When the reading starts at no, at most
                 two, and zero when the first raising move costs three or more; when it starts at
                 yes, three. And no program on this host, run from a clean start, can do better
                 when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three.
               • Prices in whole units, paid one at a time. A move that costs a million is a
                 million PAYs. The compiler also uses Minsky’s packing. Between them, those two
                 choices set how long the host takes to pay for the guest’s moves.
               • Proved; never run on a presented machine. The demonstration machine’s
                 numbers come from the two theorems above. UP itself has run on guests small
                 enough to finish; a presented machine’s compiled guest is far too large for that,
                 and nobody has run UP on one. Appendix G says what was run.


              D.3 A simpler host, with the guest step built in

              There’s a much simpler host than U, and I keep it in the book because it’s easy to
              read and it shows the copy rule in one line. Its universality is by construction: it has
              a move that runs one guest step by calling the small machine’s own step. It isn’t a
              universal Thiele machine in the sense of Definition D.1, and the reasons are exact. It
              never halts, since it has no HALT and its guest step never traps; its surcharge grows
              without bound, since it charges one even for a guest step that costs nothing; and it
              isn’t a register host, since its guest step does the computing. A host that fixed the
              first two and kept the built-in step would still fail the last (the argument after the
              definition). U is the universal Thiele machine of this book. Read it as a picture of
              what U does the long way, and as a host that starts from any guest state at all, clean
              or not.
                                                       D.3 A simpler host, with the guest step built in   563


   It carries a guest inside its own state: the guest’s program as data, the guest’s
counters, its table, its ledger, its flag. The host has one extra move, run one guest
step. In that one move it looks at the guest’s flag, takes the step, looks again, and if
the flag went from down to up, the host’s own copy of that flag goes up in the same
move, and the host pays for it.

Definition D.4 (The host). A guest is a program P of the small machine together with
a state g of it (Definition 15.2). A host state h has six parts: its own core core(h), its
ledger µ(h), its own flag own(h), the guest program P(h) held as a list of instructions,
the guest state g(h), and the mirror m(h), a yes/no copy of the guest’s flag. The host
has two kinds of move. OWN i runs the instruction i on the host’s own core, costs
what the small machine charges for i, and raises own exactly when that machine’s
flag would rise. GSTEP b costs b. If the host’s core is trapped it does nothing else.
Otherwise it moves the host to its next line and, if the guest’s next instruction costs
at most b, takes one program step of the guest, which leaves a stopped guest where
it is; in the same move the mirror becomes m(h) ∨ (¬cert( g(h)) ∧ cert( g′ )), where
g′ is the new guest state. The host’s reading is own(h) ∨ m(h). Its stored program
is U0 = [GSTEP 1; OWN (INC A); OWN (DEC A 1)]: one guest step, then two
moves that bring the host back to its first line. It loads a program P from ( x, y) with
g(h) = start( x, y) and the mirror and its own flag down.

    Every instruction of the small machine costs at most one, so GSTEP 1 runs every
guest instruction there is. Why charge the budget b? Why not the cost of whatever
instruction got fetched? Because charging the budget keeps the price a function of
the move alone, which is what the definition of Section 2 asks for: you read the
price of a host move off the move, the way you read the small machine’s prices off
its table, without peeking inside the guest. What that costs the host is easy to see. A
host that steps a guest instruction priced 0, an INC say, still pays one for the move.
    So the host’s ledger is closer to a clock than to a receipt for its guests: one unit
per guest step, whatever the step was. It never falls behind the guest’s own ledger
(part (3) of Theorem D.11 below), and it matches that ledger only when every guest
step happens to cost one. Could a cleverer host have simulation-exact accounting,
a ledger equal to its guest’s? Not with this one fixed-price move: GSTEP 1 is the
same move whether the guest’s next instruction is an INC priced 0 or a paid CHECK,
so one price can’t match both. Two moves can: one that costs nothing, takes the
guest’s step when that step costs nothing and otherwise jumps, and one that costs
one and takes it. A loop that tries the first before the second keeps the host’s ledger
equal to the guest’s at every pass. That host still has its guest step built in. U gets
the match with ordinary instructions: it pays only on the record moves it runs itself,
so its ledger equals its guest’s (Theorem D.4).
564   D The universal machines


                 And there’s one thing to say about the definition before the theorems, so you
              know which of them carry weight. GSTEP runs the guest’s instruction by calling the
              small machine’s own step on the guest’s state: the guest’s step is a primitive of the
              host. So “the host runs any guest” (Theorem D.9) is true by construction. The host
              was built to do exactly that, and the proof follows the three moves around the loop.
              The theorems with something in them come after it. From a loaded host, or any state
              where the two agree, the mirror always equals the guest’s flag (Observation D.10).
              Nothing raises the mirror unless the guest itself passes a CERTIFY inside a guest
              step the host paid for (Theorem D.12). No OWN move, in any host program at all,
              touches the guest’s state or the mirror (the second sentence of that same theorem),
              and no host move of either kind rewrites the guest’s program. And the mirror is tied
              to the guest’s earned chain: after any host run from a loaded host, if the mirror is
              up, the guest’s own run from its start contains a passing CHECK, then a COMMIT of
              the same claim, then a CERTIFY, since the mirror is the guest’s flag and the guest
              started clean (Theorem 15.11). So this host runs any small-machine program by
              construction and keeps the guest’s record by theorem, as a copy of the guest’s flag.
              The mirroring program U0 does not earn the host’s own flag; a different program
              could do so with the host’s OWN CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. U does both the
              long way: it runs the guest with its own instructions, and it earns its own flag.



              Theorem D.9 (The host runs any guest). (1) If the host’s core is not trapped, then
              after n moves GSTEP 1 the guest state is the guest program’s own run of n steps
              from g(h), the guest program is unchanged, and the host is still not trapped. (2) If
              the host’s core is at line 1 and not trapped, then 3n steps of the program U0 leave
              the guest exactly where n steps of its own program put it. (3) For every two-counter
              program M and inputs a, b: M halts from (1, a, b) exactly when the host program
              made of OWN moves of the compiled M halts, from a host whose core starts at
              ( a, b), whatever guest that host carries.

              Proof. (1) Before any move, the guest is at g(h). One untrapped guest move has
              budget 1, enough for every guest instruction, so it takes exactly the guest’s next step.
              It leaves the host untrapped, which lets the same argument apply to the next move.
              After the first move the guest has taken one step; after the second, two; and after
              n, exactly n. No such move changes the guest’s program. (2) One pass of U0 is a
              guest step, then INC A and DEC A back to line 1, so it is (1) once per pass. (3) A
              host program made only of OWN moves is the small machine, core for core, and
              Theorem 15.4 does the rest.
              Observation D.10 (The copy is the record). Say a host state h agrees when m(h) =
              cert( g(h)). Every host move takes an agreeing state to an agreeing state, so every host
                                                      D.3 A simpler host, with the guest step built in   565


trace and every stored host program does too, and a freshly loaded host agrees. In
particular, if h agrees and is not trapped, the mirror after n moves GSTEP 1 is the
guest’s flag after n steps of its own program.
Proof. One move at a time. An OWN move touches neither the mirror nor the guest.
A trapped GSTEP touches neither. An untrapped one sets the mirror to the old
mirror or the crossing, and the guest’s flag is a latch (Theorem 15.6), so if the old
mirror equalled the old flag, the new mirror equals the new flag. The last sentence
is this together with Theorem D.9.



Theorem D.11 (The host’s step collects the guest’s toll). (1) If h agrees, is not
trapped, and the guest step that budget b allows takes the guest’s flag from down to
up, then the mirror is down before GSTEP b and up after it, the host’s ledger rose
by exactly b, and b ≥ 1. (2) In the run of (1) of Theorem D.9, from a host that
agrees, if the guest’s flag goes up between its steps n and n + 1, the mirror goes up
between the host’s moves n and n + 1, and that move costs 1. (3) For every host
trace t, µ( g(run(t, h))) + µ(h) ≤ µ(run(t, h)) + µ( g(h)): the host’s ledger grows at
least as fast as the guest’s.

Proof. (1) The guest’s flag rises only on a passing CERTIFY (Theorem 15.6), which
costs 1, and the budget let it run, so b ≥ 1; the mirror was the guest’s flag, so it was
down, and the move sets it to the crossing. (2) is (1) at the matching move. (3)
Write the host’s charge and the guest’s ledger increase beside every move. When
a guest step runs, its price is at most the budget the host paid. When none runs,
the guest’s increase is zero and the host’s charge is nonnegative. Adding these
comparisons along the trace gives

                  µ( g(run(t, h))) − µ( g(h)) ≤ µ(run(t, h)) − µ(h).
Move the two starting readings to the other sides to get the stated form.



Theorem D.12 (No unpaid host certification). If the mirror is down at h and up
after a host move i, then i is GSTEP b with b ≥ 1, the host was not trapped, the
guest’s next instruction was CERTIFY, and the guest’s flag went from down to up in
that move. A trace made only of OWN moves leaves the mirror and the guest state
exactly where they were. And the host’s own flag rises only by an OWN CERTIFY
that passes on the host’s core.
566   D The universal machines


              Proof. An OWN move copies the mirror unchanged, and a trapped GSTEP does too,
              so the rise is an untrapped GSTEP b whose guest step crossed; a crossing is a passing
              CERTIFY, which costs 1 and needed the budget. The own flag moves by the small
              machine’s step line.



              Theorem D.13 (The host is a Thiele machine). For every host state and move, if
              the host’s reading goes from no to yes, the move costs at least 1; the same holds for
              the mirror alone and for the own flag alone. So the host read through own ∨ m, the
              host read through m alone, and the guest class are Thiele machines (Definition 2.1),
              and any host trace that raises the host’s reading costs at least 1.

              Proof. The mirror’s half is Theorem D.12; the own flag’s half is the small machine’s
              toll on the host’s core. The trace form is Section 2’s universal floor.

              Remark D.1 (Two guests, run). Load the guest CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero
              A; CERTIFY; HALT with both counters at 0. After two moves GSTEP 1 the mirror is
              down; after three it is up, the guest’s flag is up, the host’s own flag is still down, and
              the host has paid 3. Under the program U0 the mirror is down at host step 6 and up
              at step 7, with 3 paid. The guest CERTIFY; CERTIFY traps on its first step: after five
              moves GSTEP 1 the mirror is down, the guest is trapped, and the host has paid 5 for
              nothing.
                 That copy can’t be faked. The proof walks every host move there is, and the
              copy only rises in a guest step where the guest itself ran CERTIFY and passed. A
              host program that never touches the guest leaves the copy exactly where it was.
              From a loaded host the copy always equals the guest’s flag, and the host’s ledger
              always grows at least as fast as the guest’s, and a three-instruction loop runs any
              small-machine program one guest step per pass. Here the mirror, the crossing test
              and the charge sit in the host’s step rule, so Theorems D.11 and D.12 hold for every
              sequence of host moves, including ones that never run a guest. Everything the
              simple version gets from its built-in move, U gets from ordinary instructions, plus
              an exact ledger and a flag of its own.


              D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs
              Section 13 left the diagonal standing on any substrate, on a little family built to fit
              it, and on L, handled on its own terms rather than as a substrate. It also said what a
              machine has to supply to fill in the same shape, two things: programs that can be
              handed to programs as numbers, and a recursion theorem for the transformations it
                                                        D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   567


can carry out. This machine’s universal program reads a whole guest program out of
one register, with a numbering of programs that goes there and back (Definition D.3),
and halting is undecidable here in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.5. What’s left
are the two classical results that turn a universal machine into a place where the
diagonal bites: Rice’s theorem and Kleene’s recursion theorem. They come with a
wrinkle I should put first, because it decides which machine they’re about.
     The wrinkle is the one from Section 15, at the end of the subsection on what two
counters compute. The small machine takes its inputs straight into two counters,
and Schroeppel’s memo gives a proof that two plain counters can’t even compute
2n from n. Rice’s reduction has to keep a program’s input safe while a copy of a
halting instance runs. Kleene’s construction has to run an evaluator while keeping
its input. Two counters have nowhere to keep it. So the two theorems land where
they’re true and where I could prove them. The host machine of Definition D.2, the
one with a counter for every number that U runs on, is a fine programming system:
its programs are numbers, an input sits in register 1, and there’s room to spare. On
it both theorems hold in full. On the two-counter machine itself the story splits, and
I’ll tell it at the end of the subsection: Rice’s theorem holds on every input, by a trick
for keeping the input that I’ll show you; Kleene’s holds when inputs are written as
powers of two, the way Minsky packed them; and on plain inputs Kleene’s is false,
and that’s a theorem too.
     The host machine’s programs are numbered in the same style as U numbers a
guest’s. Write ⟨m, n⟩ for (2n + 1) · 2m . INC r is ⟨0, r ⟩, DEC r j is ⟨1, ⟨r, j⟩⟩, HALT is
⟨2, 0⟩, CHECK r is ⟨3, r ⟩, COMMIT r is ⟨4, r ⟩, CERTIFY is ⟨5, 0⟩, and a program is the
list code: the empty program is 0, and an instruction x followed by a program t is
⟨ x, code(t)⟩. An instruction number that is none of these codes reads as HALT. Then
every number decodes to some program, since a positive number is ⟨ x, n⟩ with n
smaller than it, and decoding a program’s code gives the program back. When I put
one program after another, the later one’s jumps move down by the length of what
comes before it, and a jump to a line where it has no instruction, line 0 included,
goes to the line just after it, so a stop inside it hands on to whatever follows. Say
a host program outputs y on input x when, started with x in register 1 and every
other register 0, with a clean table, it halts with y in register 0.
     Rice comes first, because it’s the shorter road. Henry Rice, whom you met
in Section 7, proved in his 1951 doctoral thesis, and published in 1953, that no
program decides any property of what programs do unless every program has it or
none does. Properties of how a program is written aren’t covered. The road from
halting is a single detour. Take a property of what programs do, a program y that
has it, and a program n that doesn’t. Given an instance of two-counter halting, a
Minsky program H with starting counters a and b, build a host program that first
loads a and b into two fresh registers (not register 1, and named by neither y nor n),
568   D The universal machines


              then runs a copy of H moved onto those registers, then empties both, then runs y.
              If H halts on ( a, b) the built program behaves like y and has the property. If H runs
              forever the built program never stops on any input, and it behaves like the program
              that loops, which lacks the property (if the looping program has it instead, swap the
              roles of y and n). Everything the built program does before y is INC and DEC, which
              add nothing to the ledger and touch no fact, channel, trap latch or flag. So a decider
              for the property would be a decider for halting, and by Theorem 15.5 that would let
              a program list every single-tape Turing machine that doesn’t halt. Two words carry
              the weight, and they’re the ones to check in the statement: what “behaves the same”
              sees, and where the program starts.

              Definition D.5 (Behaving the same, on the host). A host program ends in a state
              when it halts there, from the start with x in register 1 and the rest clean; a trap
              counts as stopping. Two host programs behave the same when for every input x, any
              state one ends in has a state the other ends in that agrees with it on every register’s
              value, the fact table, the channel, the trap latch, the ledger and the flag, and the
              same the other way round. The line number and the versions aren’t compared. A
              property of host programs is extensional when behaving the same carries it from one
              program to the other.



              Theorem D.14 (Rice’s theorem on the host machine). Let Π be an extensional
              property of host programs that some program has and some program lacks. Then Π
              is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.5.

              Proof. The reduction above. The prefix before y leaves every register but the two
              fresh ones as it found them, and empties those, so when H halts the built program
              ends in whatever state y ends in from the same input, with the same ledger, table,
              channel, trap and flag. When H doesn’t halt, the built program stops on no input.
              You don’t even need to know whether the looping program has Π: ask the decider
              about it, and its answer says which of y and n to put at the end.
                 A property that depends only on the partial function a program computes,
              whether it stops and what it leaves in register 0, is extensional, so it is covered. That
              case also follows from the recursion theorem below.
                 On the small machine itself the same road works from the clean start, and only
              from there. Say two two-counter programs behave the same from the clean start
              when, whatever state one halts in from counters (0, 0), the other halts in a state
              with the same counters, trap latch, ledger and flag, and the same the other way
              round. The fact table and the channel aren’t compared, because the prefix moves
                                                      D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   569


the versions of A and B by fixed amounts and the facts, the channel’s included,
carry versions. There is no input to keep, since the program starts at (0, 0), and H’s
instance is loaded straight into A and B.


Theorem D.15 (Rice’s theorem for the small machine, from the clean start). Let Π
be a property of two-counter programs that’s carried from a program to any program
that behaves the same from the clean start, held by some program and lacked by
some other. Then Π is undecidable in the reduction sense of Theorem 15.5. In
particular “halts from the clean start” is undecidable.

Proof. The road of Theorem D.14, with the input dropped. Take a two-counter
program H with a start ( a, b), and let y have Π and n lack it; as before, if the
program that loops has Π, swap the roles of y and n. Build the program that does
INC A a times and INC B b times, runs a copy of H with its jumps moved down
(a jump to a line where H has no instruction, line 0 or past its end, goes to the
line just after the copy), empties A and then B with a one-line DEC loop each, and
then runs y with its jumps moved down. From the clean start the copy of H begins
at ( a, b), which is H’s own start, so it stops exactly when H does. If it does, both
counters are emptied and y runs from (0, 0). Every instruction before y is an INC
or a DEC: it adds nothing to the ledger and touches no fact, channel, trap latch or
flag. It does move the versions of A and B up, each by the number of writes that
counter took before y started, and the facts y records carry versions. But a CHECK
or a COMMIT reads versions only to ask whether two versions of the same counter
are equal, and adding one fixed amount to both keeps the answer. So y takes the
same steps inside the built program as it takes from the clean start, with the same
counters, trap latch, ledger and flag at every point, and with facts that differ only
by that fixed shift in their versions. That shift is why the fact table and the channel
are left out of “behaves the same from the clean start.” If H doesn’t stop, neither
does the built program: the copy of H never reaches a HALT, and nothing before
y can trap. So the built program behaves the same as y when H stops from ( a, b),
and the same as the two-line program that loops, INC A then DEC A back to line
1, when it doesn’t. A decider for Π would then decide whether H stops from ( a, b),
with the consequence stated in Theorem 15.5; which of y and n goes at the end is
the decider’s own answer about the looping program. “Halts from the clean start” is
carried by behaving the same from the clean start, held by the empty program and
lacked by the looping one, so it’s covered.
   That theorem covers the clean start only. Every input is harder, because the
standard reduction has to keep the input safe while the halting instance runs, and
570   D The universal machines


              two counters have nowhere obvious to keep it. The way through is at the end of the
              subsection.
                  Kleene’s recursion theorem is the deeper one, and it’s a construction, which is
              Section 13’s point about Kleene’s little gem (Moschovakis’s phrase): the content is
              the building, and the contradiction in Section 13 was just the last line. It says: for
              every transformation F of programs that some program can carry out on numbers,
              there’s a program p that computes the same thing as F ( p). The shape of the building
              is the old one. From the program that carries out F, build an evaluator that reads a
              number, treats it as a program’s code, specialises that program to its own code, runs
              F’s program on the result, and runs whatever program comes back. The specialising
              step is what logicians call s-m-n: fix one input of a program and get a new program
              that needs one input fewer. Then the witness is the evaluator specialised to its own
              code. Run on any input, it builds its own code, hands it to F’s program, gets the
              code of F ( p), and runs that.
                  Each piece on the host machine comes next, with its exact premise.


              Theorem D.16 (s-m-n, and a universal program for host programs). (1) For a
              number c and a host program V, let spec(c, V ) be c copies of INC 2 followed by V
              with its jumps moved to follow them. Then for all x, y, spec(c, V ) outputs y on input
              x if and only if V, started with x in register 1 and c in register 2, halts with y in
              register 0. (2) There is a host program W made only of INC, DEC and HALT such
              that, for all c, x, y, W started with x in register 1 and c in register 2 halts with y in
              register 0 exactly when the host program numbered c outputs y on input x.

              Proof. (1) The prefix writes register 2 c times and nothing else, so it moves that
              register’s version from 0 to c. A fact records a version, so after the prefix every later
              version of register 2, and the version in every fact the run records about register 2,
              is c more than in a clean run. A CHECK or a COMMIT reads versions only to ask
              whether two versions of the same register are equal, and adding c to both keeps the
              answer, so the two runs take the same steps. The run is V’s run from the stated start,
              moved down by c lines. (2) is the evaluator. A finite algorithm decodes a number
              into a program, runs it step by step on given registers, record layer included, and,
              searching over the number of steps, returns the output of the first halting run. It
              is a finite tape algorithm, and the translation of Appendix K turns any finite tape
              algorithm into a finite program of INC and DEC on finitely many counters. The host
              runs those instructions on registers of its own, with HALT marking the returned
              output. That’s W.
                 One thing to be exact about: U is not that universal program. U runs two-counter
              guests, and a two-counter guest given its input plainly can’t run the evaluator. With
                                                       D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   571


inputs written as powers of two one can, as Theorem D.22 near the end of this
subsection shows. W runs host programs, and it can, because it’s a host program on
a machine with registers.


Theorem D.17 (Kleene’s recursion theorem on the host machine). (1) For every
host program T there is a host program e such that for all x, y: e outputs y on
input x if and only if, for some d, T outputs d on the number of e, and the program
numbered d outputs y on x. (2) So for every transformation F of host programs
that some host program carries out on numbers (on the number of p it outputs
the number of F ( p), for every p), there is a host program e such that for all x, y, e
outputs y on x if and only if F (e) does. (3) The same on numbers: for every function
 f on numbers, defined everywhere, that some host program computes, some number
e has the program numbered e and the program numbered f (e) output the same on
every input.

Proof. (1) Let E be the following program of INC and DEC, built the same way as
W from one finite evaluator, with T’s number t written in. On inputs x and c it
computes the number of spec(c, Pc ), where Pc is the program numbered c, runs T
on that number to get d, and then runs the program numbered d on x. Let c0 be the
number of E, and let e = spec(c0 , E). By (1) of Theorem D.16, e on input x does
what E does on x and c0 . And E on c0 builds the number of spec(c0 , Pc0 ), which is
the number of e, since Pc0 is E. So e hands its own number to T, gets d, and runs d
on x. (2) and (3) are (1) with T carrying out F or f .
    That fixed point is of the function: e and F (e) stop on the same inputs and leave
the same number in register 0. Their ledgers, flags and fact tables can differ: e is
all INC and DEC, so whatever F (e) pays, e only simulates. I’d like a fixed point that
agrees on the record too, and the next two theorems say how much of that can be
had. The ledger and the flag can be had, but agreement on every register can’t.


Theorem D.18 (The recursion theorem, up to the record). Let F be a transformation
of host programs that some host program T carries out on numbers. Then there is a
host program e such that, for every input x, any state e ends in has a state F (e) ends
in that agrees with it on register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of
facts in the table, and whether the channel is empty, and the same the other way
round. So e stops on x exactly when F (e) does, and the ledgers are equal exactly,
with no surcharge. T may itself check, commit and certify.
572   D The universal machines


              Proof. The construction is Theorem D.17’s, with a different evaluator. The first step
              is to see that a record is small. From a clean start, a host program that stops has a
              record I can read off five numbers, in this order: what it left in register 0; how many
              facts the table holds; what is left of the ledger once the facts, the trap and the flag are
              paid for, which I’ll call the replay allowance; 1 if the flag is up and 0 if not; and 1 if
              the trap latch is up and 0 if not. The record obeys a short rulebook, and you can read
              each rule off the price table. A run stops at its first trap, so its ledger is its passing
              CHECKs, plus its passing COMMITs, plus its passing CERTIFYs, plus one if it trapped
              (only those three can fail, and the failing one is charged). Its passing CHECKs are
              its facts, at most sixteen. Its flag is up exactly when some CERTIFY passed. So the
              allowance is the passing COMMITs plus the passing CERTIFYs less one for the flag,
              which is never negative, and the ledger is the facts, plus that allowance, plus the
              flag, plus the trap. A COMMIT needs a fact behind it, so a positive allowance means
              at least one fact. A CERTIFY needs a commitment, so a raised flag means a passing
              COMMIT, and so a positive allowance. And the channel is empty exactly when no
              COMMIT passed, which is exactly when the allowance is zero, since a CERTIFY can’t
              pass before a COMMIT has. The allowance counts repeated CERTIFYs as well as
              COMMITs; it counts the cost the replay can spend on commitments, not the original
              commitment events. Those are the only properties of a record the replay will use.
                  The second step is five blocks, one for each number. Each block reads the code of
              T, runs T on the number of the specialised program, runs the program that comes
              out on x, and returns its number. All of that happens on plain data: the blocks are
              programs of INC and DEC, built the way W was, from a finite evaluator translated
              into INC and DEC. So if T has marks of its own, they are simulated and never paid.
                  The third step is the payment. The evaluator puts 1 in a fresh register, which is
              ⟨0, 0⟩, the pair of Zero and 0, so it satisfies the host’s one property, and CHECKs it
              once for every fact; there are at most sixteen, so the table has room. It COMMITs to
              that claim once for every unit in the replay allowance. It CERTIFYs once if the flag is
              up. It copies the first number into register 0. And if the trap latch is up, it CHECKs a
              register that holds 0, which fails, since 0 is no pair, and the host traps. Everything
              before the payments is INC and DEC and costs nothing, and the payments cost what
              the record costs, so the ledger is exact. Specialise the evaluator to its own number,
              as before.
                 Try CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY, CERTIFY on a true claim. The ledger is four, the
              table holds one fact, the flag is up and the trap is down, so the replay allowance is
              two. The replay pays CHECK, COMMIT, COMMIT, CERTIFY: the same ledger of four
              and the same summary, in a different order. The theorem claims that agreement and
              no more.
                                                       D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   573


   In the replay, the trap latch is up exactly when the fifth number is 1, and the
flag exactly when the fourth is positive. Look only at the function computed and
you get the usual fixed-point statement back. There are two limits, and the second
one is a theorem. First, e pays after it has computed everything. It is not the way
U runs a guest, mirroring every move: e pays the counts, CHECKs, then COMMITs,
then the CERTIFY, whatever order F (e) used, so the order of the record’s events isn’t
preserved, and for a program F (e) that never stops, e never stops and pays nothing,
though F (e) may pay without bound. The relation says nothing about states in the
middle of a run. Second, no fixed point agrees on every register, or on what the
facts name.


Theorem D.19 (No fixed point of full behaviour). There is a transformation F of
host programs, carried out by a host program, such that no host program e behaves
the same as F (e) in the sense of Definition D.5.

Proof. Let F ( p) be the one-line program INC r, with r one above the number of
p. To carry this out on numbers, add one to the input code, encode INC with that
register, and encode the one-element instruction list. These are finite arithmetic
operations of the counter construction in Appendix K. A program’s number is at
least every register it names: the number of an instruction is above its register, and
the code of a list is above every instruction in it. So e can’t name r, the register F (e)
writes. On input 0 the run of F (e) ends with 1 in register r, and if e stops at all, it
ends with 0 there. If e doesn’t stop, then it already differs from F (e), which does.
Either way they don’t behave the same.
   A variant of F that also CHECKs register r and commits to it gives F (e) a fact and
a commitment about r that e can’t have, so no fixed point agrees on the fact table
alone, or on the channel alone, or on the versions of the registers. What survives is
what Theorem D.18 states, plus any register named in advance, or any finite set of
them: before it pays, the evaluator reads that register’s final value off the simulated
run of F (e) and writes it into its own copy of the register, keeping its scratch work
and its two payment registers elsewhere. The register F above writes is chosen by
looking at e, and that’s the one no fixed point can follow.
   And with the recursion theorem proved, the wall of Section 13 goes up on this
machine without assuming that theorem as an extra premise. Call a property of
host programs functional when it depends only on the partial function a program
computes.
574   D The universal machines




              Theorem D.20 (The diagonal on the host machine). Let Π be a functional property
              of host programs that some program has and some program lacks. (1) Read “ f is
              representable” as “some host program carries f out on numbers.” Then no function
              d from programs to Booleans whose flip is representable is right about Π on every
              program: this is the argument of Theorem 13.1, reproved for host programs, with its
              recursion premise a theorem here. (2) No host program decides Π outright: there
              is no program D that, on the number of every program, halts with a number in
              register 0 that’s 1 exactly when the program has Π.

              Proof. (1) The flip, send programs that d calls good to the program lacking Π and
              the others to the one having it, is carried out by a host program by hypothesis.
              Theorem D.17(2) gives a program e that computes what its image computes; Π
              holds of e exactly when it holds of the image, and the image lacks it exactly when d
              calls e good, so d is wrong at e. (2) From a deciding program D build a host program
              that computes D’s flip on numbers, by the finite-simulation search of Appendix K,
              reading the Boolean from the first halting run of D; then (1) applies. This one is a
              plain no: the flip (1) needs is built from D itself, so no premise about what can be
              represented is left over.
                  Rice and Kleene are the ingredients the diagonal of Section 13 asks a substrate for,
              and the wall they put up doesn’t care about the record: the base does the computing
              and the flag watches. A program’s ledger and flag are among what “behaves the
              same” sees on the host, so a nontrivial property of those is undecidable too, in the
              reduction sense of Theorem D.14, and the fixed point is up to the record, as far as
              the theorems above say and no further.
                  Now the two-counter machine itself, which I promised at the start of the sub-
              section: Minsky’s two bins of pebbles and nothing else. Rice comes first. Say a
              two-counter program behaves the same as another on a set X of inputs when, on
              every input n in X, started with n pebbles in bin A and none in bin B, one stops
              exactly when the other does, and then they agree on both bins, the trap latch, the
              ledger, the flag, and on which property and which counter each recorded fact and
              the channel are about. The versions are left out: they say which write a fact is about,
              and the trick below moves them.
                  The trick is the whole problem. Rice’s reduction has to keep the program’s input
              safe while a copy of a halting instance H runs, and there’s no third bin to keep it
              in. My first guess was bin B, and that dies at once, because H needs both bins. The
              second guess is Minsky’s own packing: keep several numbers in one bin as powers
              of different primes, H’s two counters as the exponents of 2 and 3, and the input
              as the exponent of 5. That dies more quietly. To put the input there, the program
                                                      D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   575


would have to turn n pebbles into 5n , an exponential, and Schroeppel’s memo, from
Section 15, gives a proof that two plain counters can’t even build 2n from n. I had
no way to build 5n .
    What works is to stop keeping the input beside the work. Turn n pebbles into
6n + 5, which is only adding, and then multiply in H’s counters as powers of 2 and 3.
H runs by halving the pile and splitting it in thirds and building it back up, and the
6n + 5 rides along in the middle of every one of those piles. It’s odd, and counted
off in threes it leaves two over, so no halving or thirding ever reaches into it.


Theorem D.21 (Rice’s theorem for the two-counter machine, on any inputs). For
any set X of inputs, a property of two-counter programs that’s carried from a
program to any program that behaves the same on X is undecidable in the reduction
sense of Theorem 15.5, unless every program has it or none does, and then it’s
decidable. X can be every input, the powers of two, or {0}.

Proof. For every input: given a two-counter instance H starting from counters a and
b, build a program that turns the input of n pebbles in bin A into (6n + 5) · 2a · 3b ,
runs H inside the exponents of 2 and 3, divides out every 2 and every 3 when H
stops, takes away 5, divides by 6, and then runs the program that has the property.
Because 6n + 5 shares no factor with 2 or 3, the coding never mistakes it for an
exponent, and the input comes back whole. If H halts, the built program behaves
the same as the one with the property on every input; if not, it never stops on
any input, like the program that loops. As before, if the looping program has the
property, put a program that lacks it at the end instead, and the decider’s own
answer about the looping program says which. So a decider for the property would
decide two-counter halting.
    Try input 2 while the simulated counters hold 1 and 2. The pile is 17 · 2 · 9 = 306.
Raising the first simulated counter doubles it to 612; lowering the second divides it
by three, to 204. Strip off every factor of two and three and 17 remains; subtract
five and divide by six, and the original input 2 is back.
    So 6n + 5 is the place to keep the input that two counters seemed not to have.
It isn’t beside the work but inside it, in a factor the work never touches. I like that
one more than I can justify: the input hides in the leftover that every halving and
thirding walks straight past.
    Kleene needs more than keeping an input. It needs a program that runs a
program. So write a number x as 2x pebbles and read a result as the exponent of 2,
the way Minsky did. With inputs written that way, there’s one two-counter program,
call it U2 , that, started on 2x · 3e , stops with 2y exactly when the program numbered
e gives y on x; specialising a program to a number is exact; and the recursion
576   D The universal machines


              theorem holds. (U2 is a different program from the universal host program U, which
              runs on the machine with a register for every number.)


              Theorem D.22 (Kleene for the two-counter machine, inputs written as powers of
              two). (1) For every transformation F of programs that some program carries out
              on program numbers, there’s a program e that computes the same function as F (e),
              with inputs and outputs written as powers of two. (2) The fixed point is of the
              function only: there’s such an F for which no e behaves the same as F (e) once the
              properties and counters of the recorded facts count.

              Proof. (1) The host’s three pieces, with two counters in place of registers. First, the
              universal program. Load a program’s number e and its input x together as 2x · 3e in
              bin A, with bin B empty. The evaluator of Appendix K, the one that searches budgets
              and runs the program numbered e on x, is a finite counter program on finitely many
              counters, and packing those counters into two by the prime-exponent construction
              of Appendix K.3 gives U2 : started on 2x · 3e it stops with 2y in bin A exactly when
              the program numbered e, started on 2x , stops with 2y . Second, specialising. For a
              number c and a program V, let spec(c, V ) be c copies of a block that multiplies bin
              A by three, followed by V with its jumps moved down. The block is INC and DEC
              only, so it adds nothing to the ledger and records nothing, and started on 2x the c
              copies leave 2x · 3c ; so spec(c, V ) on 2x does what V does on 2x · 3c . Third, the fixed
              point. Let T be a program that carries out F: on 2n , n the number of a program
              p, it stops with 2m , m the number of F ( p). Build E from the same finite evaluator,
              with T’s number written in, and pack it into two counters as before: on 2x · 3c it
              computes the number of spec(c, Pc ), where Pc is the program numbered c, runs T
              on that number to get d, and runs the program numbered d on 2x . Let c0 be the
              number of E and e = spec(c0 , E). On 2x , e does what E does on 2x · 3c0 : it builds
              the number of spec(c0 , Pc0 ), which is the number of e itself since Pc0 is E, hands it
              to T, gets the number of F (e), and runs F (e) on 2x . The machine is deterministic,
              so a packed output is unique, and for every x and y, e started on 2x stops with 2y
              exactly when F (e) does. (2) is the counterexample that follows.
                  The counterexample in (2) is short. Number the programs the way U numbers
              its guests (Appendix L), so a program’s number is above the code of every property
              it names. Let F ( p) be the one-line program that checks that bin A holds at least the
              number of p plus one. A program can only record facts about properties it names,
              so no e can record the fact F (e) records, and from a large enough input F (e) does
              record it.
                  Even with Schroeppel in hand, my first guess about Kleene was that the powers
              of two were a convenience, and that plain inputs would only take more work. They
                                                      D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   577


don’t take more work: with plain inputs, Kleene’s theorem is false. A transformation
is carried out if some program, started on 2n where n is the number of a program p,
stops with 2m where m is the number of F ( p).


Theorem D.23 (No plain recursion on two counters). (1) No program of n lines
stops with c · x pebbles in bin A, started on x pebbles in bin A and none in bin B, for
every x, where c is the least prime above N = 16(n + 1)(4n + 1)16 . (2) So there’s
a carried-out transformation F such that no program e computes the same plain
function as F (e).

Proof. (2) from (1): let F ( p) be a program that multiplies bin A by the constant c
determined by the length of p. Multiplication by a fixed constant is the transfer loop
of Appendix K. Decoding a finite program, counting its lines, finding the least prime
above a number and writing that loop are computable operations, so a program
carries out F on encoded program numbers. A fixed point would multiply every
plain input by the constant forbidden by (1).
    For (1), suppose an n-line program did it. Split each state into the two bin counts
and a finite control: the line (one of the n lines, or “stopped” for any line with no
instruction), the trap, whether the channel is empty, and the table read entry by
entry as a fact’s property, its counter, and whether it is current (its version is its
counter’s version now) or stale. Only properties the program names can enter the
table, at most n of them, so an entry is one of at most 4n kinds, and a table of at
most sixteen entries is one of at most ∑k≤16 (4n)k ≤ (4n + 1)16 lists. So there are at
most Q = 4(n + 1)(4n + 1)16 controls. The control and the two counts decide the
next control and counts: a CHECK writes a current fact, a write to a counter makes
that counter’s facts stale, a COMMIT passes exactly when a current fact with its
property and counter is in the table, a CERTIFY passes exactly when the channel isn’t
empty, and the ledger, the flag, the channel’s contents and the versions themselves
never decide a branch. Call the control with the two counts a configuration.
    Pick a threshold h ≥ 1 above every number k in a property Ge(k) the program
names. At h or above, a count answers every question the program can put to it (is
it zero, is it even, is it at least k, can a DEC take one off) the same way as any other
count of the same parity at h or above. Call a control together with the parities of
both counts a pattern; there are at most 4Q = N of them.
    The forced run. A stage start is a configuration with one count below h, in the
exact bin, and the other at h or above, in the large bin, which holds v. From it, run
the program while pretending the large bin can never fall below h: follow the exact
bin exactly, the large bin only by its parity, and keep a tally of the large bin’s net
change. This forced run depends on the control, the exact count and the parity of v,
578   D The universal machines


              and not on v itself. The real run does exactly what the forced run does, with the
              large bin at v plus the tally, up to the first step where v plus the tally drops below h,
