              the crossing. A move changes a count by at most one, so at the crossing the large
              bin holds exactly h − 1.
                  What a forced run does. One of three things, fixed by the stage start. (a) It stops.
              (b) It comes back to a step with the same control, the same exact count below h and
              the same parity of the large bin as an earlier step; it’s deterministic in those, so it
              repeats that stretch forever, and the exact count stays bounded. (c) Neither. Then
              it has at most 2Qh steps with the exact count below h, one per combination, so
              from some step on the exact count stays at h or above for good. Among any N + 1
              consecutive steps of that tail, two have the same pattern, at steps t1 < t2 ≤ t1 + N,
              and between them the exact count changes by some δ, even because the parities
              match. If δ < 0, the run from t2 repeats the run from t1 with the exact count
              lowered by |δ| each time round, so after finitely many rounds it goes below h, which
              the tail never does. So δ ≥ 0, and the stretch repeats forever, lifted by δ each time
              round, never dipping below h. In every case but (a), then, the forced run from some
              step on repeats one stretch forever, and each time round the exact bin changes by a
              fixed g and the large bin by a fixed amount; in (b) g = 0, and in (c) the stretch is at
              most N moves long.
                  What the real run does, once v is large enough for that stage start, meaning the
              large bin can’t reach the crossing before the forced run stops or its repeating stretch
              has gone round once in full. If the forced run stops, the real run stops the same
              way, with the exact bin at a count fixed by the stage start and the large one at v
              plus a fixed amount. If the large bin doesn’t lose each time round, the real run
              never crosses and never stops. If it loses and g = 0, the real run crosses with both
              bins below a bound fixed by the stage start. The remaining case is a transfer: each
              time round the large bin loses m > 0 and the exact one gains g > 0. That’s case
              (c), so the stretch has at most N moves, each moving one bin by at most one, and
              m, g ≤ N; both are even. Now the stage rule. Start the same stage with v + m
              in place of v. The parity is the same, so the forced run is the same, and since the
              crossing comes after the stretch has gone round once, the bin needs exactly one
              more time round to get down to h − 1. So the real run crosses one time round later,
              with the same control, the formerly large bin at h − 1, and the other bin larger by g.
              With v + km it crosses k times round later, the other bin larger by kg. After a transfer,
              the crossing is a new stage start with the bins’ jobs swapped. For example, a loop
              that takes two pebbles from the full bin and puts four in the other has m = 2 and
              g = 4: two more pebbles going in buy one more trip round the loop, and four more
              coming out.
                  Choosing the input. Apart from v, a stage start is one of finitely many things:
              a control, an exact count below h, a parity, and which bin is which. Take one
                                                       D.4 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs   579


bound V ≥ h that’s large enough, in the sense above, for every one of them, and
above every count that was called fixed or bounded above: the exact bin of a stage
that stops, and both bins at a crossing with g = 0. The configurations with one
count below h and the other below V are finitely many. If the program multiplied
every input by c, no two different inputs could pass through the same configuration,
because everything after it, the output included, would be the same, while cx ̸= cx ′ .
So only finitely many inputs pass through that finite set. Pick an input x that passes
through none of it and has cx above V. Since ( x, 0) is itself a configuration, x ≥ V.
    Following that input. The run from ( x, 0) starts a stage: bin B exact at 0, bin A
large at x. Every later stage start along the run has its large bin at V or above, or the
run would pass through the finite set. The run stops, since the program multiplies,
so no stage runs forever. No stage crosses with g = 0, since that crossing is in the
finite set. So each stage before the last is a transfer, with its own pair (mi , gi ), and
the last one stops. It stops with its exact bin below V and its large bin at its v plus
a fixed amount, and the output cx is above V, so the output bin A is the large one.
There are finitely many stages, because each takes at least one step of a run that
stops.
    The comparison. Put D = 2 ∏i mi and run the input x + D. It is x plus a multiple
of m1 , so by the stage rule the first stage crosses at the same configuration except
that the other bin is larger by ( D/m1 ) g1 = 2g1 ∏i≥2 mi , which is a multiple of m2 .
So the second stage crosses the same way, with the next bin larger by 2g1 g2 ∏i≥3 mi ,
and so on through every stage. The last stage starts with its large bin larger by
2 ∏i gi , an even amount, so it stops the same way with bin A larger by exactly that.
So the outputs from x + D and from x differ by 2 ∏i gi . But multiplication by c
makes them differ by cD = 2c ∏i mi . Cancel two:
                                    c ∏ m i = ∏ gi .
                                      i         i

Empty products are 1. Every factor on the right is between 1 and N, and c is a prime
above N, so it divides none of them, and a prime that divides a product divides one
of its factors. So c can’t divide the right side. That’s the contradiction.
   Nothing in that proof used more than this: two bins that move one pebble at a
time, finitely many controls, a next step fixed by the control and the bins, and bins
that, above some threshold, are read only through their parity. Any machine like
that has the same obstruction, and the same computable transformation F with no
program e equivalent to F (e) on plain inputs.
   I went looking for Schroeppel’s own memo and found a scan of it. As I read it, his
route is close in spirit: he trades a two-counter machine that starts with one counter
empty for a machine with one register that can only add, multiply and divide by
fixed numbers and take one away, each of those built out of one of the program’s
580   D The universal machines


              loops, and that’s the stages here under another name. I haven’t followed his proof
              line by line, so I compare the two at that level and no further; the argument this
              book stands on is the one above. The c it uses is astronomically bigger than anything
              a real multiplier needs, and finding the best bound is a question I leave alone.
                  So on two bins, Rice holds on every input; Kleene holds with inputs written as
              powers of two, for the function, and fails for the facts; and with plain inputs Kleene
              fails outright. The last one is the answer I didn’t see coming: the powers of two
              weren’t a convenience, and on two bins they’re the difference between a recursion
              theorem and none.
                  That failure has a setting computability theorists know. The mathematician
              Hartley Rogers, in his 1967 textbook, calls a numbering of the computable functions
              acceptable when every other computable numbering of them can be translated into
              it by a computable map, and in every acceptable numbering Kleene’s theorem holds.
              Read on plain inputs, the two-bin programs number something smaller than all
              the computable functions, since none of them computes 2n from n (Schroeppel’s
              theorem; compare Theorem D.23), so they fall outside Rogers’s class, and his route
              to the theorem isn’t open there. The computer scientists James Royer and John
              Case (1994) studied that territory: programming systems for classes of functions
              smaller than all the computable ones, which can’t be acceptable, and what can still
              be programmed and proved in them. And the logician and puzzle writer Raymond
              Smullyan’s two books on recursion theory and self-reference (1993, 1994) take
              the fixed-point theorems apart axiomatically, so you can see which property of a
              numbering each one leans on. The plain-input failure is a small instance on the map
              they drew.


              D.5 The universal machine’s guest interface

              I’ll say what the two universal programs cover plainly, a sentence at a time. The
              stated class of guests of U is the small machine’s programs, every one of them, from
              every clean start start( x, y). The whole-run theorems don’t cover a guest handed
              facts in its table, a commitment in its channel or a raised flag at the start; the
              one-step simulation, by itself, works from any related pair. It’s the same kind of class
              Turing’s universal machine has: a fixed instruction set, and a finite program held
              as data, here packed into one number the way Turing packed his into a description
              number. Each guest keeps its computation, its halting, its answer, its record and its
              prices, exactly: the host halts when it halts, its flag goes up when the guest’s would,
              on a chain of its own, and its ledger is the guest’s.
                   The guests of UP are every Thiele machine whose driver, step, prices and reading
              are computed by programs, with the reading decided on every state. Each keeps its
              computation and its halting; its reading becomes the host’s flag as a latch, raised on
                                                        D.5 The universal machine’s guest interface   581


an earned chain whose claim is the guest’s own reading; and its prices become the
host’s ledger, exactly, except for a surcharge at the move where the reading first says
yes: at most two when the reading starts at no, exactly three when it starts at yes.
The surcharge is zero when that move costs three or more, and it can’t always be
avoided: when the guest certifies with a ledger below three, no program on that
host, run from a clean start, matches its ledger exactly (Theorems D.7 and D.8).
Picture a clerk who’ll stamp anybody’s receipt. He copies it onto his own forms, bills
at your rates to within two when your reading starts at no and to within three when
it starts at yes, and the stamp at the bottom is one he earned by checking your own
reading, not one he copied.
    What’s outside the class is outside the theorems. A machine whose reading no
program decides (an oracle checker, say, which the definition of certified Thiele-
complete doesn’t rule out) doesn’t come in. Nor does a machine whose next move is
nobody’s computation. The two universal programs have different start conditions:
U’s whole-run result starts its guest clean; UP starts its guest where the presentation
says, even if that state already has a yes reading. The host starts clean and earns a
claim about that reading. It does not reconstruct or authenticate the guest’s earlier
history.
    And insisting on no built-in step is the point, and a plain interpreter shows why.
A plain interpreter on an ordinary computer runs guests too, but then the guest’s
record is data the interpreter’s program updates by convention, which is exactly the
position of the ordinary programmable computer from Section 14 and Section 15.13.
That’s a fact about how such interpreters are built. It says nothing about what they
can do: U and UP are fixed interpreters, and their record isn’t kept by convention.
Nothing in them raises the host’s flag except the host’s own CERTIFY, and the host’s
step won’t let that pass without a COMMIT, or the COMMIT without a CHECK on a
slot nobody has touched. The guest’s record isn’t data the host updates. It’s a record
the host earns again, under the same rule, on its own registers.
APPENDIX E




Every model

After the smallest honest machine (Section 15) and the universal programs of the
previous appendix, there was a worry I couldn’t put down. Everything in them was
built on Minsky’s two counters. The definition of certified Thiele-complete names a
two-counter window in clause (a). The universal program runs two-counter guests.
So is all of this a fact about counters? Pick a different machine to start from, a
Turing machine with its tape, a register machine, Alonzo Church’s lambda calculus,
and does the record still go on the same way, or did the definition depend on my
example?
   I chased it with a picture: a box with a panel bolted to its front. The box
computes, with levers for moves and a window showing what clause (a) asks to see,
two numbers and a line number. The panel is the example machine’s earned layer:
version tallies that click when the box writes, a rack for facts, the flag, and the three
buttons CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY at a cost of one each. The worry is whether
that panel only bolts onto the one box I built.
   So this appendix goes both ways. First the panel goes onto boxes I didn’t build,
and I say exactly what a box has to supply for it to fit. Then other boxes, panel
and all, get run inside mine. If the record is really about the record and not about
pebbles, both trips should work, and the conditions on the way should say what has
to survive the move.


E.1 From any base up

Start with the direction I care about most: the panel onto a box I didn’t build. The
box can be any machine at all that has a universal base in the sense of clause (a), and
in the picture that means two things: it shows a two-counter window, and for each
two-counter instruction it has a lever that acts on the window as that instruction
does. What else is inside, what its states look like, I don’t get to know.
    My first guess was to keep whatever the box came with. Plenty of machines have
a meter of their own, or a light on the front that means something’s done, so leave
those where they are, bolt the panel on beside them, and see what happens. It can’t
work, and the definition says why. If a lever can cost anything, computing adds to
the ledger, and certified Thiele-complete asks that it add nothing, which is a rule of
the price list, not a claim about heat. If a lever can switch on the box’s own light, a

                                  582
                                                                              E.1 From any base up   583


record went up with no CHECK behind it. Certified Thiele-complete rules out both.
So the meter and the light come off, along with everything else the box already had:
its costs, its record, all of it, except the states, the levers and what each lever does to
the state.
    Then bolt on a panel cut down from the small machine’s, and nothing else: one
version number for the whole box that every lever raises, which is the tally, a table
of facts, a channel, the flag, and three new moves, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY,
each costing one, with every lever costing nothing. The three act as on the small
machine, with the tally in place of a counter’s version: CHECK files its claim with
the tally when the checker says yes and the table has room, COMMIT puts the fact
in the channel when the table holds its claim at the current tally, and CERTIFY raises
the flag when the channel holds a fact. Call that the lift of the machine. A lever
moves the box only while the trap is down. The trap works as on the small machine:
a CHECK, COMMIT or CERTIFY that fails sets it, nothing takes it down, and once
it’s up every move, a lever included, changes nothing but the ledger.


Theorem E.1 (Every universal base lifts). (1) The lift of any box with a universal
base, over a language of claims about the box’s state (“unchanged” meaning the
box’s state is the same), with an exact equality test and a checker proved to say
yes exactly when the claim holds, is certified Thiele-complete, as long as the claims
its CHECK can ask include one that’s true at one loaded state and false at another,
and the fact table has room for at least one fact. (2) The claims “this register is at
least n” and “the program is at line n,” read off the window, always include such a
claim, so with those claims every universal base lifts. (3) Conversely, every certified
Thiele-complete machine has an interface meeting the four clauses under which
its base moves, taken alone, form a machine with a universal base. (4) The panel
leaves the box alone: from a state whose trap is down, a run of lever pulls in the lift
moves the box exactly as the box’s own run does, and the trap stays down.

Proof. (1) The four clauses, one at a time. (a) The lift keeps the box’s states, levers
and step and adds the tally, the table, the channel, the flag, the trap and the ledger.
With the trap down, a lever moves the box’s part of the state as the box’s step does,
raises the tally by one, and touches nothing else. So from a live state, which is
a state whose box part is live and whose trap is down, the window moves as the
instruction does and the state stays live; no lever changes the flag; the loaded states
are the box’s loaded states with an empty panel, so they’re clean; and the flag, once
up, is lowered by nothing. (b) Start with the panel empty. The only move that
raises the flag is CERTIFY, and CERTIFY traps unless the channel holds a fact; the
channel is filled only by a COMMIT, which traps unless the table holds its claim at
584   E Every model


              the current tally; and the table is filled only by a CHECK that passed, which files
              the claim with the tally it was checked at. So in front of the raise there’s a passing
              CHECK of some claim c, then a COMMIT of c at the same tally, then the CERTIFY.
              The trap is down from the CHECK to the COMMIT, since the COMMIT passed and
              nothing takes the trap down, and with the trap down the tally rises with every lever
              pull, so an unchanged tally means no lever was pulled in between, so the box’s
              state is unchanged, and that’s what “the thing c is about is unchanged” says in the
              lift’s language, whose claims are about the box’s state. A passing CHECK means the
              checker said yes, and the checker was proved to mean what it says. (c) is the price
              list: levers at a cost of zero, the three buttons at one each, the ledger the running
              sum. (d) Take the claim that’s true at one loaded state and false at another. From
              the first, CHECK passes and files it, the table having room, COMMIT finds it at the
              same tally, and CERTIFY raises the flag. From the second the CHECK traps, and
              a trapped machine raises nothing. (2) “A is at least 1” is true at the loaded state
              showing (1, 1, 0) and false at the one showing (1, 0, 0). A window claim is a register
              and a number, or a line number, so two claims can be tested equal, and its checker
              reads the window, which is its meaning, so the checker is sound by definition. (3)
              Take an interface the machine is certified Thiele-complete with and throw away
              every move whose kind isn’t base. What’s left has the same states, the base moves
              as levers, and the interface’s window, live states and loaded states, and clause (a)
              says of exactly these that the window follows every instruction from every live state,
              that the state stays live, and that each loaded state shows (1, a, b) and is live. That’s
              a universal base. (4) A lever pull with the trap down changes the box’s part by the
              box’s step and the tally by one, and nothing else; the trap goes up only on a CHECK
              that fails, a COMMIT without its fact, or a CERTIFY with the channel empty, never
              on a lever. So along a run of lever pulls the box’s part follows the box’s own run,
              pull for pull, and the trap stays down.
                 Of the checker’s exactness, (1) uses one half whole and the other half once: (b)
              needs the checker to say yes only when the claim holds, and (d) needs it to say yes
              on the one claim at the one loaded state where that claim is true. The theorem asks
              for both halves whole, the way every theorem about the small machine does, so one
              checker serves all of them.
                 Clause (b), the small machine’s proof with the bins swapped out for whatever
              the box has, is the part I’d braced for, and it turned out to be nothing. The chain
              CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY never looked at anything but the tally and the claim.
              The levers changed only the tally on the panel, making old facts stale; they never
              inserted a fact, made a commitment or raised the flag. Neither side of the proof ever
              needed to know it was looking at pebbles.
                                                                            E.2 What never lifts   585


   So the earned layer isn’t something two counters do. It sits on top of any box
with a universal base, and it never needed to know which one. I’d half expected to
be rewriting the proof once per model.


E.2 What never lifts
A theorem that says the panel fits every box is one I don’t trust until I’ve watched
it fail to fit something. So I went looking for boxes it won’t turn into a certified
Thiele-complete machine, and the first one I tried was the one I was surest would
work.
    It was a Turing machine, with one fixed table, and each lever does one row of
the table. That looked like the obvious base to me, and it isn’t one at all. Clause
(a) asks for a lever for every two-counter instruction, and there are infinitely many
two-counter instructions, since a jump can go to any line. A fixed table has finitely
many rows, so it has finitely many levers, and it runs out of levers long before it
runs out of instructions. The first two items below are that failure in two forms, and
the others fail for other reasons, and each is proved.


Theorem E.2 (What doesn’t lift). (1) A box with only finitely many levers has no
universal base, and no box with a universal base is finitely branching, meaning
that from every state all its levers together lead to only finitely many different
states. (2) The lift of a finitely branching box is never certified Thiele-complete,
whatever claims and fact table it gets. (3) Neither is the lift of a box whose step
ignores the state it’s in, where each lever sends every state to the same place. (4)
On a record axis where every place is at or below every other, there is no certified
Thiele-complete machine at all. (5) With a checker that says yes exactly when the
claim holds, the lift’s own non-vacuity clause holds exactly when the fact table has
room and some claim is true at one loaded state and false at another.

Proof. (1) Take a universal base and its loaded state showing (1, 1, 0). For each j
the lever for DEC A j must take it, in one pull, to a state showing ( j, 0, 0): A was
above 0, so one comes off and the line jumps to j. Different j, different window,
different state. So one state has infinitely many different successors, which is what
not finitely branching means; and since one lever lands in one place from one state,
the levers for the DEC A j are all different, so there are infinitely many of them. (2)
In the lift the moves that cost nothing are the levers, since each button costs one,
and from any state the levers together lead to finitely many states: with the trap
down, the box’s finitely many successors, each with the tally raised by one, and with
it up, the state itself. (The buttons can lead to infinitely many, one CHECK for each
586   E Every model


              claim, but each costs one.) If the lift were certified Thiele-complete through some
              interface, that interface’s base moves would cost nothing by clause (c), so they’d
              all be levers, and by Theorem E.1(3) they’d form a universal base on their own. By
              (1) a universal base has a state from which its moves reach infinitely many states,
              and levers of a finitely branching box can’t. (3) Suppose each lever lands in one
              place whatever the state. The move an interface gives an instruction is a base move,
              at a cost of zero by clause (c), while each button costs one, so it’s a lever. Pull the
              lever for INC A twice from a loaded state showing (1, 0, 0), and pull the lever for
              INC B and then the lever for INC A from the same state. Both runs end with the
              lever for INC A, so both end with the box in the one place that lever lands, with the
              tally two higher and the panel untouched: the same state of the lift. But the window
              would have to show (3, 2, 0) after the first run and (3, 1, 1) after the second, and a
              window is a function of the state. The same two runs refute the box on its own. (4)
              On a record axis, raising the record means leaving the down-set of where it stood. If
              every place is at or below every other, every down-set is the whole axis and no move
              ever leaves one; but clause (d) asks for three moves that raise the record from some
              loaded state. (5) If the table has no room, every CHECK traps and no CERTIFY ever
              fires, so (d) fails. If no claim is true at one loaded state and false at another, (d)’s
              second half has no witness. And when both hold, (d) was proved in (1).
                  So my first test case failed, and at first I read item (1) as saying a Turing machine
              can’t be a base at all. It says something narrower. A Turing machine with one fixed
              table can’t be one. A classic model comes in the other way round, with one lever for
              each program that carries out one two-counter instruction, run to its end. Pull it
              and the box runs that program from start to stop in a single move. That’s how the
              register machine below comes in, and it’s the honest reading of “a Turing machine is
              a base” too. The levers are the programs, not the rows.
                  That still leaves a worry about clause (a) itself. It asks for one lever per two-
              counter instruction, which is a fact about how the two-counter machine is presented,
              and a box that does each instruction in several pulls looks shut out for a reason
              that has nothing to do with computing. It isn’t shut out, and the fix is to let the
              pulls be grouped. Call a box a base by simulation when it has a window reading
              a two-counter configuration off each state, through any encoding at all, a class of
              live states, a finite list of its own levers for each two-counter instruction, and a live
              loaded state showing (1, a, b) for each start, such that from every live state the list
              acts on the window exactly as the instruction acts on a configuration and the state
              stays live. The grouped box has the same states, and its levers are finite lists of the
              box’s levers, a list pulled in order.
                                                                      E.3 Computation is the slice   587




Theorem E.3 (The one-lever presentation loses nothing). (1) Every box with a
universal base is a base by simulation. (2) Every base by simulation is a universal
base of its grouped box, and a run of the grouped box is the box’s run along the
joined lists. (3) So for every base by simulation, the lift of its grouped box, with
the window claims and a fact table with room for at least one fact, is certified
Thiele-complete. (4) The box with five levers, add one to A and go to the next line,
the same for B, add one to a jump target (leaving the window alone), and for each
of A and B “if it’s above 0, take one off and jump to the target, otherwise go to the
next line, and put the target back to 0 either way,” is a base by simulation, has no
universal base, and its grouped box lifts to a certified Thiele-complete machine.

Proof. (1) Each list has one lever. (2) The grouped box’s step is the box’s run along
the list, so the simulation clause of a base by simulation is clause (a) for the grouped
box. (3) is (2) with Theorem E.1. (4) INC r is one pull; DEC r j is j pulls of the
target lever, then the decrement lever for r, from a live state, where live means the
target is 0; the decrement lever puts the target back to 0, so the state stays live. The
box has five levers, so item (1) of Theorem E.2 says it has no universal base.
    So clause (a) can be read by simulation, and nothing is lost: a box that carries
out each two-counter instruction with one fixed finite list of its own moves, through
any window, is a universal base the moment its moves are grouped, and it lifts. Item
(1) of Theorem E.2 is about the presentation, and the five-lever box is the proof that
a finite lever set is not what fails. What this doesn’t give is a Turing machine’s rule
table running a tape: the five-lever box is a register box, and the next subsection is
still how Turing machines come in.
    Item (3) is a box with no memory. Pull a lever and it lands wherever that
lever always lands, whatever happened before. So a window on it can’t tell INC A
followed by INC A from INC B followed by INC A, and a box that can’t tell those
apart can’t keep two counters in its window.
    Item (4) is the trouble with bare preorders from Section 11, where the cups
stopped telling you the place, showing up one level higher. If every place on the axis
is at or below every other, the flag has no up to go to. No step ever turns a cup over,
nothing ever has to be paid for, and the earned chain has nothing to earn.


E.3 Computation is the slice

The lift says the panel goes onto any box with a universal base. Turn it round and
it says something about the box: the box is what you see of the lift when you stop
588   E Every model


              looking at the panel. That’s where ordinary computation sits in this book, so I want
              it said exactly, with a name.

              Definition E.1 (Slice). Take a machine with a ledger, a whole number for each
              state, and a loaded state for each start, and take a box with a universal base. A slice
              of the machine onto the box is a map from the machine’s states to the box’s states, a
              move of the machine for each lever of the box, called its computing move, and a class
              of the machine’s states, called working, such that: (i) each loaded state is working,
              and the map sends it to the box’s loaded state for the same start; (ii) from a working
              state, a computing move lands on a working state, and the map sends where it lands
              to where the box’s lever takes the map’s image; (iii) from some loaded state there
              are two runs whose ends the map sends to one box state, with the record up at one
              end and down at the other, and two runs whose ends it sends to one box state, with
              different ledgers.
                  When there’s a slice, I’ll say the box is a slice of the machine. The first two clauses
              say the slice runs as the box runs. Start with a working state and pull one computing
              lever. Clause (ii) says that its picture moves exactly as the box moves, and that
              the full state is working again. That last part lets you apply the same rule to the
              next lever, then the next. A whole run therefore follows the box’s run, move for
              move. Clause (i) puts the two at matching starts, so they finish at matching pictures
              too. The third clause says it can’t see what was kept or what it cost: a function of
              the box state that gave the record at the end of every run from every loaded state
              would have to give both answers at the one box state the clause names, and the
              same goes for the ledger. Nothing else is hidden in the definition. Read the box’s
              window through the map and take as live the working states whose image is live,
              and the first two clauses make the computing moves for the box’s instruction levers a
              universal base of the machine. So a machine has a slice onto some box exactly when
              it has a universal base whose window meets the third clause, and then the window
              itself is a slice onto the two-counter box, whose states are configurations and whose
              levers are the instructions. The third clause does work. A Thiele-complete machine’s
              computing moves, taken alone, are a box, and the map that forgets nothing meets
              the first two clauses onto it and fails the third, because the record and the ledger
              are functions of the state; and the window of the first clock of Observation 10.13,
              whose record is a question about its counters, fails it too.


              Theorem E.4 (Computation is the slice). (1) Take the lift of a box with a universal
              base, as in Theorem E.1(1). Forgetting the panel, which keeps the box’s part of each
              state and drops the tally, the table, the channel, the trap, the ledger and the flag,
              is a slice of the lift onto the box, with the levers as its computing moves and the
                                                                       E.3 Computation is the slice   589


states whose trap is down as its working states. Beyond that, CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY never move the box’s part, from any state; from any box state with an
empty panel, the lever runs are sent, under forgetting, to exactly the box’s own runs
from that state, lever list for lever list; and from a loaded state where the claim of
Theorem E.1(1) is true, the run of no moves and the run CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY
of that claim end on one box state with the flag down and up and ledgers exactly 3
apart, CERTIFY three times ends there too with the flag down and the same ledger
as the second run, and CERTIFY d times, for any d, ends there with the flag down
and a ledger d above the first run’s. (2) With no room in the fact table, the lift of any
box, with any claims, is certified Thiele-complete through no interface at all. (3) Let
a machine be Thiele-complete through an interface; every certified Thiele-complete
machine is (Theorem 15.23). Its computing moves are exactly its moves that cost
nothing, so they’re the same through every interface it’s Thiele-complete through;
taken alone, with the interface’s window, live states and loaded states, they form
a machine with a universal base; and the window is a slice of the machine onto
the two-counter box, with the instructions’ moves as computing moves and the live
states as working. (4) Let a machine be run as one rule: from each state, every
move leads to the same next state. It has no universal base, no base by simulation
and no slice onto any box. It obeys the toll exactly when every move costs at least
one or no state reading no steps to one reading yes, so it’s a Thiele machine only as
a clock or with a reading that never rises.

Proof. (1) The lift’s loaded states are the box’s loaded states with an empty panel
and the trap down, so they’re working, and forgetting sends each to the box’s loaded
state for its start. From a state with the trap down a lever moves the box’s part as
the box’s step does and leaves the trap down (Theorem E.1(4)), which is the second
clause. Start with any box state and an empty panel. The first pull matches the
box’s move and keeps the trap down; the next pull therefore starts under the same
conditions. Repeat through the word and every pull matches. A CHECK, COMMIT
or CERTIFY that passes changes only the table, the channel, the flag and the ledger;
one that fails sets the trap and adds to the ledger; and with the trap up every move
changes nothing but the ledger. None of them touches the box’s part. Now take the
loaded state where the claim is true. The run of no moves ends there with the flag
down and the ledger at 0. On the other run the CHECK passes and files the claim,
the table having room, the COMMIT finds it at the same tally, and the CERTIFY
raises the flag: three moves at one each, none of them moving the box, so the same
box state, the flag up and the ledger at 3. CERTIFY from a clean state finds the
channel empty and traps, and every later move changes only the ledger, so CERTIFY
d times ends at the same box state with the flag down and the ledger at d, which at
d = 3 is the chain’s ledger. So the third clause holds, for the flag and for the ledger,
590   E Every model


              and no function of the box state and the ledger together gives the flag. (2) Take any
              interface and the three moves its clause (d) names. Each costs one by clause (c), so
              each is a button. Take a loaded state from which they raise the flag; it’s clean by
              (a), so its flag is down by (b). If its trap is up, nothing passes and nothing rises. If
              its channel holds a fact, CERTIFY alone raises the flag from it: a run of one move
              from a clean state that ends with the flag up, where (b) asks for a CHECK and a
              COMMIT before the raise. If its channel is empty, some COMMIT has to pass inside
              the three moves, before the CERTIFY that raises the flag. Until then no CHECK
              has passed, because a CHECK passes only with room in the table, and no button
              moves the tally, so that COMMIT found its fact in the loaded state’s own table at the
              loaded state’s own tally; that COMMIT and a CERTIFY, run from the loaded state,
              then raise the flag in two moves, against (b) again. So the three moves raise the
              flag from no loaded state, and clause (d) fails. (3) By (C), computing moves cost 0
              and every other move costs 1, so the computing moves are the moves that cost 0,
              whichever interface the machine is read through. Throw the rest away and what’s
              left has the same states, the interface’s window, live states and loaded states, and
              a move for each instruction that acts on the window as the instruction does from
              every live state and keeps it live, with each loaded state live and showing (1, a, b): a
              universal base, as in Theorem E.1(3). The same facts are the first two clauses of a
              slice onto the two-counter box, and the third is Theorem 10.15(2): two runs from
              one loaded state end on one window, one with the record up and one with it down,
              and their ledgers differ. (4) From each state all the moves lead to one state, so the
              machine is finitely branching, and by Theorem E.2(1) it has no universal base. A
              slice would give it one, as the remark after Definition E.1 says. A base by simulation
              fails too. A list of p moves does p steps of the rule, so two lists run one after the
              other end in the same place in either order. From the loaded state showing (1, 0, 0),
              INC A and then DEC A to line 5 shows (2, 1, 0) and then (5, 0, 0), while DEC A to
              line 5 and then INC A shows (2, 0, 0) and then (3, 1, 0), and one state can’t show
              both. For the toll: if a state reading no steps to one reading yes, every move takes
              that step, so every move costs at least one, every step does, and the machine is a
              clock (Observation 10.13); if none does, the reading never rises and the toll asks
              nothing.
                 Not every part of that carries the same weight, and I’d rather say which before
              somebody else does. Some of it holds by construction. That the slice runs as the
              box runs, and that CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY leave it alone, are how the lift
              was built, and the blindness in (1) follows from the second once the chain raises
              the flag: the chain and the run of no moves end on one box state because no button
              moves the box. In (3), the window meeting the first two clauses of a slice is the
              definition of Thiele-complete read out, and so is the fact that the moves that cost
                                                                        E.3 Computation is the slice   591


nothing are the same through every interface. Three parts could have failed. That
the lift is certified at all is the earned chain of Theorem E.1, clause (b). That the
window of every Thiele-complete machine can’t see what was kept or what it cost is
Theorem 10.15, and it could have gone the other way: the first clock’s window sees
its record. That a table with no room certifies through no interface is (2). And (4),
that a machine run as one rule has no slice and is a Thiele machine only as a clock
or with a reading that never rises, is short, and its second half rests on one choice in
Definition 2.1: the toll puts the price on the move, the same from every state. With
a price that could read the state, a machine run as one rule could charge exactly its
raises.
    What “computation” means in the theorem’s name is a box’s levers acting on its
states. A model that comes with a move for each two-counter instruction is covered
as it stands, and one with a fixed list of its own moves for each is covered once
its moves are grouped (Theorem E.3). A model run as one rule, a Turing machine
stepping by its one table, is covered by (4) only: it has no slice, and it isn’t a slice of
anything. A Turing machine read the other way, with a lever for each program that
carries out one two-counter instruction, as in the previous subsection, is a box like
any other. Nothing in the theorem uses the equivalence of the seven models below
(Theorem E.6(1)), which is other people’s work; that equivalence is what says a box
with a universal base computes whatever the other models compute.
    A machine run as one rule can still run programs, and its program can keep a
flag. Whether that flag is a record the machine keeps or a bit it only simulates can
be said exactly too, once the program is part of the state.
Observation E.5 (A record or a simulated bit). Take a machine whose moves are
operations on configurations, with a reading of the configurations, and put the program
in the state: a state is a program, which picks an operation for each configuration,
together with a configuration, and one step applies to the configuration the operation
the program picks there and keeps the program. Take every program. Then the reading
never comes down under any operation from any configuration exactly when, read on
these states, it never comes down from any state.
Proof. If no operation brings the reading down anywhere, no step does, since each
step applies an operation. If an operation brings it down from some configuration,
the program that picks that operation at every configuration is one of the programs,
and the step from the state made of that program and that configuration brings it
down.
    So whether a cell is a record or a simulated bit is a fact about the one rule that
steps program and configuration together, and it takes the whole set of states to see
it. A certification cell that some program can clear, like the one a universal machine
592   E Every model


              keeps as plain data on its tape (Section 15.13), is a simulated bit, though on a run
              whose program never clears it the cell goes up and stays, as a record would.

              Why the live-state clause stays in the slice
              Go back to the blown fuse. A free lever turns the live machine’s gears and leaves
              the trapped machine still. Hide the difference between those states and one camera
              picture would have to prescribe both outcomes. Theorem 15.1 gives the exact
              consequence: hide every native CHECK globally, require autonomous free moves,
              and every projected free move becomes identity.
                  Keep the camera promise on live states instead. The computing moves act there
              and keep the machine live. A failed panel check leaves that domain. That is the
              boundary in the slice above. It lets the computational view move while the native
              failure rule keeps its power to stop the run. Restricting the promise to reachable
              states would not do this: append a failed CHECK to a run and the trapped state
              is reachable too. It is the live boundary, which that check crosses, that makes the
              difference.
                  The certificate and ledger remain passive beside the core. The trap is inside the
              core, where the gears read it. Add the publication file and you can keep which
              claims were certified, with the native lamp as its nonempty reading. The fuse still
              works as before. The file records what was published; the live-state clause says
              where the computing promise holds. Both boundaries belong in the description of
              the machine. Theorem 15.9 proves that the lamp reports whether the publication
              file is empty. Theorem 15.20 counts how many different files can sit above the same
              full native state.


              E.4 The same thing, in seven models

              Now the other direction, the one the worry was really about. Put boxes with different
              insides in a row: one with a tape, one rewriting lambda terms, one with bins. Is a
              panel riding on one of them the same as a panel riding on another? The honest way
              to ask is whether the boxes agree on what they compute.
                  My first idea was to wire the boxes to each other myself, two at a time, with a
              relation that says one box’s run keeps pace with another’s, but that’s the wrong tool.
              Section 10’s weak base equivalence is about runs keeping pace, and what I need
              here is coarser: do the boxes compute the same relations on numbers? For that the
              work is already done, and it isn’t mine. The seven models are the weak call-by-value
              lambda calculus L, Turing machines, two Minsky instruction conventions, binary
              stack machines, Conway’s FRACTRAN, and the µ-recursive functions, and that they
              all compute the same things is Minsky’s, Shepherdson and Sturgis’s, and Forster,
                                                                  E.4 The same thing, in seven models   593


Larchey-Wendling and their coauthors’ work. The translations, with how each one
writes its inputs and reads its outputs, are in Appendix K.


Theorem E.6 (The base doesn’t matter). (1) A relation on numbers that’s com-
putable in any one of those seven models is computable in all seven. (2) The box
that keeps a whole two-counter configuration in one number, with one lever for
each instruction, has a universal base, its step is computable in all seven models,
and its lift, with a table of sixteen facts, is certified Thiele-complete. (3) A register
machine of the kind Cook and Reckhow described, where each two-counter instruc-
tion compiles to at most five of its own instructions, has a universal base too, and its
lift is certified Thiele-complete. (4) Any box on numbers with a universal base lifts
to a certified Thiele-complete machine, and its step, computable in one model, is
computable in all seven.

Proof. (1) Compose the translations of Appendix K. (2) Encode a configuration as
⟨ℓ, ⟨ a, b⟩⟩. Decoding, performing one INC or DEC, and encoding the result are the
total finite arithmetic operations constructed there. So the window follows each
instruction exactly; loading is the encoding of (1, a, b). (3) Let RAM registers 0, 1
and 2 hold the simulated line, A and B, and keep register 3 equal to 1. To increment
counter register r, add register 3 to r and then to register 0. To decrement it with
target j, use these five lines, numbered 0 to 4: if r > 0 jump to 3; add register 3 to
register 0; jump to 5; subtract register 3 from r; set register 0 to j. At line 5 the finite
block has ended. A base move restarts a block at its first line, runs it for its length,
and keeps the resulting registers; an ended block stays put. The zero and positive
cases give exactly the required window, and neither changes register 3. Loading
puts (1, a, b, 1) in registers 0 to 3. (4) Apply the lift theorem to that universal base
and apply (1) to its step function.
    So the answer to the worry is that the record doesn’t care. A box with a universal
base, described in any of the models people have used to say what computing is,
takes the same panel, becomes the same kind of machine, and pays the same price,
one each, for the same three acts.
    And the trip goes back down. So far the panel went onto other boxes. Now put
another box, panel and all, inside mine. Appendix D.2 proved that the fixed program
UP on the small machine’s host runs every computably presented Thiele machine.
In terms of the seven models, that reads: if the four relations that describe a Thiele
machine (its driver, which picks the next move or says stop, its step, its cost and its
reading, on codes) are computed in any one of the seven by programs that answer
on every input, then the machine is computably presented, and UP runs it, halting
594   E Every model


              when it halts, with its flag, and with a surcharge of at most two when its reading
              starts at no.
                  So a Thiele machine described in lambda calculus runs, under one fixed program,
              on the small machine’s host, which gives model independence in both directions:
              up, by lifting any universal base, and down, by running anything presentable on one
              fixed program. When I saw both arrows close I stopped worrying that the definition
              depended on my example. A definition that did wouldn’t survive being carried both
              ways.


              E.5 Why two counters

              If the box doesn’t matter, why did I build on two bins? I wanted the smallest box
              that holds up, and the obvious smaller one has a single bin. Nothing earlier in this
              book says one bin is too few. So before I’d let myself say two is the fewest, I tried
              one.
                  Watch what a program on one bin can see. While the bin isn’t empty, it can’t
              tell how full it is: a stretch of lines that never finds the bin empty does exactly the
              same thing from a fuller bin, with the extra pebbles riding along. So the only news a
              one-bin program ever gets is the bin running dry. Between two of those moments it’s
              just walking its own lines, and among more moments than there are lines, two are
              on the same line, which is the pigeonhole again. Put those together and a one-bin
              program either stops within a count you can write down in advance, or never stops
              at all.


              Theorem E.7 (One counter is too few). (1) A program P of INC, DEC and HALT
              instructions on one bin, started with n pebbles in it, halts exactly when it has stopped
              within k (n + k + 1) steps, where k is the number of lines in P. So whether it halts is
              decidable. (2) Halting for the book’s two-counter machine is undecidable. (3) So no
              computable translation takes each two-counter program and start to a one-counter
              program and start that halts exactly when the original does.

              Proof. (1) If k = 0, the program has already stopped. Otherwise suppose it is
              still running after T = k (n + k + 1) steps, so the T + 1 configurations at times
              0, 1, . . . , T are all live. If the counter has stayed at most n + k up to time T, those
              live configurations have only k (n + k + 1) = T possibilities: k lines and n + k + 1
              counter values. There are T + 1 of them, so one repeats, and the deterministic run
              loops forever.
                  If instead the counter reached n + k + 1 by time T, take the first time it did, and
              look back to the last time before that when it was at most n. In between it stayed
                                                            E.6 The lift and its instruction interface   595


above n, so above 0. It moves at most one per step, so on the way up it arrived at
each of the k + 1 levels n + 1, . . . , n + k + 1; mark the first arrival at each. There
are k + 1 arrivals and k lines, so two arrivals have the same line ℓ, at levels a < b.
Every DEC in the stretch between them found the counter positive. Start that same
stretch at level b: every counter value is larger by b − a, so still positive, every DEC
goes the same way, and the run comes back to line ℓ at level 2b − a. Repeat forever.
Either way a run still live at time T never stops, so a run that stops does so within T
steps, and running P for T steps decides it. (2) The tape simulation, prime packing
and halting diagonal of Appendix K, carried over to the book’s instruction set line by
line. (3) Such a translation, followed by the test in (1), would decide two-counter
halting, against (2).
   So two counters are the fewest in exactly this sense: one counter can’t compute
everything, because its halting can be decided, and two, handed their inputs packed,
can. I like where the answer came from. The pigeonhole that left no spare chair in
the closed room is the same one that says why the box has two bins.


E.6 The lift and its instruction interface

The lift gives each box with a universal base an earned panel. In the other direction,
every certified Thiele-complete machine supplies a universal base through its own
base moves. The obstruction results also identify two kinds of base that never
lift. Together these describe the coverage proved here. Two further classification
questions concern bases outside those classes and the possibility of certification
through an interface other than the lift’s own.
    The tape-to-counter construction of Appendix K connects bases through what
they compute. The lift then supplies the record operations. Its tally is one edition
number for the whole box, whereas the small machine keeps an edition per counter.
That coarser tally is enough for the lift’s arguments. To run the lifted machine inside
the presented-machine interpreter, supply the four computability relations for its
chosen presentation.
    The construction lets you follow the box and the panel separately: the base
provides its computing moves, the panel earns its record, and the live projection
recovers the box’s working run.
APPENDIX F




Built from parts

Back in Section 2 I asked a question and only got halfway: bolt two Thiele machines
together, and do you get one? Everything real is built out of parts. A computer is
a processor and memory and a disk, a bank is branches, a proof is lemmas. If the
record and its toll only held for one machine at a time and fell apart the moment
you put two together, they’d be a property of toys.
   So put two Thiele machines on a bench, each box with its own panel, and wire
them up the three ways anybody wires machines. Side by side, with no wire between
them at all, so that every move is a lever pulled on one box or the other. End to
end, with the first box’s bins tipped into the second’s when the first is done. And one
inside the other, with the inner box running as a guest on the outer one. Some of it
holds and some of it provably doesn’t, and the places where it doesn’t were where I
learned the most.


F.1 Side by side
Two boxes on the bench, no wire between them. A move of the pair is a lever pulled
on one box or the other. The question is what the pair’s record should be, and my
first answer was the wrong one: a single count of how many certifications the bench
has made, one number, easy to read. I’ll come back to why it fails, because it’s in
the list of things that break. What works is to keep both panels showing. The pair’s
record is the pair of records, a place for the left machine and a place for the right
one, compared one side at a time.
    Since that record has more than two places, “certified Thiele-complete” in this
appendix means the definition of Section 15 with the record allowed to be a place
along a direction, the way Section 11 set it up. Read on a direction, clean states
all sit at one place, the floor; a record never moves below where it was; and in
clause (b) a raised record is one that isn’t at or below where the run began, with the
CERTIFY the move that first takes it out. The old definition had a single bit there,
and at two places this one is exactly the old one.




                                 596
                                                                                   F.1 Side by side   597




Theorem F.1 (Side by side). (1) The cost of any run of the pair is the left machine’s
cost of its moves plus the right machine’s cost of its moves, and the order in which
levers on the two boxes were interleaved doesn’t change where the pair ends up or
what it paid. (2) The pair obeys the toll exactly when both machines do. (3) Read
through “either flag is up,” two Thiele machines side by side are a Thiele machine
with floor one; read through “both flags are up,” a run that starts with both flags
down and ends with both up costs at least two, and two is reached when each part
can certify for one. (4) Two certified Thiele-complete machines side by side are a
certified Thiele-complete machine. (5) In that pair, call a side’s floor the place on
its record axis where its clean states sit. A run from a clean start that ends with
each side at or above a point that isn’t at or below that side’s floor makes at least
six record moves and raises the ledger by at least six. Six is reached, from suitable
loaded starts, by a three-act certificate on each side; a particular pair of target points
can need more. (6) The pair of records is the product in the precise sense: for any
machine mapping into both, preserving records, there’s exactly one map into the
pair that does both jobs.

Proof. (1) A move of the pair is a lever of one box. It moves that box’s component by
that box’s step, leaves the other component alone, and costs what that box charges
for it. So the pair’s run is the pair of the two boxes’ runs along the projections of the
trace, each box’s moves in the order they came, and the cost is the left projection’s
cost plus the right’s. Two interleavings with the same two projections end in the
same state at the same cost. (2) The toll prices a step that takes the record out of
the down-set of where it stood. A pair is at or below another when both sides are, so
the down-set of a pair is the two down-sets side by side, and a move of the left box
leaves the pair’s down-set exactly when it leaves the left down-set, the right side not
having moved. So the pair’s exits are the left exits and the right exits, each priced by
its own box, and the pair obeys the toll exactly when both parts do; for the converse,
an exit at zero cost on one side is an exit at zero cost of the pair with any state at
all on the other. (3) Read through “either flag is up,” a step from neither to either
raises one side’s flag, and that side charges it at least one, so the pair is a Thiele
machine with floor one. Read through “both flags are up,” a run from both down to
both up raises each side’s flag on some step, no move touches both, and each such
step costs at least one; when each part can certify for one, the two certificates one
after the other cost two. (4) Give the pair the interface that reads a move as its own
box reads it, takes a claim to be a claim of one side, about that side’s component
and unchanged when that component is unchanged, with both sides clean as clean,
both sides loaded as loaded, the sum of the ledgers as ledger, and the left box’s
598   F Built from parts


               window as window. Clause (a) is the left box’s clause (a), since a left base move acts
               on the left window as its instruction does and a right move doesn’t touch the left
               component, and no base move of either side changes either record. Clause (c) is the
               two price lists added. Clause (d) is the left box’s witness claim with the right box
               idle. Clause (b) is the one with work in it. Take a run from both clean that ends with
               the pair’s record raised, and cut it just after the first move that takes the pair’s record
               out of where it began. That move is one side’s, and since pairs compare side by side
               it takes that side’s record out of where that side began. Project the cut run onto
               that side: a run from clean that ends with that side’s record raised, so by that side’s
               clause (b) it contains that side’s chain, a passing CHECK of a claim c, a COMMIT of
               c with c’s component unchanged in between, and a CERTIFY. Put the other side’s
               moves back where they were. None of them touches the component c is about, so
               the chain is a chain of the interleaved run. (5) If a side ends at or above a point
               that isn’t at or below its floor, its record ends not at or below its floor either, or the
               point would be at or below the floor by passing through it. The clean start puts that
               side at its floor, so the projection onto that side is a run from clean with its record
               raised, which by that side’s clause (b) has three record moves of its own, a CHECK,
               a COMMIT and a CERTIFY. The two sides’ moves are different moves, so six record
               moves at least, and by (c) a ledger rise of at least six; a three-act certificate on each
               side, from loaded starts where each side’s witness claim holds, makes exactly six.
               (6) A record-preserving map from a machine Z into a box is a map of states with a
               monotone map of records, the record of the image being the image of the record,
               and every move of Z simulated by some run of the box. Given one into each box,
               send a state of Z to the pair of its images. The record of the pair is the pair of the
               records, and a move of Z is simulated by the left box’s run followed by the right
               box’s, which is a run of the pair by (1). That map followed by either projection is
               the map you started with, and any map into the pair with those two projections
               agrees with it on every state, which is what equal maps means here.
                  Most of that is what you’d guess from the bench. Each box keeps its own ledger
               and nobody else pulls its levers, so the costs add, and it can’t matter which box you
               happened to work on first. The six in (5) is two certifications costing three each,
               one per box, with no discount for doing them on the same bench.
                  Machines, with maps that keep the record, form a category, and item (6) says
               these pairs are its products. Ask the maps to keep the cost too and the pair stops
               being a product: a machine mapped into both boxes would pay its cost once on
               each side, twice in all. What survives is a symmetric monoidal structure, which is all
               that side by side needs. Its pentagon, triangle and hexagon laws say that regrouping
               four boxes, inserting an idle box, or exchanging groups of boxes gives the same final
               wiring whichever permitted route you take. Label the boxes and follow each wire:
                                                                         F.2 One after the other   599


every rewiring only moves boxes around, so both routes put each wire at the same
labelled terminal, at the same cost.
   That paragraph is the most formal way I know of saying “side by side composes,
and nothing about the order of the parts matters.” It’s a lot of category theory to
confirm what the bench told me in a glance, and I’m glad to have it anyway. A
glance is where I’d have missed something.


F.2 One after the other
Now wire them end to end. Run the first box, and when it’s done, tip its two bins
into the second box’s start, at no charge on the ledger, and run the second. Programs
get chained that way everywhere, and my first thought was that the tipping couldn’t
matter, because it’s plumbing: pebbles go from one bin into another, nobody checks
anything, and plumbing has no business on a record. That turned out to be half
right, and the wrong half is item (4).


Theorem F.2 (One after the other). (1) Running one certified Thiele-complete
machine and then handing its two counters to another through loads that cost
nothing gives a certified Thiele-complete machine. (2) For any two programs of the
two-counter machine, it computes the composite: some schedule leaves the first
machine’s window where the first program takes the input, and the second’s where
the second program takes that result. (3) The hand-off keeps the toll when every
state it can load into sits at one level of the second machine’s record. (4) If some
load lands the second machine at a record that isn’t at or below another load’s, the
hand-off loses the toll: it’s a certification nobody paid anything for.

Proof. (1) Give the second machine a loadable form. A state is either pristine,
holding the second machine’s loaded state for some ( a, b), or running, a state of the
second machine. A move LOAD ( a, b) turns a pristine state into the pristine state for
( a, b) and does nothing to a running one; the second machine’s own moves move a
running state as before and turn a pristine state into a running one. LOAD is a base
move and costs nothing. When the second machine is certified Thiele-complete its
loaded states are clean and stand at the floor, so a LOAD leaves the record alone;
the base, the toll and the witness claim are the second machine’s; and the chain
in front of a raise lies after the last LOAD before the second machine’s first move,
so it lifts through the projection onto the second machine’s own moves. So the
loadable form is certified Thiele-complete, and the composite, the first machine
side by side with it, is certified Thiele-complete by Theorem F.1(4). (2) A wired
schedule is the first machine’s moves, then a LOAD of the two counters its window
600   F Built from parts


               shows at that moment, then the second machine’s moves. The first stretch runs the
               first program on the first window; the LOAD puts the second window at (1, a, b) for
               the counters ( a, b) the first stretch left; the last stretch runs the second program on
               it. If both programs halt, the two windows after the schedule are the two halting
               configurations, the second’s on the first’s output, and the wire cost nothing. (3) and
               (4) are one fact read two ways. A LOAD from the pristine state for one input to
               the pristine state for another costs nothing, and carries the record from where the
               first loaded state stands to where the second stands. If every loaded state stands at
               one level, no LOAD moves the record, the composite’s exits are the two machines’
               own, and the toll is kept by Theorem F.1(2). If some loaded state stands at a record
               not at or below another’s, the LOAD from that other one to it, at zero cost, leaves a
               down-set, which is an exit nobody paid for, and the toll fails.
                  Item (4) is the one to remember. The tipping costs nothing, so it had better
               not tip in anything that counts as established. If pouring pebbles into the second
               box can land its panel somewhere that isn’t at or below where some other pouring
               would land it, the second machine gets a raised record without ever having checked
               anything, and that’s a forged certificate passed off as plumbing. My first thought
               was right about the pebbles and wrong about where they land.


               F.3 Connecting records and writers
               Joining two boxes also means deciding how to read their flags and who may write
               their workspace. The following examples trace those connections and the guarantees
               they affect.


               Theorem F.3 (What breaks). (1) Read the pair through “both flags are up” as a
               single flag, and any run that raises it from a clean start makes at least six record
               moves; the definition of certified Thiele-complete asks for a claim that three moves
               can certify, so through the pair’s own interface that reading fails the non-vacuity
               clause. (2) Two clocks side by side obey the toll with a two-counter machine inside.
               They aren’t Thiele-complete, so composing that easy bar composes nothing. (3)
               Give the small machine a second writer that changes counter A without raising its
               version, and the run “check that A is 0, let the other writer change A, commit, certify”
               raises the flag, so the earned-record clause fails when the machine is read the small
               machine’s way, with the second writer as a base move. (4) Two windows that each
               price their own machine exactly can collide as a pair, so exact pricing isn’t preserved
               by putting machines together. (5) Count the pair’s certifications with one number,
               and the count can’t tell which side certified. The pair of records can.
                                                                 F.3 Connecting records and writers   601


Proof. (1) Through the pair’s interface, a run from a clean start that raises “both
flags are up” ends with each side’s record raised, and by Theorem F.1(5) that takes
at least six record moves. Clause (d) asks for a claim whose CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY, those three moves alone, raise the record from a loaded state. Three
moves aren’t six, so (d) fails for that reading. (2) A clock is the two-counter machine
with every move priced at one and a reading over it (Observation 15.27). Two side
by side have a two-counter machine running inside, the left’s, and obey the toll by
Theorem F.1(2); and every move of the pair is a move of one clock, costing one,
while a Thiele-complete machine has a move that costs nothing (Theorem 10.12(5)).
(3) Add to the small machine a writer that changes counter A and leaves its version
alone, read as a base move. The run CHECK (A is 0), the writer’s move, COMMIT
(A is 0), CERTIFY, from a start with A at 0, passes its CHECK, finds its fact at the
unchanged version at the COMMIT, and raises the flag at the CERTIFY. The base
and toll clauses still hold, and so does the checker’s promise. What fails is clause (b).
The small machine reads “unchanged” as same value and same version, and the only
chain in that run has the writer’s move between its CHECK and its COMMIT, where
counter A, the thing the claim is about, changed its value. The COMMIT didn’t
notice, because it looks only at the version, and the version didn’t move. So a run
from a clean start raises the record with no earned chain in it. (4) Take a left box
whose only step its window doesn’t see is a certifying one, so the window still prices
it exactly, charging that unseen transition one; and a right box whose only step is a
stutter, at zero cost, leaving its down-set alone and its window unchanged, priced
exactly at zero. In the pair, the left box’s unseen certifying step and the right box’s
stutter show the same pair of windows before and after. One costs at least one and
leaves the pair’s down-set; the other costs nothing and doesn’t. So a price computed
from the pair of windows is short on the first or over on the second. (5) Replace the
pair of records by the number of sides that have certified. A run in which only the
left side certifies and one in which only the right side does both reach the count one,
with the left record raised in the first and at its floor in the second. The count can’t
tell them apart; the pair of records can.
    Item (1) puts one flag over two boxes. It costs what two certifications cost, six
record moves, and the definition wants a claim that three can settle, so a single flag
over both panels, read through the pair’s interface, is too expensive to meet the
definition. That holds for this interface; nothing here shows that no other interface
on the pair could meet it, and Theorem F.1(4) shows the pair meeting it through a
richer record. Item (4) says that a window exact for each box alone can be fooled
by the pair: two pair states with different costs can show the same pair of readings.
    Item (3) is the one with the most teeth, because it’s the bug from Section 14, the
file checked and then swapped. On the bench it’s a second hand reaching into a bin
602   F Built from parts


               while the box isn’t looking: two writers on one value, and a check that’s out of date
               by the time anybody leans on it. The small machine’s version rule is exactly the fix,
               and this is what happens without it: the commitment goes through on a claim about
               a thing that changed underneath it. Database people and the people who build
               processors have been fighting this one since at least Kung and Robinson’s paper of
               1981 and the Livermore report of 1987, and that section gave it the security people’s
               name, time of check to time of use. Here it’s a theorem about the record, and the
               version number is what makes it go away. The second hand can still reach in, but
               with the version its reach shows on the tally, and the COMMIT traps.
                  Item (5) is my first guess from the side-by-side wiring, coming back to fail on
               schedule. It’s why the pair’s record compares one side at a time. Squash the two
               records into one number and the record forgets who did the work, and a record that
               forgets who did the work isn’t one anybody can lean on.


               F.4 One inside another

               The last way to wire the bench: put one box inside the other, as a guest on a
               host. Part of this the book already has. The appendix on the universal machines
               (Appendix D.2) showed the fixed program UP runs any computably presented Thiele
               machine, and the small machine’s own programs, with the record earned again by
               the host. What’s new is putting those links in a row, a box in a box in a box, and
               asking what the outermost one pays.
                  My first guess was that it could pay less, even nothing for the guest’s climbs, since
               a host that’s clever about how it runs the guest could skip the guest’s costs. The first
               item below puts a floor under that: the host pays at least one for each step where
               the guest’s record went up. It’s a floor on rises, and it doesn’t keep the guest’s whole
               cost.


               Theorem F.4 (Nesting). (1) Let a host that obeys the toll simulate a guest faithfully:
               each guest state has an image among the host’s states and each guest record an
               image among the host’s records, the host’s record at the image of a state is the image
               of the guest’s record there, and each guest move is carried by some host run from
               the image of the state before it to the image of the state after it. Let the record map
               also reflect the order: when the image of one guest record is at or below the image
               of another, the first record is at or below the second. Say a run of the host follows a
               run of the guest when it splits into one stretch of host moves for each guest step,
               each stretch carrying the image of the state before that step to the image of the
               state after it. Every run of the guest has a host run that follows it, every such host
               run ends on the image of the guest’s end state, and every host run that follows a
                                                                           F.4 One inside another   603


guest run costs at least the number of the guest’s steps that turned a cup over. A
host run that only ends on the image of the guest’s end state can cost less. (2) In
each link the surcharge is 0 until the guest’s reading first says yes, and the bounds
below hold from then on. A small-machine guest on UP is carried with surcharge
exactly 0. A computably presented machine whose reading starts at no is carried,
through its compiled guest, with surcharge at most 2, and, when every move costs
at most one, exactly 2 once its reading has first said yes. One whose reading starts
at yes is carried with surcharge exactly 3. (3) Links compose, and their surcharges
add: a tower of k links has surcharge between the sums of their lower and upper
bounds. (4) A tower of presented machines, each level running the next on UP , adds
exactly 2 for every level above the first, on top of the first level’s own surcharge;
every level’s host run is presented by the next.

Proof. (1) The simulation gives, for each guest move, a list of host moves carrying
the image of the state before it to the image of the state after it. String those lists
together along the guest run: that host run follows it, and it ends on the image of
the guest’s end state, because each stretch ends where the next begins. Now take
any host run that follows the guest run, and a guest step that turned a cup over,
leaving the down-set of its record. Its stretch carries the image of the state before to
the image of the state after, and since the record map reflects the order, the image
after isn’t at or below the image before, or the guest’s record after would be at or
below the record before. If every host move in that stretch ended at or below where
it started, then chaining them, the end of the stretch would be at or below its start;
so some host move in it ends not at or below where it started, leaving the down-set
