of where it stood, and the host, obeying the toll, charges that move at least one.
Different guest steps have different stretches, so the charges add up to at least the
number of such steps. The end alone isn’t enough: a guest on one cup that turns
it over and turns it back has one rise and ends where it started, and the host run
that does nothing reaches the image of the end state at no cost. (2) A link from a
guest to a host matches every point of the guest’s run with a point of the host’s, with
the record bits equal there and the host’s ledger the guest’s plus a surcharge, the
surcharge 0 while the record is down and between the link’s two bounds once it’s
up, and halting and the record’s first rising matching. A small-machine guest run by
UP is a link with surcharge exactly 0: that is the ledger equality of Appendix D.1,
carried to UP . A computably presented machine run as its compiled guest is a link
with surcharge at most 2 from a reading that starts at no and exactly 3 from one that
starts at yes, which is Theorem D.8; once the reading has first said yes the surcharge
is the larger of 3 − c and 0, with c what the raising move cost, since the host pays
the larger of c and 3 there, and when every move costs at most one, c is exactly
one, the toll making it at least one, so the surcharge is exactly 2. (3) Match the
604   F Built from parts


               points through the middle: a point of the bottom run has a matching point of the
               middle run, which has a matching point of the top run; the record bits agree along
               the way; the top ledger is the bottom ledger plus both surcharges, which is 0 while
               the record is down and between the sum of the lower bounds and the sum of the
               upper bounds once it’s up; halting and the first rising pass through. A tower of k
               links is that, k − 1 times. (4) Each level above the first is, by the presentation after
               this proof, a presented machine whose run is the level below’s host run, carried as
               its compiled guest on UP . Its moves are the host’s moves, which cost 0 or 1, so by
               (2) that link adds exactly 2 once the record is up, and by (3) the additions stack on
               the first level’s own surcharge.
                   Item (1) is the cleanest sentence in the appendix. However you build the outer
               box, as long as it obeys its own toll and doesn’t lie about the inner box’s record, it
               pays at least one for every step where the inner record climbed, on every run that
               keeps pace with the inner box step by step. The keeping pace is needed. A guest
               that turns a cup over and then turns it back ends where it started, and the host can
               reach that image by doing nothing at all, at no charge on its ledger. The step by
               step floor is the guest’s rises paid one by one, and the end alone can’t see them. It’s
               a floor on the climbs, and it isn’t the inner box’s whole cost. A guest can charge
               a hundred for one rise while a host charges one for the matching rise, and both
               obey their tolls. Keeping the whole cost takes a further demand on the simulation,
               that it carry the guest’s costs too, and for UP that’s the separate ledger theorem of
               Appendix D.2, with its surcharge.
                   Part (4) looks as if it needs a premise, and it doesn’t. Two links are plainly
               unconditional: from a presented machine to its compiled guest, and from that
               guest to UP running it. Going deeper needs the host’s own run, at each level, to be
               presented as a machine the next level up can run. All the host’s states together have
               no one-to-one code in one number, since there’s a register for every whole number.
               But a loaded state has only finitely many registers that aren’t at 0 with version 0,
               and no move changes more than one of them, so the states like that are a machine of
               their own, closed under every move, and each has a code: its line, its finitely many
               live registers with their versions, its table, channel, trap, ledger and flag. Programs
               that always answer compute its step, price and flag from that code, and the driver
               reads UP ’s instruction off the line and says stop when the host has stopped. Its run
               is the host’s run, and its toll is the host’s. So every level is presented by the next,
               and the tower adds 2 a level as deep as you like. The 2 comes from the compiler’s
               rule of stopping at zero; a compiler that carried the excess forward would add 2 at
               that level’s raise and give it back as the level below paid on.
                                                                         F.5 What this adds up to   605


F.5 What this adds up to
Wired side by side, end to end, or one inside the other, a Thiele machine on the
bench stays a Thiele machine, and the tolls add the way money adds. What breaks,
breaks for reasons you could name before you saw the proof: a single flag for two
claims costs two claims’ worth, a clock is still a clock, a shared value without a
version can’t be trusted, and a hand-off that costs nothing can’t be allowed to carry
a certificate. None of those is a surprise in hindsight. All of them are now theorems,
and the composition question from Section 2 has an answer. Two Thiele machines
side by side are one under both readings I tried, “either flag” and “both flags.” The
“both flags” reading still fails the definition of certified Thiele-complete through the
pair’s interface, the second writer breaks the earned-record clause through the small
machine’s own reading, the clocks and the two counterexamples fail outright, and
simulation in general has a proved floor.
   Three of my first guesses on this bench were wrong: the single count, the
harmless tipping, and the clever host that pays nothing for a climb. The last two
leaned toward a record that says more than anybody paid for, and the first toward
one that says less than it should. I didn’t see any of the three coming; the proofs did.

Running it

Everything so far is definitions and proofs about them. Does any of it run? This
appendix is me finding out. I built the small machine twice, once straight out of the
definitions and once by hand from the same description, ran both, and compared
the whole state after every step. Then I ran the universal programs on guests small
enough to finish, and real programs through the part of the compiler that executes.
    One rule holds for the whole appendix: the runs test the builds, and the proofs
carry the theorems. A run shows what a build did on the inputs it was given, and no
theorem in the book leans on one: every theorem in it stands on its argument, on
the page.
    There are two counts to keep apart as you read. The ledger counts what the price
list charges. The number of interpreter steps counts the work this particular build
does to carry the run out. One guest step can take millions of host steps and add
one to the ledger. Every one of those host steps gives off heat on the hardware that
runs it, and the ledger counts none of that heat. The times only tell you which runs
are practical on this build. The table shows what ran and what didn’t.

G.1 Taking the coat off
The first executable is generated straight from the formal definitions, the way you’d
strip the coat off a proof and keep the program underneath. The second was written
separately, by hand, from the same description. Both implement the small machine,
the host with a register for every whole number, the host with PAY and the loaders,
and both run the universal programs; their instruction lists the second build reads as
data printed from the definitions, so it checks them by running them, not by writing
them again. The compiler below has an executable runner too.
    Whole numbers matter here. A machine word in one build is 63 bits wide, and the
guest codes U reads go up past 2100 , so ordinary fixed-width arithmetic would wrap
around and lie. The mathematical machine never overflows, so its executable uses
integers of any size, with the arithmetic chosen to match the definitions: subtraction
stops at zero and division by zero gives zero. What sits between the definitions and
the running code, the mappings, the compilers and the routines that read input and
write output, is code I had to trust.


G.2 A second machine, written by hand, to check the first
Comparing two builds step by step catches one of them disagreeing with the descrip-
tion, on the runs I tried. They’re compared on the whole state after every step: the
program line, every counter and register and its version, the fact table in order, the
channel, the trap latch, the ledger and the flag. The comparison covers exhaustive
sets of short programs, random programs and both hosts, and they agree on every
tested step. U and UP on tiny guests are compared at fifteen checkpoints two
hundred steps apart, over the first three thousand host steps of each run, instead of
after every step, and the longer runs below against a separate guest implementation,
once per pass of the loop and at the stop. I also broke the machine on purpose,
giving it a fact table one too small, a CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY that cost
nothing, a commitment that ignores versions, and a write that doesn’t bump the
version, and each break gets caught. A second set pins the boundaries this book
draws in words, and those runs come out as the words say: two runs that end in the
same state with different first certifications, a check that can’t fail certifying from
every start, a CHECK and six commitments costing seven without a flag, a write
after the commitment and a flag over a claim that’s now false, sixteen copies of one
CHECK filling the table, a CERTIFY costing one at a ledger already at two, and a
merge between two yes-states that leaves the entering state alone.
   A mistake both builds share gets past the comparison, and so does a mistake in
the definitions themselves, since both builds follow them.
608   G Running it


              G.3 U on a real guest
              Now the universal program, which is where I expected trouble. The guest I wanted
              to run first was the obvious one, a guest that goes the whole way: CHECK, COMMIT,
              CERTIFY, flag up, run inside U on the built machine. That isn’t what ran, and the
              reason is the way the guest is stored. U keeps the whole guest program as one
              number, a number that grows like two raised to the sum of the codes for the guest’s
              instructions (for a guest of one instruction it’s exactly a power of two), and it reads
              that number the only way a counter can, one unit at a time. So its speed depends
              on the code, and the code grows fast: a guest with one CHECK in it has code 224 ,
              and a guest with the whole chain has a code near 2106 .
                  So I came down to what could finish. The table below is what ran, on the
              executable host, compared against a separate guest implementation at every pass of
              the loop and at the stop: the host stopped exactly when the guest did, and at the
              stop showed the guest’s counters, trap latch, ledger and flag.
                                guest                   host       host steps   time
                                count A down from 2 U            25,953,317
                                one passing CHECK       U       402,654,059 618 s
                                one failing CHECK       U       201,327,155 305 s
                                one passing CHECK       UP      402,654,059 617 s
                                one failing CHECK       UP      201,327,155 313 s
                  The first row’s count is pinned exactly: if the build changed so that it moved by
              one step, the comparison would fail. The times are from one ordinary computer
              and are only there to give you the scale. The counts work out to about twelve host
              steps for every unit of the guest’s code each time U goes round its loop, which it
              does once for every guest step and once more to see that the guest has stopped:
              the failing CHECK traps on its first pass, 12 × 224 and a little, and the passing one
              takes two passes, 24 × 224 and a little. The growth is exponential in the size of
              the guest. A guest with one CERTIFY in it would have code 232 , about fifty billion
              host steps, and at the measured rate of about 650,000 steps a second it would take
              something like twenty-two hours, nearly a day. The guest I wanted, with the whole
              chain, has a code near 2106 , which at the same twelve steps a unit is about 1033
              host steps for each pass; at the measured rate, with this encoding on that computer,
              a run of its three steps comes to around 1020 years. So U on a guest that certifies is
              proved, in Appendix D.1, and has never been run. Runs this long only fit in memory
              at all because the build can repack the host’s register store in the middle of a run;
              repacking changes how the registers are stored, not what they hold.
                  What a run that long can be is counted. Four loop shapes do most of U’s work.
              Count from the DEC instruction that tests the loop counter; any instructions before
              that test are still counted separately. You can derive each shortcut from the arrows:
                                                                          G.3 U on a real guest   609


• In the emptying loop, a positive counter v takes one DEC back to its own test and
  becomes v − 1. At zero, one DEC exits. Thus E(0) = 1 and E(v + 1) = 1 + E(v),
  giving E(v) = v + 1.
• In the copying loop, a positive DEC jumps back one line to INC on a distinct
  destination, which returns to the test. Each unit moved therefore takes two steps,
  and the zero test takes one: C (0) = 1, C (v + 1) = 2 + C (v), so C (v) = 2v + 1.
• With two destination INCs before the test, each positive pass takes three steps.
  Thus D (0) = 1, D (v + 1) = 3 + D (v) and D (v) = 3v + 1. If the two destinations
  are the same register, it receives two increments per pass; the step count stays
  three.
• In the halving loop, two successful DECs on the source and one INC on the
  quotient return to the same test. After k = ⌊v/2⌋ such passes, 3k steps have
  removed 2k from the source and added k to the quotient. The remaining source
  is zero or one. Follow that final branch instruction by instruction.
   Each successful decrement or increment also raises its register’s version once.
The zero test does not write. So the same counts determine the version changes
as well as the counter values and next line. These loops neither charge nor change
the table, channel, trap or flag. Replacing one completed loop stretch by its derived
effect and count therefore preserves the whole endpoint and the number of steps.
Repeating that replacement throughout a run preserves both by addition.
   The numerical tally below applies those four rules and steps the other instructions
individually. It agrees with the three runs above that were also stepped all the way.
For the guest CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY, using the zero predicate on A, the passing
start (0, 0) ends with the flag up and ledger three. From (5, 0) the first check fails
and the guest stops with ledger one. Appendix L supplies the program blocks and
their guest correspondence; the displayed totals count that particular encoding.
               start                                        host steps
               (0, 0)   3,894,222,629,847,358,066,688,933,266,198,944
               (5, 0)     973,555,646,581,507,138,873,939,791,446,643
    What that table shows is a count, not a run. Nothing stepped those 1033 instruc-
tions, and the row in the table at the top of this section says so.
    Those big counts come from this encoding and from reading it one pebble at
a time. They measure the work this interpreter does, and that’s all they measure.
Whether some other interpreter, or some other base, could do the same job fast is a
separate construction with its own running-time analysis. Nothing measured here
puts a floor under every way of doing it.
610   G Running it


              G.4 From source programs to the host
              Running guests one CHECK at a time doesn’t tell you whether the built machine
              can do anything you’d recognise as a program. You’d want to hand it gcd, or a
              sort, written the way people write them, and get the answer out, and writing gcd
              by hand in INC and DEC is no way to find out. So the last piece of the build
              is a compiler. The source is a small language you could write by hand: whole-
              number variables, addition, subtraction that stops at zero, comparisons, if, while,
              and procedures that return several results, with the rule that a procedure can only
              call ones defined before it, so there’s no recursion. Each translation stage has a
              proof that it preserves the program’s result: the procedures are inlined, the result is
              flattened to assignments and jumps, that is compiled to Minsky’s counter machine
              through the counter-machine compiler, that to a program for the host machine, that
              to a two-counter guest, and the guest to a run of UP .


              Theorem G.1 (The compiler is correct). For every source program with no recursion,
              and every input: the program computes y exactly when the runner (the bounded
              evaluator of the compiled host program) halts with y for some amount of fuel;
              exactly when the compiled host program halts with y; exactly when the two-counter
              guest halts with y; and exactly when UP running that guest halts with y, with its first
              counter at 0, its ledger at 0 and its flag down. So a terminating compiled program
              delivers its answer and certifies nothing. To certify a claim about that answer, a
              target program must add a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY; this compiler does
              not insert that chain. The runner also takes exactly as many steps as the host
              program does, with the rest of its fuel left over, and a run that doesn’t halt has used
              all its fuel.

              Proof. Six arrows and a runner, each argued below, and the statement is their
              composition. Four of the arrows are between machines that take steps, and for those
              one argument does both directions, so I give it first.
                 The simulation argument. Take two machines S and T, each deterministic, where
              S has a next state from every state inside its program, and a relation ∼ between
              their states such that: a state of S inside its program is related only to states of T
              inside its program, and a state of S outside it only to states of T outside it; and from
              any related pair with S inside its program, one step of S is matched by one or more
              steps of T that land related to S’s next state. Then from related starts, S halts exactly
              when T does, and they halt related. Forward: start with the related pair. Follow the
              stretch of T that matches S’s first step; its endpoint is the related start needed for
              the second stretch. Keep joining stretches until S stops. There are only finitely many
              steps to match, so this gives a finite run of T whose final state is related to S’s final
                                                            G.4 From source programs to the host   611


state. The latter is outside its program, so the former is outside its own. Backward:
suppose T halts after k steps and S doesn’t halt. Then S takes at least k + 1 steps
without leaving its program, the matched stretches give T a run of at least k + 1
steps all of whose stretch ends are inside its program, and T, being deterministic,
has only one run from its start, which halted at step k. That’s a contradiction, so S
halts, and by the forward direction it halts related to where T did.
    Unfolding the calls. Imagine a program written on cards. A call says “carry
out the orders on that other card, then come back.” Here a card may call only a
lower-numbered card. Card zero therefore calls nothing. Replace every call on card
one by the orders from card zero; then do card two, using the already expanded
lower cards, and continue. There are finitely many cards, and every replacement
has already been built. The process ends with calls replaced by actual orders.
    The variables need their own places too. Give each active procedure a block of
numbered boxes, its frame. If the caller’s block starts at box b and uses n boxes, put
the called procedure’s block immediately after it, starting at b + n. A call becomes
four pieces: copy the arguments into that new block; set its other boxes to zero;
carry out the expanded orders using those box numbers; copy the answers back into
the caller’s named boxes. A local variable numbered x in the called procedure is thus
the global box numbered b + n + x. No assignment reaches below the procedure’s
own block.
    Why does this preserve a terminating run? Begin with the lowest-numbered
procedure. It has no calls, so its expanded orders are its original orders with
the boxes renamed. Assignments change the same values, tests choose the same
branches, and loops repeat the same bodies. Now take a procedure whose lower-
numbered calls have already been settled. Each replacement call builds exactly
the arguments and zeros that the original call would receive. The expanded lower
procedure returns the same answers, and the copy-back puts them in the same caller
boxes. The caller’s surrounding orders then continue from the same values. Working
upward through the numbered procedures settles the main program.
    The comparison works backward as well. Whenever an expanded call finishes, its
four pieces have run in their written order. The middle piece is the expanded lower
procedure, whose terminating runs I have already matched to the original lower
procedure. Its preparation and copy-back are just the original call’s input and output
operations. Replace that finished four-piece execution by the call it implements. The
surrounding assignments, branches and completed loop repetitions then give the
same original execution. A finite execution in either description therefore gives a
finite execution in the other, with the same answer. Neither can terminate when the
other does not.
612   G Running it


                  In symbols, matching a source arrangement e to the global boxes G in a frame
              starting at b means G (b + x ) = e( x ) for each local box x. The comparison above
              preserves that equality at the beginning and end of every translated statement.
                  Flattening. The flat code of a statement placed at address a: an assignment is one
              assignment; a sequence is the first statement’s code followed by the second’s; if b is
              a jump on false to the else part, the then part, a jump past the else part, and the
              else part; and while b with a body of l instructions is a jump on false to a + l + 2,
              the body at a + 1, and a jump back to a. Every jump in the code of a statement
              lands inside that code or at its end, the address just past it. Now follow a completed
              structured execution. An assignment performs the same change; a sequence joins its
              two runs; a branch follows the same test answer. For each loop iteration, the test
              falls through, the body’s code takes the run to a + l + 1, and the jump returns it to
              a. Repeat for the remaining iterations; the final false test jumps to the end. Thus
              an execution from variables e to e1 gives a flat run from address a to the end of the
              code with those same final variables.
                  Read a completed flat run in the other direction. Because no jump escapes
              past the code’s end, a run that leaves it must visit that end first. Assignments and
              branches recover their structured operations immediately; a sequence splits at the
              second statement’s first address. For a loop, the run’s first step is the test. If it is
              false, the run jumps to the end, and the loop’s derivation is the one with a false
              test. If it is true, the run enters the body’s code, which it can leave only through
              its end at a + l + 1 (the body’s own backward statement), where the jump returns
              it to a with a strictly shorter run left. Read the next iteration the same way. This
              cannot continue beyond the finite run I started with: its final test must be false,
              giving the last piece of the structured loop execution. So the flat program at address
              1 halts exactly when the structured statement has a derivation, with the same final
              variables.
                  Counter machine. Here a DEC jumps when its register is zero and goes on
              otherwise. Variable x lives in register x + 1, register 0 is kept at 0, so DEC 0 j is a
              plain jump to j, and registers above the variables are working space. The relation:
              register 0 is 0, registers 1 to n hold the flat variables, and every register above is
              0. Each flat instruction becomes a block built from small loops. Follow one pass
              and then count how many pebbles remain to be moved: Emptying a register: each
              pass takes one off, and the loop exits at zero. Moving s into d: each pass takes one
              off s and adds one to d, so s + d never changes, and at exit s is 0 and d holds the
              old sum. Copying: move s into two registers at once, then move one of them back.
              Cut-off subtraction t − u: take one off each while both are positive; at exit one of
              them is 0, and the other holds the difference, or 0. Comparison: take one off each
              in step; whichever reaches zero first, or both together, decides < and =, and the
              block empties both. Build a larger expression from these smaller jobs. A constant is
                                                               G.4 From source programs to the host   613


a fixed number of increments into an empty working register. A variable is copied
there with its original restored. For a sum or cut-off subtraction, compute the two
smaller expressions in separate working registers, combine them with the loops just
described, and empty the temporary registers. Starting with the innermost pieces
and working outward, the final value lands in register t, the registers above t return
to zero, and those below t are left alone. A test computes its comparison in the
same spare registers, chooses the true or false exit, and clears the spare registers
on either exit. Combining tests follows the selected exits of their smaller tests, each
of which has already restored the registers. Thus a test leaves the registers as it
found them and changes only which address comes next. So an assignment block
computes the value into the first working register, empties register x + 1, moves
the value in, and lands related; a jump on false runs the test’s code with the true
exit at the next block and the false exit at the block of j; a jump is DEC 0 j. The
linker places the blocks one after another and sends every jump to the start of its
target’s block. That’s the one-step matching. The flat machine has a next state from
every address in its program, and an instruction that names a variable outside the
frame just advances, so the step is total. The counter machine is deterministic. The
simulation argument gives both directions: the counter program from the loaded
inputs leaves its code with register out + 1 equal to y exactly when the flat program
halts with y in out.
    Host. The host’s DEC is the other way round: it jumps when its register is positive,
taking one off, and goes on at zero. An INC x stays INC x. A DEC x j at host address
a becomes three instructions: DEC x ( a + 3), then INC 0, then DEC 0 j′ , where j′ is
the host address of j’s block. If register x is positive, the first takes one off and jumps
to a + 3, the start of the next block, which is what the counter machine does. If it is
0, the run goes on to INC 0, which raises register 0 to one more than it held, and
DEC 0 j′ finds it positive, takes the one back off and jumps to j′ , which is the counter
machine’s jump at zero, with register 0 as it was. The relation: the same registers,
at corresponding addresses. Each counter-machine step is matched by one or three
host steps. The host program has no CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY or PAY, and INC
and DEC change only a register and the line, at no cost, so every host state in the
run has the start’s facts, channel, trap latch, ledger and flag. The counter machine’s
step is total, the host is deterministic, and the simulation argument gives: the host
program halts with register out + 1 equal to y exactly when the counter program
leaves its code with that register equal to y.
    Guest. The host program’s registers r0 , . . . , rk−1 are packed into the guest’s
                    r
counter B as ∏i pi i , one prime pi per register, with counter A the spare. That is the
packing of Appendix K.3, with the two counters’ jobs swapped. The relation: the
guest is at the start of the block for the matching instruction, B holds the code of
the registers, and A is 0. An INC on register i is the stretch that multiplies B by
614   G Running it


              pi ; a DEC on register i is the stretch that divides B by pi with remainder and takes
              the positive branch when the remainder is 0, the zero branch otherwise, restoring
              B. The appendix argues each stretch: it ends, because each of its loops empties
              the counter it counts down; it lands with A at 0; and, by unique factorisation, it
              changes the exponent of pi alone, by the right amount. The host’s step is total on
              these programs and the guest is deterministic, so the simulation argument gives:
              the guest halts with B coding registers whose register out + 1 is y, that is, with y
              the exponent of that register’s prime in B, exactly when the host program halts with
              that register at y. The guest has no record instruction, so its ledger stays 0 and its
              flag down.
                   UP . UP keeps pace with its guest the way U does, with the PAY case added (the
              proof of Theorem D.7). This guest has no PAY and no record instruction, so on it UP
              runs only branches U has, and the argument of Theorems D.2 and D.3 goes through:
              from a freshly loaded host UP halts exactly when the guest does, with its registers 0
              and 1 holding the guest’s A and B, and its ledger and flag equal to the guest’s. So it
              halts with register 0 at 0, register 1 the code with y in it, ledger 0 and flag down.
                   The runner. The runner keeps the host program and the registers in binary tries,
              a tree indexed by the bits of a number. Read the address one bit at a time: a zero
              chooses one branch and a one the other. Looking up an address follows that route
              to its stored value, or returns the default zero if no value was stored there. Storing
              at an address follows the same route and changes its final value, creating missing
              branches as needed. Every other address either branches off before that end or
              names a different node, and keeps its value. Thus the tree performs the same lookup
              and single-address update as the register map it represents. So each round of the
              runner’s loop does exactly what one host step does to the same registers, and the
              runner stops when the line leaves the program or the fuel is spent. If it halts after k
              rounds, the host run of k steps is halted at the end of the program with the runner’s
              registers, and the fuel left is the fuel given less k. If the source program has a
              derivation, the arrows above give a halting host run, of some length k, and the host,
              being deterministic, has only that run; any fuel of at least k makes the runner take
              those k steps and stop. If the runner hasn’t halted, it used every unit of fuel on host
              steps that stayed inside the program, so the host is still running after that many
              steps, and a derivation, which would give a halting host run of some length k, would
              need k larger than the fuel.
                  Composing: the program computes y exactly when the unfolded program does,
              exactly when the flat program halts with y, exactly when the counter program does,
              exactly when the host program does, exactly when the guest halts with y coded in B,
              exactly when UP halts as stated, and exactly when the runner halts with y on some
              fuel.
                                                                          G.5 What wasn’t built   615


   The theorem says nothing about how many steps the compiled program takes
next to the source; it’s about answers.
   The runner and the compiler are implemented, and the build has been run on a
set of programs I picked to be annoying: gcd, factorial, a primality program written
with procedures, an Ackermann tower, a sorting network on a list packed into one
number, and a tiny interpreter for another machine written in the source language.
Then come 220 random programs that halt, 160 random programs with loops that
might not, programs that never halt run for a fixed budget, and programs mutated
on purpose to make sure the comparison notices. Answers are compared with
direct arithmetic and separate interpreters of the source and compiled programs.
Ackermann’s function at (3, 5) is 253; the source program takes 64,768 operations
to get there, and the compiled host program takes about 119 million steps. The
executable runner does a few million host steps a second, so that’s under a minute.
   That works out to about 1,800 host steps per source operation for Ackermann,
and up to about a hundred thousand for multiplication by repeated addition, because
every addition copies a running total one unit at a time. On this build the work
grows with the size of the numbers being handled, because every operation is one
pebble at a time. How it grows with the size of the program I haven’t measured.
The last two stages, the two-counter guest and UP running it, are proved and have
never been run, and UP on a compiled guest would be slow for the same reason U
on a certifying guest is. Still, I like that 253. It came out of nothing but INC and
DEC, and a proof that they mean what the source meant.


G.5 What wasn’t built
There’s no chip. The model is not a circuit, and the lack of one says nothing about it.
The example was never cut into metal: there’s no circuit for the small machine, no
simulation of one at the level of gates, and no board ever ran any of this. The small
machine exists as mathematical definitions and executable implementations that
agree on every tested step. That’s the whole of what “it runs” means in this book.
   I’d love to see it in metal some day. But builds that can be held against each other
on every step are worth a lot to me. A board with nothing to hold it up against isn’t,
and that’s the trade I made.
APPENDIX H




The CHSH check

The example machine checks whether a number is zero, even, or at least something.
That’s a fine way to show the chain, and a modest thing to certify. This appendix
builds a check worth earning from zero, and then shows the one thing the small
machine’s host does with it, which is smaller and more exact than “it checks for
quantum behaviour,” a sentence that’s tempting and wrong. In brief, so you know
where this is going: the check never computes the famous number and never writes
down the famous bound. It tests seven facts about integers in eight counts. If they
pass, a certain five-by-five table has a property called positive semidefinite, and
that property forces the famous number under the famous bound. The wall is a
consequence of the check, and it never goes into it. Everything else is explaining
those sentences.
   Why put it in the book? Because it pulls four things apart that the small examples
keep bunched together: the counts, the relation the counts satisfy, the act of checking
that relation, and the record kept of the act. Writing a tally down costs nothing on
this machine. The checker decides a real condition about a matrix, using nothing
but integer arithmetic. The step ties the passing check to this edition of the tally,
and the earned chain costs three, the same three it costs for “A is zero.” How deep
the condition is and what the three acts cost are different numbers, and here you
can see them apart.
   And the tally on its own carries no history of where it came from. A tally
somebody made up passes the same arithmetic as one that was played. What’s
claimed here is about the numbers and what the machine does with them, and the
guarantee paragraph below says exactly how far that goes.


H.1 The game

There are two players, Alice and Bob, in separate rooms. A referee flips two
independent fair coins, independent also of the players’ plan, and hands Alice a
question x, zero or one, and Bob a question y, zero or one. Alice answers a, zero
or one; Bob answers b. No talking during the game. They may agree on a plan
beforehand, as detailed as they like. They win a round when their answers differ
exactly when both questions were one. In words: if either question is zero, match; if
both are one, differ.

                                 616
                                                                                 H.1 The game   617


   Try to win every time. A plan is a list: what Alice says to x equals zero, what
she says to x equals one, and the same two for Bob, four bits in all. Now write the
four requirements the rounds impose: a0 equals b0 (both asked zero); a0 equals
b1; a1 equals b0; a1 differs from b1. Chain the first three: a0 equals b0 equals a1,
and a0 equals b1, so b0 equals b1. But the fourth says a1 differs from b1, and a1
equals b0 equals b1, a contradiction, so one of the four must break. So any plan
loses at least one of the four question pairs, and if the referee asks all four equally
often, the best a plan can do is three out of four, seventy-five percent. Do it the
long way too: there are sixteen plans (four bits), and if you write them all out and
count wins you’ll find eight win three rounds and eight win one, and none wins
four (the broken requirements always come in odd numbers, which you can see by
adding up the four equations and keeping only whether the totals come out even
or odd, with “equal” as 0 and “differ” as 1: each of the four answers appears twice
on the left, so the left sides add to an even number, and the right sides add to one).
Sharing a coin before the game to pick a plan at random doesn’t help; a mixture of
numbers no larger than three-quarters is no larger than three-quarters. Arthur Fine,
a philosopher of physics at the University of Washington, much of whose work is on
the physicist Albert Einstein and the quantum theory, proved in 1982 that the whole
“pre-agreed answers, no influence between rooms” story is exactly the mixtures of
those sixteen lists, one scoreboard for all four questions at once; the sixteen are the
whole classical story. That one I don’t have to take on his word: the form of his
theorem that speaks of the four averages is proved in this book, and the end of this
appendix says where.
   Now the number itself: recode answers zero and one as plus one and minus one.
For each question pair, let E be the average, over many rounds, of Alice’s answer
times Bob’s. The CHSH quantity is S equals E00 plus E01 plus E10 minus E11. For
one fixed plan each win adds one to S and each loss subtracts one, so S is wins
minus losses: a three-win plan has S equal to two, a one-win plan has minus two.
With equal question frequencies, the win rate is one half plus S over eight. So
“seventy-five percent” and “S at most two” are the same fact, and the second is the
one that got the name.
   The ceiling is easy to reach and costs nothing to write down. Tally one round per
question pair with both players answering zero every time: after the recoding every
answer is plus one, so all four correlators are one. That’s the plan that answers zero
to everything, which matches on every pair and so wins the three pairs that ask for
a match, S = 1 + 1 + 1 − 1 = 2. On the small machine’s host a tally like that is a
few INCs on counters, and INC costs nothing. Nothing in it says the rounds were
played; anybody can tally anything at no charge on the ledger. The other side, that
no finite mixture of plans beats two, is Theorem I.2 in Appendix I, one direction
618   H The CHSH check


             of Fine’s result. The full equivalence, in the form that speaks of the four averages,
             appears in the last subsection of this appendix.


             H.2 Where it came from, and why anyone cared
             So who started this, and why would anybody care whether two rooms can win a
             coin game? The names come in a line, and the line didn’t mean much to me until
             I saw that each of them moved the same thing a notch: from an argument about
             what’s real, which you can only agree with or not, toward a pile of counts a referee
             can judge. Each one rests on a different piece of the game above.
                 The trail starts in 1935, with Einstein, by then at the Institute for Advanced Study
             in Princeton, and two younger colleagues there, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen,
             asking whether quantum mechanics describes everything that’s real about a pair
             of particles. Their argument: if measuring one particle lets you predict the other’s
             result with certainty, the result must already have been fixed, and the theory leaves
             that out. What they rest on is the plan in each player’s pocket, a pre-agreed list of
             answers, the plan above. And the first thing worth checking is whether the paper
             even says what Einstein meant, and by his own account it doesn’t quite. Podolsky
             did the writing, and that June Einstein wrote to Erwin Schrödinger, the Austrian
             physicist whose 1926 wave equation is at the heart of quantum mechanics, that the
             essential thing had been “smothered by formalism.” The person who lays that letter
             out is Arthur Fine, the same Fine whose theorem closed the sixteen plans above, in
             his encyclopedia entry on the argument. So Fine stands at both ends of the line: he
             checked the founding paper against what its author meant, and he proved exactly
             what the plans can do. Even the founding paper is a lead to check, not a verdict.
                 For thirty years that was philosophy. In 1964 John Bell turned it into arithmetic:
             if each particle carries pre-agreed answers and nothing travels between the rooms,
             certain averages can’t exceed a fixed number, and quantum theory predicts they
             do. What that rests on took me a few reads. His inequality rules out the pair of
             assumptions together, called local realism (answers exist before you ask, and no
             influence across the gap). Either one alone survives it. And where does a paper like
             that get published? In a brand-new journal called Physics Physique Fizika, which
             charged authors no page fees and in fact paid them by the word, ten cents a word,
             and which folded in 1968 after four volumes, or three. I went looking for that
             count, and the sources don’t agree on it: four is the number the American Physical
             Society’s archive of the journal gives, and Iulia Georgescu, writing about the journal
             in Physics World in 2026, says three. She’s also where the ten cents comes from.
             As Andrew Whitaker tells it in his biography of Bell, the journal gave out no free
             copies, so Bell spent his payment buying copies of his own paper to mail to other
             physicists. A result nobody else holds a copy of hasn’t left the room yet, and Bell paid
                                                    H.2 Where it came from, and why anyone cared   619


to send his across. In 1969 four physicists, John Clauser, then a graduate student
at Columbia, Michael Horne and Abner Shimony at Boston University, and Richard
Holt at Harvard, rewrote it as the four-average form above, S at most two, which
could be tried in a lab with imperfect equipment. It’s called the CHSH inequality,
after their initials. That notch rests on what a real lab can deliver. Shimony was in
philosophy and in physics at Boston University both, which is the whole line in one
man.
    Then the obvious next question: did anybody actually try it? Stuart Freedman,
a graduate student at Berkeley, and Clauser, by then a postdoc there too, tried
it in 1972. The physicist Alain Aspect’s group at the Institut d’Optique in Orsay,
with two colleagues there, Jean Dalibard and Gérard Roger, did it in 1982 with the
measurement settings switched while the photons were in flight, which in the game’s
terms, as I read it, is the referee handing out the questions too late for any note
about them to cross between the rooms. Before that, in 1975, Aspect went to see
Bell at CERN to tell him what he planned, and by Aspect’s own account Bell heard
him out in silence and then asked, first thing, whether he had a permanent position.
Aspect did. Bell’s reason, as Aspect tells it, was that most physicists would take the
experiment for a waste of time, or take him for a crackpot. I read that as the toll
in its oldest form: a check that could have come out the other way costs somebody
something to run, and Bell wanted to know who’d pay. And in 2015 three groups
of experimental physicists (Bas Hensen’s in Delft, with electrons 1.3 kilometres
apart; Marissa Giustina’s in Vienna; Lynden Shalm’s at NIST, the National Institute
of Standards and Technology, in Boulder) closed the two main escape routes at once.
In 2022 Clauser, Aspect and the Austrian physicist Anton Zeilinger shared the Nobel
Prize “for experiments with entangled photons, establishing the violation of Bell
inequalities and pioneering quantum information science.” The 2015 tests came out
of that line of work, and Zeilinger was one of the authors of the Vienna one. So
in under fifty years the subject went from a question you needed a permanent job
to risk to a Nobel. The lab number sits above two. A remaining escape, that the
referee’s coins were secretly correlated with the particles, is a philosophical one and
I’m not going to pretend it’s closed.
    Now put this book’s check on the same line, because that’s where my position
gives. It sits past the far end, at the counts. Those fifty years went into making the
counts worth judging, rooms really apart, questions really late, escape routes really
shut, and my check starts after all of it. It’s handed eight counts and can’t tell a
lab’s tally from one somebody wrote down at no charge. So the check is a referee of
counts, and everything that made these counts worth refereeing happened upstream
of it.
    What quantum play does: if the players share an entangled pair and choose what
to measure from their question, the best they can do is S equals two times the square
620   H The CHSH check


             root of two, about 2.83, a win rate of about eighty-five percent. Boris Tsirelson,
             a Soviet mathematician who later taught at Tel Aviv University, in a 1980 paper
             called “Quantum generalizations of Bell’s inequality,” proved that that’s a ceiling:
             quantum correlations violate Bell, but only up to there. I prove that ceiling below,
             and show the state that reaches it, with real amplitudes and with complex ones, in
             any dimension at all, infinitely many levels included (the last subsections of this
             appendix say how). The first thing proved is the algebra.
                 Then there’s the wall above that, which is the one I find most instructive. In
             1994 the physicists Sandu Popescu and Daniel Rohrlich asked: what if you only
             demand that nothing can be signalled, that Alice’s answers on their own have the
             same odds whatever Bob is asked, and the other way round? Then you can write
             down a “box” (the PR box, after their initials) that wins every round (its answers
             differ exactly when both questions are one, by fiat, each answer alone a fair coin), S
             equals four, and nothing about it lets either room send a message. So no-signalling
             on its own doesn’t explain the quantum ceiling; the PR box meets that condition and
             beats 2.83. (A box isn’t a physical theory, and nobody is claiming one that meets
             everything relativity asks.) The order is: two for plans, 2.83 for quantum, four for
             no-signalling.
                 And the box has the same kind of history as everything else in this book: some-
             body got there first. Popescu and Rohrlich’s initials stuck, but the big review of the
             field by Nicolas Brunner and four coauthors credits boxes like it to Peter Rastall,
             whose 1985 paper on locality and Bell’s theorem appeared in Foundations of Physics,
             and, separately, to Leonid Khalfin, a physicist at the Steklov Institute’s Leningrad
             branch, and Tsirelson himself, both in 1985, nine years before. Then the question
             that really matters: if relativity isn’t what stops things at 2.83, what is? People have
             tried candidates. In 2005 the computer scientist Wim van Dam, who works on the
             theory of quantum computing, argued, in a paper on the implausible consequences
             of such boxes, that with enough PR boxes, Bob could work out any yes-or-no func-
             tion of both their inputs after Alice sends him a single bit, which would make the
             whole question of how much two parties need to talk collapse, and that’s a strong
             hint the boxes are too good to be real. In 2009 Marcin Pawłowski, a physicist
             at the University of Gdańsk, and five coauthors proposed a principle they called
             information causality: Bob can’t get more information about Alice’s data than the
             bits she actually sends him. They argue that ordinary and quantum physics both
             obey it, and that any theory that beats 2.83 breaks it. How much of the rest of the
             quantum boundary it reaches is something I haven’t checked. Which principle fixes
             the whole quantum boundary, if any one does, this book won’t answer. The check
             below is a fence at the middle step.
                                                  H.3 Five sentences that are easy to say by accident   621


H.3 Five sentences that are easy to say by accident
Each one comes below with what I can stand behind beside it.
    “Faster than light.” Nothing travels. Each room alone sees fair coins; the
correlation shows up only when you lay the two columns side by side afterward.
“Quantum means random.” The average S is fixed by the state; what’s random is
each single answer; the plans are the less random side. “A Bell violation proves
nonlocality.” It rules out local realism, both assumptions together, and every real
test has loopholes with names. “A tally above two proves nonlocality.” No: S is a
population average, and one finite tally can land above two by luck. Four rounds,
one per question pair, with coin-flip answers, reach S equals four one time in sixteen.
That gap between a population bound and a finite sample is the problem Yanbao
Zhang, Scott Glancy and Emanuel Knill, at NIST in Boulder, work through for real
Bell tests (Physical Review A, 2011 and 2013), and the book doesn’t solve it. The
way they solve it is worth knowing, because it has the shape of this book’s record.
Turn each round into a small bet that no local plan can expect to win, even a plan
that remembers every earlier round, multiply the bets as the rounds come in, and the
French mathematician Jean Ville’s inequality, from his 1939 thesis, one of the works
that started the theory of martingales, says the chance the product ever climbs past
one over δ is at most δ. So a flag can go up for good the moment the product crosses,
with its error stated up front. It needs one thing the small machine doesn’t have:
settings drawn underneath the program, where the program can’t choose them. And
how much can one round tell you? Wim van Dam, Richard Gill, a mathematical
statistician who later held the chair in that subject at Leiden, and Peter Grünwald
(2005) measured exactly that, in bits of evidence against every local plan. Of the
two-party proofs they compare, CHSH comes out the strongest, “much stronger”
than the others in their words, at about 0.046 of a bit per round, a few hundredths,
so a convincing record takes hundreds of rounds, and four won’t do. About a finite
tally, this book proves only the narrow thing, that a tally above two, with every
question pair asked at least once, is not explained by one fixed plan replayed every
round, and that narrow thing is what the sentence has to stay. The bound for a finite
local model is a separate theorem, and it says nothing about one tally. And “the PSD
test proves the data is quantum.” (PSD is short for positive semidefinite, the property
of the five-by-five table from the opening of this appendix; the next subsection builds
both.) It doesn’t, and the direction matters. Passing implies the five-by-five table,
pinned in a way the next subsection explains, is PSD, and that implies S squared
is at most eight; both are proved. The correlators of a PSD table like that are the
correlators of some quantum strategy, by Tsirelson’s representation theorem, which
is proved here: the strategy is built on two systems of four levels each, or two levels
each with complex amplitudes. The exact edge of the quantum set for this game
622   H The CHSH check


             was found by Lawrence Landau, whose 1969 Berkeley thesis was on the quantum
             theory of local observables, and Lluís Masanes, then at the University of Barcelona
             (next subsection), and that’s proved here too. Failing says nothing about whether
             the play was quantum: the check is complete for the pinned matrix, the quantum
             set is wider than that, and quantum behaviour can fail it. Every one of the sixteen
             plans fails it, and I’ll show you why. What it guarantees is in one paragraph, once
             the check is on the host machine.


             H.4 The five-by-five, and what positive semidefinite means

             The mathematics the check rests on is one idea: a table of numbers could be a table
             of dot products. Take a two-by-two symmetric table with a and c on the diagonal
             and b off it. It’s positive semidefinite (PSD) when a and c are at least zero and a
             times c minus b squared is at least zero. Check two by hand: ones on the diagonal
             and one half off, the determinant is three quarters, passes; ones on the diagonal and
             1.2 off, the determinant is negative, fails. The reading: PSD means the table could
             be the dot products of some arrows, and 1.2 is too big a dot product for two arrows
             of length one. Everything else is that idea, generalised to bigger tables.
                 Now the table. Rows and columns labelled I, A0, A1, B0, B1 (the identity, Alice’s
             two questions, Bob’s two). Diagonal all ones. The I row and column zero off the
             diagonal (that’s “zero marginals”: the table takes each answer alone to average to
             zero, a fair coin; the counts record no marginals and the check doesn’t test this). A0
             with A1 zero, B0 with B1 zero (no round asks Alice both questions, so no tally holds
             that average, and the table sets it to zero). Those zeros are choices. They pin the
             table to one slice, and I’ll come back to what they cost. And the four Alice-Bob cells
             hold the four correlators E, which leaves a five-by-five with four free numbers in it.
             It splits into the one in the corner and a four-by-four block made of an identity and
             the two-by-two grid E of correlators, and PSD of that block is the same as saying
             E shrinks every vector (E is a contraction), which is three inequalities: one minus
             E00 squared minus E10 squared at least zero; one minus E01 squared minus E11
             squared at least zero; and their product at least the square of (E00 E01 plus E10
             E11).
                 Run it. All four correlators 0.6 except E11 at minus 0.6, S equals 2.4: the two
             diagonal terms are 0.28 and 0.28, the cross term zero, passes; above two, below
             2.83. All four at one over root two (E11 negative): diagonals zero, cross term zero,
             passes with no slack, S equals two root two exactly, the 2.83; nudge any entry’s
             size up and a diagonal goes negative. The all-ones plan (one, one, one, one): first
             diagonal is one minus one minus one, negative, fails, though S equals two and it’s a
             perfectly legal classical play. The PR box (one, one, one, minus one): fails the same
             way. The check is a fence at the middle step, and a fence that keeps out every one
                                           H.4 The five-by-five, and what positive semidefinite means   623


of the sixteen plans: each has all four correlators at plus or minus one, so the first
diagonal is always one minus one minus one. Of the classical plays, only diluted
mixtures of plans get through.
    That point, one over root two in size in every entry, is four real numbers, and no
tally of rounds ever lands on it. A tally’s correlators are ratios of whole numbers,
and the point needs each of them to be one over root two, which would make root
two a fraction, and you killed that fraction with a pencil in Section 5. That point
and its mirror image, every sign flipped, are the only places the bound is reached
(Remark I.2 in the appendix). So a passing tally always has S squared strictly below
eight. It can get as close as you like: the (17, 3) tally in the five examples below
has S squared equal to 7.84, and tallies of the same shape with a fraction nearer
one over root two get nearer still. Two root two is the least bound the check can
promise, and no tally the check accepts ever reaches it. Hold on to that corner; it
comes back.
    Picture what quantum play can reach as a field, and every test as a fence. In 2007
Miguel Navascués, Stefano Pironio and Antonio Acín, in a paper called “Bounding
the Set of Quantum Correlations” (NPA, after their initials), came at the edge from
outside, resting on necessary conditions. In their terms a table like this one is the
first rung of a ladder: bigger tables of expected products, each PSD, each a necessary
condition for quantum behaviour when its entries are left free, each rung tighter, and
(their 2008 paper) converging to the quantum set (strictly, the set from commuting
operators, which can differ from the tensor-product set in general scenarios). Each
rung is a fence with the whole field inside it. The check’s table is the first rung
with the marginals and the two within-party entries pinned to zero. Pinning is a
stronger demand than the rung makes, so passing puts you inside the first rung, and
a quantum point can still fail. My fence cuts across the field. Lawrence Landau in
1988 and Lluís Masanes in 2003 came at the edge itself, for this two-questions-each
case only. I’d have drawn a flat wall at 2.83. The exact boundary they found is a
curved surface (the arc-sine form) touching 2.83 at one point. It’s proved here: a
table has a PSD completion exactly when its entries lie between minus one and one
and their arcsines pass four inequalities, so those are exactly the quantum tables.
    So the obvious next question: if every rung is tighter than the last, does some
rung finally land exactly on the quantum set and stop? My first guess was yes,
at least here. A 2026 preprint by Anubhav Chaturvedi, a quantum-information
theorist at the University of Gdańsk, says no: no finite rung of the ladder captures
the whole quantum set even in this simplest case. And for the four correlators
alone, a 2008 paper by the same Navascués, Pironio and Acín works out that the
first rung already lands on Landau and Masanes’s curved edge. That looked like a
contradiction until I saw what each one fences. Landau and Masanes draw the edge
for the four correlators alone. Chaturvedi’s is the full behaviours, each room’s own
624   H The CHSH check


             odds included. So there’s the corner again from the other side: tallies never reach
             it, and, if his proof holds, rungs never close on the field. I wanted that to be one
             fact, but it’s two. Mine is root two again, about which points a count can hit. His is
             about the fences. His result backs, from outside, the caution this book keeps about
             the ladder, that no finite rung may close on the whole quantum set. It says nothing
             about my own check, though. My check’s caution, that a quantum point can fail it,
             comes from the pinning, and his paper never pins anything.


             H.5 The check, in integers

             There are eight counts: for each of the four question pairs, one counting rounds
             where the answers matched and one where they differed. A round is one bump
             to one count; nothing about the round is tested, and no marginals are recorded.
             Then the check reads the eight and tests seven integer facts. For each pair, let N be
             same plus different and D be same minus different (so E is D over N). The seven:
             the four N are strictly positive (every pair was sampled; a pair with no rounds is
             rejected outright, and never read as a correlator of zero); A, which is N00 squared
             N10 squared minus D00 squared N10 squared minus D10 squared N00 squared, is
             at least zero; B, the same with the other column, is at least zero; and with C equal
             to D00 D01 N10 N11 plus D10 D11 N00 N01, C squared is at most A times B. Those
             are the three contraction inequalities with the denominators cleared, and there’s no
             division in them, no reals, no square root and no S. Try it: counts (same, different)
             of (4, 1), (4, 1), (4, 1), (1, 4) give E of 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, minus 0.6; N is five and D is
             three (minus three for the last); A is 175, B is 175, C is zero; passes. These counts
             are the first example above, the S equals 2.4 one, written in integers.
                 The theorem chain, in words: a passed check gives PSD of the five-by-five built
             from the counts; contraction and PSD are equivalent, both directions; and PSD forces
             S squared at most eight. The names are in the statements below. The underlying
             algebra is one identity: four times the sum of the four correlators squared, minus S
             squared, is a sum of six squares, so if the row sums of squares are at most one, S
             squared is at most eight, and the point one over root two reaches it. So Tsirelson’s
             bound comes out as algebra, with no Hilbert space (the mathematical home of
             quantum states) in it.
                 The chain goes below as three statements. The derivations are in Appendix I,
             and the statements say what they prove.

             Definition H.1 (Correlators from the counts; the pinned matrix). For eight counts
             and a question pair xy, let Exy = (samexy − diffxy )/(samexy + diffxy ), read as
             0 when both are 0. For reals Exy , M ( E) is the symmetric five-by-five matrix on
             I, A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 with ones on the diagonal, Exy in the cells ( A x , By ) and ( By , A x ),
                                                                             H.5 The check, in integers   625


and zero everywhere else (Definition I.5). M is PSD when vT Mv ≥ 0 for every real
vector v, and S( E) = E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 .



Theorem H.1 (The integer check implies the pinned matrix is PSD). If eight counts
pass the seven integer facts, then M ( E) for their correlators is symmetric and PSD.

Proof. The four positivity facts make every denominator positive, so each Exy is
Dxy /Nxy , and dividing the other three facts by positive squares turns them into the
three contraction inequalities (Lemma I.15). Contraction is equivalent to PSD of
M ( E) by a Schur complement on the four-by-four block (Corollary I.13).
   In the appendix this is Theorem I.16, and Corollary I.13 gives the equivalence of
contraction and PSD in both directions.



Theorem H.2 (PSD forces the Tsirelson bound). For all real E00 , E01 , E10 , E11 : if
M ( E) is symmetric and PSD, then S( E)2 ≤ 8.

Proof. Call the four entries a, b, c, d, read across the rows. PSD means that no
choice of five weights makes the matrix’s weighted total negative. Choose weights
(0, 1, 0, − a, −b) in the order ( I, A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 ). The diagonal contributes 1 + a2 +
b2 , and the two cross terms contribute −2a2 − 2b2 . The total is 1 − a2 − b2 , so
a2 + b2 ≤ 1. Weights (0, 0, 1, −c, −d) give c2 + d2 ≤ 1. All four squares therefore
add to at most two.
    Now compare four times that sum with the squared score. Their difference is
   4( a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ) − ( a + b + c − d )2 = ( a − b )2 + ( a − c )2 + ( a + d )2
                                                   + ( b − c )2 + ( b + d )2 + ( c + d )2 .
To check it, each squared letter occurs three times on either expanded side; the cross
terms are −2ab, −2ac, +2ad, −2bc, +2bd, +2cd on both. The difference cannot be
negative because it is a sum of squares. Thus the squared score is at most four times
two, which is eight.
   This is Theorem I.14 in the appendix.


Corollary H.3 (A passed check means the bound). If eight counts pass the seven
integer facts, their correlators satisfy S2 ≤ 8. In fact S2 < 8, and passing tallies
come as close to 8 as you like.
626   H The CHSH check


             Proof. Theorem H.1 makes the pinned matrix of these four correlators PSD, and
             Theorem I.14 in the appendix, which holds of every such matrix, gives S2 ≤ 8; the
             calculation with the quadratic form is printed there. The score is a ratio of whole
             numbers, and no such ratio squares to 8, so the bound is strict. The tallies whose
             four correlators√are n/q, n/q, n/q, −n/q with 2n2 ≤ q2 pass, and their scores 4n/q
             come as near 2 2 as you like.

             Remark H.1 (Sound, and incomplete). The pinned matrix is stricter than the
             quantum question it is usually read against. PSD of M ( E) gives the correlators
             a PSD completion, since the zeros are one choice of the two free entries. The
             converse fails. The all-ones plan has a PSD completion, and every deterministic
             plan is a quantum strategy; yet its minor on rows A0 , B0 , B1 is 1 − 1 − 1 = −1,
             so M ( E) is not PSD there, and a tally of one matching round per pair gives A =
             1 − 1 − 1 = −1 in the integer check, so the check fails. The second failure is a
             named theorem on the machine: the tally of one matching round per pair is refused
             forever (Proposition H.6). Every deterministic plan fails the same way. The tally of
             one round per pair fails the check for each of the sixteen plans, and so does any tally
             of one plan replayed over any number of rounds (a pair left unsampled fails the
             positivity facts outright), because no deterministic plan’s pinned matrix is PSD. So a
             pass proves the bound, and a failure proves only that the tally’s pinned matrix isn’t
             PSD or a pair went unsampled; it says nothing about whether the play was classical
             or quantum. The tally from the start of this appendix, written down at no cost, is
             exactly such a tally: it reaches S = 2 and the check throws it out.

                None of that algebra is new, and I don’t want it to read as if it were. Mna-
             cho Echenim and Mehdi Mhalla, computer scientists at Grenoble, give a detailed
             treatment of the CHSH and Tsirelson bounds (2023). Navascués, Pironio and Acín
             already analyse this very matrix by Schur complement and discuss the level above it.
             What I think is mine here is smaller: an integer decision procedure on the counts,
             and a proved link from “the check passed” to PSD to the bound.
                The picture under the check is older still. Tsirelson showed, in a longer paper
             of 1987 after his 1980 note, that the correlations two separated quantum parties
             can reach are exactly the tables of inner products of unit vectors, one vector for
             each question on each side. With the marginals pinned to zero the pinned matrix is
             that picture, and by its Schur complement it is PSD exactly when the two-by-two
             table of correlators, read as a matrix, has operator norm at most one. The physicists
             Reinhard Werner and Michael Wolf’s survey of Bell inequalities (2001) sets out that
             correlation-matrix view for two-party inequalities in general.
                                                             H.6 The check, earned on the host machine   627


H.6 The check, earned on the host machine
Now put it on the machine. A check on the small machine is a property: a checker,
which is a little program that says yes or no, a meaning, which is a statement, and
a proof that the two agree. The version of the small machine with its property
language left open (Section 15, Theorem 15.31) takes any property language with
an exact equality test whose properties come with those three things, and for every
one of them a flag raised from a clean start stands on a passing CHECK of one
claim, a later COMMIT of the same claim with its counter untouched in between,
and a later CERTIFY, the three acts costing one each. For the game, pack the eight
counts into one counter, as a list, the way the sorted-list machine packs a list into
one number (Section 15). Let the checker be the seven integer facts read off the
unpacked counts. And let the meaning be what the facts are for: every pair was
sampled, and the pinned five-by-five is positive semidefinite. Then the proof the
generic machine asks for, that the checker says yes exactly when the meaning holds,
is the chain above with the denominators cleared in both directions, and a flag
raised on that machine from a clean start means: these counts, at this edition of
their counter, passed the check, somebody committed to that with nothing changed
underneath, and the correlators they give satisfy S2 ≤ 8. The theorems below state
that exactly, and they’re stronger than the chain above in one way I want to say
once and plainly. The earlier theorems said that a passed check makes the pinned
matrix PSD. The check is also complete for it: it passes if and only if every pair was
sampled and the pinned matrix is PSD, because clearing the denominators works
in both directions. The statement is over the machine of Definition D.2, the small
machine with a counter for every number, with PCHSH in place of its one property,
Slot. A CHECK reads one counter, which is why the eight counts have to travel in
one.

Definition H.2 (The packed tally, and the property PCHSH). Read a whole
number as a list in the list code (0 is the empty list, and 2x (2y + 1) is x fol-
lowed by the list y), and take as its tally the first eight entries, in the order
same00 , diff00 , same01 , diff01 , same10 , diff10 , same11 , diff11 , a missing entry reading
0. Every number is some tally. The property PCHSH has the checker “the tally passes
the seven integer facts” and the meaning “every question pair was sampled, and the
pinned matrix M( E) of the tally’s correlators is symmetric and PSD.”



Theorem H.4 (The check is exact). (1) The seven integer facts hold of a tally if and
only if every pair was sampled and M ( E) is symmetric and PSD. (2) For every whole
number v, the checker of PCHSH says yes at v if and only if the meaning holds of
628   H The CHSH check


             v’s tally. (3) Reading the number that packs a tally gives that    √ tally back. (4) If the
             facts hold,  the score of the tally satisfies S 2 ≤ 8 and | S | ≤ 2 2; in fact S2 < 8 and
                      √
             |S| < 2 2, and passing tallies come as close to 8 as you like.

             Proof. (1) The forward half is Theorem H.1. For the backward half, PSD gives the
             three contraction inequalities (Corollary I.13); with every N positive, multiplying
             them through by the squares of the denominators gives A ≥ 0, B ≥ 0 and C2 ≤ AB,
             which is Lemma I.15 read the other way. (2) is (1) with the packing, since every
             number is a tally. (3) is the code and its decoder being inverse. (4) is (1) forward,
             then Theorem H.2; the strict form and the closeness are Corollary H.3.



             Theorem H.5 (A raised flag stands on the check). On the machine above, let τ be a
             trace from a clean start s0 that ends with the flag up. Then, for some counter c,

                τ = pre · CHECK PCHSH c · mid1 · COMMIT PCHSH c · mid2 · CERTIFY · post,

             CHECK of PCHSH at c means the checker says yes at c’s value, which is the meaning
             by Theorem H.4(2), and the bound is (4) of the same theorem. An unchanged
             edition means an unchanged value. For the converse, the CHECK passes exactly
             when the tally passes; if it does, COMMIT and CERTIFY find their facts and the three
             acts cost three; if it fails, the trap latch goes up, and a run takes no step once the
             trap is up (as in Theorem 15.22), so the flag never rises.
