   So the one thing the machine does with the check, as this appendix’s opening
said, is that a raised flag can stand on it. Five tallies, each a theorem with its counts
written out, show the check isn’t vacuous and where its edges are.


Proposition H.6 (Five tallies). Counts are given as (same, diff) for the pairs 00, 01,
10, 11. (4,1), (4,1), (4,1), (1,4) has S = 12/5: the check passes, the flag rises, √ the
ledger reads 3. (17,3), (17,3), (17,3), (3,17) has S = 14/5 = 2.8, just under 2 2,
with S2 = 7.84: it passes, the ledger reads 3. (9,1), (9,1), (9,1), (1,9) has S = 16/5
with S2 > 8: refused forever, whatever follows. (1,0), (1,0), (1,0), (0,1), the PR
box, has S = 4: refused forever. (1,0), (1,0), (1,0), (1,0), the all-ones classical plan,
has S = 2: refused forever.

Proof. A pair’s correlator is (same − diff)/(same + diff), and S adds the first three
and subtracts the fourth. (4, 1) gives 3/5 and (1, 4) gives −3/5, so S = 12/5; the
seven facts are the worked tally after Corollary I.17, with A = B = 175 and C = 0,
so the check passes, and Theorem H.5 gives the flag and the ledger at 3. (17, 3) gives
7/10 and (3, 17) gives −7/10, so S = 14/5 and S2 = 196/25 = 7.84; with N = 20
in every pair and D = 14, 14, 14, −14, A = B = 400 · 400 − 196 · 400 − 196 · 400 =
3200 and C = 14 · 14 · 400 − 14 · 14 · 400 = 0, so the seven facts hold and the
same theorem applies. (9, 1) gives 4/5, so S = 16/5 and S2 = 256/25 > 8; the
PR box gives 1, 1, 1, −1 and S = 4; both fail the check, because a tally that passes
has S2 ≤ 8 (Corollary I.17), and a failed check traps at the CHECK, after which no
step raises the flag (Theorem H.5). The all-ones plan gives N = D = 1 in every pair,
S = 2, and A = 1 − 1 − 1 < 0, the worked tally’s second computation, so it fails
the check and is refused the same way.
    The last one is the check being stricter than the bound, as a named theorem: a
perfectly legal classical play with S = 2 is turned away.
    What the theorem doesn’t say stays what it was. The tally is placed. Nobody plays
it on the machine: the theorem starts from a counter that already holds the packing,
and no instruction plays a round, so a program can put any code in a counter at no
cost. There are no marginals. The pinned matrix is stricter than the quantum set, so
failing says nothing about whether the play was quantum, and there is no margin
for sampling noise at Tsirelson’s point.
    Writing a tally costs nothing. Each count is a counter, a round is an INC on one
of them, and INC costs nothing, so a pile of trials costs nothing to write down (what
it spends is fresh states, in a counter that never runs out of numbers); the packing
into one counter is a program’s business, and in the theorem the packed counter
is simply there at the start. What costs is the claim about the pile. On the ledger,
statistics cost nothing; the claim about them is what costs.
630   H The CHSH check


                 So what the check guarantees fits in one paragraph. If it passes, then every
             question pair was sampled, the four ratios from the counts satisfy three polynomial
             inequalities, so the pinned five-by-five is PSD, so S squared is at most eight. It
             does not guarantee that the tally came from honest play (a program can INC
             whatever counts it likes at no cost, including four rounds that put S at four). It
             does not guarantee any marginal is zero (no marginals are recorded and none are
             tested). It does not put the players’ state behind the counts. What it does give is
             a quantum strategy with the same correlators: a passing tally’s correlators have a
             PSD completion, and every point with one is the correlator table of a strategy on
             two four-level systems. And it fails the tally of every single plan, honest classical
             play included. It has no margin for sampling noise either. Honest play at Tsirelson’s
             point aims at correlators of plus or minus one over root two, and there every pair
             of squared correlators the check adds up comes to exactly one, the edge of what it
             accepts. So an honest tally aimed at that point sits right on the line, and ordinary
             luck over a finite number of rounds pushes it over most of the time. I simulated it,
             drawing each round’s answers at Tsirelson’s correlators: the check fails 92 percent
             of the time at 10 rounds per question pair, 87 percent at 100, and between 85.4
             and 85.9 percent from 1,000 to 100,000. In those simulated trials, fair coins passed
             every time from 100 rounds per pair on, and failed about 2.5 percent of the time at
             10. I saw that in the trials, and it’s no guarantee about any one tally. The limit has a
             closed form. At Tsirelson’s point the correlator matrix, read as a two-by-two, turns
             arrows without stretching them (it’s a mirror), and every one of its entries wobbles
             by the same amount, independently. To first order the largest singular value of the
             noisy matrix is one plus the larger eigenvalue of ( G + GT )/2, where G is the wobble
             turned back by that mirror, a two-by-two of independent Gaussian entries of equal
             size, and the check passes only when that   √ eigenvalue is at most zero. Write that
             symmetric matrix’s eigenvalues as u ± v2 + w2 , with u, v, w independent and of
             equal spread
                      √     (scale them to standard normals). Both are at most zero exactly when
             u ≤ − v2 + w2 . Now v2 + w2 has    √ the exponential
                                                              √     law with mean 2, so the chance
                 1         −   2 /2    1
             is 2 E 1 − e    u

             point fails with probability (2 + 2)/4 ≈ 0.854 in the long run. The arithmetic is
             on the page; the first-order step is not proved here, and the simulation is what backs
             it.

What the tolerance gives up shows in the bound: a pass caps S at 2 2 (1 + ε), a
little outside Tsirelson’s number. The exact check remains the default. With p and q
fixed for a machine instance, the tolerance check also runs as CHECK on the same
versioned registers: its CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY chain certifies exactly when
the integer tolerance test passes, costs three on success, and traps permanently on
failure. From a clean start, every raised flag has that earned chain behind it, with
the same register value at CHECK and COMMIT, and establishes the relaxed bound
above: it’s Theorem H.5 again, with the tolerance test as the checker and “every pair
sampled and operator norm at most 1 + ε” as the meaning, the scaling just described
being the proof that they agree. The check certifies a shape of the tally. What the
shape means is a question for whoever supplied the rounds.
    And notice which way the fence faces. The most practical use anyone has found
for a Bell test, certified randomness, needs the opposite bound. Stefano Pironio and
colleagues (2010) argued, and backed with an experiment, that a Bell violation,
with settings the devices can’t choose, certifies that the outputs are random, and a
group of quantum cryptographers, Rotem Arnon-Friedman, Frédéric Dupuis, Omar
Fawzi, Renato Renner and Thomas Vidick (2018), made the accounting tight with
what they call entropy accumulation. A string printed in advance passes no such test,
so it’s the cleanest case I know, outside this book, of a check that can fail, separating
output that was established from output that was printed. That needs S bounded
from below, with an error probability. This check bounds S from above and fails
every single plan, so it’s a fence that keeps out the super-quantum and the fixed
plan. As a nonlocality test it’s no use. The deployed version exists, too: Gautam
Kavuri and colleagues, physicists at NIST and the University of Colorado (2025),
run a public randomness beacon whose outputs each trace back through a Bell test
to a public record, the nearest working system I know to a certified claim written
down for good. And records cut both ways there. Jonathan Barrett, Roger Colbeck
and Adrian Kent, working on quantum cryptography (2013), pointed out that a
device which keeps its own memory of earlier rounds can leak it through outputs it
makes public later, so reusing a device can undo a guarantee the user thought was
settled. A permanent record in the wrong box is an attack.


H.7 A rational stand-in for an irrational number
One useful rational bound: 5657 over 2000, which is 2.8285, and two root two is
2.82842... It’s the four-decimal round-up, chosen so that rational arithmetic can test
632   H The CHSH check


             “above the Tsirelson bound” without square roots, and it’s safe because 5657 squared
             is 32,001,649 and eight times 2000 squared is 32,000,000, so the fraction sits above
             root eight by about seven hundred-thousandths. It’s used in a few rational theorems.
             It is not used in the integer check, and the real-number theorems use root eight.


             H.8 Two more tests, as mathematics

             The second rung: a nine-by-nine table on I, the four questions, and the four Alice-Bob
             products, with the correlators and five extra free numbers for three- and four-body
             entries. Its two four-body entries are tied, one the negative of the other. That
             tie is a constraint, ⟨{ A0 , A1 } ⊗ { B0 , B1 }⟩ = 0: the zero entries of the first rung
             don’t imply it, and a classical strategy breaks it. So the second rung is level 1+AB
             on that slice, and that’s what I mean by level 1+AB everywhere in this book. Its
             PSD is again equivalent to a contraction-like condition. The check for it proves
             something stronger, that the matrix is positive definite, by a cascade of two Schur
             steps down to a four-by-four that Sylvester’s criterion closes. Sylvester’s name on a
             test about matrices fits in a way I enjoy, because the word matrix is his. In 1850, in
             the Philosophical Magazine, the English mathematician James Joseph Sylvester used
             it for an “oblong arrangement of terms” out of which you cut square blocks and take
             their determinants, and matrix was already an old word for the place something
             grows from. The test does exactly that: it cuts the top-left square blocks out of the
             big grid, one row deep, two, three, four (the leading minors), and asks each one’s
             determinant to be positive. Was he the first to state the test? The name doesn’t settle
             that; names stick to people for all kinds of reasons, and I’d treat this one as a lead.
             There’s also a fact that’s easy to list without noticing what it means: with all five
             extra numbers at zero, the condition certifies a strict subset of the classical set (the
             ball where the four correlators’ squares sum to at most one), forcing S at most two;
             it can’t certify anything above the classical line. To get a point above two you have
             to supply the extras (S equals 2.4 with one extra at minus one half). Appendix I has
             the algebra.
                 The two sizes are one test. A single positive-semidefinite predicate takes the size
             as a parameter, and the five-by-five and the nine-by-nine are it at two sizes.

             Definition H.3 (The size-generic PSD test). A claim is a top index n and a ma-
             trix M indexed by naturals. It is realizable when Mij = M ji for all i, j ≤ n and
             ∑i≤n ∑ j≤n vi Mij v j ≥ 0 for every real vector v. The CHSH claim of E is top index 4
             with the matrix M ( E) of Definition H.1; the level-1+AB claim uses top index 8 and
             the nine-by-nine matrix.
                                                                               H.9 The quantum set   633


Corollary H.7 (The level-1 test is the size-five case). For all real E00 , E01 , E10 , E11 :
the three contraction inequalities hold if and only if the CHSH claim of E is realizable.
The same holds at size nine for the level-1+AB contraction condition and its claim.

Proof. Top index 4 means the five indices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The double sum visits each
of their twenty-five cells once, multiplies it by its row and column weights, and
adds the results. That is precisely the weighted-total test for the five-by-five matrix.
The completed-square calculation in Corollary I.13 equates that test with the three
contraction inequalities. Top index 8 similarly visits the eighty-one cells of the nine-
by-nine matrix. Theorem I.19 writes its total as three squares plus the residual and
proves that its test is exactly the residual condition. The same definition therefore
asks the same question at either size.
    The third thing is the elliptope, the set of correlators for which some choice of
the two missing entries (A0 with A1, B0 with B1) makes the five-by-five PSD. Every
one of the sixteen plans is inside it, mixtures stay inside, every point inside obeys
S2 ≤ 8, Tsirelson’s point is inside and reaches it, the PR box is out, and it’s strictly
bigger than the classical set. There’s a certificate checker for it with a soundness
proof, in two branches: a strict Sylvester check with the completion supplied, and
a rational factorisation certificate of the completed matrix, checked in integers.
What’s proved is that a pass puts the correlators inside the set and that no choice
of inputs gets the PR box through, and, by computation, that some named points
pass, the all-ones plan and a point that the arc-sine boundary puts exactly on the
quantum edge among them. And every point with a rational PSD completion has
such a certificate: peel the completed matrix a row at a time, as in Section I.8, but
keep each pivot instead of taking its square root; a zero pivot forces its row to zero,
and every number that comes out is rational. The certificate checker is sound and,
on rational completions, complete, as mathematics; none of the small machine’s
properties is the elliptope check.


H.9 The quantum set

Three descriptions of the same set have been running through this appendix: the
tables some quantum strategy can produce, the tables whose five-by-five matrix has
a PSD completion, and the tables inside Landau and Masanes’s curved edge. They
are the same set, for strategies on finitely many levels, and the next subsection takes
away the “finitely”. Each piece is taken in turn below, because the constructions are
the part worth seeing.
   Quantum tables are inside the completion set. A strategy’s correlator is the inner
product of two unit vectors: Alice’s observable applied to the shared state, and Bob’s
applied to it. Four unit vectors always have a PSD table of inner products, so every
634   H The CHSH check


             quantum table has a completion, and Tsirelson’s bound follows from that: S2 ≤ 8
             for every strategy, and its level-one moment matrix passes the PSD test with the
             marginals in. Quantum mechanics uses complex amplitudes, and the complex case
             goes through by a plain trick: a complex vector of length n is a real vector of length
             2n, its real parts followed by its imaginary parts, and the real part of a complex
             inner product is the ordinary inner product of those longer real vectors. So the real
             argument
               √        runs unchanged. The two-qubit strategy written out in Appendix I reaches
             2 2 in both readings.
                 The completion set is inside the quantum tables. This direction is Tsirelson’s
             representation, and the construction is his. Take a table with a PSD completion. A
             PSD matrix is a table of inner products of vectors, always: peel off one row at a time,
             and a zero on the diagonal forces its whole row to zero. So the completion hands
             over four unit vectors, a0 , a1 for Alice and b0 , b1 for Bob, with a x · by equal to the
             table’s entries, and they fit in three dimensions: slide one of the two entries the table
             leaves open to the end of the range that keeps the completion PSD, and there the
             completion is singular, which puts the four vectors in a space of three dimensions.
             Appendix I, Section I.8, gives the factorization and the measurements explicitly.
             Now comes the trick. There are three real four-by-four matrices, built from the
             two-by-two ones that swap two entries or flip the sign of one, that each square to
             the identity and anticommute in pairs: multiply any two of them in either order
             and the answers differ only in sign. Use a vector’s three components to mix those
             three matrices, and you get an observable that squares to the identity, a legitimate
             measurement. Give Alice and Bob a maximally entangled pair of four-level systems,
             and the correlator of two such observables comes out as exactly the inner product of
             their vectors. So the strategy built from the four vectors produces the table, for both
             real and complex amplitudes. Four levels on each side is always enough, and with
             complex amplitudes two are.
                 The curved edge is the same set again. Each correlator is the cosine of an angle,
             the angle between one of Alice’s vectors and one of Bob’s. Walk the loop a0 , b0 , a1 , b1
             and back to a0 : the angle across any one leg can’t exceed the sum of the other
             three, because angles on a sphere obey the triangle inequality. Flip one of Alice’s
             vectors to its opposite and walk the loop again, then do the same with her other one,
             and between them you get the other four inequalities, with 2π in them. Written in
             arcsines, those eight inequalities are Landau and Masanes’s four. Going the other
             way, any four angles that pass them can be met by actual vectors: choose an angle
             between Bob’s two that meets both pairs of constraints, build each of Alice’s from the
             two angles it has to make with them, and check that the determinant that says such a
             triangle exists comes out nonnegative. So a table has a PSD completion exactly when
             its arcsines pass the four inequalities, and those are exactly the quantum tables. The
             point (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) sits on the edge, because arcsin 53 + arcsin 45 = π2 by
                                              H.10 Any number of levels, and one converse that fails   635


the 3-4-5 triangle, and so does Tsirelson’s point. The interval construction, including
both endpoint cases, is in Section I.9.


H.10 Any number of levels, and one converse that fails
Nothing here cares about dimension. Quantum mechanics also allows systems
with infinitely many levels, and the arguments don’t need finitely many. Whatever
the dimension, a shared state v gives an expectation on the operators the players
measure with: x 7→ Re ⟨v, x v⟩. That one line is the whole step. The proofs use only
what that expectation always has: you can add, multiply, scale and take adjoints,
the product spreads over sums, and the expectation of x ∗ x is never negative. Each
measurement is its own adjoint with the expectation of its square at most one,
which covers unsharp measurements too, and Alice’s commute with Bob’s. That last
demand is weaker than putting them on two separate systems, so the result covers
the wider, commuting model as well. On that  √footing Tsirelson’s sum of squares goes
through, and the CHSH value is at most 2 2. The same nonnegative form, with
each diagonal entry raised to one, completes the correlator table to a PSD matrix, so
the four arcsine inequalities hold, and with a unit the full first-level moment matrix,
marginals and all, is PSD. The other direction needs no help from infinity: every
point inside the arcsine edge is reached on two four-level systems.
    Also, the finite-mixture theorem proves only one direction, that a finite local
model satisfies the bound, and its converse as stated is false: a table with S = 0 that
no local model produces. Fine’s own theorem, in the form that speaks of correlations,
is proved separately as an equivalence: a table of four correlators comes from a local
model exactly when each is between −1 and 1 and all eight CHSH inequalities hold.
Section I.10 constructs the finite distribution. And one more thing about tallies,
which the guarantee paragraph above already used: a tally loaded at no charge is
not thereby classical (the four rounds with S equal to four). The correlators (one,
one, one, minus one) are the PR box, which no classical model has as its averages,
though coin-flip play lands on that four-round tally one time in sixteen; the classical
vertex this appendix used, which fails the check like every plan, is (one, one, one,
one).
    That covers the game, the number, the two walls, and the check. The derivations
come in full in the next appendix, Appendix I; what all this costs against physics
was Section 19.
APPENDIX I




The CHSH derivation, in full

Appendix H tells the story; this appendix does the algebra. Each item gives the
statement with its hypotheses and the steps you need to check it. Nothing here says
that a matrix is a physical state. Where quantum strategies come in, I say exactly
how they stand to the matrices.


I.1 Setting and notation

Start with four piles of tally sheets, one for each pair of settings Alice and Bob can
be given. On each round their answers either agree or disagree. Give agreement a
score of +1 and disagreement a score of −1. In each pile, add the scores and divide
by the number of rounds. That pile’s average is its correlator. It says how strongly
the two answers agree for that pair of settings.
   For example, three agreements and one disagreement give a total of two over
four rounds, hence an average of one half. The four averages make a little square
table: Alice’s setting chooses the row, Bob’s chooses the column. The score I will
study adds three cells of that table and subtracts the bottom-right one. Here are the
names for those quantities.

Definition I.1 (Settings, outcomes, correlators). Alice receives a setting x ∈ {0, 1}
and Bob a setting y ∈ {0, 1}. Each answers a bit, recoded as an outcome a, b ∈
{+1, −1} (bit 0 becomes +1, bit 1 becomes −1). The correlator Exy is the average
of the product ab over the rounds with settings ( x, y). The CHSH quantity is

                             S = E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 .
I collect the four correlators into the 2 × 2 matrix

                                          E10 E11

whose rows are indexed by Alice’s setting and whose columns by Bob’s. The rows of
E are ( E00 , E01 ) and ( E10 , E11 ); the columns are ( E00 , E10 ) and ( E01 , E11 ).

Definition I.2 (Counters). There are eight counts: for each setting pair, samexy
counts rounds whose two answer bits matched and diffxy counts rounds whose bits
differed. A round adds one to exactly one of the eight. Write
                                                                           Dxy
        Nxy = samexy + diffxy ,      Dxy = samexy − diffxy ,       Exy =       .

    A matched round contributes ab = +1 and a differing round ab = −1, so Dxy
is the sum of the products and Dxy /Nxy is their average. Since | Dxy | ≤ Nxy , every
correlator from counters lies in [−1, 1]. When a bucket is empty, its correlator is
defined as 0. The score is E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 .


I.2 The classical bound
Write a fixed plan on a card: Alice’s answer to setting zero, her answer to setting one,
and Bob’s two answers. Each answer is a sign, plus or minus. Before multiplying
anything, look at Bob’s pair. Either the signs agree or they differ. If they agree,
adding them gives plus or minus two and subtracting them gives zero. If they differ,
the sum is zero and the difference is plus or minus two. One of those two quantities
vanishes; the other cannot exceed two in size. The next calculation uses exactly that
split.



Lemma I.1 (Deterministic strategies). Let a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ∈ {+1, −1}. Then a0 b0 +
a0 b1 + a1 b0 − a1 b1 is 2 or −2.

Proof. Factor: a0 b0 + a0 b1 + a1 b0 − a1 b1 = a0 (b0 + b1 ) + a1 (b0 − b1 ). If b0 = b1
then b0 + b1 = ±2 and b0 − b1 = 0; if b0 ̸= b1 the other way round. In both cases
exactly one of the two brackets is ±2 and the other is 0, so the expression is ±2
times a sign, which is +2 or −2. There are sixteen sign choices, and every one of
them gives exactly ±2. None gives 0 or ±4.
   You can also just list the sixteen sign choices and add each one up. Nothing in
the argument needs real numbers: the signs are whole numbers, so the bound holds
the same way whether you read the correlators as rationals (what a counter gives)
or as reals.
   A fixed card is only the first case. You can shuffle among several cards, perhaps
using some more often than others. Every card still tells each player an answer using
that player’s setting alone. The shuffle changes how often each card contributes; it
does not change the score that a particular card would produce. Since each card’s
score lies between minus two and two, their average must stay between those same
ends. The following definition writes out that weighted shuffle.
638   I The CHSH derivation, in full


               Definition I.3 (Finite factorizable model). Four real correlators E00 , E01 , E10 , E11
               are factorizable when there are a natural number λmax , weights p(λ) and re-
               sponse signs A( x, λ), B(y, λ) for λ = 0, . . . , λmax such that: 0 ≤ p(λ) ≤ 1;
               ∑λmax

               Exy = ∑λλmax

               ity p(λ), and each player reads an answer off the card using only their own setting.
               Only the correlators are modelled.



               Theorem I.2 (The classical bound for a finite local model). If E is factorizable, then
               −2 ≤ E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 ≤ 2.

               Proof. Substitute the factorization: S = ∑λ p(λ)Sλ , where Sλ is the deterministic
               expression of Lemma I.1 at the signs A(·, λ), B(·, λ). Each Sλ ∈ [−2, 2], the weights
               are nonnegative and sum to 1, so −2 = ∑λ p(λ)(−2) ≤ S ≤ ∑λ p(λ) · 2 = 2.

               Remark I.1 (Scope of the classical bound). Fine’s 1982 theorem is an equivalence
               between several descriptions of local models and the Bell inequalities. The preceding
               theorem proves one direction: a finite factorizable model obeys the bound. The
               converse of this single inequality is false: (1, 1, −1, 1) has S = 0, but it breaks
               another of the sign variants (E00 + E01 − E10 + E11 = 4), so no local model gives it.
               The correlation-form equivalence needs each correlator between −1 and 1 and all
               eight inequalities; with those, Section I.10 builds the local model. The preceding
               theorem is stated for finitely many hidden cards (λ ≤ λmax ), and that loses nothing.
               Whatever the hidden variable is and however it is drawn, the correlators see it only
               through its four answer signs, so lumping together the cards that carry the same
               four signs gives at most sixteen cards and the same four correlators. All the lumping
               needs is a probability for each of the sixteen sign patterns.
                  The finite-tally statement concerns one fixed strategy replayed on every recorded
               round.

               Definition I.4 (A tally consistent with one local plan). For bits a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ∈ {0, 1}
               and a counter record w, w is locally consistent with ( a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ) when, for each
               setting pair ( x, y): if a x = by then diffxy = 0, otherwise samexy = 0; and every
               bucket is sampled, N00 , N01 , N10 , N11 > 0.

Theorem I.3 (A tally above 2 is not one replayed strategy). Let w be a counter
record whose rational score S(w) is greater than 2. Then for all bits a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ,
w is not locally consistent with ( a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ). Every locally consistent record has
S(w) = 2 or S(w) = −2; the first statement is that fact turned around.

Proof. Under local consistency each sampled bucket is pure: if a x = by every round
in the bucket matched, so Exy = Nxy /Nxy = +1; otherwise every round differed
and Exy = −1. In signs, Exy = α x β y with α x = (−1) ax and β y = (−1)by . The score
is then the deterministic expression of Lemma I.1, which is 2 or −2. A score above 2
contradicts this.
   The theorem rules out one explanation, a single four-bit plan used on every
round. It says nothing about a local model that redraws its hidden state every round;
Appendix H gives a four-round coin-flip tally with score 4. The clause that every
bucket is sampled does work here. An empty bucket reads as 0, and the plan that
answers 0 to everything, never asked the pair 11, would score 1 + 1 + 1 − 0 = 3.


I.3 Tsirelson’s bound from algebra
Now put the cards aside and look just at four numbers in the square. I want to
bound their three-plus-one-minus score from their squared sizes. The useful trick
is to write the proposed allowance minus the squared score as a pile of squares.
A square cannot be negative. If the difference really is that pile, the score cannot
outrun the allowance.
    The identity below is the receipt for that trick. The letters a, b, c, d are the four
entries read across the first row, then across the second. It holds for any four real
numbers. After proving it, I will put in the two bounds on row length that this part
of the checker supplies.

I.4 The zero-marginal 5 × 5 moment matrix

The four averages fill only the Alice–Bob part of a larger table. Give that table five
labels: a constant reading 1, Alice’s two possible readings, and Bob’s two. Each cell
records an average product of its row and column readings. A reading multiplied by
itself is 1, so the diagonal is all ones. The four averages measured fill the cross-player
cells and their reflected partners.
    Other cells are still empty. This particular check fills them with zero: each player’s
average answer against the constant reading, and the cells between that player’s
two settings. These are choices of the check; the four cross-player averages alone
did not supply them. I will later let the two within-player cells vary and ask whether
any filling works. For now, write down this one fixed filling and test it.

Definition I.5 (The pinned level-1 matrix). Take rows and columns I, A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 .
Put 1 on the diagonal and the four correlators in the Alice–Bob cells, and set the
four one-party entries (each player’s own average answer) and the two within-party
entries (A0 against A1 , B0 against B1 ) to zero. The resulting matrix is:


                                        I A0 A1 B0 B1 
                                 I       1 0    0   0   0
                                A0     0 1     0  E   E   

                   M( E) =             

   What do I ask of this table? Choose five numbers, one beside each row and one
beside the matching column. For each cell, multiply its entry by its row’s number
and its column’s number, then add all twenty-five results. Do this with any five
numbers you like, positive, negative or zero. I require the total never to be negative.
That requirement is called positive semidefiniteness, abbreviated PSD.
   Write the five chosen numbers as a column v. The superscript T turns a column
into a row, so ordinary matrix multiplication writes that same weighted total as
vT Mv. The condition is therefore vT Mv ≥ 0 for every choice of v. The table is
symmetric too: reflect it across its diagonal and the entries agree.
642   I The CHSH derivation, in full


                  The first row and column have only one nonzero entry, the corner 1. Their
               contribution is the square of the first chosen number. The remaining four rows and
               columns can be tested on their own. Grouping them gives
                                                       !                        !
                                                 1 0                  I2   E
                                       M( E) =             ,   G =                  .
                                                 0 G                  ET   I2

                   Here I2 is the two-by-two identity table: ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
               The superscript on E again swaps rows and columns. The weighted total for M ( E)
               is the first number’s square plus the weighted total for G. If every total for G is
               nonnegative, adding a square keeps it nonnegative. If some total for G is negative,
               choose the first number to be zero and the same negative total appears for M ( E).
               Thus the two tables pass or fail together.
                   The next operation is completing a square, with several numbers at once. For
               one number, u2 + 2uw + rw2 becomes (u + w)2 + (r − 1)w2 . The first square
               cannot hurt, and choosing u = −w makes it vanish. So the whole expression stays
               nonnegative for every choice exactly when the remaining part does. The matrix
               formula below does the same job for two groups of numbers.
                   Here positive definite means that the weighted total for P is strictly positive
               for every nonzero choice of weights. In particular, P has an inverse, written P−1 :
               applying it undoes multiplication by P. The matrix left after completing the square
               is called the Schur complement. Its name is less useful here than the operation that
               produces it.

Lemma I.9 (The 2 × 2 test). If α ≥ 0, δ ≥ 0 and αδ − β2 ≥ 0, then αu2 + 2βuw +
δw2 ≥ 0 for all real u, w.

Proof. If w = 0 the form is αu2 ≥ 0. Otherwise put t = u/w, so the form is
w2 (αt2 + 2βt + δ). If α = 0, then − β2 ≥ 0 forces β = 0 and the bracket is δ ≥ 0.
If α > 0, αt2 + 2βt + δ = α(t + β/α)2 + (αδ − β2 )/α, a sum of two nonnegative
terms.

               Lemma I.11 (Discriminant). If a + 2bt + ct2 ≥ 0 for every real t, then b2 ≤ ac.

               Proof. If c < 0 the quadratic tends to −∞, so c ≥ 0. If c = 0, the line a + 2bt is
               nonnegative for every t only if b = 0, and then b2 = 0 = ac. If c > 0, evaluate at
               t = −b/c: a − b2 /c ≥ 0, so b2 ≤ ac.



               Theorem I.12 (PSD implies contractive). If M ( E) is positive semidefinite, then
               p ≥ 0, q ≥ 0 and pq − s2 ≥ 0.

               Proof. Feed the quadratic form three test vectors, written in the order
               ( I, A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 ). Each is the choice x = − Ey that zeroes both completed
               squares in the proof of Theorem I.10, so only yT ( I2 − ET E)y is left.
                    First, v = (0, − E00 , − E10 , 1, 0) gives vT Mv = p, so p ≥ 0.
                    Second, v = (0, − E01 , − E11 , 0, 1) gives vT Mv = q, so q ≥ 0.
                    Third, for each real t, v(t) = (0, −( E00 t + E01 ), −( E10 t + E11 ), t, 1) gives
               v(t)T Mv(t) = p t2 − 2s t + q ≥ 0. Apply Lemma I.11 with a = q, b = −s, c = p:
               s2 ≤ pq.



               Corollary I.13 (The equivalence). For all real E00 , E01 , E10 , E11 , the symmetric
               matrix M ( E) is positive semidefinite if and only if the correlators are column
               contractive.

               Proof. Theorem I.10 is one direction and Theorem I.12 the other.
                  The equivalence above is about the columns. The bound can go through either
               the rows or the columns: the six-square identity only needs the four squares to add
               to at most 2, and the two row bounds give that, and so do p ≥ 0 and q ≥ 0.

Remark I.3 (What PSD of the pinned matrix means). M ( E) is the level-1 moment
matrix with the two within-party entries ⟨ A0 A1 ⟩ and ⟨ B0 B1 ⟩ pinned to zero. Its PSD
is sufficient for the correlators to admit some PSD completion (Section I.7), and it is
not necessary: the all-ones plan has a completion but fails here. So a check built on
M ( E) is sound for the completion set and not complete for it, and it rejects some
honest classical tallies. That correlators with a PSD completion are exactly those
reachable by quantum measurements is Tsirelson’s theorem, and both halves are
proved here in finite dimension. For real and for complex amplitudes, a strategy’s
correlators are inner products of unit vectors (with complex amplitudes, use real
vectors of twice the length) and its level-1 moment matrix is PSD, so they have a
PSD completion. The other half, that every PSD completion comes from a quantum
strategy, comes from this construction: the strategy is built on two four-level systems
from the completion’s Gram vectors (Section I.8).

               I.5 The integer check
               The machine has whole-number tallies. The three conditions above were written
               using averages, which are fractions. You can test the same conditions without
               ever dividing: first make sure each denominator is positive, then multiply it away.
               Multiplying by a positive number cannot turn a passing inequality into a failing one
               or a failing one into a passing one.
                  For the first column, the condition starts as one minus two squared averages.
               Multiplying by the product of their squared denominators leaves three whole-
               number products. I call that result A. The second column gives B the same way.
               The cross-column term is a sum of two products of averages; multiplying by all four
               denominators leaves a whole number I call C. The last condition becomes C2 ≤ AB,
               because both sides have had the same positive denominator removed. Four positive
               bucket sizes and these three comparisons make seven checks. Here are the products
               to calculate.

               Definition I.7 (The seven-integer check). From the counters of Definition I.2, with
               all arithmetic in Z, let
                                            2   2     2   2     2   2
                                       A = N00 N10 − D00 N10 − D10 N00 ,
                                            2   2     2   2     2   2
                                       B = N01 N11 − D01 N11 − D11 N01 ,
                                       C = D00 D01 N10 N11 + D10 D11 N00 N01 .
               The check is the conjunction of seven facts, in this order: 0 < N00 , 0 < N01 ,
               0 < N10 , 0 < N11 , 0 ≤ A, 0 ≤ B, and C · C ≤ A · B.

                   There is no division, no real number, no square root and no S in it.


               Lemma I.15 (The seven facts are the three conditions with denominators cleared).
               Assume N00 , N01 , N10 , N11 > 0 and put Exy = Dxy /Nxy . Then, with p, q, s as in
               Definition I.6,

               C2 ≤ AB ⇐⇒ s2 ≤ pq.

Theorem I.16 (Soundness of the integer check). If a tally w passes the seven-
integer check, then its four correlators Exy = Dxy /Nxy are column contractive.
Consequently its pinned matrix is positive semidefinite.

Proof. The first four tests say that every bucket contains a round, so each average
is its signed total divided by a positive count. The next two tests say that A and B
are nonnegative. Dividing each by its positive denominator gives p ≥ 0 and q ≥ 0.
The last test says AB − C2 ≥ 0. Divide that difference by the positive square of the
product of all four counts; the result is pq − s2 ≥ 0, as the preceding calculation
shows. Those are exactly the three column conditions, and Theorem I.10 shows that
they make the matrix pass the nonnegative-total test.



Corollary I.17 (A passed check implies the Tsirelson bound). If a tally w passes
the seven-integer check, the correlators of w satisfy S2 ≤ 8. It is the composition of
Theorem I.16, Corollary I.13 and Theorem I.14.

   Two of the seven facts carry the bound by themselves. With every pair sampled,
0 ≤ A and 0 ≤ B are p ≥ 0 and q ≥ 0, so the four squared correlators add to
at most 2 and Lemma I.4 gives S2 ≤ 8. The fact C · C ≤ A · B is what positive
semidefiniteness adds, and the bound doesn’t use it. For the form this takes on the
small machine, where a raised flag has to stand on a passing check, see Appendix H.
648   I The CHSH derivation, in full


                  A worked tally. Take (same, diff) = (4, 1), (4, 1), (4, 1), (1, 4) for the pairs
               00, 01, 10, 11. Then Nxy = 5 for all four, D00 = D01 = D10 = 3, D11 = −3,
               and the correlators are 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, −0.6 with S = 2.4. Compute:
                              A = 25 · 25 − 9 · 25 − 9 · 25 = 625 − 225 − 225 = 175,
                               B = 25 · 25 − 9 · 25 − 9 · 25 = 175,
                               C = 3 · 3 · 5 · 5 + 3 · (−3) · 5 · 5 = 225 − 225 = 0.
               All seven facts hold: four positive N, 0 ≤ 175 twice, and 0 ≤ 175 · 175. Dividing
               back, p = 175/625 = 0.28 and s = 0, the second row of the table in Section I.4.
                   Two more, for contrast. One round per pair from the all-ones plan, (1, 0) four
               times, gives N = D = 1 everywhere and A = 1 − 1 − 1 = −1 < 0: the check
               fails. The tally (4, 1), (9, 1), (9, 1), (1, 4) gives correlators 3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5,
               with N = 5, 10, 10, 5 and D = 3, 8, 8, −3: A = 25 · 100 − 9 · 100 − 64 · 25 = 0,
               B = 100 · 25 − 64 · 25 − 9 · 100 = 0 and C = 3 · 8 · 10 · 5 + 8 · (−3) · 5 · 10 = 0. It

               I.6 Level 1+AB

               The first table had one place for each player’s answer. Enlarge it by giving each
               Alice–Bob product a place too. There are four such products, so the five places
               become nine. A cell still asks for the average product of its row and column labels.
               Some of those products reduce to entries I already have; five more numbers are
               needed for the particular filling below. Call them γ1 through γ5 . The longer labels
               say which products they stand for.
                  The five additional parameters name the moments γ1 = ⟨ A0 A1 B0 ⟩, γ2 =
               ⟨ A0 A1 B1 ⟩, γ3 = ⟨ A0 B0 B1 ⟩, γ4 = ⟨ A1 B0 B1 ⟩ and γ5 = ⟨ A0 A1 B0 B1 ⟩. These are
               labels for the entries; the definition below does not construct operators.

               Definition I.8 (The level-1+AB matrix). The 9 × 9 real matrix on rows and columns
               I, A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 , A0 B0 , A0 B1 , A1 B0 , A1 B1 , with the following entries:
                                                                                                 I.6 Level 1+AB   649



                         I A0 A1 B0 B1 A0 B0 A0 B1 A1 B0 A1 B1
                  I      1  0   0  0   0  E00 E01   E10   E11
                 A0      0  1   0 E00 E01  0   0    γ1    γ2
                 A1      0  0   1 E10 E11 γ1  γ2     0     0
                 B0      0 E00 E10 1   0   0  γ3     0    γ4
                 B1      0 E01 E11 0   1  γ3   0    γ4     0
                A0 B0   E00 0 γ1 0 γ3      1   0     0    γ5
                A0 B1   E01 0 γ2 γ3 0      0   1   −γ5     0
                A1 B0   E10 γ1 0   0 γ4    0  −γ5    1     0
                A1 B1   E11 γ2 0 γ4 0     γ5   0     0     1
    Two constraints are fixed by this layout. First, the four-body cells carry opposite
signs: +γ5 at ( A0 B0 , A1 B1 ) and −γ5 at ( A0 B1 , A1 B0 ). In a real moment matrix
those two cells are ⟨ A0 A1 B0 B1 ⟩ and ⟨ A0 A1 B1 B0 ⟩, so the tie says ⟨ A0 A1 ( B0 B1 +
B1 B0 )⟩ = 0, which for a real matrix is ⟨{ A0 , A1 } ⊗ { B0 , B1 }⟩ = 0. The level-1
pinnings don’t imply it. Take a classical strategy: Alice’s two answers a0 , a1 are
independent fair signs, and Bob copies them, b0 = a0 and b1 = a1 . Every pinned
cell of its moment matrix is 0 and both four-body cells are 1, so no choice of the
nine numbers gives its matrix. So the matrix here is level 1+AB cut down to the
slice ⟨{ A0 , A1 } ⊗ { B0 , B1 }⟩ = 0, and that is what “level 1+AB” names in this book.
The slice holds whenever A0 and A1 anticommute. The soundness theorems below
are about this matrix, so they stand as stated. Second, the matrix keeps the level-1
pinning: every cell whose label reduces to a marginal or to ⟨ A0 A1 ⟩ or ⟨ B0 B1 ⟩ is zero,
for instance ( A0 , A0 B0 ), ( A0 B0 , A0 B1 ) and ( A0 B0 , A1 B0 ). The displayed matrix is
symmetric.
    I want to test this larger table with the same operation as before: put a weight
beside each row and column and add the weighted cells. The first three weights will
each be collected into one completed square. Everything involving the other six will
be left over. That leftover is what I call the residual; it is the part whose sign I still
need to settle.
    Write a vector as (v I , v A0 , v A1 , v B0 , v B1 , v00 , v01 , v10 , v11 ), where v xy is the coor-

                          L1 = E00 v00 + E01 v01 + E10 v10 + E11 v11 ,

                          L3 = E10 v B0 + E11 v B1 + γ1 v00 + γ2 v01 .

               Definition I.10 (What the integer check computes). The supplied moments arrive
               as bucket pairs: γk = Ngk /Dgk with Ngk = samegk − diffgk and Dgk = samegk +
               diffgk . Watch the letters: for these five buckets N names the numerator and D
               the denominator: the difference and the count, the reverse of Section I.1. Let
               K = ( N00 N01 N10 N11 Dg1 Dg2 Dg3 Dg4 Dg5 )2 . The check computes the 21 integers
               KHij , the 15 integers of S(6) at scale K2 and the 10 integers of S(5) at scale K4 , each
               by h11 hij − h1i h1j on integers. The decider is the conjunction of: Nxy > 0 for the
               four pairs; Dgk > 0 for k = 1..5; − Dgk < Ngk < Dgk for k = 1..5; and six strict

                                                                                    I.6 Level 1+AB   653


integer S(5) . The full check combines the seven-integer check of Definition I.7 with
this decider.
   Each cleared integer, read as a real, equals the corresponding real quantity times
the stated positive power of K. A k × k leading minor of a matrix scaled by c > 0
scales by ck . So every integer positivity holds exactly when the real one does.
   Two parts of the full check are there to fail early, and no proof below needs
them. A passing decider makes H positive definite (Remark I.4), and the top left
two-by-two block of H has p and q on its diagonal and −s off it, so p > 0, q > 0
and pq > s2 , and the seven-integer check passes. And with H positive definite, the
nine-by-nine form is zero only at zero: it is three squares plus R (Lemma I.18), so
where it is zero the six inputs of R are zero, then so are L1 , L2 and L3 , and then so
are v I , v A0 and v A1 . So the nine-by-nine matrix is positive definite; with ones on its
diagonal, that puts every γk strictly between −1 and 1, which is the bucket bound
− Dgk < Ngk < Dgk .


Theorem I.22 (The full 1+AB check implies PSD). Let the counts make every Nxy
and every Dgk positive, and let the decider just defined pass on them. Then the
matrix of Definition I.8 at the four correlators and γk = Ngk /Dgk is symmetric and
positive semidefinite.

Proof. The bucket conjuncts make every denominator positive, the scaling remark
just above carries the six integer positivities over to the real cascade, and Lemma I.20
twice plus Lemma I.21 give R ≥ 0, and so positive semidefiniteness by Theorem I.19.


Remark I.4 (Interior only). Every test in the cascade is strict, so a passing check
certifies that H is positive definite, which is stronger than semidefinite. A point
where H is PSD but singular cannot pass, and neither can a moment with |γk | = 1.
For example, the tally of Section I.5 with correlators (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) has
H11 = 1 − 9/25 − 16/25 = 0, so the full 1+AB check fails on it for every choice
of γ, though the level-1 check of Section I.5 accepts it. The argument establishes
soundness only; no converse is stated.

I.7 The elliptope completion

Go back to the two within-player cells I filled with zero. Leave them blank this time.
Keep all four measured cross-player averages fixed, and ask whether there is any
way to fill those two blanks that makes the table pass. A failure with zeros no longer
settles the question; another filling may work.
     Call the first missing number x and the second y, and copy each into its reflected
cell so the table stays symmetric. The collection of averages that admit a passing
filling has a name, the elliptope completion set. Membership means that at least one
choice of those two numbers works. It does not require every choice to work, or
require the zero choice to work.

Definition I.11 (Completion and membership). Complete the matrix of Section I.4
by setting the within-party entries to free reals: x in the ( A0 , A1 ) cells and y in the
( B0 , B1 ) cells, marginals still zero. The correlators are elliptope realizable when
some x, y make the completed matrix symmetric and PSD.

                  Its quadratic form at v = (v0 , . . . , v4 ) is ∑k v2k + 2xv1 v2 + 2yv3 v4 + 2E00 v1 v3 +
               2E01 v1 v4 + 2E10 v2 v3 + 2E11 v2 v4 . The pinned matrix is the case x = y = 0, so PSD
               of M ( E) implies membership.


               Theorem I.24 (Deterministic plans are inside). If a20 = a21 = b02 = b12 = 1, then
               ( a0 b0 , a0 b1 , a1 b0 , a1 b1 ) is elliptope realizable, with x = a0 a1 and y = b0 b1 .

               Proof. With these entries the form equals v20 + ( a0 v1 + a1 v2 + b0 v3 + b1 v4 )2 . Ex-
               panding the second square gives a20 v21 + · · · on the diagonal, which is v21 + · · · by
               the unit squares, and the cross terms 2a0 a1 v1 v2 = 2xv1 v2 , 2a0 b0 v1 v3 = 2E00 v1 v3 ,
               and so on for all six pairs. A sum of two squares is never negative.
                  The all-ones plan is one instance. The classical mixture (1, 0, 1, 0) has a comple-
               tion at x = 1, y = 0, with form v20 + (v1 + v2 + v3 )2 + v24 .


               Theorem I.25 (Convexity and finite mixtures). For 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1, if E and F are ellip-
               tope realizable, so is λE + (1 − λ) F. For finitely many members with nonnegative
               weights summing to at most 1, the weighted sum is realizable. Every finite mixture
               of deterministic plans is realizable.

               Proof. The form is affine in ( E, x, y) for each fixed v. Take the completion (λx1 +
               (1 − λ) x2 , λy1 + (1 − λ)y2 ); the form at the mixture is the same mixture of two
               nonnegative forms. For several members, weight each one’s completed matrix by its
               assigned share and add them. If the shares total less than one, give the missing share
               to the zero-correlator point with both missing entries zero; its completed matrix is
               the identity. The diagonal of the weighted matrix is then one, its cross entries are
               the desired weighted correlators, and every weighted total is a sum of nonnegative
               totals with nonnegative weights. It therefore supplies the required completion. The
               last statement combines this with Theorem I.24.
                                                                          I.7 The elliptope completion   657




Theorem I.26 (Tsirelson’s bound holds on the completion set). If E is elliptope
realizable then S2 ≤ 8.

Proof. For a symmetric PSD matrix the bilinear form obeys Cauchy-Schwarz,
B(u, w)2 ≤ Q(u) Q(w), because Q(u + tw) = Q(u) + 2t B(u, w) + t2 Q(w) ≥
0 for all t and Lemma I.11 applies. Take u1 = e A0 and w+ = e B0 + e B1 :
B(u1 , w+ ) = E00 + E01 , Q(u1 ) = 1, Q(w+ ) = 2 + 2y. Take u2 = e A1 and
w− = e B0 − e B1 : B(u2 , w− ) = E10 − E11 , Q(w− ) = 2 − 2y. So c21 ≤ 2 + 2y
and c22 ≤ 2 − 2y with c1 = E00 + E01 , c2 = E10 − E11 , and both budgets are
nonnegative. Then c21 c22 ≤ (2 + 2y)(2 − 2y) = 4 − 4y2 ≤ 4, so c1 c2 ≤ 2, and
S2 = (c1 + c2 )2 = c21 + 2c1 c2 + c22 ≤ (2 + 2y) + 4 + (2 − 2y) = 8.
   The completion can make a row of E longer than 1 (the all-ones plan has rows
of squared length 2), which is why this proof does not use the row bounds of
Section I.4.


Corollary I.27 (The PR box is outside). (1, 1, 1, −1) is not elliptope realizable,
since its S2 = 16 > 8.



Theorem I.28 (Strictly beyond the classical bound). (3/5, 3/5, 3/5, −3/5) is
elliptope realizable and has S = 12/5 > 2.

Proof. At x = y = 0 the form equals v20 + (v1 + 35 v3 + 53 v4 )2 + (v2 + 35 v3 − 35 v4 )2 +

25 v3 + 25 v4 . Check: the two middle squares give v3 coefficient 25 + 25 = 25 , plus

25 is 1; the v3 v4 terms are + 25 and − 25 and cancel; the cross terms are 2 · 5 v1 v3 ,
2 · 53 v1 v4 , 2 · 35 v2 v3 and −2 · 35 v2 v4 , as the entries require.
   By Theorem I.2 no finite factorizable model has S > 2, so this point is not a finite
mixture of plans, while Theorem I.25 puts every such mixture inside. The completion
set then strictly contains the finite classical set, and the PR box lies outside it. It sits
inside the no-signalling set, for the plain reason that every correlator in it is between
−1 and 1 (the vector that is 1 at A x and ∓1 at By gives 2 ∓ 2Exy ≥ 0), and any four
such numbers come from the no-signalling box that answers ( a, b) at settings ( x, y)
with probability (1 + ab Exy )/4, each player’s own answer alone a fair coin.
   The elliptope gate is an integer decider with a soundness proof. Its completion
entries arrive as bucket pairs, and an empty bucket is read as 0/1, so unlike
Section I.5 it does not require every pair to be sampled.

               Definition I.12 (The two branches). The positive-minor branch: with the comple-
               tion supplied as buckets and all entries scaled to integers by a positive common
               factor K, the four leading minors of the 4 × 4 block on A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 are strictly
               positive. The factorization branch: with the completion and a rational certificate
               supplied (six subdiagonal entries over a common positive denominator, four pivots
               dk ≥ 0 over another), the ten entry equations of M = LDLT hold in cross-multiplied
               integer arithmetic. The full gate is their disjunction.



               Theorem I.29 (Soundness of the gate). If the full gate returns yes on a counter
               record, any completion buckets and any certificate, then the four correlators of the
               record are elliptope realizable. On the PR box tally the gate returns no for every
               choice of the remaining arguments.

               Proof. In both branches it is enough to show the 4 × 4 block on A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 gives
               a nonnegative form, because the I row and column are 1 on the diagonal and 0
               elsewhere. The first branch: dividing by the positive factor K (a k × k minor scales
               by K k ) gives four positive leading minors of the real block, and Lemma I.21 applies.
               The second: cross-multiplying by positive denominators changes no equation, so
               M = LDLT holds over the rationals with L unit lower triangular, and the form
               is vT LDLT v = ∑k dk Pk2 with P = LT v and every dk ≥ 0. The PR statement is
               soundness followed by Corollary I.27.
                   Examples by direct computation: the all-ones plan passes through the fac-
               torization branch at x = y = 1 with pivots (1, 0, 0, 0); the classical mixture
               (1, 0, 1, 0) passes through the same branch at x = 1, y = 0 with pivots (1, 0, 0, 1);
               the 12/5 point passes through the positive-minor branch at x = y = 0; and
               (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) passes through the factorization branch at x = y = 0 with
               pivots (1, 1, 0, 0), since B0 = 35 A0 + 54 A1 and B1 = 45 A0 − 35 A1 reproduce every
               entry.
                   That’s all the gate is: no property of the small machine is built from it.


               I.8 The four-vector construction
               Put two equal-length pencils down with their ends together, and draw a line along
               one of them. Keep that pencil still and turn the other. Use the square corner of a
               sheet of paper to bring the moving pencil’s tip straight across to the line, and mark
               where it lands. The mark moves from a full pencil-length forward, through the
               joined ends when the pencils make a square corner, to a full pencil-length backward.
               Call those readings 1, 0 and −1. That is the signed shadow I want. Between
                                                                     I.8 The four-vector construction   659


those positions the reading is the cosine of the angle. A dot product of unit vectors
measures that shadow.
   Now ask for four directions, two labelled Alice and two Bob, with a prescribed
shadow for each Alice–Bob pair. Try this request: Alice’s first points exactly along
both of Bob’s; Alice’s second points along Bob’s first and exactly against his second.
Each request alone is easy. Put them together and your hands cannot do it: Bob’s
pencils would have to point both the same way and opposite ways. Four numbers in
range need not describe four directions that can coexist.
   Write those four readings as x = E00 , y = E01 , z = E10 and w = E11 . I haven’t
specified the shadow between Alice’s own two directions, or between Bob’s own
two. Those are the two blanks, t and u, in the following table. Can they be filled so
that the whole table comes from directions? The pencils let you ask it in a plane;
the construction will allow four coordinates. A completion is a positive-semidefinite

The extra row and column labelled I in Section I.7 have diagonal 1 and all other
entries zero, so they do not change this condition.
   Why positivity? Lay arrows end to end, allowing a backward arrow when its
weight is negative. Square the length from the start to the finish. Expanding that
square adds up the arrows’ pairwise shadows, with their weights. It cannot be
negative. A proposed shadow table that gives a negative answer for some choice of
weights cannot come from arrows. That is the PSD test. A Gram matrix is simply
the table of all those pairwise dot products.
   The converse has to build the arrows. Pick the first direction as a baseline. Give
every other arrow the component along it that its shadow demands, then build the
remaining components perpendicular to it. What remains to be fitted is a smaller
shadow table. Here is that construction, including its boundary. If its first diagonal
entry is zero, positivity of h11 a2 + 2h1j ab + h jj b2 for every a, b forces h1j = 0: with
b = 1, a nonzero h1j would let the linear term go negative without bound. Delete
that zero row and column, construct vectors for the smaller matrix, and put back
the zero vector. If h11 > 0, set

                  Three dimensions are always enough. The table fixes the cross entries and leaves
               two entries of G open, a0 · a1 and b0 · b1 . Hold the first and let the second be t.
               The values of t that keep G PSD form an interval: if two values do, so does every
               value between, because the quadratic form at a mixture is the same mixture of the
               two forms; the set is closed, because a form that is nonnegative at every value of a
               convergent sequence is nonnegative at its limit; and it is bounded, because a PSD
               matrix with ones on its diagonal has every entry between −1 and 1. At an end of
               that interval G is singular: if it were positive definite there, it would stay positive
               definite under every small enough change of t, on both sides. Take G at an end. A
               singular PSD G has a nonzero c with cT Gc = 0, and cT Gc is the squared length of
               ∑i ci vi for the four vectors vi , so that sum is zero and the four vectors lie in a space
               of at most three dimensions. Coordinates in an orthonormal basis of that space keep
               every inner product, so a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 can be taken in R3 .
                  The next question is harder: how do directions become a prescription for a
               quantum measurement? Start with two signed cards in a row. One move swaps
               them; another changes the sign of the card in the right-hand place. Start at (+, +).
               Swap then change the right sign: (+, −). Start again, change the right sign then
               swap: (−, +). Every sign is reversed. Try unequal numbers on the cards: the two
               orders still give negatives of each other. “Anticommute” means exactly that relation
               between the two moves. Do either move twice and everything is back.
                  Write the swap as X, the sign change as Z, and doing nothing as I:
                                               !                      !                  !
                                         0 1                   1 0                  1 0
                                X=               ,     Z=               ,    I=            .
                                         1 0                   0 −1                 0 1

               For the larger construction, label four places by the two-bit words 00 through 11
               and put a signed number at each. An X in one bit-position swaps each pair of places
               differing at that bit; a Z reverses the signs at places whose bit there is 1. The two
               positions give the following three moves, written as real 4 × 4 matrices:
                                       Γ1 = X ⊗ I,   Γ2 = Z ⊗ X,     Γ3 = Z ⊗ Z.

               The tensor product has entries ( A ⊗ B)(i,k),( j,l ) = Aij Bkl . Each Γi is symmetric and
               squares to the identity. For i < j, the first position where the two products differ has
               X against Z, and XZ = − ZX; all other positions commute. So Γi Γ j = −Γ j Γi . For a
               unit vector a, the symmetric matrix A( a) = ∑i ai Γi then satisfies A( a)2 = ∑i a2i I = I.
               Its two-outcome measurement has projectors ( I + A( a))/2 and ( I − A( a))/2: they
               are symmetric, square to themselves, are orthogonal, and sum to the identity.

    What would that mean at a bench? Prepare the stated shared state, choose one
of the two specified measurements on each side, and write down the two signs
returned. For each pair of settings, count agreements as +1 and disagreements as
−1. Their average is the correlator. The model predicts the four averages x, y, z, w;
a finite tally fluctuates around its expectation. The signed-card moves let you check
the measurement algebra by hand. Realizing that state and those measurements in
a device, and comparing its tallies with the predictions, is the physical experiment.
    Conversely, in a normalized quantum state ψ with self-adjoint measurements
A x = By2 = I on separate systems, put a x = ( A x ⊗ I )ψ and by = ( I ⊗ By )ψ. They
  2

are unit vectors and Re⟨ a x , by ⟩ = Exy . Replace each complex coordinate by its real
and imaginary parts. This preserves those real inner products, and their Gram
matrix is a completion. A mixed state gives the same construction by taking the
direct sum of the vectors of its pure components, weighted by the square roots of
their probabilities. So the completion condition and finite-dimensional quantum
realizability are equivalent.
    The necessary direction does not require finite-dimensional vectors. If a
positive normalized expectation ω on an algebra has self-adjoint A x , By , with
ω ( A2x ), ω ( By2 ) ≤ 1, then the real symmetric matrix with entries Re ω ( Xi X j ) is
PSD: its quadratic form is ω (C ∗ C ) ≥ 0 for the real linear combination C of the
four observables. Increasing each diagonal entry to 1 preserves PSD. When Alice’s
observables commute with Bob’s, its cross entries are precisely the real correlators.
This supplies the same G. Including the unit as a fifth observable also gives the
level-1 moment matrix with its marginals. The sufficient direction already used only
two four-level systems.

               I.9 The arcsine boundary, in both directions
               Keep Bob’s two directions hinged at one end. Alice’s first direction has to make a
               specified angle with each. How far can Bob’s hinge open while that is possible? Hold
               Alice’s direction upright and sweep each of Bob’s around it at its required angle.
               Point them towards the same side to close the hinge as far as it will go; point them
               towards opposite sides to open it as far as it will go. There is a whole interval of
               openings between those limits. Alice’s second direction asks for another interval.
                  Draw both intervals on one strip marked from 0 to 180 degrees. If they miss, no
               hinge setting satisfies both. If they overlap, choose an opening in the overlap and
               construct each Alice direction at that opening. The algebra below permits each its
               own perpendicular component in four dimensions. The pencils show why the shared
               opening is the question; they need not fit the entire construction on a tabletop. In
               the impossible request above, one interval is just 0 degrees and the other just 180.
               There is nowhere to put the hinge.
                  Assume x, y, z, w ∈ [−1, 1], and put s x = arcsin x, with analogous notation for
               the other three entries. A unit vector making angles α, β ∈ [0, π ] with two unit
               vectors can exist at an angle δ between those two exactly when
                                        |α − β| ≤ δ ≤ min(α + β, 2π − α − β).
               To see this, decompose the two vectors along and perpendicular to the first. Their
               inner product ranges from cos α cos β − sin α sin β to cos α cos β + sin α sin β, by
               Cauchy–Schwarz; every value in that interval is attained by choosing the angle
               between their perpendicular components. Taking arccosines gives the displayed
               interval, including zero perpendicular components.
                  Apply this to Alice’s first vector and Bob’s two. Since α = π/2 − s x and β =
               π/2 − sy , Bob’s angle must lie in

                                             I0 = [ |s x − sy |, π − |s x + sy | ].
               Alice’s second vector gives I1 = [ |sz − sw |, π − |sz + sw | ]. Each interval is nonempty
               because | a − b| + | a + b| = 2 max(| a|, |b|) ≤ π for a, b ∈ [−π/2, π/2]. They
               intersect exactly when
                               |s x − sy | + |sz + sw | ≤ π,       |sz − sw | + |s x + sy | ≤ π.
               Using | a| + |b| = max(| a + b|, | a − b|), these are the four inequalities
                                 |s x + sy + sz − sw | ≤ π,        |s x + sy − sz + sw | ≤ π,
                                 |s x − sy + sz + sw | ≤ π, | − s x + sy + sz + sw | ≤ π.
               So a completion implies all four.

I.10 The finite local model, in both directions
Make sixteen cards, each with four boxes labelled A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 , and put every
possible arrangement of plus and minus signs on them, one arrangement per card.
Draw a card before choosing which setting to ask each player about. Alice reads her
chosen box; Bob reads his. Neither needs the other’s setting. How often each card is
drawn is the only choice left in this model.
   Try to get perfect agreement for the first three pairs and perfect disagreement
for the fourth. Any card that ever gets drawn would need A0 = B0 , A0 = B1
and A1 = B0 , which makes A1 = B1 too. Changing how often you draw the
cards cannot fix it. For less extreme requests the question is quantitative: can you
assign nonnegative weights to the cards, adding to one, that give all four requested
averages? The following construction supplies those weights exactly when all eight
CHSH inequalities hold and the correlators are in [−1, 1].
   There is a useful way to assemble the deck. First allow only Bob’s first question
and make a distribution of the three answers A0 , A1 , B0 . Then do the same for his
second question. Both smaller decks must draw Alice’s answer pairs in the same
proportions. The adjustable number t is Alice’s agreement-minus-disagreement
average across her two boxes. Choose it in both intervals
     J0 = [ −1 + | x + z|, 1 − | x − z| ],        J1 = [ −1 + |y + w|, 1 − |y − w| ].

Each interval is nonempty. They overlap exactly when | x + z| + |y − w| ≤ 2 and
|y + w| + | x − z| ≤ 2, which expand to the eight CHSH inequalities. For a0 , a1 , b ∈
664   I The CHSH derivation, in full


               {−1, 1} set
                                                             1 + ta0 a1 + xa0 b + za1 b
                                         P0 ( a0 , a1 , b) =                            ,
                                                                         8
                                                             1 + ta0 a1 + ya0 b + wa1 b
                                         P1 ( a0 , a1 , b) =                             .
                                                                         8
               When a0 = a1 , nonnegativity of P0 is 1 + t ≥ | x + z|; when a0 = − a1 , it is
               1 − t ≥ | x − z|. These are precisely t ∈ J0 . The same check for P1 uses J1 . Summing
               signs shows that both distributions have mass 1 and the desired pair correlators.
               Their common Alice marginal is PA ( a0 , a1 ) = (1 + ta0 a1 )/4.
                  To join the two smaller decks, first draw Alice’s pair with its common probability.
               Among the first deck’s cards bearing that pair, draw Bob’s first answer; among the
               second deck’s cards bearing the same pair, draw his second. Those conditional
               draws give a four-answer card. A pair that never occurs needs no card. Written as
               probabilities, this procedure is
                                           (
                                             P0 ( a0 , a1 , b0 ) P1 ( a0 , a1 , b1 )/PA ( a0 , a1 ), PA ( a0 , a1 ) > 0,
                  P( a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ) =
                                             0,                                                      PA ( a0 , a1 ) = 0.
               If PA = 0, nonnegativity forces both corresponding triple distributions to be zero.
               Otherwise summing over either Bob answer cancels the denominator. So P has the
               two triple distributions as marginals and total mass 1. Sample one of its sixteen
               answer quadruples and let each party answer with its assigned sign. This is a finite
               mixture of deterministic local plans with exactly the four required correlators.
                   The other direction is one line per card. On a single card, A0 ( B0 + B1 ) + A1 ( B0 −
               B1 ) is ±2, because one bracket is 0 and the other is ±2. Each of the other seven
               CHSH expressions is this one with the boxes relabelled or a sign flipped, so it is ±2
               on every card too, and any weighting of the cards keeps all eight averages between
               −2 and 2 (Theorem I.2 is the first of them). So a deck exists exactly when the
               correlators are in [−1, 1] and the eight inequalities hold.


               I.11 Scope of the constructions
               The constructions above pin down the correlators. What follows is where they stop:
               they aren’t a completeness claim for the integer check, they say nothing about full
               behaviours with marginals, and they say nothing about data from a lab.
                  The arcsine boundary. For two settings and two outcomes per side, Tsirelson,
               Landau (1988) and Masanes (2003) give theorems characterizing the correla-
               tors reachable by quantum measurements: | arcsin E00 + arcsin E01 + arcsin E10 −
               arcsin E11 | ≤ π and its sign variants. The characterization holds as an if and only if
               with the completion set and, through Tsirelson’s representation, with the quantum
               set. The point (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) is on the boundary: arcsin 53 + arcsin 45 = π2
                                                                                I.12 Prior work   665


by the 3-4-5 triangle, so the sum is π; Tsirelson’s point is on it too. The necessary
direction holds in any dimension, for any expectation on an algebra of observables
in which Alice’s commute with Bob’s.
    Equality with the quantum set. That the completion set of Section I.7 is exactly
the set of quantum correlators is Tsirelson’s representation theorem, and it is proved
in finite dimension: for both real and complex amplitudes, with two four-level
systems enough for every point, and two two-level ones with complex amplitudes.
That PSD of the level-1 moment matrix is necessary for quantum behaviour is
proved for strategies in finite dimension, with real amplitudes and with complex
ones, and in any dimension, marginals included, for any expectation on an algebra
of observables.
    Achievability. Theorem I.6 is a point of R4 . A state       √ and measurements that
reach it are explicit:
                  √     the two-qubit state (|
                                            √  00 ⟩ + | 11 ⟩) /  2 with√A0 = √
                                                                             Z, A1 =√X,
B0 =√( Z + X )/ 2√and B1 = ( Z − X )/ 2 has correlators 1/ 2, 1/ 2, 1/ 2,
−1/ 2 and S = 2 2, and every strategy in finite dimension has S2 ≤ 8, with real
amplitudes and with complex ones. Both are arithmetic about the model. How close
a real laboratory comes, and what that costs in loopholes closed, is the story told in
Appendix H.
    Completeness of the checks. The 1+AB cascade and the elliptope gate are proved
sound. The cascade has no proved converse; the gate’s factorization branch accepts
every rational PSD completion, by the row-peeling of Section I.8 with each pivot
kept. The level-1 integer check is the exception: on the small machine the same
seven integer facts hold exactly when every pair was sampled and the pinned matrix
is positive semidefinite (Theorem H.4), so that check is complete for what it tests.
The 1+AB cascade is strict and misses boundary points. The two 1+AB checks
don’t sit inside one another. The full check accepts the 12/5 tally above, which the
zero-moment check refuses, and it refuses the tally with E00 = 1 and the other three
correlators 0, where H11 = 0, which the zero-moment check accepts.
    Finite levels. For full behaviours, marginals included, the NPA levels are relax-
ations. Chaturvedi (arXiv 2607.14569, 2026) argues, in a preprint, that no finite
NPA level characterizes the complete quantum set even in this simplest Bell scenario.
I haven’t gone through that proof, and nothing here rests on it.
    Statistics and physics. Nothing here says how many rounds make a tally infor-
mative, and nothing says the counters came from honest play; a program can INC
whatever counts it likes.


I.12 Prior work

Tsirelson’s 1980 paper gives the bound 2 2 for quantum correlations, and his
theorem says that quantum two-outcome correlators are inner products of real unit

               vectors. Landau (1988) and Masanes (2003, arXiv quant-ph/0309137) each give a
               condition that, by their proofs, characterizes the quantum correlators exactly for two
               settings and two outcomes. Wehner (2006, arXiv quant-ph/0510076) gets Tsirelson

               of those vectors. Navascués, Pironio and Acín (2007, arXiv quant-ph/0607119;

               paper applies a Schur complement to the level-1 matrix of this scenario, recovers
               the arcsine condition, and discusses the 1+AB level. I went back to each of those
               papers for these points, and that is what I found in them. The results are theirs.
               Two of them are proved again here, in finite dimension: Tsirelson’s representation
               and the arcsine characterization; the rest of their proofs are not redone. Echenim
